11512-o-henry-memorial-award-prize-stori:
Chosen by the Society of Arts and Sciences with an introduction by Blanche Colton Williams, this 1922 volume prints the O. Henry Memorial Award prize stories of 1921. Edison Marshall, Charles Tenney Jackson, Maryland Allen, Thomas Beer, and Wilbur Daniel Steele are among the winners.

Stories range from a marriage in Kairwan and a man who cursed the lilies to a get-away, a tribute, and fifty-two weeks for Florette. The committee, founded in 1918 by John F. Tucker, set out to honour the short story each year, and this volume shows the form at its early 1920s best.
15365-a-psychiatric-milestone-bloomingda:
Printed privately by the Society of the New York Hospital in 1921, this volume marks Bloomingdale Hospital's centenary from 1821 to 1921. A Lucretius motto on mind growing and aging with body fronts the book. An invocation, a historical review by Edward Sheldon, and talks by Adolf Meyer and Lewellys Barker follow.

Meyer speaks on psychiatry's aid to life problems, Barker on its place in general medical practice. An 1808 building for mental patients appears in an illustration. Medical historians will find the milestone a rich record of American psychiatry at a turning point.
15451-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
This April 1, 1897 number of The Great Round World is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls, sold for five cents in New York. Publisher William Beverley Harison aimed it at young readers and their teachers, in magazine form, with pictures. Front matter advertises manuals of vertical writing by John Jackson, a system then winning ground in schools.

Inside, the paper explains the week's events in bright, simple language, so pupils can follow political and scientific questions of the day. That purpose, plain in its own pages, sets it apart from a story magazine: news first, told for children. The issue gives a snapshot of 1897 as American schoolchildren met it, week by week, in short and clear reports.
16213-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch for April 21, 1920, volume one hundred fifty-eight, sorts Irish criminals in its Charivaria column into three classes. There are those you cannot catch and those caught but not convicted. Then come those convicted but not kept in prison. America gone dry prompts a joke about Scotsmen pinning stamps to envelopes, while Bonar Law's boast about the Slough works sale meets a dig about keeping The Daily Mail waiting.

A Deptford man who offers to walk to Brighton with a jar on his head, presumably having mislaid his hat, earns another quip. Cartoons and satire would have carried the same brisk tone through the weekly. The issue is a neat, funny record of British and Irish politics in the spring of 1920.
16271-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch for January 21, 1920, volume one hundred fifty-eight, opens its Charivaria column with a Frenchman. He lost his temper so completely in a pistol duel that he threatened to shoot his opponent. That earned him suspension from similar encounters for six months. A man who received half a ton of coal without warning was removed to an asylum, treated for coal-shock, while Wrexham's education committee declined Welsh in elementary schools.

Doubts had arisen whether Welsh would ever serve as the League of Nations' medium, Punch adds. A Daily Mail movement to brighten boys' dress draws a note on fuller waists from Smith Tertius. Cartoons and verses would have kept the same brisk tone. The issue is a neat, funny record of postwar Britain.
17449-mining-laws-of-ohio-1921:
The Department of Industrial Relations of Ohio compiled this volume of mining laws in 1921, printed in Columbus by the F. J. Heer Printing Company and bound at the State Bindery. A foreword from the department introduces the acts that governed mining in the state. The book gathers the law as it stood in 1921, for use by operators, inspectors, and officials.

Readers get a working legal reference, not a narrative: statutes, rules, and duties for mines and miners in industrial Ohio. The volume suits legal historians, labour historians, and anyone tracing how states regulated dangerous work after the First World War. Its plain, official form matches its purpose.
2121-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle closes his history with the afternoon and evening of Frederick's life, from 1763 to 1786, after the twelve labours of war are done. Twenty-three years of reign remain, full of importance for Prussia, though not for world history. Frederick lived to 1786, ruling Prussia for forty-six years in all.

America, Carlyle says, shall be English and Prussia a nation, while France sinks into torpor after failing to cut Germany in four. The volume gives the old king's last years, ruling a state his wars had made. His last years, though quiet in Europe, shaped Prussia's schools, laws, and army for decades.
22149-the-journal-of-negro-history-volum:
Carter G. Woodson founded The Journal of Negro History in 1916 to give Black history scholarly standing. Volume 6, for 1921, gathers a year's articles, reviews, and documents. One essay opens bluntly: the citizenship of the Negro in America is a fiction. The Constitution promises him every right, the writer argues, while the federal government evades its duty to guard those rights.

Other pieces study slavery, Reconstruction, Black soldiers, and African backgrounds. Woodson's journal printed the evidence on which later history would build. In 1921 almost no white university would touch these subjects. The volume shows Woodson's enterprise at work: exact, angry, and determined to make a record.
23659-21:
Dr. Frank Crane built this short book from his American Magazine article If I Were Twenty-One, revised by the author and published in 1930. Its premise is plain: wisdom need not wait for old age. The experience of others can serve as well as one's own, and a young person can choose a good course early.

Ten chapters give his counsel in order. Do the next thing, adjust yourself, care for your body, train your mind, and be happy. Then marry, save money, study the art of pleasing, resolve to be a thoroughbred, and make a lasting, friendly arrangement with your conscience. It is brisk, quotable self-help from a popular preacher-essayist of the day.
26032-american-cookery-november-1921:
American Cookery for November 1921, formerly the Boston Cooking School Magazine, serves Thanksgiving menus and recipes with household advice. Contents list windows and their fittings, editorials, and a Rumford baking powder ad claiming success in baking rests on a pure and perfect leavener. The powder, the ad says, gives dough a fine, even texture and brings out natural flavor.

Recipes run practical. Cranberry sauce simmers butter and chopped cranberries for fifteen minutes. Pumpkin fanchonettes mix pumpkin, sugar, eggs, molasses, ginger, butter, cinnamon, salt, and milk in pastry tins, and pilgrim cookies soak seedless raisins overnight. The number is a homely guide to a 1921 Thanksgiving table, with ads and hints beside the food.
28023-pictorial-photography-in-america-1:
Published in New York in 1921, Pictorial Photography in America gathers photographs chosen by the Pictorial Photographers of America. Its editorial board included Clarence H. White, Henry Hoyt Moore, Dwight A. Davis, and John Paul Edwards. Short essays frame the pictures, including Arthur Wesley Dow on painting with light.

The pictures range from portraits and city views to farms, harbours, and quiet rooms at home. Each print names its maker and home city, so the album doubles as a survey of American camera clubs and tastes in 1921. Readers get a clear view of what serious photographers then prized: soft light, plain subjects, and careful craft.
28253-mcgill-and-its-story-1821-1921:
Cyrus Macmillan wrote McGill and Its Story, 1821-1921, for the university's centenary, published in London, New York, and Toronto in 1921. Macmillan traces McGill from James McGill's will and the Royal Institution for the Advancement of Learning, through delay, anxious years, and the first buildings, to the larger university of his day. He dedicates the book to McGill men who fell in the war of 1914 to 1918.

Chapters cover Sir William Dawson's making of McGill, college life at mid-century, and higher education for women. Appendices print McGill's will, the charter, and memorial addresses. The book serves as a clear, affectionate history of a Canadian university.
30650-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume twenty-one of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works was printed in London in 1912. Its Roman date is MDCCCCXII, and it follows the limited pattern: two thousand sixty copies printed, two thousand for sale. An illustration shows Stevenson on the forward deck of the schooner Equator.

Contents open with The Story of a Lie, moving from introducing the admiral and a letter to the papers to action in the admiral's name. Esther on the filial relation follows, with the prodigal father making his debut at home. Stevenson blends adventure, family, and moral irony in a collected volume for readers of his complete works.
32554-history-of-the-kentucky-derby-1875:
John L. O'Connor's History of the Kentucky Derby, 1875-1921, copyrighted in 1921, recounts the race from its first running. The first Derby day in May 1875 dawned cloudless, with a cool breeze over a course in splendid order, and by half past eleven crowds already filled the stands.

O'Connor counts no fewer than ten thousand persons on the course, from bankers and merchants to butchers and bakers, with ladies in bright costumes like parti-colored butterflies. The volume carries the story forward through the forty-sixth Derby in 1920, tracing a Kentucky festival from its hopeful first day to an established annual race.
33497-from-xylographs-to-lead-molds-a-d-:
From Xylographs to Lead Molds, AD 1440 to AD 1921, copyrighted in 1921 by the Rapid Electrotype Company of Cincinnati, traces printing from wood blocks to cast-metal type. Its pages, with illustrations and illuminations, open with individual movable cast-metal type, and the art of writing that came before it. The book tells how printers learned to mold letters in lead, a craft that spread books far and wide.

The volume suits readers of printing history, offering a short, illustrated survey of nearly five centuries of type. Its tone is practical and proud, written by makers for makers. For book lovers, it is a pleasing history of the press itself, from carved wood to the lead molds that made modern publishing possible.
5295-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
La Fontaine's twenty-first volume gathers The Spectacles, The Bucking Tub. The Impossible Thing completes the trio, opening with a vow to leave the nuns alone, since their freaks have so often filled his page. The author admits the subject may fatigue the mind, yet his muse still holds the veil to public view, pursuing scene after scene among the sisters.

Soft amours and artful tricks follow, and La Fontaine confesses the tales would be endless if fully told. Readers get three stories of convent comedy, in which the author both apologises for his subject and indulges it once more, with his usual wit.
5924-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
A cart of death drives chapters eleven through fourteen of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter eleven treats the strange adventure Quixote had with the car or cart of the Cortes of Death, pursued dejected beyond measure as he turns over the cruel trick enchanters played him. His lady Dulcinea, changed into a vile shape in his mind, haunts the journey, while chapters twelve through fourteen bring further strange adventures and the Knight of the Grove.

We follow a melancholy knight whose delusions grow darker, even as Sancho's loyalty holds. The cart of players, dressed as death and devils, becomes a mirror for Quixote's own fears. This part suits readers following volume two, since its grove knight and death cart prepare the famous duel of mirrors ahead.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: James Buchanan, Lancaster lawyer and Dickinson graduate, fills this fifth volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. Born to a Scotch Irish farmer from Donegal, Buchanan practiced law and spoke in public from his youth. The volume prints his messages and papers as president. It closes the pre war record of a presidency tested by division.

Rutherford Hayes, Kenyon College debater and student of logic, fills this seventh volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. Born in 1822 after his father's death, Hayes studied Latin and Greek and entered Kenyon in 1838. The volume prints his messages and papers as president. Richardson's series keeps Hayes's official record in print.
a-psychiatric-milestone-bloomingdale-hos: The Society of the New York Hospital marks one hundred years of Bloomingdale Hospital in this centenary volume, covering 1821 to 1921. Its contents pair a historical review by Edward Sheldon with addresses by Adolf Meyer on psychiatry's contribution to life problems and by Lewellys Barker on psychiatry in general medical practice. An invocation and anniversary committee open a privately printed record of a hospital's first century.
akhmatova-chetki-rosary-1921:
Anna Akhmatova published Rosary, her second book of poems, in Russian, and the 1921 printing holds the lyrics that made her famous. She wrote in clear, strict forms at a time of war and revolt. Love, loss, and a sense of doom fill these short poems.

Many lines speak in a woman's voice to a lover who is absent or untrue. Others hint at the dark years closing in on Russia. One famous line vows that she is not among those who fled. Generations of Russian readers learned these poems by heart, and they still anchor her fame.
anderson-triumph-egg-1921:
The Triumph of the Egg, published in 1921, is Sherwood Anderson's second story collection, following Winesburg, Ohio. Its tales of small-town and farm people carry his signature figure: the grotesque, a person twisted by one truth taken too far.

The title story turns an egg-sorting father's failure into grotesque comedy. 'I Want to Know Why' gives a boy's view of racehorses and the men who handle them, and other tales follow teachers, farmers, and wanderers. Anderson writes in a plain style that gropes toward feeling. These stories helped define the modern American short story.
aratus-phaenomena-mair-1921:
A. W. Mair translated Aratus's Phaenomena for the Loeb series in 1921. The volume adds works by Callimachus and Lycophron beside Aratus. Aratus composed his astronomical poem around 275 BCE at a Macedonian court.

The Phaenomena maps the constellations in elegant Greek verse. Weather signs drawn from animals, winds, and the moon fill its second half. Farmers and sailors used the poem as a practical almanac. It became the most-read poem of antiquity after Homer, roughly speaking. Saint Paul even quotes a line from Aratus in the New Testament. Mair's Loeb gives Greek facing English throughout the volume. Science as poetry describes the Phaenomena's lasting appeal.
arxiv-2412-00021:
Supravat Sarkar, in a solo paper from 2024, classifies certain smooth geometric structures built from projective bundles. A projective bundle attaches a projective space to every point of a base space. The paper asks when such a bundle can also be seen as a blow up of another space.

Working under a well-known conjecture, Sarkar classifies the bundles over projective spaces with that double identity. Under extra assumptions, the classification extends to bundles over arbitrary smooth bases. For bundles of small twisting measure, he verifies the property directly, with no extra assumption. The work also produces new examples of spaces carrying both structures.
arxiv-2412-01621:
Angel Yahir Loredo Lopez, Tyler McDonald, and Ali Emami turn a newspaper word game into a test of careful reasoning, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. The game, Connections from the New York Times, asks players to sort words into hidden groups that share a theme.

The authors gathered three hundred fifty-eight of these puzzles into a benchmark called NYT-Connections. The puzzles look simple but punish quick, gut-level answers, the fast style of thought psychologists call System 1. They tested six recent language models, a plain machine learning heuristic, and human players. Each faced single tries, repeated tries, and repeated tries with hints. Even the best model fell nearly a third short of human scores. Fancy prompting tricks like chain-of-thought helped less and less as puzzles grew harder. The benchmark isolates basic reasoning in a form anyone can grasp.
arxiv-2412-03621:
Feiran You, Hongyang Du, Kaibin Huang, and Abbas Jamalipour trim phone prompts for cloud language models while saving radio power too, in work from 2024. Long prompts improve answers but cost airtime and delay on mobile links. Their frame treats prompt size and signal power as one joint problem.

A small on-device model squeezes the prompt before sending. A learning agent then sets the squeeze level and the transmit power to match network conditions. The extended version refines the prompt in rounds, dropping the least useful words step by step for deeper cuts with control. Tests show shorter service time with answer quality largely kept. The work targets snappier mobile AI service.
arxiv-2412-03821:
Massive stars of types O and B can pulsate, and their pulsations reveal what is happening inside them. Xiang-dong Shi and co-authors searched data from the TESS, LAMOST, and Gaia surveys for stars. They identified one hundred fifty-five pulsating stars or candidates, nearly all new. The set includes thirty-eight Be stars, which spin fast and shed gas. Most of the rest split into two classes, SPB and BCEP stars, told apart by their pulsation patterns.

Plotted on diagrams, the stars sit in the instability zones and on the main sequence. Their masses run from two and a half to twenty times the mass of the Sun. Two objects pulsate like one class but sit where the other class belongs. The team derived period and brightness relations for both classes. They argue these diagrams are useful sorting tools for future finds.
arxiv-2412-04021:
Qian Li and five colleagues use deep learning to restore missing information in 21-centimeter intensity mapping data. Foreground contamination wipes out regions of Fourier space, and in interferometric observations the so-called foreground wedge causes heavy data loss. Those missing modes can damage baryon acoustic oscillation reconstruction, a key cosmological measurement.

The team trains a U-Net to recover the lost modes before reconstruction runs. The restored temperature map correlates with the original signal at about 0.9 at the tested scale. Reconstruction on restored data performs nearly as well as on clean data. A model trained on coarser fields even transfers to finer fields, which the authors link to scale-invariant mode coupling.
arxiv-2412-04421:
Smith and co-authors report single-qubit gates with errors below one part per million in a trapped-ion processor, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The qubit sits in a calcium ion held over a chip trap at room temperature. Microwave control comes from a resonator built into the chip itself.

Gate times ranged from about four to thirty-five microseconds, trading speed against accuracy. The best error per gate hit about one and a half in ten million. Calibration errors were pushed far lower still. Remaining error came from qubit decoherence, leakage, and measurement. No magnetic shielding was used, the team notes.
arxiv-2412-04721:
Jarred Roberts and a large team of colleagues extract gamma-ray source measurements from a balloon-borne telescope's difficult flight data. The COSI balloon payload flew for forty-six days in 2016, observing the Crab Nebula, Cygnus X-1, and Centaurus A through a variable balloon background. The team pulled source fluxes from that background and produced images using Richardson-Lucy deconvolution.

Spectra were fitted jointly with data from other instruments. The Crab's spectrum follows a broken power law; Cygnus X-1 fits a cutoff power law with a cutoff near 138 kilo-electronvolts. Centaurus A matches a simple power law. The results validate the Compton imaging approach ahead of the COSI satellite mission.
arxiv-2412-05121:
Cui, Qing, Feng, and Zhang joined two phase tricks in twenty twenty-four to make swirl light beams with flat patterned plates. Swirl beams serve grip tools, fast links, and quantum work. One past trick ignores light tilt, while the other hangs on it.

Their blend hits the same goal with a tunable grip on that tilt. Plate shape facts map straight to the swirl count of the beam. Tests showed the blend works and bends the tilt rules as planned. Swirl making gains a wider design space from the pair, they show.
arxiv-2412-06121: Ahmed Shokry, Amr Elmasry, Ayman Khalafallah, and Amr Aly present a fast way to check shortest path claims in a graph. Their 2024 paper gives a certifying method that runs in linear time. It handles graphs whose edge weights can be positive, negative, or zero, a wider range than earlier linear-time checks allowed.
arxiv-2412-07121:
Zirun Guo, Tao Jin, Wenlong Xu, Wang Lin, and Yangyang Wu adapt sentiment models while they run in a 2024 computing paper. Multimodal sentiment analysis reads feeling from text, voice, and face together. Models trained once decay when the data stream shifts, as real streams do. Retraining usually needs the original data, which may be private or huge. Test-time adaptation fixes the model on the fly, using only what it sees now.

Their two strategies enforce consistency across modalities and mint cautious pseudo-labels to learn from. Across experiments the pair lifted performance steadily. Adapting at run time suits live settings like monitoring interviews or calls, where yesterday's data no longer matches today's speakers.
arxiv-2412-10221:
Jerzy Kąkol and Arkady Leiderman published a 2024 mathematics paper on when products of function spaces keep a prized smoothness property. Some spaces are Asplund: their functions are differentiable in a strong, well-behaved way almost everywhere. The paper first tidies the definitions, systematizing the equivalent forms of differentiability spaces and their weak variants for locally convex spaces.

Then come the applications, extensions of a classical theorem of Mazur. If one factor is a separable Baire space and the other is any product of separable Fréchet spaces, the combined product is weakly Asplund. For products of Banach spaces, the answer is exact: the product is Asplund precisely when every factor is. Analogues hold for the smaller sigma-products as well. Such permanence results matter because analysts build big spaces from small ones daily. Knowing which virtues survive multiplication saves rediscovering failures the hard way.
arxiv-2412-10421:
Food data come in scattered pieces, which blocks a full account of how energy flows from farm to body. Maxwell Kaye, Graham MacDonald, and Eric Galbraith built one energy ledger for the world food system. They harmonized data on ninety-five foods across growing, processing, feed, and eating. Human metabolism was estimated from body size, age mix, and activity. The ledger closes the loop from sunlight to digestion.

The share of food calories never metabolized doubled between nineteen ninety and twenty nineteen, reaching about twenty percent. Food supply grew faster than bodies burned energy. Half of humanity's needs could in theory be met within the local grid cell. The open framework can test ways to trim waste.
arxiv-2412-10521:
Mara Sherlin Talento and her four co-authors, publishing in 2024, build a sturdier way to measure how two brain regions move together. Each region produces many signals at once, from different neurons or channels. The classic tool for comparing such bundles assumes straight-line links and breaks down when signals have wild outliers. Brain signals often do.

Their method, KenCoh, swaps in a rank-based measure of association, Kendall's tau, inside the classic framework. Ranks shrug off outliers and catch curved links too. In simulations, the method matched the standard estimator on clean data and beat it on heavy-tailed data. Applied to human brain waves during a virtual driving task, and to mouse cortex recordings during sounds, it revealed distinct patterns of regional linkage across frequency bands and brain states.
arxiv-2412-11521:
Andrea Perin and Stéphane Deny ask how deep networks learn symmetries in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Many data sets carry symmetries, transformations that leave labels unchanged. Using them promises better predictions. The authors study standard networks trained in the standard supervised way, with no symmetry built in.

Their setup partially hides the symmetry during training. Some classes show all transformations of a cyclic group, others only a subset. In the infinite-width limit, kernel methods describe the network's behavior. Analyzing the kernel's Gram matrix in the Fourier domain gives a simple formula. Generalization error splits into class separation, the signal, and class-orbit density, the noise. Readers get a theory of when symmetry is learned from data alone.
arxiv-2412-12321:
Chamsi Hssaine, Huseyin Topaloglu, and Garrett van Ryzin study online sharing of resources capped by rate, not by budget. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Jobs arrive one by one and must be sent to a resource at once. Each resource has a target rate that shifts over time, and straying from it draws a penalty on top of the task cost.

They show that standard tools for the budget form can fail badly here. Their new method uses proxy tasks: each new arrival stands in for future ones inside a primal-dual scheme. It hits the best regret rate when costs come from a fixed spread. Tests on synthetic and retail fulfilment data show it works in practice.
arxiv-2412-13221:
Shyamal Biswas revisits Gauss's law for moving surfaces in two thousand twenty-four. The law links the flux of an electric field through a closed face to the charge inside. He studies charges that move in and out while the face grows, shrinks, and bends. The Maxwell equations frame the whole setup.

Biswas works out the flux integral as it changes in time. He gets an equation for how that flux grows or falls. The flux turns out to depend on growth or shrink of the face. It does not depend on how the face bends. The paper is written as a clear teaching style check of a classic law.
arxiv-2412-14621:
Zhichao Carton Zeng, Annika Peter, Xiaolong Du, and a wider team wrote this astronomy paper, published in 2024. It asks how dwarf galaxies would look if dark matter could interact with itself, rather than only pulling through gravity.

In this model, the centers of dark matter halos first hollow out, then collapse to high density over time. The authors ran simulations with both dark matter and star particles, for lone dwarfs and for dwarfs orbiting a bigger galaxy. The stars' spread in size, brightness, and motion came out much wider than under standard cold dark matter. That wider spread could explain why real dwarf galaxies look so varied. The team also found shared paths in how orbiting dwarfs evolve, which could be layered onto much larger universe simulations.
arxiv-2412-14721:
Hoppe and a large team of co-authors model the particle balance of runaway electron beams in the TCV tokamak after a disruption. Their paper from twenty twenty-four studies the low-Z benign termination scheme. That scheme first drops the free electron density, so a later instability can scatter the runaways thinly on the wall. Measured density, though, bends in an odd non-monotonic way with neutral pressure.

Runaway-driven ionization explains the bend in their model. More neutral targets mean more fresh ions as runaways strike. Scans over runaway density and energy show only density moves the needle. Density also tracks how heat spreads at termination. The cause of the scheme's upper pressure limit stays open, though. The paper firms up one link of a fusion safety chain.
arxiv-2412-15421:
Julian Steele and a large team of co-authors report superconductivity in germanium films hyperdoped with gallium, grown as orderly epitaxial layers, in a two thousand twenty-four physics paper. Doping group four semiconductors into superconductors could marry quantum devices with standard chip tech.

Molecular beam epitaxy made films with extreme hole concentrations, about eighteen percent gallium swapped in. The films superconduct below 3.5 kelvin. Synchrotron X-ray measures show gallium atoms sit substitutionally in the germanium lattice, slightly distorting its cells, rather than clumping messily. First-principles calculations support the picture that this order opens a narrow band enabling superconductivity, making the material a clean superconductor-semiconductor platform.
arxiv-2412-15621:
Bhupendra Acharya and co-authors map donation scams on social media in this 2024 study. Charities and individuals now raise funds on platforms, and scammers exploit that trust. The team gathered data from five platforms over two months in 2024. Their haul covered more than one hundred and fifty thousand accounts and three million posts. From that mass, they picked out more than eight hundred scam accounts.

The scammers used classic tricks, such as fake fundraisers for real disasters. The team traced the phone numbers, emails, and links those accounts shared. Shared contact points helped link accounts into wider fraud networks. Many accounts were made fresh for the scam season, the data showed. The authors argue platforms need checks tuned to donation appeals. Their data set offers a base for building such checks.
arxiv-2412-15721:
Kristina Lerman and colleagues compare eating disorder discussions on three social platforms with different moderation styles. Online spaces can offer real support for people with eating disorders, but they can also spread content that glamorizes harmful behavior. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team analyzed posts and community patterns on a lightly moderated service, a middle-ground forum site, and a video platform. They looked at how users express concern, seek support, and cluster around pro-anorexia themes under each moderation regime.

Support seeking looked similar everywhere. The lightly moderated platform, however, let toxic echo chambers form that amplified pro-anorexia rhetoric, while stricter settings contained it better. The authors conclude that moderation choices shape community health in sensitive mental health spaces, a finding aimed at platform designers and policymakers. The paper carries a reader warning about its subject.
arxiv-2412-16621:
Lee derives in twenty twenty-four explicit upper bounds on how fast the Fourier transform of fractal-based probability measures fades at high frequency. Such decay rates matter because faster fading yields stronger results in metric number theory and related fields. He focuses on measures spread over self-similar sets, the copies-of-themselves shapes built by repeated shrinking.

The new bounds improve on earlier work for this class. They are stated in concrete terms a reader can apply directly. An example shows the payoff: numbers whose digits in a continued-fraction-like expansion come from a fixed finite set. The author presents the bounds as tools for sharper results about such thin sets.
arxiv-2412-16921:
Tanayveer Singh Bhatia and co-authors present a 2024 astrophysics paper simulating starspots in three dimensions. Starspots are dark, magnetized patches on cool stars. They dim and distort the light curves telescopes record. The team runs realistic radiative magnetohydrodynamic models with the MURaM code. Their spots carry substantial penumbrae, the fringed edges real spots show. The setup improves on earlier flat-slab models. Umbra, penumbra, and quiet surface come out distinct in brightness and temperature.

The layers also differ in their heat content and flow patterns. Stellar physicists get spot models fit to feed into light curve interpretation. Transit surveys hunting planets must subtract spot noise, so better spots mean cleaner planet signals. Large-scale structure is the focus: how the whole spot hangs together, not just its core. The step from slabs to curved, layered models narrows the gap between simulation and telescope.
arxiv-2412-17321:
Nicolas Devatine and Louis Abraham gauge how much work humans put into fixing AI text, in work from 2024. Old gap scores count letter swaps well but miss big block moves, which take real effort. Their new score leans on text compression, in the style of a classic squeeze method, to weigh the data gap between draft and edit.

On real edit records, the score tracked true edit time and effort closely. It also beat older scores at catching complex edits, at lean compute cost. A side find: models seem to sense edit speed in a way that matches the score. Code and data are shared in public.
arxiv-2412-18821:
Yu Sang and Hai-Nan Lin probe whether magnetar bursts remember their past. Magnetars, hyper-magnetic neutron stars, fire repeated soft gamma-ray bursts. The timing and energy of those bursts encode the source's activity. The team gathered burst records from four soft gamma repeaters.

Rescaled range analysis finds long-term memory in both waiting times and energies, a first for these sources. Randomness and chaos tests add nuance. Waiting times are never fully random, while two sources' energies look completely random. Both series show weak chaos throughout. In the randomness-chaos plane, the magnetars sit where repeating fast radio bursts sit. No significant gap separates the two families. That statistical kinship hints at a physical link between magnetar flares and the repeating radio bursts.
arxiv-2501-00021:
Junchao Chen, Suyash Gupta, Daniel Hughes, and Mohammad Sadoghi argue that distributed systems can keep partial progress during network splits, softening a famous trade-off. Their paper appeared in 2024, though the catalog lists 2025. The CAP theorem says a system under partition must drop either consistency or availability. The authors conjecture that a middle path exists: the system stays responsive to a subset of clients and keeps nonzero throughput through failures.

They present CASSANDRA, a consensus protocol that lets separated replicas keep ordering client requests. Fully coordination-free designs avoid the dilemma but fit few real applications, most of which need coordination. The authors say partial progress, not total availability, is the honest goal for systems that must keep working while the network is broken.
arxiv-2501-01321:
Konstantin Getman and a large team test in 2025 whether young stars need freakishly strong magnetic fields to power their biggest flares. Earlier models, lacking direct field measures, strayed from a known law linking X-ray brightness to magnetic flux. Simulations blamed extra-strong fields during flares.

The team watched four young Orion stars with an X-ray telescope and a near-infrared instrument at nearly the same time, catching them during or just after powerful flares. The measured fields were ordinary for young stars, ruling out the strong-field idea. The law-breaking, they argue, comes from huge active regions and giant loops, not stronger fields. Solar flares break the law the same way, only less.
arxiv-2501-02021:
Aditya Prakash builds a weakly supervised method to classify large graphs from few labels. Graphs can stand for images, with nodes as cell nuclei and edges as their links. Often only the whole graph bears a label, such as a cancer type. The label is set by small zones inside the graph, not the whole.

Two ways pull subgraphs from each big graph: a sliding window and a breadth-first walk. An attention network then weighs which subgraphs matter most for the call. Graph labels are passed down to subgraphs, so no fine notes are needed. The frame suits pathology, where expert marks are scarce and costly. Tests in the work back the design for graph-level calls.
arxiv-2501-02421:
Saber Jafarizadeh optimized how fast random walks settle in a 2025 paper on Markov chains. A reversible chain wanders a graph and gradually forgets its start, approaching a target distribution. The fastest mixing problem asks which step probabilities reach that equilibrium quickest, a design question for sampling and network gossip alike. Solving it exactly usually needs semidefinite coding, which grows heavy on elaborate topologies.

Jafarizadeh shows that enlarging a base graph by lifting its cliques changes nothing essential: the problem reduces to the base graph. The best mixing time stays identical. Whole groups of topologies sharing a base are thus solved at once. For subgraphs of a larger graph, best edge probabilities can even be fixed without looking at the rest of the network.
arxiv-2501-04921:
Jihao Fan, Wei Cheng, Gaojun Luo, Zhou Li, and Meng Cao present a 2025 study of quantum error-correcting codes built by stacking two codes together. Their codes also borrow pre-shared entanglement, a resource that boosts what a code can protect. By choosing the inner and outer layers with care, they beat earlier codes of the same length and data rate. The outer layers come from two flexible code families whose lengths vary more freely than the standard choice.

The authors build several new families this way. Some reach maximal entanglement, which happens when both layers are maximal, and some sit just one step below the best possible error distance. Two families stay strong as codes grow without bound. The paper closes by proving the construction meets a known long-run performance bound.
arxiv-2501-05121:
Matthias Velsink, Maksym Illienko, Komal Chaudhary, and Stefan Witte tackle a spectroscopy problem in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Pump-probe spectroscopy watches ultrafast shifts in materials. But the pump pulse can harm light-sensitive samples for good, so the signal is capped by what the sample can stand. The team set out how to lift signal-to-noise in a time span while keeping harm low. Their test bed was ultrafast photoacoustics in solid thin films.

They changed pump and probe pulse energies, mean pump fluence, and the laser's repetition rate. Each material type backed a distinct best path, hung on which harm route ruled. One key lever stood out: the repetition rate should be fit to the sample. The upshot is a design plan for pump-probe tests. Pulse settings should be tuned to how weak the sample is, not set by one stock recipe.
arxiv-2501-06121:
Finding the closest matches to a query among millions of vectors powers search and recommendation tools, and doing it exactly is too slow. Leonardo Delfino and co-authors release kANNolo in this 2025 paper, a library for approximate nearest neighbor search written in Rust with researchers in mind.

The library is built like a kit: similarity measures, compression tricks, and index structures snap together in any mix, for both dense and sparse data. Despite that freedom, tests show speed and accuracy on par with the best specialized tools. The authors offer it as a bench where new search ideas can be tried quickly without giving up performance.
arxiv-2501-07121:
Hornek and co-authors present a 2025 study of how grid-scale batteries can earn money in Europe's fast intraday power market. In that market, power trades until minutes before delivery, and prices swing sharply. The team built a trading method driven by price forecasts, updated in rolling windows. They compared it with a perfect-foresight benchmark and with earnings in other spot markets, using real German market data from 2023.

A one-megawatt test system using the method earned about 146,000 euros over the year studied. That result came within 11 percent of the perfect-foresight ceiling, which no real trader could reach. The method beat the other markets and the standard market indices. The authors conclude that careful forecasting makes the complex intraday market worth trading in.
arxiv-2501-07421:
Lukas Rustler, Vojtech Volprecht, and Matej Hoffmann benchmarked four stereo depth cameras head to head for robotics work, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Each camera recorded over three thousand depth frames across three scenes: a flat surface, a plastic doll, and a set of household objects. The contenders were two Intel RealSense models, a StereoLabs ZED 2, and a Luxonis OAK-D Pro.

For tabletop work within a meter, the RealSense D435 won, holding error under a centimeter in every scene. At longer range the other three pulled ahead, with the ZED 2 keeping error under three centimeters even at four meters, though it needs a host computer with a graphics card. The full dataset is public.
arxiv-2501-07721:
Vlad-Andrei Badoiu and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on a language model for Romanian. Big open models often lag in tongues with little training text. Romanian is one such case. The team built a bilingual base model tuned to Romanian from the start.

The paper records the full build: gathering the text corpus, picking the model shape, and tuning its settings. After base training, the model was fine-tuned for translation. On English-to-Romanian tasks it beat the existing tools the team compared. Its scores also rivaled much larger open models on Romanian tasks. The authors say a small, focused model can serve a language community well at low cost.
arxiv-2501-08021:
Jean-Pierre Rozelot, Alexander Kosovichev, and Irina Kitiashvili review the Sun's near-surface shear layer, with focus on a thin sublayer called the leptocline. Their 2025 paper recalls that the sunspot cycle has been tied to inner solar dynamics since its discovery. Recent work keeps finding change in how the outer layers rotate.

The leptocline sits only a few megameters deep, marked by a sharp change in rotation speed at mid latitudes and by self-organized flows. Ionization of hydrogen and helium, a drop in sound speed, and shifts in the seismic radius all crowd into this layer. It may also help shape the butterfly pattern of sunspots across the cycle. The authors present the layer as a rich target for systematic study of solar activity.
arxiv-2501-09421:
Jack King, Robert Poole, Cláudio Fonte, and Steven Lind study, in a 2025 preprint, how uncertainty grows inside elastic turbulence. Elastic turbulence is the chaotic flow of stretchy fluids, like polymer solutions, even at slow speeds. It can boost mixing and heat transfer, so engineers want to steer it. Forecasting such flow means knowing how fast small errors swell. The authors borrow an approach lately used on ordinary turbulence. They derive equations for how measures of uncertainty evolve.

Computer experiments revealed four regimes of error growth. Errors first rush to large scales, then get eaten by dissipation, then grow at all scales at once, and at last level off. Stretchy effects feed the growth while viscosity and relaxation drain it. Slowing the flow raised early uncertainty but mattered less later. Stronger elasticity and larger domains sped late growth.
arxiv-2501-10621:
Mehrad Mortazavi, David Cappelleri, and Reza Ehsani present a farm robot in 2025 that takes leaf samples on its own. Reading the light reflected by a leaf can reveal a crop's health, water stress, and nutrient needs. Doing this by hand in orchards is slow, and farm labor is scarce.

Their robot, RoMu4o, drives on the ground and carries a six-joint arm with a vision system. It spots a target leaf, plans a safe path, grips the leaf, and shines a sensor on it that reads many colors of light at once. In lab trials it succeeded in most attempts, and in a pistachio orchard it managed about seven in ten. The team sees it as a step toward automated crop checks.
arxiv-2501-10821:
Jean Rozelot, Alexander Kosovichev, and Ali Kilcik wrote this 2025 paper on the changing shape of the Sun. The Sun is slightly flattened at its poles, a trait called oblateness, and studies of it reach back to the nineteenth century. How that flattening changes over the solar cycle is still poorly known.

The team used data from sound waves inside the Sun, the most precise probe of its structure. From those data they inferred how the flattening rose and fell over time. The changes trailed the solar activity cycle by about three years. Oddly, the Sun was more flattened in the quieter recent cycle than in the stronger one before it.
arxiv-2501-11921:
Jiazheng Chen and Wanchun Liu schedule wireless transmissions round goals, not raw data, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Goal-oriented communications judge a network by if the application succeeds, not by bit accuracy. To schedule devices over many channels is hard, as state and action spaces blow up in size. The team sets out form traits of the optimal policy. They weigh channel states and Age of Information. That is a measure of data freshness.

They prove the optimal value function is monotone in channel states and asymptotically convex in age states, and the optimal policy is monotone in channel quality. Those traits guide their method, SUDO-DRL. It joins on-policy stability with off-policy sample efficiency in one reinforcement learning method. Runs showed up to forty-five percent better performance and forty percent faster convergence than alternatives. It scaled to systems where off-policy methods failed.
arxiv-2501-13421:
Anoop Mishra and Deepak Khazanchi build a way to measure whether people see machine learning development as fair. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Unfair results can come from biased data, sloppy data handling, wrong assumptions, or hidden bias in the team. Yet fairness in building these systems is a fuzzy idea. No shared scale exists to judge it.

The authors held online focus groups with developers and read past research on fairness. They also drew on justice theory, which covers fair process and fair shares. From this they name three parts of perceived fairness. These are openness, being answerable for choices, and fair representation. Each part breaks into smaller concepts that can be rated. They then test the scale with both builders and users of these systems.
arxiv-2501-14221:
Tatsuhiko Shirai and Takashi Mori compute chaos probes in quantum spin systems with an approximation method, in a 2025 paper. The probe, an out-of-time-order correlator, tracks how information scrambles. Exact computation is costly in big systems. Their method adapts a discrete phase-space technique. The systems studied interact across long range. Coupling fades with distance as a power law. A squared commutator of local operators serves as the measure.

The method matched exact dynamics in strongly long-range cases. It captured the average spread of information at all times. In weakly long-range cases it missed details. The fastest scrambling front escaped it. The team used it on system-size scaling. Scrambling time scaling changed character with interaction range. That split was qualitative, not just numeric. The work gives simulators a new tool for scrambling studies. Its limits are mapped as carefully as its wins.
arxiv-2501-14321:
Mann Patel, Divyajyoti Panda, Hilay Mehta, Parth Patel, and Dhruv Parikh ask whether small trained modules can be merged to cover combined domains. Their 2025 project uses light fine-tuning methods that train only a compact add-on to a large model. Each add-on becomes an expert on one trait domain.

The test case is a well-known personality scheme with sixteen types built from four trait pairs. The team trained an add-on for each single trait, then merged add-ons with simple math on their weights, with no further training. They checked both single and merged modules with an online personality quiz. Merged modules produced the intended combined types well enough to support the approach. The work suggests a cheap way to build new domain mixes from parts already trained.
arxiv-2501-14521:
Anna Clevenhaus, Claudia Totzeck, and Matthias Ehrhardt wrote a 2025 paper on fitting finance models to market prices. Their test case is the Heston model, a standard model in which market volatility itself moves at random. Few of its settings can be read off prices directly, so fitting means solving a hard search problem with many local traps.

Their trick, called space mapping, pairs the true model with a cheaper stand-in. The stand-in prices a simpler option with a fast equation, while the true model prices an Asian option through a costlier route. Steps taken on the cheap model steer the fit of the true one. Test runs suggest the method can make such fits faster and more reliable, a daily need for trading desks.
arxiv-2501-14721:
Church calls peers to widen what paired text banks can do in this twenty twenty-five talk paper. Such banks hold like texts in two tongues with no line match. Most work mines them for word pairs and flat drill files.

Inside, the talk tours the banks' past from their first builds on. Fresh paths then fan out for peers to take up and test. He frames the banks as a field ripe for new hands and aims. The piece is a key talk text from a shop meet that year. It asks the field to think past stock uses of the banks.
arxiv-2501-14921: Souza and Costa wrote a 2025 letter on index coding, where a broadcaster serves receivers who each already hold some messages as side information. Good codes cut what the sender transmits by using what receivers know. The pair build a scheme from a layered lattice construction over the integers, with a remainder-style encoding, named CRT lattice index coding. They derive a ceiling for the gain side information can give and state when it is the same for every receiver, a trait called uniform gain. Examples show the scheme in action.
arxiv-2501-15121:
Chen Wang, Yuanyuan Ma, Zhijun Wang, and Yanjun Sun compute the internal shape function of a scalar meson in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The distribution amplitude describes how momentum is shared inside the K meson in question, treated as a quark-antiquark ground state. Sum rules are the tool of choice.

The authors add a correction for the distance between the quarks, refining the moments of the amplitude. They then use light-cone sum rules to compute form factors for a related B meson decay. The decay results line up with the amplitude they derived, which supports its reliability. The work feeds into predictions for rare decays where this meson appears. Precise amplitudes help test the standard model against experiment.
arxiv-2501-15621:
Shikun Cui and Dmitry Pelinovsky study when rippling waves in a nonlinear equation stay stable and when they break down. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The equation is the modified Korteweg-de Vries equation, a classic model for waves that keep their shape as they travel.

Two families of repeating traveling waves exist in the model. Earlier work checked their stability only against disturbances with the same period. Cui and Pelinovsky use tools from the theory of integrable systems to test disturbances of any period. One family proves stable under every setting. The other is always unstable, and the authors show how its instability bands change shape as the wave crosses into a new regime.
arxiv-2501-16921:
Wouter Weekers, Alessandro Saccon, and Nathan van de Wouw present a 2025 paper on control methods that hunt for the best setting of a system with fewer tests. Classic hunting methods nudge the input again and again and read the output each time. Those readings can be slow and costly to gather.

The authors use data gathered during normal runs to build a stand in for the hidden cost curve. The stand in, built with a kernel method, lets the controller plan its next steps with fewer fresh readings. The method works in sampled steps rather than in a steady loop. Tests in the paper show the savings in readings while the hunt still lands near the best point.
arxiv-2501-17821:
Ajinkya Khoche and co-authors build a method to track motion across far scenes for self-driving cars, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Motion tracking in three dimensions matters most at long range, where object tools fail on sparse far points. Dense grids grow too fast with range, so the team uses a sparse method built for scattered points.

Sparse maps from two scans clash in size and order, so dummy points fill the gaps before the maps merge. A scoring rule also gives far points more weight. Results on a large public driving set set a new best for long-range motion tracking. Readers in vehicle sensing get a design that scales.
arxiv-2501-18121:
Surveys that promise privacy must add noise to their averages, and smart sampling can shrink that noise. Yu-Wei Chen, Raghu Pasupathy, and Jordan Awan design sampling plans for private mean estimates. Their plan splits the population into strata and samples each at its own rate. Because sampling itself boosts privacy, each stratum can use a different noise budget for the same final promise. Three noise methods are covered.

Ignoring privacy when planning strata can inflate error badly. The team proves their error goal has a clean shape, then gives an algorithm that finds the best whole-number plan. The structure of the best plan is also described. Privacy work like this helps official surveys stay both safe and accurate.
arxiv-2501-18521:
Grigoriy Mazhorin, Andrei Kugut, Artyom Polyanskiy, Ilya Moskalenko, and Ilya Simakov measure how qubit anharmonicity bends Rabi oscillations under weak, near-resonant drives. Their paper from twenty twenty-five serves the operating regime of two-qubit entangling gates. The squared Rabi frequency is tracked against drive amplitude and detuning. A clean linear law emerges, linking the ratio to detuning over anharmonicity, and data agree with analytics.

The practical stakes ride on the controlled-Z gate in fluxonium qubits, driven through the coupler. Mistuned Rabi frequencies leak population and spoil phase, both quantified here. Precise control of real qubits depends on exactly this sort of calibration science. The results hand gate engineers a verified formula where folklore used to sit.
arxiv-2502-00021:
Trevor McInroe and Samuel Garcin present PixelBrax in two thousand twenty-five. PixelBrax is a set of control tasks where agents learn from pixels alone. It joins the Brax physics engine with a renderer built in JAX. The whole loop thus runs on the graphics chip.

Thousands of worlds can run side by side with drawn views. Speed runs about a hundred fold past CPU based rivals. All chance in the worlds is handled in the open, so runs repeat exactly. Color and video clutter can be added to test broad skill. Code for the tasks and for learning methods is shared in the open.
arxiv-2502-00221:
Jocelyn Shen and five co-authors test home robots that pass along other people's stories, in a 2025 study. Loneliness is widespread despite constant connectivity. Companion robots usually chat as friends themselves; this team tried a different role, the robot as a messenger between strangers.

Forty robot stations lived in users' homes for two weeks. The companion shared emotionally relevant stories from other people and guided reflection on them, following five design dimensions. Interviews showed users felt connected to the narrators' lives, spotting parallels with their own and hearing views they would never meet otherwise. The authors call such machines social proxies and offer design guidance. The finding reframes robots as bridges to humanity, not substitutes for it.
arxiv-2502-00421:
Turi Abu, Ying Shi, Thomas Fang Zheng, and Dong Wang release Sagalee, an open speech recognition dataset for the Oromo language, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Oromo is widely spoken in Ethiopia and neighboring regions yet lacks recognition resources.

Crowd-sourcing gathered one hundred hours of real-world recordings with transcriptions, mixing read speech in clean and noisy conditions from diverse speakers. Baseline experiments train a Conformer model, reaching word error rates between fifteen and nineteen percent depending on the loss. Fine-tuning Whisper does much better at about eleven percent. The dataset is public, giving Oromo speech technology its first solid benchmark.
arxiv-2502-00521:
Vitalii Vertogradov, Ali Övgün, and Daniil Shatov construct exact collapse solutions that form black holes with no singularity inside, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their models describe ordinary matter with a pressure law that varies with radius and time. Matching the interior to a regular exterior spacetime yields a self-consistent dynamical black hole.

The pressure profile grows outward and eventually breaks a standard energy condition beyond a critical surface, so an external junction keeps the whole spacetime well-defined. Inside, the collapse stays non-singular throughout. The models' photon sphere and shadow both grow as the pressure parameter rises, and the matching surface hints at a phase change that can delay the horizon's formation. The authors flag shadow signatures future observations could test.
arxiv-2502-00721:
Jorge Vila-Tomás and four co-authors propose a Turing test for artificial nets that model human vision in two thousand twenty-five. Claims for nets as brain models run ahead of proof, they argue. Open snags span where to read outputs and how to test them. A low level data set of retina to cortex facts is their fix.

Three models with like builds face ten psycho and physio facts. A parametric model tuned by maximum differentiation hugs human acts closest. Its receptive fields and nonlinear color acts lead the pack. Two rivals tuned for opinion and segmentation trail on those facts.
arxiv-2502-00921:
Marvin Li and co-authors offer a simple theory for why AI generators suddenly settle on key features, in this 2025 paper. Language models can veer off course in a blink, and image models decide core features within narrow windows of their process. Past explanations leaned on heavy assumptions about the data.

The new theory uses a general sampling frame that fits both text and image models. It shows the effect arises naturally as generation narrows onto a sub-group of the modeled distribution. The math needs only basic tools and sharpens older bounds even for image models. Tests back the prediction, and the authors note a link to sudden shifts seen in statistics.
arxiv-2502-01721:
Early galaxies grew mostly by making their own stars, not by swallowing each other, concludes a 2025 arXiv study by Dávid Puskás and co-authors. Using deep survey images, the team counted close companion pairs among galaxies seen as they were three to nine tenths of the way back to the Big Bang.

Pair rates rose, flattened, and in lighter galaxies turned down across that era, which converts to a few mergers per galaxy per billion years at the plateau. Set against star formation, the merger contribution stays secondary. The authors title the finding plainly: in situ star formation dominates the growth story.
arxiv-2502-01821:
Runxiang Cheng and seven co-authors automate bug reproduction at Google in twenty twenty-five. Bug reports rarely include enough detail to reproduce a defect. A reproduction test that fails before the fix and passes after is gold for debugging. Such tests are almost never attached to reports, in open source or industry.

The team works with real bugs from Google's internal tracker. Generating reproduction tests in a huge proprietary codebase is the challenge. They adapt a state-of-the-art technique called LIBRO to the setting. Their own agent-based system uses a fine-tuned language model to write the tests. Readers in software engineering get evidence on automated program repair where the code base is industrial scale and the bugs are real.
arxiv-2502-01921:
Xiao Cao and ten colleagues wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on a candidate pair of active black holes in one disk galaxy. Dual active galactic nuclei are usually found in major mergers of similar-sized galaxies. Minor mergers, where a big galaxy absorbs a dwarf, should be far more common, yet the unequal black hole pairs they create are rarely found.

The candidate reported here has a mass ratio of about seven to one. The authors weigh the evidence that both black holes are actively feeding and estimate their masses. Finding more such pairs matters because most galaxy growth happens through minor mergers. This case gives astronomers a rare look at an unequal pair caught mid-merger.
arxiv-2502-02121:
Ruth Wan Theng Chew, Quoc Phong Nguyen, and Bryan Kian Hsiang Low present BILBO, a Bayesian optimizer for two-level problems with black-box parts. Their paper from twenty twenty-five explains the shape: an upper problem whose feasible set is set by the lower problem's best replies. Such stacks fill real design work. Re-solving the lower level at each probe wastes samples, and guessed replies can mislead.

BILBO tunes both levels in one pass. Trusted sets from confidence bounds cap how far the lower reply can stray. One query per round is chosen with the lower level's doubt in mind. A conditional reassignment of the query stirs exploration where needed. Regret bounds hold for standard kernels. Tests on synthetic and real tasks back the design.
arxiv-2502-02421:
Amin Heyrani Nobari and five co-authors introduced Activation-Informed Merging in twenty twenty-five, a method for combining fine-tuned language models more wisely. Merging averages the weights of models tuned for different skills, gaining versatility for free. But uniform merging can overwrite weights the base model truly needs.

Their technique consults the models' activation patterns on a task-agnostic calibration set to judge which weights matter, then protects the essential ones during merging, borrowing ideas from continual learning and compression. It layers onto any existing merging method. Across benchmarks, merged models with this protection gained up to forty percent in performance. The authors argue activation space, not just weight space, should guide how models are combined.
arxiv-2502-02721:
Landman, Brown, Chung, and Nagy introduced a new Krylov method for large-scale inverse problems in twenty twenty-five. Inverse problems reconstruct a hidden cause from observed data, such as an image from scanner signals. Krylov methods solve them step by step in a growing search space.

Classic versions rely on inner products, costly calculations that slow parallel computing and can break down at low precision. Earlier inner-product-free versions minimize a stand-in quantity, not the true mismatch to data. The new method pairs an inner-product-free projection with a randomized sketch-and-solve step for the smaller problem. Its target quantity sits closer to the true residual norm, the mismatch that matters statistically. Numerical tests show it solves large problems efficiently without inner products.
arxiv-2502-03121:
Emilia Pruszyńska-Karbownik and her eleven co-authors, publishing in 2025, carve a light-trapping grating from an unusual crystal, MoSe2. The material bends light strongly and absorbs almost none in the near-infrared, which suits tiny optical devices. Until recently, no one could grow large, even sheets of it. The team grew a sheet by molecular beam epitaxy and etched a grating just 42 nanometers thick.

Their light measurements confirm the grating holds a bound state in the continuum, a mode that theory says should trap light indefinitely. The same structure also boosted a frequency-tripling effect more than a thousandfold compared with a plain sheet. The authors point to compact lasers, wavefront shaping, and exotic light states as uses. The work shows a van der Waals material can now be patterned like a conventional photonic chip.
arxiv-2502-03521:
Larisa Jonke and Eric Lescano derive the first corrections to Einstein's gravity from a doubled copy of a deformed gauge theory in this 2025 paper. The double copy trick builds gravity by squaring a force theory, and it works strikingly well. Their version starts from Yang-Mills theory on a noncommutative space, where coordinates fail to commute by a small parameter.

They compute how that deformation bends the theory's three-particle vertex, step by step in the small parameter and up to three fields. Squaring the result gives a gravity-like theory written in a doubled geometry, with two star products matching the doubled coordinates. Imposing the level matching condition merges the products and yields the first true corrections to the doubled gravity action. They then take the pure gravity limit in four dimensions and study what the deformation does to ordinary spacetime physics.
arxiv-2502-03721:
Ziyang Wei and four co-authors tackle a security flaw in a new kind of communication system. Their 2025 paper concerns semantic systems, which send meaning rather than raw data with help from AI models. Such systems can be attacked through poisoned training data. Hidden triggers in the data make the system err on marked inputs while clean inputs pass as normal.

Older defenses carry costs: some cut parts of the model and hurt clean work, while others demand strict data forms. The new defense watches for odd gaps in the meaning space of inputs and flags marked samples by a set threshold. It leaves the model and the data forms untouched. Tests found high catch rates across many poisoning levels. The work offers a light guard for meaning-based networks.
arxiv-2502-04521:
Valiyeh Nezhad and co-authors proposed FedGAT in 2025, a way for hospitals to train scan models as a team without sharing patient data. Models that rebuild MRI scans from partial data work well at one site but often fail at new sites. Team training fixes that, yet most forms force every site to use the same model shape.

FedGAT first trains a shared model that learns what good MR images look like. Each site can then plug that shared core into its own model shape, tuned to its gear and needs. Sites swap model updates, never raw scans, so privacy holds. The design aims for strong rebuilds across sites with unlike tools.
arxiv-2502-06721:
Brian Colquhoun, Christine Davies, G. Peter Lepage, and Sophie Renner, with the HPQCD Collaboration, present a 2025 paper bounding a hypothetical light particle using supercomputer simulations of quantum chromodynamics. The particle, an axion like one, might couple to charm quarks. A charm bound state's decay into light plus the new particle is a key search channel.

The team computed the key form factor for that decay on a space time lattice, a first for this process. Their value holds across nearly the full mass range for the new particle, with error under two percent. The sharper theory turns past and future decay searches into tighter bounds on the particle's coupling.
arxiv-2502-06921:
Arghadip Das and five co-authors published a 2025 paper on running graph neural networks on small devices. These networks learn from data shaped as graphs, such as networks of linked items. They power tools for recommendations and speech tasks. Running them on laptops or other edge devices keeps data private and avoids the cloud.

The trouble is that graph data is irregular, sparse, and always changing shape. The small AI chips in edge devices were built for tidy, regular work, so they struggle here. The team's framework, GraNNite, tackles the problem in three steps. First it splits the graph work so the chip can run it at all. Then it tunes the work for speed, cutting wasted memory trips. Last, it trades a little accuracy for further savings where that trade is worth it. The result is faster graph learning on limited hardware.
arxiv-2502-07021:
Jeremy Kulcsar and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on running a classic transport algorithm across machines that cannot pool their data. Sinkhorn iterations solve entropy-regularized optimal transport, but the kernel matrix here is split row-wise among workers. The team design two exact protocols that pass only slices of the scaling vectors around.

One protocol has every worker talk to every other; the other routes through a central server. For both, the authors derive closed-form costs for computation, communication, and memory, and prove the distributed iterates match the centralized algorithm exactly. Experiments on CPU and GPU clusters confirm the cost model, and show the repeated global exchange becoming the bottleneck as workers multiply. Optional extras cover a bounded-delay asynchronous mode and a privacy layer.
arxiv-2502-07221:
Qifeng Zhou and co-authors turn chat-style vision models into search tools for mixed image-and-text pathology queries, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Real clinic queries blend slides with words, but paired encoders cannot fuse them. The team names this composed search task and builds a test set for it.

Their frame, HOMIE, adapts any such model into a retrieval expert without rebuilding it. A small two-billion-part version beat bigger health models and paired encoders by wide gaps. Plain single-mode search stayed strong too. The pitch is proof-based answers over black-box calls. Readers get an interpretable search route for tissue diagnosis.
arxiv-2502-07321:
Salvatore Capozziello, Anupam Mazumdar, and Giuseppe Meluccio show how a nonlocal form of gravity can sidestep a famous barrier in cosmology. Weinberg's no-go theorem says no local field theory can solve the cosmological constant problem without fine-tuning. The constant drives the observed speeding-up of cosmic expansion, yet its small value defies natural explanation. Nonlocal interactions fall outside the theorem's assumptions.

The authors point to infinite derivative gravity, where the gravitational interaction spreads over a region rather than acting at a point. In that frame, the cosmological constant can be read as a nonlocal gravitational effect on very large scales. The observed acceleration then fits inside an effective field theory. No fine-tuned parameters and no extra matter fields are needed. The paper offers this as a fresh route to understanding cosmic acceleration.
arxiv-2502-07621:
Morgan Giese, Will Thompson, Dariusz Lis, and Susanna Widicus Weaver dissect the chemistry of a massive star-forming region in a paper from 2025. Interferometer observations of W75N resolved several dense cores. Over twenty molecules were identified and fitted for abundance, temperature, and line width. Complex organic molecules appeared in two cores for the first time. Maps of six well-fitted molecules exposed the region's structure.

One core splits chemically: sulfur-bearing molecules mark one half, organics the other. Another core shows two emission peaks, hinting at twin young stars. The work follows up a single-dish survey of many such regions. Detailed numbers like these feed models of how stars and planets inherit chemistry.
arxiv-2502-09121:
Yichao Huang opens a series of papers on the tail behavior of Gaussian multiplicative chaos measures, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. These random measures arise in probability theory and in Liouville conformal field theory. Huang studies a bulk measure that has a uniform singularity along a boundary.

The focus here is on quotients between bulk and boundary versions of the measure. Huang establishes preliminary joint moment bounds for these quotients. A key tool is a localization trick applied at the boundary. The paper also records a generalization of Kahane's convexity inequality, noted as independently useful. Later papers in the series will use these bounds to pin down the exact right tail profile.
arxiv-2502-13021:
Simon Caron-Huot and co-authors present lectures on asymptotic observables, the measurable quantities quantum field theory predicts at the largest scales. In theories with a mass gap and quiet behavior far out, these include scattering amplitudes, cross sections, and readings of operators pushed to infinity. The lectures argue these quantities form one family.

Analytic continuation links the family members, in new versions of an old idea called crossing symmetry. As a worked case, the notes show how the infrared divergences of quantum electrodynamics combine and exponentiate for inclusive observables, using folded time contours. The authors close by sketching how a classic transform method could map the analytic structure of these observables systematically.
arxiv-2502-14621:
Azaïs and Denis unify rival methods for estimating jump rates in a class of random processes in this 2025 paper. Piecewise-deterministic Markov processes move along smooth paths, then jump at random times. Their jump rate is a key unknown in applications from networks to cell biology.

Earlier nonparametric estimators grew from separate theories, blocking fair comparison. The authors build one framework holding them all and prove fresh consistency and normality results inside it. No method wins everywhere, even within a single model. Simulations on the classic TCP network model back the theory. Real data on Escherichia coli growth and division show the same trade-offs in practice.
arxiv-2502-14921:
Matthieu Meeus and co-authors audit whether synthetic text from a language model can leak facts about the private data used to fine-tune it, in a 2025 paper. Synthetic data is often shared as a privacy-safe stand-in. The team assumes an attacker sees only the synthetic output and tries to infer which records trained the model.

Their membership attacks worked well enough to show real leakage. Planted canary records designed for direct model access proved weak here, because they rarely surface in useful synthetic text. The authors craft better canaries, with natural openings and odd endings, that leave detectable traces. The work sharpens how such releases should be audited.
arxiv-2502-15821:
Keane Ong, Rui Mao, Deeksha Varshney, Erik Cambria, and Gianmarco Mengaldo tackle greenwashing in company sustainability reports. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that ESG scores rest on these reports. Firms can pad them with claims that are vague, inflated, or false. Past text tools often take such claims at face value.

The team built A3CG, a data set that pairs each sustainability aspect with the acts claimed for it. This pairing forces checks against real deeds, not rhetoric. The set also tests whether models hold up when firms shift focus to new areas. Tests of taught models and large language models show clear limits. Both kinds miss or misread claims in set ways. The authors map what future work must fix for ESG checks that resist spin.
arxiv-2502-18221:
Kassaie and Tompa present a paper from twenty twenty-five on cleaning data in free-text documents. Loose text lacks fixed meaning, so quality checks are hard to run. Their plan uses extraction programs to design and explain cleaning steps. For a simple update model, they set terms a rule-based extractor must meet. Extractors that meet those terms can join their cleaning framework safely. They prove those terms are enough for the job. Tests run on medical records as the trial case.

The framework spots and fixes quality problems in the records. The authors say the method shows practical worth in real settings. It turns extraction rules into updatable views over documents. Cleaning then stays tied to the source text, not a detached copy.
arxiv-2502-18821:
Dung Nguyen and co-authors merge expert models with an eye to the curve of the space they live in, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Big models are often built as teams of experts that are later merged. Old merges treat the weight space as flat, which can bend the merge off course when the true space curves.

Their method, CAMEx, steers merges by natural slopes that hug the curve, with no need for the heavy matrix that curve tools crave. A live design also shifts how experts join across training stages to save compute. Tests across language tasks show the curved merge beats flat ones in both first training and fine tuning. The team frames it as scale ready expert craft.
arxiv-2502-20621:
Kang, Wang, Seung, Wang, and Abuadbba propose EPhishCADE, a privacy-aware framework for detecting email phishing campaigns, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Phishing emails lure victims to fake sites for data theft. Campaigns hide links between seemingly unrelated attacks. Their system clusters attacks using structure plus context.

A graph layer reveals textual, numeric, time, and place similarities. Only phishing URLs are used, never private sender or content data. Organizations can collaborate on detection without exposing personal information. Analyst fatigue drops as reports are streamlined automatically. Benchmarks against an established structure-based study show clear effectiveness.
arxiv-2502-21021:
Seungki Kim and Phong Nguyen wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five tightening the hunt for a counterexample to the Mertens conjecture. The conjecture, a once-plausible claim about the Mertens function's growth, is known to be false, but no explicit counterexample has ever been exhibited. Knowing where the smallest one must lie guides the search.

Using state-of-the-art lattice algorithms, the authors improved the upper bound on the lowest counterexample. The new bound sits near exp of about two times ten to the nineteenth. That is far below the earlier conjectured scale set by Kotnik and van de Lune, near exp of about five times ten to the twenty-third. The improvement shrinks the range in which the first violation can hide.
arxiv-2502-21321:
Komal Kumar, Tajamul Ashraf, and a large team survey post-training methods for large language models that reason. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Pretraining on huge web data gives a model its broad base. The field now turns to steps after that base, to sharpen skill.

Post-training spans fine-tuning, learning from reward, and extra compute at test time. These steps can lift reasoning, fact care, and fit to user aims and ethics. The survey sorts the methods, weighs their gains, and names their traps, such as lost old skill and gamed rewards. It maps new paths in alignment and scale, and gives a live list to track the fast field.
arxiv-2503-00121:
Drew Weninger and four co-authors design a coupler for linking light between chips and fibers. Their 2025 paper serves co-packaged optics, where light and electronic chips share one package. Such packages aim at huge data rates for data centers. Scaling needs many light channels, yet fiber arrays and hand alignment hold that back.

Their coupler uses a graded-index lens plus a fading-field link to pass light vertically between chips. The design allows flip-chip assembly with no active alignment. Simulations show losses under three tenths of a decibel across an eleven-micron gap. Tolerances for placement error span a few microns, and the working band is wide. The results suggest a path to dense, low-loss optical packaging.
arxiv-2503-02621:
Atienza and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about screening for a hidden heart rhythm problem with little labeled data. Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation comes and goes, so it is easy to miss. The team used single-lead heart signals recorded remotely during normal rhythm. Labeling medical data takes experts and raises privacy limits. That makes large labeled sets hard to build for new questions.

They tried self-supervised learning, where a model learns patterns before any labels are used. They compared it with standard supervised methods on their small group.
