Self-supervised models did better on the screening task. The authors stress a second point as well. Weak supervised results on tiny groups can mislead researchers. Self-supervision offers a safer first look at fresh clinical questions.
arxiv-2503-04921:
Armin Ariamajd, Raquel López-Ríos de Castro, and Andrea Volkamer introduce PyPackIT in two thousand twenty five. Scientific software often suffers from thin funding and time. Research code quality then lags behind the science it supports. PyPackIT automates research software engineering for Python projects.

The cloud tool follows FAIR and open science principles. It ships a build ready package skeleton for new projects. Documentation and test suites come fully operational out of the box. GitHub Actions drive continuous integration, deployment, and maintenance. A control center lets teams tune the setup dynamically.
arxiv-2503-05121:
Alan Frieze and Xavier Pérez-Giménez pinned down a threshold in random hypergraph theory in 2025. A hypergraph links groups of points at once, and a loose Hamilton cycle is a ring that visits every point while consecutive hyperedges overlap in exactly one point. The question is how many random hyperedges a hypergraph needs before such a spanning ring almost certainly exists.

The authors show that once the number of hyperedges passes a precise edge, growing with the number of points and its logarithm. A loose Hamilton cycle appears with high chance, for every uniformity of three or more. The bound is asymptotically best possible: just below it, isolated points almost certainly remain, and a cycle visiting every point is then impossible. Threshold results of this kind are the backbone of random form theory.
arxiv-2503-05721:
Marco Antonio Stranisci and Christian Hardmeier present a 2025 benchmark study of the filters used to scrub harmful content from language model training data. Filtering is a front line of safety for large models. Yet its effect on groups at risk of discrimination had never been measured in a systematic way.

The authors reviewed fifty-five technical reports to catalogue the filtering strategies in use, then built a test setting to run them. They measured how much harm each strategy removed and what it cost the groups the filters are meant to protect. The paper gives builders a clear view of a trade-off that is usually invisible.
arxiv-2503-06721:
Vincent Drach, Sofie Martins, Claudio Pica, and Antonio Rago present HiRep v2 in a 2025 arXiv paper. HiRep is open-source software for lattice field theory simulations with Wilson fermions in higher representations. Such simulations probe physics beyond the Standard Model.

The new version fully supports GPU acceleration for both configuration generation and measurement. It runs on NVIDIA and AMD cards. Improved actions, advanced solvers, and Monte Carlo methods with speed-ups are built in. Scaling across many GPUs and nodes stays strong with little loss. The authors offer it as a sturdy tool for large-scale studies.
arxiv-2503-07121:
Khanna, Goldstein, Pesci, and Gov measure how cicadas decide together to start their dawn chorus, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Choruses erupt each morning in many habitats, but onset rules were unquantified. The team records choruses over weeks and tracks singing growth with a time-frequency order parameter. Onset times follow sunrise with striking precision.

Choruses start in civil twilight at a fixed sun angle below the horizon. Scaled curves from all days collapse onto one sigmoid with a one-minute rise. Singing probability versus ground light shows a narrow susceptibility peak. Fluctuations peak at the same point, hinting at a fluctuation-dissipation link. A decision model with acoustic coupling matches the data quantitatively.
arxiv-2503-07221:
Christian Pötzsche and Robert Skiba link two tools from the theory of bifurcation, in two thousand twenty-five. Bifurcation theory studies when solutions of an equation split into new branches. One tool, parity, works in an abstract operator setting, while the Evans function is a workhorse for the stability of traveling waves.

The pair show how the two tools relate, and they use that link to give a flexible test for local bifurcations. Their test produces bifurcations that are truly time-driven, since steady or repeating forcing cannot meet its conditions. They also tie the Evans function to a spectrum that governs bounded solutions. Non-trivial examples show the methods at work.
arxiv-2503-07521:
Irina Aref'eva, Ali Hajilou, Alexander Nikolaev, and Pavel Slepov study how a strong magnetic field affects the strong force's coupling in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their tool is a bottom-up holographic model, using a magnetized Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton background to mimic heavy quark dynamics. The running coupling describes how the interaction strength changes with scale. The authors track it at fixed temperature and chemical potential while varying the field.

Like the earlier light-quark model, the heavy-quark coupling decreases in a strong external magnetic field. The main difference between the two models is where their phase transitions sit. Near first-order phase transitions, though, the coupling behaves alike in both cases, jumping by amounts that depend on temperature, chemical potential, and field strength. The results inform holographic modeling of quark matter under extreme conditions.
arxiv-2503-08121:
Huy Nguyen and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 presenting a large new test set for matching people across drone and ground video. Security teams often need to tell whether a person seen from the air is the same one a street camera caught. Viewpoints, scale, and sharpness all swing wildly between those feeds. Their set holds more than six thousand people and over nine million frames from drones, fixed cameras, and body-worn ones.

Drone heights in the set range from near rooftop level to high above the street. The team also built a matching network with three streams for motion, appearance, and scale. Their network beat past methods on the new set and on older video benchmarks. Scores still dropped on the new set for every method, marking it as a hard test.
arxiv-2503-08321:
Ivica Obadic and co-authors present a 2025 paper on image models that explain themselves. Graph-based vision models read an image as linked patches. They score well but hide why they chose an answer. The team builds a version whose reasons can be read. It limits each node to a small local window of the image.

A tight bottleneck with sparse attention picks the links that matter. The picked subgraph shows which patches drove the call. Tests cover scene sorting and number guessing tasks. Images include normal photos and remote sensing views. Scores and pictures both back the claim that clarity costs little skill. Image teams get a model that shows its work. That matters where a wrong call must be checked, such as land mapping or site surveys from the air.
arxiv-2503-09321:
Models that answer questions about video must truly use both the picture and the sound. Yet many benchmarks let them pass on vision alone, and their single scores hide where the failure lies. Gorjan Radevski and co-authors built DAVE, a diagnostic benchmark for audio visual evaluation. Its questions are constructed so that both channels are needed to answer correctly. The scoring is split into small, atomic categories, so a model can be shown to fail at hearing, at seeing, or at aligning the two.

Testing leading models on DAVE exposed specific failure modes that ordinary benchmarks blur. The authors offer the dataset and framework as a standard diagnostic tool, so developers can aim repairs at the true weak point instead of chasing a single aggregate number. The benchmark is public, with data and code released for other teams to use.
arxiv-2503-09721:
Manish Nagaraj and three co-authors pick the training samples that matter most for deep learning. Their 2025 paper proposes a score called Loss Trajectory Correlation. Big training sets are costly to use in full. A coreset, a small stand-in subset, can train nearly as well if chosen with care.

Their score compares how each sample's loss moves during training with how the validation loss moves. Samples that track the validation path earn a place in the coreset. The score comes free as a byproduct of training. On two image benchmarks, coresets picked this way matched or beat rival methods. The picks also carried across many network designs with small losses.
arxiv-2503-10321:
Some groups in algebra can be fully told apart by their finite snapshots, a property called profinite rigidity. Julian Wykowski proves in this 2025 paper that finitely generated free metabelian groups have this property in the strongest sense.

These groups are the freest ones where commutators themselves commute. Wykowski shows no other well-behaved group shares exactly their finite quotients. The proof leans on his earlier result about rigidity for modules over tidy rings, plus a known description of these groups through homology. The result adds a clean infinite family to the short list of groups known to be rigid this way.
arxiv-2503-10421:
Zhenwei Wang and co-authors teach a neural system to solve vehicle routing in a 2025 paper. Routing fleets through many stops faces huge option counts and hard real-world limits. Classic solvers are slow or need hand-crafted rules, while some learning methods stumble on strict constraints.

The head of the text frames the method as constraint-based adaptive hypergraph learning. Its encoder rebuilds links among stops and constraints as it learns better representations. A double-pointer decoder then builds routes step by step. Training uses reinforcement learning, so the system improves from its own trial routes. The end-to-end design aims to respect hard limits while keeping solution quality high on practical routing tasks.
arxiv-2503-12421:
Yuri Antonacci and five co-authors build a method for tracking group-level interactions in body networks as they change over time and frequency. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Most tools study pairs of signals and assume steady behavior, missing brief, frequency-bound teamwork.

Their framework models the network with a time-varying autoregressive system. A recursive estimator with a forgetting factor follows the drift. From the model they separate shared, redundant information from synergy, where the group knows more than its parts. Simulations show the method catching short bursts of synergy in set bands. In rat brain recordings, shared information timed to whisker touches appeared on the opposite brain side. The tool suits any shifting network.
arxiv-2503-12821:
Mingyang Song, Xiaoye Qu, Jiawei Zhou, and Yu Cheng tackle, in a 2025 paper, the long-tail problem in the training data of large vision-language models. Such data are lopsided: a few common concepts appear again and again, while rare ones barely show. Models then shine on the common and stumble on the rare. The authors study this in modern chat-style vision models and broad tasks such as visual questions.

Their analysis pins the skew on two roots: too much head data and too little tail data. Their fix works in two stages. First, crowded data are trimmed to match how concepts truly spread. Second, diffusion generators and the few real rare images are used to build fresh tail examples. Across eleven benchmarks, the treated model gained over four percent on average, with no growth in data volume.
arxiv-2503-14721:
Aaron Dunbrack, Pauli Virtanen, and Tero Heikkila study an odd form of superconductivity in a twenty twenty-five paper. In helical superconductivity, the phase of the superconducting state twists through space, like a corkscrew. Such states break time-reversal symmetry, the rule that physics looks the same run backward.

The math of the twist rests on a term in the free energy called the Lifshitz invariant. In simple one-band cases it comes from the energy spectrum near the Fermi surface. The team shows that in multi-band cases, quantum geometry adds a part, and that part rules when the bands are flat. The same idea drives shifts in density wave patterns.
arxiv-2503-15721:
Teklishyn and co-authors present a 2025 report on a silicon tracking detector built to add as little material as possible while covering a large area. The detector serves the CBM experiment, which faces very dense particle traffic. Its eight layers span four square meters, yet the material budget is only two to seven percent of a radiation length, a benchmark for how much a particle is disturbed. Thin double-sided silicon sensors with more than two thousand channels each do the sensing.

Feather-light cables carry the signals to a custom chip that records arrival times near five nanoseconds and charges across a wide range, all in free-streaming mode. About a third of the modules are built and tested. The authors also note uses in another Japanese experiment and in medical imaging telescopes.
arxiv-2503-16621:
Shomik Jain, Margaret Wang, Kathleen Creel, and Ashia Wilson test a hopeful idea in fair machine learning in a 2025 paper. Many models often tie for best accuracy while treating people differently; this Rashomon set of near-equal models is said to promise fairer choices. The authors look instead at allocations: when qualified candidates outnumber scarce resources, many fair-seeming distributions reach the same utility.

A healthcare case study shows the model set does not reflect that wider space of allocations. Sampling limits, the habit of picking the lowest-risk people first, and shared biases across models all shrink the promise. Equally good models, the authors warn, can still lock in the same winners and losers.
arxiv-2503-17121:
Kagome metals, built on a lattice of corner sharing triangles, can become superconducting. Their band structure has special points where the density of electronic states spikes. Jae-Ho Han and SungBin Lee study how having several electron orbitals in play changes which superconducting states such systems prefer. Experiments on kagome metals under doping and pressure motivate the work. The authors use parquet renormalization group analysis, which tracks how electron interactions grow and compete as the energy scale drops.

The analysis finds eight distinct superconducting instabilities, each with an order parameter that mixes the orbital degrees of freedom. In one region of parameters, the leading state pairs electrons in a pattern that resembles d-wave symmetry in its orbitals, while the spins align in a triplet arrangement. Related states there can break time reversal symmetry, echoing chiral triplet superconductivity but driven by orbitals.
arxiv-2503-17721:
Future wireless nets plan to sense and talk through the same waves, which doubles what a spy can steal. Yongxiao Li and seven co-authors survey in 2025 how smart walls that bend radio waves can guard such nets at the signal level itself. These reconfigurable intelligent surfaces reshape the air around a link, boosting the true path and starving the spy's. The survey lays out the base facts of the walls, of signal-level guards, and of the merged sense-and-talk nets.

Work is split by wall kind: still walls that only bend waves, and active walls that also boost them. For each kind the team weigh gains in speed, secrecy, and sense strength under set limits. They close with the hard parts left and the paths new work might take toward sixth-era nets.
arxiv-2503-17921:
Whitmore and co-authors build templates for reading the ages of star clusters from their light in this 2025 paper. Two space telescopes together span ultraviolet to mid-infrared, which should date young clusters well. The catch is that newborn stars blow their birth gas and dust away, muddying the signal.

Working on a nearby spiral galaxy, the team assembled energy profiles for compact clusters from 275 nanometers to twenty-one micrometers. Clusters aged one to four million years could be told apart in the infrared. In most cases a dust glow feature tracked the hot gas signal, and its dust was largely gone by four million years, cleared by starlight before any supernova. Nearly hidden clusters sat beside slightly older visible ones, suggesting triggered birth. Ages from the templates matched both gas bubble speeds and theory models.
arxiv-2503-18021:
Florian Kogelbauer and Ilya Karlin find the best way to shrink a linear dynamical system onto its slow backbone, in a 2025 paper. Many systems mix fast and slow motions, and modelers often keep only the slow part, which lives on a surface called the slow manifold. Projecting the full motion onto that surface can be done many ways, and the choice decides how faithful the small model stays. The authors derive the projection from a variational principle, an optimization over time, and show it is the dynamically optimal one.

Their projection follows the full system's passing behavior, not just its settled state. Reduced paths computed with it hug the true paths far more closely than standard choices. The authors demonstrate the gain on explicit examples, including a three-component linear system from the kinetic theory of gases, known as Grad's moment system.
arxiv-2503-18221:
Wen-Tse Chen and four co-authors teach a team of four-legged robots to tow a load on cables through messy, crowded ground, with no central guide. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Cables let the team slip through tight gaps, by going slack when they must. But the load's pull flips between taut and slack, and the joint task grows fast as robots are added. The team built a planner taught by reward, with many agents at once. It is taught as a group but runs one robot at a time. The system can steer a team of any size, and handles the flip of the cables as it goes.
arxiv-2503-18821:
Chenyi Li and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper that formalizes the optimality conditions of smooth constrained optimization inside the Lean4 proof assistant. These conditions, known as the KKT conditions, state what must hold at a local minimum. A machine-checked version gives optimization theory a precise and reusable base.

The build starts from the Lagrangian function and constraint qualifications, then formalizes the geometric view through tangent cones. A key step proves that the tangent cone matches the linearized feasible directions under the right conditions. The Farkas lemma then delivers the KKT conditions. A dual problem and weak duality are formalized as well.
arxiv-2503-19021:
Marcel Augusto Pinto, Giovanni Luca Sferrazza, Daniele De Bernardis, and Francesco Ciccarello wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies how a qubit sheds light into a lattice of coupled cavities whose tones tilt step by step, so photons feel a fake force.

For a strong force, the shed light bounces back and forth in a clean, time-cycled patch that spreads left or right by the qubit's tone, as in a Jaynes-Cummings tale. For a weak force, the decay turns messy, with revivals like those a mirror would cause, though no mirror is there. The band's finite width traps the photon and plays the mirror's part. A delay equation with Bloch swing terms fits the weak case well.
arxiv-2503-19221:
Yong Yang and a large team of co-authors explain the odd shape of the Ophiuchus star stream in two thousand twenty-five. The stream is a thin trail of stars torn from a cluster as it orbits the Milky Way. It shows a side spur, a spread-out tail, and a shorter length than its age would suggest.

New spectra from a southern survey, paired with models, point to the bar of stars at the galaxy's core. The bar has slowed over time, and its pull can swap the stream's two tails from one side to the other. Stars lost long ago stay bunched, which explains the short length, while the spur and spread come from tails built at distinct times.
arxiv-2503-21721:
Jaywon Koo and his four co-authors, publishing in 2025, propose a better scorecard for AI image and video generators. The standard scores split the job badly. One measures picture quality but ignores the prompt. Another checks prompt match but ignores quality. Learned preference scores need constant retraining and may not transfer to new models.

Their metric, cFreD, folds both demands into one number. It extends a classic distance between image distributions so the comparison is conditioned on the text. Across many recent generators and prompt sets, its rankings tracked human judgments better than rival scores, including ones trained on human preferences. The authors release their toolkit and benchmark. They pitch the metric as a durable standard for a field whose models change every few months.
arxiv-2503-21821:
Kaiyue Feng and co-authors introduced a benchmark called Physics in this 2025 paper. The set holds 1,034 open-ended problems taken from PhD qualifying exams across six core areas of physics. Solving them takes real domain knowledge plus multi-step math, and each problem ships with a worked solution and checked answers.

An automated grader, itself a language model, scores numeric, symbolic, and text answers for single parts and whole problems. The team ran 53 leading models, both commercial and open. Top scores clustered in a small group of reasoning-focused models, with the best open models nearing the commercial ones. Most open models still solved fewer than half of the figure-free problems, and misread figures were a common failure.
arxiv-2503-21921:
Marconcini and co-authors (2025) studied the gas around the active center of the galaxy NGC 424 using three major telescopes. Data from the James Webb Space Telescope, the Very Large Telescope, and the ALMA radio array let the team trace cold, warm, and hot gas in the galaxy's central region. Emission lines from carbon monoxide, hydrogen, oxygen, and neon showed how the different gas phases sit and move together across scales from a few parsecs to several kiloparsecs.

The team modeled the disc's rotation and estimated a total mass near 1.09 times ten to the tenth solar masses. They found a compact outflow of hot ionized gas moving at up to a thousand kilometers per second, with no matching outflow in the colder gas. Gas speeds also spread widely along the galaxy's minor axis, which the authors link to energy the outflow injects into the disc.
arxiv-2503-22621:
Maximilian Ruff published a 2025 mathematics paper sharpening the error guarantees for numerical schemes that handle rough solutions. Some wave equations start with data too jagged for classical methods. Low-regularity integrators are built for such data, but their proven accuracy was fractional, worse than what computations suggested. The paper closes that gap for two famous equations.

For the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, it analyzes an exponential-type scheme from 2018; for the wave equation, a corrected splitting method from 2023. Both are shown to converge at their full order, one and two respectively, for solutions of modest smoothness. The proofs lean on space-time bounds for the underlying linear problems: a Strichartz inequality in one case, a null-form estimate in the other, the latter a first in numerical analysis. Better guarantees matter because simulations of rough waves, from optics to fluids, rest on them.
arxiv-2503-23221:
Rolando Rubilar-Torrealba, Lisandro Fermin, and Soledad Torres modeled stock market drops in a 2025 paper. A drawdown is the fall from a past peak to a later low, and the largest such fall is a key risk gauge for traders. The authors track the chain of record values of that largest fall over time.

They model the chain with a process that flows in a smooth way but jumps at random times. From that model they derive the mean and spread of the record chain. They also build ways to fit the model values from data and test them in computer runs. A real market case shows the full steps, from data to fitted risk figures.
arxiv-2503-23921:
Shoto Aoki, Hidenori Fukaya, and four colleagues compute a famous topological index for lattice Dirac operators using K-theory, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The index counts a mismatch between left- and right-handed zero modes, and the Atiyah-Singer theorem ties it to the geometry of the underlying space.

Their approach treats the Wilson Dirac operator of lattice gauge theory as an object in K-theory, and shows its spectral flow equals the index. Unlike the standard lattice formulation, theirs needs no Ginsparg-Wilson relation. It also extends to systems with boundaries and to mod-two versions of the index in general dimensions. Numerical checks confirm the formulas reproduce the known continuum theorems. For the first time, they compute the Atiyah-Patodi-Singer index with curved boundaries, and its mod-two cousins, directly on a lattice. The work gives lattice practitioners a cleaner topological toolkit.
arxiv-2504-00321:
Oscar Jed Chuy, Matthew Hale, and Ricardo Sanfelice wrote a paper from 2025 on control schemes that steer a system while computing their moves in steps. Feedback optimization reads a system's output live and adjusts its input to hold a goal, which helps cancel disturbances. Past work usually put both in the same kind of time. Real setups often mix them: the system flows on, while a computer updates in ticks.

Their model joins the two clocks for linear systems. They first show the model is well posed, that solutions run their full course, and that the system cannot tick infinitely fast. They then prove the state settles quickly toward a ball of known size around the goal. The scheme also stands up to noise in the readings, to errors in the system's own numbers, and to jitter in when inputs land. Simulations back the claims.
arxiv-2504-01121:
Two robot trash barrels rolled through a public space, and Fanjun Bu, Kerstin Fischer, and Wendy Ju studied how people made sense of them. The team reviewed video of two hundred and seventy-four encounters and interviewed sixty-five people or groups who met the robots. People reacted not just to what the robots did, but to the whole idea of robots doing trash duty.

Visitors wanted background: who sent the robots, why, and what the bigger plan was, since those answers changed how they chose to act. The team draws lessons for anyone putting robots in public, and offers their field study as a worked example of how to read such encounters. The robots' odd job, not just their moves, drove the response.
arxiv-2504-02421:
Morteza Davari, Phablo Moura, and Hande Yaman study how to split a weighted network into balanced, connected parts, in a 2025 paper. The classic version weights the vertices; theirs weights the edges. The goal is a set of connected groups whose heaviest member is as light as possible, or whose lightest is as heavy as possible. Both versions, they prove, are hard even on very simple graphs, and no fast shortcut exists under standard assumptions.

For the min-max version they give an approximation algorithm with a tight guarantee. They also build several exact solvers: compact and extended integer programs, plus branch-and-cut and branch-and-price methods. A final experimental section races the solvers against each other. The full implementation is released as open code for others to use.
arxiv-2504-04921:
Katja Karhu, Jussi Kasurinen, and Kari Smolander published this review in 2025. AI tools have become everyday aids for writing code, but their use in software testing lags behind. The authors mapped recent industry studies, from 2020 onward, on how AI is actually adopted in testing work. They grouped the findings by theme, covering real use cases, reported benefits, and the gap between promise and practice.

The map shows that AI is still lightly used in testing, and few industry studies exist. Promising uses include generating test cases, analyzing code, and automating tests intelligently. Yet reported deployments and measured benefits remain limited compared with expectations. The review also flags a search problem: the phrase artificial intelligence pulls in many false hits in research databases. The authors conclude that testing teams need more grounded evidence before AI earns a central place in their workflow.
arxiv-2504-05521:
Andrei Neagu, Frédéric Godin, and Leila Kosseim run a fair race between eight deep reinforcement learning algorithms. The arena is a finance task: dynamic hedging, where a trader keeps rebalancing assets to cancel the risk of an option. Framing hedging as step-by-step decisions suits learning agents, but past studies tested only one or two methods, so no honest ranking existed.

The field covered policy gradient methods, four variants of deep Q-learning, and two variants of an actor-critic method, two of them new to this task. Prices were simulated with a volatility model, and the classic Black-Scholes delta hedge set the bar. A Monte Carlo policy gradient method won, with a proximal method second. The winner was the only agent to beat the classic baseline within the given computing budget, which the authors link to the task's sparse rewards.
arxiv-2504-06021:
Kang and five co-authors built this image classifier in twenty twenty-five that keeps knowledge outside the model. Most classifiers bake facts into their weights during training. New classes then demand retraining. Their learner stores knowledge in an external memory of web images and text instead.

At run time the model pulls memory items that match the input photo. Swapping the memory contents retargets the classifier to new classes with no retraining. Training taught it to classify from noisy web data for classes it had never seen. Tests covered zero-shot and few-shot tasks, fine-grained sorting, and step-by-step class additions. The authors report strong, versatile results across all of them.
arxiv-2504-07221:
Abdel-Ghani, Abbas, and Maksymov compute with a single oscillating gas bubble in twenty twenty-five. Artificial intelligence demands ever more energy, motivating physical computing hardware. A computing reservoir needs nonlinear behaviour to model complex patterns. Their reservoir is one bubble trapped in liquid.

An acoustic pressure wave both feeds in data and excites the bubble. The bubble's complex motion transforms the input for a simple readout. The system forecast benchmark time series and classified patterns accurately. Chaotic oscillation, where motion is rich and irregular, worked best. Orderly regimes performed worse on the same tasks. The authors validate the idea theoretically as a low hardware route to computing.
arxiv-2504-07621:
Sayantan Bhattacharya and Sudip Bhattacharyya asked why some neutron star binaries stay bright for decades in 2025. These systems, where a neutron star siphons gas from a light companion, normally flare for weeks then go quiet, driven by an instability in the gas disk. One famous case stayed in outburst at least twenty-three years, rested sixteen, and returned, which strains that story.

Comparing long-term X-ray light curves across many short-period systems, they measured outburst length, feeding rate, and disk mass. Long-outburst systems separated cleanly from short ones in four combined views of those measures. The authors conclude ordinary disk instability cannot explain the long events, so another mechanism must sustain them.
arxiv-2504-08221:
Andrés Salcedo and two co-authors forecast what cosmic voids can teach when paired with galaxy counts, in a 2025 cosmology paper. Voids are the vast empty zones between galaxy webs. They respond to both cosmic rules and the link between galaxies and their dark halos, which makes them tricky but rich probes. The team model the pair-up with a forward scheme that fills halos with galaxies by set rules.

Their forecast uses a coming sky survey's fifth-year data. Joining void counts, void-galaxy pairing, and galaxy pairing pins two key cosmic values to about one percent. The joint fit also solves for the galaxy-halo link from the same data, which breaks old trade-offs. A stacked lensing check on voids adds a further test. The authors say voids deserve a central place in survey plans.
arxiv-2504-08621:
Tao Zhang, Zhenhai Liu, Yong Xin, and Yongjun Jiao automate engineering simulation with language model agents in a paper from 2025. The target software, MOOSE, runs finite element simulations for heat, mechanics, and coupled physics. Setting up runs takes expert knowledge and much manual work. Their framework, MooseAgent, splits the job among cooperating AI agents. The agents read a plain-language request, draft input files, and verify them over several rounds.

A searchable database of annotated examples helps curb model errors. Tests covered heat transfer, mechanics, phase field, and multi-physics cases. Simple single-physics problems succeeded at high rates. The code is open source. The authors aim to lower the entry barrier for simulation work.
arxiv-2504-08721:
Jasper Bussemaker and four co-authors improve how engineers optimize complex system designs. Their 2025 paper targets architecture choices tested by costly physics simulations. Some test runs fail outright, leaving no score to learn from. These hidden failures, called hidden constraints, break standard surrogate methods.

Surrogate-based optimization swaps pricey simulations for a fast stand-in model. Bayesian methods with Gaussian processes guide the search. The team reviews tricks for mixed variables, many goals, and tiered choices. For failures, three plans compete: drop failed points, replace them, or predict the failure zone. Tests, including a jet engine design, favor a mixed approach. Handling failures openly beats pretending they never happened.
arxiv-2504-09021:
Lee and six co-authors trained a racing agent in this paper from twenty twenty-five for Gran Turismo 7. Earlier champion agents in the game leaned on exact position data from outside the car. That help will not exist on real roads. Their agent drives from camera views and onboard sensors alone.

A memory-based actor network keeps track of the course and rivals from those local views. During training only, a critic network sees the full global picture to guide learning. In races the agent beat the game's built-in drivers consistently. The authors claim the first vision-based agent at champion level in competitive racing. The gap between training help and driving inputs is the design's core trick.
arxiv-2504-10121:
Soham Ghosh, Sujay Mukhoti, and Pritee Sharma present a 2025 study on forecasting rice production under rainfall risk in Maharashtra, India. Farm output in the region leans heavily on the monsoon. The team asked whether adding rainfall data to time series models sharpens forecasts of crop production.

They used yearly data from 1962 to 2021 and built four models. Two were standard forecast models, with and without rainfall as an input. Two more added a volatility layer that lets risk itself shift the average. Forecasts ran one to three years ahead and were scored by two error measures. Models with rainfall did better, most clearly in the extended versions. The authors urge climate-aware forecasting for planning.
arxiv-2504-11721:
Daisuke Murakami and co-authors (2025) build climate scenarios that life insurers can use to stress-test their books. The team took the DICE model, a standard climate-economy model, and tuned it to the five shared socioeconomic pathways. Its emissions paths were aligned with six leading integrated assessment models. The result is a set of global temperature trajectories. Variants add policy targets, such as reaching net-zero carbon by a set year.

Temperature paths then convert into extra deaths from climate change, region by region. Those mortality shifts plug into insurance portfolios. The authors demonstrate the chain on synthetic life and annuity books. The point is practical: regulators increasingly ask insurers to show climate resilience, and most firms lack a tractable scenario engine. A calibrated, well-known model offers one that actuaries can defend. The paper lays out the calibration so others can reproduce and adapt the scenarios.
arxiv-2504-11821: Yi Huang and Xinhang Tong extend a thermodynamic uncertainty relation, in a 2025 preprint, to a wider family for entropy. Such relations cap how steady a current can run, given the entropy a process makes. The authors rebuild entropy production with generalized f-divergences, gaps between probability laws, and derive relations. A value called symmetry entropy enters, tying the bound to how the process treats time reversal. The result widens where precision-versus-cost trade-offs can be shown in stochastic thermodynamics.
arxiv-2504-12221:
Mei and co-authors design a quantum processor built from hole spins in pure germanium, in work from 2025. The bits sit in tiny gate-made dots, and sound waves in carved crystal blocks link them across long spans. Strong spin-orbit effects in the holes let plain electric signals steer each bit.

Models built on band theory and finite-element tools set the key numbers for the design. Coupling strengths, cavity quality, and spin life times all reach strong values in the models. Crystals grown in-house at high purity cut noise from stray nuclei. The team frames the plan as a path that fits standard chip making.
arxiv-2504-12321:
Charlotte Siska and Anush Sankaran wrote a 2025 computer science study on how to stop trick prompts that make language models break their own rules. Such attacks, called jailbreaks, hide harmful requests inside clever wording. Most defenses can block them but cannot explain why a prompt looks harmful.

Their method, called AttentionDefense, watches how a small language model pays attention to its own system instructions. Odd attention patterns help flag an attack and explain the flag at the same time. Tests on standard attack sets found detection as good as or better than older methods, at lower cost. The approach offers a clearer and cheaper guard for model safety.
arxiv-2504-13521:
Markets speak in many tongues at once: charts, order books, news, and trade counts. Kasymkhan Khubiev and Mikhail Semenov ask in 2025 how deep nets can hear them all. (The catalog spells the lead surname with one more letter than the head byline.) Their focus falls on the order book, the live list of bids and asks. They turn runs of book states into picture-like stacks that a net can read as one input.

That trick, with learned codes for the book's parts, hit the top mark on fast-trading tests in their runs. Charts and news still feed the wider frame around the book reader. The pair pitch deep nets as fit for the book's flood, where hand rules drown. The wider claim, that all market tongues can be heard at once, rests on this one strong case.
arxiv-2504-16121:
Muhammad Rafsan Kabir and co-authors build a question-answering system for multilingual legal documents in this 2025 paper. Language technology has barely touched legal and regulatory work. Their test bed is the Bangladesh Police Gazettes, written in both English and Bangla. The system pairs search with generation, a design called retrieval augmented generation. Retrieved passages ground the answers the model writes. An advanced variant of that design sharpens retrieval further.

Better retrieval means answers cite the right rule more often. Bilingual records are common in government but hard to search by hand. The framework aims at fast, precise answers from such archives. Staff could query regulations in either language. The work is a systems paper with a working prototype. It targets low-resource language settings often ignored by legal tech.
arxiv-2504-16521:
Yigit Ertugrul, Kamil Kapusuz, and Claude Desset lead a team assessing irregular antenna arrays for wireless links above one hundred gigahertz. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. At such frequencies antennas shrink to chip size, breaking the neat half-wavelength grid. Irregular layouts, thinned or clustered, work around the clash.

They weigh those layouts inside multi-user systems with hybrid beamforming. An optimization tunes element placement against a dial between data rate and sidelobe spill. Clustered layouts were arranged by both a genetic search and a brute-force method. A printed circuit prototype checked the designs in full-wave simulation. Fair comparisons matched thinning ratios against cluster sizes. The study gives engineers numbers, not just intuition, for terahertz-era arrays. Such links are candidates for dense future networks. Hardware realism is the paper's through-line.
arxiv-2504-17321:
Smith and co-authors fine-tune a satellite time-series model to map tree canopy cover as it changes, in this 2025 paper. Their variant, Dargana, starts from the EarthPT foundation model. It used under three percent of the original training data and five percent of the compute.

The model labels canopy at ten-meter detail and tells conifer from broadleaf trees. Tested on Cornwall imagery it had never seen, it scored near the top on standard accuracy measures. It spotted fine features like hedgerows and young woods below the training sample size. It also tracked change over time, such as new planting. The authors pitch it for land and conservation work.
arxiv-2504-18521:
Shintaro Shiba, Quan Kong, and Norimasa Kobori present a real-world dataset for event-based visible light communication and localization, in twenty twenty-five. Event cameras suit optical communication because of their high spatial and temporal resolution. They can decode modulated LED signals and locate the camera relative to LED markers. No public benchmark dataset existed for these tasks.

Their dataset combines an event camera, a frame camera, and precisely synchronized ground-truth poses. Recordings cover varied camera motions, sensitivity settings, and brightness conditions, indoors and outdoors. The authors also propose a localization method built on the contrast maximization framework. Experiments show LED-based localization with events beats conventional marker-based localization with frames. They hope the dataset becomes a standard benchmark for event camera research.
arxiv-2504-18721:
Ellis Owen, Yoshiyuki Inoue, Tatsuki Fujiwara, and Albert Kong weigh what galaxies together contribute to the high-energy sky's background glow, in a 2025 paper. Starburst galaxies shine in gamma rays. Colliding cosmic rays there make the light through particle decays. The same collisions should also make neutrinos. Old, quiet galaxies may glow too. Their dead stars leave pulsars, a top gamma source in our own galaxy. The team models the combined output of both galaxy types.

Galaxies, they find, supply only a fraction of the neutrino background. But they can form a major part of the gamma-ray background. Contrary to the standard view, much of that light may be electron-driven. Dead galaxies contribute through their pulsar populations. The result reshapes how the background is read. It suggests old stellar systems are not dark at high energies. Future telescopes can test the split.
arxiv-2504-18821:
Riasat Ali, Xia Tiecheng, and Rimsha Babar study radiation from an exotic black hole in a paper from 2025. The black hole comes from Horndeski gravity, a theory that extends Einstein's picture, and it carries extra fields nicknamed hair. The team uses a tunneling picture, where charged particles slip through the horizon. They ignore the recoil of the hole as particles leave.

From the tunneling rate they derive the hole's temperature and entropy. A first-order correction appears once quantum gravity effects are included through a generalized uncertainty rule. Standard approximations support each step of the calculation. The results show how such corrections shift the hole's heat traits. The work is theoretical, aimed at testing gravity ideas.
arxiv-2504-19221:
Jiawang Li designed a line of paired antennas to focus wireless power at close range, in a solo paper published in 2025. Large intelligent surfaces are a leading path to improve 6G in low frequency bands. His study lines up dual-polarization antennas in a row and drives them with matched phases. Earlier work on such focusing considered the direct path alone.

With a long row, the focus point on the center line settles at a fixed depth. He grades the width of the focus spot for two wave polarizations and tests slanted and circular foci. A two-ray path, with a reflected twin, makes the model more realistic. Rules for row placement and the focus spot come out of the mathematics. Simulation runs support the plan, and the parts pair with small cross-talk. The work grounds surface-based power beams.
arxiv-2504-19321:
Avigail Gil and Erez Berg wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies a two-dimensional electron gas with one spin and one valley, tuned so its Fermi level sits on a van Hove peak in the density of states.

With three or six such peaks linked by symmetry, the fate turns on the sign of the interplay between electrons there. If that interplay is positive, the gas stays stable. If it is negative, the gas breaks into a charge density wave or a pair density wave, set by the shape of the spread at the peaks. One pair wave form, with three wavevectors at once, can host tiny fractional vortices. The work maps how Fermi surface shape drives the order.
arxiv-2504-19621:
Haroui Ma, Francesco Quinzan, Theresa Willem, and Stefan Bauer build a statistical test for hidden bias in medical image AI, in a 2025 paper. A diagnostic model might lean on a patient's demographics instead of the disease, and standard accuracy checks will not notice. Their framework uses counterfactual invariance: a fair model's answer should not change if only a sensitive trait changed. A diffusion model generates the counterfactual images, and hypothesis testing measures any real dependence.

The method needs no actual counterfactual patients, only the model and data at hand. Tests ran on synthetic data and on large chest X-ray collections. Hospitals adopting imaging AI need exactly this kind of audit before a biased model quietly skews care.
arxiv-2504-20021:
Ryan Spieler maps the phases of two-dimensional theories guarded by a two-fold symmetry and time reversal, in this 2025 paper. The phases split into bosonic ones, living on surfaces that may lack orientation, and fermionic ones, sensitive to finer structure. Moving between them takes special operations.

Starting from seed theories, Spieler applies the operations step by step and names the theory at each border crossing. The survey yields eight phase diagrams for each family, tied together by trading bosons for fermions. Many borders host critical theories enriched by symmetry. The work also writes down fermionic versions of known bosonic moves for the first time.
arxiv-2504-20721:
Mattia Cafasso and Carla Mariana da Silva Pinheiro studied random grid figures at a key edge in 2025. For unitary random grids, eigenvalues crowd along an interval and thin out at its ends. At a key edge point the limiting density vanishes with an unusual five-halves power law, producing a special determinantal point process. The authors look at the multiplicative figures of that process, amounts built from products over its points.

They prove these figures are governed by the first three equations of the Korteweg-de Vries ranking, the celebrated group of nonlinear wave equations that recurs throughout integrable systems. The paper then analyzes the asymptotic actions of the related answers. The result ties an edge case of random grid theory to soliton math, giving exact handles on swings where the spectrum is at its most delicate.
arxiv-2504-21521:
Sun and Zou wrote in twenty twenty-five about adaptive neural control that approximates using desired signals instead of actual ones. Neural networks help controllers handle unknown dynamics in machines. Classic designs need the true system state to stay in a known region. That requirement can be hard to guarantee in practice. Their desired approximation approach feeds only the target state into the network. An integral Lyapunov design then builds the adaptive controller around tracking error.

Detailed theory covers both integral and incremental adaptation versions. All closed-loop variables are proven bounded under their schemes. Transient tracking performance is quantified analytically in the paper. The tracking error settles into an adjustable small set. No knowledge of the region where real variables evolve is needed. Initial conditions on states and weights are also freed from restrictions.
arxiv-2505-00221:
Aktaş and Kroer study in twenty twenty-five a greedy algorithm for maximising a strongly convex function over a bounded set. Such maximisation is unusual, since most tools assume minimisation. The greedy method moves step by step toward the best corner point at each stage, with a full step each time.

Under smoothness and a key slope condition, they prove the method's outputs settle at the right limit from any start. They also derive a speed rate that depends on the shape of the problem. To show the value, they prove new results for a sparse data method and a sensing method. They also design a new method for a relaxed form of a classic graph cut problem.
arxiv-2505-00321:
Large AI models have broad skills, but running them from distant data centers adds delay that 6G services cannot afford. Edge large AI models split and distribute these models across nearby edge devices, using their combined communication and computing power. The five authors survey the opportunities and the hurdles: edge hardware is limited, the models carry vast numbers of trainable neurons, and shipping updates eats bandwidth.

They propose collaborative fine-tuning and full-parameter training frameworks, plus a microservice-assisted inference design, to make deployment practical. They also test edge models inside the air interface itself, on channel prediction and beamforming. The paper offers these frameworks as a route to real-time intelligent services in 6G networks.
arxiv-2505-01121:
Kwang Hyun Cho, Hyukjoon Kwon, and Changbong Hyeon study a precision limit for a pair of coupled qubits in a 2025 physics study. The thermodynamic uncertainty relation ties how steady a current runs to how much entropy a process produces. In classical systems the bound has a fixed floor, but quantum coherence can lower it, as earlier work on a single driven two-level system showed.

The authors extend that setting to two qubits coupled quantum mechanically, sitting in a bath of light. Coupling adds a new channel that can reshape fluctuations of the irreversible current. Their analysis asks how far the uncertainty bound can loosen in the coupled system.
arxiv-2505-01221:
Giorgia Callegaro and co-authors model how firms should invest in cyber defense when attacks come in clusters, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Real attacks bunch together, with one hit raising the chance of more. A classic model of security spending is extended to capture that bunching.

Each attack may breach the system, with odds tied to how exposed the system is. Spending cuts that exposure, and the team solves for the best spending path over time. Policies that heed clustering reacted faster and worked better than static plans or plans that assume random, even attack timing.
arxiv-2505-01421:
Tobias Géron and a large team report a 2025 arXiv study of bars in disc galaxies seen by the JWST space telescope. Volunteers in the Galaxy Zoo project looked at color images and marked whether each galaxy had a strong or weak bar. The team studied hundreds of galaxies across a wide range of redshift.

After correcting for effects that hide bars, the bar share fell from about 25 percent in the nearest group to about 3 percent in the farthest group. The authors treat these shares as lower bounds, since faint bars are easy to miss. Still, they found clear bars up to redshift 2.5. That suggests many early discs were calm or rich in normal matter, so bars could form. Weak bars also grew rarer with redshift.
arxiv-2505-02921:
Francisco Aros, Enrico Vesperini, and Emanuele Dalessandro simulate how the stellar generations inside globular clusters slowly blend, in a 2025 paper. Clusters host several populations with distinct chemistry, and the younger ones often start more concentrated. Over time the differences fade, at a pace set by each cluster's dynamical age. The team tracked the mixing in energy and angular momentum space across simulations.

They compare the true phase-space blending with three observable gauges. One established gauge tracks spatial differences; two new ones track spin-axis spread and velocity anisotropy gaps. Present-day differences, they show, still encode how the populations began and how the cluster evolved. But reading formation history off today's snapshot takes care, since dynamics rewrites the evidence as it mixes.
arxiv-2505-04521:
Kuen Sum Cheung and colleagues weighed the carbon cost of coding with AI help in a 2025 study. Language models write code fast, but running them burns energy in data centers, while a human at a keyboard burns comparatively little. Using competitive programming tasks as a stand-in for development work, the team measured emissions for manual solving against model-assisted solving of the same problems.

On average, the assisted workflow produced a far larger carbon footprint than the manual one, by the authors' reported factor. The gap also grew with task complexity in a clear correlation, since harder problems invite more model calls and longer outputs. The study urges teams to count inference emissions as a real project cost, not a free lunch.
arxiv-2505-05121:
Jasper Rou, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, tests how accurate deep learning solvers are for the equations behind option pricing. Such solvers promise fast prices, but their real-world accuracy is poorly understood.

Rou compares two neural network methods, the Deep Galerkin Method and the Time Deep Gradient Flow method. Tests run under both the Black-Scholes and Heston models. He measures convergence rates and training time against sampling stages, sample counts, network layers, and nodes per layer. For the second method he also varies the discretization order and time steps, giving practitioners concrete guidance on solver settings.
arxiv-2505-05921:
Aritra Majumdar and Krishanu Maulik published this mathematics paper in 2025. It studies a random walk with memory: at each step, the walker looks back at its own past steps and often repeats one. How far back the memory reaches is set by a sequence whose weight fades in a regular way.

The authors find a sharp phase change in how the walk behaves. With weaker memory, the scaled walk settles toward a smooth bell-curve process. With stronger memory, it locks onto a random multiple of a power curve instead. Near the border between the two regimes, the usual timing and scaling rules break down, and the right scale can be smaller or larger than classic results suggest. They also prove matching laws for the walk's center of mass.
arxiv-2505-06521:
Satoshi Mishima and Kin-ya Oda offer a 2025 arXiv letter on errors on errors in physics data. When experiments disagree, analysts often inflate the quoted errors, but the standard recipe lacks a firm base. Two fixes exist, one Bayesian and one frequentist, and each adds gamma-distributed helper variables to model doubt about the errors themselves.

The authors show the two fixes match parameter by parameter and are structurally the same. That match lets a Bayesian prior choice be read as a frequentist sampling assumption, and the reverse. The result gives one shared framework for handling doubt about quoted variances.
arxiv-2505-07321:
Six researchers teach a small race car to drive itself on a real track in a paper from 2025. Most self-driving race systems train first in computer simulation, which often fails on real roads. Their system learns on board the car instead, using a method called reinforcement learning. A classic controller gives a base driving style, and the learner adds small fixes in real time.

Tests used the F1TENTH scale racing platform. The learning controller beat the base controllers and cut lap times by more than a tenth against prior best results. It needed only twenty minutes of training to get there. A version with no base controller also topped earlier marks. The team sees wider use in fast, changing tasks.
arxiv-2505-07621:
Leonardo Kuffo and Peter Boncz wrote a paper in 2025 on getting the best value for money from vector search on cloud CPUs. Vector search retrieves items by their position in a high-dimensional space of features, and it underpins many artificial intelligence tools. Cloud providers rent many different CPU types, and no fair benchmark had compared them for this workload.

The researchers benchmarked the processors across two kinds of search index and several compressed forms of the data. One maker's processor won by a wide margin on one index type, then lost on the other. When performance was scored as queries per dollar spent, a third maker's processor was the best option for most configurations, even beating its own newer successor. The work serves as a buyer's guide for teams deploying vector search in the cloud.
arxiv-2505-08921:
Austin King and Benjamin Bromley model how a star's flare can light up its planet-forming disk twice, in a 2025 paper. When a young star flares, light reaches us directly and then again after bouncing off the surrounding disk, a light echo. Earlier echo models treated flares as instant flashes. Real flares rise and fade over time, so the authors build echoes from extended, time-resolved flares. They test the model on two disk-bearing stars observed by the Kepler mission's K2 campaign.

For one star, the fitted disk properties matched known values, a good sign for the method. The second star's restless brightness after the flare peak made fitting unreliable. Together the cases show both the promise and the limits of echoes as a way to probe disks that telescopes cannot image directly.
arxiv-2505-09021:
Maria Dhakal and co-authors present a way to improve comments in computer code with AI tools, in a paper from 2025. Good comments help readers grasp what code does, but many comments are vague, stale, or missing key facts. Rewriting them by hand at scale is slow.

The team first studied what makes a comment good, using a survey of cases and a grounded analysis to name quality axes. They then used a large language model to rewrite comments along those axes. The results were distilled into a smaller model that firms can run in-house, keeping code private. Tests showed both the large model and the small one lifted comment quality. All data and code were shared in a public repository.
arxiv-2505-10121:
Mohamed Meguebel and co-authors present a theory study from two thousand twenty-five on entangling photons by their frequencies. Entanglement links particles so that measuring one reveals facts about the other. The authors use a quantum dot, a tiny semiconductor island with atom-like energy levels, coupled to a waveguide that carries light.

Their design tunes the dot so that single-photon processes fade out while two-photon processes are boosted. The result acts as a gate that entangles the frequencies of single photons passing through. They grade the gate by splitting its output state into parts, which exposes a trade-off between how often entanglement forms and how pure it is. They also show the gate can build entangled states with more than two levels.
arxiv-2505-11021:
Tungsten trioxide is a plain oxide with a flexible crystal, and squeezing it in a film can wake new behavior. Ewout van der Veer and co-authors grew such films under shear strain from the layer below. The strain settled the crystal into a low-symmetry form that carries electric polarization. That form held up even in thick films and at high temperatures. At the atomic scale, oxygen cages tilt in a new pattern to allow the change.

Under the microscope the film shows striped polarized regions with needle-like forks. The walls between stripes conduct electricity far better than the bulk. Those walls also host a predicted particle-like state tied to missing distortion. The findings open routes toward oxide electronics built on this common material.
arxiv-2505-11221:
Donghoon Lee, Tung Luu, Younghwan Lee, and Chang Yoo introduced LVLM2P in twenty twenty-five, a framework that lets a big vision-language model teach a small reinforcement learning agent. Large multimodal models reason well about decisions but are too heavy for lean real-world systems. Plain reinforcement learning is light but wastes trials flailing early on.

In their setup, the large model acts as a teacher over trajectories the agent collects, suggesting instructive actions that cut pointless exploration. Because the teacher reads visual input directly, no one must hand-write text descriptions of the scene. Experiments show baseline agents learn markedly faster with this guidance. The approach aims to bring foundation model wisdom to agents that must run cheaply on site.
arxiv-2505-12621:
João Eduardo Batista, Emil Vatai, and Mohamed Wahib present SAFE, a 2025 framework that ties each sentence a language model writes to the source sentence behind it. Models used in science often answer without clear sources, or cite the wrong ones, which blocks trust in high-stakes work. Fine-grained credit, down to one sentence in a source, is what users need to check claims as they read.

SAFE works in two steps while the text is being written: it first predicts how many references a sentence needs, then assigns them. The first step hit ninety-five percent accuracy, and the full method lifted the accuracy of every attribution method tested. On real document sets with hundreds or thousands of sentences, it still linked sentences to their sources well. The code and training data are public.
arxiv-2505-12921:
Yingxiang Hu and Mohammad Ivaki wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five on a problem about the shape of convex bodies that meet a wall. The capillary setting studies bodies that touch a flat boundary at a set angle, like a droplet on a surface. The Minkowski problem asks how to rebuild a body from data about its surface curvature.

The authors solve a weighted version of that problem for a range of exponents and contact angles. Their route is iterative: start from the known solution of the basic case, then apply a family of curvature image operators. The fixed points of those operators are exactly the bodies the problem seeks.
arxiv-2505-13421:
Si-Yang Liu, Qile Zhou, and Han-Jia Ye let a language model referee among tabular prediction models one row at a time, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Tables are the bread and butter of machine learning competitions and business data, yet the best model swings wildly from dataset to dataset.

Practitioners cope by averaging several models, but fixed blending rules cannot adapt to individual cases. The authors' in-context ensemble works differently. For each instance, the language model sees the rival models' predictions in context and integrates them dynamically. It does this without access to the raw features or their meanings. The ensemble's judgment is thus case-specific rather than one global recipe. The framing turns leaderboard know-how, which model to trust when, into a learned skill. The paper targets the stubborn variability of tabular tasks head-on.
arxiv-2505-14721:
Omar Malik examines how American firms are taking up artificial intelligence in a 2025 study drawn from a Census Bureau survey of business trends. He tracks adoption by state, by industry, and by firm size, looking for where the tools are spreading and where they lag.

Adoption stays low overall: only about seven percent of firms use AI today. Still, the share is climbing steadily, and more firms plan to start. Knowledge-heavy fields such as information work and professional services lead, along with larger firms, while construction and small firms trail. Malik reads the pattern as a quiet revolution: a slow, widening spread of AI with real stakes for output and policy.
arxiv-2505-14921:
Mateus Pelicer, Veronica Dexheimer, and Joaquin Grefa introduce a calculation engine for dense matter and neutron stars, in a 2025 paper. Neutron stars pack more than a sun's mass into a city-sized ball. What matter does at such density is still deeply uncertain. The engine, called MUSES, is free software that chains models together in workflows users can compose.

The team used two matter models plus a module that balances particles with leptons. A joining module blended the models in four different ways, from smooth steps to bumps. They then computed star structure for each blend. The choice of blending shape changed the results, which shows why such tools matter. The engine lets researchers swap parts and test dense matter ideas openly.
arxiv-2505-15221:
Christoph Jabs presents RustSAT, a software library that makes advanced SAT solvers easy to use from the Rust language, in a research paper from 2025. SAT solving decides whether a set of logical conditions can all hold at once. Top solvers crack many real problems, but their low-level input forms and expert setup form a barrier.

RustSAT helps users build SAT and MaxSAT problems, and read or write them as files. It links to several leading solvers through one shared Rust interface. It also supplies ready encodings for common higher-level rules, such as at-most-one, counting limits, and weighted sums. Those encodings are also open to C and Python programs, which widens the library's reach.
arxiv-2505-15621:
Shuyin Ouyang and co-authors built a tougher test for AI models that write data science code. Existing coding benchmarks lean on tidy puzzles, while real data work is messy and library-heavy. Their benchmark, DSCodeBench, holds one thousand problems drawn from real GitHub projects across ten popular Python data libraries, with longer, more realistic solutions and stronger test suites.

A construction pipeline mixed automated drafting with careful human editing to keep problems accurate. In trials, bigger models steadily outscored smaller ones, showing the benchmark separates ability levels well. Even the best model tested, GPT-4o, passed only about thirty-nine percent of problems on its first try. The authors offer the set as a trustworthy yardstick for progress in machine-written data science.
arxiv-2505-16021:
Braden Weight and Yu Zhang apply a quantum Monte Carlo method to systems where light and electrons interact strongly in a 2025 chemistry study. When light couples tightly to matter, hybrid polariton states can change reactions and light-driven behavior. Standard electronic structure tools have been extended to include light, with mixed accuracy.

Their method adds photon degrees of freedom to auxiliary field Monte Carlo, a stochastic approach known for careful ground state estimates. Benchmark chemical systems serve as tests of electron-photon correlation. Getting that correlation right matters for predicting how cavity light might steer chemistry, a goal drawing wide interest in quantum optics and materials work.
arxiv-2505-16921:
Some galaxies shine in X-rays far brighter than a normal stellar black hole should allow, and their flicker can reveal what feeds them. Hamza El Byad and co-authors mine ten years of NuSTAR observations of the galaxy M82 in this 2025 paper, home to two of these ultraluminous sources.

They track a quasi-periodic wobble from one source as it drifts between twenty and three hundred cycles per thousand seconds. No other timing features appear beyond broad low-frequency noise. The wobble behaves like the low-frequency oscillations seen around both black holes and neutron stars, tying this extreme source to the wider family of feeding compact objects.
arxiv-2505-17421:
Zhen Qiao and co-authors present a deep learning method for channel estimation in future 6G networks in this 2025 paper. Channel estimation means judging how a radio signal changes as it travels. In vehicle networks the channel shifts fast. A good method must balance accuracy against cost on limited hardware.

Their network, called ICENet, uses an implicit layer that can run for more or fewer rounds. Poor channel data gets more rounds, and clean data gets fewer. That keeps memory low while holding accuracy high. The paper closes with open problems for this line of work. The design targets vehicle to everything communication, where resources are tight.
arxiv-2505-17721:
Dekai Zhu, Yan Di, Stefan Gavranovic, and Slobodan Ilic present a 2025 model called SeaLion that creates three-dimensional point clouds with part labels attached. Diffusion models have grown strong at making point clouds for tasks like data enrichment and model editing. Yet they rarely add the fine labels that say which points form a leg, a wing, or a handle.

SeaLion works in a compressed latent space and uses the model's own internal features during cleanup. At each step it predicts both the noise to remove and the part label for each latent point. The cleaned points are then decoded into a cloud shaped by those labels. The authors also propose ways to grade such labeled clouds. Labeled output makes generated shapes far more useful for editing and training.
arxiv-2505-18321:
Kun Huang and co-authors design, in a 2025 numerical paper, a simulation method for a classic plasma equation that tracks how particles spread and collide over the long range. The method belongs to a family that lets the solution jump at cell edges, which complicates the duty to conserve mass, momentum, and energy exactly. Their scheme keeps those laws while staying stable.

The trick leans on the jump terms themselves: an upwind choice steadies the computation, and the jumps absorb the tension between stability and conservation. The authors recast an older structure-keeping idea in plain numerical terms and extend it to this method family. Benchmark runs test the scheme's behavior.
arxiv-2505-18521:
Li and five co-authors sped up training of diffusion image models in twenty twenty-five. Diffusion models learn by removing noise along many trajectories; when trajectories mix freely, the denoising task gets harder and training slows. An earlier method reduced mixing with a costly matching procedure that scales poorly.

The team generalizes the idea: miscibility can be cut at any layer and by many means, not just matching. They show the denoising process is one-to-one under their scheme, so image diversity is preserved. Cheaper implementations include nearest-neighbor noise selection and image scaling. Across generation, editing, and robotics planning tasks, training ran up to more than four times faster. The authors also explain how optimal transport methods help training through the same lens, and released their code openly.
arxiv-2505-18821:
Samit Ghosh and Arjun Paul define a generalized kind of connection on bundles in a 2025 mathematics study. Their setting is a smooth complex projective variety carrying a holomorphic principal bundle for an algebraic group. A connection tells how to compare bundle data at nearby points, and here its values live in a Lie algebroid, a structure mixing tangent directions with symmetry.

The authors study basic properties of these connections, including how they behave when the structure group is extended or reduced. They then seek criteria for a connection to exist on bundles over curves. Such criteria organize when extra geometric structure can be added.
arxiv-2505-19121:
Seunguk Yu, Juhwan Choi, and Youngbin Kim build a multilingual data set to test ethical bias in language models. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Social bias in such models is well logged, but whether it shifts with the tongue in use was less clear. They guess that tongue-linked gaps drive part of the bias.

Their set draws news pieces on human rights themes and turns them into touchy questions and answers in many tongues. Two strict tests then weigh bias across tongues and themes. In most cases, the tests rule out the no-bias claim. Bias shows across tongues and across models alike. The set is free for later work.
arxiv-2505-19321:
Solar and four co-authors simulate how supermassive stars form in the first star clusters, varying gas temperature, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such stars may seed the giant black holes already seen in the early universe. Whether the gas fragments into a cluster instead of feeding one monster star was unsettled.

Their simulations mix gas physics with star dynamics in a collapsing primordial cloud. Central objects of about ten thousand solar masses formed across temperatures, fed by both gas inflow and star collisions. Warmer gas favored disk shapes and a bigger collision share. In the most unstable runs the central object captured nearly all available mass. The authors link colder, unstable conditions to heavier black hole seeds.
arxiv-2505-19521:
Dongzhe Zheng and Wenjie Mei present, in a 2025 paper, a geometry-based way to learn how a system moves when the rules that bound it are known only locally and with doubt. Robots face this problem when sensors give only nearby, noisy facts. Past methods either demand full knowledge of the bounds or filter the noise without using the shape of the problem.

Their frame ties measures, bounds, and motion into one bundle structure over the state space. Safety functions then adapt to local sensing quality. A neural model learns the motion while respecting the bounds, with theory backing both learning and safety. Simulations beat older methods on speed of learning and on staying within bounds.
arxiv-2505-19821:
Zhou Feng and five co-authors craft a backdoor attack on neural networks that works with almost no poisoned data, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Backdoors plant a hidden trigger so a model misbehaves on cue while acting normal otherwise. Older attacks need heavy access to training data and often show.

Their attack, named ShadowPrint, targets the model's internal feature patterns instead of its raw inputs. A clustering method aligns those patterns so the trigger takes hold. In tests it reached perfect attack success at poison rates as low as one in ten thousand samples. Clean accuracy barely dipped, and detectors caught it rarely. The authors frame the result as a warning that defenses must guard the feature space itself.
arxiv-2505-19921:
Roland Berger and Jun Maillard work on duality theorems for a class of algebras studied in modern algebra. Their paper came out in 2025. The duality in question, named after Calabi and Yau structures in geometry, links an algebra to a shifted copy of itself.

An earlier theorem by Berger and a collaborator assumed that certain derived constructions exist. Berger and Maillard now prove that existence directly. They show that the categorical framework behind the calculus is equivalent to modules over a differential graded algebra, a graded algebra with a built-in differential. That equivalence defines the strong version of the property without extra assumptions. As a check, they prove that a polynomial algebra has the property. The result firms up the foundations of Koszul calculus, a method for studying algebras through resolutions.
arxiv-2505-20121:
Johannes Niederhauser and Aart Middeldorp extend a termination proof tool for higher order rewriting to work on normal forms, in work from twenty twenty-five. Rewriting systems replace terms by rules, and proofs that they always stop are key for trust. Matching under beta and eta rules adds hard twists.

The new order, called NCPO, handles systems where its cousin tool fails, even when that cousin is paired with a strong transform trick. The authors argue that NCPO is far easier to automate with SAT and SMT solvers. Their prototype is the first to automate both NCPO and the older order with its transform. Worked examples show the order in action. The paper is the full version of the study.
arxiv-2505-20221:
Xiao Shou, Yanna Ding, and Jianxi Gao treat neural network training as a moving system whose path can be learned and forecast, in work from 2025. Training is costly because gradient steps repeat so many times. If the path of the weights could be extrapolated, runs could be cut short.

Their method learns the update rules of common optimizers as smooth flow fields. It bakes the shape of gradient updates into the learning goal, unlike black-box sequence models. From partial training runs, it forecasts final weights well. Scores rivaled transformer models and beat older sequence baselines. The method also carried across network designs and starts, which the authors offer as a base for studying training itself.
arxiv-2505-22821: Achim Blumensath studies two classes that lie inside the wider class of automatic structures, in a solo work from two thousand twenty-five. One class holds the ones with polynomial growth, and the other holds the Presburger structures. For both classes, he gives algebraic characterisations of the groups in them. He gives the same kind of account for the equivalence structures in them too.
arxiv-2505-23921:
Víctor Martínez-Lahuerta and co-authors scrub a stubborn error out of atom interferometers, ultra-precise sensors built on matter waves, in a 2025 paper. These devices split atoms with Bragg diffraction, which inherently opens several paths at once. The stray paths imprint a diffraction phase that corrupts the reading. Optimal control theory had already hardened the devices against vibration and acceleration.

Here the same control tools target the phase itself. In a realistic model with a warm incoming wavepacket, the method pushed the phase below a microradian for slow atoms. That erases one of the leading systematic errors in the field. The authors say metrology-grade interferometers gain accuracy without new hardware.
arxiv-2506-00121:
Adam Boesky and three co-authors present a 2025 paper on SPLASH, a fast system for classifying supernovae by their host galaxies. A coming sky survey will spot millions of exploding stars, far more than telescopes can check one by one with spectra. Quick photo-based sorting is essential for picking young events to follow up. SPLASH uses only the host galaxy's light measurements to judge the explosion type.

The pipeline links each event to its host, estimates the host's mass and star formation with deep learning, then classifies with a random forest. It reached seventy-six percent accuracy on the basic two-way split between supernova types. Keeping only its most confident calls yields very pure samples. It can classify about five hundred events per second. The authors also note the host data let scientists select events by environment, aiding studies of how stars die.
arxiv-2506-00921:
Leyou Xu and Bo Zhou wrote this 2025 paper in graph theory, the study of networks made of points and links. They look at connected graphs and one measure of their shape, the girth. Girth is the length of the shortest loop in the graph. They also study the graph's Laplacian eigenvalues, a set of numbers that capture much of its structure.

The authors count how many of those numbers fall inside a set range tied to the girth. For graphs with girth at least four, they prove the count stays at or below a bound set by the graph's size minus its girth. They also pin down which graphs reach the bound in the first two cases. A last part settles the same question for graphs of girth three.
arxiv-2506-01921:
