Minghao Liu and four co-authors build a benchmark for editing medical images by text instruction. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Text-guided editing thrives on natural images but lags in medicine. Clinical uses beckon: surgical planning, teaching, and patient communication. No standard test has graded such editors. Reliability in a clinic demands hard evidence.

Their MedEBench holds over a thousand curated image-prompt pairs. Seventy editing tasks span thirteen anatomical regions. Grading covers editing accuracy, context preservation, and visual quality. Each case carries a written intent and a region mask. Seven leading models are compared on the set. The benchmark exposes where medical editors still fail.
arxiv-2506-04221:
Tai-Hsuan Yang, Bowen Shi, and Jong Yeon Lee propose axioms for topological phases in open quantum systems, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. For closed systems, such phases are classed by ground states of gapped Hamiltonians. Open systems, which leak to their surroundings, lacked a base set of principles.

Their three axioms cover local recoverability, no long-range correlations, and spatial uniformity. States that meet them act as fixed points, and coarse-graining turns each into a full phase. Rich topological data emerge from the axioms and stay robust when they are relaxed. Each state supports logical memories with distinct responses to operations. Large simulations showed weakly decohered states meet the axioms after coarse-graining. The work starts a classification program.
arxiv-2506-04321:
Dominik Hahn, Ryan Sweke, Abhinav Deshpande, and Oles Shtanko give efficient quantum Gibbs sampling with local circuits in two thousand twenty-five. Thermal states of quantum systems are a central open challenge. Provably fast thermal prep came only of late, via crafted dissipative processes. Those methods lean on pricey block encoding steps.

Their route runs the same spirit with dense local circuits alone. Spatial truncation and Trotter steps mimic the exact dissipative process. Proofs show the swaps barely dent fast mixing at high heat. Error to the true thermal state stays small and bounded. Simulations hint near term hardware can run it.
arxiv-2506-04521:
Di Wu, Seth Aycock, and Christof Monz test whether human-style reasoning helps machine translation in a 2025 computing paper. A popular recipe asks language models to translate step by step, drafting and refining like a person. That recipe topped a recent world contest. The authors doubt the steps themselves deserve the credit, and they run two simple experiments to check.

Asking the model to simply translate again and polish its own output beat the step-by-step recipe. Following the steps faithfully helped in some ways and hurt in others. The gains, they argue, come from the extra pass, not from copying human habits. The result warns builders not to assume that what helps people helps models too.
arxiv-2506-04821:
Zhen Hao Wong leads a team training language models on logic puzzles to reason better elsewhere. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Models shine on practiced tasks yet wobble on fresh structured problems. Ordinary fine-tuning teaches narrow habits, not general thinking. The team's play-to-learn setup uses seven custom puzzles. Each puzzle targets a distinct skill, like constraint tracking or symbolic deduction.

Reinforcement learning grades each attempt with a simple right-or-wrong reward. Models learn to test hypotheses and revise them. Out-of-distribution performance rises notably after training. The skills transfer beyond the puzzles themselves. Logic training thus builds sturdier general reasoning. The work argues for practice grounds, not just bigger datasets.
arxiv-2506-05321:
Maxwell Xu and a large team trained a foundation model on messy wearable sensor data in a 2025 paper. Wrist and body sensors promise health insight, but real recordings are full of gaps from charging, removal, and glitches, and self-supervised models usually demand complete inputs. Their second-generation large sensor model learns directly from incomplete streams, with no need to fill gaps first.

A masking scheme uses learnable tokens to represent both gaps already present and gaps added on purpose during training, teaching the model to reason around missing pieces. Pretraining covered tens of millions of hours of day-long, multi-sensor recordings. Across varied downstream tasks the model performed best among rivals, per the authors.
arxiv-2506-07921:
Ariel Caticha and Hassaan Saleem present a 2025 physics paper on relational quantum mechanics. In this view, the state of a system is not absolute but depends on relations to other systems. The authors rebuild that idea inside entropic dynamics, a framework that derives motion from probability, entropy, and information geometry.

Their models keep some fixed structure, such as a shared time slicing and flat space geometry. Within that limit, particle positions stay definite, as in classical physics. The team defines a new measure of mismatch between successive states, tuned to the geometry of quantum phase space. They show the models treat time relationally and can be made neutral under shifts and rotations in space.
arxiv-2506-09721:
Guglielmo Padula and Gianluigi Rozza use generative models to shrink the parameter lists that slow down fast solvers for partial differential equations. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. When a domain's shape is set by many parameters, solvers that map parameters to solutions lose accuracy. Each added knob makes the map harder to learn.

Their fix grows fresh geometries from a generative model, which needs fewer knobs by design. Solvers trained on those shapes inherit the smaller parameter space. One solver type learns straight from data, the other bakes physics into a network. For the data-driven one, accuracy rose with the trimmed space. For the physics one, they give a method that speeds convergence too. A test case bends the famous Stanford bunny shape. The work suits design loops that sweep many shapes.
arxiv-2506-09821:
Avni, Kumar, and Dagan tracked heavy particles in a swirling vortex for this paper from twenty twenty-five. Their vortex is a rotating cylinder flow, a stand-in for ocean eddies. Particles were followed one by one in simulations. Five forces acted on them: drag, buoyancy, virtual mass, Coriolis, and rotational lift.

Whether particles gathered or escaped hinged on both their inertia and the flow settings. Rotational lift, often ignored for round particles, took over at middling particle response times. It set up slow vertical bobbing in position and spin. Steady orbits appeared, split, or vanished as conditions shifted. The authors say the model can inform marine transport and industrial mixing.
arxiv-2506-11021:
Chaitanya Ravuri and Saman Amarasinghe wrapped code models in a checker in a 2025 paper to cut hallucinated bugs. Coding models solve many tasks now, yet they still slip in subtle flaws that make their code unsafe to run alone. A guard that knows when to hold back is the missing piece.

Their wrapper draws many candidate programs and runs each on a test suite the system writes itself. Programs that act the same on all tests form a cluster, and the biggest cluster's share serves as an exact confidence score. One threshold then trades how often the tool answers against how often it is right. The wrapper needs no view inside the model.
arxiv-2506-11221:
Weibing Zheng and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on grading medical students. Students practice talking with patients through chat-based simulations. Grading those talks by hand is slow, and human judgment is soft and graded, not black and white.

The team tuned a language model to grade student lines using fuzzy logic. Fuzzy logic scores traits by degree, not by a hard pass or fail. Human raters scored talks on four traits: being professional, staying on topic, acting with care for ethics, and drifting off task. The tuned model matched those scores with over eighty percent accuracy. On main traits, it topped ninety percent. The authors say fuzzy scoring helps machines grade more like doctors do.
arxiv-2506-11721:
Dillon Chen, a solo author, proves a limit on a learning method used for planning tasks, in a paper from 2025. The method uses relational graph neural networks to learn value scores that carry over to new problems in the same domain. Its design was motivated by a known link between such networks and a logic with two variables and counting.

Some planning domains have best value scores that can be built from features of that logic. Past tests suggested the networks could learn such scores. Chen shows that, in fact, they cannot. The proof also points to older network designs that may learn these value scores better. The result helps match network choice to the structure of a planning problem.
arxiv-2506-11821:
Martina Paccini, Simone Cammarasana, and Giuseppe Patané build a digital twin of the human muscle and bone system. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, aims at personal care for disorders of movement. Such disorders are a top cause of disability worldwide. A digital twin is a live computer copy of one patient's body mechanics.

Their frame merges motion capture, ultrasound, muscle signals, and scans. It extracts spine motion, posture, and muscle action in fine detail. A visual platform lets doctors explore the measures and track change over time. Tests show the twin pulls precise motion and tissue traits from the data. The tool may sharpen diagnosis and rehab plans per patient.
arxiv-2506-12921:
Sukrit Chakraborty, Prasanta Choudhury, and Arindam Mukherjee extend shortest path ideas from graphs to richer shapes built from triangles and higher blocks, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such block sets can model tangled systems better than plain graphs. The team first gives clear meanings for a weighted block set and for a path through it.

Search methods for plain graphs are adapted to the new setting. Two new methods then find the shortest path, modeled on the classic Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford graph methods. Uses in shared computing and neural nets built on blocks are noted. Readers get a base step for bringing graph tools to higher shapes.
arxiv-2506-13821:
Giovanni Bernardi, Adrian Francalanza, Marco Peressotti, and Mohammad Reza Mousavi published this chapter in 2025. Under its head title, Software is infrastructure, it makes the case for formal verification of programs. Software now underpins banking, transport, health, and power, and its failures carry staggering price tags.

The authors recall major software disasters of the past forty years, from lost spacecraft to trading glitches, tallying their human and financial costs. Against those numbers, they argue, the price of mathematically proving programs correct looks small. Program analysis, checking code against precise specifications, is their favored branch of the formal methods family. They support the pitch with industrial success stories where verification caught errors testing missed. The chapter addresses students and practitioners alike: it maps software's social role, prices its failures, and presents verification as a mature, underused answer rather than a curiosity.
arxiv-2506-14521:
Korbinian Pfab and Marcel Rothering ask whether current AI research methods can deliver working factory tools, in a case study paper from 2025. Their test case is false call reduction for automated optical inspection, where good parts get flagged as faulty. The authors review peer work in that area and probe its weak spots.

They name seven flaws common in past studies and show what each flaw costs in practice. Run by the standard playbook, the project would fail on this use case. Among their fixes are metrics tied to business goals, clear success bars set in advance, and close study of how data shift over time. The paper urges applied AI teams to audit their methods before trusting results.
arxiv-2506-14821:
Vision-language models answer questions about images, but fine detail escapes them, and big models are costly to run. Sunil Kumar and co-authors teach smaller models to call a zoom tool in this 2025 paper, using reinforcement learning tuned for groups of attempts.

The winning recipe pairs that learning with a simple reward, an easy tool interface, extra room to read the zoomed result, and training data loaded with hard visual cases. The tool-using models beat similar-sized rivals on some question-answering tests. The work shows that smart tool habits can partly replace raw model size when compute is tight.
arxiv-2506-15621:
Samuel Bronstein, in a solo paper from twenty twenty-five, proved a sharp inequality on a wide class of curved spaces. The work deals with a kind of rearrangement of functions on spaces with a curvature bound. That move obeys a Pólya-Szegő type rule, where spread can only fall. He uses it to prove a Moser-Trudinger type inequality on many metric measure spaces that meet a set curve and size bound.

As a fruit of that proof, he sorts which smooth spaces with Ricci curvature bounded below admit such an inequality. The sort is a full characterization, not a one way test. Readers in geometry get a bridge from curved space bounds to a classic sharp bound.
arxiv-2506-15921:
Andy To and a team of co-authors tracked a rise in plasma speed before solar flares start. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, used a space telescope that reads light from the Sun. They built a catalog of one thousand four hundred forty-nine flares from twenty eleven to twenty twenty-four. That large set let them study the phase before a flare across flare sizes. They read speeds at the foot points of flare loops from the width of light lines.

They fit the pre flare speeds with bent line fits across many hot lines. The rise came in a steady, shared pattern before onset. Readers who forecast solar storms get an early sign that a flare is near. That sign may help warn of space weather that can harm satellites.
arxiv-2506-16421:
Jan Skvrna and Lukas Neumann present the winning solution to the S23DR Challenge in two thousand twenty-five. The task: predict a house roof wireframe in 3D. Inputs are a sparse point cloud plus semantic segmentations. Their method works direct in 3D space throughout.

Vertex candidates come from the point cloud via Gestalt segments. A PointNet style model refines and classifies those candidates in local cubes. A second model predicts edges from cylinders between vertex pairs. The two stage deep approach topped the private leaderboard. Its hybrid structure score led the field for the year.
arxiv-2506-16821:
Can Lin and co-authors present a method from two thousand twenty-five that helps soccer robots find the ball without hand-labeled training data. Humanoid robots in outdoor RoboCup matches must spot the ball fast and reliably under changing light and motion. Hand-labeling thousands of images is slow and costly, which limits supervised training.

Their framework starts from a pretrained model that writes rough pseudo-labels on its own. Practice tasks such as colorizing images, finding edges, and matching triplets then teach strong visual features. A meta-learning step helps the detector adapt quickly to new fields with little extra supervision. The team released a dataset of ten thousand labeled outdoor match images. Their pipeline beat baseline models on accuracy and overlap measures.
arxiv-2506-17521:
Shrinking a computation graph while keeping its math is a core task in automatic differentiation. Matthias Bentert and co-authors settle the difficulty of two versions of that task. One asks for the cheapest way to build a Jacobian by vertex removal. The other asks for the smallest graph overall. Both are proven NP-complete, closing long-open questions. Their proof for the first problem makes no assumptions about links between the local derivatives.

The team also gives exact algorithms whose running time is close to best possible under a standard hypothesis. A cleanup rule removes twin vertices back to back safely. Hardness results tell tool builders to aim for good-enough answers, not perfect ones.
arxiv-2506-19321:
Seung Yeon Cho and co-workers derived two-phase fluid math rules from a kinetic gas model in a 2025 paper. Mixtures of two gases, each with its own heat capacity actions, need math rules for compressible two-phase flow in engines and pipelines. Their BGK-type model relaxes the mixture toward equilibrium through a function chosen by entropy minimization under moment constraints, a principled way to bake thermodynamics into the kinetics.

A formal expansion recovers the two-phase Euler math rules plus Navier-Stokes-like dissipation. The relative entropy method then makes the inviscid limit rigorous, with quantitative convergence rates under regularity assumptions. Number-based tests with an implicit-explicit scheme confirm the model preserves the asymptotic limit, sliding from kinetic to fluid actions as resolution demands.
arxiv-2506-19821:
Victor Blanco, Alfredo Marin, and Justo Puerto tackle matrix seriation with exact methods in place of rough rules. Seriation swaps the rows and columns of a matrix to reveal hidden structure. It is a core tool to view linked data. Its uses span clustering and the search for odd cases. Old methods rest on rough rules and give no pledge of the best result.

The team builds one frame based on math-based search for the best result. Their models state seriation goals and limits with high fidelity. They bring in models for stress based on near rows, in both curved and straight forms. For set patterns of near rows, they give a new form based on a Hamiltonian path. Tests on fake and real data show the forms lift result quality.
arxiv-2506-19921:
Michael Brown and co-authors read carbon dioxide ice on eight mid-sized moons of Saturn with the Webb telescope, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Solid carbon dioxide should not last at those heats unless trapped in a host. The moons share sunlight but differ in ice, organics, and birth place, which makes a clean test set.

The main band showed on every moon, and a second band on all but two faces. Band shifts split the trapped gas into four types. Inner moons hold gas in fresh ring ice and in dark stuff, while outer moons show gas made from burnt organics and gas held in water ice. Lab work is still needed, the team notes.
arxiv-2506-20621:
Alonso, Santos Alves, Romao, Lopes, and Kalinowski present Define-ML, a method for planning machine learning products in twenty twenty-five. Machine learning systems depend heavily on data and uncertain behaviour. Standard planning methods like Lean Inception ignore those concerns. That gap can produce unrealistic product visions.

Define-ML adds three activities to the Lean Inception workshop format. Teams map data sources, link features to those sources, and map learning tasks. It was tested on a toy problem and in a real industrial case. Participants said it clarified data issues and aligned goals with feasibility. Everyone surveyed intended to adopt the approach. A learning curve was noted, eased by expert facilitation. The method is openly available for other teams.
arxiv-2506-20921:
Tong Zeng and four co-authors let a team of AI agents optimize a chemical plant on paper, in a 2025 study. Tuning a process means balancing cost, yield, and safety limits, but the limits are often unwritten, which stalls conventional solvers that demand exact bounds. Their framework starts from a plain description instead.

Specialized agents, all powered by a strong reasoning model, split the labor: one drafts operating constraints, another validates settings, others run simulations and steer the search. Tested on a standard industrial process, the system matched conventional optimization on cost and yield while running thirty-one times faster than grid search, finishing in under twenty minutes. Its reasoning even surfaced sensible trade-offs, such as where utility costs bite. The work suggests language models can supply the judgment solvers lack.
arxiv-2506-21221:
Florian Bertrand, Martin Kolář, and Francine Meylan add new examples, in a 2025 preprint, to a problem about how much local data fixes a mapping. The setting is CR geometry, which studies certain surfaces inside complex spaces. A key question asks when a map between two surfaces is fully set by its first few derivatives at one point. That data is called its jet. Recent results cover maps between smooth, weakly curved hypersurfaces. The authors distill a general problem from those findings and show it on examples.

They then build a fresh case that falls outside the neat setting. It is a real surface of codimension seven inside ten-dimensional complex space. The surface is not strictly pseudoconvex. Still, any symmetry map of it is fixed by its 2-jet at a given point. Such examples test where jet determination holds and where it breaks.
arxiv-2506-22921:
Xulong Yuan's 2025 paper sharpens a test for telling apart two impostors in future gravitational wave data. When pairs of massive black holes spiral together, their signals can be bent by nearby matter, such as a spike of dark matter dragging on the orbit. Modified gravity theories can bend the same signals in similar ways. Mistaking one for the other would corrupt both astrophysics and fundamental physics.

Yuan works with a statistic that measures how scattered the inferred parameters are across many events. An earlier study used it against one pair of rival effects. This paper extends the contest to three effects that enter at the same order: dark matter drag, an extra dimension of space, and a slowly varying gravitational constant. It also sets the decision threshold more carefully and tests different source populations. The verdict: the effects remain separable, but by less than before, so thresholds matter.
arxiv-2506-23021:
Fontes and Szafron hone the tail end of muon loss in bound flight paths. New tests will hunt muon flips with sharp reach not seen yet. Sharp tests need sharp sums for both the hunt and its noise. The sole hard noise is muon loss in path, near its tail end. High-grade sums for bound states have long fought clean rank. The pair built a field frame to rank such sums in past work.

That frame served muon flips first, in the prior text. Here it stretches to the loss tail, a more hard case. The end state holds a ghost pair, which adds new terms. Their sum is the most sharp read of that noise yet. It hits next-tier log-prime grade for light-charge fix terms.
arxiv-2506-23921:
Germans Savcisens and Tina Eliassi-Rad probe what language models really encode about truth in a 2025 paper. People speak as if these models know facts, but their knowledge is a trained probability pattern. Tests that probe internal signals for truth have rested on shaky assumptions.

The authors name three flaws in common probing and build a sturdier tool. Their framework sorts statements into true, false, or neither by reading internal representations. Tests spanned sixteen open models and three fresh data sets. Simple probes often failed to transfer and sometimes lost to plain prompting. Truth and falsehood also proved asymmetric inside the models. A third signal, distinct from both, showed up as well, hinting that neither is a real category models track.
arxiv-2507-00021: Villa-Morales and Ramírez-Aranda apply fractional calculus, a form of maths that allows steps between whole derivatives, to the classic theory of column buckling in twenty twenty-five. They swap a fractional measure of curve into Euler's buckling equation and solve the result. For some values of the fractional setting, a critical buckling force still exists, as in the classic theory. They also give a numerical method to estimate that force accurately.
arxiv-2507-00121:
Coloretti, Crivellin, and Iguro hunt pair produced charged Higgs bosons through double Higgs searches in twenty twenty-five. A bump in top quark decays hints at a charged Higgs near one hundred thirty giga electron volts. Flavor data point the same way. A two doublet model with loose flavor rules fits the hints.

Such a model predicts a fat rate of charged pairs at the Large Hadron Collider. Recast double Higgs searches can test the space, though yield per event runs low. The team finds most of the sweet spot reachable with current or next run data. A dedicated search could land a discovery, they argue.
arxiv-2507-01021:
Kumarmanas Nethil, Vaibhav Mishra, Kriti Anandan, and Kavya Manohar present an open-source framework for command-style dictation, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Courtrooms need dictation that is responsive, unlike slow batch processing. Online systems, meanwhile, are resource-intensive. Their framework aims to close that gap while running fully offline.

Voice activity detection first segments incoming audio into speech pieces. Whisper models then transcribe those segments in parallel. The design also works with most other speech recognition architectures, including CTC-based models. Parallel multiplexing raises compute utilization as more users dictate at once. The system is deployed in a notable share of India's courtrooms, around fifteen percent by the authors' account. Live evaluations showed latency falling as user concurrency increased.
arxiv-2507-01421:
Jeremy Mould and Bhashin Thakore present a study from twenty twenty-five on primordial black holes as a slice of the dark matter in the Coma galaxy cluster. If a tenth of a percent of the cluster's dark matter were such holes in a set mass range, their slow boil off could make the GeV glow seen from the cluster. Light holes glow at high energy, which fits the band.

They then test if the haze of unresolved gamma rays across the sky holds the same mark. Cross checks with weak lensing maps from a sky survey span twelve years of space data. The signal found fits known bright sources, like blazars. A hole based share would need an unreal count of holes.
arxiv-2507-02221:
Steven Song and co-authors introduce GDC Cohort Copilot, an AI assistant that builds patient cohorts from the Genomic Data Commons from plain-language requests. The commons holds harmonized cancer genomics data organized around cohorts. Its graphical builder is powerful, but new users struggle to find the right descriptors among hundreds of fields. Many can describe the cohort they want in words far more easily.

The copilot turns a free-text description into the exact filter the commons needs, then exports the cohort back for analysis. An interactive interface lets users refine the result. The team develops and tests several large language models for the job. Their locally served open-source model beats GPT-4o prompting at generating correct cohorts. The tool ships as a containerized app on a public hub, with model weights and source code openly shared.
arxiv-2507-02321:
Nina Konovalova, Maxim Nikolaev, Andrey Kuznetsov, and Aibek Alanov tighten spatial control over AI image generation in a 2025 paper. Tools like ControlNet let users guide pictures with edge maps or depth maps. A refined version checks the match only at the final steps of generation, leaving early steps unguided.

Their strategy, InnerControl, trains small probe networks to read the control signal back out of the model's middle layers at every step. Even from very noisy drafts, the probes recover the guides well enough to score alignment. Training then pushes every step toward the target, not just the last. Paired with the refined baseline, the method sets new marks across control types while also lifting image quality.
arxiv-2507-03821:
Maria Gabriela Damaceno and four co-authors test optical computing with light in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Demand for fast, real-time data work in neural networks and control systems drives the search for options beyond electronics. Their scheme encodes data in the wavefront of light, shaped by spatial light modulators.

They first built an optical XOR logic gate that works on binary matrices. By testing matrices up to three hundred by three hundred elements, they measured error rates and bit depth limits. They also showed image encryption and decryption with a one-time pad on large matrices. The results support work toward a high-dimensional matrix optical processor. Redundancy in the data played a role in keeping errors down.
arxiv-2507-04021:
Niklas Vaara, Pekka Sangi, Miguel Bordallo Lopez, and Janne Heikkila describe a new radio signal simulator in a 2025 paper. The tool uses ray tracing, which follows radio waves as they bounce through a space. Instead of a hand built model, their tool works straight from point clouds that map real rooms.

The simulator is fast and can be adjusted by learning, since its calculations can be tuned by a computer. In two indoor tests, it traced paths with up to five bounces in less than ninety milliseconds each. The team also shows how labels that mark walls, floors, and objects can help the tool learn the radio traits of each material.
arxiv-2507-05321:
Kwangsuk Park and Jiwoong Yang grade programming homework with a committee of AI agents instead of one, in a 2025 paper. Vision-language models stumble on code assignments that mix runnable parts with graded criteria. Their system, AGACCI, splits the judging into specialized roles that share the work. Each agent checks the work against stated rubric points and drafts feedback.

The test set held 360 graduate assignments from sixty students, each scored by human experts. The committee beat a single strong model on rubric accuracy and on the relevance, consistency, and coherence of its comments. Results varied by task type. The authors argue multi-agent grading can scale expert-like assessment without flattening its depth.
arxiv-2507-05421:
Harrison Green, Claire Le Goues, and Fraser Brown teach fuzzers to resize test files without wrecking them, in a 2025 paper. Fuzzers find bugs by mutating inputs and watching which paths a program takes. Many file formats carry length fields, and a naive mutation that changes data but not its declared length creates garbage the program rejects at the door. Their technique, FrameShift, detects those relation fields and keeps lengths consistent during mutation.

The method is light, needs no extra instrumentation, and was built into two leading fuzzers. Over twelve CPU-years of testing, it improved bug-finding performance. Fuzzing is a workhorse of software security, so removing a whole class of wasted mutations raises the yield of every campaign.
arxiv-2507-05521:
Chun-Khiang Chua (2025) studies how heavy mesons decay into exotic four-quark states. The LHCb experiment recently observed several open-charmed tetraquarks, particles whose makeup cannot be a simple quark pair. Chua asks which decays of B and Bc mesons could produce them. The approach is topological: each decay is broken into a set of standard diagram shapes, and the unknowns are fitted once and reused. Strong decays of the tetraquarks into ordinary particles are decomposed the same way first.

Weak decays are then built from the same pieces. The method covers anti-B decays with a D meson plus a tetraquark, and Bc decays into two tetraquarks. With the amplitudes in hand, Chua highlights the decay modes whose flavor pattern can only come from an exotic state. Those modes give experimenters clean places to confirm the tetraquarks' nature. The paper is a roadmap for searches at flavor factories.
arxiv-2507-05621:
Six researchers wrote a computer vision paper in two thousand twenty-five on making images for narrow, expert fields. General image models often miss fine points of meaning in such fields and can invent wrong details. The authors call that failure mode hallucination, and they set out to cut it down with a system named AdaptaGen.

The system joins two steps that older work kept apart: shaping the text prompt and adapting the model. It sorts meaning from both a broad and a fine view, using a matrix-based method. A cross-modal step helps the model keep the core subject of a field while it builds the picture.
arxiv-2507-05821:
Dobson, Hujdurović, Imrich, and Ortner studied distinguishing sets in cubic graphs of given girth in twenty twenty-five. A distinguishing set is a set of vertices that only the identity symmetry preserves; its smallest size is the distinguishing cost. Girth is the length of the shortest cycle in the graph.

Vertex-transitive cubic graphs, highly symmetric networks where each vertex has three edges, are partly understood. Costs are known for some families, but graphs of larger girth with two edge orbits were mostly open. The authors prove such graphs of girth five have distinguishing cost two. They also prove no infinite cubic graph can be 3-arc-transitive with girth six. These results narrow a long-standing classification effort in algebraic graph theory.
arxiv-2507-06221:
Yuxuan Lu, Yifan Wu, Jason Hartline, and Michael Curry work on honest forecasting when the forecast is written in words. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Scoring rules reward numeric forecasts so that telling the truth pays best. Newer work maps text forecasts onto those numeric rules. Yet a rule can be honest and still clash with what people judge as good text.

The team designs an Aligned Scoring rule for text. It starts from a proper scoring rule, then bends it toward a reference score such as human judgment. The bend is chosen to cut the squared gap between the two. Tests show better fit with human taste than earlier methods. Honesty is kept while the fit improves. The work matters as language models report beliefs in prose.
arxiv-2507-06721:
Avi Kadria and Liam Roditty wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives faster ways to build distance oracles, compact stores that answer near-true distances in a graph within a set stretch.

The classic store of Thorup and Zwick takes a set space and gives distances off by at most a set factor. Past builds took quadratic time in the worst case. The authors give three builds with the same space but much less time. One is the first truly subquadratic build for a wide range of the stretch knob. The others run near the edge count on many graphs, with first linear-time builds for some stretch values. A third serves very large knob values.
arxiv-2507-07621:
Junyu Luo and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on moving graph learning from a labeled domain to an unlabeled one where the data has shifted. Graphs from a new setting rarely match the old, and models trained on the old one stumble. Worse, real drivers of the labels are tangled with domain-specific noise, and blunt alignment of the two domains smears both. The team built a method that untangles them first.

Their method, named SLOGAN, draws a sparse causal map and keeps only the stable features that drive the labels. A bottleneck rule squeezes out spurious links tied to one domain. A generative step recombines features across domains to break leftover false couplings. A calibration step adapts to label noise so errors do not snowball. On real data sets, it beat past baselines clearly.
arxiv-2507-10021:
Liu, Li, Zhang, and Xiao present a paper from twenty twenty-five on solving gas flow under outside force across scales. Such flows shift from smooth to thin and sparse along the force direction. Solvers must stay exact and fast in both regimes, a long-standing hard task. Their method blends a spectral way to capture off-balance particle spreads with a multi-scale flow model. Special grid points and weights suit the spectral step. The blend links the computing method tightly to the physical model.

The new solver runs up to fifty times faster than the classic method at like accuracy. It keeps key balance traits of forced gas systems intact. Tests span shock tubes, heat flow, and channel flow cases. The authors see wide engineering use for the method.
arxiv-2507-10321:
Viktor Sinitsyn, Nils Schlautmann, Florian Schwaiger, and Florian Holzapfel wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It streamlines how flight software for large drones is built, from one shared source of interface facts to code made by machine.

New aerospace firms face an old pain: the digital links between onboard boxes must be described clearly, or the parts will not mesh. Hand work here is slow and error prone. The team's process keeps one consistent account of each interface, then automates the steps from that account to working code. Design assurance rules are kept in view throughout. The chain has already served in several finished projects. The gain is less drudge work and fewer mismatched links.
arxiv-2507-12021:
Aleix Alcacer and Irene Epifanio add fairness limits to archetypal analysis, a method that sums data as mixes of extreme patterns. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes a risk: the learned mix can smuggle in sensitive group traits. Their FairAA form adds a penalty that shrinks group signal in the projections. A kernel variant, FairKernelAA, handles curved data spreads.

Tests run on synthetic sets with linear, curved, and multi-group layouts. Group separability falls under both new methods, by gap and by classifier gauges. Explained variance barely moves, so the archetypes stay faithful. A real body-measure set from ANSUR confirms the trade in practice. The authors pitch fair archetypes for sensitive uses where plain summaries could encode bias.
arxiv-2507-13821:
Jacob Antony and co-authors share short notes on oriented line graphs and their matrices in two thousand twenty-five. An oriented line graph turns the edges of a graph into nodes and gives each a direction. It ties closely to a matrix that tracks walks which never double back.

For regular graphs, the spectrum of that graph links to the poles of a known counting function, the Ihara zeta function. The authors work out the full characteristic polynomial of a broad family of matrices built on the oriented line graph. The family covers both the plain adjacency case and a Hermitian version. They also show a use in star coloring, a way to color graphs so that no two-color path of length three appears.
arxiv-2507-13921:
Jenny Frediani and a large international team report what the James Webb Space Telescope found in the planet-forming disk of a young star being blasted by its giant neighbors. The disk orbits an F-type star in a massive cluster, where ultraviolet light from outside is about a thousand times stronger than near the Sun. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team analyzed mid-infrared spectra and fitted simple slab models to the molecular fingerprints. Stellar properties came from a ground-based optical spectrum matched against model atmospheres.

Carbon dioxide gas glows brightly: four rare variants of the molecule were detected together for the first time in such a disk, tracing cool gas. Carbon monoxide is faint and water is strikingly scarce, capped at a low total amount. The dry, carbon-rich inner zone challenges expectations for how terrestrial planets assemble under harsh external light.
arxiv-2507-14621:
Oguzhan Akgun, Alain Pirotte, Giovanni Urga, and Zhenlin Yang build forecast tests for panel data in this two thousand twenty-five econometrics paper. Staff ask if forecast methods do as well in each cluster of countries or firms. A catch comes when the clusters are worked out from data. Here a panel k-means method does that work. Standard tests miss that step, and so can mislead. The team takes a selective conditional inference frame to treat the step.

First they set out a Wald-type test for pairwise equality of forecast skill, and show its conditional limit spread is a truncated chi variable, with the cut set by quadratic inequalities. For the clustered claim, they join p-values from pairwise and overall tests. Computer runs showed good size control and power. A use on exchange-rate forecasts shows the worth, setting time-series models off against machine learning methods.
arxiv-2507-15021:
Soheil Radfar and co-authors build a flood model in a 2025 paper on coastal risk. Compound floods strike when surge, tide, rain, and river flow arrive together, overwhelming coasts. Full physics models are accurate but slow, while plain learning models are fast but can break physics in extremes.

Their model, ALPINE, bakes the full shallow-water equations, Newton's laws in fluid form, into a neural network. A layered design reads space patterns and tracks time, trained with a loss that balances data fit and physics fit. Six past storms trained and tested the system, one held back unseen. Errors fell and skill rose against plain networks, above all at peak storm intensity. The authors aim at forecasts fast enough for real decisions.
arxiv-2507-15521:
Robertson and Wolff test whether language models use internal world models for mechanical reasoning in twenty twenty-five. They adapt methods from human mental model research to pulley problems. Diagrams of pulley systems were rendered for the models to judge. The first study asked models to estimate mechanical advantage.

Top models scored just above chance, and their estimates tracked true values. Estimates also tracked the number of pulleys, suggesting a counting shortcut. In a second study, models could tell a working system from a jumbled fake one. In a third, they failed to tell a working system from one that transfers no force. Performance there was at chance level. The authors conclude model world models are brittle for fine structure.
arxiv-2507-15921:
Stefano Souza and co-authors study a broadened turn-off in the color charts of star clusters. The turn-off is where stars leave the main sequence as they age. In young and mid-age clusters it spreads wide, a trait with no agreed cause. Past work focused on heavy clusters, so this team turns to light ones in the Magellanic Clouds.

Widths were read as age spreads by a standard method and checked against space telescope data. The trait shows in low-mass clusters too, on the known age and mass trends. The lightest cluster in the set shows no such spread. That fact backs a link with how fast stars can escape the cluster. Ground and space reads agreed, which validates the survey method.
arxiv-2507-17121:
Faisal Ahmed tackles uneven class sizes in grading diabetic eye disease, in this 2025 paper. The disease can blind if missed, and automated grading of eye photos can catch it early. Training data, though, hold far more mild cases than severe ones, which skews learning.

Ahmed pairs image augmentation with transfer learning from pre-trained networks. Several network families were tested on a public 2019 data set. The best model scored near ninety-nine percent on the simple sick-or-not task and about eighty-five percent on the harder five-level grading. Two compact networks gave the best balance of accuracy and speed, a useful trait for screening clinics.
arxiv-2507-18121:
Diksha Bansal and Bibekananda Maji extend a classic proof about the Riemann zeta function to the wider world of number fields, in a 2025 paper. In 1914, Hardy used a relation between two theta functions to show that the zeta function has endless zeros on its critical line. The authors ask whether the same trick works for the Dedekind zeta function, which belongs to a general number field.

They first prove a number field version of the theta relation. With it, they show the Dedekind zeta function also has endless non-trivial zeros sitting exactly on the critical line, for any number field. They also prove the theta relation is equivalent to a striking identity credited to Hardy, Littlewood, and Ramanujan.
arxiv-2507-19821:
Yanrui Yu and co-authors build a traffic video search system driven by plain language, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. City cameras pour out vast footage daily, and database-style queries are too rigid for open questions. Users can ask for targets in their own words instead.

Three parts do the work: smart sampling to find the right segments, an open-world detector for objects, and a tracker that links sightings over time. A new benchmark with rich language labels backs the tests. Scores beat the most accurate rival on key measures, and speed ran near ten times faster.
arxiv-2507-20221:
Uzzal Saha and Surya Prakash combine three deep learning networks into one system for telling harmless lung nodules from cancerous ones in CT scans. Each network first learned from general images and was then adapted to scan patches. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors add a two-stage attention step that learns how much to trust each network overall and for each class. A small final learner polishes the verdict. Training tricks include a loss focused on hard cases, blended-image augmentation, and repeated test-time views of each scan.

On a standard public lung scan data set, the combined system scored accuracy and discrimination near the top of the reported range. It cut errors well below prior best methods by their count. Sensitivity and specificity were both high and balanced, including cases where radiologists had disagreed. The authors offer the system as a screening aid for radiologists.
arxiv-2507-21221:
Rivlin, Engineer, and Baumann study a famous quantum thought test with a friend inside the lab, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. In the test, one observer measures a quantum system inside a sealed lab. A second observer treats the whole lab as a quantum system. Recent theorems use this setup to question if events are absolute.

Most past work used a toy friend made of one qubit in a perfect lab. The team adds a noisy environment and a fuller interaction model. They use a frame where many observers copy the same record from the surroundings. The friend's result grows more objective as copying spreads. Noise also hides true quantum effects and adds strict limits. A new effect that uses friend-environment links appears as well.
arxiv-2507-22721:
Davide Carazzato, Nicola Fusco, and Aldo Pratelli prove a regularity result for a class of energies in a 2025 paper. The energies mix attraction and repulsion between points on a line. Points that balance these forces are called critical points, and their behavior inside their support was in question.

Under set assumptions on how the interaction kernel grows near zero, the authors show bounded critical points are continuous. That means the balanced configurations have no jumps within the region they occupy. The result is stated for one-dimensional problems with a Riesz-type energy. Such theorems underpin models of charged particles, droplets, and other systems where long-range forces compete. The proof adds a firm piece to that theory.
arxiv-2507-23221:
Charles O'Neill and four co-authors find a single internal direction that flags made-up statements. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Contextual hallucinations claim things the given context does not support. Their trick uses a second model as an observer. One forward pass plus a linear probe does the detection. The probe reads the observer's residual stream.

A single linear direction separates false from faithful text. It transfers across generators and beats baselines clearly. The signal peaks in middle layers and holds across model sizes. Tracing it points to sparse late-layer activity. Pushing along the direction changes how often generators hallucinate. Detection thus comes with a steering knob attached. Interpretability gains a concrete, usable signal.
arxiv-2507-23321:
Feyzollah Younesizadeh and Davoud Kamani wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, though the catalog names no creator for it. It tests D-brane inflation inside a fresh modified gravity, in which the action is a set function of a scalar field and the trace of matter.

The team works through slow-roll inflation in that gravity by way of the D-brane model. They compute the scalar spectral index and the tensor-to-scalar ratio, the two gauges Planck data pins best. The model's zone covers the left-hand side of the Planck plot well. The dynamics of reheating, the hot phase after inflation ends, is also traced. The paper adds one more check of brane ideas against sky data.
arxiv-2508-00621:
Adrià Gómez-Valent and Alex González-Fuentes wrote this letter in two thousand twenty-five. It shows that a seeming peak in dark energy's density need not mean a true crossing of the phantom divide.

Sky data from Planck, a galaxy survey, and supernova sets hint that dark energy shifts with time, with a hump at a set epoch. The authors split the read into two parts: standard quintessence, plus a negative kind with negative density and positive pressure that fades toward zero. The mix makes the same hump, with no phantom cross at all. The fit beats the standard model at a strong level, on par with a known two-knob form. Odd fields may thus be at play in today's cosmos.
arxiv-2508-00821:
Gautham Varma K, Mohd Hashim Raza, and Azaz Ahmad study a nonlinear Hall effect tied to the chiral anomaly in a class of metals, in work from twenty twenty-five. The metals lack a center of symmetry and have strong spin orbit coupling. The anomaly was once tied to special semimetals, but now looks like a surface trait of these metals too.

Within a semi classical transport frame, the Hall response grows with the square of the magnetic field and stays negative. Magnetic scatter sites change the size of the signal, not its shape. A tilt in the energy bands makes the response depend on direction, with sign flips in weak and strong cases. The findings help plan lab tests for direction tuned conduction.
arxiv-2508-01921:
Conor Wallace, Isaac Corley, and Jonathan Lwowski test a unified vision-language model for factory inspection in a 2025 paper. Such models promise to handle many visual tasks through one language-driven interface, cutting the clutter of separate task models. Their model was trained on a new large inspection dataset covering classification, detection, and point location tasks.

The model competed well on whole-image classification and structured point tasks. But it fell short of classic image models on core inspection measures. It behaved brittly when prompts varied little, produced degenerate output on fine detection, and often fell back on memorized language regardless of the image. The authors doubt current models are ready for precision inspection.
arxiv-2508-03121:
The-Hai Nguyen and co-authors present a 2025 paper on merging several trained neural networks into one model without retraining. One merging method treats each layer as a regression problem and gives an exact, fast answer. That method, though, merges each layer on its own and ignores how early layers feed later ones.

Their upgrade, called RegMean++, folds both within-layer and cross-layer links into the merging goal. Tests across many settings, including new domains, step-by-step merging, large tasks, and shifted data, showed the upgrade beat the older method every time. It also held its own against other advanced merging methods while staying simple and explainable.
arxiv-2508-03221:
Jia Wu, Yu Pan, Junjun Yang, and Yi Du poison image generators cheaply by corrupting only part of the network, in a 2025 paper. Backdoor attacks plant a hidden trigger: show it, and the model produces the attacker's chosen image. Full-network poisoning is expensive and often detectable.

Their attack retrains only selected blocks of the model's core network, leaving the rest untouched. It needs thirty percent of the usual computing and a fifth of the graphics time, putting backdoors within reach of consumer hardware. Success rates stayed high, image quality barely dipped, and leading defenses, including attention-based detectors, missed it. Block-by-block tests showed some layers matter far more than others for planting the trigger. The paper is a warning that model supply chains need block-level audits.
arxiv-2508-03921:
John Kelleher, Matthew Nicholson, Rahul Agrahari, and Clare Conran test two ways to stretch small training sets, in a 2025 paper. Their task is spotting anomalies in time-series data from a new field where labeled examples are scarce. One method borrows a model trained elsewhere, and the other picks the most useful new examples to label.

The authors find that gains from picking examples are real but slower than earlier papers claimed. They credit their stricter design, which keeps the picking pool and the test pool apart. Grouping data into clusters before picking did not help; a single group worked best. Adding borrowed knowledge helped at first, then gains faded as more target examples joined training. The study tempers hype about easy wins from clever sampling.
arxiv-2508-04421:
Branko Juran proves a recognition principle that tells when an algebraic object with symmetries really comes from loops in a symmetric space. The objects are algebras over an operad built from framed disk embeddings inside a representation space. Looping a space repeatedly in that representation direction always produces such an algebra. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Juran proves the converse under one condition. Take fixed points under every subgroup where the representation still has room. If each fixed-point space is group-like, the algebra is a genuine loop space. The theorem generalizes earlier work by dropping the assumption that the representation contains a trivial direction.

The proof's engine is an equivariant approximation theorem, now established for all representations and all based symmetric spaces. Earlier proofs needed extra hypotheses. The result completes a chapter of equivariant homotopy theory.
arxiv-2508-04521:
Noufal Asharaf, Hartmut Führ, and Vaishakh Jayaprakash settle when two wavelet systems yield the same family of analysis spaces, in this 2025 mathematics paper. Coorbit spaces measure how well generalized wavelet systems can approximate signals. Knowing when different systems give the same spaces saves duplicated theory. The paper answers that question fully for continuous wavelet transforms in two dimensions.

The transforms studied come from matrix groups acting on the plane. For that whole class, the authors classify exactly which systems share their coorbit scales. The answer is presented as exhaustive, closing the two-dimensional case. Results of this kind guide the choice of wavelet systems in signal analysis, since the space, not the system, sets the approximation power.
arxiv-2508-04921:
Zixuan Feng and six co-authors offer a roadmap for open source communities facing generative AI in a 2025 paper. AI coding tools are transforming how software is written and governed, and communities without a framework risk being swamped. The authors view each community as a socio-technical system and read the change through McLuhan's tetrad, which asks what a technology enhances, obsoletes, retrieves, and reverses.

Scenario work across four arenas, software practice, documentation, community engagement, and governance, maps plausible impacts of the tools. From those scenarios the authors draw a roadmap for sustaining communities through the shift. The aim is to help leaders shape the change rather than merely react to it.
arxiv-2508-05721:
Debarshi Mukherjee and co-authors extract the pion's energy spectrum from lattice QCD simulations. The pion is the lightest hadron, and its energy at each momentum tests theory. Two-point correlation data from lattice runs hold those energies in hidden form. Plateau fits to energy-over-time curves pull the values out.

Eigenvalues across momenta then draw the pion's dispersion curve. Plotted points are checked against the shape theory predicts. Agreement marks where the lattice method can be trusted. Mismatch zones flag momentum ranges that need care. The report shows the full pipeline from raw correlations to a checked physics curve.
arxiv-2508-05921:
Rout speeds stiff math cures with a net form that keeps its shape bent and firm in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such cures oft fail not for lack of reach, but for bad tune health in the fit. Stiff and mixed-grade tasks make that ill health worst of all.

Inside, a light net type with fixed-form fits gets a wave-code gate at its mouth. The gate lifts the fit grid's rank and reach while its bent shape stays put. Reach in one test law grew by more than two size steps in the run. Fault in wave-mix drills fell by up to six size steps as well. The team says health, not depth, is the true neck in such cures.
arxiv-2508-06821:
Nonexpansive maps never stretch distances, a property that guarantees resting points useful across optimization and imaging. Anish Banerjee and co-authors widen that family in this 2025 paper with a new class judged by perimeter-style conditions rather than pairwise ones.

They show the new class is considerably larger than the classic nonexpansive and quasi-nonexpansive families. Working in normed spaces, they link periodic points to fixed points to prove existence results. The headline theorem says every map of the new kind on a closed, bounded, rounded region of a Hilbert space must have a fixed point, anchoring the class in theory.
arxiv-2508-07521:
Xiaoliang Zhang and Haechan Park compute how lattice vibrations affect a quantum bit in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The bit is an electron spin in a lutetium compound, tuned to a clock transition where it resists noise. Such bits can hold their state for a long time, which suits quantum computing.

Using first-principles methods, the team measures how vibrations change the coupling that links the spin to its nucleus. They then compute relaxation and coherence times and how they shift with temperature. Their results match the observed peak in coherence near a certain field, though the values differ from experiment. The analysis shows which vibration types matter most for each kind of loss.
arxiv-2508-08621:
Dickson polynomials are a classic family in finite field theory, valued in coding and cryptography. Wayne Peng and Yen-Ju Chen study what happens when these polynomials are applied again and again in this 2025 paper, treating the repeats as a dynamical system.

They compute the exact period of the resulting sequence, a measure of when the pattern starts over. A classic identity links their behavior to simple power maps on a larger field, which lets the authors describe the group formed when these polynomials act as permutations. They also prove partial results for the messier cases and derive several fresh identities, capped by a symmetry property.
arxiv-2508-08721:
Yuqian Zhao, Xun Chen, Zongtang Wan, Zhaohua Ma, and Yuesheng Li wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, though the catalog names no creator for it. It reports a giant magnetocaloric effect in GdZnPO, a honeycomb crystal held to be a spiral spin liquid hope.

Spin liquids swirl among many like ground states, so a field that locks them into one state dumps a flood of entropy. Near the lock-in field the crystal cools hard, past known cooling materials, and it keeps working up to a few degrees. A frustrated spin model of the lattice fits the effect. Cycled in a tight field range, the crystal could chill gear to a hair above zero.
arxiv-2508-09921:
Savyaraj Deshmukh and co-authors trace why light pulses hop between coupled tiny resonators, in work from 2025. Such resonators make frequency combs for future optical chips. In paired or tripled rings, pulses can jump back and forth in a steady loop called soliton hopping. The team treats the system with tools honed on fluid flow and turbulence.

They map the loop paths and their branch points for pairs and triples. In pairs, hopping grows from a stable pulse branch. In triples, it grows from an unstable one, which shifts the pump power needed. Branch shapes also explain why scans show jumps and mixed states at the same settings.
arxiv-2508-10321:
James Tian studies random kernels in operator theory, in work from 2025. A kernel is a tool that measures how points in a space relate, and the random form he defines must stay positive only on average, not in each draw. The paper also links these kernels to moment dilations, a way to lift operators to a larger space.

Tian proves basic traits of the new class, such as how it behaves under mixing and sampling. A split result holds under a size condition on the kernel. He then builds dilation triples for random operators that keep mixed moments true on average. The setup ties chance-based moments to unitary motion.
arxiv-2508-11721:
Zou and a large team of colleagues grade and fuse big eye-scan models in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such base models now abound for eye care, but which one wins was not clear. No one had yet tried to fuse them all into one stronger tool.

Inside, four top base models were run on shared sets from a range of lands. Tasks span eye ills like lens-age spots and body ills like high blood push read from eye scans. Two models led the pack, and one held up best on fresh out-of-bank sets. A gate-style fuse gave small gains on some eye and body tasks. Body ill calls from eye scans stayed hard on new groups.
arxiv-2508-15021:
Mark Van der Merwe and Devesh Jha apply in-context learning to dynamic manipulation in two thousand twenty-five. Big language models can learn from a few examples placed in a prompt. That skill works past text, for general patterns too. Dynamic tasks, though, have high dimension, complex motion, and partial views.

The pair take an iterative route to the problem. The model reads past tries and predicts tweaks to a policy with set knobs. Tests run both in simulation and on a real robot. In the low data range, their method beat rival methods. The work shows a path to robot skills that adapt from scant trials.
arxiv-2508-15621:
Sahu, Gupta, Schall, Maitra Bhattacharyya, and Chikkadi trace in twenty twenty-five how dense particle suspensions lose their solidity under shear, down to the local packing patterns. What makes a glassy material flow is a core physics puzzle. The team sorted particles in crystals and glasses by their local shape motifs and matched each motif to how deep a cage its neighbours form around it.

In glasses, the most symmetric twenty-faced motifs sat in the deepest cages, deeper than crystal patterns. Under shear, big clusters of near-stable motifs broke into smaller ones, driving the shift from solid-like to liquid-like behaviour. Particles escaping stable clusters had shallow cages and rearranged most easily. The authors name motif break-up as the engine of flow.
arxiv-2508-16221:
Chris Guiver and Hartmut Logemann study, in twenty twenty-five, when Lur'e systems with feedthrough have well-behaved solutions. Lur'e systems couple forced nonlinear differential equations with an algebraic equation for the output. Feedthrough means the output appears inside its own equation, so it may have no explicit formula. The authors ask basic questions: do solutions exist, can they be continued, can they blow up in finite time, are they complete going forward, and are they unique? Simple examples show that answers good enough without feedthrough can fail with it.

They give sufficient conditions for each property. The proofs use global inversion theorems from real analysis, plus tools from non-smooth analysis and differential inclusions, which handle set-valued dynamics. Examples illustrate the theory.
arxiv-2508-16721:
Guillermo Arias-Tamargo and Maxwell Velásquez Cotini Hutt analyze symmetries in a class of field theories in a 2025 paper. Their models are two-dimensional non-linear sigma models with a Wess-Zumino term. Such models map a surface into a target space, and they show up across physics. The shape of that target space decides what symmetries the theory holds.

When the target has a round symmetry with no fixed points, the theory holds a pair of group-like symmetries. Many such theories also hold non-invertible symmetries, a newer kind tied to self-duality under gauging. The authors show how the target's topology and the extra term decide whether the group-like symmetries run continuous or in steps. They chart the anomalies, the quantum flaws in those symmetries, alone and mixed. They also show the whole symmetry frame survives the gauging step.
arxiv-2508-16821:
Sam Earle and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on puzzle games as tests for smart software. Puzzle games are easy for people to grasp but can be deep and hard to master. The team built an engine that runs such games fast on graphics chips.

Their engine compiles any game written in a small design language. That language follows a popular free tool used by game makers since 2013. The team ported several hundred games from that tool into their engine. They then tested search methods, learning agents, and language models on the games. Many games that look simple proved very hard for all three kinds of software. The engine gives a broad, human-made test bed for reasoning research.
arxiv-2508-17421:
Colin Rogers and Adriana Briozzo solve moving boundary problems tied to a special nonlinear equation in a 2025 mathematics study. Stefan-type problems track a front, like melting ice, whose motion depends on the field it bounds. Their target equation is third order and modulated in time, a harder setting than the classic heat case.

A symmetry reduction through a classical Ermakov equation yields exact solutions of Airy type. The Ermakov system's nonlinear superposition principle builds new solutions from old ones. Involutory transformations then widen the solvable class. An appendix derives partner problems linked by reciprocal transformations, each exactly solvable as well.
arxiv-2508-18221:
Beibei Li builds a fast solver for magnetized plasma around black holes in a 2025 paper. General relativistic magnetohydrodynamics covers gas and magnetic fields in warped spacetime. Around spinning black holes, those equations must evolve together with Einstein's own.

The solver uses a high-order spectral method on mapped grids. That choice yields exponential accuracy as the grid grows finer. Matter and spacetime evolve inside one unified framework, fully coupled. Convergence tests confirm the spectral accuracy and that entropy stays stable. Diagrams of flow crossing the horizon check the physics against expectations. 3D views show tangled plasma structures near rotating holes. The approach targets the next supercomputers for sharper strong-gravity simulations.
arxiv-2508-18321:
Maojia Song and co-authors published a 2025 study on how language models behave under peer pressure. Such models now often work in teams, where each one sees what the others answer. Earlier work looked at simple copying of peers. This study asks broader questions about trust, rapport, and picking out good advice.

The team built a quiz-style test bed called KAIROS. In it, fake peer agents can be set to act friendly, pushy, or misleading. The setup tracks how past chats and current peer moves sway a model's answer. The authors tried plain prompting, extra training on examples, and a form of trial-and-error training. Bigger models held their ground better and gained from prompting tricks. Smaller models stayed easy to sway. Only the carefully tuned trial-and-error training made small models steadily more robust.
arxiv-2508-19221:
Isabel Cachola, Daniel Khashabi, and Mark Dredze ask whether the standard formulas for grading readability actually match human judgment, in a 2025 paper. Plain-language summarization leans on old metrics like the Flesch-Kincaid grade level. The team surveyed the field's habits, then tested eight metrics against human ratings of summary readability. Most metrics, the favorite included, correlated poorly with what people found readable.

Language models judged far better, the best reaching a solid correlation with human scores. On real summary datasets, the models also caught deeper demands like background knowledge, and they reversed some conclusions the formulas had suggested. The authors recommend new best practices for judging plain-language work, and they release their data and code.
arxiv-2508-19721:
Carlos Carvalho and eleven co-authors introduced CAMÕES in twenty twenty-five, the first open evaluation framework for speech recognition in European Portuguese. Existing resources skew heavily toward Brazilian Portuguese, leaving the European variety and others under-measured. The team assembled a benchmark of forty-six hours of European Portuguese test speech across many domains, plus a curated four hundred twenty-five hours for training.

They benchmarked foundation models in zero-shot and fine-tuned modes against E-Branchformer models trained from scratch. Fine-tuned foundation models and the from-scratch models performed comparably. The best systems cut word error rates by more than thirty-five percent relative to the strongest zero-shot model, setting a new state of the art for European Portuguese and other varieties.
arxiv-2508-21521:
Gigante, Leofante, and Micheli propose counterfactual scenarios for automated planning in twenty twenty-five. Counterfactual explanations show the smallest change that flips a model output. In planning, past work changed a plan to meet a different goal. Such explanations diagnose faults but miss high level traits of the problem.

Their scenarios instead change the planning problem itself, with minimal edits. The goal is a problem that admits plans with desired properties, stated in a temporal logic. They give two qualitative versions based on explicit quantification over plans. Complexity results cover varied allowed changes to the problem. Generating scenarios is often no costlier than computing a plan. The authors argue the framework can support practical explanation tools.
arxiv-2509-00421:
Maxime Meyer, Mario Michelessa, Caroline Chaux, and Vincent Y. F. Tan study the memory limits of prompt tuning in transformers in 2025. Prompt tuning adapts a pre-trained model by learning a short prompt of extra tokens, leaving weights frozen. Prior theory stresses universal approximation, which matches weight tuning, but says little about memory.

The team proves the information a transformer can memorize grows at most linearly with prompt length. More importantly, they give the first formal proof of a widely observed flaw: performance degrades as contexts grow long. Transformers thus have inherently limited memory for prompt-tuned facts. The bounds set realistic hopes for prompt-based adaptation at scale.
arxiv-2509-00621:
Osama Abu Hamdan, with three co-authors, Hao Che, Engin Arslan, and Md Arifuzzaman, presents FLEET, a testbed for federated learning, where many clients train a shared model without sharing private data. A gap remains between algorithm design and real performance because evaluation tools often ignore realistic network conditions.

FLEET couples a framework-agnostic learning component, usable with diverse machine learning tools, with a high-fidelity network emulator that models real topologies and background traffic. It records holistic metrics, linking training outcomes to network statistics such as bandwidth limits, latency, and packet loss. Abu Hamdan and his co-authors argue the platform lets researchers study convergence and efficiency under changing infrastructure in a reproducible way.
arxiv-2509-00821:
Yong-Xin Zhang, with two co-authors, studies photon effects in the quantum Rabi-Stark model. The model couples light and matter strongly. It includes a nonlinear Stark coupling as a key term. The team uses a quantum dressed master equation to track photons. They focus on effects that are nonclassical in nature.

They analyze correlation functions of second and higher order. The Stark coupling strongly modulates photon statistics in their results. It induces tunable antibunching and bunching of photons. Those patterns describe whether photons avoid or favor arriving together. Transition signatures in the correlations could probe quantum phase transitions. Stark coupling also controls photon squeezing directly. It can enhance squeezing or suppress it as needed.
arxiv-2509-00921:
David Dukic, with two co-authors, proposes supervised in-context fine-tuning for generative sequence labeling. Sequence labeling assigns labels to tokens in text. Named entity recognition is a classic example. Such tasks are usually tackled with encoder-only models. They seem to need bidirectional context to work well.

Generative labeling is more natural for causal language models, though. Their SIFT method casts labeling as constrained response generation. It combines in-context learning from demonstrations with supervised fine-tuning. SIFT beats both in-context learning and decoder-as-encoder baselines. Tests span a range of standard labeling tasks. Long context hinders generative labeling in both settings. Removing the instruction mitigates that deficiency, the team finds. Instructions prove largely unnecessary for strong SIFT performance.
arxiv-2509-01221:
Many open language models exist, but picking the best one to fine-tune for a specialist task is slow and costly to test directly. Wei Huang, Huang Wei, and Yinggui Wang introduce DaMoC, a framework that chooses by compressing both the data and the candidate models. Smaller stand-ins let the team judge fit before committing to full training.

On the data side, they sort filtering methods into three families and raise the density of key tokens, then rewrite text with a model's help to sharpen it. On the model side, they score each layer's importance, drop weak layers, and merge what remains sparsely to keep skill. Wide experiments back the approach. DaMoC aims to make model choice fast and grounded.
arxiv-2509-01421:
Diffusion models dominate image generation, but their quality drops when asked for sizes unlike those they trained on. Guohui Zhang, with six co-authors, traces that failure to information: different resolutions carry different amounts of it, so the conversion steps must adapt. Their framework, InfoScale, generates variable-scale images with no extra training.

The team analyzes three parts of the process. Dilated convolutions lose high-frequency detail at larger sizes, attention struggles to adjust how it gathers information, and the starting noise spreads information in a pattern misaligned with the target scale. InfoScale addresses each issue by using information more effectively across the pipeline. Zhang and the co-authors aim for one model that can produce images at many resolutions, higher or lower than training, without the usual quality penalty.
arxiv-2509-01621:
Gradient-based methods promise fast, scalable discovery of causal structure from data, but skewed data can quietly mislead them. Tim Schwabe, Moritz Lange, Laurenz Wiskott, and Maribel Acosta identify two distributional biases in the simple case of two categorical variables. One arises when the variables' entropy differs; the other when repeated interventions shift some variables faster than others.

With Dirichlet priors, the team shows both biases can appear even in controlled synthetic data. Two simple models that learn causal factorizations from marginal or conditional distributions prove susceptible to both. The authors also show how the biases can be controlled, and an empirical check of two related existing methods suggests removing competition between rival factorizations helps. The study warns causal discovery tools to audit their data before trusting their arrows.
arxiv-2509-01721:
Austin Meek, Carlos H Mendoza-Cardenas, and Austin J Brockmeier extend a tool that aligns brain wave recordings across unlike setups. Brain wave data, called EEG data, shifts with sensors, gear, and filters, which can confuse sorting tools. Their base tool reshapes signal spectra so data sets line up better. The new work offers two ways to pick the target spectrum that all signals are mapped toward.

One way averages channels into a shared center point, and the other picks the closest matching person. The filters can also bridge data sets with different channel counts. In tests, sorting of signal parts into brain and non brain groups improved a lot. Cleaner sorting helps remove artifacts in care for epilepsy and other brain conditions.
arxiv-2509-02121:
Junyi Shen, Noppanat Wadlom, and Yao Lu bring batch query optimization to agentic language model workflows. Agentic workflows chain reasoning, tools, and multiple specialist agents. Serving engines tune single calls in isolation, while agent frameworks ignore system level planning. Repeated prompts, overlapping contexts, and split hardware execution waste resources in batch analytics.

Their Halo system casts each workflow as a query plan graph and merges batched queries into one consolidated graph. A cost model weighs resource limits, prefill and decode costs, cache reuse, and placement. Plan level optimization then cuts redundant execution across the batch. Adaptive batching, cache sharing, and fine pipelining raise hardware use further. Benchmarks show large speedups without quality loss.
arxiv-2509-02321:
V. V. Vien, T. Phong Nguyen, and T. D. Tham present a 2025 particle theory paper building an extension of the Standard Model, the current best description of basic particles. Their version adds a symmetry group that shapes how neutrinos, extremely light particles, get their masses.

Mass comes through two routes, a seesaw mechanism and a Weinberg-type term. Together they force a simple relation among entries of the neutrino mass matrix. Scanning allowed settings, the authors find ranges for mass splittings, the lightest neutrino mass, and phase values that match current limits. Both normal and inverted mass orderings get predictions. The same scan estimates coupling strengths, which the authors say can explain why charged lepton and neutrino masses differ so much.
arxiv-2509-03621:
In a 2025 theoretical physics paper, Vijay Balasubramanian and four co-authors argue that purely GHZ-like entanglement cannot occur in holographic systems. Holography links a gravitational theory in a volume to a non-gravitational theory on its boundary. GHZ states, named for Greenberger, Horne, and Zeilinger, share entanglement evenly across three or more parties in one rigid pattern.

The authors derive a relation that any holographic signal of three-party entanglement must obey. Proposed geometric duals for those signals let them prove the relation with a geometry argument. Pure GHZ states violate that relation. Time-symmetric holographic states therefore cannot be purely GHZ-like. The result is presented as the first inequality restricting pure three-party entanglement structure in holography. Similar relations for four parties are also discussed, narrowing what kinds of quantum states gravity can describe.
arxiv-2509-03721:
Cédric Join and one co-author devote a 2025 research paper to avoiding unexpected obstacles without reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning teaches machines by trial and error, and a quoted remark from Yann LeCun notes it needs enormous numbers of trials for any new task. The authors ask whether advanced control theory can steer a simple vehicle around surprises far more cheaply.

Their test vehicle is the classic Dubins car, a model that moves forward at fixed speed with a limited turning radius. Two controllers are tried: a flatness-based design with a special feedback setting, and a newer model-free predictive control approach. Computer experiments look convincing for both, with the model-based version only slightly ahead. Robustness against random mismatches and disturbances is satisfactory for one method and excellent for the model-free one.
