Both approaches also carry a low computational burden, a practical advantage over heavy learning pipelines.
arxiv-2509-03821:
Nitro, a tamper-evident logging system built for high performance, occupies a 2025 research paper by Rui Zhao and three co-authors. Audit logs prove what a computer did, and tamper-evident designs make later edits detectable. Existing systems impose heavy overhead, lose data under load, detect tampering only coarsely, and demand recompiling the kernel to install.

Nitro detects log tampering at fine grain while avoiding kernel recompilation through eBPF, technology for running small vetted programs inside the kernel. A new definitional framework states what security a logging system should provide, and their cryptographic construction meets it. Cryptography is co-designed with log processing, so system-level optimisations apply across the pipeline. Evaluations show tenfold to twenty-five-fold gains under high stress, and two to ten times better performance in real-world scenarios, with near-zero data loss. A variant adds in-kernel log reduction to cut overhead further.
arxiv-2509-04221:
Leonard E C Romano and one co-author, Andreas Burkert, re-date the Local Bubble and ask what it did to nearby star birth in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The Local Bubble is a vast hollow in the gas around the Sun, blown by exploding stars. Earlier estimates gave it about fourteen million years. The authors rebuild its shape and motion from public three-dimensional dust maps, then compare with simulated supernova remnants from the SISSI project.

Their younger age, only a few million years, demands many more explosions in less time. Star clusters tallied from Gaia data could supply that rate. Most local star formation seems to have finished before the bubble formed, they conclude. Its expansion likely smothered ongoing star birth rather than triggering it.
arxiv-2509-04421:
The XRISM Collaboration maps gas motions inside the Perseus galaxy cluster with its new X-ray observatory in a 2025 research paper. Galaxy clusters are the universe's largest structures, filled with gas heated to tens of millions of degrees. Black hole feedback and mergers stir that gas, but the stirring pattern stayed largely unknown. XRISM's sharp spectral mapping covers the bright Perseus cluster across its cool core, measuring how fast gas moves at each radius.

Two distinct drivers appear. In the inner region, a small-scale driver likely comes from the central supermassive black hole, heating far more strongly than the second. In the outer core, a large-scale driver traces to mergers. Turbulence from the black hole could offset cooling losses.
arxiv-2509-04821:
Spoken language understanding must find intent and slots in speech despite scarce labelled data. Yan Xie, lead author with three co-authors, propose an adaptive feature distillation framework in a 2025 paper. The method transfers rich semantic representations from a large text embedding teacher model to a lightweight student model suited to deployment.

A dynamic adapter with a residual projection network aligns the two feature spaces. A distillation coefficient adjusts strength in real time based on intent and slot prediction feedback. On a Chinese benchmark, the system reports leading intent accuracy, slot score, and overall accuracy, addressing both data scarcity and deployment cost.
arxiv-2509-05321:
Synthetic brain signals matched to video clips are released by Yunfei Guo and three co-authors in a 2025 paper on emotion data. Brain-computer interfaces and emotion studies need paired video and EEG data, recordings of electrical activity from the scalp, which are costly to collect.

Their open framework starts from the SEED-VD collection of video stimuli and generates personalised EEG signals with a self-play graph network joined to a diffusion model. An engineering pipeline aligns each video with its signals in time. The released set holds more than a thousand samples with many-channel EEG and emotion labels. The data support video and brain alignment, data augmentation, and interface research.
arxiv-2509-05521:
Solutions that are too rough for school calculus are given a firm definition for port-Hamiltonian systems by Timo Reis in a solo 2025 systems theory paper. These systems model energy exchange through ports, with state, flows, and efforts living in spaces that may have no finite size.

Reis sets out a weak solution concept from a shape-based viewpoint. In that framework the state's derivative naturally lives in an extension space, a larger space borrowed from evolution theory. Worked examples show the new notion matches the weak solution framework used for partial differential equations. The result extends energy-based modelling to settings where strong solutions do not exist.
arxiv-2509-05621:
An unknown link strength between two quantum sites can be read from the direction of a circulating current, Vipul Upadhyay and Rahul Marathe show in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Their device echoes a Wheatstone bridge, the classic circuit that finds an unknown resistance by balancing a network.

Geometric asymmetry in a small fermionic system ties an extra energy degeneracy point to the current's circulation. When baths are tuned near that point at low temperature and bias, the circulation reverses exactly at the balance condition, revealing the unknown hopping rate. Moderate environmental noise and losses are tolerated, and quantum Fisher information analysis supports the design. The bridge keeps working at higher voltage and temperature too.
arxiv-2509-05721:
Automatic reports full of charts are produced by a team of specialised agents rather than one monolith, in a 2025 prototype paper by Péter Ferenc Gyarmati and three co-authors. Single-agent systems for visual data reporting are brittle, and the authors pursue a human-AI partnership instead.

Their hybrid design moves logic out of the language models into deterministic modules, including a rule-based system for principled chart design. Output comes in two forms: an interactive web report readers can explore, and executable notebooks that let analysts trace every step. The granular design keeps the pipeline automatic yet auditable and steerable. Code and examples are public for reproducibility.
arxiv-2509-06021:
A single quantity, the resonance density range, organizes when a laser-driven plasma instability grows unchecked, according to a 2025 paper led by C. Yao with six co-authors. The instability is absolute two-plasmon decay, where laser light splits into two plasma waves inside nonuniform plasma. The resonance density range is the density interval where the resonant modes still grow as they would in uniform plasma.

Linear fluid simulations across wide parameter ranges confirm the range marks the spatial growth region. The authors then study pulses with intensity modulations, typical of broadband lasers built to suppress such instabilities. They link the range to a threshold time gap between intensity peaks beyond which absolute growth is suppressed, giving laser designers a concrete target.
arxiv-2509-06421:
Oscillations that persist against noise pay for coherence in dissipated energy, and Ryuna Nagayama and Sosuke Ito derive the exact exchange rate in a 2025 paper. For stochastic limit cycles, rhythmic systems buffeted by noise, they prove two trade-offs in the weak-noise limit. One bounds the entropy produced per period by how many oscillations survive before correlations fade.

The second, a thermodynamic speed limit, bounds entropy production by the cycle's geometric length. Both drop out of one uncertainty relation by inserting dual observables drawn from the cycle's stability, making the two trade-offs precise duals of each other. Numerical tests on the noisy Rössler model and applications to stochastic chemical systems, including degenerate diffusion, confirm and extend the theory.
arxiv-2509-06521:
A question about groups linked to the Yang-Baxter equation is settled in part by H. Meng and two co-authors in a 2025 algebra paper. A group counts as an involutive Yang-Baxter group when it matches the permutation group of a certain well-behaved solution to that equation. Cedó and Okniński had asked whether soluble groups with mild Sylow subgroups always qualify.

The authors study finite soluble groups whose Sylow subgroups, the largest subgroups tied to one prime, have nilpotency class at most two. They prove such a group is a Yang-Baxter group when its nilpotent residual contains no copy of the quaternion group of order eight. They also prove the result when the Sylow subgroup for the prime two is exactly that quaternion group. Together the two theorems cover the cases left open by the question.
arxiv-2509-06721:
A blank patch in the sky map of fast radio bursts is traced to our own galaxy's plasma by Swarali Shivraj Patil and twenty-eight co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The team analyzed about thirty-six hundred burst sources from the CHIME telescope's second catalog. Burst positions were not spread evenly across the sky.

A roughly circular gap, centered near the galactic plane, lines up with Cygnus X, a plasma-rich star-forming region in the Milky Way. Hot gas there raises sky temperature, and turbulent ionized plasma smears burst signals until they become undetectable. Simulations suggest only a handful of bursts should have been seen in the gap given that temperature, and a lower limit on the scattering time explains the rest. Similar suppression appears along other plasma-heavy sightlines. Bursts, the authors note, can serve as probes of the galaxy's warm ionized gas.
arxiv-2509-06921:
Combining neural networks with symbolic logic for cyber defense is reviewed by Safayat Bin Hakim and four co-authors in a 2025 systematic review. Security work needs both fast pattern recognition and careful reasoning, and purely neural or purely symbolic systems each supply only one side. The review analyzes over a hundred publications on neuro-symbolic AI in cybersecurity.

A three-tier taxonomy organizes the field by how deeply learning and logic are integrated, and an analytical lens grades grounding, instructibility, and alignment. Multi-agent and structured-integration designs beat single-agent ones in complex scenarios, causal reasoning enables proactive defense, and knowledge-guided learning improves data efficiency and explainability. A dual-use analysis warns that autonomous offensive systems already achieve notable success at low cost. Barriers include weak evaluation standards and high computing costs, and a research roadmap is proposed.
arxiv-2509-07221:
Jack Heinzel and 1 co-author warn in 2025 about when Monte Carlo approximations can mislead hierarchical Bayesian inference. Hierarchical inference combines many observations into one population picture, a key task for gravitational wave astronomy, which expects thousands of new detections. The method relies on Monte Carlo sampling, random draws that stand in for exact sums, and those draws are already costly.

From first principles, the authors derive an error estimator that measures how much information the sampling approximation loses. They advise keeping that loss at or below about 0.2 bits for reliable results. They also show the common likelihood estimator is biased but can be corrected. Tests on synthetic gravitational wave populations show simple models with strong assumptions resist sampling error better. A free software package lets analysts compute the error measure on their own data.
arxiv-2509-07321:
Casey D. Majhor and 1 co-author put an off-road navigation system through 30,000 simulated trials in a 2025 evaluation. The system, MUONS, plans paths from point clouds, three-dimensional maps built from sensor points, for an autonomous ground vehicle. Rough terrain makes planning hard, since slopes and obstacles can trap a vehicle that picks a poor route.

Three demanding terrain maps and twenty combinations of seven planning settings make up the simulation campaign, followed by real field tests. The vehicle succeeded in 98 percent of simulated runs and had no failures in the field. One setting, the expansion radius of the initial search, mattered most for planning time and path length. Patterns from simulation matched field behavior well, which supports tuning such vehicles in simulation before risking hardware outdoors.
arxiv-2509-07621:
When Earth's magnetic field lines snap and reconnect, particles can be flung to high energies. Nadja Reisinger and Fabio Bacchini compare models of that process with spacecraft data in a 2025 research paper. Their event comes from NASA's Magnetospheric Multiscale mission, which flew through a reconnection site in Earth's magnetotail. The team ran fully kinetic models, tracking single-particle physics, seeded with the observed plasma values.

The models match the overall shape of the ion and electron energy spread. They understate the highest-energy tail of the electrons, though. Changing run settings barely moved the results, while starting heat mattered much more. The authors conclude that two-dimensional setups have limits. Three-dimensional models will likely be needed to match the observed energization fully. The study sharpens a natural laboratory for reconnection physics.
arxiv-2509-07721:
R. X. Zhai and 2 co-authors derive an exact bound in 2025 on the trade-off between power and efficiency in heat engines that run in finite time. Power and efficiency pull against each other: maximum efficiency demands an infinitely slow cycle, which delivers vanishing power. A quantitative bound on the compromise would let engineers benchmark real engines against what physics allows.

Working with low-dissipation finite-time heat engines, the authors analytically derive the exact constraint linking the two quantities. The bound specifies the maximum power attainable at any prescribed efficiency. Such a benchmark has theoretical weight for thermodynamics and practical weight for engine design, since it separates losses that better engineering can remove from losses that no design can escape. The letter format keeps the argument focused on the bound itself.
arxiv-2509-07921:
Maciej Wlodek extends a bordered version of symplectic field theory for knots in a solo 2025 mathematics paper. Legendrian knots are knots constrained by a contact structure, a geometric twist condition, and their invariants are often computed from an algebra built from disks bounded by the knot. Cutting the knot's front picture in half should let each half carry its own algebra.

Wlodek constructs such an algebra for each half-knot and shows the full theory's algebra arises by gluing, formally a pushout, the two halves together. The construction adds disks with several positive punctures to the differential, going beyond the earlier bordered Chekanov-Eliashberg algebra. Gluing formulas let mathematicians compute big invariants from manageable pieces.
arxiv-2509-08121:
Aditi Laddha and 1 co-author find new upper bounds for a famously hard count in a 2025 paper. The count is the permanent of a matrix. It looks like the determinant, but with no minus signs to cancel terms. Exact values are out of reach for large inputs. Bounds are the next best thing.

The work starts from a new formula in the style of Schur, built on a new kind of matrix inverse. A step-by-step process, much like Gaussian elimination, then gives bounds a computer can find. The bounds are best when the matrix is close to diagonal in shape. Permanents count matchings in networks and arise in quantum optics, so tighter bounds have real use.
arxiv-2509-08221:
Reinforcement learning for self-driving, as practised inside one popular simulator, is surveyed by Elahe Delavari and 2 co-authors in a 2025 review. Around one hundred peer-reviewed papers that train, test, or validate driving policies in the open-source CARLA simulator are analysed systematically, because the field lacked a clear account of its own habits.

Papers are sorted by algorithmic family: model-free, model-based, hierarchical, and hybrid. More than four in five studies still rely on model-free methods. Benchmarking and evaluation practices are charted alongside the algorithms. A map like this shows newcomers where the crowded roads are, and it exposes how much of the field's confidence rests on a single simulator's version of reality.
arxiv-2509-08421:
Pedestrians tracked across many cameras keep losing their identities, and Keisuke Toida with 4 co-authors fix the fusion step in a 2025 computer vision paper. Multi-view tracking merges camera images into a bird's-eye view, but projecting features from several angles distorts them unevenly, so the fused representation becomes unreliable exactly where views overlap awkwardly.

ATLASFusion performs location-aware sparse fusion that weighs reliability region by region, aggregating tracks across space and time. Consistent identities across views are the whole point of multi-camera systems in stations, stadiums, and smart intersections. A fusion method honest about where its evidence is thin should hand downstream counting and safety systems fewer phantom people.
arxiv-2509-08621:
Advertisement videos form a new test for large language models in a 2025 paper by Xinwei Long and 12 co-authors. Ads pack marketing logic, persuasion, and audience cues into short clips. The team builds AdsQA from more than fifteen hundred ads and nearly eleven thousand clips.

Five tasks probe understanding beyond plain objects in a scene. The authors also build ReAd-R, a model trained with rewards to reflect on questions before answering. Fourteen leading models are benchmarked on the set. ReAd-R scores best by a clear margin. The benchmark pushes models toward deeper, domain aware video understanding.
arxiv-2509-08921:
Ali Karoobi and 2 co-authors develop a theory of operator realizations about a matrix centre in a 2025 paper. Realizations are linear models for analytic functions whose variables do not commute. Earlier theory covered rational functions in finite dimensions.

A non-commutative function has such a realization around a matrix tuple exactly when it is uniformly analytic near that point. Uniformly open neighborhoods give the right setting for the test. The result extends finite dimensional realization theory as far as possible, to all uniformly analytic functions. The work is pure operator theory. It clarifies when a linear model can capture a function's local behavior.
arxiv-2509-09321:
Hangyi Jia and 5 co-authors build TAM Bench, a benchmark for machine learning agents, in a 2025 paper. Agents now run full ML workflows end to end, from data prep to model training. Old benchmarks lack the task range, domain spread, and rigor to judge them fairly.

A web agent plus language models harvest and structure tasks from sites such as Kaggle. Leaderboard counts and score spread set each task's difficulty grade. Scoring checks task score, format, rule adherence, and transfer to new tasks. One hundred fifty tasks form Lite, Medium, and Full sets. The Lite set, with balanced modes and grades, suits daily use.
arxiv-2509-09421:
Mehdi Djellabi and 2 co-authors extend quantum feature kernels for graphs in 2025 using neutral-atom machines. Their setting works with attributed graphs, where nodes and edges both carry extra information. Edge traits are placed into atom positions, while node traits enter as local detuning fields in a Rydberg Hamiltonian, a design the authors show can sharpen what the kernel can express.

Alongside an existing evolution kernel read from global measures, they propose a correlation kernel built from local ones. Pooling readings from several stages of the evolution lifts scores further. Simulations on two molecular data sets, MUTAG and PTC_FM, matched leading classical methods and, with pooling, moved ahead of them.
arxiv-2509-10321:
Jonas Flechsig and Maximilian Pilz extend conformal prediction to settings without labeled calibration data in this 2025 paper. Conformal prediction wraps a model's output in a set that is guaranteed to contain the true answer at a chosen rate. Normally that guarantee needs a labeled calibration set, which can be expensive or impossible to get.

Their method swaps the true calibration scores for careful estimates built from unlabeled data. For classifiers, they prove the prediction sets still cover the truth at a rate reduced only by the model's own error. The same guarantee carries over to regression with a matching exactness measure. A final section shows how practitioners can apply the results with models they already have.
arxiv-2509-10521:
Sai Puppala and 3 co-authors propose a geometry-first approach to personalized federated learning in this 2025 paper. When each client's data skew toward a few labels and keep shifting, one global model fits nobody well. Their framework, called VGM2, starts by learning a custom low-dimensional map of each client's data.

On those maps, the method models distances between same-class and different-class pairs, and clients share only small statistical summaries of those distances, with uncertainty attached. The server merges the summaries into global priors for the next round, in a way the authors prove is stable under wide differences between clients. Across eight vision data sets with skewed splits, the method matched or beat strong baselines while sending little data.
arxiv-2509-10621:
Planetary nebulae, the glowing shells of dying sun-like stars, serve as backlights for Alexander Csukai and three co-authors in this 2025 astronomy paper. Their subject is extinction, the dimming of the central star's light by dust along the way. They assembled a complete sample of two hundred sixty-two large, well-measured nebulae and identified the central stars of one hundred sixty-two.

For each, the team built a spectral energy distribution from survey data and fitted reddened model spectra, pinning extinction down to a few hundredths of a magnitude. The values track interstellar extinction closely, with only one nebula showing clear extra dust of its own. Along the way they found four new close binary central stars, put the binary fraction between roughly a quarter and a third, and double-checked older identifications of central stars in the literature.
arxiv-2509-10921:
Entropy for gravity itself is Sangmin Choi and Malcolm J. Perry's subject in this 2025 paper. Black hole horizons carry entropy. The usual derivations lean on temperature. The authors formulate the entropy of a horizon, classically, as a Noether charge. A Noether charge is a conserved quantity tied to symmetry. No temperature is required. Their definition reaches horizons that do not belong to black holes at all.

Getting there needs a fix. The covariant phase space formalism needs a correction. The correction accounts for how the charge's generating vector field depends on the configuration. That vector field connects to Bousso's proposal. A region's gravitational entropy is set by the lightsheet at its boundary, on his view. The lightsheet is the sheet of light rays leaving the region. The authors test their formula on a range of horizons. Black hole and cosmological horizons both appear.
arxiv-2509-11121:
Benjamin Berger is the sole author of this 2025 computer science paper. It concerns content-defined chunking. Storage systems use chunking to cut files into pieces. Repeated pieces can then be stored only once.

His algorithm is called Chonkers. It promises strict guarantees on two things at once. Chunk sizes stay within proven bounds. Edits also stay local. Change a small part of a file, and only nearby chunks change. The design is layered. It can combine with older chunking methods. Berger pairs it with Yarn, a deduplicated string representation. Yarn is built as a merge tree. On three test collections, Chonkers beat its own proven bounds in practice. It deduplicated versioned data well.
arxiv-2509-11221:
Santiago Matheus, Francesco Bottacin, and Edoardo Provenzi revisit a cornerstone result in this 2025 mathematics paper. Relative entropy never increases under a quantum channel. That fact is called monotonicity. Several proofs exist. The authors compare two famous ones in a single finite-dimensional framework.

The first half examines Petz's strategy. His original argument used an operator inequality. The authors pinpoint a subtle gap in that step. They show how the fix restores the argument. The second half develops Uhlmann's approach. It rests on interpolation of positive forms. It also handles density operators that cannot be inverted. Petz's route is more direct. Uhlmann's is more general. The paper aims to make both proofs easier to follow.
arxiv-2509-11421:
Yusuf Emir Sezgin and 2 co-authors design predictive maintenance for 6G small cells that keeps telemetry local in this 2025 paper. Sixth-generation networks promise autonomy and reliability, but streaming sensitive operating data to central servers costs bandwidth and privacy. Their framework trains failure prediction models at each base station instead, coordinated through a knowledge-defined networking design.

Each station learns from its own signal quality, jitter, delay, and block size readings, with an encoding scheme that can flag several faults at once. A simulator with a millimeter-wave module and injected faults tested realistic deployments. Federated training matched centralized accuracy and per-label precision while sharing no raw data and sending far less traffic, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-11721:
Alessandro Foradori and three co-authors run image classification on a network of light rings. This 2025 photonics paper treats silicon microring resonator networks. Photonic neuromorphic hardware promises low power and wide parallelism. Scalable nonlinearity and long-term memory are hard to get. Ring networks offer both, using space, time, and wavelength at once.

Images are encoded as time sequences. They feed through the ring network. A simple linear classifier reads the result, in reservoir computing style. Several output ports strengthened the classifier. Multiple laser wavelengths helped. Varied input powers helped too. The test sets were MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. A single-pixel setting was also explored. There the physics supplies the memory, so inference needs no digital memory.
arxiv-2509-12021:
Scratch's colorful blocks make programming friendly for learners but awkward for language models, which read text. Benedikt Fein, with two co-authors, bridges that gap in 2025 with LitterBox+, a framework that extends the Scratch static analysis tool LitterBox.

The trick is translation: block programs are converted into a text form a language model can digest. Learners can then ask questions about their own code, hear explanations of quality problems the analyzer flagged, and request suggested fixes. Everything is reachable both through a programming interface and directly inside the Scratch environment students already know. The design stays open, so new prompts, other model providers, and fresh features combining static checks with generation can be plugged in later.
arxiv-2509-12321:
A charged particle in a magnetic field can only occupy stacked energy bands called Landau levels, the root of the quantum Hall effects. In a solo 2025 letter, Farokh Mivehvar couples those levels, for a neutral particle in a synthetic gauge field, to the light inside an optical cavity.

The coupled system turns out to be exactly two quantum harmonic oscillators with a strong nonlinear link, so the full quantum problem stays solvable. The hybrid states, named Landau polaritons, keep part of the band degeneracy and show entanglement between light and matter plus squeezed fluctuations. Depending on settings, the driven system settles into several distinct steady states.
arxiv-2509-12521:
A picture can be tuned to steer what a multimodal model prefers to say. The answer need not look harmful. Yifan Lan and four co-authors name that attack Preference Hijacking in 2025. They present Phi, a method that crafts such an image. It bends a model's response preferences at inference time. The model itself is not changed.

The team also builds a universal perturbation. It is a reusable component. It can be embedded in different images. It pushes answers toward any preference an attacker picks. The outputs stay on-topic and plausible. That makes the manipulation hard to spot. Tests across tasks show the steering works.
arxiv-2509-12621:
Perturbation theory works best from a starting point that can be solved exactly, and for qubit systems that starting point is a stabilizer state. Xuzhe Ying and two co-authors build a systematic stabilizer perturbation theory in 2025, using the local Schrieffer-Wolff transformation as the engine.

The transformation can be carried out efficiently through a binary encoding of the Pauli algebra, the arithmetic of qubit operators. Benchmarks on the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising chain validate the method. It is then applied to the toric code on square and kagome lattices, probing whether its anyon excitations stay free or become confined under perturbation.
arxiv-2509-13021:
Phung Duc Luong, Le Tran Gia Bao and five co-authors launch xOffense in 2025, a team of AI agents that tests system security on its own. Hand pen tests are slow and need scarce experts. Full auto flow can scale with compute.

A tuned mid-size open model drives thought and choice. Split agents handle scouting, flaw scans, and attacks. A lead layer keeps steps in sync. Chain-style tuning teaches exact tool calls and multi-step plans. On two hard benchmarks the team cleared near four fifths of sub-tasks. That beat lead rivals by clear gaps at lower cost.
arxiv-2509-13121:
Faruk Alpay and Hamdi Alakkad probe in 2025 whether every reflexive Banach space forces a fixed point for non-stretch maps. The open question has resisted classic attacks for years. Reflexive spaces bend back on themselves in a weak sense that may or may not pin such maps.

Two new gauges track how far a free orbit hull can collapse. If either gauge stays positive across cases, the space holds a copy of a banned sequence space. It then cannot be reflexive. Finite checks and coded routines bound the gauges. Good and bad cases show where old paths fail and what stays open.
arxiv-2509-13321:
Stefano Bondani and Sergio Cacciatori explore in 2025 whether clock drift can reveal gravitational waves in async gauges. Time-time metric wobbles become explicit when gauges desync. Drift between a hit clock and a calm reference is the target signal.

Current timing and data-keeping tools are surveyed for a feasibility path. Non-local geodesic reach sets the bar. A prototype mix at the best tech point is sketched. The sweet band sits near one hertz. Mid-mass black hole pairs are among hoped sources. The study is a first step, not a built detector.
arxiv-2509-13521:
Manu Stalport, Michael Cretignier and two co-authors release ARDENT in 2025, a Python package for fast dynamical detection limits from radial velocities. Planet system architecture informs formation, yet survey completeness caps statistical claims about giants versus inner small planets.

ARDENT refines classic data limits with orbital stability limits, via analytic and numeric criteria. Stability can rule out whole zones that data alone allows. On TOI-1736, with a cold giant and inner sub-Neptune, no extra planet past a set period survives the giant gravity. Completeness sharpens and follow-up targets narrow. The package is user-friendly across systems.
arxiv-2509-13621:
Antonin Sulc, Thorsten Hellert, and Steven Hunt introduce an automated fault analysis system for the Advanced Light Source in a 2025 paper. The Advanced Light Source is a synchrotron facility. Its control system, EPICS, pours out event logs in real time. For a human operator, picking those chains out is hard.

The system starts by treating each log entry as a piece of language. Embedding techniques then turn the entries into vectors, numbers that carry the meaning of an entry in its context. Next, a neural network that understands sequences reads the stream. It learned only from records of normal running, and it gives every new event a score for how anomalous it looks, right away. Operators can then move fast to the event chains that matter most. The detector learns what normal looks like, and reports the rest, which is what makes the learning unsupervised.
arxiv-2509-13821:
Frederik Møller and five co-authors teach a neural network to read quantum simulator data in a 2025 physics paper. Analog simulators realize many-body dynamics beyond classical computation, but extracting physics from their noisy, partial measurements is hard, especially when the microscopic model is not fully known.

Their tool is a variational autoencoder, a generative model that compresses data into a small latent space. Trained without labels on interference snapshots of tunnel-coupled one-dimensional Bose gases, the latent variables it found tracked the system's equilibrium control parameter closely. On quenched, out-of-equilibrium runs, the latent space exposed frozen-in solitons after rapid cooling and anomalous dynamics that standard correlation methods missed, offering a complementary probe of quantum matter.
arxiv-2509-14121:
Marco A. Gomez and Christopher D. Cruz-Ancona design safe sliding mode control for double integrator systems in a 2025 control paper. A double integrator, the textbook model of a mass pushed by a force, must be steered robustly while never entering an unsafe region, despite disturbances and uncertainty pushing back.

When the constraints concern position alone, the authors show a safe sliding domain can be built from the dynamics of a simpler, already safe integrator system. On that domain, closed-loop trajectories stay robustly safe. They then design a controller gain that drives the system into the domain while steering around the forbidden set. The construction starts with first-order sliding mode and generalizes to an adaptive version that keeps trajectories within a fixed neighborhood of the domain, safely outside the unsafe region.
arxiv-2509-14221:
Silan Hu and three co-authors introduce GEM-Bench in 2025, a test set for a new kind of online marketing. Chatbots and search tools built on large language models can now place ads inside their answers. Until now there was no shared test built just for judging those ad filled answers.

GEM-Bench brings together three data sets covering chat and search, a set of scores for user satisfaction and engagement, and several starting methods in a shared framework. Early results show a trade off. Simple prompting can raise clicks but often lowers satisfaction, while writing an ad free answer first and adding ads later protects satisfaction at extra cost. The sets and tools are public for later work.
arxiv-2509-14321:
Jonathan Roberts and twenty-two co-authors present new orbit fits in 2025 for two directly imaged companions, YSES 1 b and HR 2562 B. Both objects sit near the border between planet and brown dwarf. Distant companions move slowly, so their orbit shapes are hard to pin down.

Fresh astrometry from the GRAVITY instrument, plus radial velocity and proper motion data, feed revised fits made with the orbitize software. For YSES 1 b the added data give the first full orbit fit, with a moderately eccentric path. The team also estimates a small tilt between the star spin and the orbit. For HR 2562 B the new fit agrees with earlier work. Sharper orbits help test how such wide companions formed.
arxiv-2509-14521:
Ali Baheri and Alireza Vahid put forward a fully spread out Sinkhorn method in 2025 for Wasserstein barycenters, a shape aware way to average chance spreads. Agents in a spread out system hold unlike local spreads and must fuse them over sparse, weak links. Plain averaging in flat space can mislead.

Sinkhorn sums give a close form for such averages, but they tend to need a centre to run them. Their version rewrites the key mean step as a plain average in log space. Agents then swap log notes with near peers in gossip rounds, mixed with local Sinkhorn steps. No centre is needed. Shape aware fusion suits robot and sensor fleets whose beliefs are spreads, not points.
arxiv-2509-14721:
Gengchao Yang and four co-authors present a multiscale super resolution framework in 2025 for reconstructing fluid flows with deep networks. Instead of upscaling finished flow fields, their method works on the mesoscopic density functions of the lattice Boltzmann method. Coarse simulations could then be sharpened after the fact.

Two network designs, a standard convolutional network and a deeper residual dense network, upscale distribution functions by factors of two, four and eight. Velocity, pressure and vorticity are recovered from the sharpened functions by one model. On flow past a cylinder, the deeper network cut distribution error by an order of magnitude against the plain network and avoided spurious pressure wiggles. Cheap coarse runs plus learned sharpening promise high fidelity flow data at lower cost.
arxiv-2509-14821:
Andrea Cavallo, Samuel Rey, Antonio G. Marques, and Elvin Isufi introduce Precision Neural Networks in a 2025 machine learning paper. Earlier covariance neural networks filter data on a graph built from the covariance matrix, which captures how variables vary together. Covariance graphs are dense, hide conditional independence, and are usually fixed before training.

Precision matrices, the inverses of covariance matrices, naturally show which variables are directly linked and are often sparse. The proposed networks filter on the precision graph instead. Learning is joint: the network weights and the precision matrix are updated in turn, so the graph adapts to the task. The authors bound the estimation error at each step and test the idea on synthetic and real data, where joint learning beats fixing the graph first.
arxiv-2509-15221:
Zhaoyang Liu and a large team of co-authors scale up open-source computer use agents in a 2025 AI paper. Such agents operate graphical interfaces directly, clicking and typing like a person, but progress has been throttled by scarce open training data and models. ScaleCUA attacks the data problem head-on.

The dataset spans six operating systems and three task domains, built by a closed loop where automated agents and human experts refine each other's work. A model trained on it operates across platforms without per-system retraining. Reported results beat prior baselines by wide margins on web and interface benchmarks and set new best marks on several standard suites. Data, models, and code are promised for release, betting that open scale will do for computer use what it did for chat models.
arxiv-2509-15321:
Joe Boninger links two ways of studying knots and braids. One is the Burau map, an old tool that turns a braid into a table of numbers. The other is knot Floer homology, a newer tool that grades groups tied to a knot. Both tools trace back to the same older method, called Fox calculus, but the link had not been made plain.

Boninger shows that a Floer type theory can be built whose graded count gives a chosen minor of the Burau table. He does the same for a second, related map. He then ties the Burau map to a quantum group and shows a tangle tool of his recovers its braid action. The proof is short and based on shapes.
arxiv-2509-15421:
Carlos Blanco and three co-authors revisit neutrinos from the galaxy NGC 1068. A large ice based detector in Antarctica has seen these particles from that galaxy. Their soft energy spread was read as a sign that the source speeds protons only to modest energy. The team offer a different reading of the same data.

They propose the source may speed protons far higher. The charged particles made in crashes then lose energy to strong magnetic fields before they can decay. That loss cuts the neutrino energies down to what is seen. The fields needed would be huge. The plan also shifts the mix of neutrino types, so future large detectors can test it.
arxiv-2509-15621:
Tomoya Yamashita leads a team that erases whole concepts from a language model. Past erasing work removed set sentences, which needs the exact text to be named. Broader targets, like a person or an event, could not be handled that way. The team define concept unlearning with the help of knowledge graphs, where facts sit as linked triples.

To erase a concept, the graph nodes for it and their links must go. Their method asks the model itself to write triples and short accounts of the target. Erasing then runs on those self made items, matching the model's own inner store. Tests on real and fake data sets show the method works. It removes concepts with less harm to other knowledge.
arxiv-2509-16421:
Agents that watch live video must judge each moment as it comes, with no peek at what follows. Aiden Chang, Celso De Melo, and Stephanie M. Lukin present Aha, a system that scores each frame's relevance to a task stated in plain language. Light prediction heads rank frames for informativeness and doubt, while a caching trick keeps memory flat over endless streams.

On highlight benchmarks the online system beat even offline rivals that see the whole video. Gains were clear on two standard sets. Trials with robot video suggest the frame scorer could guide real-time planning and long-horizon scene understanding for machines in the field.
arxiv-2509-16621:
Hiun Kim, Tae Kwan Lee, and Taeryun Won study word lists inside search tools in a 2025 paper. Learned sparse search maps queries and documents into lists of weighted terms. A recent variant lets the model grow its own custom word list. The team ask how the size and starting state of that list shape search quality.

Their tests show the list does more than hold words. It sets how queries and documents are spelled out for matching. That framing was not the list's first purpose. Still, it drives how well the engine works. The finding opens a new lever for faster and better search. Builders can now tune lists on purpose.
arxiv-2509-17321:
Paweł Budzianowski and six co-authors built a benchmark for judging how far a robot task has progressed. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds on generative value learning, which asks vision-language models to grade task progress from camera views. Good progress scores could sort and label the flood of robot data now being recorded in the wild.

Their benchmark, OpenGVL, covers varied hard manipulation tasks with both robot and human actors. They test publicly available open models on it and find a clear gap: open model families reach only a fair share of the closed models' scores. The authors also show the benchmark at work as a curation tool, filtering large robot data sets by quality. The full benchmark and code are released for public use.
arxiv-2509-17421:
Fei Zhao leads a team of eleven co-authors on a 2025 arXiv paper that builds a Chinese benchmark for multi-image understanding. Most multi-image test sets are in English, and no Chinese one existed. Their set, RealBench, draws on real user content, so the tasks stay close to daily use rather than lab scenes.

RealBench holds thousands of samples and tens of thousands of images. Its scenes, resolutions, and image layouts vary widely, which raises the bar for models that must reason across pictures. The team graded twenty-one multimodal models of many sizes, from closed systems to open visual and video models. Even the strongest closed models struggled with the Chinese multi-image tasks. Open models trailed closed ones by a wide average margin. The authors offer RealBench as a base for closing that gap.
arxiv-2509-17521:
Philip Schätzle and five co-authors grow diamond films with a new knob: distance from the plasma. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses chemical vapor deposition, where a plasma feeds the growth of diamond on a seed. By placing the sample at a set distance from the reactor baseplate where the plasma couples, they found two growth regimes no one had reported.

Just a few millimeters below the plasma, growth slows but nitrogen enters the crystal far more readily. That mix yields delta-doped layers thinner than a few tens of nanometers, and every layer shows NV emission tied to the nitrogen content. Farther away, growth stops, yet nitrogen-rich species still coat the surface and enter the next grown layer. The tricks suit thin, heavily doped films for quantum sensing and sparse NV layers for quantum computing. Other dopants, such as phosphorus, could follow the same route.
arxiv-2509-18121:
Nikhil Garg and 7 co-authors train neural nets on brain-like memory chips that sip power. Their 2025 paper deals with wearables and implants that must run AI at the edge, with no cloud. New memristive parts can merge memory and compute, which cuts costly data moves.

The team feeds lab-measured updates from ferroelectric parts into net sims. Short pulses cost less energy per update and less in total, though they need more rounds. Plain training lost score next to a mixed-precision form. A fix that shifts the symmetry point of updates won that score back. The trade among score, speed, and energy is mapped in full.
arxiv-2509-18321:
Tiny magnetic waves called magnons can carry signals at very small scales. That makes them tempting parts for brain-like computing. David Breitbach and 11 co-authors report a neuron built only from magnons in this 2025 paper. Past magnon parts were hard to link into chains, so connected magnon neurons had not been shown before.

Their neuron takes in magnon signals and fires a stronger magnon pulse once a threshold is passed, then resets itself. It sits on a low-loss garnet film and uses a shift in wave frequency for its on-off action. Light-based tools showed a memory that fades at a tunable rate. A small change in pump power shifted the memory time by a factor of a thousand. The team linked three neurons in a chain and triggered them in sequence.
arxiv-2509-18521:
Training large language models with reinforcement learning spends most of its time generating sample answers. Yuzhen Zhou and 17 co-authors present APRIL, a system that cuts the waste in that step. Their 2025 paper names the core problem: a few very long answers stall whole batches, leaving graphics chips idle. Rollouts, as these samples are called, take over ninety percent of training time.

APRIL asks for more samples than needed and stops once the target count is reached. Partial answers are not thrown away; they are recycled and finished in later steps. That rule keeps every chip busy and wastes no work. Across three common training algorithms, rollout throughput rose by about a fifth on average. Final accuracy also edged up slightly. The system works across frameworks and chip brands. It is already built into an open training framework.
arxiv-2509-18621:
The unit disc carries a classic curved geometry, the Poincaré metric of hyperbolic space. Alok Kumar Pandey, Ashok Kumar, and Bankteshwar Tiwari study a deformed version of it in this 2025 paper. The deformation is the Apollonian weak metric, another way to measure distance inside the disc. They ask what Finsler structure, a generalized length rule, this metric carries.

They find the structure is of Randers type, a Riemannian metric nudged by a one-form. In fact, the Apollonian version is the Poincaré metric deformed by a closed one-form. A neat consequence follows: its shortest paths agree point by point with the hyperbolic ones. The team then computes several curvature measures for the structure. Its S-curvature stays above a fixed bound, while its flag curvature stays below negative one. That makes the disc a Hadamard space in this structure.
arxiv-2509-19021:
Sorting numbers fast is a basic job inside high-throughput software, and small gains there spread everywhere. Atharv Pandey and Lakshmanan Kuppusamy study radix sort, which sorts digit by digit instead of by comparing values. Their target is a flaw in the base-n variant: when data are skewed, padding short numbers with zeros wastes work. They build a model that prunes that waste as it goes.

Their method, SP-LSD, runs a stable partition at each digit step, starting from the least significant digit. From it they derive a decision frame with three crossover points. The frame says when each method beats comparison-based sorts, when the new model's overhead pays off, and when pruning wins overall. Tests on skewed and even data match the predicted boundaries. The result is a clear roadmap for picking the right sort for a given dataset.
arxiv-2509-19321:
G. Tutberidze, writing alone, proves new bounds for maximal operators built from averaged Fourier sums in the Vilenkin system. Vilenkin systems generalize the Walsh functions used in digital signal analysis, built on groups rather than the circle. T means are weighted averages of partial sums, here with monotone weights. Maximal operators, which take the largest value along a sequence of averages, are the standard tool for proving that averages converge almost everywhere.

The new inequalities are of Hardy-space to weak-Lebesgue type, weighing the input and output differently. From them, almost-everywhere convergence of these T means follows. The author also shows the results are best possible in a precise sense, so the exponents cannot be improved. Applications recover several known theorems and add new ones. The work sits in harmonic analysis over Vilenkin groups.
arxiv-2509-19421:
Attis V. M. Marino and three co-authors simulate ultracold atoms in a one-dimensional lattice that is almost, but not quite, periodic. Such quasi-periodic lattices sit between order and disorder and host unusual phases. The team controls lattice depth, interaction strength, and filling with precision, then abruptly switches on a second, mismatched lattice and watches the many-body dynamics unfold. Their solver follows the full quantum evolution with a multi-configuration method built for bosons.

Four distinct localization stories appear. A smooth superfluid at mismatched filling collapses and revives as it localizes. A fragmented superfluid at matched filling freezes into a Mott pattern. A strongly fragmented Mott state merely melts under the new lattice's pressure. Strangest, in the fermionized regime, correlations inside each double well stay unexpectedly robust. The findings map new localization mechanisms for engineering exotic quantum behavior.
arxiv-2509-19521:
Waving two hands to steer a robot could beat joysticks in tight or risky workplaces. Najeeb Ahmed Bhuiyan and three co-authors built a two-hand gesture system for a mobile robot arm. The left hand steers the base by tilt and finger bends, read by small sensors. The right hand guides the arm, with its motions read by a tiny neural network on low-power hardware.

Both jobs run at once, unlike older one-task-at-a-time setups. The system runs on the ROS robot platform and drives a seven-joint arm. The authors stress low cost, low power, and open code. Uses range from factory floors to aid for people with limited mobility. Work in hazardous zones, where distance keeps people safe, is another target.
arxiv-2509-19621:
Database schemas can loop back on themselves, and loopless ones behave in welcome ways. Albert Atserias and Phokion G. Kolaitis study the subtlest of three classic loopless notions, gamma-acyclicity. They extend recent work on annotated relations, where each row carries a tag from an algebra of values. Tags can track things such as provenance or multiplicity.

Their main finding is that the good behavior of gamma-acyclic schemas carries over to annotated relations. One condition is needed: the tag algebra must allow a flow-like balancing act called the transportation property. The result completes a pattern seen for the other acyclic notions. Acyclic schemas support fast, safe query evaluation and updates. Extending those guarantees to annotated data matters for modern databases that track where each fact came from.
arxiv-2509-19921:
Federated learning pays contributors by score, but Balazs Pejo and four co-authors show those scores are fragile. One risk is innocent: advanced aggregation methods, built to handle unreliable clients, silently shift the final scores. The basic averaging that most studies assume is not what real systems run. A second risk is hostile: poisoning attacks can inflate an attacker's score or deflate rivals.

Experiments across datasets and architectures confirm both distortions. Fair credit is the incentive that keeps hospitals, banks, and phone users contributing data. If scores bend under method choice or attack, that incentive rots. The authors argue contribution scoring needs the same security scrutiny as the learning itself. Their results map where the fragility enters.
arxiv-2509-20121:
Peter Mayr and Nik Ruskuc wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in pure mathematics. They study automorphism groups, the full sets of symmetries of certain algebraic structures. The structures are Boolean powers built from a finite simple Mal'cev algebra, such as a finite simple group or ring. The paper asks whether these symmetry groups have ample generics, a strong richness property.

They prove that the answer is yes. The proof splits into abelian and non-abelian cases. The abelian case uses module representations and a theory of n-systems from earlier work. The non-abelian case decomposes the group into a semidirect product of simpler parts. Along the way, they extend a known result about the homeomorphism group of Cantor space. The work sits in descriptive set theory and universal algebra.
arxiv-2509-20421:
Legal contracts written as code can be checked like software, and Reiner Hahnle, Cosimo Laneve, and Adele Veschetti show how in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their language, Stipula, models contracts with asset transfers and obligations. Informal review cannot guarantee such contracts behave as intended. Formal verification can, if the contract is translated faithfully.

Their method translates Stipula contracts into Java code annotated with formal specifications. The deductive verification tool KeY then checks partial and total correctness. For contracts whose cycles are disjoint, a large and useful subset, both translation and verification run fully automatically. The work demonstrates that a general-purpose verifier can serve legal software through translation. It points toward contract platforms where correctness is proven, not merely tested.
arxiv-2509-20521:
Splitting a whole number into ordered parts, with rules on neighboring pieces, is a classic counting game. Brian Hopkins and Augustine Munagi generalize one such rule set in a 2025 arXiv note on Arndt compositions. Jorg Arndt introduced compositions restricted by inequalities between certain part pairs in 2013. Variations have multiplied since. This note scales the defining relation by two parameters at once.

The scaled compositions turn out to match compositions whose parts come from certain congruence classes. The authors establish recurrence relations for the counting sequences on both sides. Those recurrences give new combinatorial meanings to several integer sequences already in the catalogs. They also produce simple sequences nobody had recorded. The note is short and closes with directions for further study.
arxiv-2509-20621:
A young companion thirty times Jupiter's mass orbits far from its star, and Vidya Venkatesan, the ExoGRAVITY collaboration, and many co-authors refine that orbit in a 2025 arXiv paper. GQ Lup B circles at about one hundred astronomical units, where planet formation theories strain to build cores. Sparse coverage over a long period left its orbit degenerate. The team combined every available measurement.

High-resolution spectra gave the companion's radial velocity, while interferometric astrometry from GRAVITY pinned its sky position with fresh precision. Adding the velocity broke the tie between tilt and eccentricity that astrometry alone could not. The eccentricity estimate tightened to a moderate value. The orbit sits strongly misaligned with the star's disk and spin, but closer to the plane of a wide third companion. That pattern favors formation by cloud fragmentation over orderly core growth.
arxiv-2509-20821:
Pointfree topology studies spaces through algebra instead of points, and two constructions extend it in parallel ways. Anna Laura Suarez compares those constructions in a solo-authored 2025 mathematics paper. The constructions are Raney extensions and strictly zero-dimensional biframes.

Both frameworks faithfully extend the dual of the category of T0 spaces. Suarez describes each as a frame paired with a chosen family of sublocales. She then proves an adjunction, a structured link, between certain sublocales on one side and codense sublocales on the other. The result clarifies how the two extensions relate rather than merely coexist. The paper serves specialists in pointfree topology who want a cleaner map of these abstract tools.
arxiv-2509-21121:
The two-dimensional Euler equations describe ideal fluid flow, and Yudovich's theory is the classic proof that their solutions behave well. Theodore Drivas and Joonhyun La revisit that theory in a 2025 note, taking the Lagrangian view. That view follows single fluid particles, not fixed points in space.

The authors re-prove Yudovich's existence and uniqueness result for weak solutions with bounded vorticity, and allow mildly unbounded vorticity too. Their proof tracks the flow map built from the velocity field. As a byproduct, they show how smoothly the solution depends on the initial data and on the shape of the domain. Such stability supports both pure theory and trust in simulations of two-dimensional turbulence in fluids.
arxiv-2509-21221:
Nikolay Blagoev and 3 co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on training large language models across many sites. Normal training uses one data centre with matched machines. Their setting is different. Volunteers offer varied machines from many places, and they may join or leave at any time. Links between sites can also fail.

The team presents GWTF, a training framework built for that rough setting. Its core is a flow method that picks routes for small batches of data. The routes aim to train the most batches with the least delay. Tests used GPT style and LLaMA style models across ten places. The method cut training time by a large share in hard cases with much churn.
arxiv-2509-21821:
Recovering the meaning of a program from its low-level form is slow, expert work. Xinyu Hu and four co-authors survey how large language models might help with that work, called reverse engineering. Analysts use it to take apart compiled code, undo disguises, and check software for security flaws. This 2025 survey gathers what is known so far and where the gaps lie.

The authors sort forty-eight published studies along six lines, from the task each study aimed at to the quality of its data. They pull out each study's setup so that others can compare results and repeat the work. The survey then maps the open problems in the field. It points to what must improve before language models can be trusted on real security work.
arxiv-2509-22021:
The PICOLON Collaboration reports a stability check of an ultra-pure crystal detector built to test a famous dark matter claim. The DAMA/LIBRA experiment long ago reported a yearly rhythm in its signals, hinting at dark matter particles called WIMPs, but no other experiment has confirmed it. Checking the claim needs crystals of sodium iodide as pure as DAMA's own, and purity that stays put over long runs.

PICOLON grows such crystals, and one ingot reached the DAMA purity level in 2020. A six-month measurement confirmed that the radiopurity of that crystal line stays stable over time. The paper presents the background stability of a newer detector crystal made by the same purification method. It also reports the experiment's first search for the annual modulation signal itself. The authors argue that stable purity is a real advantage for a proper check of the DAMA result.
arxiv-2509-22421:
Leonel Giacobbe, Jingdao Chen, and Chuangchuang Sun teach two robot arms to grasp soft and fragile things together. Most grasp systems suit stiff objects and fail when an item bends or tears. Single-arm touch-based grasping also cannot lift large or heavy items. The team pairs two GelSight Mini touch sensors with a learned predictive controller for both arms.

The sensors report texture and stiffness in real time. From that touch data, the system infers contact state and how much the object gives. It then adjusts force and position in a closed loop. Tests beat plain and single predictive baselines on keeping stable grasps across varied sizes and stiffness.
arxiv-2509-22521:
Jonas Lammers and 6 co-authors give a recipe for a universal light-based processor built on quantum walks. Large multi-port interferometers are needed for photonic quantum computing. Quantum walks were known in theory to serve as a universal base, but no build plan linked them to lab hardware. The team shows how to turn any linear transformation into the coin and step operations of a walk.

Those operations then map onto the knobs of a time-multiplexed platform. The design encodes data in several degrees of freedom at once, which keeps it scalable and light on resources. They also prove the system tolerates lab imperfections well. Comparisons favor it over existing layouts.
arxiv-2509-22621:
Aayush Mishra, Daniel Khashabi, and Anqi Liu borrow the inner life of in-context learning to improve fine-tuning. Fine-tuning trains weights to give target replies. In-context learning instead adapts at run time from prompt examples, often generalizing better with little data. The team first showed the two methods produce distinct activation patterns inside the model. That gap suggests they adapt through different mechanisms.

Their method, IA2, distills in-context activation patterns into a fine-tuned model before training starts. The priming step pushes the model toward in-context-like internal reasoning. Across twelve benchmarks and two model families, IA2 raised both accuracy and calibration of outputs. The finding also offers a window into how adaptation works inside these models.
arxiv-2509-23021:
Robots have far fewer training demos than humans, whose motion data fill the web. Xiao Hu and 3 co-authors bridge that gap with shared motion primitives. Their framework, UniPrototype, finds common building blocks in human and robot motion. Soft assignments let several primitives fire at once, which captures blended skills. A selection rule adjusts how many primitives a task gets.

That keeps the code compact for simple tasks and richer for hard ones. Tests ran in simulation and on real robot systems. Robots that learned through the shared primitives picked up skills faster. They also beat prior transfer methods on task performance.
arxiv-2509-23121:
Vision-language-action models unify seeing, reasoning, and control, but factory floors test them hard. Shuai Li and 6 co-authors review how top VLA models fare in industry. They judge the models from a deployment standpoint. Limits are sorted into data collection issues and architecture issues. Fine-tuned models kept basic grasping skill in industrial scenes.

Complex settings, varied object types, and precise placing still lag far behind needs. The gap shows where task-specific work is required. Robustness, generalization, and precision all need gains. The review gives practical guidance for adapting these models to real plants.
arxiv-2509-23221:
A quiet crystal that breaks its own symmetry at low temperature is the puzzle in CoSn2. Suman Nandi and 10 co-authors trace that break to the electrons, not the lattice. Resistance data bend away from standard behavior below about twenty-five kelvin. X-ray diffraction then finds weak superlattice spots near twenty-two kelvin. The cell doubles along two axes into a fourfold superstructure.

Symmetry drops from tetragonal to monoclinic with no visible distortion. Magnetoresistance turns twofold where it was fourfold before. Calculations show no phonon softening, but electronic susceptibility rises. Polarized photoemission points to strong orbital anisotropy. An electronic instability drives the change, they conclude.
arxiv-2509-23321:
Fusing sharp gray satellite images with coarse color ones should be cheap enough for small devices. Yizhen Jiang and 5 co-authors binarize the fusion network to cut that cost. Two flaws block naive binarization. Spectral mismatch between the image types distorts color. Standard binary kernels also blur the multi-scale, directional shapes in remote sensing scenes. Their custom convolution answers both flaws.

A spectral redistribution step fixes the color statistics with learned scale and shift. A Gabor-based amplifier handles varied scales and angles. Stacked into S2BNet, the blocks form a full binary pan-sharpening network. Wide tests show high fusion quality at low cost.
arxiv-2509-23421:
A lambda baryon decaying into a proton, a lepton, and an antineutrino encodes six form factors worth pinning down. M Ahmadi, Z Rajabi Najjar, and K Azizi compute all six in quantum chromodynamics. The factors govern the low-energy matrix elements of the decay. Their momentum-transfer dependence is traced across the full physical range. Two parametrizations, a z-expansion and a polynomial fit, carry the results.

Decay widths for electron and muon channels come out of the fits. Branching ratios follow from those widths. The muon-to-electron width ratio lands near zero point two in both fits. The z-expansion value agrees especially well with Particle Data Group averages.
arxiv-2509-23621:
Tools that build machine learning pipelines on their own promise wider access to AI, but security work is a stern test. Sherif Saad and 3 co-authors put eight open-source AutoML frameworks through eleven public cybersecurity data sets. The tasks cover intrusion detection, malware sorting, phishing, fraud, and spam. Scores varied widely across tools and data, with no single winner.

The authors say the hard choice has shifted from picking a model to picking a framework, given gaps in speed, automation, and features. The tools favored tree-based models, which risk overfitting and murky reasoning. Adversarial attacks, drift, and weak feature work round out the problems, and the paper ends with best practices.
arxiv-2509-23821:
Should a home robot be raised by a host home, the way foster care raises a child? Federico Pablo-Marti and Carlos Mir Fernandez propose that idea as Robot Fostering. Hosts would run a set course of daily tasks with the robot over months. The point is to gather long, rich records of how the robot acts in real homes.

Rules come first in their plan, ahead of the tech. They set clear scores for how good a record is, and checks that match EU-grade norms. The paper is a plan, not a test: it lays out cheap first steps and pilots to run later. No trials have been run yet.
arxiv-2509-24021:
Cosmic ray showers make more muons than simulations predict, and extra strangeness in particle collisions is one suspect. Ken Ohashi and 2 co-authors build a framework to test that scenario against both cosmic-ray and collider data. Using the MCEq shower package, they locate the phase-space regions of hadronic collisions that drive muon counts. A strangeness rise starting around a million to ten million GeV could fit the newest cosmic-ray results, they find, but it demands substantial enhancement at LHC energies.

They then compute how precise the kaon-to-pion ratio must be at LHCb and FASER for Run 3 data to settle the question across most of the viable parameter space.
arxiv-2509-24621:
Retrieval models usually need heavy extra training to turn a general multimodal model into a search engine. Yuhan Zhu and 8 co-authors ask whether an off-the-shelf multimodal large language model can retrieve well with no training at all. Their framework, FreeRet, runs retrieval in two stages: grounded embeddings from the model itself give fast candidate search, then the model's reasoning reranks the candidates precisely.

Three advances support it: skipping lexical alignment layers for faithful embeddings, conditioning generation on explicit priors, and neutral framing to curb bias in reranking. On large mixed-modality benchmarks, FreeRet beat models trained on millions of pairs. It works across model families and keeps their generative skills.
arxiv-2509-24821:
Rui Jia and a team of co-authors built a model to judge student mastery from class talk. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with cognitive diagnosis. In its classic form it reads neat test data to say what a student knows. Real class talk is dynamic and messy, far from a test sheet. No frame fit that world, and key signs are hard to pull from long chats.

Their model, DiaCDM, adapts a known class pattern: the teacher starts, the student replies, the teacher weighs in. A graph code joins the teacher's asks to the knowledge points at stake. Readers in education tech get a way to read mastery from the talk that fills real lessons.
arxiv-2509-25021:
Ben Keller and co-authors test the long flexible cables that read out a desert telescope's first camera, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The camera will field over ten thousand cold detectors, and the full array near one hundred thousand. Half-meter low-heat cables bridge the cold and warm ends.

Heat flow through the cables was measured and fitted across cold ranges. Signal pass and cross talk checks traced extra cross talk to small board joints, not the cables. Copper traits in the traces let the team price heat loads for both test and full cameras. The verdict backs the cables for dense arrays. Readers in instrument building get vetted parts data.
arxiv-2509-25321:
When a red giant star mixes its interior during the first dredge-up, the carbon and nitrogen at its surface end up tied to the star's mass and age. John Roberts and co-authors turn that link into a clock. They calibrate a relation between the carbon to nitrogen ratio and age, using survey abundances and ages measured from starquakes for a reference set. The relation dates other red giants from their spectra alone.

The method recovers starquake ages between one and ten billion years with typical errors near one and a half billion years. It works across evolutionary states with only modest offsets. Using it, the team maps how the Milky Way's chemistry changed with birth time and place. After removing likely migrant stars, they find few migrators and weak chemical change over the last ten billion years across much of the disk.
arxiv-2509-26421:
Eva Stafne and Juliette Becker show that Einstein's general relativity can rescue close-in planets around white dwarfs from a runaway greenhouse, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The habitable zone of a dead star sits very near it, so any slight oval in a planet's orbit stirs tidal heat. A companion planet can pump that oval rhythmically, and earlier work warned that even a whisper of it could boil a surface ocean.

The authors add the relativistic twist that near a compact star, orbits precess fast. That steady swing can break the companion's rhythm before the oval grows. For some system layouts, they find, relativity stands guard over habitability. The result matters for picking targets in the hunt for life signs.
arxiv-2510-00121:
Curt Healey wrote this 2025 mathematics paper reviewing a proof of Löwner's theorem, a cornerstone of operator theory. The theorem links functions that preserve order between matrices to a rich analytic structure. It also underpins Kubo-Ando theory, which studies special averages of positive operators. The pieces of the classic proof sit scattered across many sources, which frustrates new readers.

Healey gathers those pieces into one continuous, self-contained account of the proof. Every needed component is presented in place, in the order the argument requires. The aim is clarity and efficiency for anyone learning this material. No new theorem is claimed, and the paper does not pretend otherwise. Its value lies in making a hard, central proof genuinely readable in one sitting. Such reviews matter because later work in Kubo-Ando theory leans on this theorem constantly.
arxiv-2510-00421:
Dessislava Kochloukova and Aline Pinto wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the homology growth of certain pro-p groups. Pro-p groups are infinite symmetry groups built from p-group approximations, central to modern number theory. The question is whether homology ranks can grow without bound across finite-index subgroups. Unbounded growth would signal wild internal complexity in the group.

The authors study groups that are nilpotent-by-abelian, a layered and comparatively tame class. For subgroups of finite index, they bound the torsion-free rank of homology in each low degree. The bound holds uniformly, with the degree limit set by the nilpotency class and a finiteness condition. Their condition asks a certain quotient to be of type FP, a finite presentation-like property. The result adds these groups to the map of families with controlled homological growth. Such control matters wherever pro-p groups model Galois symmetries.
arxiv-2510-00621:
Gao, Chen, and Zhang introduce FAME in this 2025 arXiv paper, accepted at NeurIPS 2025, on function-on-function regression. That task predicts one continuous curve from another, such as forecasting a full daily pattern from sensor traces. Older methods fix basis functions in advance or treat curves as plain grids of numbers, which loses their smooth nature.

FAME learns the curves directly with a neural controlled differential equation paired with a mixture of experts. Multi-head cross attention then links features across the input and output functions. On synthetic and real-world benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy among the methods they tested. The model also stayed robust when observations were sampled at irregular points along each curve, a common problem in real functional data.
arxiv-2510-00821:
Corrada-Emmanuel develops a logic for judging experts without an answer key in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI safety. When two graders agree, almost nothing follows about who is right. When they disagree, at least one must be wrong, and that asymmetry carries usable information. His framework turns the observed pattern of agreements and disagreements into a linear programming problem over possible true outcomes.

Universal axioms, stated as linear equalities, constrain every finite test alongside the obvious counting limits. Solving the problem reveals which group performance levels remain logically possible. As a practical demo, he builds alarms that need no ground truth at all. Applied to language model judges grading MT-Bench outputs, disagreement patterns from twenty-five pair comparisons triggered alarms whenever grading quality fell below thresholds that the user sets in advance.
arxiv-2510-01021:
Bandeira surveys random matrix theory and the intrinsic freeness phenomenon in this 2025 arXiv lecture text, written for his invited talk at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia in summer 2026. Random matrices underpin work in statistics, physics, and computer science, from sample covariance in the 1920s to Wigner's semicircle law for nuclear physics. The hard part is usually bounding the largest eigenvalue of a random matrix with certainty, not just on average.

Bandeira explains how intrinsic freeness yields sharp, easy-to-use bounds that hold at finite sizes. The key point is that many random matrices behave almost like free variables from operator algebra, even in modest dimensions. He walks through the main theorems in plain steps and gives two applications in high-dimensional statistical inference. Open problems, including a conjecture for general finite groups, close the lecture.
arxiv-2510-01421:
Guo and co-authors find two satellite gas halos glowing beside giant nebulae around galaxy groups when the universe was young. Lyman-alpha emission traces massive dark matter halos at redshift three, and giant glowing nebulae mark the biggest. Follow-up spectroscopy targeted four such giants and found company beside two.

Each satellite halo sits a few hundred thousand light-years from its giant, sharing nearly the same velocity. Their sizes span tens of thousands of light-years, with halo masses near the group scale. Small velocity offsets suggest filaments of cosmic structure connect each pair. Simulations predicted exactly this abundance of massive satellites. MUSE spectroscopy followed up the earlier wide-field discoveries. One central galaxy sits puzzlingly quiet amid the glowing gas. Halo mass estimates place both satellites at group scale. Occurrence rates match what structure-formation simulations expect. Nebulae advertise halos too faint to see directly.
arxiv-2510-01521:
Maji and co-authors present Carbon X, an open tool that forecasts the carbon intensity of electricity grids worldwide. Carbon-aware computing shifts work to cleaner hours, but it needs fine-grained forecasts for each grid. Older tools demand grid-specific fuel data, train a separate model per grid, and give no sense of their own uncertainty.

Carbon X leans on time series foundation models, which transfer patterns learned across many series. One general model, fed only past carbon data, forecasts and fills gaps for over two hundred grids. Zero-shot accuracy landed near the best specialist tools on benchmark grids. Calibrated intervals tell users how much trust each forecast deserves. Forecasts reach three weeks ahead, long enough for planning flexible workloads. Imputation fills missing stretches in grid records, a common headache for smaller utilities. Code and data are released for other sustainability researchers.
arxiv-2510-01721:
Mandal, Murthy, and Srikant give the first finite-time guarantees for a robust learning method in this 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning agents are often trained in one environment and deployed in a slightly different one. Distributionally robust methods guard against that gap by optimizing for the worst plausible environment. Temporal-difference learning is the classic way to judge a policy's long-term reward.

The authors combine robustness with temporal-difference learning under linear function approximation. Their setting measures environment drift with total-variation and Wasserstein distance sets. The algorithm is model-free and needs no simulator access to the environment. It pairs a two-time-scale update with an outer loop that refreshes a target network. They prove a sample complexity bound for reaching a chosen accuracy. The result closes a gap between the practical success of robust methods and the guarantees available for ordinary ones.
arxiv-2510-02221:
Li, Tan, Liu, and Ren route sound-like vibrations one way through a chiral nanohelix using phonon spin in this 2025 physics paper. Controlling nanoscale heat and vibration flows is central to nano-energy devices and sensing. Phonons carry a spin angular momentum that couples to other spinful fields, such as circularly polarized light. That coupling offers a handle most phononics ignores.

Shining circularly polarized infrared light converts photon spin into collective phonon spin in the chiral structure. The interference excites axial phonons traveling in one direction only. In the smallest chiral carbon nanotube, the rectification rate approaches one hundred percent. Molecular dynamics simulations confirm the near-ideal one-way routing.
