Using theory and particle in cell simulations for a cold, collisionless plasma, the team derives a formula for growth rates. They find an aligned external field always slows the mushroom instability, though it resists the field far more than a smaller scale instability does. The analysis also covers related modes and clarifies when jets can still amplify their fields.
arxiv-2510-24321:
Ivica Dimitrovski and two co-authors explore prompt learning as a cheap way to adapt the vision language model CLIP to remote sensing scene classification with few labels. Deep learning for this task is limited by scarce labeled data and costly annotation across regions and sensors. CLIP transfers well in general, but a large domain gap makes its direct use on satellite imagery suboptimal.

Prompt learning adjusts only small text prompts, leaving the big model frozen. The team systematically evaluates several representative prompt methods in the few shot setting. They assess how well each adapts CLIP's semantics to remote sensing scenes, offering guidance for low label earth observation tasks.
arxiv-2510-24521:
Nicolas Nessi and Peter Reimann, two authors, study typical motion in lattice systems. Their systems are classical, with smooth variables on grid sites. Start states are drawn at random, with each variable drawn alone. The pair ask if most starts lead to near-identical histories. They track bulk traits, the large-scale values a lab would measure.

Their proof says yes: most random starts give the same history. Measure concentration, a math fact about high dimensions, drives the proof. It bounds how far any start can stray from the typical path. The one demand is that local changes fade fast with distance. The result covers Hamiltonian systems and many dissipative ones too. Two worked examples, a map lattice and coupled rotors, show the scope.
arxiv-2510-24621:
Ziyi Fang, Lingxiao Huang, and Runkai Yang work on a short form of a large data set that still gives good cost reads. Their goal is the strong middle point task, where a few wild points should not pull the answer off course. Past short forms grew in size as the wild point count grew.

Their new short form drops that tie to the wild point count when the data set is large enough. They also give a best size for the one line case, and stretch the result to group tasks. In tests, their method beat past ones on size, score, and speed.
arxiv-2510-24821:
Inclusion AI leads a large team that built Ming-Flash-Omni, a sparse model that reads and makes text, image, and sound in one frame. Most of its vast weight set sleeps at each step; just a small share wakes per word piece. That sparse plan lets the model grow large while each run stays cheap.

Next to its past form, the new model scores far higher on joint sight and word tests. It can switch tasks mid chat with no restart. For sound, it reads speech with place and tone sense, and can make speech, sound, and music in one stream. For sight, it adds new make and edit tools.
arxiv-2510-25421:
Lewis Cockram led eight co-authors on driver fatigue. Yueteng Yu, Jorge Pardo, and Xiaomeng Li helped. Andry Rakotonirainy, Jonny Kuo, and Sebastien Demmel followed. Mike Lenne and Ronald Schroeter complete the team. Their 2025 paper studies conditional automated driving. Passive fatigue can compromise driver readiness and safety. Drivers must resume control when automation requests it.

A language model conversational agent checked in with drivers. It aimed to re-engage them with surroundings. The study ran on a real test track. Forty participants drove in automated scenarios there. In-car video, sleepiness ratings, and interviews were analyzed. The agent helped support vigilance during passive fatigue. Interactions shaped driver alertness in observed sessions. Acceptability analysis revealed three user preference profiles. Those profiles affect future intention to use agents. Adaptive design should serve diverse user groups, they argue. Natural language can support context-aware interaction in cars.
arxiv-2510-25721:
Yi W Ren led twenty-three co-authors observing a distant galaxy. Akio K Inoue, Javier Alvarez-Marquez, and Takuya Hashimoto helped. Their 2025 astronomy paper uses JWST readings. The galaxy SXDF-NB1006-2 sits at redshift seven point two. Near-infrared camera and spectrograph data were studied.

Spectral energy distribution fitting derives physical traits. The target is a young starburst galaxy. Its age is about two million years only. An intense radiation field characterizes the starburst. Multiple nebular output lines are detected in spectra. A robust broad oxygen output part appears. That indicates ionized gas outflows from galaxy. Gas depletion time is a few hundred million years. The target could progenitor massive quiescent galaxies later. Optical and far-infrared output morphologies differ spatially. Varied critical densities and inhomogeneous distributions explain that. Likely old stellar populations may explain metallicity. Future mid-infrared readings can confirm their presence.
arxiv-2510-25821:
Avery J. Tishue, Charuhas Shiveshwarkar, and Gilbert Holder examine a snag in using galaxy motions to probe the early universe. The method uses the kinetic Sunyaev Zeldovich effect, where moving gas slightly shifts the cosmic microwave background, to rebuild large scale velocity fields. Recent rebuilds came out weaker than models predicted, which hints that the link between galaxies and free electrons was overstated.

Tishue and the team test what that overstatement means for limits on local primordial non Gaussianity, a measure of unevenness in the early universe. With standard assumptions, future surveys would sharpen the limits a lot. With the weaker electron link, the gains can shrink in an important way.
arxiv-2510-25921:
Nikola L. Kolev, Tommaso Rodani, Neil J. Curson, Taylor J. Z. Stock, and Alberto Cazzaniga use machine learning to repair and sharpen images from a scanning tunneling microscope. This microscope images surfaces at atomic scale, but its sharp tip degrades and its slow serial scanning limits speed. Large voltages used in making samples can also blunt the tip, forcing time consuming reconditioning.

Kolev and the team train flow matching and diffusion models, two kinds of generative image models, on synthetic data built with physics input. They start from only thirty six clean real images of a hydrogen covered silicon surface. The trained models restore damaged images and rebuild sharp images from sparse samples, cutting acquisition time by a factor of two to four.
arxiv-2510-26021:
Michael Ion and Alex McDonough study chip firing dynamics on a special combinatorial object called the R10 matroid. Chip firing is a game like process where chips pile on vertices and spill to neighbors when a pile grows too tall. A matroid is an abstract structure that captures independence. R10 is a ten element, rank five example that a theorem by Seymour shows is a basic building block for all regular matroids.

Ion and McDonough give a simple description of chip firing on R10 using complex numbers placed on the vertices of a pentagon. They also give an easy set of representatives for each of the one hundred sixty two classes in its sandpile group. They also link to an app for hands on play.
arxiv-2510-26221:
Pushpendra Yadav, working alone, presents a thesis on exciton dynamics in two dimensional materials, in both calm and strongly driven regimes. An exciton is a bound pair of an electron and a hole, and such pairs govern how non conducting solids absorb and emit light. Behavior at high exciting density, where an electron hole liquid can form, is far less studied than the balance case.

Using first principles methods, the GW approach and the Bethe Salpeter equation, Yadav shows how rising photo excited carrier density drives a redshift to blueshift crossing point in exciton energies. Electron phonon links reshape optical spectra and life spans at finite temperature. Combining these effects, an electron hole liquid forms above a critical density and below a critical temperature, held stable to higher temperatures by strong links in two dimensions.
arxiv-2510-26321:
Oscar Veenema leads twenty six co-authors in a study of shock heating in the star forming regions around the center of the galaxy NGC 7582. The galaxy is a dust obscured Seyfert 2, an active galaxy whose central engine is hidden. Using combined integral field spectroscopy from two Webb telescope instruments, they map pure rotational lines of molecular hydrogen across the nuclear and surrounding regions.

Temperature distributions follow a characteristic power law in each aperture. Two southern star forming regions show unexpectedly high molecular gas temperatures, comparable to the active nucleus itself. Veenema and the team test direct photoionization, ultraviolet fluorescence from young clusters, and shock excitation as heat sources. They find shock heating most plausible. Several infrared tracers and dense gas in their models support that view.
arxiv-2510-26921:
Moonsoo Jeong, Dongbeen Kim, Minseong Kim, and Sungkil Lee improve 3D Gaussian Splatting by splitting its primitives more cleverly. The method renders scenes from many soft three-dimensional blobs, and its adaptive density control decides where to split them. The standard rule looks only at the size of positional gradients, which can split wastefully.

Jeong and his three co-authors add directional consistency, the angular coherence of those gradients, to the decision. That better captures local structural complexity and avoids redundant splitting. When a split is needed, the same measure places the children to align with local structure instead of at random. In their experiments, the method cut the number of primitives by up to thirty percent while greatly improving reconstruction fidelity.
arxiv-2510-27421:
Aditya Parikh, Sneha Das, and Aasa Feragen audit fairness in automated breast tumor segmentation labels from the MAMA-MIA dataset. Fairness checks usually stop at classification, yet biased segmentation can quietly degrade care quality for some groups and compound across clinical decisions and model iterations. The team evaluates automated segmentation quality across age, ethnicity, and data source.

Their analysis reveals an intrinsic age-related bias against younger patients that persists after controlling for confounders such as data source. Physiology may contribute, a known challenge for radiologists and automated systems alike. Aggregating multiple data sources also shifts site-specific ethnic biases in the results. The authors stress granular, subgroup-level data investigation as necessary practice before deploying segmentation models in diagnostic workflows.
arxiv-2511-00521:
Bao Nguyen, Hieu Trung Nguyen, Ruifeng She, Xiaojin Fu, and Viet Anh Nguyen tackle a meta-problem: for each new query, which reasoning method should a language model use? Common practice samples many candidate answers and aggregates them, assuming more candidates means more accuracy. The authors test that assumption with a rigorous analysis and derive accuracy bounds for standard aggregation under fixed generation settings.

On that foundation they build EPIC, a planning framework that learns a shared space linking queries, reasoning methods, and model abilities through contrastive learning. Their probability bounds enter as a regularizer, balancing accuracy against computing cost. Across varied math reasoning tasks, EPIC consistently picked the best method for each query, improving accuracy while cutting overhead. Smart selection, the work suggests, beats brute sampling.
arxiv-2511-00721:
Thanh Nha To and four co-authors design fair, secure links for systems that sense and communicate at once. Integrated sensing and communication shares spectrum between radar-like sensing and data service. Their design adds two tools: surfaces that transmit and reflect signals simultaneously, and rate-splitting access that divides messages into common and private parts. Each sensing target doubles as a potential eavesdropper, a realistic threat.

The team jointly optimizes base station beamforming and the surface coefficients to maximize the minimum secrecy rate across users, fairness built into the objective, while holding a floor under sensing beam quality. The non-convex problem yields to alternating optimization with a majorization-minimization method. Simulations verify fast convergence and significant gains in secure communication performance.
arxiv-2511-01021:
Sainik Karak and Tanmoy Paul study extension problems for p-compact operators between Banach spaces. The question is when an operator defined on a smaller space can be extended to a larger domain. It must keep its special compactness property. A second question asks the same for the operator's adjoint.

Much of the analysis assumes the spaces involved are projection friendly spaces of a standard type. The authors ask whether extensions, when they exist, can be chosen to almost preserve the norm. Often an operator can be extended to a larger domain if the codomain is enlarged as well, and under extra assumptions the range can be kept the same. They also derive necessary and sufficient conditions for a Banach space to be an L1-predual.
arxiv-2511-01221:
Kazuki Hiroe and Daisuke Yamakawa study wild character varieties, spaces that parametrize certain equations with irregular singularities on compact Riemann surfaces. The tame cousins, with only regular singularities, are far better understood, and bridging the two has been an open problem in the geometry of these moduli spaces.

The authors construct Poisson maps from wild to tame character varieties by unfolding each irregular singularity into regular ones. They then show these unfolding maps are Poisson birational equivalences, meaning the wild and tame spaces match up at the level of their Poisson geometry away from small excluded sets. The result answers yes to a conjecture posed by Klimes, Paul, and Ramis.
arxiv-2511-01421:
Arda Kosay and colleagues steer city traffic without charging tolls. Connected and automated vehicles make intersections programmable, and their framework uses that: roadside units adjust timestamp based scheduling, in effect delaying or advancing vehicles on particular paths. That nudges drivers' routing choices toward flows that are better for everyone.

A hierarchical design separates real time intersection control from network level coordination, and the model becomes a congestion game with path dependent node costs. The authors prove equilibrium flows exist and are essentially unique, removing ambiguity and making a tractable two level optimization for designing the incentives. On the standard Sioux Falls test network, the scheme cut the gap between selfish user equilibrium and the system optimum by up to about seventy one percent.
arxiv-2511-01721:
Thierry Goudon and Antoine Mellet analyze flocks in the extreme where attraction and repulsion between individuals become very strong. Their starting point is a mean-field kinetic model of a population, organisms or particles. The population is pushed around by mutual interactions and an external velocity field. They study the singular limit as the interaction forces grow.

For well-prepared initial data, the population piles up inside a moving domain. The domain's shape is fixed by minimizing the interaction energy, while its center of mass rides the external field. Inside the domain, the organisms' flow obeys a classical hydrodynamic model, the lake equation. That result needs only existence and uniqueness of energy minimizers. It holds for general interaction kernels. The internal-flow part uses a modulated energy method, under stricter assumptions.
arxiv-2511-01821:
Soham Chanda and Amanda Hirschi build a new algebraic structure for contact geometry, a branch of math that studies spaces with a special twisting structure at each point. Their starting point is contact homology, a tool that counts closed orbits of a flow on such a space to tell spaces apart. The paper adapts a method called global Kuranishi charts to this contact setting.

For any closed contact manifold with no degenerate orbits, the pair build what they call a flow category. Its building blocks are the Reeb orbits of the manifold and the spaces of pseudo-holomorphic buildings that link them. The construction lifts contact homology, so it keeps that older tool's information in a richer form. It is also natural: an exact symplectic cobordism between two manifolds yields a matching flow bimodule between their flow categories.
arxiv-2511-01921:
Roberta Fiandaca and Manil Dev Gomony shrink neural radio receivers so they can run on constrained hardware. Neural receivers beat classic designs but carry heavy compute cost. The authors attack the cost from two sides, quantization and compression, both keyed to the Fibonacci coding scheme.

They introduce uniform and non-uniform quantization schemes. One is Fibonacci code word quantization. Another is a refined, fine-grained version of incremental network quantization. It recovers accuracy lost in the process. Two new lossless squeezing algorithms then exploit the patterns in sequences of Fibonacci-quantized weights. Quantizing alone cut multiplier power by about 45 percent. It cut area by about 44 percent. Squeezing reduced the memory footprint by about 63 percent. The receiver still outperformed a standard one.
arxiv-2511-02021:
Daniel Klocke and a large international team report a landmark climate computation: the first global simulation of the full Earth system at kilometer scale. Their model resolves the planet at a grid spacing of 1.25 kilometers, coupling atmosphere, ocean, and land so that energy, water, and carbon flow through all three at a resolution where storms and ocean eddies appear explicitly.

The run harnessed two of the world's largest GPU installations. One had 8,192 graphics processors on the Alps system. The other had 20,480 on JUPITER. The team used the ICON code base, its components balanced across Grace CPUs and Hopper GPUs. A separation-of-concerns redesign halved the code's complexity while raising performance and portability. The machine sustained about 146 simulated days per real day. That time compression beats even earlier atmosphere-only simulations at similar resolution. It opens long, fully coupled Earth system studies.
arxiv-2511-02121:
Anastasia Matveeva studies when sequences defined by recurrences with polynomial coefficients consist only of whole numbers. These are tied to their generating functions, which satisfy differential equations. Whether they stay bounded decides much of their arithmetic nature. Classical work gave an integrality test for Motzkin-type sequences, but elsewhere ad hoc methods ruled.

Matveeva revisits that test with tools from differential algebra and builds a unified approach to boundedness and algebraicity across a wider holonomic class. The central product is an algorithm that decides whether all, none, or a one-parameter family of cases for certain second-order recurrences stay bounded. It succeeds on several well-known cases listed in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences.
arxiv-2511-02221:
Lei Tan and six co-authors trawl a major Chinese spectroscopic survey for a distinctive class of stars. Be stars are fast-spinning B-type stars whose spectra show hydrogen emission lines from material they have flung into a disk, and they matter for understanding how stars evolve and form disks. The team built a labelled dataset from the eleventh data release of LAMOST, a telescope that records spectra in bulk.

A classifier combining convolutional and memory networks reached 97.86 percent accuracy on held-out spectra. Applied broadly, then cross-checked with an automated classification tool and by hand, the pipeline confirmed over forty thousand B-type spectra. Matching against published emission-line catalogues produced a sample of 8,298 Be stars, more than half of them new discoveries, which the team further split into classical and Herbig types using colour information.
arxiv-2511-02521:
Romy Peled, Daniel Kroening, Michael Tautschnig, and Yakir Vizel put language models to work on one of hardware verification's most manual chores: finding the inductive invariant that proves a chip design correct. Their system, a neurosymbolic pipeline, has the model propose candidate lemmas and invariants through two prompting frameworks. A formal symbolic tool checks every proposal, so nothing unverified slips through.

With enough reprompting, the models produced provably correct inductive arguments for mid-size open-source register-transfer-level designs. At least one of the two prompting setups succeeded on eighty-four percent of the problem set. The authors frame the result as practical relief for formal verification engineers. The creative search for lemmas can be partly automated, while the guarantee of correctness still comes from the symbolic checker, not from the language model's confidence.
arxiv-2511-02721:
Translators often add small explanations so readers in another culture can follow a text. Doreen Osmelak and four colleagues built PETra, a multilingual corpus for that habit, called pragmatic explicitation, and describe it in a 2025 paper. It spans eight language pairs drawn from TED talks and European Parliament records.

The corpus tags additions like short entity descriptions, converted measurements, and translator remarks. The team found candidates where words had no direct match in the source, then refined them with active learning and human checks. Entity and system-level additions proved most common. Active learning lifted classifier accuracy by seven to eight points, reaching 0.88 accuracy in the best cases. The resource makes a slippery habit measurable.
arxiv-2511-03421:
Shihai Wang and Tao Chen present LQPR, a light tool that turns written performance demands into checkable numbers automatically. Engineers must quantify such demands for tuning and testing, yet hand quantification is slow and error prone because wording stays vague. LQPR reframes the job as classification under a new theoretical frame.

Rather than lean on large language models, the tool exploits the short, patterned phrasing that performance demands tend to use. A linguistically induced matcher reads those patterns directly. Trials against nine rivals test speed and accuracy on real requirement sets. Fast, cheap quantification could let teams check far more demands than manual review ever allows.
arxiv-2511-03521:
Mohamed Swailem and Alastair M Rucklidge add seasons to the classic predator-prey model and watch order give way to chaos. Carrying capacity now pulses with time, standing in for seasonal swings in food or nutrients. Steady coexistence disappears under that pulsing, though letting the predation rate pulse as well can restore a balance point.

That balance can still break through parametric resonance into slower or matched cycles, even when predation stays constant. Period-doubling steps and outright chaotic swings appear across the parameter map. Letting numbers vary across space, with diffusion added, yields spatial patterns on top of the timing chaos. Seasonal forcing, the work shows, is not a small wiggle on the classic model but a driver of rich behavior.
arxiv-2511-04021:
Sergio Demian Lerner and Ariel Futoransky present OTS-PC, a bidirectional payment channel design for the Lightning Network based on one-time signatures over state sequence numbers. Payment channels let two parties transact off-chain, and the widely used Poon-Dryja construction carries well-known complexity in stored data and privacy.

The new construction is described as simpler than Poon-Dryja while keeping compatibility with Lightning routing. Storage per channel stays constant rather than growing with use, and information leakage is kept minimal. Those properties matter for scaling everyday Bitcoin payments, where channels may update many times and operators cannot retain ever-growing revocation data for every channel they hold.
arxiv-2511-04121:
Sayed Shafaat Mahmud, Adiba Amira Siddiqa, and Cosmin Ilie present the photometry first part of a neural search for dark stars. These are hypothetical first stars powered by dark matter annihilation, if dark matter consists of weakly interacting massive particles. Such stars could grow supermassive and shine like galaxies.

Earlier chi-squared fitting had flagged three photometric candidates in deep survey data from the James Webb Space Telescope. A feedforward network trained for the same search reconfirmed two of those candidates by goodness of fit. The network ran about ten thousand times faster than the Nelder-Mead minimization used before. Speed matters because the public high-redshift datasets needing screening are very large.
arxiv-2511-04621:
Ankan Pandey and two colleagues chart complex dynamics in a triad of Stuart-Landau oscillators. These equations are a basic model for synchronization and emergent order. The triad is coupled in one direction only, and its members are non-isochronous, so speed depends on amplitude.

Steady states and their stability anchor the team's analysis. Coupling strength, network shape, and frequency gaps all shape the outcome in tangled ways. They trace a route into quasiperiodic synchronization, where rhythms lock in a layered pattern. Bridging such theory with experiments is a stated aim, since real systems rarely match simple coupled models.
arxiv-2511-04821:
Aatiya Ali and her co-author clean energetic proton data from the GOES satellites with machine learning. GOES has watched space weather from geostationary orbit for over thirty years. Its proton channels, though, suffer contamination when higher-energy protons leak false signals.

That leakage inflates low-energy flux readings, including the key ten to fifty megaelectronvolt band. Earth's magnetosphere adds further distortions on top. No universal correction exists in the public data today. Their regression approach aims to remove both effects, giving solar particle event forecasts the clean inputs they need to be trustworthy.
arxiv-2511-04921:
Yu Li leads six authors with AgentExpt, an agent that automates AI experiment design. Language model agents now handle retrieval and complex reasoning on the web. Designing experiments needs the right datasets and baselines, chosen with judgment.

Older recommenders harvest candidates only from public portals, missing many used in papers. They also lean on surface similarity, which can pick poorly suited resources. AgentExpt retrieves resources with an agent that reads how the field actually cites them. Collective practice in published work guides the picks. Better starting resources could save researchers weeks of setup on each new study.
arxiv-2511-05021:
Leixin Wu and co-authors study secure key exchange at terahertz rates with many antennas, in a form that needs no trust in the measuring device. Detector flaws can open holes in quantum key systems, even when the core math is safe.

Their plan hands all measurement to an untrusted third party, which removes detector attacks. Beam shaping turns the many-antenna link into a set of parallel lossy channels for key sharing. They derive key rates for two protocol styles, in both long-run and finite cases, and stress antenna layout and detector quality in tests.
arxiv-2511-05621:
Daniil Yurshevich gives an algorithm to list all finite groups of matrices whose entries lie in a quadratic number field. Such fields extend the rationals by a single square root, and they host many matrix groups of math interest. A full classification method for finite matrix groups over number fields is the paper's stated goal.

The algorithm rests on the representation theory of finite groups, the study of how groups act through matrices. By leaning on that theory, the method can in principle determine every finite example over the field in question. The work is a short, focused contribution to computational group theory, aimed at readers who classify symmetry groups given in matrix form.
arxiv-2511-05821:
Rujiphart Charatvaraphan and co-authors present PyGress, a web tool that grades the Python skill level shown in open-source projects. Judging developer proficiency helps explain how projects evolve and where expertise sits. PyGress builds on an existing analyzer that scores code against language-learning levels from beginner to advanced.

A user submits a GitHub repository link. The tool then pulls the commit history, scores the code level across it, and draws summaries for each contributor and the whole project. It also tracks how the project's code level moves over time. The authors offer PyGress as an interactive way to explore coding levels in Python repositories, with source code and a video demonstration made public.
arxiv-2511-05921:
Ankan Mullick and co-authors cut the human labeling cost of teaching voice assistants new intents. Voice agents act on a fixed set of user intents. When confidence runs low, requests get rejected and need manual labels. Over time, rejected requests also hide new intents the agent should learn, and labeling everything is impractical.

Their framework, IDALC, detects intents with light supervision and uses active learning to pick which rejected requests are worth human labels. Across benchmark data sets it beat baselines on accuracy and macro-F1 by clear margins. Labeling cost stayed at a small share of the unlabeled pool. The authors present the system as a practical way to keep voice agents current without armies of annotators.
arxiv-2511-06921:
Siddhartha Mahajan, Harsh Raj, and Sonam Tanwar investigate traffic congestion around the North Campus of Delhi University. Rather than counting cars at a few moments, they simulate vehicle movement continuously in the UXSim platform, letting cars interact intersection by intersection. The study concentrates on several key junctions where congestion recurs.

Within the simulated campus network, the team tested standard remedies rather than new construction. Optimizing traffic signal timing and modestly reconfiguring certain intersections produced measurable gains in flow. The authors present the work as useful guidance for local traffic managers, and as evidence that continuous-time simulation can inform both quick actions and longer-term planning for crowded university districts.
arxiv-2511-07521:
George Andrews and colleagues refine a key operator in supersymmetric field theory. For a special class of four-dimensional theories, the Kontsevich-Soibelman operator encodes how particle spectra jump between chambers. The authors add a refinement suited to theories whose quiver diagrams split into sources and sinks.

Traces of the refined operator appear tied to the Macdonald index, a refined count of protected states. Closed-form guesses are offered for Argyres-Douglas theories across a broad family. Evidence gathered supports the link. A proven connection would let physicists compute hard indices from operator data, streamlining the study of strongly coupled quantum systems.
arxiv-2511-07821:
Lu Gan and Xi Li manufacture a voice-command dataset without recording studios. On-device keyword spotting for tiny hardware needs many labeled commands, yet collecting human recordings is slow and expensive. Their SynTTS-Commands dataset is synthesized entirely with a modern text-to-speech system.

Speaker embeddings borrowed from public corpora diversify the synthetic voices across English and Chinese commands. Benchmarks across efficient acoustic models test whether fake voices teach real skills. Strong results would validate synthetic data as a scalable stand-in for recordings. Voice interfaces for low-power devices, appliances, and toys depend on exactly this kind of cheap, multilingual training material.
arxiv-2511-08021:
Josselin Garnier and Laurent Mertz propose a control variate method to speed Monte Carlo estimates for stochastic differential equations. Such estimates average many simulated paths, and cutting their error without huge cost is a constant goal. Their method pairs a fine time step simulation with a cheaper coarse one driven by a parabolic picture of Brownian motion.

Both simulations share the same fine Brownian increments, so they stay strongly coupled. The coarse expectation comes from a separate Monte Carlo run. The authors characterize how squared error falls with budget and step orders, and numerical tests on representative equations confirm the efficiency gains.
arxiv-2511-08621:
Gaëtan Caillaut and six co-authors release a family of language models tuned for finance, where general models often stumble on domain language. The LLM Pro Finance Suite holds five instruction-tuned models from eight to seventy billion parameters, trained on a curated corpus that is more than half financial text in English, French, and German.

Rather than training from scratch, the team builds on strong general models and preserves their instruction following and safety behavior. On a broad financial benchmark suite the models beat the compared state-of-the-art baselines, including on financial translation tasks. General-domain skill stays intact, so the models can drop into existing workflows. Two of the smaller models are released publicly to support further financial language research.
arxiv-2511-08821:
Ismail Lamaakal and four co-authors reframe neural network compression as a problem of managing uncertainty about the weights. Quantization shrinks models by storing weights in few bits, and BayesQ is built to choose those bits by minimizing the loss expected under a posterior distribution over the weights.

A lightweight Gaussian posterior, fitted by a Laplace approximation, is used to whiten the weights before codebooks are designed for least expected distortion. A greedy knapsack then hands out mixed precision bit by bit where each bit buys the most expected-loss reduction. Optional distillation on calibration data alone aligns the small model with the full one. At three to four bits per weight on image and language benchmarks, BayesQ edges out strong baselines such as GPTQ by small but consistent margins.
arxiv-2511-09121:
Molla Basir Ahamed and Partha Pratim Roy study meromorphic functions that stretch the disk in a controlled way. The class at hand holds univalent meromorphic functions on the unit disk with a pole of prescribed order at an interior point. Each admits a quasiconformal extension to the whole Riemann sphere with bounded distortion.

Using the area theorem and convolution methods, the authors prove a generalized area-type inequality and extract explicit analytic conditions for membership in the class. The convolution theorem is pushed to a modified Hadamard product of several such functions. Sufficient conditions keep the product inside a related class. That class is set by the factors' distortion constants and the pole position. A criterion covers sense-preserving harmonic mappings on convex domains, and the sharp Schwarzian norm is computed for the simple pole case, improving a 2016 result.
arxiv-2511-09221:
Vukan Ninkovic and Dejan Vukobratovic teach a small autoencoder to design binary error-correcting codes for noisy channels. Autoencoder approaches learn encoders and decoders end to end, but forcing binary codewords breaks gradient flow during training. Their fix is a simple two-stage procedure with no gradient approximation tricks.

Training starts with continuous pretraining, followed by direct binarization and fine-tuning. For the seven-bit, four-information-bit configuration over a binary symmetric channel, the learned pair recovers a rotated version of the optimal Hamming code. It reproduces that code's linear structure and distance properties, and matches its block error rate under maximum likelihood decoding. Compact autoencoders, the result suggests, can find algebraically optimal codes through stable training.
arxiv-2511-10521:
Shahar Hod studies how long a disturbance can linger around a charged black hole. Working with the Reissner-Nordström spacetime, he considers a massive scalar field around the hole and focuses on the large-mass regime, where the field's mass far exceeds the inverse size of the hole.

Hod proves analytically that the combined system supports quasi-resonances, perturbation modes whose lifetimes can be arbitrarily long. For each fixed ratio of the black hole's charge to its mass, he determines a critical mass spectrum that characterizes these long-lived modes. The result gives an exact handle on a system where resonances normally have to be computed numerically, and it clarifies how charge shapes the slowest-decaying disturbances a black hole can hold.
arxiv-2511-10721:
Sheng-Yu Wang, Aaron Hertzmann, Alexei A. Efros, Richard Zhang, and Jun-Yan Zhu make data attribution practical for text-to-image models. Attribution asks which training images most influenced a given generated picture, a question with legal and creative stakes, but existing methods burn heavy computation on every single query.

Their idea is distillation: take a slow attribution method based on unlearning. Its judgments are compressed into a feature embedding space where influential training images can be retrieved with fast indexing and search. At deployment, no expensive attribution algorithm runs at all. Tests on models trained on MSCOCO and on Stable Diffusion trained on LAION matched or beat prior methods. They answered in a few seconds, thousands to hundreds of thousands of times faster than the methods they compared against.
arxiv-2511-10821:
Iván Olarte Rodríguez and five co-authors introduce MECHBench, a benchmark suite for black-box optimization drawn from structural mechanics rather than invented math problems. Most established suites use abstract made-up functions, which only partly reflect the messy problems engineers actually optimize, limiting what algorithm developers learn from them.

The suite's current cases come from vehicle crashworthiness, scenarios whose non-smooth, highly nonlinear models force the use of gradient-free methods. For each benchmark, the paper describes the physical context, writes out the optimization problem precisely, and gives clear guidelines for using the suite correctly. The authors aim to give the optimization community test problems with real engineering stakes. Search behavior measured on the bench should then say more about performance in practice.
arxiv-2511-10921:
Ming Zhong, Zhemin Zhang, and their colleagues present MERA, a tool that builds quantum programs with care for mid-run checks. Those checks let a chip reuse qubits and steer the work, but they also bring noise from nearby qubits, waiting, and resets. The error rate differs a lot from qubit to qubit on one chip.

MERA first maps the error rate for each qubit, then uses that map to place work, route links, and set timing. It also adds shielding steps to cut noise while qubits wait. Across twenty-seven test programs, it raised the chance of a right answer by about a quarter to a half over the standard tool.
arxiv-2511-11121:
E. Tahtali, C. Kreuzig, and their colleagues describe a platform that recreates the weak gravity of asteroids and comets inside a drop tower on Earth. Such small bodies draw growing interest, fed by missions to visit them, but their feeble pull is hard to copy in a lab. The platform targets pull levels far below Earth's, held for a few seconds at a time.

A motor-driven rig with spindle axes moves a comet-like sample so the felt acceleration matches the target level. The work sits inside a project on comet activity under partial gravity. Getting the timing and load right is the core engineering task, and the setup now carries its full test load.
arxiv-2511-11221:
Tyler Wheeler, Michelle Kuchera, and their colleagues test sparse neural networks for turning particle detector data into compact vector summaries. Time projection chambers rebuild charged-particle tracks in a gas and serve many nuclear physics experiments. Good event summaries would speed up searches for rare decays and reactions in that flood of signals.

A sparse ResNet design gave useful structured summaries even with random weights, and light pre-training on a simple physics task improved them further. The team trained on one detector tuned for low-energy decays and probed the summaries for rich event structure. The same encoder also handled a second detector well, with gains when trained on the first.
arxiv-2511-11421:
Lan Li, Tao Hu, and their colleagues present BOFA, a framework that lets the vision-language model CLIP learn new classes step by step without forgetting old ones and without adding parts. Extra learnable modules usually raise complexity and forgetting risk, and the strengths of the visual and textual sides are rarely fused well. BOFA confines all adaptation to CLIP's existing cross-modal bridge layer, so no parameters or inference cost are added.

Inside that layer, an orthogonal low-rank fusion rule constrains updates to a safe subspace built to be orthogonal to past task features. Knowledge then accumulates stably with no replay of old data. A cross-modal hybrid step further joins the two sides.
arxiv-2511-11621:
Pedro Antunes and six co-authors introduce AIvailable, a platform for serving large language models from a mixed pool of older and varied graphics cards. Most inference frameworks assume uniform, powerful hardware, an assumption that fails in universities and other budget-limited settings.

A software-defined design runs models fully on GPUs, across both NVIDIA and AMD nodes, with no fallback to slow CPU work. Four components, including a unified client interface, present all deployed models as one logical service while squeezing full use from each card's memory. For labs holding mixed hardware, the platform offers a low-cost route to dependable language model service.
arxiv-2511-12121:
Wanlong Fang, Tianle Zhang and Alvin Chan ask a direct question about multimodal learning: does forcing different kinds of data to align always help? Models often align text, image and other representations so they can be combined. Past work mostly watched alignment that arose on its own, rather than testing enforced alignment itself.

The authors add a contrastive module whose alignment strength they can set during training. Tests on synthetic and real data show the effect depends on how much the modalities repeat each other. Too much or too little alignment can hurt, and the best level balances shared signals with signals that belong to one modality alone.
arxiv-2511-12221:
Qin-Sheng Zhu and four co-authors build a quantum diffusion model for preparing quantum states, framed through open system dynamics. In diffusion models, a clean state is gradually corrupted and a learned reverse process restores it. Here the forward step is read as natural decoherence, described by quantum master equations.

Their model treats each step as a quantum channel written with Kraus operators, and keeps those channels physically valid by optimizing on a special manifold. Tailored training and losses use that structure for faithful reconstruction. Tests from single qubits up to entangled seven-qubit states report very high fidelity under both random and depolarizing noise.
arxiv-2511-12421:
Xiaoyu Huang, Blake Jackson and Kyu-Hwan Lee show how machine learning can help discover a combinatorial bijection, an explicit one-to-one matching between two families of objects. Many problems in algebraic combinatorics reduce to building such a matching. Traditionally researchers stare at data until a pattern appears, but patterns may only emerge at scales beyond human inspection.

As a proof of concept, they train a transformer on paired Dyck paths, lattice paths that never drop below the diagonal. Patterns in what the model attends to lead them to a new algorithmic description of the classical zeta map, which they call the Scaffolding Map. The workflow offers a template for similar searches.
arxiv-2511-12521:
Michal R. Wrobel presents a human-centered method for mapping named emotions onto the continuous valence-arousal-dominance space, the three scales that describe feeling from unpleasant to pleasant, calm to excited, and weak to strong. Discrete labels and dimensional scores are hard to combine, which blocks the merging of useful datasets for training emotion models.

The proxy method asks people to make a simple geometric animation that stands for a given emotion, then rate their own animation on the three scales. Those user-made artifacts bridge the two models without a purely computational mapping. Two iterative user studies validated and refined the approach, and their combined data yield a full mapping between the label and dimensional systems.
arxiv-2511-13021:
Sachin Vashistha and four co-authors test whether language models keep track of a conversation's world. Following a dialogue means maintaining a local model of who did what, what changed, and what was implied. PragWorld applies seven minimal linguistic alterations to real conversations and asks yes-no questions about the result, building two benchmarks that probe whether models update their internal picture or coast on surface patterns. Across a wide range of open and closed models, accuracy proved fragile.

Models particularly failed to track entities through alterations. The authors then locate the problem inside the transformer: some layers help and others hurt, with harmful layers encoding spurious signals and shortcuts. The most damaging alterations are the ones those layers influence. Two fine-tuning strategies that regularize the harmful layers follow from the diagnosis. Conversation looks easy for language models; this benchmark shows how thin their grip on it can be.
arxiv-2511-13321:
Liu Liu, Xueyu Zhu, and Zhenyi Zhu present a bi-fidelity neural method for the semiconductor Boltzmann equation and its inverse problems. The equation spans several scales, and earlier asymptotic-preserving networks handled that split with a micro-macro view. Their weak point was slow settling of the overall density when the Knudsen number is tiny.

The new design splits the density into a main part that can be pretrained well and a small correction learned by a compact network. That split speeds training and sharpens forward answers near the fluid limit. Tests on two related systems showed much better and steadier inverse results than the standard method, even with partial data.
arxiv-2511-13621:
Dimitrios Koutsianos and 3 co-authors adapt alpha-divergence losses for face and speaker verification. Verification scores are usually driven by margin-based softmax losses such as CosFace and ArcFace. Alpha-divergence losses can induce sparse posteriors, which helps memory, but adding an angular margin to them is not obvious.

They find two clean routes: put the margin in the reference measure, giving Q-Margin, or in the logits, giving A3M. A sparsity-driven training instability in A3M is fixed by reinitializing prototypes in a simple way. Both losses gained strongly on hard face benchmarks and on speaker tests, with the largest wins at low false acceptance rates that matter for banking-grade security.
arxiv-2511-13921:
Xin Xiang, Jon M. Miller, Ehud Behar, and four co-authors dissect a fast wind blowing out of an active galaxy. Such ultra-fast outflows stream from near a supermassive black hole at a sizable fraction of light speed and can shape the whole host galaxy. The team studied an 18,000-second X-ray snapshot of the Seyfert galaxy Markarian 877 taken by XMM-Newton.

Their analysis finds three distinct wind layers moving at different speeds and ionization levels, imprinting absorption across soft and hard X-ray bands. Even on cautious assumptions, the fastest layer carries enough power to drive strong feedback. Patterns in the data suggest the wind is pushed by both radiation and magnetic forces.
arxiv-2511-14621:
Xuanjing Chu and ten co-authors develop analytic methods to measure reactive load impedance with superconducting resonators beyond the perturbative limit. Such resonators probe capacitors and solids through shifts in resonance. Past analysis assumed tiny perturbations, which fails for strong loads. The new framework gives closed form links between frequency, participation, and quality factor.

No full wave simulation is needed to extract circuit parameters and loss. The team validate with circuit models, finite element work, and lab measurements. They recover the dielectric constant and loss of hexagonal boron nitride in line with past values. Multi mode self calibration improves consistency. Design rules for raising energy participation are also provided.
arxiv-2511-14921:
Mohamed Rouili and three co-authors present RAID, an in network detector for random access signaling storms in 5G Open RAN. Open radio access networks split and virtualize control functions, creating new attack surfaces. A burst of fake connection requests can saturate central unit processing within a short window. Controller based defenses react too slowly due to long control loop delays.

RAID places detection and mitigation directly in the network path for timely response. That placement avoids tens to hundreds of milliseconds of controller latency. The design targets latency sensitive services that storms would otherwise disrupt. By acting in line, RAID aims to preserve connection success during attacks. The paper frames in network defense as essential for open 5G systems.
arxiv-2511-15421:
Ethan Hicks, Joseph Oglio, Mikhail Nesterenko, and Gokarna Sharma ask a simple Bitcoin question: how long should a user wait before trusting that a payment will not be undone? A payment sits in a block, but a split in the chain can still erase it. That risk falls as more blocks pile on top, yet it never reaches zero, and most users just wait six blocks.

The authors study chain splits in simulations and in real Bitcoin data to link block depth to the chance of reversal. They then use prospect theory, a model of how people weigh gains and losses, to tie a safe waiting depth to payment size and personal risk tolerance.
arxiv-2511-15521:
Christian P. Clear, Gillian Nave, and four co-authors present a major new measurement of the spectrum of neutral manganese, the light pattern that identifies the element. Precise wavelengths and energy levels for manganese matter for reading the makeup of stars from their light. The team recorded discharge spectra with two high-resolution methods covering a wide range from ultraviolet to infrared.

They extracted wavelengths for many thousands of lines with errors at least ten times smaller than before. Combining all lines, they classified over two thousand transitions, refined hundreds of known energy levels, and established eighteen new levels reported for the first time. The sharper data should enable far more accurate studies of manganese in cosmic spectra.
arxiv-2511-15921:
Chelsea Zou, Yiheng Yao, and Basant Khalil develop a self correcting framework to reduce hallucinations during multi step thinking in language models. Judging only final answers misses unfaithful intermediate steps. Their method reads fine grained uncertainty signals in real time. Self assessed confidence alignment and token level entropy spikes flag unreliable thinking as it forms.

A composite reward penalizes unjustified high confidence and entropy spikes. Stable, accurate trajectories are rewarded instead. Reinforcement learning with that reward makes the model more introspective. Generation behavior shifts toward coherent, faithful chains, not just lucky answers. Experiments show gains in both final accuracy and thinking calibration. The approach targets trust in settings where the thinking path matters as much as the result.
arxiv-2511-16021:
Taihei Oki and Tamás Schwarcz generalize a classical exchange property for matroid bases. A base is a maximal independent set, and the multiple exchange property says parts of one base can be swapped with parts of another while both stay bases. That result feeds many algorithms beyond matroid theory itself, motivating a stronger common form.

Their first generalization lets both sides pre-select portions to include in the swap, with the exchanged sets equal in size and bounded by the rank of the combined chosen parts. Their second contribution builds a framework extending a Grassmann-Plücker identity for matroids representable over characteristic-zero fields. New exchange and reconfiguration properties follow, with reconfigurations reachable through a sequence of symmetric exchanges.
arxiv-2511-16321:
Ching-Heng Cheng, Jen-Wei Lee, Chia-Ming Lee, and Chih-Chung Hsu present WWE-UIE, a compact network that cleans up underwater photographs. Water absorbs and scatters light unevenly, so underwater shots lose contrast and take on a blue-green cast. Recent hybrid methods restore such images well but cost too much computation for real-time use.

The design combines three readable priors. Adaptive white balance counters the color loss. A wavelet block splits the image into bands to recover both broad structure and fine texture. A gradient-aware module uses Sobel edges with learned gating to protect sharp boundaries. On standard benchmarks the network matched heavier methods with far fewer parameters and operations, making real-time enhancement on small devices practical.
arxiv-2511-16421:
V. Sunko and J. Orenstein argue in a perspective article that linear magneto-birefringence offers a direct probe of altermagnetic order. Altermagnets split electronic bands by spin without net magnetization or strong spin orbit coupling. That hidden order needs probes that access the order setting itself. Optical birefringence under a magnetic field provides such access, the authors show.

Momentum space spin textures correspond to ferroic magnetic multipoles in real space. Other wave symmetries of the splitting yield distinct optical responses. A symmetry approach finds geometries and field setups that isolate named multipole components. Domain imaging becomes possible with those setups. Theoretical benchmarks for interpreting readings are also provided for this rapidly growing magnet class.
arxiv-2511-16521:
Fan Yang and five co-authors solve a calibration chore for indoor camera systems: registering ceiling-mounted cameras to the floor plan of the room they watch. Manual registration is slow, and automatic visual localization can fail where a space looks repetitive. Their method, named YOWO for You Only Walk Once, turns one walk into both a map and a registration.

A person wearing a head-mounted depth camera walks the whole scene once while the ceiling cameras record the same walk. The head camera yields the scene layout and a world-coordinate path; the ceiling views give matching paths and relative camera poses, aligned by timestamps. A factor graph then jointly refines camera poses, layout, and registrations. The team also releases the first benchmark dataset for this paired task.
arxiv-2511-16621:
Tahere Fallahi Serish and four co-authors test a non-separable version of k-inflation against the newest cosmic microwave background data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. In this model the inflaton's kinetic and potential parts interact through a coupling that ties them together, unlike the standard separable templates.

In slow roll the setup keeps a constant sound speed while shifting the predicted spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio in a controlled way. The authors derive closed formulas for both observables for two monomial potentials. They check them against exact numerical integration, finding agreement at the sub-per-mille level for the spectral index. With negative mixing, both observables drop. That lets otherwise marginal potentials fall inside the region favored by combined ACT, Planck, and baryon acoustic oscillation data.
arxiv-2511-16721:
Saavanth Velury and Yuxuan Wang propose a variational quantum eigensolver built to find quasiparticle excitations, the dressed particles that carry energy in interacting quantum materials, rather than just ground states. Their framework works in momentum space and uses the Hamiltonian's translational symmetry.

A variational circuit starts from a free-fermion particle-hole state of definite momentum and evolves it toward the interacting excited state at the same momentum. It uses a fermionic Fourier transform circuit joined to a Hamiltonian variational ansatz. Benchmarks on the XXZ chain, which maps to a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid, recover the low-lying two-spinon dispersion at several interaction strengths. The velocity read from the spectrum matches Bethe ansatz theory closely, and the authors sketch extensions to other interacting systems.
arxiv-2511-16821:
Johannes Krotz and Ryan G. McClarren present a hybrid method for time-dependent particle transport that marries Monte Carlo estimation with a deterministic discrete ordinates solve, and upgrades the sampling with quasi-Monte Carlo low-discrepancy points. Each half covers the other's weakness: Monte Carlo handles complex physics, the deterministic stage converges smoothly.

A tunable scatter limit decides how many collisions the Monte Carlo leg handles before handing a scattering-free streaming problem to the deterministic stage. A scatter-free Monte Carlo step between time steps then relabels the solution for the next round. Swapping pseudorandom draws for quasi-Monte Carlo points inside the existing sampling maps needs only modest, localized code changes. The payoff is significant accuracy and convergence gains at practically no extra cost, beyond what comparable non-hybrid solves achieve.
arxiv-2511-17221:
Adam Lilja and three co-authors present QueryOcc, a method that learns three-dimensional semantic occupancy from images without human labels. Knowing which space around a vehicle is occupied, and by what, is core to autonomous driving, but annotating 3D scenes at scale is prohibitively expensive. Earlier self-supervised approaches either let 3D structure emerge only indirectly from 2D rendering, or relied on voxel grids built from lidar, limiting precision.

QueryOcc instead asks independent queries at points in space and time across neighboring frames, learning a continuous representation directly. Supervision can come from pseudo-point clouds made by vision foundation models or from raw lidar. A contractive scene representation keeps memory constant while preserving near-field detail. On the standard self-supervised benchmark, QueryOcc improved the main semantic score by about a quarter over previous camera-based methods, at a practical frame rate.
arxiv-2511-17321:
Jia Liu and four co-authors propose an unusual way to learn about fundamental physics parameters: read them off from entanglement in particle decays. When an unstable particle decays, its outgoing spins and colors carry a definite amount of entanglement, which depends on the underlying couplings and masses. Using Higgs boson decays as the test case, the authors compute that entanglement across all decay channels, after averaging over kinematics, and apply a criterion favoring near-maximal entanglement entropy.

Within the standard model, the entropy peaks close to the observed Higgs mass and the measured W boson mass, the latter standing in for the weak gauge coupling. In a two-parameter deformation of the model, the same criterion picks out the standard-model-like balance between vector and fermion couplings. The authors suggest entanglement extremality could become a complementary handle on the parameters of fundamental theory.
arxiv-2511-17421:
Christopher Boland, Sotirios Tsaftaris, and Sonia Dahdouh attack shortcut learning in medical image analysis. A model there may grade scans by some irrelevant but correlated feature instead of the disease signs. Such shortcuts, whether smeared across the image or localized in one corner, can make models fail dangerously on new hospitals' data. The authors observe that different shortcut types surface in different layers of a neural network, so defenses should target the intermediate layers where each shortcut lives.

Their framework distills knowledge from a specialist teacher, fine-tuned on a small set of task-relevant data, into the intermediate layers of a student trained on a large, bias-corrupted dataset. Across chest X-ray, skin lesion, and synthetic benchmarks and several architectures, the method beat standard training and other bias defenses. It often matched a model trained on bias-free data, even on out-of-distribution tests.
arxiv-2511-17621:
Brendan Gho and eight co-authors propose running groups of language model agents like a market. As model agents are set to work together, trust and accountability become hard to keep with central watchers or adversarial judges, which scale poorly and hide how choices form. In the market design, each agent trades in stated beliefs, updating and exchanging them as if quoting prices, so the group settles toward shared, truthful outcomes.

Because each agent's reward lines up with the group's aim of getting things right, orderly and checkable reasoning can arise without outside force. The team tests the idea on factual reasoning, ethical judgement, and common sense tasks. They present market making as a scalable frame for multi-agent systems that must stay safe and aligned.
arxiv-2511-17721:
Shreya Sinha-Roy, Richard Everitt, Christian Robert, and Ritabrata Dutta address a hard step in forecasting: updating a deep generative model when new data arrive. Such models predict well for weather and other changing systems, but their hidden likelihood makes standard Bayesian updating hard to use.

They introduce prequential posteriors, built from a loss that scores forecasts in order over time. Under mild conditions the method settles near the best predicting values. Tests on fake time series and on real weather data show the approach works in practice and can scale to large models used for complex systems.
arxiv-2511-18521:
Core Francisco Park, Manuel Perez-Carrasco, Caroline Nowlan, and Cecilia Garraffo compress hyperspectral satellite data with a variational autoencoder, a neural model that squeezes data into a small latent code and rebuilds it. A geostationary instrument produces terabytes daily across more than a thousand wavelengths, straining storage and sharing.

Their model compresses the data by a factor of several hundred with errors far below the signal. Probes of the latent code recover cloud fraction and ozone well, while nitrogen dioxide and formaldehyde, with weaker signals, are harder. Information is stored in a partly nonlinear way, and extra supervision during training helps little.
arxiv-2511-18721:
Adarsh Kumarappan and Ayushi Mehrotra make a safety pledge for a jailbreak defense more honest. SmoothLLM guards a model by checking many tweaked copies of a prompt, and it ships with a certificate. That pledge rests on a strict stability claim about attacks that in practice rarely holds, which makes the certificate hard to trust.

The pair swap the strict claim for a chance based one, with a small slack built in. A new lower bound on defense odds draws on fitted models of attack success, for both gradient built and sense based jailbreaks. Users can then set pledge thresholds that track real attack behavior. Workable guarantees beat perfect ones that assume a world that is not there.
arxiv-2511-18821:
Xilai Li, Loris Del Grosso, and David E. Kaplan map stable round orbits that sit off the equator of a magnetically charged black hole. A magnetic charge warps the field so charged particles need not circle in the equatorial plane, a path barred near standard holes. For a still, round hole they derive an exact formula for orbit latitude by radius.

Electrons and protons can stray far in latitude at the innermost stable orbit and stay stable while they shed synchrotron light, even for a tiny hole charge. For spinning holes, numeric runs trace the forward and backward orbit branches and show how frame dragging reshapes their stability zones. Off plane rings would be a telltale sign of magnetic charge.
arxiv-2511-19521:
Tesla Zhang and five co-authors mechanize a verification system for timed message-passing protocols, the rules devices use to exchange messages within set time windows. Semantic typing with logical relations can certify such protocols, even mixing typed and untyped parts, including physical objects. Earlier work added timing predicates and computable paths between time points.

What that system lacked was a machine-checked formalization. Mechanizing it would prove the framework sound and make it easier to scale. The present work carries out that mechanization for the proof-relevant logical relation, turning paper proofs about timed protocols into artifacts a computer can check.
arxiv-2511-19721: Pedro Marun, Saharon Shelah, and Corey Bacal Switzer work in set theory on forcing extensions built by adding many Cohen reals. Adding aleph-omega many such reals and adding aleph-omega-plus-one many must give different models, for density reasons about the underlying Boolean algebras. That abstract argument, the authors note, does not name a concrete principle separating the two models. The paper supplies such a principle, pinning the difference between the two extensions to a specific mathematical and combinatorial statement.
arxiv-2511-19821:
Aashish K Gupta, Christopher Ness, and Sina Haeri study how trapped metal powder escapes from printed lattice parts. The parts use triply periodic minimal surface designs, whose complex inner cavities hold powder after printing. Removing that powder is a major problem in metal additive manufacturing.

Using discrete element simulations, the team models powder draining under gravity from single cells of several designs. They vary the cohesive energy of the powder to see how stickiness shapes the flow. The Schwarz-P and Gyroid designs clear powder best and resist cohesion-driven blockage. The authors also examine particle motion, overlaps, and contact forces in those two cells.
arxiv-2511-19921:
Arijit Chakraborty works on counting field extensions, a problem guided by Malle's conjecture. The conjecture predicts how many extensions with a given symmetry group occur, sorted by discriminant size. For the group built as a wreath product of a two-element group with a permutation group H, Jürgen Klüners had already proved the predicted count under mild conditions.

Chakraborty gives a different route to the same counting problem over an arbitrary number field. His method produces the explicit main term and an error term that saves a power, which makes the estimate sharper. The approach also weakens the assumptions placed on H, so the result covers more groups than before.
arxiv-2511-20421:
Cota, Matos, and Vieira classify a family of algebras by how fast their identities grow. Their 2025 paper works in PI theory, the study of polynomial identities. Every algebra obeys certain polynomial equations for all inputs. The codimension sequence counts how many such rules are independent at each degree. Its growth rate is a key fingerprint of the algebra. Graded algebras with a matching symmetry operation are the focus here.

The authors classify unitary algebras whose growth is quadratic. Their method links minimal varieties to character decompositions. Nonzero multiplicities in the proper cocharacters carry the key data. A complete classification up to sameness is achieved. Every variety of at most quadratic growth decomposes nicely. It is generated by a direct sum of minimal pieces. Each piece itself has at most quadratic growth. The funding came from Brazilian agencies FAPESP, CAPES, and CNPq. Such classifications organize a sprawling landscape of structures.
arxiv-2511-20621:
Karvonen, Reuter, Rinberg, Marks, Garriga-Alonso, and Warr check whether AI providers run models honestly. Their 2025 paper tackles inference verification for large language models. Re-running a model gives slightly different outputs each time. Numerical noise blurs honest variation and cheating. Customers need proof the advertised model actually ran.

Token-DiFR compares generated tokens against a trusted reference implementation. Syncing the sampling seed tightly constrains what outputs are valid. The output tokens themselves then serve as free audit evidence. Simulated bugs, sampling errors, and quantization all get caught. Four-bit quantization shows up within three hundred output tokens. Detection quality there reaches near-perfect scores above 0.999 AUC. A second scheme compresses activations into compact fingerprints. Random orthogonal projections make those fingerprints cheap to send. Activation-DiFR spots quantization from just two output tokens. Communication costs fall by a quarter to three quarters. An open-source vLLM integration ships alongside.
arxiv-2511-20821:
Samuele Dell'Erba and Andrew D. Bagdanov ask in 2025 whether text-to-image generators really need a trained prior, the costly network that translates a text prompt's embedding into a visual one before decoding. Such priors demand big training sets. Their alternative, Optimisation-based Visual Inversion, starts from random pseudo-tokens and reshapes a latent visual representation until it matches the prompt embedding, with no training.

Two added constraints keep the optimisation realistic. One uses Mahalanobis distance, which measures how unusual a point is relative to a distribution. Another uses nearest neighbours in image data. Tested on the Kandinsky 2.2 generator, the constrained methods beat a raw text-embedding baseline on visual fidelity. The nearest-neighbour version matched or beat the data-efficient trained prior on scores. The study also exposes a flaw in the T2I-CompBench++ benchmark, where the raw text embedding scores surprisingly high despite worse images.
arxiv-2511-20921:
Mitzi Urquiza-González and a large collaboration report in 2025 precision laser measurements on fermium-255, one of the heaviest nuclides reactors can breed. The isotope lives just 20 hours, and fermium, element 100, is the heaviest element available in weighable amounts. At the RISIKO separator in Mainz, the team probed hyperfine structure in two ground-state transitions, at 398.4 and 398.2 nanometres, using a high-resolution ion source. Atomic theory calculations supplied the hyperfine fields needed to read off nuclear moments.

The magnetic dipole moment came out at minus 0.75 nuclear magnetons, with an uncertainty of 0.05 in the final digit. The electric quadrupole moment measured plus 5.84 electron-barns, plus or minus 0.13 at the same precision. The magnetic value points to the neutron occupying the 7/2 Nilsson orbital, and the hefty quadrupole moment confirms a stable, strongly prolate shape. The results revise earlier data and benchmark nuclear theory for the heavy actinides.
arxiv-2511-21121:
Document search systems usually start by running optical character recognition over every page, then fight brittle rules for chunking, tables, and layout. Anup Roy and three colleagues present VisionRAG in 2025, a retrieval system that skips text extraction and indexes pages as images. A three-pass pyramid builds compact semantic vectors from page-wide summaries, fact-level cues, visual hotspots, and section headers. At query time, ranked fusion merges the pyramid levels, and the winning page images go straight to a multimodal model for the final answer.

VisionRAG keeps just 17 to 27 vectors per page, where patch-based rivals store hundreds. On financial document tests it reached 0.8051 accuracy at rank ten on FinanceBench. Recall at rank one hundred on TAT-DQA reached 0.9629 in the same runs, so nearly every answer-bearing page was found. The authors argue summary-guided, OCR-free retrieval is a scalable replacement for text-first pipelines.
arxiv-2511-21721:
Gao Mo and eight coauthors present PeerCoPilot, a language-model assistant built for peer-run behavioral health organizations, in 2025. Such organizations pair mental health care with help on income, jobs, and housing, but thin funding and staffing leave many needs unmet. Peer providers, who draw on their own lived experience, carry heavy day-to-day workloads.

PeerCoPilot helps providers draft wellness plans, build step-by-step goals, and find matching resources. A retrieval pipeline grounds its answers in a database of over 1,300 vetted resources. In evaluations with 15 peer providers and 6 service users, over 90 percent backed using the tool. It also gave more reliable, specific information than a plain baseline model. A group of 5 to 10 providers at CSPNJ, an organization serving over 10,000 people, now uses it daily.
arxiv-2511-21921:
Frontiere and colleagues extend the GPU cosmology code CRK-HACC to simulate ordinary galaxy-forming matter at survey scale. Sky surveys measure the universe so precisely that ignoring gas, stars, and black hole feedback distorts the predictions those surveys are tested against, especially for cross-correlated, multi-wavelength analyses of large-scale structure. Exascale supercomputers make full-physics runs over volumes feasible, if the software is built for them.

The team added subgrid models, treatments of processes too small to simulate, covering radiative cooling, a multiphase interstellar medium, stochastic star formation, galactic winds, and two-mode black hole feedback. The models were calibrated to reproduce the galaxy stellar mass function from redshift 0 to 2 and the cluster populations surveys probe in their validation. It is presented as the baseline for exascale survey-volume simulations.
arxiv-2511-22121:
Li, Wang, Huang, and Rehg, computer vision researchers, ask which visual cues modern single-image 3D generators actually use. Humans infer shape from one picture using shading, texture, silhouette, perspective, and edges, but deep models that now produce impressive 3D objects from a single photo might lean on entirely different shortcuts. Their Cue3D framework systematically perturbs each cue, dilating silhouettes, shuffling pixels, occluding parts, and measures how much the generated 3D output degrades for seven state-of-the-art methods.

The headline finding is that shape meaningfulness, not texture, drives generalization, and geometric cues, above all shading, are crucial for good 3D output. Models also over-rely on the provided silhouette, and sensitivity to perspective and local continuity varies sharply across model families, regression-based, multi-view, and native 3D alike. By dissecting these dependencies, Cue3D points toward more transparent, robust, and controllable single-image 3D generation.
arxiv-2511-22221:
Isichei and Magueijo, cosmologists, ask what happens if emergent gravity is allowed to do work. In the thermogravity view, Einstein's equations arise as an equation of state from heat exchange across local horizons, making general relativity look like a degenerate thermodynamic cycle with only heat legs. The authors add the missing ingredient, work-producing legs, and find the additions are not free. They generate controlled violations of local Lorentz invariance and of energy-momentum conservation.

Those violations are features, not bugs, because their cosmological consequence is late-time acceleration of the universe's expansion, the phenomenon usually blamed on dark energy or a cosmological constant. The paper discusses what the framework implies for the cosmological constant problem and for structure formation. For local observations that tightly constrain Lorentz violation, it positions thermodynamic cycles as a generator of genuinely new, testable gravity theories rather than a mere reinterpretation of Einstein's.
arxiv-2511-22321:
Meuser, Weil, Lahiri, and Paraschiv teach a quantum network to route entanglement using only what each node can see locally. Distributing entangled pairs across repeaters is probabilistic and links decay quickly. So hand-written routing heuristics either need global topology knowledge or perform poorly. RELiQ trains a reinforcement learning agent with a graph neural network centrally, then lets nodes decide from local observations plus message exchange with neighbors, building an implicit picture of the network.

Trained only on random graphs, the agent transfers to unseen topologies without retraining, beating local heuristics and matching global ones by reacting faster to changes. Routed-pair counts and end-to-end fidelity both hold up as swap success rates, link generation, and memory quality vary. The design points toward quantum internets that adapt on the fly rather than recomputing routes from a central map.
arxiv-2511-22521:
Mohammadshirazi, Guha Neogi, Kulshrestha, and Ramnath teach a small model to answer document questions like a big one. Document question answering needs the answer's location on the page, not just its text. Large vision-language models ground answers well but are costly to deploy, while compact students lose that locating skill. Their framework, DocVAL, distils a teacher's reasoning into a student, with validation at every stage.

A validator checks each trace for correctness and geometric consistency, using text detection only in training, and returns pixel-level error feedback. The student learns from the cleaned traces, then improves through rounds of validator-guided correction. The resulting 12-billion-parameter Gemma-3 student scored 91.4 percent on text accuracy and 82.4 percent on localisation quality on DocVQA, with no OCR needed at deployment. Ablations credit validation with a 6.3 point localisation gain and refinement with 9.7 more, and the team releases 95,000 verified traces.
arxiv-2511-23021:
Shah and colleagues rethink generative recommendation, where a model predicts the next item a user will pick from the history of what they have clicked or bought. Items are represented by semantic IDs, short token codes built from their descriptions. And the standard approach generates those codes one token at a time, which is slow and leans heavily on short-range patterns.

Their method, MADRec, instead learns with masked diffusion: some tokens in a user's sequence are hidden. And the model learns to restore them all at once, treating the hidden tokens as independent given the visible ones. That allows several codes to be predicted in parallel at serving time. In experiments on Amazon Beauty, Sports, and Toys data plus MovieLens-1M, MADRec consistently beat the one-at-a-time approach, with the largest gaps when training data was scarce and on coarse-grained recall.
arxiv-2512-00121:
Johannes Hagel studies a nonlinear oscillator whose forcing changes in an irregular, non-repeating way, in a 2025 study. The system is a parametrically forced equation with a quadratic term. Hagel asks how such an oscillator behaves over long times.

The forcing term depends on a strictly positive solution of a weakly forced companion equation. The study examines the phenomenon named in its title, tube rupture, through theory and simulation together. Results of this kind matter for understanding driven mechanical and electrical systems that can drift into failure when forcing never settles into a pattern. Hagel's approach combines proof with numerical experiment, each checking the other. That pairing suits a system whose long-run behavior is hard to guess.
arxiv-2512-00421:
Epidemics unfold together with human beliefs and behavior, each shaping the other. Mulin Tian and Ajitesh Srivastava present TrendGNN in 2025, a graph neural network aimed at understanding epidemics, beliefs, and behaviors together.
