arxiv-2603-00421: Zhou and Han use a large cosmological simulation to ask how a dark matter halo's past growth shapes its depletion radius, the edge where surrounding matter thins. Rescaled by virial size, the inner depletion radius tracks the recent accretion rate closely and halo mass only weakly. Its link to accretion steepens at late times, driven by recent major mergers that shrink stacked radii for fast growers. Slow growers answer mainly to accretion rate, while fast growers also answer to shape, spin, concentration, and formation time.
arxiv-2603-00521: Liu and six colleagues build Phys-Diff, a physics aware latent diffusion model that splits hidden features into track, pressure, and wind speed parts, for tropical cyclone work. Cross task attention weaves physics style links among those attributes, curing the physical inconsistency of purely data driven forecasts. Past storm records, ERA5 reanalysis, and FengWu fields feed a Transformer encoder decoder. Tests on global and regional sets lead the field.
arxiv-2603-00621: Zhukova and three colleagues unify fragmented cross document coreference data sets into uCDCR, a single English corpus in one format with standard metrics and protocols. The unified set covers entity and event coreference, fixes known inconsistencies, and fills missing attributes for reproducible research. Comparing data sets on lexical traits shows ECB+, the leading benchmark, has among the lowest lexical diversity, with middling complexity on a same head lemma baseline. Annotation rules that drive high diversity, and their effect on that baseline, are also examined.
arxiv-2603-01021: Kukusta, Bekenov, and Antonov compute the electronic structure of the layered trimer iridate Ba4NbIr3O12 with density-functional theory including strong correlations. Corner-linked trimers of face-sharing octahedra produce bonding and antibonding states, with a wide gap at the Fermi level and a nonmagnetic singlet ground state. Their calculated X-ray absorption and resonant inelastic scattering spectra match key features, including sharp low-energy peaks from transitions within iridium levels and a peak near 3.2 electronvolts from a higher transition.
arxiv-2603-01221: Qiao and nine colleagues ask how debate between AI agents changes each agent's reasoning, splitting answer uncertainty into epistemic gain and aleatoric cost. Across agent setups they find good debate needs high epistemic gain under controlled aleatoric cost, explaining puzzles like accuracy rising with token entropy. They then build a reinforcement learning algorithm for multi-agent debate that uses uncertainty guidance to lower aleatoric cost and use epistemic information better. Tests show it lifts each agent's accuracy and makes debate more productive, giving a Bayesian lens on multi-agent debate.
arxiv-2603-01321: Seo and five colleagues propose using strong lensing of dark sirens to measure the Hubble constant. Dark sirens are gravity-wave events without identified light signals, studied with strong lensing of galaxies. The constant is read from lensed dark siren brightness ranges and host galaxy redshifts, pooling events for stronger pooled claims when multiple events are at hand. Lensed events improve sky pinpointing and brightness figures with good lens maps, tackling the Hubble tension between early and late Universe measures.
arxiv-2603-01421: Lin and five colleagues offer SciDER, a multi-agent system running the research life through a data-centric approach and a dynamic multi-mode skill system across four sub-agents. An idea agent makes guesses via Evolutionary Idea Search, a data agent shapes raw data, a lab agent writes runnable code from dataset traits, and a critic agent drives looping self-polish. They release OpenSciDER-SFT-8K, a high-quality run path dataset, with the OpenSciDER-27B fine-tuned model. Across six benchmarks, SciDER and OpenSciDER obtain leading results.
arxiv-2603-01621:
Inda Kreso, Mehran Tarif, Fatemeh Moradi, and colleagues guard factory control systems against stealthy data attacks. Their 2026 work targets false data that stays inside normal physical bounds, so it looks safe. Deep learning guards often smooth over such subtle fakes, while classic checks scale poorly on linked sensor data.

Their digital twin watches a live copy of the plant and flags shifts in the data pattern. A closed-form score measures how far the live pattern drifts from the twin in both mean and cross-links. Tests on two public plant data sets beat a deep learning rival on precision and on a balanced score. The math runs fast on plain hardware with tiny memory, which suits small edge controllers in plants.
arxiv-2603-01921:
Linnea Heitmeier and Jan Gabriel simulate a shaken box of plastic spheres and compare it with light-scattering experiments. Their 2026 work vibrates polystyrene spheres inside a cubic container at varied shaking strengths. Packing fraction tracks how densely the grains settle as shaking proceeds over time.

Simulations use the Discrete Element Method, which follows each grain and its contacts directly. Mean-squared displacement reveals whether grains diffuse normally, crawl subdiffusively, or surge superdiffusively. Simulated displacements run far above the values measured by diffusing wave spectroscopy in the lab. Rotational displacement, though, matches the measured scale closely, which flips the usual reading of the signal. The authors propose the lab signal reflects rotation, not translation, and note the system locks into a constrained state well before close packing.
arxiv-2603-02221:
Zizheng Zhang, Yiming Li, Justin Xu, and colleagues improve clinical prediction tables in this 2026 paper. Good features, built by hand from raw columns, often beat deep models on health data. Language models can suggest new features using medical knowledge. Older tools search blindly, ignoring how the final model learns and which features matter.

Their system, MedFeat, loops feedback from the final model back into feature search. Importance scores from a standard explainer guide which ideas to try next. Past wins and losses are tracked so search does not repeat dead ends. Across many clinical tasks, scores rose steadily over baselines. New features stayed meaningful and held up across years and patient groups, from intensive care to general wards.
arxiv-2603-02621:
Isaac Llorente-Saguer presents a GPU framework for testing Goldbach's conjecture in this 2026 paper. The conjecture claims every even number is a sum of two primes. It has been verified to huge ranges, but GPU tools hit a memory ceiling. A monolithic prime table consumed all video memory near a hundred billion.

His framework packs primes densely as bits, cutting memory sixteenfold. A segmented double sieve then removes the video memory ceiling entirely. Inverting the verification loop plus a fast primality oracle does the heavy lifting. Exhaustive checks reached a trillion on one consumer graphics card, with no counterexamples. Each segment needs only a tiny slice of memory. A rigorous CPU fallback guarantees completeness, and data-center tests scale cleanly across many GPUs.
arxiv-2603-02821:
Alphonse Duleau wrote this obituary for Augustin Fresnel, the French engineer and physicist known for his work on light. The preserved text opens with an editor's preface tracing Duleau himself, who was born in Paris in 1789 and trained as a bridge and road engineer. Duleau met Fresnel in 1810 while both were young engineers posted away from Paris.

The preface follows Duleau's postings to Bordeaux and the Garonne district, then back to Paris for canal work, including swing bridges. He later became a professor of construction and an editor of the engineers' annals. Read as a primary source, the obituary gains weight from this closeness: its author knew Fresnel personally from the start of their shared careers in French public works.
arxiv-2603-03321:
Nardine Basta and Dali Kaafar present DIALEVAL, a system for checking whether language models follow instructions. Judging that well means splitting an instruction into small checkable requirements, a job still done by hand with one-size-fits-all rules. Human judges, the authors note, actually apply different standards to different kinds of requirements. Their 2026 framework automates the job with formal types.

Two language model agents split the work: one extracts typed requirements under strict rules of atomicity and independence, the other scores each type its own way. Content items pass on matching meaning; numbers must match exactly. The method extends to multi-turn dialogue, where older tools fail. Validation shows about ninety percent accuracy and a much closer match to human judgment on complex instructions.
arxiv-2603-03421:
Shahar Hod proves a floor under the size of a black hole's shadow. The shadow is the dark disk framed by the photon ring, now photographed around real black holes by the Event Horizon Telescope. His 2026 paper asks how small that shadow can be, relative to the horizon, for black holes surrounded by matter fields, the so-called hairy case, in spherical symmetry.

Assuming the matter obeys the weak energy condition, Hod shows the shadow radius must be at least a fixed multiple of the horizon radius, more than two and a half times it. The familiar bald Schwarzschild black hole, with no surrounding matter, lands exactly on that floor, saturating the bound. The result gives observers a clean theoretical benchmark: any measured shadow smaller than the floor would break the assumptions behind it.
arxiv-2603-03521:
Jonathan Klawitter and four others ask how many truly separate trees a Bayesian evolution study has sampled. Such analyses explore evolutionary trees with Markov chain Monte Carlo, and consecutive samples resemble each other. The effective sample size corrects for that stickiness, but trees are discrete and high-dimensional, so usual estimators falter. Their 2026 study compares current tree gauges against new ones built on conditional clade distributions.

A further new gauge reads clade frequency differences between independent chains. Simulated chains with known answers grade every method, and real data sets test stability. The clade-distribution gauges match current approaches, and two of them vary less by averaging many estimates. The chance-based gauge and two previously recommended methods cost too much on long chains. Multimodality and poor mixing can badly distort all the gauges' readings, the authors warn.
arxiv-2603-04021: Bisatt and colleagues classify Galois images of non-split Cartan curves via p-adic Hodge theory. For p-adic curves with mod p image in a non-split Cartan normalizer, they classify images via torsion. Potentially supersingular reduction gets special attention, with a novel filtered-module algorithm from a Weierstrass model. Rational curves with non-split Cartan mod p image and no complex multiplication must have image equal to the full preimage of a mod p-power normalizer. Adelic bounds sharpen via the Weil height of the j-invariant.
arxiv-2603-04121: Kim and Weidner prove sharp regularity near the grazing set for kinetic Fokker-Planck equations. They establish optimal regularity for linear kinetic Fokker-Planck equations on bounded domains. First, they prove sharp one-half regularity under diffuse reflection or set in-flow boundary conditions, where previously only small Hölder regularity was known. Second, they characterize solution behavior near the grazing set through higher-order expansions beyond the one-half threshold. These results first show solutions stay smoother all the way to the grazing set by the incoming boundary.
arxiv-2603-04421: Yuan and colleagues test mixed vendor teams for clinical diagnosis. Single vendor teams risk correlated failures that reinforce shared biases. Three doctor agents from different vendors face single model and single vendor rivals on RareBench and DiagnosisArena. Mixed teams consistently win, reaching leading recall and accuracy. Overlap shows mixed teams pool complementary biases, surfacing diagnoses that uniform teams miss. Vendor diversity is thus a design rule for robust diagnosis systems.
arxiv-2603-04621: Dexter and colleagues rebuild linear programming for GPUs with DuaLip-GPU. Earlier work like ECLIPSE and DuaLip showed ridge-regularized dual ascent can scale with first-order methods. The old code tied to few schemas on a CPU stack, blocking extension and accelerator use. The redesign splits problem specification from the engine for GPU execution. An operator model expresses LP forms with blocks for dual scoring and projection steps. GPU techniques, plus primal scaling, row normalization, and a continuation scheme, yield at least 10 times faster than the CPU solver.
arxiv-2603-04721: Nishioka and Tanaka build a phone motion app for physics labs. Smartphone sensors offer teaching chances. Common apps give accel only in the device-fixed system, hindering motion analysis. The new app provides accel in a fixed global system by logging accel and Euler angles, turning them to fixed accel. A second app handles summing and plots. Both apps are install-free. Tests across sliding, thrown, and round motion show fixed accel rebuilds speed and distance. Classroom use showed deeper grasp.
arxiv-2603-05121: Adel Moumen and colleagues measure decoder layer redundancy in SpeechLLMs, where the decoder typically holds over 90% of total parameters. Across two LLM families and three scales, redundancy largely comes from the pretrained LLM, and text and speech inputs show similar redundant blocks. Pruning decoder layers with post-pruning healing shows 7-8 billion models keep good ASR with only 60% of decoder layers, with less pruning tolerance at smaller scales. The same layer blocks prove redundant across encoders, tasks, and languages, enabling a single pruned backbone.
arxiv-2603-05221: Clotilde Bizière and colleagues study reachability in VASS+Z, vector addition systems with integer counters, with nonnegative plus unrestricted counters. With the nonnegative count fixed, reachability is NP-complete with one such counter under unary or binary encoding. Beyond one, a KLMST-based algorithm places reachability in a fast-growing dimension-indexed class, improving on a naive Ackermannian bound by simulating integer counters nonnegatively. Integer counters also lower the hardness bar: unary 2-counter reachability is PSPACE-hard, unary 3-counter reachability TOWER-hard, bounds otherwise known only at higher dimensions.
arxiv-2603-05321: Ian Steenstra and team design an intervention giving teens voice in HPV vaccination choices with parents. Teens face preventive choices yet their views are rarely solicited. Most digital HPV interventions target parents, treating teens as passive recipients. Embodied conversational agents tailor per audience: parents meet a physician using motivational interviewing, while teens choose an age-appropriate doctor or a fantasy game conveying HPV facts through play. A clinic pilot with 21 dyads finds high satisfaction, better knowledge, and lifted intent to vaccinate. Design effects for teen participation and agency follow.
arxiv-2603-05821: Ding and colleagues propose ImKWS, a test-time adaptation method for keyword spotting under imbalance. Keyword spotting serves voice assistants, but noise degrades accuracy, and standard adaptation demands labeled audio. Test-time adaptation uses only unlabeled audio, yet current methods fail when rare keywords meet frequent background sounds. Standard entropy minimization then grows overconfident and biased toward the frequent background class. ImKWS splits entropy handling into reward and penalty branches with separate update strengths, enforcing consistency across audio transformations. Google Speech Commands tests show reliable adaptation in imbalanced scenarios.
arxiv-2603-06321: Zhan and his team put forward unsupervised point cloud semantic splitting driven by a prototype library, with structure learning and consistent reasoning. Consistent learning links points to that prototype library through high quality feature selection. This work builds a link matrix for clear and ambiguous groups, keeping such consistency through constraints on both. The method was tested on S3DIS, SemanticKITTI, and ScanNet sets, with top scores.
arxiv-2603-06721: Rayhan Ahmed and colleagues study linear preserver problems on Toeplitz matrices over the real and complex fields. They characterize maps that preserve rank-one matrices and maps that preserve the determinant within this structured matrix space. The paper also reports related results and open questions for other structured matrices. By pinning down which linear maps keep these key traits intact, the work clarifies the rigid shape of Toeplitz preservers.
arxiv-2603-06921: Derajić and colleagues propose a composite neural control barrier function for robot navigation in changing environments. Barrier filtering is easy to deploy but hard to design, so they offer a simple neural design. Multiple barrier functions combine into one function. Each is trained on offline data from Hamilton-Jacobi reachability to approximate the safe set for moving obstacles. A neural architecture ensures the safe set does not intersect its failure set. Tests for a robot and a quadrotor compare the method against baselines.
arxiv-2603-07221: Ashlagi and colleagues ask what minimal structure makes margin-based learning generalize regardless of parameter count. They start with a simple problem in arbitrary metric spaces: concepts defined by a center point, classifying points by whether distance falls below r or above R. Whenever R exceeds three times r, the class is learnable in any metric space, so a large margin makes learnability rest on the triangle inequality alone. They extend this to bounded linear combinations of distance functions, revealing a sharp margin threshold.
arxiv-2603-07421: Leca, Johnston and Santos review how empathy is taught and discussed in engineering and software engineering courses. They synthesize forty-three primary studies and find one field frames empathy as ethical thought tied to social duty, while the other turns it into structured, design-oriented, measurable practice. Teaching empathy lifts collaboration, ethical reasoning, bias spotting and motivation in both fields. Yet low course priority, hard measures and scarce resources still limit it.
arxiv-2603-07921: Awad and colleagues make transfer learning less pessimistic when an agent moves to a new environment. Standard robust optimization widens its uncertainty set under large shifts, yielding policies too cautious to perform well. Their framework instead builds estimate-centered uncertainty sets from limited target samples plus side information about source-target dynamics: bounds on feature moments, distributional distances, and density ratios. That side information tightens the estimates, and the authors prove error bounds and a finite-sample guarantee for the policy. Tests on Gym environments and control problems beat baselines.
arxiv-2603-08021: Wu and colleagues make human grasping poses showing object geometry and user interaction semantics, for natural hand-object use. Existing semantic grasping methods struggle with the gap between 3D objects and textual instructions. They often lack clear spatial or semantic constraints, yielding invalid or wrong grasps. Their AffordGrasp framework starts with an annotation flow that adds to hand-object sets with structured labels showing interaction intent. It joins an affordance-aware model of hand poses with a dual diffusion process that reasons over geometry, spatial uses, and task semantics.
arxiv-2603-08221: She presents SplitAgent, a privacy-preserving distributed architecture for enterprise-cloud agent collaboration. Business use of cloud AI agents faces a dilemma: cloud models demand sharing sensitive data, while local processing limits power. Current frameworks like MCP and A2A assume complete data sharing, making them unfit for confidential business settings. SplitAgent splits work between in-house privacy agents and cloud-side reasoning agents, with dynamic sanitization that adapts protection to task meaning. Tests show 83.8% task accuracy while keeping most private data protected.
arxiv-2603-08421: Deng and colleagues present CliCooper, a multiclient split learning framework for data owners. Split learning offloads under privacy constraints, and newer versions spread across clients. That work runs on partial trust: owners hide labels and data, while trainers supply checked artifacts and ownership proofs. CliCooper closes gaps in two ways. Privacy-based activation protection with label obfuscation guards privacy without harm. A dynamic chained watermarking links stages across trainers, securing trust and copyright. Tests keep accuracy, cutting cluster success to zero, slashing inversion match, and holding copies near random guessing.
arxiv-2603-09121: Yifan Han and colleagues present DexHiL, a human-in-the-loop framework for post-training vision-language-action models on dexterous robot tasks. Multi-finger control is high-dimensional and contact-heavy, so past dexterous systems stayed unreliable when moved to new jobs. DexHiL lets a person correct both arm and hand within one system through a light teleoperation interface. Its sampling favors corrective segments, and real-robot tests beat offline-only fine-tuning by a wide margin in success rates.
arxiv-2603-09321: Beth Biller and colleagues make the case for a UK-led near-infrared integral field spectrograph on the Habitable Worlds Observatory coronagraph. Finding life on rocky planets in nearby habitable zones needs several molecular features at once, since no single spectral sign is unambiguous. A wide wavelength span covers multiple features per molecule and gives context for the full suite. The UK instrument would cover the infrared arm while the US leads the optical arm of the flagship search.
arxiv-2603-09721: Minh Khoa Le and his coauthors tackle the cost of making sharp videos with diffusion models. Their Matrix Attention treats a whole frame as one matrix, so attention runs across frames rather than across small tokens. Two FrameDiT designs use this idea, one pairing it with local attention for fine motion. On standard video tests the combined design leads rivals while staying fast.
arxiv-2603-09821: Chengyu Shen and a large team introduce One-Eval, an agent system that turns a plain request to test a language model into a full run. Choosing benchmarks, fixing data formats and reading scores normally take much hand work. One-Eval plans the test, fetches and normalises the data, then reports more than bare scores. Human review points and kept sample trails support checking and rollback.
arxiv-2603-09921: Shan Ning and coauthors revisit contrastive methods for naming the Wikipedia entity shown in a photo. Generative approaches do this well but cost too much compute for wide use. WikiCLIP uses language model embeddings for entities, tuned by an adaptor that aligns text meaning with image patches. Hard negative examples, made to look alike yet differ in meaning, sharpen training; the model beats strong baselines much faster.
arxiv-2603-10121: Lhachemi and Cano unify sum rules and bounds for optical, heat and charge flow through quantum geometry. Their single object, a generalised time dependent quantum geometric tensor, is built from links of projected particle and heat polarisation terms. Flow tensors then split into a Berry curvature part that survives at zero rate and a quantum metric fix. Hilbert Schmidt form yields an uncertainty rule and a clean geometric cap on response over finite time.
arxiv-2603-10221: Nuno Crokidakis models how rule breaking, from traffic violations to defying legal limits, persists in a society. His replicator dynamics weigh personal benefit against institutional punishment and social sanctions inside each utility function. With positive social feedback, the system is bistable: broad compliance and broad violation are both stable, with a sharp first order style jump between them. Negative feedback instead gives a smooth transition driven by rising collective cost.
arxiv-2603-10721: Kangke Cheng and co-authors present a sample-and-search algorithm for learning-augmented k-median clustering in high dimensions. A predictor first labels points with a known error rate, and clustering then works from those hints. Their sampling-based method sharply improves the time complexity of earlier algorithms for this problem. It also removes the exponential dependence on the dimension of the space, a key bottleneck before. Experiments against leading methods show much lower cost in practice, together with lower clustering cost.
arxiv-2603-10821: Julian F Schumann and co-authors evaluate randomized smoothing as a defense against adversarial attacks on trajectory prediction for autonomous driving. Even top models are highly vulnerable to mildly perturbed inputs, and defenses remain little studied. The defense wraps models in randomized smoothing, a method proven in other domains, and the team tests several variants. Across multiple base models and datasets, robustness consistently improved. Accuracy in normal settings was not compromised. The authors present smoothing as a simple, cheap defense.
arxiv-2603-11021: Tycho van der Ouderaa and coauthors compress large language models with vector quantization built on the Leech lattice, a 24-dimensional lattice famed for optimal sphere packing. Scalar quantization hits information-theoretic limits, while lattice schemes encode blocks of weights without storing a codebook. They extend a Golay-code-based search for indexing and angular search over lattice shells, and add a fully parallel dequantization kernel. A reinterpretation of shape-gain quantization with Hessian corrections, acting on directions, rounds it out. It beats recent quantization methods.
arxiv-2603-11221: Matt Wilson and James Hefford show that two constructions of higher-order maps in quantum theory, one built from causality constraints and one from compositionality constraints, amount to the same thing. They build a functor from higher-order causal categories into strong profunctors over first-order causal processes. The functor preserves the compositional structure and proves full and faithful when the base category is additive. For the standard quantum process category, the embedding respects the sequencer. One-way signalling constraints can be expressed through the profunctor calculus.
arxiv-2603-11321: Yuning Wu and coauthors fix a stability trap in teaching reasoning models with teacher help. Mixing off-policy teacher data into on-policy training leaves an off-policy gradient that can collapse learning. Their Hindsight-Anchored Policy Optimization treats teacher intervention as temporary scaffolding. A Beta-Binomial confidence rule gates when help is allowed. Interventions swap the group's worst rollout for a verified teacher trajectory. Thresholds anneal the support away within a horizon. The method lifts three mixed-policy methods across six math benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-11421: Yang and co-authors present ShotVerse, a two-part system for text-driven video with camera control across shots. Text prompts alone give loose control, while hand-drawn camera paths take heavy effort and often fail. A planner agent first maps out film-like camera paths from the text. A controller then renders those paths into multi-shot video through a camera adapter. The team built ShotVerse-Bench, a film data set with a three-track test plan, and reports gains in camera accuracy and consistency.
arxiv-2603-11621: Soni, Datt, and Sankaranarayanan study a hybrid sum tied to a cubic number field. They prove an asymptotic formula for its discrete mean square. The field K is non-normal and cubic, given by a cubic polynomial with negative discriminant. The sum runs over integers n that split as a sum of eight squares, weighted by a_K(n) squared. For large x, their formula pins the discrete mean square down with a tight error term.
arxiv-2603-11821: Rosbach and co-authors test how AI advice sways pathology experts judging tumor cell percentages. Twenty-eight experts estimated percentages alone, then again with AI support, some under time strain. AI help raised accuracy overall, yet a 7% automation bias rate appeared: wrong AI advice overturned right first calls. Time pressure did not raise how often this happened, but the drops tied to leaning on AI grew worse. A mixed-effects model also showed moderate anchoring on the AI output, stronger under time pressure.
arxiv-2603-12021: Thennal DK, Biemann, and Hatzel merge translation and label projection into one step with XML tags. Their LabelPigeon system carries span labels across languages while the text itself is translated. Older split pipelines were said to hurt translation quality, a claim this work re-tests head on. A new direct scoring scheme shows LabelPigeon beats the baselines and lifts translation quality in 11 languages. Gains in cross-lingual transfer held across 27 languages and three downstream tasks.
arxiv-2603-12121: Zheng, Shen, and Chen ask how classical bulges shape bar growth in disk galaxies. A suite of N-body runs evolves model galaxies with bulges of varied mass and compactness. Heavier, tighter bulges raise central speeds and stability while the disk share falls. Bars then start later and grow more slowly, and strong bulges can stop them outright. Young bars in such galaxies spin faster at first, then slow down faster too. Once a dilution effect is removed, later pattern speeds look much alike across bulges.
arxiv-2603-12521: Kegalle, Salim, Sanderson, Chan, and Hettiachchi adapt Value Sensitive Design to location-based services. Ride-sharing, food delivery, and similar platforms spill impacts onto people who share the same physical spaces. Designers must handle value tensions in shared spaces plus conditions that vary by locality. Their framework, LA-VSD, offers three heuristics for this dual challenge. It helps teams spot stakeholders, adapt field methods to local context, and align interactions across digital and physical layers. An e-scooter sharing case from Melbourne, Australia, shows the approach in use.
arxiv-2603-13521: Chengshuai Yang and Xin Yuan claim a universal structure for computational imaging systems. Such systems span five carrier families, from coded-aperture cameras to cryo-electron microscopes. They prove each imaging forward model can be built as a directed acyclic graph from exactly 11 physically typed primitives, no more and no fewer. They further prove every failure of reconstruction traces to just three root causes: information deficiency, carrier noise, and operator mismatch. The three gates map to the system lifecycle, guiding design and deployment calibration.
arxiv-2603-13621: Sarafa A. Iyaniwura and Zhiwei Peng study splitting probabilities for chiral active Brownian particles in confined domains. Active particles propel themselves, so their motion differs from passive Brownian motion at a basic level. With the backward Fokker-Planck equation, they study a one-dimensional interval and a two-dimensional corrugated channel. Closed solutions cover the interval in several asymptotic regimes. A Fick-Jacobs reduction covers narrow channels, while wider ones are handled numerically. Channel shape, activity, and chirality all shift which exit a particle takes.
arxiv-2603-13921: Sieyra and co-authors simulate the birth and rise of a solar flux rope behind a real eruption. The event, on 18 December 2014, followed an M6.9 flare in active region NOAA 12241. Their model starts from a non-force-free field built from a photospheric magnetogram taken minutes before the flare. A flux rope forms from the sheared arcade under the Lorentz force, with no pre-made rope assumed. It rises at 350 km/s, carrying dense lower-atmospheric material with it.
arxiv-2603-14921: Abe and the T2K team describe the Super Fine-Grained Detector for the ND280 near detector upgrade. About two million centimeter cubes of scintillator form the tracker. Three crossing wavelength-shifting fibers read each cube. Nearly 56,000 photon counters catch the scintillation light. Charged particles from neutrino hits draw 3D tracks in the array. Protons down to about 330 MeV/c register clearly. Sub-nanosecond timing spots Michel electrons and times neutron flight. Neutron energy reconstruction is a first for neutrino detectors, they note.
arxiv-2603-15021: Rausch and Wittek report lessons from industry projects on documenting agentic AI systems. Such systems mix specialized agents that trade artifacts, call tools, and pass quality gates. Standard sketches miss these style-defining parts as systems grow old and change. The authors give a modeling vocabulary and a small set of views for agents, artifacts, and tools. They align the views with the C4 method across levels of detail. Industrial examples show how the approach keeps documentation clear and maintainable.
arxiv-2603-15421: Roh and co-authors present CLAG, a memory system where a small language model agent sorts its own stored experiences into clusters. Single global memory pools can dilute or corrupt what an agent knows, and small models suffer most from stray context. A router sends each new memory to a fitting cluster, and the agent writes a profile for each one. Retrieval first picks clusters by profile, which cuts the search space. On several question datasets with three small backbones, CLAG beat prior agent memory systems and stayed light.
arxiv-2603-15721: Khadka and Das tackle a privacy clash in blockchain services. Regulated on-chain services demand identity papers, which then link real names to public records. Their Selective Disclosure Framework splits eligibility checks from identity reveal. A prototype named ZK-Compliance makes zero-knowledge proofs inside the browser. Users prove single facts, like being over 18, with no raw data shared. A Grant, Verify, Revoke cycle keeps consent in user hands. Proofs took under 200 milliseconds on plain hardware.
arxiv-2603-15921: Bansal and co-authors grade how well vibe coders can find and fix bugs. Their VIBEPASS study splits debugging into two linked tasks. First, a model must craft a test that exposes a hidden fault. Second, it must repair the code under set diagnostic help. Twelve frontier models faced competition problems with flawed AI solutions. Valid test inputs came at near-ceiling rates. Discriminative tests that expose faults collapsed instead. Fault hypothesis building, not output checking, forms the bottleneck. Witnessing tests make self-repair match outside-guided repair.
arxiv-2603-16021: Van Clief and McDermott swap agent frameworks for plain folder structure. Code-heavy orchestration fits concurrent systems with many moving parts. Step-by-step human review workflows gain little from that weight. Their Model Workspace Protocol numbers folders as pipeline stages. Markdown files carry prompts and context. Local scripts do the mechanical steps, no AI at all. One agent, fed the right file at the right time, does framework-scale work. Unix pipes and literate programming inspire the design. The protocol ships open under the MIT license.
arxiv-2603-16221: Rajapakse compares two sets of operations on Khovanov homology of a link. Lipshitz and Sarkar built one set from a stable homotopy type. Their Sq2 is the first square not fixed by homology data alone. Morán built a rival set from cup-i products on a cochain complex. His first two squares match the classic Steenrod squares. Rajapakse proves the two Sq2 operations agree.
arxiv-2603-16321: Kesiku and Garcia-Zapirain ask how much of quantum circuit learning is truly quantum. Gains might come from plain architecture growth instead. Their causal framework splits performance gaps into direct and indirect parts. Indirect parts flow through measures like entanglement entropy and purity. Across five circuit designs and three datasets, direct effects won by 13.1 to 1. Quantum-mediated gains averaged just 0.82%. Current circuits, they argue, run far below their quantum potential.
arxiv-2603-16621: Williams and co-authors classify data with Gaussian processes via a simplex map. Class chances live on a simplex, which resists standard tools. Aitchison geometry maps those values into open Euclidean space. Classification then becomes a regression problem there. The map uses fewer latent dimensions than standard multi-class models. Inference stays conjugate, with no shortcuts in the setup. Output chances come out well calibrated. Sparse process tools keep the method scalable.
arxiv-2603-16721: Prabhu and co-authors hunt multi-hit mutation combos that drive cancer. Tumors rarely trace to one mutation; hits accumulate in sets. Checking all combos explodes combinatorially across 20,000 genes. Their Pruned Depth-First Search exploits the sparsity of tumor data. Infeasible gene subsets get cut early in the search. A weighted set cover then scores the surviving combos. Bitwise tricks and a supercomputer push the method to four hits and beyond. Visited combos fell 90% to 98%, with a 183-fold speedup.
arxiv-2603-16821: Hatakeyama and co-authors estimate quantum states from measurement records alone. Their setting is a mechanical oscillator in a detuned cavity, read out by homodyne measurement. This approach verifies a state without assuming the true state. They combine causal and anticausal Wiener filters into one estimate operator. They compute its variance and define a reconstruction bias. Within realistic parameter ranges, they show the bias is small enough to neglect. They test the method on proposals for macroscopic entanglement and momentum squeezed states.
arxiv-2603-17321: Pham and Darriulat introduce two new parameters for the shape of the rising branch of light curves of Long Period Variables. These pulsating stars evolve along the Asymptotic Giant Branch, and their light curves carry clues to that evolution. The new shape parameters correlate strongly with period, regularity, amplitude, temperature, and mass loss rate. They also shed light on humps on the rising branch. One parameter, q, tracks evolution along the branch with notable efficiency. A simple global picture emerges in the plane of period against q.
arxiv-2603-17421: Okamoto improves how supernova feedback injects momentum in galaxy formation simulations. Vector momentum input can break energy conservation in two common ways. His scheme computes energy gains in each gas element's own rest frame. That fix breaks momentum conservation, so large-scale coupling gets a thermal fallback instead. Dwarf galaxy runs at two resolutions then agree on star formation history, he reports. A Milky Way-mass run still forms too many stars.
arxiv-2603-17721: Lopez-Gomez and Sahuquillo track a principal eigenvalue as its domain shrinks to zero size. The problem mixes boundary types on domains nested inside one fixed open set. When the weight stays positive, the eigenvalue runs off to plus infinity, they prove. When the weight stays negative, it dives to minus infinity instead. That flip clashes with classic Dirichlet-only intuition. For constant weights on balls, they pin the exact scaled limit.
arxiv-2603-17821: Rahman and co-authors bolt recurrent networks onto language-model embeddings for code tasks. Plain embeddings lean on position and can miss long-range order in source code. Their hybrid reprocesses embeddings through RNN layers to stress sequence sense. RoBERTa-BiGRU hit 66.40 percent on defect detection, about 5.35 points past its base, they report. CodeT5-GRU reached 67.90 percent on the same test. Three real-world sets show the same lift pattern.
arxiv-2603-18521: The BESIII team reports the first sighting of a rare Ds decay into a charged pion, two neutral pions, and an eta. The data come from electron-positron hits at 4.128 to 4.226 GeV, with 7.33 inverse femtobarns in all. A fit to the decay shapes finds a branch share near 0.98% for the a0 plus f0 path, at over ten sigma. The main path goes through an a1 state plus eta, at 1.77%. The finds shape views of light scalar mesons.
arxiv-2603-18621: Żeberek and Wójcik examine topological superconductivity at a lanthanum aluminate and strontium titanate interface. The two-dimensional electron gas there may host Majorana zero modes. Their multiband tight-binding model includes orbital structure plus atomic and Rashba spin-orbit coupling. In a full 2D system, only an out-of-plane field part drives the topological shift. Side confinement relaxes that rule, and edge modes depend on field direction. Some wire subbands show very long Majorana localization lengths. That length may hide bound states in wires of typical lab size.
arxiv-2603-19221: Liu and co-authors study online learning when the learner sees only a ranking of actions, not numeric scores. Such feedback fits settings with humans in the loop or privacy limits. They prove that with rankings from current scores, low regret is not possible in general. The same holds for average-score rankings when choices are near fixed. New methods do reach low regret when scores change slowly over time. In games, joint use of the methods leads play toward a coarse correlated balance.
arxiv-2603-19421: Parsa and co-authors push a diamond optomechanical cavity to swing far wider than usual limits allow. Driven resonators that self-oscillate are normally clamped by nonlinear effects. The team steers the system through its bistable phase space to a high-energy state. That move lifts the swing by nearly ten times at room temperature. The motion also spawns an optical frequency comb via cascaded phonon scattering. The work frames attractor design as a path to strong phonon sources. Uses span sensing and spin interfaces in diamond.
arxiv-2603-19721: Alfaro and co-authors report a HAWC study of the pulsar wind nebula G32.64+0.53. The nebula sits near the ultra-high-energy source eHWC J1850+001. It shows in X-rays and gamma rays, but not in radio, optical, or GeV bands. That pattern points to a non-thermal origin driven by fast electrons. The team used 2,860 days of HAWC data with a careful diffuse-emission model. They measured its spectrum up to 270 TeV. Their fit marks it as a PeV accelerator.
arxiv-2603-20121: Liu and co-authors build a guide dog robot that watches for hazards at human height, not just ground level. Robot sensors near the floor miss dangers like bent branches above them. The team calls this the viewpoint asymmetry problem. Their Co-Ego system fuses the robot's ground view with the user's raised first-person view. It runs on a quadruped robot platform. A study with blindfolded sighted users compared no aid, single view, and fused views. Cross-view fusion cut collision time and lowered mental load a lot.
arxiv-2603-20421: Badash and co-authors present Hawkeye, a system for reproducing GPU arithmetic exactly on a CPU. GPU matrix multiplication is non-deterministic, which blocks exact third-party checks. Hawkeye replays the exact operations behind model training or inference. It does so with no precision loss and no owner overhead. Crafted tests probe rounding direction, subnormal handling, and accumulation order. Tests span Ampere, Hopper, and Lovelace chips at several precisions. In every case, CPU reproduction of tensor core results was perfect.
arxiv-2603-20921: Zhang and co-authors argue that direct training on outcomes can beat self supervised pretraining for clinical prediction. Health models often copy pretraining goals from text and image fields. Their method instead shapes the learned features to split outcome classes widely, with small spread inside each class. Across tasks on long term health records, such as death and readmission, it beats masked, autoregressive, and contrastive baselines. It also improves calibration and sample efficiency, and training needs just one stage.
arxiv-2603-21021: Chern and co-authors prove new minor summation formulae of determinantal and Pfaffian type. Their results generalize at once the Pfaffian minor summation formula of Ishikawa and Wakayama and a recent formula by Byun. The proofs rest on factorization formulae for the determinant of a sum of a skew-symmetric matrix and a rank-1 matrix. As an application, they obtain a Cauchy-type identity for skew Schur functions.
arxiv-2603-21121: Lahti and co-authors prove a weak Harnack inequality for nonlocal minimizers in metric measure spaces. The setting is a complete, connected, doubling space, and the functions are fractional Sobolev subminimizers. As a corollary, such subminimizers are semicontinuous once a good pointwise representative is chosen. They then prove Cartan-type properties for superminimizers. The theory closely parallels the local case of BV minimizers. The authors note the results seem new even in the classical Euclidean setting.
arxiv-2603-21321: Karimi and co-authors present Engram, an agentic system that designs system heuristics over long horizons. Language models struggle here through local optima traps and context decay over long runs. Engram splits exploration across a sequence of agents that design, test, and analyze mechanisms. Each run ends with code, logs, and results stored in a persistent archive. A compact research digest carries the key insights to the next agent, which starts with a fresh context. Engram performs strongly across multi-cloud multicast, inference request routing, and database cache reuse tasks.
arxiv-2603-21421: Kamtikar and co-authors present HyReach, a robot arm that mixes rigid and soft continuum segments for reaching in cluttered spaces. The system pairs vision-based perception and 3D scene reconstruction with shape-aware motion planning. A learned controller drives the arm to target poses, using the soft part's flexibility and the rigid part's precision. It needs no retraining for new scenes. In real-world trials, reaching errors stayed below 2 cm across varied cluttered setups, the team reports.
arxiv-2603-21821: Grošelj and co-authors use smooth Powell-Sabin splines to solve boundary value problems on flat and curved domains. The splines are cubic, once differentiable, and built on unstructured triangulations. The team reviews how polynomial and rational forms of these splines are constructed. They then show how the same splines can describe the domain geometry itself with care. That geometry feeds an isogeometric solver for Poisson and biharmonic problems. Results suggest these splines rival standard Lagrange elements and NURBS as a flexible tool for surface problems.
arxiv-2603-21921: Rojas and Lee revisit the temporal difference error of reinforcement learning, and show its two classic readings can split apart. Sutton in 1988 defined it two ways: the gap between successive predictions, and the gap between a bootstrapped target and a prediction. The second reading is now the standard critic loss. The authors show that deeper, more nonlinear networks make the two values drift further apart. The choice then changes results in methods that reuse the error, such as average-reward algorithms. Defaults from theory need care in deep settings.
arxiv-2603-22021: Rathi and co-authors present a theory framework for computing the energy levels of muonic atoms. A muonic atom swaps an electron for a heavier muon. The framework targets medium-mass nuclei, from Z of 3 up to about 30. It blends a Zα expansion with an all-order method in the Furry picture. The authors add improved quantum electrodynamics effects and nuclear polarization corrections. They also assess the theory uncertainty in a systematic way. It supports current and planned spectroscopy experiments.
arxiv-2603-22321: Toschi and co-authors build a dataset for testing AI help during hands-on assembly. Their dataset, M2AD, pairs furniture manuals with assembly videos. Each step carries labels and links to the right manual pages. The team uses it to grade open multimodal models as live assistants. Three skills are tested. Models must follow step progress and point to the right manual page. Some models grasp the step order well. Yet the authors find hard limits from model design and hardware.
arxiv-2603-22521: Cruz and co-authors simulate perchloric acid solutions with an extended force field. The model pairs Madrid-2019 parameters for the perchlorate and oxonium ions with a standard water model and scaled charges. They predict densities, structure, diffusion, and viscosity across several concentrations. Densities match experiments closely up to high strength. The team also maps the temperature of maximum density at each strength. Predicted viscosities agree well with measured values at lower strengths, and the authors note where the model strains.
arxiv-2603-22621: Dardeno and co-authors propose a way to transfer health knowledge between very different structures. The field is population-based structural health monitoring. Direct transfer fails when two structures share little in common. Their idea uses middle structures that bridge the gap. By slowly changing material traits and shape, one structure can morph into another. They show the method on simulated bridge designs. A second case links a simple bridge model to an aeroplane model. The results show positive transfer can occur even between highly unlike systems.
arxiv-2603-22821: Shi and co-authors present SpaHGC, a model that predicts spatial gene expression from pathology images. Direct spatial transcriptomics is costly, so image-based prediction is attractive. SpaHGC builds a heterogeneous graph over spots within and across tissue slices. It uses local context plus cross-slice links from a pathology foundation model. Masked graph contrastive learning sharpens the features and aids transfer. Tests on seven matched datasets beat nine prior top methods on all metrics. Predictions also enrich many cancer-related pathways.
arxiv-2603-23121: Yu and Zheng study the free boundary in a p-obstacle problem with subcritical exponents. They first prove that non-negative weak solutions exist. The proof uses a mountain-pass lemma and a penalty method. Bounds and local smoothness for solutions follow from an iteration method. Near the free boundary, they prove local porosity from growth and non-degeneracy traits. Gradient level set estimates then give the key size result. At least one solution has a free boundary with locally finite Hausdorff measure of dimension N minus one.
arxiv-2603-23221: Vakarjuk and Pankova design PRETTINESS, a system for revoking digital credentials in the European Digital Identity Wallet. Wallet users hold attested credentials and show them to relying parties. Short-lived credentials can replace revocation, but they are awkward in some cases. PRETTINESS offers a separate revocation service that runs on a single server with secure channels. The authors prove its security in the universal composability model. They also gauge its cost with a working proof-of-concept build.
arxiv-2603-23321: Kanno gives a complete characterization of graphs whose edge ideal quotient has regularity 3. For a graph G, the edge ideal I(G) collects the graph's edges as algebraic data. The regularity of the quotient ring R over I(G) measures the complexity of its resolution. Graphs with regularity exactly 3 form a special borderline class. Kanno pins down exactly which graphs fall into that class. The result sorts all graphs by this algebraic test with no cases left open.
arxiv-2603-23521: Khan and eight co-authors release Chitrakshara, a dataset for Indian languages. Most vision-language training leans on English and on one image at a time. Chitrakshara covers 11 Indian languages drawn from Common Crawl. Its interleaved part holds 193 million images and 50 million documents for pretraining. A caption part adds 44 million image-text pairs. The team detail how they gathered, filtered, and cleaned the data. Their checks probe how well each language is covered. The goal is models that serve Indic users better.
arxiv-2603-23721: Pourhassan and three co-authors add quantum fixes to the heat bookkeeping of AdS black holes. The fix bends the entropy by an exponential tail on the classic area law. Heat capacity keeps its classic blow-up point, yet shrinks by over three quarters at small radii. The fix also births a Hawking-Page switch that the classic view lacks. Free energy dips below zero for small holes, a channel with no classic twin. Work during evaporation flips sign as holes shrink.
arxiv-2603-23821: Rozner and Shain propose a new way to find representations inside language models. Instead of reading activation patterns, they treat representations as paths for learning. They fine-tune a model on one adversarial example and watch how the change spreads to other examples. This perturbation test makes no geometric assumptions. It finds no false structure in untrained models. In trained models, it reveals transfer at several language levels. They argue models gain linguistic abstractions from experience alone.
arxiv-2603-24021: Gao and co-authors release QuadFM, a large text-linked motion dataset for quadruped robots. It holds 11,784 curated clips covering locomotion, interaction, and expressive behaviors such as dancing and stretching. Each clip has three layers of annotation, for 35,352 descriptions in total. Past datasets held only a few basic moves. Their Gen2Control RL framework trains a motion controller and a text-to-motion generator together. On a real robot with an NVIDIA Orin chip, the system makes motions in under 500 milliseconds.
arxiv-2603-24221: Somma and co-authors use language models to automate penetration testing of robotic systems. Robots are networked cyber-physical systems, so their security matters in industry and logistics. Their multi-agent design is grounded in the test environment. During a run, the agents build a shared graph memory of topology, channels, flaws, and tried exploits. They test the system on a robotics Capture-the-Flag setup with ROS and ROS2. The system solved the challenge in all five runs, they report, while keeping traceability and human oversight.
arxiv-2603-24421: Chugg and co-authors argue that e-values deserve a place among standard evidence measures. P-values, likelihood ratios, and Bayes factors each have defenders in a long-running debate. E-values combine across studies with ease, handle composite hypotheses, and carry long-run error rates. They can also be read as the wealth of a bettor wagering against the null. The sequential form, the e-process, also handles optional stopping. The authors test both against the wish lists of rival traditions and find they merge key strengths.
arxiv-2603-24721: Zhou and co-authors propose QuatRoPE, a positional embedding that helps language models reason about 3D spatial relations. Prior methods either encode absolute positions and fuse features too early, or encode all pairwise relations and scale poorly. QuatRoPE keeps input length linear in the number of objects. Pairwise relations emerge through dot products inside the attention layers. Its holistic vector encoding of 3D coordinates preserves the scene's geometric consistency, and a gated extension adds further gains.
arxiv-2603-25021: Gao and co-authors present VideoTIR, a method that helps video models answer questions about long footage. Such models often invent facts when a video floods them with frames. VideoTIR instead trains the model, with reinforcement learning, to call tools that pull out key segments, frames, and regions. A new training rule, TAGPO, cuts wasted tool calls by scoring each step and reusing failed tries. A sandbox pipeline makes practice runs for training. Tests on three long-video question sets show gains in both accuracy and speed.
arxiv-2603-25221: Nguyen and co-authors speed up robust support vector machines by safely dropping easy training points. Robust training guards against noisy features, but the worst-case setup costs far more time. Their screening rules prove some points sit fully on one side of the margin, noise set and all. Those points cannot change the final model, so they can leave the problem early. The rules come from Lagrangian duality, since the robust form breaks standard tools. A gap-based version proves practical. Training runs much faster with accuracy intact.
arxiv-2603-25721: Carrion and co-authors test the alpha-Starobinsky inflation model against modern cosmology data. They combine Planck data, ACT DR6 lensing, and DESI DR2 baryon acoustic data. Their sampling puts priors on the primordial observables rather than on the potential itself. A modified CLASS code then solves the exact inflation dynamics. With the full dataset, the pure Starobinsky case shows strain, they report. It needs more than 60 e-folds after horizon crossing. Letting alpha vary gives a clear one-sigma preference for log alpha above zero.
arxiv-2603-26221: Chen and co-authors ask whether open agentic systems can be trusted. Such systems mix language model planning with tools, long-term memory, and broad rights to act. They review 50 papers on attacks, tests, defences, and audits, sorted into six groups. From that review they draw a doctrine for building agent platforms that stay secure by design. They also offer a scorecard for rating platform security, and flag weak spots in controls and memory safety.
arxiv-2603-26621: Gheorghe, Alanwar, and Stoican propose tests for when one constrained polynomial zonotope sits inside another. Set operations are well understood for convex sets, but non-convex shapes lose that clean structure. Constrained polynomial zonotopes strike a balance, since they can trace complex non-convex forms yet keep an algebraic handle. The authors build nonlinear encodings that give sufficient conditions for inclusion. Their encodings are shaped to drop neatly into optimisation frameworks, so inclusion checks can ride along inside larger design or control problems.
arxiv-2603-26721: Ahmad and Khan classify stress levels from ECG signals with a vision transformer. They turn raw heart signals into 2D spectrograms with a short-time Fourier transform, then slice them into patches for the encoder. Rival models include a 1D CNN and ResNet-18, tested under leave-one-subject-out validation on WESAD and RML data. That setup is hard because people vary widely in their signals. The transformer handles the variation far better than the CNN models and beats past state-of-the-art results by a clear margin.
arxiv-2603-27021: Rahman and Rehman present the Pashto Common Voice corpus, the first open speech resource for Pashto. Pashto has over 60 million speakers but almost no open speech technology. A community effort from 2022 to 2025 built the corpus release by release. It now totals 147 hours from 1,483 unique speakers. The newest release holds 107,781 clips across 13 content domains. Outreach included interface localization and targeted recording of often-dropped characters. Fine-tuning Whisper Base cut the Pashto word error rate to 13.4 percent.
arxiv-2603-27521: Yi and co-authors test how matter recipes shape lambda hyperon polarization. In off-center heavy-ion crashes, lambda particles gain global spin alignment. That signal may shift with the equation of state. The team runs the SMASH transport model with three recipes. Only the hadron resonance gas matches low-energy data well. It fits even below the free production threshold. Polarization maps at 3 GeV agree with measured data. A peak near 2.4 GeV is also predicted.
arxiv-2603-27621: Jalalzadeh and co-authors deform quantum mechanics to study black hole heat. A q-deformed algebra at a root of unity bounds the state space. The mass spectrum becomes finite and capped. Entropy gains a universal log correction term. A minimum temperature and a maximum entropy appear. Max entropy matches the de Sitter bound. A cold remnant stays stable as radiation fades. The picture links quantum gravity to cosmology.
arxiv-2603-28021: Chen and five co-authors present CoLMbo-DF, an audio language model that detects deepfake speech and explains its calls. Older detectors give a bare yes or no and hide their grounds. CoLMbo-DF feeds the model text summaries of low-level sound traits, such as pitch patterns and spectral cues, so its reasoning rests on stated evidence. The team built a dataset of audio pairs with step-by-step notes. Their smaller model beat larger audio language model baselines.
arxiv-2603-28221: Bold and Shanahan describe new tools for simulating the scrape-off layer of stellarator fusion devices in the BOUT++ code. The layer's tangled magnetic geometry makes transport modeling hard. A flux-coordinate-independent method already worked on simpler shapes. The new work improves grid generation, the physics model, and the library itself, aimed at realistic shapes like Wendelstein 7-X. The authors close with a look at modeling now under way with these features.
arxiv-2603-28621: Carloni Calame and co-authors compute radiative corrections for two-pion production with a hard photon in electron-positron annihilation. They include the pion's non-perturbative structure in the one-loop calculation. A generalized vector meson dominance model inserts the pion form factor into loop integrals. The treatment covers final-state radiation and initial-final interference at next-to-leading order. They compare their results with a naive factorized scalar QED approach. It can help gauge model uncertainty in radiative return experiments at flavour factories.
arxiv-2603-28721: Faulend, Buljan, and Štrkalj explain slow dynamics deep inside many-body localized systems through quantum beats. Slow motion seen in simulations had raised doubts about localization in large systems. They trace it to interaction-driven modulation of single-particle hopping swings. The mechanism links to local integrals of motion and survives at large distances between them. It fits stable MBL at large scale. New runs use quasiperiodic potentials. Their model explains number entropy growth and quasiparticle spreading. It also clarifies why the two potential types behave differently.
arxiv-2603-28821: Scally and co-authors present HAMMR-L, a post-processing method that cuts noise in quantum computer outcomes. Noise grows as circuits get deeper and qubit counts rise. Past work showed that faulty outcomes show patterns in Hamming space. HAMMR-L applies Richardson-Lucy deconvolution on a state graph whose nodes are measurement results linked by Hamming distance. Their early implementation beat the cutting-edge QBEEP post-processor. It also works for any circuit and hardware, which QBEEP does not.
arxiv-2603-28921: Pasichnyk tests critical damping as a momentum schedule for SGD training. The damped harmonic oscillator model gives a schedule with no tuned parameters. Across five seeds on ResNet-18 with CIFAR-10, it reached 90 percent test accuracy 2.34 times faster than constant momentum. Final accuracy fell by 0.46 points, a real cost. A hybrid recipe uses critical damping until 90 percent, then constant momentum. That recipe removed the deficit and kept the speedup. A separate exhaustive test on surgical layer selection found no benefit over random choice. Gradient signals did help avoid harmful layer choices.
arxiv-2603-29321: Li and Shen test whether the universe favors prime numbers in cosmic structures. The cosmological principle says the universe favors no place or direction. Earlier work by Shen suggested a tilt toward parity-odd states. The team turns to large catalogs of galaxy groups. They ask whether group galaxy counts are prime more often than chance allows. The authors report a preference, with a signal above 4.1 sigma. They suggest the cosmological principle may need revision. They also link the finding to the Riemann zeta function.
arxiv-2603-29621: Munch and co-authors solve Stokes and Navier-Stokes equations with the deal.II finite element library. They lean on its multigrid, adaptive mesh, and matrix-free tools. Stationary Stokes flow uses hp-adaptive meshes with an hp-multigrid solver. Transient Stokes flow uses space-time elements and space-time multigrid. Incompressible Navier-Stokes flow runs on locally refined meshes. A monolithic multigrid solver handles that case. The examples show how flexible the multigrid setup is. The design stays modular across problem types.
arxiv-2604-00021: Fukui studies how language models process ethical instructions, in over 600 simulations across four models, four formats, and Japanese and English. Analysis matched a prior study's Llama Japanese dissociation pattern, but no other model matched it, marking it model-specific. Three metrics, Deliberation Depth, Value Consistency, and Other-Recognition, revealed four types: Output Filter, Defensive Repetition, Critical Internalization, and Principled Consistency. The central finding is a link between power and format: low-deliberation models show none, while high-deliberation models show opposite effects from norms and virtue framing.
arxiv-2604-00421: Mohamud and colleagues ask whether mixture-of-experts models really need a trained router. In these layers, each token wakes just a few experts, picked by a learned router from the token's hidden state. Self-Routing removes that router projection and instead reads expert scores straight from a chosen slice of the hidden state, leaving the rest of the layer untouched. Tests on language modelling across expert counts and model sizes, plus ImageNet-1K classification, compare it against the learned-router baseline, random routing, and dense models.
arxiv-2604-00721: Dupont-Bouillard tackles co-3-plexes in chordal graphs. A co-3-plex is a vertex subset inducing a subgraph of degree at most 2. Since chordal co-3-plexes induce triangles and induced paths, he reduces the search to maximum stable set search in an auxiliary graph of exponential size. That yields a variable-sized linear programming formulation for maximum weighted co-3-plexes. The pricing subproblem reduces to a maximum vertex-edge weight induced path problem, solvable in polynomial time.
arxiv-2604-00921: Lewis, Gregor, and Santos-Villalobos propose a simple training-free method to slim image vectors using a post-hoc canonical correlation analysis step. By using shared structure between two trained models, the method finds linear maps that keep shared meaning while dropping extra parts. Vectors shrink by more than 75 percent in size with better downstream results. They beat standard and PCA versions alike, with scores up to 12.6 percent.
arxiv-2604-01421: Saroha and colleagues present EgoFlow, a flow-matching system making plausible trajectories from first-person video. It uses a hybrid Mamba-Transformer-Perceiver design to model motion, scene shape and meaning. Gradient-guided steps enforce physics constraints such as crash dodging and motion smoothness. That yields smooth, steerable motion without post-hoc cleanup or extra labels. Tested on HD-EPIC, EgoExo4D and HOT3D, it beats diffusion and transformer rivals in accuracy, generalization and physical realism. It cuts crash rates by 79 percent.
arxiv-2604-01621: Li and colleagues present DWDP, an inference plan keeping split-data runs while shifting mixture-of-experts weights across peer GPUs and fetching missing experts on demand. By dropping joint inter-rank syncing, DWDP lets each GPU progress alone. They address real costs with two fixes for split-weight handling and early remote-weight prefetch. Built in TensorRT-LLM and tested with DeepSeek-R1 on GB200 NVL72, DWDP improves end-to-end output TPS/GPU by 8.8 percent at similar TPS/user under 8K input and 1K output sequence lengths.
arxiv-2604-01721: Sümer and colleagues design phase-shifted pilots for uplink sensing and communication networks with non-orthogonal access. Interleaved pilots with such access raise efficiency but blur sensing resolution through sparsity, and the nulling fix helps only little. Their phase-shifted design and its nulling variant puncture sensing signals at transmitter pilot spots to preserve early channel estimates and allow a dense data overlay. Adapted cancellation then untangles multi-transmitter interference, keeping sensing intact while cutting receiver computing cost by 18.8 percent against the older baseline.
arxiv-2604-01821: Ito and colleagues propose a two-stage method for sharing educational data under privacy constraints. But educational data are fragmented, small-sample and high-dimensional, so tailored methods demand engineering. Their method first generates synthetic data with LLM-based private generation, then offers on-demand validation, where researchers submit code for checks. It adapts to multi-shot synthesis across cohorts. Three years of tests plus a case study find LLM-based generation comparable to a deep baseline, cheaper. Yet only 36 percent of synthetic findings validate on real data.
arxiv-2604-02421: Bhandari, Borah and Saha give collapsing domain walls a new bias origin from matter antimatter gap. Spontaneous symmetry breaking spawns bad wall networks, made unstable by a bias term. Here the bias arises at finite temperature from radiative shifts of a Dirac fermion with a large number density gap. The case opens a new viable region for wall collapse and gravity waves within reach of future tests. Success also hinges on the temperature when it was generated, so future wave data could probe both its amount and its heat.
arxiv-2604-02521: Baiget Orts presents SESCC, which dates ancient star catalogues through the link between stellar speeds and position errors. At the true date the two are unrelated, so the best date is the trial date that minimizes their correlation. Validated against the catalogues of Tycho Brahe and Ulugh Beg, the method applied to the Almagest points mostly to pre-Christian dates, favoring a Hipparchan origin over a Ptolemaic one.
arxiv-2604-02621: Shen, Tu and Wang propose reinforcement learning for reasoning distillation that replaces ground-truth rewards with continuous scores from a judge language model. Their continuous chain-of-thought reward comes from a single-token logit of the judge, giving a scalable online signal for large volumes of unlabeled data. With a strong judge it matches verifiable rewards, and combining both in a semi-supervised setup beats either alone.
arxiv-2604-02821: Liu, Wang and Manchester present goal-conditioned neural ordinary differential equations for all-pairs motion planning, where start and goal may be any points in a safe set. Built from bi-Lipschitz diffeomorphisms, the model guarantees global exponential stability and safety. The safe set stays forward invariant for any goal, with clear bounds on convergence rate, tracking error, and vector field size. Demonstration data can be folded in. A 2D corridor task illustrates the method.
arxiv-2604-02921: Gao, Jiang and Yan propose debiasing language models by supervised fine-tuning to correct systematic extrapolation bias in forecasts. Prompt-based fixes appear limited against this bias. They train off-the-shelf models with low-rank adaptation on instruction sets built from rational benchmark forecasts. Intervening at the parameter level changes how models map observed information into forecasts. Fine-tuning corrects that bias out-of-sample in controlled experiments and stock return prediction. The method is low-cost and broad.
arxiv-2604-03221: Anagnostopoulos and colleagues build a fully noninvasive, patient-specific blood-flow model from a single cuff reading plus physics-informed neural networks. The inverse model solves flow and pressure across an eight-artery tree in minutes, training at least ten times faster than leading models. Validated against a reference solver and clinical data, it recovers cardiac output and central systolic pressure with strong agreement.
arxiv-2604-03421: Singh and Diamond show that nonlinear spectral back-transfer from zonal modes to turbulence limits how long zonal shearing fields stay coherent. Back-transfer bursts scatter the phase and amplitude of zonal shear, and the transfer distribution is non-Gaussian, with positive triangularity far more intermittent than negative. Negative-triangularity plasmas suppress back-transfer, gaining longer coherence and tougher turbulence regulation despite lower zonal energy.
arxiv-2604-03721: Luca Bergen and colleagues proposed a test for whether two factors stay linked once a third factor is held fixed. Older kernel tests lean hard on one fitting method that is slow when tuned and shaky when untuned. Their Generalised Kernel Covariance Measure works with many fitting methods. It maps the factors into a rich space, strips out what the third factor explains, and checks what is left. In simulations with tree-based fits, it often beat leading tests on false alarms and power.
arxiv-2604-04021: Shaikh Saad and Vasja Susič examined the minimal Yukawa sector of SO(10) grand unified theories with Higgs fields in the 10, 120, and 126 representations. Taking the 10 and 120 fields as real scalars, they derived reality conditions for their weak-doublet parts and found a sign difference between the two doublets in the 120 field. Four independent routes, including a Pati-Salam embedding map and an SU(5) oscillator calculation, all gave the same result. A broad numerical scan then matched observed fermion masses and mixings, including recent JUNO solar oscillation data.
arxiv-2604-04121: Leonardo Bitzki and team built NetSecBed, a box-native testbed for same-again security tests. Public data sets usually sit static, with weak support for set re-runs and tracking across rules. It packs 60 attack cases, 9 target services, and benign traffic makers into single-purpose boxes with plain-text specs. Its line does runs, packet capture, log grabs, probing, feature pulls, and data set merging, cutting day-to-day bias.
arxiv-2604-04221: Narayanan and Vaidya build a controller that helps four-legged robots walk blind over rough ground. Their RK-MPC method pairs a simple template model with a small data-learned correction for contact and terrain surprises, then runs the combined model inside a predictive controller at 500 hertz on board. Tests in simulation and on a Unitree Go1 robot cover grass, gravel, snow and ice, and the correction improves prediction over standard Koopman baselines.
arxiv-2604-04321: Hirst, Sá Earp and Silva introduce a neural flow that reshapes closed surfaces to minimize Willmore energy, the squared magnitude of mean curvature. Neural networks model maps from flat two-dimensional domains into three-dimensional space, trained with a physics-informed loss on the energy of the embedding. Training recovers the expected round sphere for genus zero surfaces and the Clifford torus for genus one. The genus two experiment offers a new route to hunt for minimal Willmore surfaces, an open problem.
arxiv-2604-04521: Illi and Qaraqe survey pinching antenna systems, a new channel-shaping technique for next wireless generations. Pinching antenna systems extend a base station's reach by linking radio-frequency chains to long guides, with aerials pinched at custom positions, overcoming missing line-of-sight and path loss. Channel tuning thus lifts sensing, coverage, data rate and resilience against snooping. The survey sorts research by objectives: reach, data rate, secure transmission, sensing, joint sensing-communication, and energy efficiency. It weighs schemes, drawing lessons on potential and limits, and future deployment directions.
arxiv-2604-04821: Cao and four colleagues model hidden-charm pentaquarks, exotic particles made of five quarks. They treat the Pc and Pcs states as loosely bound molecules. Solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation with coupled channels, heavy-quark spin symmetry, and a local hidden-gauge approach, they trace pole paths, wave functions, and sizes. For Pc states, full coupled-channel effects prove essential and shift decay widths, while the strange Pcs system behaves more simply, with its main bound channels coupling mainly to higher decay routes.
arxiv-2604-05621: Delitzas and ten colleagues rebuild usable 3D twins of indoor scenes from head-worn RGB-D videos of people handling objects. FunRec spots jointed parts, gauges joint motion, and rebuilds still and moving shapes with no staged setups or CAD priors. It tops prior work by up to 50 mIoU points on part segmentation with far smaller joint errors.
arxiv-2604-05721: Zhang and six colleagues grow 3D Gaussians from point clouds with text guidance, enforcing geometric accuracy from the start. A multi-view diffusion model supplies consistent appearances, view-fusion artifacts are curbed at overlap regions, and unseen areas are inpainted from the largest un-grown regions. Tests on synthetic and real-scanned clouds show strong text-guided generation.
arxiv-2604-05821: Lee and five colleagues improve cross-lingual retrieval with CLEAR, a reverse-training loss for multilingual embeddings. Standard contrastive adaptation misses deep alignment and can harm strong languages like English. CLEAR uses an English passage as a bridge to tie target languages to English, gaining up to 15 percent in cross-lingual tests, most in low-resource languages, with little English loss.
arxiv-2604-06021: In 2026, Gao and three colleagues made the first measurement of parity-odd kurto spectra in galaxy survey data. It tests whether the universe breaks mirror symmetry at cosmic scales. They use two composite-field spectra from BOSS and DESI luminous red galaxies. The method compresses the four-point signal so its covariance can be estimated directly from mock catalogues. Null tests and cross-patch checks find no parity-violating signal in either survey. DESI scatter runs about four times below BOSS, as its denser sample predicts.
arxiv-2604-06221: Dyck and five colleagues benchmark 13 lossless compression implementations for 4D-STEM microscopy, whose huge datasets strain storage and transfer. Across five datasets, gzip-9 gives the highest compression ratio but runs slow. Blosc-zstd matches its ratio while compressing and reading far faster. Compression follows a power law with sparsity, from 5 times to 35 times as data grows sparser. They name six top implementations and argue compression alone cannot sustain high-throughput workflows: future systems need inference-driven representations keeping only what an inference requires.
arxiv-2604-06421: Singh and eight others introduce Arabic-DeepSeek-R1, an open-source Arabic model on sparse experts. It tops the Arabic LLM board. Four-phase chain-of-thought distillation weaves Arabic checks and norms into a 372-million-token Arabic-English mixture. The model tops the seven-benchmark suite, with MadinahQA beating GPT-5.1. Sparse experts, culturally-informed distillation, and bilingual curation let an open-source model beat GPT-5.1 on most benchmarks, the first such demonstration for Arabic models. Arabic deficit stems from under-specialization, not architecture, and adaptation reaches without industrial pretraining.
arxiv-2604-06721: De Pas, Dipierro, and Valdinoci refine long-run bounds for minima of a far-reaching energy class with a weak wavy double-well shape. The shape obeys power control on its second slope near the wells, and the kernel belongs to a broad sized class modeled on the part Laplace. The authors prove their better bounds are optimal.
arxiv-2604-07121: Li and three colleagues propose Mixed Initiative Context, a way to treat chat context in human AI teamwork as a shaped object both sides can steer. Today, multi turn context is flattened into a time ordered list, so dead threads linger in a small window and clash.
