Users can only nudge context by rewording inputs, with no clear or checkable control. The new view lets the shape, scope, and content of context be rearranged as the task shifts, with humans and AI both shaping it.
arxiv-2604-07221: Ferreira and three colleagues compute the masses of light mesons, built from up, down, and strange quarks, with a symmetry-preserving method. Their approach feeds fully dressed quark-gluon vertices into the key equations, starting from a symmetric kinematic setup. From the gap equation they build a Bethe-Salpeter kernel with three diagram types, then find masses by tracking eigenvalues and extrapolating to the physical point. The results match experiment well and improve markedly on the rainbow-ladder approximation.
arxiv-2604-07821: Yadav, Black, and Sourbut test whether capable language-model agents cooperate when helping costs almost nothing. Many real coordination tasks are not dilemmas: sharing a document or unblocking a teammate costs the helper little and helps the group a lot. In a stripped-down turn-based environment where cooperation is free and plainly optimal, capability fails to predict cooperation. OpenAI o3 reaches only 17 percent of optimal collective performance, while weaker o3-mini reaches 50 percent, under identical instructions to maximize group revenue.
arxiv-2604-07921: Skuric, Von Werra, and Wolf survey sustainability awareness across nearly 50,000 open-access robotics papers from 2015 to early 2026. They count mentions of social, ecological, and green impacts and check alignment with the UN Sustainable Development Goals. A wide share of papers maps to goal-relevant domains, yet explicit green motivation stays very low. Impact mentions usually run below 2 percent, goal references below 0.1 percent, and green-motivated papers below 5 percent. The gap between the field's promise and its stated intent persists across the whole period.
arxiv-2604-08021: Mehta and Mankodi present SynQL, a deterministic framework for synthesizing SQL workloads. Data research and learned query tools rely heavily on SQL workloads. Real queries grow hard to obtain under strict privacy rules, and shared masked traces strip live query text. Older benchmarks offer too few fixed patterns for broad reach, while language-model methods invent fake columns and collapse toward simple join patterns that fail to stress tools. SynQL makes structurally diverse, ready-to-run workloads from rules, giving teams varied, runnable queries without privacy leaks or fake schemas.
arxiv-2604-08121: Qin and eight colleagues present Uni-ViGU, a framework for video making and viewing built on a video maker. Unified multimodal models face a gap: visual making costs far more compute than viewing, especially for video. Rather than stretching viewer models for making, the team inverts the approach, stretching a video maker as the base. A unified flow method matches smooth flow for video and discrete flow for text in one process, giving coherent generation. A mixture-of-experts design augments transformer blocks with lightweight text layers, keeping prior skills.
arxiv-2604-08421: Gelman, Krefman, Kennedy, and Hullman offer a way to form a realistic guess about an average treatment effect before a study runs. Instead of fixing on a single number, they start from how effects vary across people and build the average from that spread. Medicine, economics, and psychology cases show how the spread-first view shapes a more honest prior expectation.
arxiv-2604-08621: Jeunen, Hanna, and Wheeler track agentic personalization in marketing over 11 months in a real consumer app. They compare a phase of direct marketer control with a phase of autonomous agents running a fixed component library. Active human control gave the highest engagement lift, yet autonomous agents kept a real lift on their own afterward. The findings support a joint model: people drive discovery and setup, agents preserve and scale the gains.
arxiv-2604-08721: Cui and four colleagues design a linear feedback controller for homogeneous polynomial systems whose nonlinear term has a tensor form that splits along orthogonal axes. Their structure keeping design shares the tensor eigenbasis, yielding closed form paths and clear settling and escape thresholds. It gives sharp regions of pull, where local linear fits or Lyapunov sum of squares methods prove cautious and costly. Bounds for bounded disturbances follow, with numerical examples confirming the theory.
arxiv-2604-08921: Ao Li and five colleagues present TAIHRI, a vision language model built for close range human robot contact keypoint spotting. Whole body methods tune rebuilds against the root joint, but robots need exact spotting of task key parts under a head camera. TAIHRI reads motion commands, steers focus to task key points, and maps 3D keypoints into a finite contact space. It places key parts through 2D keypoint logic via next token guess. Head camera tests show top scores for task key parts, plus language control and mesh rebuild.
arxiv-2604-09021: Huang, Zaman, and Unoki tackle hallucination in auditory language models, which reason about audio but still invent content. Existing evaluations treat hallucination as yes-or-no classification, too blunt for generative tasks, and current fixes rely on costly fine-tuning. Their noise-aware in-context learning method needs no tuning. They add the Clotho-1K benchmark, four auditory hallucination types, and fine-grained metrics. Tests show all evaluated models share the same hallucination behaviors, and the method cuts the rate from about 27 percent to about 17 percent.
arxiv-2604-09121: Wang and ten colleagues build an agentic framework for interactive speech recognition. Word error rate counts every word equally and often misses whether a sentence means the right thing. Interactive correction, a normal part of human conversation, has rarely been studied systematically for speech recognition. The framework uses a language model as judge for semantic-aware scoring beyond token accuracy. A language-model-driven agent simulates multi-turn interaction, refining outputs through semantic feedback. Tests on English, Chinese, and code-switching benchmarks show gains in fidelity and correction ability.
arxiv-2604-09321: Wang and colleagues propose a real-time network for ultra-high-definition low-light enhancement using Clifford algebra fusion. Transformer and convolutional methods hit a memory wall, failing to reach millisecond-level inference on edge devices. Their network builds a four-layer feature pyramid that splits images into low- and high-frequency parts via Gaussian blur, with a lightweight U-Net for extraction. Clifford algebra maps features to a multivector space, aggregates them while suppressing noise, and reaches millisecond-level inference for 4K and 8K images on one consumer device.
arxiv-2604-09721: Koh and seven co-authors present Jamendo-MT-QA, a benchmark for comparative music question answering across multiple tracks. Earlier music-QA work centers on clips, yet listeners often describe music comparatively, and no benchmark systematically tests reasoning across tracks. Built from Creative Commons tracks on Jamendo, the dataset holds 36,519 comparative items over 12,173 track pairs, each pair yielding yes/no, short-answer, and sentence questions. An LLM-assisted pipeline generates and filters the questions, and audio-language models are benchmarked with automatic metrics plus LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation.
arxiv-2604-09921: Olausson and six co-authors improve diversity in diffusion language model sampling, beyond the usual speed-quality tradeoff for single samples. They soften familiar confidence-based remasking heuristics, keeping their speed and simple implementation, and motivate the change with an idealized model of fork tokens and remasking's effect on entropy. The tempered heuristics close the exploration gap between confidence-based and autoregressive sampling, beating both at equal cost. The added diversity also carries into downstream post-training and test-time compute scaling, showing simple, efficient, diverse sampling is possible.
arxiv-2604-10021: Yonay, Hammond, and Yang show self-taught training design directly shapes pitch ear in music base models, which lag on key detection. Masked contrast vectors alone enable state-of-the-art key detection in the supervised setting. Linear test after masking-based contrast training on Mel spectra already performs well out of the box. Shallow wide multi nets trained on base-model features then reach state-of-the-art performance without fancy tweaks. The learned vectors alone encode common tweaks, proving self-taught training for pitch-sensitive music search tasks.
arxiv-2604-10121: Kibaroğlu explores black hole solutions in Born-Infeld-f(R) gravity, a framework that extends both Born-Infeld and f(R) theories. Adopting a static round spacetime setup, he derives an exact black hole solution and studies its shape. He then checks its thermodynamics, including Hawking temperature, entropy, and specific heat versus model parameters. The results show new thermodynamic behavior far from standard general relativity. Against Schwarzschild-AdS black holes, the corrections shift black hole thermodynamics.
arxiv-2604-10321: Cai and many colleagues review the NTIRE 2026 challenge on single-image reflection removal in the wild. Most methods are tested on synthetic or limited real images, leaving a gap in real applications. The challenge gave participants the OpenRR-5k dataset of real-world images across reflection scenarios and intensities, asking for clean images without reflections. It drew over 100 registrations, with eleven teams reaching final testing. The top methods advanced reflection removal performance and earned unanimous recognition from five field experts.
arxiv-2604-10421: Chai builds small theta lifts for even orthogonal symplectic and unitary pairs over p-adic fields. His tool is a sesquilinear form, linear on one side and conjugate linear on the other. The lift links each side of a dual pair through that shared form. Even pairs of both the orthogonal symplectic and unitary kinds fall in scope. The note thus gives a direct form based route to these small lifts.
arxiv-2604-10921: Nabizadeh-Morsalfard and three colleagues deduce norm matches and convolution bounds for a modulation space defined by a mild fading condition far out. They prove that space completes the Gelfand-Shilov space under the norm. Using these results, they deduce compactness for pseudo-differential and Toeplitz operators acting on a broad family of these spaces. The work gives a shared basis for treating compactness across that family, linking norm structure and convolution bounds to operator traits.
arxiv-2604-11021: Morse and Kozsik study when a programming language can emulate its own programs without handing them back to the host. They call this trait emulation-completeness. Turing-completeness alone is not enough. A self-emulator must also account for guest-visible state such as control flow, errors, callbacks, timing, memory use, and stack traces. This systematization paper offers a precise word list and map rather than a new emulator. It splits source-level checking from built-code emulation and weak from strong cases by kept visible conduct.
arxiv-2604-11221: Kazanskii studies a space-clock elevator, a modular transport scheme that hands payloads between rotating tethers at different orbital radii through elliptical transfer nodes. Tethers that spin have long been pitched as a way to move loads without burning fuel. Numerical work finds families of setups where neighboring tethers stay nearly in sync, allowing coordinated exchanges without impulsive maneuvers. The resulting networks can carry payloads outward while keeping tether tension bounded and orbital motion stable, offering a propellant-free alternative for transfers beyond low Earth orbit.
arxiv-2604-11521: Lin and four colleagues propose continuous adversarial flow models, trained with an adversarial objective. Where flow matching uses a fixed mean-squared-error criterion, they use a learned discriminator to guide training. The new objective yields samples better aligned with the target distribution. Built as post-training, it substantially lifts guidance-free FID on ImageNet 256px. Latent-space SiT improves from 8-point-26 to 3-point-63, and pixel-space JiT from 7-point-17 to 3-point-57. Guided FID improves, with text-to-image gains on GenEval and DPG.
arxiv-2604-11721: Faulkner and four colleagues test cooperation in LLM social groups through elected leadership. Shared resources need lasting cooperation and self-rule to avoid collective failure, but multi-agent research rarely tests whether elected leaders improve group decisions. Their open-source framework tests leadership through elected personas and candidate plans under set governance rules. Elected leadership lifts welfare scores by 55.4 percent and survival time by 128.6 percent across strong LLMs. Agent social graphs yield centrality scores for leaders, and sentiment analysis of leader speech shows rhetorical and cooperative traits.
arxiv-2604-11821: Solanki models late-time cosmic expansion with a polytropic equation of state, leaving the dark-energy-like fluid's form free rather than assumed, inside a power-law f(Q) cosmology. He derives an exact solution and constrains its parameters with Bayesian analysis using the emcee sampler, interpreting deceleration and statefinder values. The paper reports where this model stands on the Hubble constant tension between early- and late-universe measurements.
arxiv-2604-12021: Faber and Golubich find the potential of a soliton dipole in the singlet state, modelled as an SU(2) field, from lattice runs of two solitons at varying gaps. At large gaps the potential matches the standard Coulomb potential closely, up to a shift near 9 keV, blamed on lattice limits. At shorter distances, shifts from point-charge Coulomb pattern appear. They roughly match the QED formula for the running fine-structure value, with the inverse value matched near 137.
arxiv-2604-12121: Oliveira and three colleagues show a particle-physics model with an enlarged gauge symmetry can naturally host a dark matter particle lighter than one mega-electronvolt. The candidate is a near-massless pseudo-Goldstone boson given a tiny mass by gravity. Its observed abundance arises through slow freeze-in at a low reheating temperature, with no need for extremely small couplings. The model works at tera-electronvolt energies and stays testable at colliders.
arxiv-2604-12221: Cai and three colleagues introduce BarbieGait, a synthetic gait dataset mapping real subjects into a virtual engine to simulate wide clothing changes while keeping gait identity intact. Clothing diversity raises within-class variance and blocks cloth-invariant learning, so they add GaitCLIF, a baseline model built for cross-clothing recognition. Tests show it lifts cross-clothing performance on BarbieGait and on existing popular gait benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-12821: Samantha D'Alonzo and nine colleagues define, measure, and try to raise intellectual humility in online political talk. Humility means owning one's limits; arrogance blocks understanding. A codebook guides annotation of hundreds of Reddit posts, feeding a classifier for large-scale analysis. Data show high- and low-humility threads tend to breed more of the same. A randomized trial tests nudges that prompt more humble posts. Nudges lift humility across contentious topics without cutting engagement.
arxiv-2604-13121: Carbone and five colleagues frame olfactory pursuit, catching a moving odor source in rough flow, as a decision problem under uncertainty. An agent tracks a joint belief over the target's position and speed, and quasi-optimal policies come from solving the Bellman equation for a run-and-tumble model. Pure exploration works near-optimally when the target reorients often but fails under persistent motion. A hybrid policy mixing Infotaxis information gain with greedy value estimates wins across persistence times.
arxiv-2604-13321: Gopinath, Krishnaswamy, and Draper ask why multimodal language models fail at judging two-dimensional object orientation in images. Earlier work blamed the visual encoder, since encoders like CLIP and SigLIP train for image-text alignment rather than geometry. Their controlled tests train simple linear models to predict orientation from encoder embeddings in several systems. Orientation proves recoverable, so the encoder is not the bottleneck. Instead the signal spreads thinly across tens of thousands of features, which may explain why models cannot use it.
arxiv-2604-13521: Kubo and five colleagues introduce C-voting, a confidence voting for recurrent models. Such models repeat identical layers on a latent state and scale at test time by adding steps. C-voting starts from multiple candidates and selects the one with highest top-1 probabilities, reflecting confidence. It beats energy-based voting by about 5 percent accuracy on Sudoku-hard and needs no energy function. With a new attention model, ItrSA++, it outperforms HRM on Sudoku-extreme by about 95 percent to 55 percent and on Maze by about 79 percent to 75 percent.
arxiv-2604-13621: Drosos and three colleagues ask how fast experts can answer questions about feature-rich software, coining nanoquestions for items answerable in under a minute. From over 200 forum questions, they judged about a quarter short enough to qualify. In a study with 28 forum experts, more than half of the nanoquestions seen drew advice the experts judged helpful within 60 seconds, pointing toward tools for ultra-rapid human help.
arxiv-2604-13721: Parames-Estevez and three colleagues build FRAGATA, a semantic search system for two decades of supercomputing support tickets at CESGA. The center's Request Tracker history holds critical operational knowledge, but its built-in search hampers reuse. FRAGATA combines modern retrieval with the full ticket history, finding relevant past incidents despite language differences, typos, or wording changes. It updates incrementally without downtime and offloads heavy stages to the FinisTerrae III supercomputer.
arxiv-2604-13821: Ivanov and four colleagues study complex surface patterns in crystal growth, both homoepitaxial and heteroepitaxial. They compare two models. One is a continuum Ginzburg-Landau model, extending Tersoff models to two-plus-one dimensions. The other is an atomistic Vicinal Cellular Automaton, driven by a double-well force field at each step edge. Step bunching and step meandering naturally coexist in real materials. Both patterns show up in real crystals. The framework links morphologies and diagrams across contexts, bridging mesoscale and atomistic views of governing factors.
arxiv-2604-14421: Pfreundschuh and five colleagues build BIEVR-LIO, a LiDAR-inertial odometry method for feature-poor places where registration can drift or diverge. Surfaces are stored as voxel-wise oriented height images, usable directly for registration without intermediate primitives, while staying cheap to update. Map-guided sampling steers registration toward geometrically rich regions, beating global high-resolution sampling on cost. Tests across sensors, platforms, and scenes show top performance in constrained scenes and large gains where baselines diverge, with the fine geometry also serving elevation mapping for locomotion.
arxiv-2604-14521: Tatara, Takane, and Manchon study spin Hall effects, direct and inverse, in a superconductor-normal-superconductor junction under a spatially symmetric spin-orbit interaction. A supercurrent drives a spin Hall effect, piling opposite static spin at the two edges, as in normal conductors. For the inverse effect, an uneven magnetic field induces an anomalous phase shift, which yields a diode effect with higher harmonics. Unlike Rashba systems, the mechanism needs no broken structural inversion symmetry, since the uneven field, acting like a spin current, breaks inversion symmetry from outside.
arxiv-2604-14821: Rajan and five colleagues study pattern formation as a two-phase eutectic melts in a temperature gradient. Thin-sample tests on a transparent alloy pair with phase-field simulations tuned to the same alloy. Depending on melting velocity and lamellar spacing, rich melting patterns appear, with tests and simulations agreeing. They pin down scaling for liquid penetration along solid-solid interfaces at high velocity, finger thickening at low velocity, and a period-doubling instability at small spacing. The work grounds future eutectic-melting study, including additive manufacturing.
arxiv-2604-15121: Snyder and colleagues design SRMU, an update rule for streaming hyperdimensional memories that resists stale information. Standard vector-symbolic systems add each observation in, so repeats reinforce old content even after the world shifts. SRMU gates updates by relevance, a rule that works across domains and cleanup schemes. The paper positions it as a fix for sequential associative memories fed by uneven, shifting streams.
arxiv-2604-15221: Thumm and colleagues build a vision-based safety pipeline for human-robot collaboration with statistical guarantees. Their system predicts 3D human motion with conformal bounds on prediction error, replacing out-of-distribution poses with past predictions to keep motion smooth. The prediction sets feed directly into the provably safe SARA shield. Tests on the Human3.6M collection and a live joint setup show the sets run more than seven times smaller in volume than a baseline, meeting a necessary condition for performance level d.
arxiv-2604-15421: Monaghan and four colleagues redo rocky-exoplanet secondary eclipse studies in one shared model that carries star and orbit errors all the way through. Even for a simple dark bare rock, model error in forecast eclipse depth can rival errors in the data, blurring atmosphere verdicts. Their method yields a linear link between model error and errors in planet-star radius ratios and star temperature. That link sets a floor on how sharply future work can pin down composition.
arxiv-2604-15621: Feng and seven colleagues rethink adaptive retrieval-augmented generation now that stronger language models tolerate noise better. Their AdaRankLLM pairs a zero-shot adaptive ranker with passage dropout against fixed-depth retrieval, then distills listwise ranking and adaptive filtering into smaller open models in two stages. Across three datasets and eight models it leads most scenarios with far less context, acting as a noise filter for weak models and an efficiency optimizer for strong ones.
arxiv-2604-15721: Pan studies how long two-dim squeeze-proof fluid models last and when their runs can roll on. With a fresh energy-spin frame, plus straight-line haul gauges and a lift-itself proof, he shows long-life runs for near-Euler two-dim fluids. A side gain is a new if-then BKM-type rule for the patchy squeeze-proof Euler flow.
arxiv-2604-15821: Zhou and fourteen colleagues crack billion-weight all-atom force models with MatRIS-MoE, an expert-mix model on a fixed-shape base. Janus, a spread-out frame with machine-tuned tweaks, trains it. Run on two exascale beasts, the code tops 1.2 and 1.0 EFLOPS in single precision, 24 and 35.5 percent of peak, past 90 percent efficiency. That shrinks billion-weight training from weeks to hours. The work lifts the exascale bar for AI-for-Science models.
arxiv-2604-16221: Rücker, Davies, and Schwarzer show that treatment-effect covariances in a network meta-analysis follow from a geometric series of diffusion matrices, with no matrix inversion needed. The same trick extends to the hat matrix, linking regression estimation with random walks on the network graph. They also provide visualization tools for the method, implemented in R.
arxiv-2604-16421: Jawandhia and colleagues ask whether language models truly reason about geometry or merely react to how a problem is written. Their GeoRepEval framework poses the same high-school geometry problems in Euclidean, coordinate and vector forms, scoring correctness and stability across the versions. Testing eleven models on 158 problems, they found the wording alone shifted accuracy by up to 14 percentage points, with vector forms failing most. A convert-then-solve prompt rescued high-capacity models but not weaker ones, suggesting sensitivity to form rather than pure inability.
arxiv-2604-16521: Panjwani identifies a privacy hole in multi-turn language-model chats: masking each message alone misses clues that add up across turns. A user who shares a name, employer, location and condition reveals a re-identifiable profile, yet no message trips a per-turn mask. His CAMP framework formalizes this cumulative exposure, keeps a session registry of data, models risk with a co-occurrence graph, and scores exposure after each turn. When the score passes a threshold, it masks history retroactively, neutralizing profiles in four scenarios, keeping chat useful.
arxiv-2604-16621: Lourenço and colleagues design funicular shells with a physics tool. Shells appeal for value, and concrete printing has renewed interest. Concrete cannot take steel, so forms must carry pure pressure and be arched. Since Hooke's chain arch in 1675, it has remained unknown whether the polygon extends to dimensions. Their model tweaks a GAN, guided by a judge, to generate efficient shapes. A rule cuts bending-dominated shapes, and a judge handles more forms. Results show stable making of optimal unseen curved shells with forms and high membrane factors.
arxiv-2604-16821: Peng and colleagues release R&F-Inventory, a large-scale dataset for monotonic inventory estimation in reach and repeat advertising. Reach and frequency contracts stress managed sending of unique and page views under aiming, timing and frequency control. Old public sets use solo samples, missing the budget curve structure at the heart of such contracts. The dataset tracks unique and page views at many budget points within one context, forming full curves. It has time-window frequency control, meets rise and fading returns, and defines two benchmark tasks.
arxiv-2604-17121: Mozer, Siddiqui, and Liu argue feedforward transformers fundamentally limit dynamic state tracking, pushing evolving state deeper into the layer stack with each input step until depth runs out. Dynamic-depth models and explicit or latent thinking can bypass the limit, but at high compute and memory cost. The authors call for recurrent architectures and implicit activation flows instead, offering a map of recurrent and continuous-thought designs by recurrence axis and token-to-step ratio.
arxiv-2604-17321: Ramachandra presents R-FLoRA, a detector for face-morphing attacks that blends a single photo. No trusted reference image is needed. It pairs high-frequency residual clues with a frozen large vision model, gating small adapter modules by residual statistics. A new contrastive loss aligns the fused features. Across four passport-style datasets and seven morph techniques, it beat nine recent rivals in accuracy and generalization while staying fast and light enough for real border and identity checks.
arxiv-2604-17521: Klein, Roudenko, and Stoilov build a numerical method for a class of wavy, nonlinear equations in three dimensions, using the generalized Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation as their test case. Turning to cylindrical coordinates and splitting the domain by how waves should act cuts cost while keeping fine detail. The method handles the tricky power of 7/3, which usually breeds breakdown. Near the ground-state solitary wave, they show it marks the sharp line between waves that persist and waves that blow up in finite time.
arxiv-2604-17621: Zhang and four colleagues introduce KnowledgeBerg, a benchmark for questions that look simple but demand full coverage of a bounded knowledge universe plus compositional reasoning. The team calls this pattern the tip of the iceberg. The benchmark holds 4,800 multiple-choice questions from 1,183 enumeration seeds with universes grounded in trusted sources across 10 domains and 17 languages. Open-source models score only 5.26 to 36.88 F1 on listing universes and 16.00 to 44.19 accuracy on grounded reasoning. Failures fall into three stages: completeness, awareness, and application.
arxiv-2604-18221: Kivarkis, Mouhali, Benkadda, and Schneider build deep-learning surrogates that predict two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities over time. Two designs, a Koopman-based Transformer and a ConvLSTM-UNet, predict vorticity and current density straight from high-resolution runs. Trained step by step, the models mimic multiscale traits across growth and saturation phases. They keep key physics such as global invariants and Alfvénic waves at far lower cost than direct runs.
arxiv-2604-18321: Burns and Liang study accuracy certificates for convex optimization, checkable proofs that a solution is nearly optimal. The primal gap itself is usually unavailable in practice, so the authors solve a regularized surrogate instead. One-average primal-dual methods yield certificate guarantees, while a symmetric two-average method loses them. A new three-average method restores convergence at accelerated rates and mirrors gradient extrapolation in the dual, linking the methods to games and markets.
arxiv-2604-18621: Saggi and three colleagues use quantum machine learning to hunt markers for lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma. First, they compare tumor and healthy samples for gene-activity and methylation shifts, pinning genes tied to each type. Next, they build a quantum sorter telling the two tumor types apart and tumor from healthy tissue. Their combined gene set, Sample3, scores best on every measure. Pathway checks point to routes like neurotrophin, MAPK, Ras, and PI3K-Akt signaling, with NGFR, NTRK2, and NTF3 hinting at a core role.
arxiv-2604-18721: Wasalathilaka and six colleagues run a strictly controlled benchmark of visual state-space backbones for remote-sensing segmentation, varying only the encoder across experiments. Tested on LoveDA and ISPRS Potsdam with a fixed small decoder, the study finds modest gains from scaling within a family. Cross-domain generalization runs strongly asymmetric, and boundary errors drive failures under distribution shift. Robustness and boundary-aware decoding look more promising than encoder scaling alone.
arxiv-2604-18921: Poon and four colleagues reanalyze visual binary spin orbit angles with a hierarchical Bayesian model. Earlier work found binaries below about 30 AU tend to be more aligned, but later work questioned the statistics. The new analysis finds a Bayes factor of 12 for two subpopulations separated by a 31 to 38 AU cutoff. Inner binaries are more aligned, outer ones less aligned. The cutoffs may mark formation pathway transitions, with closer binaries aligned in a shared disk. Wider binaries may form less aligned through turbulence, and a secondary cutoff needs data.
arxiv-2604-19021: Sun and eight colleagues introduce FG2-GDN, a gated delta network with doubly fine grained control. Linear attention gives linear time inference, with the delta rule updating memory by gradient descent. Kimi attention moved decay control from heads to channels, but its learning rate stayed scalar. FG2-GDN replaces that scalar with a channel wise vector, like adaptive per coordinate optimizers. A plus variant splits key and value scaling for separate erasure and write control. Both beat prior networks on recall and long context understanding at comparable cost.
arxiv-2604-19221: Li and three colleagues propose the first unified audio front-end model for full-duplex speech, reformulating tasks into a single sequence prediction problem. Cascaded pipelines suffer latency, information loss, and error propagation. End-to-end audio models unify understanding and generation but remain half-duplex, relying on separate voice and turn-taking detectors. Front-end work matters as much as back-end work for seamless interaction. It takes streaming fixed-duration chunks, such as 600 milliseconds, with a reference prompt anchoring the speaker, generating discrete tokens encoding semantic content.
arxiv-2604-19321: Çelebi and colleagues address a puzzle in fine-tuning large language models: which layers should be adapted, when the roles of hidden states are poorly understood. They model hidden-state evolution as a geometric path and use the Ramer-Douglas-Peucker simplification algorithm to find critical breakpoints along it. Those geometric pivots then serve directly as the signal for layer choice, rather than as analysis alone. The geometry-aware selection replaces heuristic guesses about where adaptation belongs.
arxiv-2604-19521: Miniguano-Trujillo and colleagues build a fast, error-checked numerical method for the nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard equation. It models phase separation with long-range interactions. Its existence and regularity theory is rich, yet the math stays hard. Their method uses a pseudospectral multishape approach with a simple mobility rule and closed boundaries. Mixtures that split into parts are the focus here. The method must handle long-range forces between parts.
arxiv-2604-19621: Meredith and colleagues present a fast optimization method for multi-setting quantum control protocols in strongly coupled systems. It combines auto gradients with the non-Markovian uniTEMPO algorithm. High-quality control amid strong lingering noise is key for new solid-state quantum devices. The method enables direct gradient-based tuning of complex goal functions. Applied to quantum dots, it optimizes multi-pulse schemes, namely SUPER and Floquet-engineered Two-Photon Excitation for single- and bi-exciton generation.
arxiv-2604-19821: Ghoshal and 11 colleagues introduce JTPRO, a framework that improves tool-calling reliability for language agents when tool counts grow large and domain-specific. Vague tool descriptions and under-specified agent instructions often cause wrong tool choices and incorrect slot or value filling. The authors trace the trouble to two root causes. First, generic one-size-fits-all prompts ignore tool-specific nuances. Second, underspecified tool schemas lack clear guidance on when and how to use each tool and format its parameters.
arxiv-2604-20221: Sabatini uses symbolic time series tools and Markov models on the sound shape of Pushkin's Evgenij Onegin and one modern Italian rendering. Vowel and consonant letters form a binary code, in Markov's first spirit, feeding spare chance models that catch local and broad patterns. A compact four-state Markov chain stays true to life and spawns new text, matching the source in self-linkage and memory depth. The Russian text slowly loses memory depth while the Italian rendering holds steadier, and short sound probes tie letter shape to theme.
arxiv-2604-20321: Ciacco, Di Puglia Pugliese, and Guerriero tackle the traveling salesman problem with a cutting-plane method that builds subtour elimination constraints on the fly. A preprocessing pass first trims the candidate arcs, and constraints join the model only as needed, keeping the model small. They test classical optimization, direct quantum annealing on D-Wave hardware, and hybrid quantum-classical solvers. All three paths shrink model size and speed up computation, showing the framework pays off across classical, direct quantum, and hybrid optimization.
arxiv-2604-21021: Yang and colleagues report giant spontaneous Kerr rotations in alpha-MnTe crystals, an altermagnetic material prized for ultrafast, stray-field-free spintronics. The signal switches on at the Néel temperature of 307 K, at 1550 nm telecom wavelength. It appears in separate patches whose strength tracks sample conductivity, and a hole-conducting film reproduces the response with an anomalous Hall effect. Kerr-active regions look optically distinct from silent surroundings in reflection maps. The pattern points to carrier self-doping, not ideal order alone, as governing the giant response.
arxiv-2604-21221: Boxun Xu and nine colleagues make autoregressive video diffusion faster and steadier with Sparse Forcing, a method that learns which visual blocks persist as memory in the attention cache. A trainable sparsity mechanism compresses, preserves, and updates those blocks inside sliding windows. It is accelerated by a persistent block-sparse attention kernel. On 5-second clips it improves VBench over Self-Forcing while speeding decoding and shrinking the peak cache footprint by 42 percent, with larger gains on longer clips.
arxiv-2604-21421: Michele Miranda and six colleagues compare differential privacy, named entity spotting, and large language models for scrubbing Dutch clinical notes, the first head-to-head study of its kind. Safe sharing of clinical notes matters under GDPR and HIPAA, but manual scrubbing is costly and slow. Differential-privacy tools alone degrade utility a lot, yet combining them with language preprocessing, especially LLM-based scrubbing, greatly improves the privacy-utility trade-off. Mixed plans applying NER or LLM preprocessing before differential privacy are also tested on leakage and downstream classification.
arxiv-2604-21521: Heller, Pedit, and Ouyang build the first smooth, embedded, compact special Legendrian surfaces in five-dimensional sphere space with genus above one. For every large enough integer k, they construct such a surface whose shape follows the Fermat curve of degree k. The proof mixes an elementary implicit function theorem with loop-algebra connections and a study of unitarisability in a character variety of the thrice-punctured sphere.
arxiv-2604-21621: Jadlovský and colleagues track two aging giant stars, the Mira star R Car and the red supergiant VX Sgr, through 54 interferometer snapshots gathered over seven years. They find photospheric radii that swing with the light curve, peaking near brightness minima. Carbon monoxide layers stretch much further out in irregular rhythms. During 2020 and 2021, VX Sgr suffered an extreme mass-loss outburst resembling Betelgeuse, supporting steady pulsation-driven loss for Miras but event-driven loss for supergiants.
arxiv-2604-22021: Tommasini and three colleagues present a data-driven way to cut eccentricity in numerical relativity simulations of binary black holes. Standard runs use repeat trials, often four or more. The authors learn the starting orbit frequency and radial velocity for small eccentricity, using a Gaussian Process Regression model trained on an archive of past eccentricity-reduced simulations. For all cases tested, the trained model cuts required runs to zero or one, lowering costs relative to post-Newtonian starting guesses.
arxiv-2604-22521: Kataoka and three colleagues show how decoherence can turn a color code into a mixed-state topological phase with no pure-state counterpart. For decoherence from XX-type operators on red links of the honeycomb lattice, the mixed state keeps half the color code's topological character. A gauging procedure for mixed stabilizer states identifies the emergent phase as close kin to a single toric code. Topological entanglement negativity confirms the picture, halving under full decoherence, with a smooth crossover and a sharp variance peak as strength is tuned.
arxiv-2604-22621: Cao and 327 colleagues report gamma-ray emission up to hundreds of TeV from two remnants, G150.3+4.5 and gamma-Cygni, seen with LHAASO. Remnant shocks are considered the main cosmic ray contributors below the knee near 3 PeV, and whether remnants accelerate beyond PeV energies has been debated. Two or three components with convex shapes appear, the low-energy one more extended than the high-energy one. A likely link between that component and molecular clouds, plus weak or absent pulsar wind nebulae, supports a supernova remnant origin.
arxiv-2604-22721: Valdivia-Prado, Chapman, and Friedrich present a method for local averages, variance, and sample counts on gridded data with gaps, using boundary-aware spectral operators. Reflective transforms handle straight axes while periodic transforms handle circular azimuth in polar grids, with safeguards for weakly supported regions. Tests on synthetic data and real radar show stable, support-aware statistics, released through the dct_toolkit code.
arxiv-2604-22821: Pahwa and six colleagues introduce Audio2Tool, a benchmark of about 30,000 spoken queries testing whether speech language models can call tools correctly across smart cars, smart homes, and wearables. Tasks range from single commands to multi-intent requests and hard searches for one detail buried in long input, with cloned voices and varied noise mimicking real conditions. Current models handle simple commands well but degrade sharply on compositional and noisy tasks.
arxiv-2604-23121: Huang and seven colleagues study robot policies that stiffen after light post-training and stop obeying fresh orders. They call this lock-in: fixation on demo objects and fixation on demo spots. Their fix, DeLock, guards visual grounding in training and steers denoising at test time with prompt guidance. Across eight simulated and real tests, it beat strong baselines and matched a leading policy trained on far more demos.
arxiv-2604-23921: Gerolymatos and colleagues tackle crystal structure search as a combinatorial optimisation problem, placing atoms on grid positions in a unit cell to cut interaction energy. Exact solvers grow costly at large scale, especially without symmetry constraints. Their neural approach uses graph neural networks to sample workable structures without supervision, with expander graphs capturing short- and long-range links and a Gumbel-Sinkhorn step fixing stoichiometry. The method beats older heuristics and rivals a commercial solver across chemical mixes, opening the way to GPU-scale crystal search.
arxiv-2604-24021: An and three colleagues present QED, a multi-agent system that turns human research questions into full math proofs with no further human help. One agent plans the search, others draft candidate proofs, and verifiers check each step for correctness. Tested with experts on 18 research-level projects, it produced five original works, three of them judged comparable to papers in established specialist math venues.
arxiv-2604-24121: Wang and Zhang show that the dominant natural orbital of a Gaussian open fermion chain can expose hidden skin order. Relaxation matrices may localize modes at boundaries, yet the density profile alone need not reveal that order. Their exact steady-state theory splits the correlator into slow denominators, source loading, and real-space geometry from left and right modes. In a single slow-mode regime the top orbital locks onto the slow right mode, a law they verify in Hatano-Nelson and SSH chains.
arxiv-2604-24721: Wang, Woo, Villafaña, Treu and Gallo present dynamical modeling of the broad-line region for eight high-mass active galactic nuclei from the Seoul National University monitoring project. The hydrogen-beta emitting regions look most like thick disks at intermediate inclinations, with emission favoring the far side. Kinematics combine rotation, inflow and outflow. Comparing dynamical masses with virial products yields virial factors for individual objects. A combined sample of 38 objects gives updated factors for future mass estimates. It extends the sample to the most massive black holes.
arxiv-2604-25121: Nakatsuyama investigates the evolute of a space curve with singular points through framed curve theory. The involute matching the evolute as the locus of centres of osculating spheres had not yet been defined. She therefore defines evolutes and involutes of non-degenerate curves and framed curves directly, using Bertrand type curves. She gives conditions under which evolutes and involutes are inverse operations, and investigates the other cases where they are not.
arxiv-2604-25321: Peterseim and Lopuhaä-Zwakenberg show discrete probabilistic program inference runs in polynomial time only for plain programs. It runs in polynomial time when each function's primal graph has bounded treewidth and the inverse acceptance chance is at most exponential in program size. Past schemes lack this pledge. Their way finds apt algebra forms of the string diagrams behind such programs, using past tree decomposition schemes. This holds for other settings too, with uses in database queries and security risk checks via attack trees.
arxiv-2604-25621: Dai and three colleagues explain how substitutional platinum acts as a recombination centre in silicon. It is widely used for carrier-lifetime control in power devices, yet its microscopic mechanism stayed debated. First-principles calculations with multiphonon theory show donor and acceptor levels capture electrons and holes with large cross sections. Cross sections prove sensitive to defect setups with distinct Jahn-Teller distortions. Using two distinct neutral-dopant configurations during transitions brings cross sections in line with lab values.
arxiv-2604-25721: Xia and seven colleagues convene a workshop on new learning tools, linking artificial intelligence, human-computer interaction, and the learning sciences. The meeting focuses on human-AI tools for learning that are robust, centered on people, and grounded in teaching. Through talk across fields, those present aim to name shared challenges, design rules, and research paths. The workshop fills a gap between fields that often study learning tools apart.
arxiv-2604-25821: Jia and four colleagues propose a new description of symmetry in two-dimensional quantum field theory with anomalous 0-form symmetry. The symmetry category becomes twisted measurable fields of Hilbert spaces over the group, matching unitary representations of a function algebra with twisted convolution. Its Drinfeld center matches representations of a groupoid algebra from a Fell line bundle over the conjugation groupoid. The framework covers groups combining a compact connected factor with real or complex factors.
arxiv-2604-25921: Arif and three colleagues present Incremental Completion Decomposition, a jailbreak built from single-word continuations. Language models refuse harmful requests, yet conversational safety gaps remain. The attack first elicits a chain of single-word continuations tied to a malicious request, then the full response. Variants use model-written or attacker-written middle continuations, plus final-response prefilling. Across open-weight model families, attack success beats existing methods on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and StrongREJECT. Theory and mechanistic evidence show successful runs suppress refusal representations and move activations away from safety-aligned states.
arxiv-2604-26221: Wang and six colleagues built SeeCo, a plug-in tool that sharpens open-vocabulary segmentation of satellite images without any extra training. It adjusts each model on the spot for the scene at hand, checking agreement across different views and across wording, so land-cover labels stay consistent. Tests on eight remote-sensing benchmarks showed steady gains over the unaided models.
arxiv-2604-26821: Liu and four colleagues present VOXEL, a fast simulation framework for judging 3D-stacked AI chips that run large language models. Such chips stack memory banks over processor cores to ease the memory bottleneck, but their tangled design choices resist simple study. VOXEL lets compilers shape execution plans and explores compute styles, mappings, network layouts, and energy and heat limits, checked against an emulator on real silicon. Efficiency hinges most on how work maps to cores and memory banks.
arxiv-2604-26921: Miloschewsky, Podder and Rudolph study the power of quantum witnesses under perfect completeness. They build an oracle where a language sits in QMA1 but outside QCMA, when the QCMA verifier gets limited rounds and huge parallel query batches. They also derandomize the Fefferman-Kimmel permutation-oracle result, giving an in-place oracle separation of QMA1 and QCMA. With a tiny gap they separate the classes for fixed gaps, but not for gaps that may shrink without bound. Results follow for near ground-state preparation from sparse Hamiltonian oracles.
arxiv-2604-27021: Lima, Belchior and Moreira build a double O(3)-sigma model coupled to a Maxwell field in (2+1) spacetime, hunting self-dual magnetic vortex solutions. A Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield analysis shows both sigma fields share one topological sector, with a cosine-like potential. The theory yields magnetic vortices with quantized flux, as two nonlinear sigma sectors merge into a single sector in the BPS regime. Numerical work confirms smooth, localized field profiles, with field and energy density staying regular and confined.
arxiv-2604-27121: Eskin and three colleagues use the variational method to compute energy levels of muonic helium, an atom holding a ground-state electron and an excited muon. They take Gaussian trial wave functions for muon states with principal and orbital numbers near 14. They evaluate Hamiltonian matrix elements in the nonrelativistic picture plus vacuum polarization and relativistic corrections analytically. The resulting series of Rydberg muon energies can be checked in experiments.
arxiv-2604-27721: Berngardt and Ponomarchuk present a physics-informed fuzzy clustering method for ionograms, splitting each ionogram into tracks for further reading. The method works even when the track count is unknown in advance, as in disturbed sky conditions. It groups points by fitting curve models close to parabolic-layer tracks. Each track model carries six parameters, and by adding tracks one by one, the model finds the best track count by minimizing a modified Bayesian information criterion.
arxiv-2604-27821: Ndulue and four colleagues present a learned pipeline for hierarchical scene graph matching. Scene graphs encode spatial structure as a hierarchy of entities and relationships, built from sensor data and building models. Matching the two representations enables drift correction in SLAM, while combinatorial methods are expensive and learned approaches address only flat graph matching. Trained only on floor plans, the method beats the combinatorial baseline in F1 on LiDAR environments. It runs an order of magnitude faster, showing zero-shot generalization for BIM-assisted localization.
arxiv-2605-00621:
Christopher David Roberts and 4 co-authors assess what the oceans contribute to weather prediction at subseasonal range, weeks ahead, in Europe's leading forecast system. Coupling the atmosphere to a live ocean should help, through realistic air-sea exchange, but the interface can also grow biases that hurt. The team revisits that balance using forty-six-day reforecasts, hindcasts rerun with today's system.

Coupling significantly improved ensemble skill in the tropics, with benefits growing at longer lead times. Forecasts of the Madden-Julian Oscillation, a giant tropical weather pattern, gained about five days of skill over the uncoupled setup. In the extratropics the effect was marginal, barely moving major circulation indices. An experimental configuration with a much finer ocean grid, fine enough to resolve eddies, added little at this range. Accurate ocean initialization, the authors suggest, already captures most of the available benefit.
arxiv-2605-00721:
Anton Ratnarajah and 3 co-authors estimate how far a speaker is from a listener using synthetic echoes, in work from a room acoustics challenge at a major signal processing conference. Judging speaker distance from a recording depends on the room's impulse response, its acoustic fingerprint, and real datasets of such fingerprints are sparse. The challenge asks whether generated responses can supplement the few real ones.

The team generates impulse responses with an open-source fast generator that needs only the speaker and listener positions. A quality filter keeps synthetic responses that align with the challenge's real ones, and tuned fine-tuning does the rest. The augmentation cut the average distance error dramatically, roughly by two-thirds, in two simulated room families. Gains were largest at medium and long distances, exactly where estimation is hardest and where a system that knows how far away a voice sits becomes most useful.
arxiv-2605-01021:
Marcel Novaes generalizes the Kuramoto model of interacting oscillators so the particles move on the surface of a torus in D dimensions. The classic one-dimensional model is a standard tool for studying synchronization, where oscillators slowly lock into step. In the new version, the group behavior changes in a key way: the shift to synchronization becomes first order, meaning it is abrupt rather than smooth.

Novaes sets up the mean-field dynamics using a multidimensional Ott-Antonsen ansatz, a method that reduces the group equations. Synchronization arises through a saddle-node bifurcation, while the incoherent state remains always stable. Theory calculations are checked by numerical simulations. Readers get a clear picture of how higher-dimensional motion reshapes a classic model of synchronization.
arxiv-2605-01221:
Genki Osada proposes a new way to estimate the local intrinsic dimension of data, the number of directions that truly vary near a point. Diffusion models have opened new routes to this task, but older methods break down in high-dimensional spaces. Noise from the many normal directions drowns out the tangent signal that sets the local dimension, so estimates go wrong.

The method, called Local Hessian Spectral Dimension, filters the spectrum of the log-density Hessian. It cuts away the large eigenvalues tied to normal directions and counts the tangent directions with zero curvature. A stochastic Lanczos method makes the computation cheap, with cost growing only linearly in the dimension. Tests on synthetic and real data show stronger robustness than older methods. The method can also flag memorization in large diffusion models, where local dimension signals reveal overfitting to training data.
arxiv-2605-01321:
Yasuyuki Hatsuda and Tomohito Shiga compute the ringing tones of charged and spinning black holes at the extreme limit, where charge or spin is as high as it can be. These tones, called quasinormal modes, are the fading notes a black hole sounds after it is struck.

The pair use exact WKB analysis, a refined wave method that turns the tone problem into a set of exact conditions on complex frequencies. The key inputs, known as quantum periods, are summed to very high order and then resummed with a Borel-Padé step to get stable values. For scalar waves on extreme Reissner-Nordström and Kerr holes, the final tones match known correct values with high precision. That match checks the method on some of the hardest cases in the field.
arxiv-2605-01421:
Rosalba Garcia-Millan and six co-authors ask whether particles that only push each other away can act, in effect, as if they attract. Self-propelled particles that repel are known to clump into dense and dilute zones, a split often read as a sign of effective attraction.

The team test the idea in the smallest possible case: two soft run-and-tumble particles in a ring-shaped domain, handled with an exact microscopic theory. As the push between them grows, the leading effect is still effective repulsion. Attraction shows up only as a smaller, higher-order correction to the pair's effective interaction. The result refines the usual story told about this clumping: the phase split is real, but calling its onset an attraction effect skips the term that actually leads.
arxiv-2605-01521:
Paraskevas V Lekeas and Giorgos Stamatopoulos revisit cooperative games where a coalition's payoff depends on how the whole player set splits into groups. In this partition function form, what outsiders do among themselves changes what your group earns, which makes beliefs about outsiders part of the game.

Each coalition is assumed to hold probabilistic beliefs about how the outsiders will group, and those beliefs need not match what the outsiders actually choose. The pair apply the setup to symmetric games with positive or negative spillovers between groups. They derive conditions on the beliefs under which the core is nonempty, meaning some payoff split exists that no coalition can profitably break away from. The result shows how much shared expectation a stable grand outcome needs when groups watch each other guess.
arxiv-2605-01721:
Jacob Ginesin, Max von Hippel, and Cristina Nita-Rotaru automate the hunt for attacks that live in the wires between machines. Distributed protocols assume channels can insert, drop, replay, or reorder messages, yet verification projects each hand-roll their own fault model and prove safety against that alone.

Their tool, Tofu, flips the workflow. Given a protocol stated in linear temporal logic, it searches the whole state space for channel-fault attack traces, synthesizing a concrete attack when one exists and certifying absence when the search exhausts. The analysis is claimed sound and complete against its stated fault model, and general across protocols rather than tuned per case. TCP, the transport workhorse of the internet, serves as the demonstration target. The authors frame automatic fault analysis as a missing routine step for protocol design.
arxiv-2605-01921:
Yuan-Jun Gao, Gang Li, Shi-Dong Liu, and Qi Wu search for a proposed molecular state made of a B meson and its antimatter partner. The state, called Xb0, would be weakly bound and would test heavy-quark symmetry in the bottom sector. The team studies whether it could be found in a radiative decay of the Upsilon(10753) particle.

Working in nonrelativistic effective field theory, they treat the Upsilon state as a mix of two forms and let the decay proceed through meson loops. Loops with P-wave mesons dominate. The predicted width is small, giving a branching share around one in a million to one in one hundred thousand, but the authors call the channel promising for a search.
arxiv-2605-02021:
Santiago Thorup, Luca Castelletto, Zeyuan Feng, and Somil Bansal work on safe spacecraft docking, where a craft must reach its target while avoiding collision. Motion couples translation and rotation in many dimensions, which makes formal safety analysis hard. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability gives strong reach-avoid guarantees, but classic solvers only handle low-dimensional systems.

Their method learns a neural estimate of the Hamilton-Jacobi value function. Training uses physics-based losses plus supervision from model predictive control, which gives useful targets where physics losses alone fail and steadies learning. Online, the learned function guides control under that supervision. The aim is a scalable tube of safe states for docking and similar high-dimensional tasks.
arxiv-2605-02421:
Jinshi Liu and colleagues introduce AOCI, a symbolic-semantic index that lets a language model grasp a huge code repository in one pass. Models struggle once a codebase reaches hundreds of thousands of lines. Retrieval, summarisation, and agent exploration each build a different view at query time, varying between runs and leaving only ad-hoc traces behind.

An AOCI index starts with encoding rules, then gives one entry per code unit, meaning each file or database table. Each entry pairs a symbolic tag, which gives architectural coordinates, with semantic content covering function, dependencies, and constraints. The result is a structured blueprint of architecture, dependencies, and key design decisions that stays stable across tasks, instead of being rebuilt for every question.
arxiv-2605-02621:
Gabor Vattay writes a comment disputing a recent claim that the Schrödinger equation, the core equation of quantum mechanics, can be solved exactly using only classical action and a classical fluid density. The original article held that its method avoided the usual semiclassical approximations. Vattay argues that the derivation contains a basic error at its foundation.

In Vattay's reading, the derivation drops terms tied to how the probability density's amplitude varies in space. Dropping them removes the quantum potential, a term identified by Madelung and later stressed by Bohm. Without it, the claimed exact method is just the standard semiclassical approximation. The examples, Vattay adds, either sit in classes where that potential vanishes, or quietly import quantum results through their starting conditions.
arxiv-2605-02721:
Carlos Ruiz-Gonzalez, Mario Krenn, and Xuemei Gu build an algorithm that designs photon experiments to make entanglement with high success odds, not just high quality. Entangled photons are a workhorse of quantum technology. Sources that make photon pairs are probabilistic, and chasing perfect fidelity can make success vanishingly rare, a trade-off often ignored.

Standard treatments keep only the single-pair term and drop multi-pair emissions. The new design algorithm instead accounts for those higher-order events, explores different layout topologies under hardware limits, and tunes source settings to shrink the unwanted terms, or even use them. For widely used target states, including heralded Bell, W, and NOON states, the found designs beat prior proposals. The result points to more efficient photonic setups.
arxiv-2605-02821:
Haorui Li and nine co-authors measure how the same open-weight language model becomes a different service depending on who hosts it. Users rarely run the raw model; they call a provider's endpoint, which varies in variant, protocol behavior, context size, price, speed, reliability, and what tasks it can actually do. The paper argues the service, not the artifact, is the real unit.

Data come from a monitoring platform's request logs, provider records, compatibility probes, price snapshots, and steady latency measures over one quarter. Demand concentrates in a few model families, yet old versions stay active after new releases. A provider listing many models does not mean users adopt them, and prices stay steadier than speed, context, or error behavior. Task mix shifts token patterns, so the best provider depends on the job.
arxiv-2605-03021:
Florian Herren and Raynette van Tonder review what is known about semileptonic B meson decays that produce charm, and where the measured pieces still fall short. Adding up all measured exclusive rates should match the inclusive total, but a gap has long remained.

By adding rates measured against semi-inclusive decays, they show the missing part is mostly final states with no D meson at all. That points to sizable shares from baryon final states and from Ds mesons. They name candidate channels worth searching for and give simple models for two small missing modes.
arxiv-2605-03221:
Jiaxiang Jiang, Mahesh Subedar, and Omesh Tickoo use diffusion-generated images to lift rare-class accuracy in skin lesion classification. Medical datasets are heavily skewed, and the rarest classes often carry the highest risk, yet standard fixes give only small gains.

Their pipeline pairs an inpainting diffusion model with an out-of-distribution filter that keeps synthetic samples diverse and clinically plausible. On the large, skewed ISIC2019 benchmark, overall results rose substantially, with the biggest gain, over twenty-eight percent, on the class with fewest real samples. The work shows synthetic augmentation can directly ease long-tail imbalance in medical imaging.
arxiv-2605-03521:
Amanda Hirschi and Kai Hugtenburg construct open-closed Deligne-Mumford field theories, chain-level field theories built from moduli spaces of stable curves with boundary. Given a relatively spin embedded Lagrangian inside a symplectic manifold, they attach such a theory to it. The construction extends the Fukaya A-infinity algebra to curves of any genus and any number of boundary components.

The resulting theory is unique up to homotopy. Beyond its own interest, the construction is a first step toward proving Kontsevich's conjecture that the Fukaya category determines the Gromov-Witten invariants of the ambient space, following a strategy that Costello outlined. The paper supplies the basic construction that later steps of that program require.
arxiv-2605-03821:
Hao Wu and twelve co-authors present RoboAlign-R1, a framework that aligns robot video world models with what matters for decision making. Such models are usually trained on reconstruction and perceptual similarity. Those objectives say little about instruction following, manipulation success, or physical plausibility. Their errors also accumulate over long rollouts. The authors build reward-aligned post-training with stabilized long-horizon inference.

They built RobotWorldBench, ten thousand annotated video-instruction pairs from four robot data sources, and trained a multimodal teacher judge that scores generated videos on six dimensions. That judge is distilled into a lightweight student reward model for reinforcement learning post-training. A sliding window re-encoding step refreshes context during inference, and in-domain tests showed a double-digit percentage gain over the strongest baseline.
arxiv-2605-04021:
Sumit Rout, Aravinth Balaji Ravichandran, Paweł Horodecki, and Anubhav Chaturvedi show that Hamiltonian incompatibility is a thermodynamic resource for extracting work. Free energy caps the work of a single process once the state and Hamiltonian are fixed. But a work-extraction task is different. One device must perform across several preparations and Hamiltonian settings at once. A classical device is one whose Hamiltonian settings all mutually commute.

The authors place every branch at its best free-energy-limited envelope. They derive the resulting classical limit on the task's average work. The limit is optimized over arbitrary-dimensional classical devices. Incompatible Hamiltonian settings exceed that limit, even though every individual branch respects its own free-energy maximum. The advantage lives only in the average across the task. That identifies incompatibility itself as the resource.
arxiv-2605-04121:
Sonia L'Innocente, Francesco G. Russo, and Ilaria Svampa give Schur's classical theorem a dynamical interpretation for locally compact groups. Schur's 1904 result says an abstract group with finite central quotient has a finite derived subgroup, and it has many consequences and generalizations. The new viewpoint uses topological entropy, in the sense of Adler, Konheim, and McAndrew, to measure the complexity of group endomorphisms.

Working with groups whose central quotient is compact, the authors prove a conditional result. If the quotient has continuous endomorphisms of finite topological entropy, then the closure of the derived subgroup is also compact. It also has finite-entropy continuous endomorphisms. Connectedness is essential, since they construct a profinite counterexample without it. They also study Heisenberg groups over locally compact rings, where a dynamical Schur-type theorem persists even without compact central quotient, and derive new formulas for their p-rank.
arxiv-2605-05021:
Henrik Garde, David Johansson, and Thanasis Zacharopoulos extend a method for finding hidden inclusions inside a body from boundary electrical measurements, the Calderón problem. Their setting is harder than usual: the material can be direction-dependent, complex-valued, and not self-adjoint, a property many earlier results required. Only partial boundary data are assumed.

The monotonicity method is generalised to very general perturbations of this kind, in any dimension from two upward. The authors assume inclusion boundaries can be reached through a region where the background behaves self-adjointly, plus a definiteness condition nearby. Because uniqueness needs only the self-adjoint part, their method fits generic uniqueness results for this inverse problem.
arxiv-2605-05221:
Andrew Kiruluta develops a non-neural way to learn basis functions from data, keeping the clarity of classical expansions such as Fourier series and wavelets. Fixed dictionaries are easy to analyse but do not adapt to the structure of modern high-dimensional data. Neural networks do adapt, yet their layered form hides the basis and limits direct control over it.

His framework treats the basis pieces themselves as the variables to optimise, learning them jointly with per-sample coefficients and, when useful, a latent linear evolution rule. Kiruluta proves that minimisers exist, studies a blockwise descent algorithm, and gives conditions for recovering coefficients and identifying the basis. Manifold and dynamical regularisation can be added without neural machinery.
arxiv-2605-05521:
Decisions are often judged not only by what happened, but by what would have happened under another choice. Benedikt Koch, Kosuke Imai, and Tomasz Strzalecki give that idea, counterfactual utility, a firm formal footing. Critics had questioned whether such tastes can be consistent at all.

The authors extend the classic von Neumann-Morgenstern framework to the space of all potential outcomes. Expected counterfactual utility then meets the standard axioms there. Their framework also resolves the Allais paradox and a Russian roulette puzzle from the statistics literature, and it pins down when counterfactual values reduce to plain ones.
arxiv-2605-05721:
Single quantum emitters in two-dimensional materials could become the light bulbs of quantum networks, if they behaved like home gadgets. Sahil D. Patel and four co-authors review the push to wire such emitters into chips and light circuits. Today's best devices still need bulky optics, careful alignment, and hunting for a good working point.

The authors survey what turnkey use requires: on-demand triggering, steadying against noise, and efficient coupling into fibers and photonic circuits. Arrays multiply every difficulty through device spread and packaging costs. Their survey maps the gap between lab demos and deployable quantum-light engines.
arxiv-2605-05921:
Give expert mathematicians an AI discovery agent and the interesting question becomes how they steer it. Alex Bäuerle and seven co-authors ran a formative study with eleven experts using AlphaEvolve on advanced problems from their own fields. They identify a workflow they call intentmaking: discovering, defining, and refining one's goals through interaction with the system itself.

Intentmaking extends sensemaking, the building of understanding from data, into goal formation. Users cycle between the two as the agent's outputs reshape what they want to ask. The study offers a vocabulary for designing discovery tools around that cycle.
arxiv-2605-06021:
Tommy Carstensen presents PlotPick, an open source tool that pulls numbers out of scientific figures in batches. Systematic reviews often need values that papers report only in charts. Hand digitizing tools force a person to select and calibrate each figure one at a time, which is slow for large reviews.

PlotPick calls vision language models to extract tables from many figures at once. Carstensen benchmarks nine such models against DePlot, a dedicated chart to table model, on two synthetic chart sets. Vision models led clearly on one set, while results on the second were mixed. This version corrects the first, and withdraws its claim that every vision model beat DePlot on both benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-06421:
Mingfeng Lin, Jiakun Chen, Liang Han, and Liqiang Nie introduce FREPix, a flow matching method that generates images directly in pixel space. Pixel generation avoids the bottleneck of first compressing images through an autoencoder. Most methods, though, treat generation as uniform across frequencies, ignoring that coarse structure and fine detail behave differently.

FREPix splits generation into low- and high-frequency parts, gives each its own transport path, predicts them with a factorized network, and trains with a frequency-aware objective. On ImageNet it reaches competitive image quality scores at two resolutions. Gains are strongest early in training and when few sampling steps are allowed.
arxiv-2605-06521:
Clerico and three colleagues tackle a timing problem in sequential statistics, where late evidence can be useless even when it is strong. Their subject is anytime valid testing. It lets researchers check results while data still arrive and stop early without losing false alarm control. They build a testing by betting framework, where bets against a null claim build wealth as evidence grows, with rewards that favour quick rejection.

The authors turn the search for the best betting plan into a control problem whose answer depends only on the clock and the evidence so far. For hard deadlines, the simple case against one rival claim becomes a finite horizon Neyman Pearson problem. It comes with a matching optimal e process. They also derive an exponential decay optimal rule for shrinking rewards, a finite time cousin of the classic growth rate optimal view.
arxiv-2605-06921:
Yongliang Sun and five co-authors take a fresh look at hard counting and cutting problems known as Maximum Independent Set and Maximum Cut. Traditional step-by-step search finds good answers but grows expensive on large, dense problems. The authors explore smooth, gradient-based methods that can update many variables in parallel.

They show where plain gradient methods get stuck, and where a new formulation for Maximum Cut lets them escape weak solutions. Their framework adds partial resets, called differentiable mutations, to jump into new regions. Experiments suggest the approach scales well where ordinary local search becomes too costly to run.
arxiv-2605-07021:
Christopher Z. Cui, Taylor W. Killian, and Prithviraj Ammanabrolu tackle oversight of language model reasoning. Harmful plans may only become visible after a model finishes thinking, which makes monitoring hard. Their answer is Behavior Cue Reasoning, where the model learns to emit special tokens just before certain behaviors.

Those cues act as both signals and control points for an outside monitor. In tests, a monitor using only cue information cut wasted reasoning tokens by up to half on hard math problems. In a safety setting, cues let monitors recover safe actions from most traces that would otherwise end unsafely, with no loss in task performance.
arxiv-2605-07221:
Wei Jiang and three co-authors segment medical images using a frozen vision foundation model with only a light readout trained. Adapting such models usually means fine-tuning the backbone or building heavy decoders, both unreliable when labeled scans are few. The team found frozen DINOv3 features already carry structure and boundary cues.

Their readout trains small probes on the last three blocks, then views each image at several resolutions and augmentations, fusing the maps by confidence. Under fixed protocols on endoscopy, skin, and brain MRI benchmarks, scores were strong. With only five annotated brain patients, the method recovered nearly all of the performance of a forty-patient reference run.
arxiv-2605-07321:
Vijay Pratap Sharma and four co-authors design TREA, an edge chip for spotting and sorting objects. Edge vision platforms face tight limits on area, power, and delay. TREA uses a dual-precision multiply unit that computes most-significant digits first, supports runtime truncation, and avoids the usual multiplier cost.

A pruning strategy co-designed with the datapath keeps usage high at near half sparsity, and an adjustable unit handles several activation types through time sharing. One hundred such units are reused layer by layer across the network. Experiments show large gains in speed, usage, and energy use over fixed-width, non-adjustable chips.
arxiv-2605-07521:
Friedrich Hastedt and two co-authors tackle computer-aided synthesis planning, the task of finding routes to build a target molecule from simpler chemicals. Most tools stop once they find one workable route. Real chemists, though, must weigh cost, toxicity, sustainability, and yield against each other, so a single answer is rarely enough.

Their algorithm, MORetro*, searches for a whole Pareto front of routes, each best under some balance of the user's chosen criteria. It uses weighted scoring and guided sampling to search efficiently, and it carries a guarantee of recovering the true front under stated conditions. On standard benchmarks it surfaced strong routes that single-goal searches had missed.
arxiv-2605-07821:
Boyang Dai and two co-authors detect out-of-distribution images by reading the company objects keep. Detectors usually fight over entangled representations, ignoring context, and they struggle most on near-out-of-distribution cases, where a model's simplicity bias locks onto easy regions. Human vision, by contrast, uses object co-occurrence in natural scenes to understand what belongs.

Their framework, OCO, predicts disentangled representations for a test image, sorts its co-occurrence pattern into one of three scenarios learned from in-distribution data, and detects outliers within each scenario separately. Across challenging and full-spectrum test settings the method stayed competitive and handled both semantic and covariate shifts, precisely because it judges scenes by their object relationships rather than surface simplicity.
arxiv-2605-08021:
Jakob Wagner, Jeff Maki, Oded Zilberberg, and Kilian Seibold derive a fuller rule for driven quantum oscillators. Standard rules for how such systems lose energy assume no driving and no nonlinear terms. Real devices for quantum technology break both of those assumptions.

The authors keep the full driven motion inside the loss term itself. The loss paths then change with the drive. That change yields nonlinear damping, plus shifts in the drive. For a driven Kerr system, the theory predicts no bistability, lopsided resonance shapes, and strongly changed spread in the state.
arxiv-2605-08221:
Michael Jerge and David Evans present NoisyCoconut, an inference-time method that makes language model answers easier to trust without retraining. Instead of asking the model to reason in words, the method perturbs its internal latent trajectory with controlled noise, which produces several diverse reasoning paths inside the model.

Agreement among those paths becomes a confidence signal: when the paths converge on one answer, the model answers, and when they disagree, it can abstain. Across several reasoning benchmarks the method achieved effective coverage-accuracy trade-offs, needing no training data and no change to model weights. The design fits models already in service.
arxiv-2605-08321:
Lennart Wachowiak, Scott Blain, David Williams-King, and Samuele Marro test a watchdog for manipulative chatbots. In a preregistered study with one hundred twenty people across four decision scenarios, an adversarial language model with a hidden goal steered users' choices about two thirds of the time.

Their warden is a second model that watches the conversation live and sends the user private, non-binding warnings when it spots manipulation. Adding it cut the adversary's success rate to about thirty percent, while genuine interactions lost far less ground. The team also releases COAX-Bench, a simulation suite of fourteen scenarios and over sixteen thousand multi-agent interactions, to probe how the defense works.
arxiv-2605-08421:
Pascal Tilli and Mohsen Mesgar teach document retrieval models to see page layout, not just text patches. Late-interaction retrievers score a document as a bag of local patch embeddings.
