The review gathers evidence that vessel risk factors overlap heavily with Alzheimer risk factors, and that the vessel lining itself changes in the disease.

The lining of brain vessels acts like a chemical factory, releasing signals that can calm or inflame nearby tissue. In Alzheimer disease that lining appears to malfunction and release inflammatory and toxic products into the brain. Chronic inflammation links vessel disease and brain degeneration in both directions. The author argues this vessel and neuron partnership deserves the attention drug hunters have lavished on plaques. New treatments may come from fixing the vessel side of the disease.
europmc-pmc3094421:
Power and coauthors linked in 2011 long term exposure to traffic pollution with weaker thinking in older men. They studied close to seven hundred veterans in a long running aging study who took a battery of thinking tests over a decade. Exposure was estimated from a validated model of black carbon, the sooty marker of traffic exhaust, at each man's home.

For each doubling of exposure, the odds of scoring poorly on a standard mental screening test rose by about a third. Scores on a combined measure of the other tests also fell, by an amount similar to the effect of roughly two extra years of age. The screening result held after accounting for past lead exposure, while the combined score link weakened slightly. The authors add cognition to the list of harms tied to traffic air, and note the exposure is one cities can actually reduce.
europmc-pmc3116821:
Ole Vang and many co-authors issued recommendations on a grape and wine compound in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The compound had won fame for possible benefits against cancer, heart disease, and diabetes, and people were buying it as a supplement. Experts meeting in Denmark in 2010 asked what the published evidence actually supports.

Their verdict was cautious: results in animals look hopeful for several diseases, but human evidence is too weak to advise taking the compound beyond normal food amounts. Open questions include the right dose, side effects, and how the compound acts in the body. The group calls for proper human trials and clearer safety work before any health advice can be given.
europmc-pmc3128121:
Brett Williams and colleagues uncovered a two-stage chemical trick used by a crop fungus in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The fungus attacks an unusually wide range of plants and kills tissue to feed, relying on an acid it secretes as its main weapon. That acid seemed to both block and trigger plant defence chemistry, a puzzle the team set out to solve.

Using plants engineered to glow as their cell chemistry shifted, they showed the acid first makes host cells more chemically reduced, muting alarm signals and wall defences. Once settled, the fungus flips the setting, sparking harmful oxygen chemicals that drive host cell death, which feeds it. A mutant unable to make the acid failed entirely, unless researchers chemically reduced the tissue for it.
europmc-pmc3130021:
Maria Van Kerkhove and colleagues pooled hospital data from nineteen countries to find who fared worst in the 2009 flu pandemic, in a 2011 paper in PLoS Medicine. The new virus spread worldwide within months, and early reports disagreed on which patients were most at risk of severe illness. Their dataset covered roughly seventy thousand hospitalised patients.

Severe outcomes clustered in people with long-term illness, especially heart disease, chronic lung disease, and diabetes, echoing the risk pattern of seasonal flu. Newer signals, including obesity and pregnancy, appeared often in some countries, and indigenous communities were over-represented among severe cases in places. The authors aim the findings at vaccination and drug planning, so the highest-risk groups get protection first in future pandemics.
europmc-pmc3143121:
George Rogers and colleagues adapted a plate-based oxygen meter for isolated cell power stations in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. New machines can track breathing in many tiny wells at once, but they were built for whole cells stuck to the plate. Isolated mitochondria, the cell's energy engines, allow tighter control of fuel and demand, so the team rebuilt the method around them.

Working with mouse liver mitochondria, they found assay conditions quite unlike classic single-chamber methods. Only a few micrograms of material per well gave clean readings of resting, working, resting-again, and fully driven breathing, added step by step through injection ports. The protocol turns a cell tool into a fast screening platform for drugs and proteins that tune metabolism.
europmc-pmc3170621:
Andy Dickens and colleagues reviewed programmes tackling loneliness and isolation in older people in a 2011 paper in BMC Public Health. Isolation harms health and well-being, and a quarter of the population will soon be over sixty. Thirty-two trials and comparison studies of social interventions, published before mid 2009, met their criteria.

Group-based programmes improved at least one health outcome far more often than one-to-one schemes. Programmes where older people take an active part, rather than passively receiving visits, also did better, as did those built on a stated theory. Activity and support groups beat home visiting, and internet training fared worst. Oddly, programmes aimed squarely at isolated people did worse than open ones. Study quality was shaky overall, so the authors demand better trials.
europmc-pmc3210621:
Marcel Ale, Jørn Mikkelsen, and Anne Meyer wrote this 2011 critical review in Marine Drugs on fucoidan, a sulfated sugar chain found in brown seaweeds. Fucoidans have attracted interest for possible benefits such as fighting tumors and preventing blood clots. But batches differ widely, and the authors argue that how a fucoidan is extracted shapes what it can do.

They explain how the source seaweed, the chain's composition, and the number and placement of sulfate groups all influence biological activity. Extraction methods can preserve or damage those features, yet this step is often overlooked when results are compared. The review connects structure to function, giving researchers a guide for producing fucoidan with the properties a given application actually needs.
europmc-pmc3216421:
Val Jenkins and colleagues followed women with early breast cancer for three years. They tested whether additional treatments harm thinking and memory. The study appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. They assessed eighty-five women scheduled for chemotherapy, forty-three receiving hormone therapy or radiotherapy, and forty-nine healthy controls, before treatment and at later points.

On group averages, the treated women performed no worse than controls once age and intelligence were taken into account. Looking person by person, a minority in every group showed reliable decline on several tasks shortly after treatment, and fewer did later. Women whose treatment triggered menopause were more prone to early decline. Self-reported mental failures tracked distress and quality of life, not test scores. The authors conclude most women are unaffected or improve.
europmc-pmc3234221:
Michael Ziller and colleagues charted an understudied form of DNA methylation across human cell types in this 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Most methylation research concerns one sequence context, CpG. Methylation at other cytosines, called non-CpG methylation, was poorly mapped. The team analyzed seventy-six genome-scale methylation maps from stem cells and differentiated cells.

Non-CpG methylation proved to be largely a feature of pluripotent cells. It faded as cells specialized and nearly vanished in adult cell types. Then it reappeared when cells were reprogrammed back to stem cells. Its patterns varied a lot between stem cell lines and tracked the levels of the DNMT3 enzymes; reducing those enzymes cut it sharply. The mark also clustered near ordinary CpG methylation. The study clarifies where this extra layer of marking exists and what controls it.
europmc-pmc3245621:
Tao Liu and colleagues built Cistrome, a web platform for studying how gene activity is regulated, in this 2011 paper in Genome Biology. Experiments that map where regulatory proteins bind DNA, known as ChIP-chip and ChIP-seq, were generating data faster than labs could analyze them in a standard, reproducible way. Cistrome was designed to close that gap.

Built on the open-source Galaxy framework, the platform adds twenty-nine tools specific to these binding experiments. They span the whole workflow. The tools run from first-pass peak calling and correlation checks to linking binding sites with genome features. They also compare sites with gene expression and hunt for the short DNA motifs proteins recognize. The authors offer Cistrome as a shared, integrative workspace for transcriptional regulation studies.
europmc-pmc3295821:
Ramirez and co-authors examined how gut bacteria shape dengue infection in mosquitoes, in work published in 2012. Dengue virus spreads between people through Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and puts billions at daily risk. The mosquito gut hosts microbes that it needs to develop, and those microbes also interact with its immune defenses.

Mosquitoes carrying certain bacteria taken from wild mosquitoes were much less likely to become infected with dengue. The bacteria seemed to switch on a low level immune activity that worked against the virus. Infection itself then changed how many bacteria the gut carried. The results point to the gut community as a possible lever for breaking dengue transmission.
europmc-pmc3311621:
Lam and a large team linked leaky gut walls and changed gut bacteria to fat inflammation in obese mice, reporting in 2012. Belly fat in obesity becomes inflamed and drives insulin problems, but what starts that inflammation is unclear. The team fed mice a diet rich in saturated fat and measured gut barrier strength, gut bacteria, and inflammation in several fat depots and organs.

Fat fed mice developed weaker colon barriers, with looser seals between gut cells and more inflammatory signals in the colon wall. Their gut bacteria shifted too, with one helpful genus falling and another rising, and both shifts tracked the barrier weakness. Fat hugging the gut became packed with immune cells and inflammatory signals, while fat under the skin stayed quiet. The authors argue that gut trouble helps ignite the metabolic problems of obesity.
europmc-pmc3334621:
Cloonan and colleagues investigated whether variant forms of tiny gene regulating RNAs do real work or are mere noise, in a 2011 study. Deep sequencing often finds these variants, called isomiRs, which differ slightly from the standard form of a microRNA. Their patterns are too orderly to be random, hinting at a function, but none had been proven.

Sequencing ten adult human tissues with a custom analysis pipeline, the team found variants behaving much like the standard molecules and tracking their levels closely. Variants were found riding the cell's protein making machinery just as often as standard forms. When the team fed both kinds into cells and measured the effects, they suppressed heavily overlapping sets of genes and pathways. The verdict is that variants are working partners, which helps explain how such short molecules achieve precise control.
europmc-pmc3338721:
Sikweyiya and Jewkes asked people who had answered a survey about gender based violence how the experience felt, reporting in 2012. Ethics boards worry that asking about abuse and trauma may distress participants or put them in danger at home. The study was nested inside a South African household survey on violence, and the team interviewed thirteen men and ten women in depth afterward.

Most participants valued the interview as a rare safe chance to tell their story, and nobody said the questions caused lasting emotional or physical harm. Some did relive painful events and felt temporary sadness. A gender split appeared around risk: some women feared a partner's anger if the survey's full contents came out, and a few received threats, though none were assaulted. Men reported no such reactions. The authors urge protocols that build in support and protection for this minority.
europmc-pmc3410521:
Ngugi, Bottomley, Kleinschmidt, Sander, and Newton pooled epilepsy surveys in 2010 to size the world's burden of the condition. Epilepsy is among the most common brain disorders, yet world estimates were rough and rarely separated active cases needing treatment. Their meta-analysis sorted studies into developed countries and urban or rural areas of developing ones.

Lifetime epilepsy ran several times more common in rural developing areas than in rich countries. Active epilepsy in rich countries affected roughly five people per thousand, amounting to millions of cases, while developing-country totals ran far higher. Small studies and rural settings reported the largest rates, and adult studies outscored child ones. The numbers, they argue, should guide treatment planning.
europmc-pmc3444121:
Liu and colleagues surveyed gas sensing technology in 2012, the instruments that sniff out gases for industry, safety, and research. Each sensing principle suits some jobs and fails others, so engineers keep refining calibration and design. The review sorts the field by the physical change each sensor exploits.

Methods that read electrical changes get the fullest treatment, split by sensing material. The roster runs from polymers and carbon nanotubes to metal oxide semiconductors and moisture-absorbing films. Optical, heat-based, sound-based, and chromatography approaches are sketched more briefly. The authors compare technologies on sensitivity and selectivity, the two scores that matter most, and dissect what drives each. Several routes to better scores are listed, along with directions for future development.
europmc-pmc3460821:
Yang and a large team reported in 2012 that small molecules switching on the protein SIRT1 can cool inflammation by stripping tags from a master immune switch. Chronic inflammation feeds many diseases of aging, and the switch, NF-kB, sits at its center. SIRT1 was already known to quiet the switch by removing an acetyl tag from its p65 part.

The team built a cell assay to measure that tag directly. Their activator compounds sped tag removal, blunted the switch's response to an inflammatory trigger, and cut release of a key cytokine from stimulated cells, all dependent on SIRT1. In mice given a bacterial toxin, one compound lowered two inflammatory cytokines. The work validates a fresh class of anti-inflammatory drugs.
europmc-pmc3566921:
Yu-Meng Sun, Kang-Yu Lin, and Yue-Qin Chen reviewed the miR-125 family of microRNAs in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology in 2013. MicroRNAs are tiny strands that tune gene activity after a gene is read. The miR-125 family is ancient, kept from worms to humans, and has three human members. Its levels fall in many diseases, yet in some settings the same family helps disease along, so context decides its role.

Targets include transcription factors, enzymes that clear paths through tissue, and members of the BCL2 survival family. When miR-125 goes wrong, cells may grow, spread, and invade unchecked, feeding cancers. The family also shapes immune defense against bacteria and viruses. Weighing both faces, the review assesses miR-125 as a possible marker in blood tests and a target for future drugs. Readers see how one small RNA can guard health in one tissue and threaten it in another.
europmc-pmc3580721:
Martin Schulz and colleagues compiled safe and dangerous blood levels for nearly a thousand drugs in Critical Care in 2012. When a patient arrives poisoned, or a drug level comes back from the lab, doctors need a fast reference. It must say what concentration is expected on treatment, what signals toxicity, and what may be fatal. Scattered papers make that lookup slow in an emergency. Their table gathers the ranges into one place.

Data came from original papers, textbooks, earlier compilations, and the authors' own forensic and clinical laboratory, built over more than twenty years. This revision updates the earlier edition and adds over one hundred seventy substances, including drugs marketed since 2003 and illegal drugs behind recent poisonings, with over two hundred new references. Elimination half-lives ride alongside the ranges. A measured level, they note, predicts a poisoning's severity better than the guessed swallowed dose.
europmc-pmc3585121:
Christopher Schardl and a large team of collaborators read the genomes of plant-associated fungi in PLoS Genetics in 2013. The fungal family Clavicipitaceae includes species that live inside grasses, species that attack plants, and the ergot fungi of grain. Many make alkaloids, potent chemicals that deter insects and, in the ergot case, poison mammals. The grass dwellers vary wildly in which alkaloids they make and how they treat their hosts, from partners passed through seed to outright parasites.

Genomes from ten grass symbionts, three ergots, and two relatives were compared. Gene clusters for four alkaloid families shared stable cores that build each chemical skeleton, while edge genes, sitting near restless repeat DNA, varied and shuffled, producing the chemical variety. Losses, copies, and new functions clustered at those edges. The pattern explains how one fungal family became such flexible chemical engineers.
europmc-pmc3615021:
Jasmohan Bajaj and colleagues traced how a gut-selective antibiotic changes the liver-brain axis in PLoS ONE in 2013. In cirrhosis, gut products leaking into blood help cloud thinking, a state whose mild form is minimal hepatic encephalopathy. Rifaximin, an antibiotic that stays in the gut, improves thinking in these patients, but by what chain of changes was unclear. Twenty patients took it for eight weeks while the team profiled stool microbes, blood and urine chemistry, bacterial toxin levels, and thinking tests.

Six of seven thinking tests improved, and blood toxin levels fell. Gut microbe membership shifted only modestly, yet the web of correlations between microbes and chemical products rewired substantially, and blood fatty acids rose across many kinds. The drug seems to retune what the gut community produces, more than it replaces the community. Systems analysis of all layers at once is the paper's methodological point.
europmc-pmc3618321:
Sonja Hänzelmann, Robert Castelo, and Justin Guinney introduced a pathway scoring method called GSVA in BMC Bioinformatics in 2013. Gene set analysis condenses thousands of gene readings into the activity of pathways, which biologists interpret more readily than single genes. Older methods compare groups of samples, faltering when samples are highly varied, the normal state of real cohorts. GSVA instead scores pathway activity sample by sample, with no group labels needed, turning a gene table into a pathway table.

Benchmarks against the leading sample-wise methods showed sturdier performance, and worked examples applied the scores to differential pathway hunting and survival analysis. The method swallows both microarray data and RNA sequencing counts without special casing. Released as free software in the Bioconductor project, GSVA is pitched as a starting point for pathway-centered modeling.
europmc-pmc3652521:
Leaf pores that open and shut set a plant's water bill, and Daszkowska-Golec and Szarejko review their control in a 2013 Frontiers in Plant Science article. Two guard cells ring each pore and swell or shrink to size it, trading gas intake against water loss. Plant hormones carry much of the control traffic, and drought stress leans on that traffic hard.

One hormone, abscisic acid, is the best-known closer of the pores in dry times. The review shows it does not act alone: jasmonic acid and nitric oxide join its signal, while genes in its path cross-talk with ethylene, cytokinin and auxin routes. Other hormones, among them brassinosteroids and cytokinins, tune the response too. Gaps in the signal web are marked at the end, giving plant scientists a clear list of what to test next.
europmc-pmc3669621:
Nitric oxide can feed cancer or fight it, Choudhari, Chaudhary, Chaudhary, Bagde, Gadbail and Joshi review in a 2013 World Journal of Surgical Oncology article. The gas is a short-lived signal made by body cells, and tumours often show high output of the enzymes that make it. Dose decides its face: at some levels it drives vessel growth, cell division and spread; at others it helps kill tumour cells.

Cancer kinds covered include breast, cervical, stomach, bowel and head and neck cancers. For each, the authors set out how the gas acts on vessel growth, cell death, invasion and spread to new sites. Plans to raise or lower the gas in the body for treatment gain are weighed next. Firm proof from trials is still missing, they warn.
europmc-pmc3679821:
Long-term air pollution raises death rates, above all from heart disease, Hoek and six colleagues find in a 2013 review and meta-analysis in Environmental Health. The team gathered cohort studies to January 2013 on fine and coarse particles, nitrogen dioxide and elemental carbon, and pooled the fine particle results. Each step up in fine particle exposure, set at ten micrograms per cubic metre of air, carried about 6 percent excess risk of death from all causes.

For heart and vessel death the excess ran about 11 percent. Lung death links were weaker and unsure. Nitrogen dioxide and elemental carbon, markers of traffic burning, showed smaller rises of about 5 percent. Coarse particles showed little link. Effects looked larger in less schooled and obese groups, with no clear sex gap.
europmc-pmc3682121:
Brain waves can be nudged by a matching electric rhythm, Herrmann, Rach, Neuling and Strüber review in a 2013 Frontiers in Human Neuroscience article. Brain oscillations at set frequencies track many mental acts, from sensing to memory. Their tool, transcranial alternating current stimulation, sends a sine-wave current through the scalp at one chosen frequency. Unlike blunter methods, it can thus test cause: if tuning a wave changes a mental act, the wave plausibly drives it.

The review covers how the current is thought to entrain brain rhythms. It then sorts studies that tuned basic motor and sense processes. Higher acts follow: memory, ambiguous perception and decision making. The authors weigh what the method has proven and where its limits lie.
europmc-pmc3781321:
Silvia De Rubeis and a large group of co-authors reported a study in Neuron in 2013 on CYFIP1, a protein tied to brain development. The CYFIP1 gene sits in a chromosome region linked to intellectual disability, autism, and schizophrenia. The protein has two jobs that look unrelated: it holds back local protein synthesis and it promotes remodeling of the cell skeleton.

The team showed that a growth signal, BDNF, releases CYFIP1 from the protein-synthesis brake complex. Freed, it shifts into a second complex that drives skeleton remodeling, and a signaling protein called Rac1 flips its shape to seal the switch. Both processes are needed for dendritic spines, the tiny protrusions where neurons connect, to form correctly. A map of CYFIP1's partners included many proteins tied to brain disorders.
europmc-pmc3820521:
Leiyu Shi wrote a solo focused review on primary care in Scientifica in 2012. Primary care is the first-contact, ongoing care that anchors a health system. In the United States it has long sat in the shadow of specialty care, and Shi asks what proof says about its worth.

Shi searched journal sources and followed citation trails to gather the proof. Across rich and poor countries, strong primary care links to better access, better health results, fewer hospital stays, and fewer emergency visits. It also softens the health harm that comes with poor income. The review sorts proof by themes such as quality, cost, and fair access. Its verdict backs reform plans that put primary care first.
europmc-pmc3823921:
Qing Ji and a team of co-authors test a plant compound against colon cancer in PLoS One in 2013. The compound is resveratrol, drawn from a Chinese herb. They ask how it slows cancer cell invasion and spread, with a long non-coding RNA called MALAT1 in focus.

Working with two colon cancer cell lines, the team raised and lowered MALAT1 levels to trace its role. Resveratrol lowered MALAT1, which kept a growth signal protein out of the cell nucleus. That damped the Wnt signal path and its target genes, and cell invasion fell. The chain of effects gives lab proof for resveratrol as a possible aid in care, though tests so far are in cells, not patients.
europmc-pmc3876121:
Jie Li, Wuliji O, Wei Li, Zhi-Gang Jiang, and Hossein A. Ghanbari review oxidative stress in brain disease in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2013. Living cells make reactive oxygen forms as they burn fuel. At low levels these forms do useful work, but in excess they turn toxic.

The brain is an easy target. It uses much oxygen, keeps weak antioxidant shields, and its neurons cannot be replaced once mature. Excess reactive forms thus feed many nerve diseases. Cancer drugs can also harm nerves by the same route, in both brain and limbs. The review weighs whether antioxidant drugs can shield nerves, and closes with gaps that must be filled before such drugs earn a clinic place.
europmc-pmc3885521:
Robert J. DeRubeis, Zachary D. Cohen, Nicholas R. Forand, Jay C. Fournier, Lois A. Gelfand, and Lorenzo Lorenzo-Luaces present a treatment choice index in PLoS One, with the record dated 2014. Depression can be treated with drugs or with talking therapy, and patients differ in which suits them. The team build a way to turn group data into a personal pick.

Using data from a past trial of drugs against therapy, they model each patient's likely outcome under both options, leaving that patient's own data out of the model. Five traits that forecast a split response feed the math. The gap between the two forecasts is the Personalized Advantage Index. For most patients, one option won by a margin large enough to matter in clinic. The demo shows how trial data can guide single-patient choices.
europmc-pmc3885921:
Eiji Yoshihara, So Masaki, Yoshiyuki Matsuo, Zhe Chen, Hai Tian, and Junji Yodoi review a redox switch in Frontiers in Immunology, with the record dated 2014. Thioredoxin proteins keep cells safe by undoing oxidative marks. A partner protein, Txnip, binds them and blocks that work. Together they form a switch for the cell's redox state.

The pair sits in both the main cell body and the power units, in nearly all cell types. Fresh work ties the switch to a major inflammation trigger that fires in a redox-dependent way. The authors name the pair a redoxisome, a unit that links redox balance to disease starts and spread. Diseases from diabetes to immune disorders show the switch out of tune. The review maps its roles as a drug target candidate.
europmc-pmc3894221:
Carolina Arias leads a team of co-authors in remapping a virus genome in PLoS Pathogens, with the record dated 2014. Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus drives a cancer seen in immune-weak patients. A full infection cycle remakes the virus's gene activity in waves, and the old genome map missed much of that detail.

Using RNA sequencing and ribosome profiling across the active cycle, the team watched which viral genes switch on and get built into proteins. Control proved mostly at the RNA level. Surprises included ribosomes on non-coding RNAs, many small and upstream reading frames, RNA editing, and alternate start sites that stretch the coding stock. The refined map, dubbed KSHV 2.0, resets start and end sites for known and new features alike.
europmc-pmc3899021:
Catherine H. Mercer leads a team of co-authors in a survey report in The Lancet in 2013. Sexual behavior and attitudes shape wellbeing and shift with social norms. The report pools Britain's three National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles, run across two decades, to trace change over time and across the life course.

The newest survey used a careful probability sample with home interviews and private self-completion for the most tender items. Younger adults were oversampled to sharpen their picture. Across the surveys, partner counts, same-sex experience reports, and attitudes toward sex outside marriage all moved in more permissive directions, with gaps between men's and women's reports narrowing. The long view lets health services plan for real behavior, not myth.
europmc-pmc3964421:
Shaghayegh Vahdat and three colleagues review patient involvement in health care choices. Their paper appeared in the Iranian Red Crescent Medical Journal in 2014. Involvement means patients help pick among treatments. They get full information first. They can voice feelings and signs. They help direct their own care. They do not just follow orders. Such involvement is said to empower patients. It is also said to improve services and outcomes.

The team screened one hundred sources for this review. They kept thirty-five articles and two books. The field fell into six themes. The themes cover what participation means and why it matters. They cover what helps it and what blocks it. They cover how it is done and how it is measured. The last theme covers what it achieves. The review gives clinicians a clear entry point into shared decision-making.
europmc-pmc3965421:
Danuta M. Skowronski and a large Canadian team explain a weak flu vaccine year. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. The season was 2012-13. Weak years are usually blamed on drift in the wild virus. The team used Canada's test-negative network to test that idea. They measured protection against each flu type. Then they sequenced the season's viruses. Antibody tests compared them with two strains. One was the recommended prototype. One was the strain grown in eggs for production.

Overall protection was about 50 percent. Against the main H3N2 type, it was 41 percent. Wild H3N2 viruses matched the prototype well. The egg-grown strain did not. It had picked up three mutations at key antibody sites. The authors conclude the flaw was built in during egg growth. Drift in the wild virus was not the cause.
europmc-pmc3968321:
Jacques Ravel and colleagues built a day-by-day record of the vaginal microbiome around episodes of bacterial vaginosis, in Microbiome in 2013. Bacterial vaginosis, an imbalance of the vaginal community, is the commonest vaginal condition in women of reproductive age, yet after fifty years its cause is still not pinned down. That gap blocks better treatment and prevention. The team followed twenty-five women for ten weeks with daily self-collected samples.

Fifteen women had symptomatic vaginosis during the study, six had it without symptoms, and four stayed free of it. Sequencing those daily samples produced a rare fine-grained movie of communities shifting before, during, and after episodes. The authors offer the dataset as a shared resource for understanding the condition's natural history and improving diagnosis.
europmc-pmc4013121:
Giuseppe Grosso and eight co-authors pool trials of omega-3 fats for depression, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Omega-3 fats, found in oily fish, had been put forward as a help for low mood. Past results pointed both ways, so a fresh pooled check was due.

The team searched four databases for randomised trials in people with depression signs, up to 2013. Trials in patients with a firm diagnosis of major depression showed a clear gain from omega-3 over placebo. Trials in people with symptoms but no diagnosis showed a smaller gain. A fat called EPA drove the benefit more than its kin DHA. Use alongside standard care beat use on its own. Benefit also showed in bipolar disorder trials. No link appeared with trial size, length, dose, age, or starting severity. No gain was found for young people or for depression around childbirth.
europmc-pmc4015721:
Joanna IntHout, John P. A. Ioannidis, and George F. Borm argue that a less-used pooling method beats the standard one for meta-analysis, in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2014. Meta-analysis merges many trials into one result. The standard random-effects method, named for DerSimonian and Laird, is known to give false alarms too often.

The rival method, named for Hartung, Knapp, Sidik, and Jonkman, was known to do better when trials are of like size. In made-up tests of two to twenty trials with uneven sizes, the rival held error rates near the set level. The standard method's false alarm rate could top thirty percent against a five percent target. In close to seven hundred real Cochrane meta-analyses, a quarter of the standard method's positive finds turned non-positive under the rival method. A simple swap converts old results, so routine use is urged.
europmc-pmc4040921:
Laam Li, Nilmini Mendis, Hana Trigui, James D. Oliver, and Sébastien P. Faucher review bacteria that stay alive yet refuse to grow in the lab, in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2014. This state, viable but non-culturable, was first described in 1982 in two species. Cells in it keep intact membranes and DNA but form no colonies on routine agar.

Standard plate counts miss them, so living counts in samples come out too low, a health risk if the cells later wake. The review sets out how these cells differ from both growing cells and dead ones, and which tests can detect them. Stress such as cold or starvation can trigger entry into the state. The right stimulus, from warmth to host signals, can bring cells back to growth.
europmc-pmc4053721:
Charity W. Law, Yunshun Chen, Wei Shi, and Gordon K. Smyth present voom, a method that lets RNA sequencing data use microarray-era statistics, in Genome Biology in 2014. Gene counting by sequencing replaced chip arrays, but the chips left behind a rich, trusted toolkit for finding genes whose activity changes.

The barrier is noise shape: count data grow noisier in a pattern that plain linear models dislike. Voom estimates how spread changes with average count level, turns each observation into a precision weight, and hands the weighted data to the limma pipeline. That unlocks linear models, gene set tests, and strength-borrowing across genes for sequencing studies. In simulations, voom matched or beat purpose-built count methods, even on data made to suit those rivals. The pitch: years of refined array statistics need not be discarded in the sequencing era.
europmc-pmc4107921:
Robbie P. Joosten, Fei Long, Garib N. Murshudov, and Anastassis Perrakis made PDB_REDO, a web tool that polishes the 3D models that labs file for large bits of life. Their paper came out in IUCrJ in 2014. To solve such a shape takes many calls of judgement, so filed models are often far from the best they could be.

The tool re-runs the fit with tuned settings and re-builds parts of the model. New maths made this heavy task fit for a web tool. It flags big changes at the scale of the whole model and at the scale of one link in the chain. Early users saw clear gains in fit to the raw data and in shape soundness. The tool gives a shared, cheap second pass over filed shapes.
europmc-pmc4154221:
Ghassan B. Hamra, Dana Loomis, and colleagues systematically reviewed studies linking outdoor particle pollution with lung cancer. Their meta-analysis appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2014. An international agency had just classed particulate matter as a proven carcinogen, but without a quantitative summary of the evidence.

Eighteen studies met their rules, each estimating how lung cancer incidence or death changes with exposure. Pooling them, a standard rise in fine particles, PM2.5, came with about a nine percent higher lung cancer risk. The coarser PM10 fraction gave a similar figure with wider uncertainty. Effects were estimated with random-effects models that allow studies to differ. The authors say the numbers further justify cutting air pollution from its many sources.
europmc-pmc4165321:
Stefan Niewiesk, writing alone, reviewed maternal antibodies, the protection mothers pass to newborns, and the problem they pose for vaccination. His review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Newborns have immature immune systems and lean on transferred antibodies early in life.

As those antibodies fade they can block vaccines, as seen when measles vaccination fails to convert in their presence, in humans and animals alike and across vaccine types. The block hits antibody production while T cell responses usually survive. It works through a cross-link between the B cell's receptor and an inhibitory Fc receptor, formed by vaccine-antibody complexes. Animal work shows partial rescue with a tailored IgM antibody. Niewiesk reviews clinical workarounds and new vaccine strategies built on this mechanism.
europmc-pmc4177621:
Andrés Ruiz-Linares led a large team that measured ancestry and appearance across Latin America in PLoS Genetics in 2014. The region's people descend from a mix of Native American, European, and African ancestors, layered unevenly by place and social class. The study linked genes, looks, and how people describe their own roots.

The team tested 7,342 volunteers in Brazil, Chile, Colombia, México, and Perú, recording ancestry shares, physical traits, and self-described ancestry. Ancestry shares varied strongly by region, and they shaped most traits measured, though usually only modestly. What people said about their own ancestry matched the gene results overall, but visible traits such as skin colour swayed self-description away from the genetic estimate. The work gives a baseline map of diversity in the region.
europmc-pmc4223021:
Basem Azab, Emanuela Taioli, and two co-authors normed a blood inflammation ratio in PLoS ONE in 2014. The neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio, from a routine blood count, predicts outcomes in surgery and cancer. But nobody had set its normal range in a broad population, or checked whether it differs by ancestry.

Using national survey data from 9,427 United States adults, they found an average ratio of 2.15. Non-Hispanic Black participants averaged 1.76 and Hispanic participants 2.08, both clearly below the 2.24 average for non-Hispanic Whites. Diabetes, heart disease, and smoking each came with higher ratios. Links between the ratio and smoking or body mass also differed by group. The authors say cut-offs for risk should account for these baseline gaps.
europmc-pmc4271521:
Simon H. Martin, John W. Davey, and Chris D. Jiggins test a popular statistic used to find genes that crossed between species. Their study appeared in Molecular Biology and Evolution in 2015. The ABBA-BABA test spots shared derived alleles, but labs had begun applying it to small genome regions, a use it was not built for.

Using simulations and butterfly genomes, the team shows the statistic inflates in regions where diversity is low, so false hits cluster there. They propose a modified statistic that avoids this bias and finds truly crossed loci more cleanly. The paper is a caution and a fix for a widely used tool in evolution research.
europmc-pmc4284921:
Gary S Collins, Johannes B Reitsma, Douglas G Altman, and Karel GM Moons present the TRIPOD statement, a checklist for reporting medical prediction models. It appeared in BMC Medicine in 2015. Such models estimate the chance that a disease is present or that an event will happen, and doctors use them to guide choices.

Reviews had shown that most reports of these models leave out key facts, so readers cannot judge bias or usefulness. TRIPOD lists what a report must cover, from how the data were gathered to how the model was built and checked. The statement covers models that diagnose, models that forecast, and updates to either kind.
europmc-pmc4326421:
Aaron C Ericsson and eight co-authors compared the gut microbes of lab mice bought from two big suppliers and bred on different genetic backgrounds. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Mouse gut microbes shape the results of disease models, and puzzling differences between labs had been blamed on where the mice came from.

Using DNA based profiling of droppings, the team found strong differences in microbe richness and mix between suppliers. Many bacterial groups differed by vendor, by mouse strain, or by both together. The results mean two labs can run the same experiment on paper while their mice carry different inner ecosystems. The paper urges researchers to report and control mouse sourcing in microbe sensitive work.
europmc-pmc4380921:
Anita Melnyk, Alex Wong, and Rees Kassen pooled studies on the fitness costs of antibiotic resistance, in Evolutionary Applications in 2015. When bacteria gain resistance through a mutation, the change often slows their growth or weakens them in drug-free settings. Such costs decide whether resistance fades when treatment stops. The team ran a meta-analysis of studies that measured the cost of single resistance mutations across drugs and bacterial species.

On the whole, resistance mutations were costly, the pooled results showed. But the average hid real variety: several drug classes and bacterial species showed no clear cost at all. Where costs are low, resistance is more likely to linger after drug use falls. The authors call for more work on second mutations that repay the cost, since those compensations shape how resistance can be managed in clinics.
europmc-pmc4409221:
Manuel Stemmer, Thomas Thumberger, Maria del Sol Keyer, Joachim Wittbrodt, and Juan Mateo presented CCTop, a CRISPR target picker, in PLoS ONE in 2015. CRISPR/Cas9 editing is steered by a 20-letter guide sequence, but that sequence can recur in a genome, and the complex tolerates some mismatches, so off-target cuts are a real risk. Choosing the site well on a computer first is key to success at the bench. CCTop was built to overcome limits of earlier tools.

From a pasted query, it finds and ranks all candidate guide sites by off-target quality, with sensible defaults that users can tune, and documents each fully. The team validated it experimentally across gene inactivation and both major repair outcomes. An interface meant for bench biologists, not programmers, is the point: fast, reliable picks without specialist software skills.
europmc-pmc4418721:
Yibing Hu and eight co-authors reported a laboratory study in PLoS ONE in 2015 on why colorectal cancer can resist chemotherapy. They focused on cancer stem cells, a small set of tumor cells marked by the protein CD133, and on fibroblasts that sit near tumors and support their growth.

Cancer stem cells taken from patient-derived grafts and cell lines survived drug treatment on their own. Fluid from fibroblasts, and the exosomes in that fluid, made the stem cells grow, form colonies, and build tumors more readily under two standard drugs. Blocking exosome release weakened those effects. The authors argue that treatment should target fibroblast signals as well as the stem cells.
europmc-pmc4435621:
Charles Lai and six co-authors built glowing reporters to watch tumor vesicles move between cells, reporting in Nature Communications in 2015. Cells shed tiny packages called extracellular vesicles that carry RNA and protein to other cells. Seeing where those packages go, and whether their RNA cargo is actually used, needs labels that work in living cells and animals.

The team attached a membrane anchor to green and red glowing proteins. That let vesicles of different origins be told apart. They also tagged a cargo RNA so it lights up when a partner protein binds it. Light-based reporters added a view inside living animals. Cancer cells took up vesicles quickly, and cargo RNA was being turned into protein within an hour of transfer. Communication by vesicles, the work shows, runs in both directions and is fast.
europmc-pmc4489921:
Sevil Sofueva and nine co-authors showed how the protein cohesin helps organize chromosomes in The EMBO Journal in 2013. Inside the nucleus, chromosomes must open the regions being read while packing the rest tightly. Recent maps had revealed megabase-scale domains separating active from inactive stretches, raising the question of what builds and holds those domains.

Very specific long-range contacts, the team finds, are anchored where cohesin and another protein, CTCF, sit together, but not where either sits alone. Those contacts form loops that mark out the domains and create intricate structure inside them. When cohesin was disabled in resting nuclei, the contacts vanished and domains relaxed. Gene activity then went awry across the genome, in genes with and without cohesin bound. Domains, the authors argue, stabilize the gene programs inside them.
europmc-pmc4496821:
Ana Pilar Betran and a team of co-authors asked what caesarean rate a population actually needs, in Reproductive Health in 2015. In 1985, the World Health Organization said there was no justification for rates above ten to fifteen percent of births. Since then caesarean rates have climbed worldwide to unprecedented levels, and the validity of that old threshold has been challenged from both sides.

Searching four databases for ecological studies, analyses that compare rates and outcomes across whole populations, published between 2000 and 2014, the team found only a handful that met their rules. Most were cross-sectional snapshots, and they related caesarean rates to maternal, newborn, and infant mortality, low birth weight, and stillbirth. The review appraises each study's quality and synthesizes what such population-level data can and cannot say about an optimal rate, calling for better evidence than ecological correlations can provide.
europmc-pmc4523921:
Anna Vangone, Alexandre M. J. J. Bonvin, and Michael Levitt present a contact-based way to predict how tightly two proteins bind, in eLife in 2015. Protein pairs run nearly every job in the cell, yet the energy of their joining is still hard to forecast. Knowing binding strength helps explain healthy and diseased states alike.

Their method counts the contacts where the two proteins touch, sorted by type, and adds features of the surface that stays exposed. Tested against a standard benchmark of measured pairs, accuracy swung with how the measurements were made and how much the proteins change shape on binding. On a cleaned subset with trusted values, the model beat all other methods tried. Simplicity, the authors argue, can outscore more complex energy models.
europmc-pmc4620521:
Brian P. Best wrote a solo 2015 review of the harm done by the chemicals that keep tissue from freezing solid. These agents, called cryoprotectants, stop ice when organs cool to very low heat levels. But the strong doses needed are themselves toxic. That harm is now the main block to storing organs frozen for transplant.

Best sums up what is known about how the agents hurt cells and the main ideas behind the harm. He also weighs the fixes tried so far, such as tuning cooling speeds or the timing of each dose. None yet solves the problem. Frozen storage could add greatly to the pool of organs for transplant. He argues that beating this harm is the key task in the field.
europmc-pmc4655321:
Bryan Williams and colleagues reported the PATHWAY-2 trial in 2015, testing which added drug works best for resistant high blood pressure. Resistant cases stay high despite three standard drugs. The team suspected excess salt retention and predicted the diuretic spironolactone would win. The double-blind crossover trial ran at fourteen United Kingdom sites. The work appeared in The Lancet.

Each patient rotated through twelve weeks each of spironolactone, bisoprolol, doxazosin, and placebo on top of their usual drugs, with doses doubled halfway. Home blood pressure readings, averaged over four days, formed the main comparison. The design gives each patient as their own control across all four options. The trial was built to settle which fourth drug doctors should reach for first in resistant hypertension.
europmc-pmc4701921:
Deena Khan and S. Ansar Ahmed wrote a mini review on estrogen and the immune system in Frontiers in Immunology in 2015. Women's immune systems generally react more strongly than men's, and women develop autoimmune disease more often. Sex hormones are a leading suspect for the gap. Estrogen can act on nearly every immune cell type, through its receptors and through other routes. The review maps which receptors sit on which cells and which signaling paths estrogen uses.

Two diseases frame the puzzle. In multiple sclerosis and in systemic lupus erythematosus, both more common in women, estrogen's effects point in opposing directions. The authors work through the mechanisms that could explain why one hormone helps in one setting and harms in another. The contrast matters for treatment: hormone-based ideas must be tailored to the disease, not applied as a blanket rule.
europmc-pmc4737121:
Gráinne S. Gorman, Andrew M. Schaefer, Yi Ng, and nine colleagues counted adult mitochondrial disease in the Annals of Neurology in 2015. Mitochondrial disorders, caused by faults in either the mitochondrial genome or nuclear genes, were thought common but had resisted firm counting because symptoms and genetics vary so much. The team assessed every adult referred with suspected mitochondrial disease in the North East of England over more than two decades, and computed minimum prevalence for 2011.

Mitochondrial DNA mutations sat at about one in five thousand people, matching earlier estimates. Nuclear mutations added roughly three per hundred thousand adults with clear disease. Combined, about one in forty-three hundred adults carries disease-causing mitochondrial faults, putting these disorders among the commonest inherited neurological conditions of adulthood. The authors stress the planning consequences: services, trials, and health policy must budget for a burden this size.
europmc-pmc4766421:
Yunhao Qin and four colleagues test a bone-healing signal in Scientific Reports in 2016. Cells shed tiny parcels called extracellular vesicles, which carry messages to other cells. Whether parcels from bone marrow stem cells could push bone growth was little studied, so the team collected them and put them to work in dish and animal tests.

The parcels raised bone-building gene activity in bone-forming cells and sped their maturing, without changing their growth rate. Fitted into a delivery setup and placed in skull gaps in rats, they grew more new bone than controls. One small RNA inside the parcels, miR-196a, proved key to the effect. The team proposes parcel therapy as a tool for repairing bone.
europmc-pmc4775221:
Ed Reznik leads a broad author team in eLife in 2016 surveying the small genome inside mitochondria across human cancers. Each cell holds many copies of this second genome, which codes for parts of the cell's energy machinery. Whether tumors gain or lose copies, and what that means, had not been mapped across cancer types.

Drawing on a large shared cancer atlas covering 22 tumor types, the team found some cancers, notably of bladder, breast, and kidney, run low on mitochondrial DNA next to matched healthy tissue. Low counts tied to certain gene faults and to shifts in energy and immune gene activity. Some tumors seemed to make up the loss by boosting energy proteins another way. The map, they argue, points to treatment angles based on a tumor's energy setup.
europmc-pmc4848621:
Marie-Caroline Smith and co-authors reviewed how mold toxins, called mycotoxins, occur together in food and animal feed, and what mixed exposure does. Most past work and most rules treat one toxin at a time. Yet surveys worldwide find several toxins in the same grain lots. The review sums up 127 reported combinations in cereals and their products.

The most common pairings join aflatoxins with fumonisins, or deoxynivalenol with zearalenone, among others. Lab tests of mixes show effects that can cancel, add up, or multiply, shifting with species, cell type, dose, and time. Rules that judge each toxin alone may thus miss real risk, and the review presses for mix-aware testing.
europmc-pmc4868821:
Sophie Petropoulos and co-authors mapped gene activity cell by cell in early human embryos in 2016. They read 1,529 single cells from 88 embryos made before implantation. Mouse work had shaped ideas about first cell fate choices, but human data were scarce. The map follows cells as the first three lineages form.

Cells first pass through a mixed state where lineage genes sound together. Then three groups, trophectoderm, epiblast, and primitive endoderm, settle at the same time as the blastocyst forms. Female cells calmed their double X chromosome output before implantation, by a route unlike the mouse. The atlas gives a base for fertility and stem cell research.
europmc-pmc4885021:
Matthew A. Apps, Matthew F. Rushworth, and Steve W. Chang argued in 2016 that one strip of the anterior cingulate cortex, its gyrus part, tracks how motivated other people are. The wider region serves many tasks, yet its social role was fuzzy. Anatomy and activity proof point to the gyrus strip as a social specialist.

Their model says the strip estimates others' drive and updates the estimate when events prove it wrong. Costs, benefits, and errors in social exchanges all register there, in brain scans and single cell reads alike. The model makes testable calls about why social skill varies in health and illness. Social thought, on this view, runs on motive tracking.
europmc-pmc4890321:
Dane W. deQuilettes and co-authors showed in Nature Communications in 2016 that light reshuffles the halide parts inside perovskite solar films. The material, a lead iodide perovskite, already tops 21 percent solar efficiency, yet films hold loss sites and shift oddly under light. With glow microscopy plus chemical imaging, the team watched glow and makeup change together in lit films.

Lit spots brightened as halides moved, and glow lifetime rose near tenfold over time. The reshuffle seems to heal or bypass some loss sites, a self-improving quirk. Grasping ion movement under light is key to stable, lasting perovskite cells. The work ties a visible glow change to a chemical cause.
europmc-pmc4919521:
Kojiro Mukai and eight co-authors pin down a step that switches on STING, a sensor for stray DNA inside cells. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. STING is needed for the type I interferon response, a first line defense against DNA viruses. When STING senses DNA, it moves from one cell compartment toward the nucleus, but why that move matters was unclear.

The group shows that STING gains a fatty tag, called palmitoylation, at the Golgi, and that this tag is required for activation. A drug that blocks the tag, 2-bromopalmitate, shut down the interferon response. Mutating two cysteine sites had the same effect. Disease linked STING variants found in patients with autoimmune disease were also blocked by the drug or the mutation. The authors suggest the step could guide new treatments for inflammation driven by the body's own DNA.
europmc-pmc4931321:
Dongliang Chao and ten co-authors build a fast, high capacity anode for sodium ion batteries from thin sheets of tin sulfide. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Sodium ion batteries could cost less and be safer than lithium ion ones. Most sodium electrodes, though, charge slowly because sodium ions move sluggishly and swell the material. The team grew ultrathin layered tin(II) sulfide sheets as an array on graphene foam.

The anode stored about 1,100 milliamp hours per gram at a low current. At a very high current it still held about 420, beating even its own lithium storage results. Tests showed most charge was stored at surfaces, a fast process called pseudocapacitance, tuned by the thin sheet design. The authors suggest the same surface led design may lift other layered materials for sodium storage.
europmc-pmc4937821:
Charity W. Law and six co-authors show a full RNA sequencing analysis built on three Bioconductor packages. Their workflow article appeared in F1000Research in 2016. RNA sequencing counts how active each gene is in a sample. Turning counts into sound claims takes cleaning, exploration, testing, and pathway checks. The authors run the whole chain on mouse mammary gland data, so readers can follow real output at each step.

EdgeR imports, filters, and normalizes the counts. Limma, with its voom method, then fits models and tests which genes differ between groups. Glimma adds interactive plots, so users can click into single samples and genes instead of reading static charts. The authors pitch the trio as an easy route from raw counts to biological insight. They stress that open, shared code keeps such analyses checkable by others.
europmc-pmc4959521:
Matthew J. Memoli leads a team testing which flu antibodies truly track with protection. Their study appeared in mBio in 2016. Flu vaccines are judged by the HAI titer, a measure of antibodies against hemagglutinin, the virus's main surface protein. A titer of 1:40 or more counts as protective. Recent weak vaccine seasons raised doubts about that single marker. The team used a human challenge model at the NIH Clinical Center, giving healthy volunteers a wild type 2009 H1N1 virus through the nose.

Volunteers starting at or above the threshold were less likely to develop mild to moderate flu disease. The titer did not cut symptoms alone, though. Antibodies against the second surface protein, neuraminidase, tracked better with every severity measure the team checked. The authors argue vaccine testing should weigh neuraminidase antibodies too. Relying on one correlate, they say, can misjudge how well a vaccine will work.
europmc-pmc5023321:
Andre F. Marquand, Iead Rezek, Jan Buitelaar, and Christian F. Beckmann propose normative modeling in Biological Psychiatry in 2016. Most brain studies split people into patients and controls, as if each group were uniform, but real patient groups vary widely. Normative modeling instead charts the normal range of a trait, then measures how far each single person sits from that range.

To show the method, the team mapped the link between impulsivity and reward-related brain activity in 491 healthy people. Some people fell far outside the normal pattern, and the size of that gap tracked hyperactivity symptoms of attention-deficit disorder, though not inattention. Disease, on this view, is an extreme or personal departure from normal function rather than a fixed box. The approach lets researchers study one patient at a time without forcing the whole group into two camps.
europmc-pmc5075021:
Rafael Sanjuán and Pilar Domingo-Calap explain what sets viral mutation rates in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences in 2016. Some viruses adapt to new hosts with startling speed because they generate fresh diversity fast, while others barely change. The review gathers the machinery behind that spread: RNA viruses mutate faster than DNA viruses, single-stranded faster than double-stranded, and larger genomes tend to mutate more slowly per site.

Rates are tuned at many levels, from the copying enzyme's accuracy and proofreading to the template's shape, the cell's chemistry, and access to repair after copying. Host enzymes that edit viral genomes can dump in bursts of change, and some viruses carry their own diversity-generating parts. Mutation rates are not fixed traits: they evolve under pressure, as shown by accuracy variants selected under mutagenic drugs. The big patterns are clear, the authors close, while several mechanisms remain unmapped.
europmc-pmc5119021:
Akinobu Ito and seven co-authors explained how a new antibiotic smuggles itself into bacteria, reporting in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy in 2016. Cefiderocol is a cephalosporin drug carrying a chemical hook that grabs iron. The target was Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a hospital germ often resistant to many drugs.

The drug worked far better when iron was scarce, and labeled drug built up inside the bacteria under those conditions. Cefiderocol binds iron tightly, and the bacteria's own iron transport systems hauled the iron-drug complex inside, like a Trojan horse. A chemically altered version that could not grab iron lost the boost, confirming the route. Hiding in an iron carrier lets the drug slip past defenses that normally keep antibiotics out.
europmc-pmc5137221:
Dagfinn Aune and nine co-authors pooled studies on nut eating and death risk in BMC Medicine in 2016. Nuts had been linked to less heart disease, but evidence on rarer causes of death was scattered. The team combined twenty prospective studies and modeled risk by dose.

For each extra 28 grams of nuts a day, the pooled risks fell for coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease overall, total cancer, and death from any cause. Deaths from respiratory disease, diabetes, and infections also dropped, while stroke showed no clear change. Tree nuts and peanuts looked alike. If the links are causal, the authors estimate 4.4 million early deaths in 2013 across several world regions could be tied to eating under 20 grams of nuts a day.
europmc-pmc5153921:
Melanie Y. Bertram and six co-authors weighed cost-effectiveness thresholds in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2016. Health funders compare treatments by the health gained per unit of money, and a 2001 World Health Organization commission suggested judging value against multiples of a country's income per head.

In practice, some countries hardened those guide numbers into funding rules. Experience shows that hurts: the thresholds ignore local conditions, and the underlying cost estimates are themselves uncertain, so the wrong services can win funding. The authors argue cost-effectiveness should sit inside a transparent national process alongside budget impact and feasibility, backed by law and stakeholder support, rather than deciding alone. They urge each country to build its own context-specific way of choosing.
europmc-pmc5224921:
Angela J. Churchill, Giselle Dominguez Gutiérrez, Ruth A. Singer, David S. Lorberbaum, Kevin A. Fischer, and Lori Sussel used mouse genetics to order two pancreas transcription factors in eLife in 2017. The pancreas makes hormone-producing islet cells, including insulin-making beta cells, through a chain of progenitor stages. Two switches, Neurog3 and Nkx2.2, are both essential, but which one directs the other was unclear.

The team deleted Nkx2.2 only in cells that had switched on Neurog3, the marker of endocrine progenitors. Many beta cell network genes that collapse in full Nkx2.2 knockout mice stayed normal in these mice, yet beta cell development still failed in the same way. That pattern places Nkx2.2 mainly downstream of Neurog3 while also showing it has extra essential work inside the endocrine progenitors themselves. The authors describe Nkx2.2 as part of a modular program that assigns islet cell fates.
europmc-pmc5266721:
Andrea Majoros, Ekaterini Platanitis, Elisabeth Kernbauer-Hölzl, Felix Rosebrock, Mathias Müller, and Thomas Decker reviewed non-standard JAK-STAT signaling in Frontiers in Immunology in 2017. The JAK-STAT pathway relays cytokine signals, including interferons, the body's antiviral messengers. In the textbook version, JAK enzymes tag STAT proteins, which pair up, enter the nucleus, and switch on defense genes. Recent work breaks that tidy picture in several ways.

JAKs can act without their enzyme activity. STATs can work without the phosphate tag, in and out of the nucleus, and mixed STAT groups unlike the classic pairs also control genes in interferon-treated cells. The review gathers how these side routes serve the innate antimicrobial defense interferons provide. It also touches on pathway proteins moonlighting elsewhere: IRF9 in metabolism, a kinase-dead form of TYK2 steering natural killer cells, and alternate phosphate forms of STAT1 with separate jobs.
europmc-pmc5286221:
James W. Dawson and John W. Struthers published a long study of generalised osteitis fibrosa in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in October 1923, from the research laboratory of the Royal College of Physicians in Edinburgh. The case at its center joined a widespread bone-softening disease to a tumour of the parathyroid gland and to calcium deposits lodged in other tissues, a rare and obscure combination.

After the clinical history, X-ray, and post-mortem notes, the pair dissect the tissue changes. They trace how bone is removed, how fibrous tissue replaces it, how new bone forms, and how giant-celled tissue and cysts arise. A long discussion then tests what kind of process the disease is: inflammatory, a faulty rebuilding akin to rickets, or a growth akin to tumours. It compares the disease with a shelf of other bone disorders. Their summary orders its stages and causes.
europmc-pmc5307821:
Euridice Martínez Steele, Barry M. Popkin, Boyd Swinburn, and Carlos A. Monteiro studied diet quality in the United States in Population Health Metrics in 2017. Their focus was ultra-processed foods, factory-made items built from refined parts and additives. Such foods supply a growing share of meals worldwide. The team asked if that share tracks the health of the whole diet.

They used food records from a national survey of more than nine thousand people from 2009 to 2010. Foods were sorted into four groups, from plain raw items to ultra-processed goods. As the ultra-processed share rose, the diet's content of key nutrients worsened, both one by one and as a whole pattern. The authors conclude that cutting that share is a sound way to improve diet quality in the country.
europmc-pmc5395521:
Tong He, Marten Heidemeyer, Fuqiang Ban, Artem Cherkasov, and Martin Ester present a method called SimBoost in a 2017 paper in the Journal of Cheminformatics. Drug hunters need to know how tightly a compound grips its target protein. Lab tests are slow and dear, and most candidate drugs fail. Past computer tools mostly gave a yes or no answer, which blurs weak and strong binding.

SimBoost instead predicts a graded binding strength, using traits of the drug and the protein and how alike each is to known pairs. A sister version also gives a range that shows how much to trust each guess. On three test data sets the method beat older models. The authors offer it to rank compounds before lab work begins.
europmc-pmc5512621:
Sheikh and co-authors present a review in Materials on how the body reacts to implanted materials. Every implant triggers inflammation and wound healing at its surface. Macrophages arrive first and stay for the device's whole life. Some fuse into giant cells that attack the material surface. A fibrous capsule often seals the implant off in the end.

Surface traits steer the strength of this foreign body reaction, they explain. Roughness, chemistry, and shape all play a part. Protein coating and cell sticking start the chain of events. Grasping these steps could guide implants the body accepts better. Tissue engineering gains the most from such designs.
europmc-pmc5541421:
Jay, von Saucken, and Landreth present a review in Molecular Neurodegeneration. Their subject is TREM2, a receptor found only on immune cells. Gene variants in TREM2 raise the risk of Alzheimer's disease. They also link to other brain diseases that break down nerve cells.

The review sums up what is known about TREM2 expression and signaling. It notes a key split in the evidence. Lab dish studies often show one effect on inflammation, while studies in living tissue show another. The authors then weigh how TREM2 shapes disease and care. Readers get a full map of an immune pathway now central to brain research.
europmc-pmc5591521:
Dunstan, Scott, and Todd reassess two screening tools in BMC Psychiatry. The Zung scales ask people to rate their own depression and anxiety. They are widely used, but clinics often apply their cut-offs wrongly. The study tests them against a rival scale and a diagnostic questionnaire.

A total of 376 adults filled in all the forms. Eighty-seven were already in psychological treatment. The rival DASS scales predicted diagnoses a bit more strongly. The Zung scales still performed well. They caught more true cases, while DASS missed fewer healthy people. Stricter Zung cut-offs would even out that trade. The authors urge more testing against full clinical interviews. Readers get practical guidance on fair screening.
europmc-pmc5596521:
Sellers and co-authors review influenza's effects beyond the lungs in Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses. Flu is classed as a breathing-tract illness. Case reports keep tying it to harm in distant organs. The true burden is likely undercounted.

The team searched the medical literature by organ system. They reviewed 218 reports, from case studies to autopsy work. The most often described problems were heart-muscle inflammation and brain inflammation. Other syndromes strike the nerves, muscles, and more. Some appear with the infection itself. Others, like Guillain-Barré syndrome, follow weeks later. Spotting these states matters for care. Each organ needs its own support plan. Readers get a tour of flu's hidden reach, organ by organ.
europmc-pmc5600021:
Mackenzie and co-authors extend a crystal-analysis tool in IUCrJ. CrystalExplorer computes model energies for the forces between molecules in a crystal. Such energies help explain why crystals pack as they do. The models now reach a much wider range of solids.

The team tuned the CE-B3LYP and CE-HF models against density functional results. Test pairs came from 171 crystal structures. The range covers metal coordination compounds, organic salts, and solvates. Open-shell systems are included too. The CE-B3LYP energies strayed from the reference values by just 2.4 kilojoules per mole on average. That held across a huge span of pair energies. Energy frameworks can now be drawn for these harder crystals. Readers get a faster, trusted route to mapping crystal forces.
europmc-pmc5622121:
Wise and co-authors pool brain imaging studies of the two main mood disorders in Molecular Psychiatry. Major depression and bipolar disorder share many symptoms, yet it was never clear how far their patterns of brain change overlap, and single studies often pointed in different directions.

The team combined fifty study sets on depression, covering more than four thousand people, with thirty-six sets on bipolar disorder. Both groups showed less grey matter than healthy people in a shared set of areas. The losses centered on inner frontal regions that guide emotion. The insula on each side shrank in both disorders. Depression carried wider losses beyond that shared core. They reached the side frontal cortex and the hippocampus. Parts of the back and lower brain differed too. The result is a map of what the two illnesses share and where they part, drawn to guide scan-based diagnosis.
europmc-pmc5627421:
Zielezinski and co-authors guide alignment-free sequence comparison in Genome Biology. Comparing sequences usually means aligning them letter by letter. Alignment breaks down in known ways, though. Rearranged genomes violate its order assumptions. Distant relatives fall into a twilight zone of weak matches.

Alignment-free methods skip the letter matching entirely. They compare sequences through word counts and related statistics. Uses span whole-genome family trees and protein family sorting. They also flag transferred genes and viral mixes. Speed makes them fit the flood of sequencing data. Many researchers still find the methods opaque. This guide explains how they work under the hood. It sets them against alignment-based rivals fairly. A catalog of current tools closes the tour. Readers can pick a method with open eyes.
europmc-pmc5645121:
Náfrádi and co-authors ask whether patient empowerment helps people take medicine as prescribed. Their systematic review treats self-efficacy and health locus of control as core parts of empowerment. Health locus of control means who a patient sees as in charge of their health. The team searched two large databases for studies on these links.

The search found 4,903 papers, and 154 met the review's tests. High self-efficacy and a strong internal locus of control were linked to better adherence. Belief that doctors control health also helped. Chance and God-based control beliefs mostly hurt adherence. The authors propose a joint empowerment approach shared by doctor and patient.
europmc-pmc5708621:
Hu and co-authors report five years of virus surveillance in a bat cave in Yunnan, China. Their study tracks SARS-related coronaviruses in horseshoe bats. Such viruses found elsewhere differ from the human SARS virus in key genes. None looked like its direct ancestor.

The team sequenced full genomes of 11 new strains from this one cave. The strains varied widely in the S gene and in accessory genes ORF3 and ORF8. Some matched the human virus closely in the spike protein's key regions. Others matched in ORF3 and ORF8. Signs of frequent gene swapping appeared across the group. Three new strains could enter cells using the human ACE2 receptor. The authors propose that mixing built the SARS ancestor.
europmc-pmc5738221:
Page and Moher map research on the PRISMA statement, a guide for reporting systematic reviews. Seven extensions of the guide have appeared, with eight more in the works. Their scoping review asks how far the guide is used. It also asks how well reviews follow its items.

They found 100 studies on uptake and impact. Most data cover how well reviews stick to the main statement. Pooled results show many items are still reported poorly. Even reviews after 2009 often miss key items. The authors suggest an updated statement plus tools to help journals enforce it.
europmc-pmc5816021:
Tsukasaki and co-authors show bone-eating T cells defending the mouth. Gum disease, or periodontitis, is driven by mouth bacteria. In arthritis, TH17 cells damage bone and cause harm. The team asks if that bone damage ever helps.

In a mouse model, invading bacteria sparked special TH17 cells. Those cells roused mucosal defenses against the germs. They also broke down bone around the tooth. Losing the tooth itself removed the germs' safe foothold. So the same cells protect and destroy at once. Readers get a fresh, two-sided view of immune bone damage.
europmc-pmc5830921:
Wang and co-authors report a structural study of TDP-43, an RNA-binding protein that forms aggregates in ALS and Alzheimer's disease. The work appeared in The EMBO Journal. It focuses on the protein's folded N-terminal domain. That domain links subunits into head-to-tail chains and supports the protein's role in RNA splicing.

A single phosphomimic change at serine 48 broke up those chains. The altered protein resisted liquid-liquid phase separation in test tubes. In cells, it made nuclear droplets of TDP-43 more fluid. Its splicing activity also fell. The team solved an NMR structure of an engineered dimer that fills the normal joining surface. That structure gives a detailed view of how the domain assembles, and the soluble full-length protein built here opens new in vitro assays.
europmc-pmc5861821:
Pollock and co-authors seek shared best practice for 16S microbiome studies. Their short review appeared in Applied and Environmental Microbiology. Such studies read a marker gene to profile microbial communities. Fast sequencing tools have made the approach very popular. Yet each lab step can bias the final data. Collection, storage, and processing choices all play a part.

The authors gather findings from the literature step by step. They give broad advice for future metabarcoding experiments. Sampling site matters, since communities vary even within one organ. Method choices can skew which microbes seem common. Newcomers to the field get a grounded guide to design choices. The aim is consensus on how such studies should run.
europmc-pmc5874321:
Nurgali and co-authors introduce a research topic on chemotherapy side effects. The editorial appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Modern cancer drugs improve survival, they note. Yet side effects and lasting harm remain a major worry. Current remedies often work only partly. Some add fresh side effects of their own. The collection gathers progress on easing treatment burden.

Nausea and vomiting get early attention in the piece. Delayed sickness is common, feared, and poorly controlled. Animal studies of a drug called netupitant are summarised. Gut injury from treatment is another focus area. Mouth and bowel sores can cause pain, weight loss, and sepsis risk. Safe prevention for such injury is still lacking. The editors frame the topic as an urgent need.
europmc-pmc5918521:
Gallo and co-authors warn that marine plastic litter and its toxic chemicals need urgent prevention. Their paper appeared in Environmental Sciences Europe. It was prepared as a background paper for treaty talks in 2017. Plastics last for hundreds of years at sea. They break into micro and nano pieces over time. Sea life then takes those pieces up the food chain.

Plastics can carry additives and pollutants, the authors note. Some disrupt hormones at very low doses. Those harms threaten ecosystems, biodiversity, and food supply. Proof is already strong enough to act, they argue. Rising production and poor waste systems worsen the flow. A deep rethink of plastic use is urged.
europmc-pmc5933221:
Howard, Cao, and Browne ask what mechanochemistry can offer molecular synthesis. Their perspective piece appeared in Chemical Science. Mechanochemistry drives reactions with direct mechanical energy, often by milling. The method is known for cutting solvent use. The authors argue it can do much more than that.

They highlight reactions that behave unlike the same reactions in solution. Some give products that heat or light would not predict. Milling can open chemical space that other methods cannot reach. The piece gives a short guide to milling devices and reaction types. It invites chemists to treat mechanical force as a tool in its own right.
europmc-pmc5949321:
McFarland, Evans, and Goldstein test whether probiotic benefits depend on the strain and the disease. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in Frontiers in Medicine. Reviews often pool very different probiotics together. That pooling can mislead readers about what works. The authors searched the literature from 1970 to 2017. They kept strains tested in at least two controlled trials per condition.

They included 228 trials in the analysis. Clear strain-specific effects appeared for preventing antibiotic-linked diarrhoea in adults, they report. Some Lactobacillus mixtures worked while other strains did not. Disease-specific variation also showed for well known strains. Guidelines should report results by strain and disease, they argue.
europmc-pmc5954021:
Hsu and co-authors trace how PD-L1 builds up on cancer stem cells and shields them from immunity. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Cancer stem-like cells carry extra PD-L1, which helps them evade attack. The route behind that enrichment was unclear. The team followed an epithelial-mesenchymal transition pathway. It runs through beta-catenin to the enzyme STT3.

STT3 adds sugar chains that stabilise PD-L1, they report. The effect is stronger in stem-like cells than in other cancer cells. They also found the drug etoposide can reverse the pathway. That reversal lowered PD-L1 across cell types. It made cancer cells more open to anti-Tim-3 therapy.
europmc-pmc5966421:
