Nguyen and co-authors profile human breast epithelial cells with single-cell RNA sequencing to map their diversity. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Breast cancer starts in epithelial cells that gain genetic changes. The full range of cell types in the human breast stayed unclear. The team sequenced 25,790 cells from reduction mammoplasty tissue. Seven individuals supplied the samples. Unbiased clustering sorted the cells by their gene activity.

Three epithelial populations emerged from the data, they report. One was basal and two were luminal types. The luminal sets split into secretory and hormone-responsive cells. Rebuilt trajectories joined them into one lineage tree. The atlas forms a base for tracing cancer origins.
europmc-pmc5978021:
McKenzie and a large team of co-authors test how captivity changes the mammalian gut microbiome. Their study appeared in Integrative and Comparative Biology. Captive life alters diet, treatment, and contact with other animals. Such shifts can reshape gut bacteria and host health. Earlier work hinted at lower diversity in captivity. Few species had been checked, though. The team paired wild and captive samples across six mammal orders.

Diversity held steady in bovids, giraffes, anteaters, and aardvarks, they report. It fell in canids, primates, and horses. It rose in rhinoceros. Community makeup shifted for most groups surveyed. Host type, diet, and gut design strongly shaped the patterns.
europmc-pmc6022321:
Wang and co-authors review how mesenchymal stem cells calm the immune system. Their review appeared in Stem Cells International. These stem cells can renew themselves and form several cell types. They live in nearly all tissues and help repair damage. They also interact with cells of both the innate and adaptive immune systems.

The cells release cytokines, growth factors, and chemokines. These signals suppress many effector immune responses. The review sums up recent lab findings on such effects. It also covers clinical trials for immune-related diseases. Trials have grown fast after early reports of safety. Readers get an update on where this therapy now stands. They also see why its value still draws debate.
europmc-pmc6069421:
Masten and Barnes survey resilience science from a developmental view. Their article appeared in Children, a pediatrics journal. Resilience means adapting well when challenges threaten development. Interest has surged as evidence grows on adverse childhood experiences. Such experiences can shadow health for life.

Findings stress how much adversity a child faces. Everyday adaptive systems matter as much as rare traits. Timing shapes which supports help most. Families, doctors, and teachers guard the front lines. The authors call resilience common and changeable. It grows from many systems working together. Readers in child health get practice and training lessons. Well-timed support, they argue, can shift a child's path.
europmc-pmc6099221:
Watson and co-authors report lessons from perfusing donor livers outside the body. Their study appeared in the American Journal of Transplantation. Warm perfusion may let teams judge livers before transplant. The group perfused 47 human livers. Twenty-two went on to transplant.

Damage enzymes in the fluid predicted later peaks in patients. Nearly all livers cleared lactate within three hours. Glucose rose early in most runs. Three livers needed heavy bicarbonate support to hold pH. One of them failed outright after transplant. Bile amount meant little on its own. Bile acidity did flag later bile duct damage. Readers get working criteria for judging borderline livers.
europmc-pmc6107321:
Van Dyne and co-authors report a study in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on cancers linked to human papillomavirus. The virus is known to cause cervical cancer. It can also cause cancers of the throat, vulva, vagina, penis, and anus. The team tracked how often these cancers occurred in the United States.

They used cancer registry data from 1999 to 2015. The data cover most of the U.S. population. Cases rose from about 30,000 in 1999 to about 43,000 in 2015. Cervical cancer rates fell each year. Throat and anal cancer rates rose for both men and women. The authors urge continued tracking of these cancers.
europmc-pmc6143021:
Cowan and co-authors present a systematic analysis in JAMA Oncology on the global burden of multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells in the blood. It causes real harm and death, yet its worldwide scale was not fully mapped. The study belongs to the Global Burden of Disease project.

New cases and deaths rose from 1990 to 2016. Middle-income countries added most of that increase. Rates varied widely from country to country. Treatment is very limited in countries with low social and economic development. The authors say better access to diagnosis and effective therapy is a pressing need. The work is a reference for health policy and resource choices.
europmc-pmc6143921:
Ni and Lu wrote a review in Cancer Medicine on interferon gamma in cancer immunotherapy. Interferon gamma is an immune signal made by T cells. Checkpoint drugs can raise its levels in tumors. That rise helps clear cancer cells. Yet the same signal can also help tumors hide.

The review surveys five years of studies on both faces of this signal. On one side, it aids immune watch and can starve tumors of blood. On the other, it can switch on escape programs. Resistance to therapy can stem from faults in this pathway. The authors say grasping both sides can improve treatment design.
europmc-pmc6156521:
Anand and Mande wrote a review in Frontiers in Microbiology on diet, gut microbes, and the gut-lung connection. The gut microbial community shapes metabolism and immune responses. Diet strongly shapes that community. Its products reach far beyond the gut.

The review explains how gut microbes help digest nutrients humans cannot. Their by-products tune immunity in the gut and in distant organs such as the lung and brain. An imbalanced gut has been tied to lung diseases, including allergy, asthma, and cystic fibrosis. Talk between gut and lung runs both ways. Some probiotics seem to help lung health. The authors call for deeper study of this axis.
europmc-pmc6166321:
Leal and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Physiology on myokines, signals released by exercising muscle. Exercise helps metabolic diseases, and doctors often pair it with drug treatment. How exercise produces its benefits is not fully understood. Myokines, peptides made by muscle fibers as they contract, may be part of the answer.

The review covers myokines such as IL-6, IL-10, and IL-1ra, which mediate many effects of activity. These signals act locally and across the body. Talk between muscle and fat tissue is a central theme. Inactivity seems to blunt the myokine response, which may help explain the harms of sitting. The authors draw out lessons for health and metabolic care.
europmc-pmc6178621:
Gralinski and co-authors present a research article in mBio on the complement system in SARS coronavirus disease. Severe SARS cases end in acute respiratory distress, a lung failure driven by the immune response. The complement system is an early part of host defense against infections. Its role in this disease was untested.

In a mouse model, animals lacking complement developed far less respiratory disease. Their viral loads were unchanged. Their lungs held fewer neutrophils and their bodies showed less inflammation. The result supports the view that SARS damage is immune-driven. The authors suggest that blocking complement signaling might form an effective treatment strategy for such infections.
europmc-pmc6211121:
Yap and co-authors review immune cells in rheumatoid arthritis. This long-term disease inflames the joints. It can deform joints and cut quality of life. No cure exists yet. Drugs can calm the inflammation and slow harm. The review appeared in Cells.

Each immune cell type plays a distinct role in the disease. Cells release signal molecules called cytokines. Those signals drive much of the joint harm. The authors link cell roles to current treatments. They also stress the need for early diagnosis. Early drug treatment gives far better outcomes. New markers could help find the disease sooner. They could also track how active it is.
europmc-pmc6238021:
Kruk and co-authors measured deaths from poor-quality health care. Universal coverage aims to improve health in poorer countries. Coverage only helps if care is good. The study covered 137 low- and middle-income countries. It appeared in The Lancet.

The team used Global Burden of Disease data for 2016. They compared death rates for 61 treatable conditions. Reference rates came from 23 rich countries with strong systems. Excess deaths passed 15 million in total. About 9 million deaths were amenable to health care. About 5 million of those were due to poor-quality care. The rest were due to non-use of care. The authors say quality must rise with coverage.
europmc-pmc6245421:
Hamman reviews the gel found inside Aloe vera leaves and its many uses. His review appeared in Molecules. The gel is rich in long sugar chains called polysaccharides. Many health claims for the plant rest on those chains. Reported effects include wound healing support and lower blood sugar. Anti-inflammatory and immune effects have also been claimed.

Newer work looks at how the gel changes drug uptake. Whole leaf and inner gel forms may help compounds cross the gut wall. The gel may also help drugs pass through skin. Dried gel powder can serve as a base in slow release tablets. Hamman weighs the evidence for each use with care. The review helps readers sort firm findings from early promise.
europmc-pmc6255921:
Martin and Badovinac review what defines a memory CD8 T cell. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Memory cells are immune cells that met a germ before and persist for years. They guard the body against repeat infection. The memory pool is not uniform. Single cells differ in surface marks and in what they do.

Age of a memory cell shapes its traits, the authors argue. How long ago it first met its target matters. Repeat meetings, through infection or vaccines, reshape the pool further. Host genes and past microbe exposure add more variety. The review sorts the known subsets by their marks and jobs. It also urges wider use of less sterile mouse models. Such models may match human immune variety more closely.
europmc-pmc6302221:
The GBD 2017 Influenza Collaborators estimate the global toll of flu-linked chest infections. Their analysis appeared in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine. It covers lower respiratory tract infections tied to influenza. The team modelled cases, hospital stays, and deaths. Coverage spans every country from 1990 to 2017.

They estimate flu-linked infections killed about 145,000 people in 2017. Death rates were highest in adults over 70. These infections caused about 9.5 million hospital stays that year. They made up roughly one in nine such infection episodes. The authors urge more vaccine use and prevention. Seasonal flu, they stress, deserves as much care as pandemic planning.
europmc-pmc6314821:
Vande Voorde and co-authors test a blood-like culture medium for cancer cells. Their study appeared in Science Advances. Standard lab media hold nutrients at levels unlike human blood. Those gaps can distort how cancer cells behave. The team built a medium called Plasmax. It carries over 50 nutrients at blood-level amounts.

They grew triple-negative breast cancer cells in Plasmax. A standard rich medium served as the comparison. Cell metabolism shifted closer to real tumor behavior. One trace nutrient, selenium, changed cell survival. It stopped a form of cell death called ferroptosis. Colony growth changed as a result. The authors urge labs to use more faithful media.
europmc-pmc6371621:
Si and co-authors review microRNAs and cancer drug resistance in Clinical Epigenetics. Small RNAs of about twenty units can tune many genes at once. Drug resistance blocks most cancer cures, and the authors link these small RNAs to that failure.

Resistant cells may take in less drug or repair DNA damage faster. They may also change cell cycle checks or fix altered drug targets. MicroRNAs can drive each of these shifts by targeting the genes involved. Some microRNA patterns may warn doctors that a drug will fail. Others could be blocked or replaced to restore drug response.
europmc-pmc6372921:
Taylor and co-authors present a population cohort study in The BMJ. They tracked 55,959 UK patients aged 45 and over with a new heart failure diagnosis between 2000 and 2017. Primary care records were linked to hospital and death data, with matched controls for comparison.

Survival improved only modestly across the period. One-year survival rose from 74.2 percent to 80.8 percent, and ten-year survival reached just 26.2 percent. Patients who avoided hospital admission near diagnosis lived a median 2.4 years longer. A deprivation gap of half a year separated the richest and poorest groups. The authors call timely diagnosis and treatment a policy priority.
europmc-pmc6407021:
Ginwala and co-authors review flavonoids for chronic inflammation, in Antioxidants. Lasting low-grade inflammation feeds cancer, diabetes, heart disease, and brain disorders. Many current drugs for these conditions carry harsh side effects of their own.

Flavonoids are plant compounds used as remedies for centuries. The review gives special focus to apigenin, found in many herbs and vegetables. Lab work shows it can calm inflammatory signals. The authors weigh that proof against the lack of strong human trials. Safer and cheaper plant-based options remain the goal they set for the field.
europmc-pmc6429521:
Zeng and co-authors compare two families of gut bacterial products, secondary bile acids and short chain fatty acids, and their opposing effects in the colon. Bacteria convert leftover bile acids into forms such as deoxycholic acid, which high-fat diets raise. Fermenting dietary fiber instead yields acetate, propionate, and butyrate, linked to calmer tissue.

At chronically high levels the bile acids promote inflammation and cancer, while the fatty acids mostly protect against both. Sections trace how each class steers cell growth, immune activity, and the microbiome itself. The contrast helps explain why fiber-rich eating may offset some colon cancer risk created by fat-heavy diets.
europmc-pmc6430821:
Berhanu and co-authors build an artificial photosynthetic cell that makes its own energy for protein synthesis. Earlier artificial cells could copy parts of living systems but always ran on supplied fuel. Here a giant vesicle holds a cell-free protein-making system plus tiny proteoliposomes fitted with ATP synthase and bacteriorhodopsin.

Light drives the pigments to produce ATP, which then powers transcription and translation inside the vesicle. Among the proteins made are bacteriorhodopsin itself and parts of ATP synthase, the very components doing the energy work. Those fresh parts slot into the membrane and raise ATP output further, a positive feedback loop. The design marks a step toward an energetically independent artificial cell.
europmc-pmc6449421:
Jefferies reviews the interferon regulatory factors, a family of nine gene switches that turn on virus-fighting interferon programs and steer how immune cells develop. IRF3, IRF5, and IRF7 drive type I interferon output when sensors spot viral traces, while IRF9 manages the response to interferon itself. Other members shape the myeloid cells that carry inflammation.

Since too much or too little IRF activity feeds autoimmune disease, the review focuses on the brakes. Some brakes tag the factors for disposal; others are microRNAs that trim their output. In lupus, losing certain microRNAs lets alarm signals pour out unchecked. Keeping IRF levels on a fine leash thus stands out as a drug strategy worth chasing.
europmc-pmc6465321:
Hack-Lyoung Kim and Sang-Hyun Kim review pulse wave velocity, the speed of the pressure wave through arteries, as a window on atherosclerosis. Risk scores and imaging each miss part of early disease: imaging is costly, slow, or involves radiation and contrast. Stiffening and atherosclerosis feed each other, since stiff walls suffer endothelial damage and plaque-friendly stress.

Pulse wave velocity is simple, non-invasive, and reproducible to measure, and cohort studies tie it to coronary, cerebral, and carotid disease. Longitudinal data show it predicts future cardiovascular events beyond standard risk factors. The authors position the measure as a screening tool for picking out people headed toward silent disease.
europmc-pmc6466021:
Ferronato and Torretta review bad handling of solid waste in poorer countries, where open dumping and open burning stay the main ways to get rid of it. The survey spans waste streams rather than one stuff type, tracing harm to sea water, air, soil, and well water, plus heavy metals staying in soil and plants near dump sites.

The informal sector gets steady focus: waste pickers recover value while handling harmful loads bare-handed, with proven health risks. City and countryside face different forms of the problem, from mixed factory dumping in Dar es Salaam to pesticide jugs in farming areas. Case studies serve as a guide for planners who design joined collection and treatment systems.
europmc-pmc6482321:
Bouarab-Chibane and co-authors measure how 35 polyphenols affect six bacteria that spoil food or poison people, then teach a model to predict the effects from chemistry alone. At a fixed dose and a day of growth, the compounds ranged from feeding germ growth to holding it back. Response split by species: Listeria monocytogenes folded against most polyphenols, while Pseudomonas aeruginosa shrugged nearly all of them off.

Structure-activity models succeeded for four species, with fat-loving character and electronic charge traits doing the work. The two Gram-negative models resembled each other, hinting at shared toxic paths. Surface checks on the bacteria echoed the modeling split.
europmc-pmc6723421:
Malik and Hu update the evidence on sugar-sweetened drinks and heart and metabolic health. Such drinks carry little nutrition. Past work ties them to weight gain, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and some cancers. The authors recheck the evidence, including the murkier link to metabolic syndrome.

Large cohort studies back a strong link to weight gain and to diabetes and coronary heart disease. The link holds even apart from body weight. Links to metabolic syndrome are less steady, and stroke risk looks higher in women. Short trials on risk factors support the pattern. Cutting these drinks should improve population health, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc6743121:
Chen and co-authors studied how a malaria-derived drug kills glioma cells, and how the cells fight back. Dihydroartemisinin, or DHA, causes ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death marked by harmful oxygen buildup. The team tested DHA on glioma cells and probed the defense the cells mounted.

DHA did trigger ferroptosis, with iron-dependent death and fat damage. At the same time, it stressed the cells' protein-folding compartment. That stress switched on a pathway, PERK and ATF4, which raised a heat shock protein called HSPA5. HSPA5 in turn boosted GPX4, an enzyme that neutralizes the fat damage. This feedback blunted the drug's killing effect.
europmc-pmc6801921:
Wegh and co-authors review postbiotics and their potential uses in early life nutrition and beyond. Postbiotics are bioactive compounds made during microbial fermentation. The umbrella term covers metabolites, short-chain fatty acids, cell fractions, functional proteins, and cell wall pieces, among others. Unlike prebiotics and probiotics, the term still lacks a consensus definition. The authors propose a working one.

Evidence so far points to direct immune effects. Postbiotics have been tried for infant colic, atopic dermatitis in adults, and several kinds of diarrhea. Results in young children with diarrhea are mixed, urging care. Heat-killed bacteria plus their culture fluid are among the products tested. The review gathers compounds, mechanisms, and clinical findings to date.
europmc-pmc6814821:
Shi and co-authors report a study in Nature Communications on a protein called YTHDF1. The protein reads a chemical mark on RNA and helps control which proteins a cell makes. Genes for it changed fast in Tibetans and in six Tibetan domestic mammals, a sign of life at high altitude where air is thin. The same gene is switched on in many cancers.

The team focused on non-small cell lung cancer. Blocking YTHDF1 slowed cancer cell growth and tumour growth in mice. It did so by cutting production of cell-cycle proteins such as CDK2, CDK4, and cyclin D1. The work links a high-altitude trait to cancer growth.
europmc-pmc6857221:
Curtis and co-authors argue for cultural safety in healthcare, in the International Journal for Equity in Health. Health gaps for indigenous and ethnic minority patients persist in many countries. Laws and training often demand cultural competency from practitioners. Yet the two terms, competency and safety, are used with mixed meanings. The authors review the literature to sort them out.

Competency usually centres on the practitioner's skills and knowledge. Safety, by contrast, is judged by the patient receiving care. It also confronts power imbalance and institutional racism in the system itself. The authors offer a recommended definition of cultural safety. They argue it, not competency, is the standard that can deliver fair outcomes.
europmc-pmc6869321:
Chenthamara and co-authors review nanoparticles in medicine, in Biomaterials Research. Particles under 100 nanometres across can carry drugs through the body in ways bulk materials cannot. They are now basic tools for watching and treating disease. Yet the choice among carrier types is bewildering for newcomers. This review aims to give them a map.

It explains the most common nanomaterials, natural and synthetic, and what each does well. Coating a particle's surface can extend its time in the blood and steer it to a target. That helps it dodge the liver and the immune system's engulfing cells. The authors then compare routes of administration, from injection to inhalation, and how each changes a treatment's effect.
europmc-pmc6881321:
Jonsson and co-authors report a study in Nature Communications on predicting age from brain scans. A trained algorithm can estimate age from a structural MRI. When the estimate runs ahead of true age, that gap may flag brains ageing faster than they should. The gap has been linked to disease. What genes shape it was unknown.

The team built a deep learning method trained on scans of healthy Icelanders. Transfer learning tuned it for two further datasets, IXI and the UK Biobank. A genome-wide scan in the Biobank data then tied the age gap to specific DNA variants. One variant also related to cortical thickness and area patterns. The work connects a scan-based measure to inherited biology.
europmc-pmc6893721:
Izquierdo and co-authors revisit leptin 25 years on, in the journal Nutrients. Leptin is a hormone made by fat tissue. It tells the brain to eat less and burn more, and it first looked like a ready-made obesity cure. The catch emerged quickly: people with obesity already carry high leptin levels. Their bodies simply stop answering it, a state called leptin resistance.

For leptin to work, it must cross the blood-brain barrier and reach the hypothalamus. The review examines where that transport and the later signalling break down. Animal models show partial successes for several repair strategies. None has yet become a clinical treatment, the authors note, which keeps resistance a central puzzle.
europmc-pmc6898321:
Praveschotinunt and co-authors engineer a gut bacterium in Nature Communications. Healing the gut lining matters in inflammatory bowel disease, fistulae, and ulcers. Most current drugs damp the whole immune system and bring side effects. Agents that repair the lining itself are scarce. The team turned a friendly gut resident into a local repair crew.

They modified Escherichia coli Nissle 1917, a long-used probiotic strain. The bacteria weave fibrous mats of curli fibres studded with trefoil factors, proteins that protect the gut wall and spur its repair. The engineered strain secreted the mats in dishes and in mice, and stayed harmless. It protected mice against chemically induced gut injury better than the plain strain.
europmc-pmc6964821:
Basisty and co-authors build an atlas of what aging cells secrete, hunting markers of aging itself. Their study appeared in PLoS Biology. Cells that stop dividing, called senescent, release a cocktail known as the SASP. It drives many age-related conditions, from brain decline to cancer. Studies usually measure only a few dozen of its proteins, badly undercounting it.

The atlas profiles secreted proteins and vesicle cargo from several cell types, aged by different triggers. Each profile holds hundreds of mostly distinct proteins, plus a core set raised in all of them. Several candidates matched aging markers in human blood. Proteins called GDF15, STC1, and SERPINs tracked with age in a long-running Baltimore study cohort. The database, the authors say, can help gauge how many senescent cells a body carries.
europmc-pmc7079521:
Adhikari and co-authors scope the early COVID-19 literature in Infectious Diseases of Poverty. The disease was identified as the cause of a respiratory outbreak beginning in Wuhan in December 2019. By 31 January 2020 it had reached 19 countries, with 11,791 confirmed cases and 213 deaths, and the World Health Organization had declared an international emergency. Research poured out quickly.

Following the Arksey and O'Malley framework, the team analysed 65 research articles published before 31 January 2020. Most, 89.2 percent, were written in English, and 38.5 percent concerned the causes of the disease, while 67.7 percent came from Chinese scholars. Early work concentrated on causes; prevention and control studies followed as weeks passed. The review summarises what that first wave established about epidemiology, causes, symptoms, diagnosis, and control, including reproduction number estimates higher than SARS. It preserves a record of what was known in the outbreak's first month.
europmc-pmc7145621:
Vallenet and co-authors describe new features of MicroScope, a platform for annotating and exploring microbial genomes, in Nucleic Acids Research. Launched in 2005, the system mixes automatic gene annotation with expert hand curation and maps of metabolic networks. It now holds data for more than 11,800 microbial genomes, with over 4,500 user accounts.

Improvements cover genome choice, browsing, and the expert annotation screens. New tools help assign functions to genes and regions, and compare hundreds of genomes through pangenome graphs, which capture the variation strains share and do not share. The platform supports teamwork in curation, so microbiologists can pool corrections instead of each group annotating alone.
europmc-pmc7162821:
Al-Shayeb and co-authors report hundreds of unusually huge bacterial viruses, phages, found across Earth's ecosystems, in Nature. Phages normally carry small genomes and lean on their bacterial hosts to copy themselves. Sequencing DNA from many environments turned up phage genomes over 200 kilobases long, including one of 735 kilobases, the largest described to date.

Thirty-five genomes were finished by hand into complete circles. These phages carry their own CRISPR-Cas immune systems, transfer RNAs, and even ribosomal proteins, equipment ordinary phages skip. Their CRISPR systems may silence host genes or attack rival phages. The team defines the major family groups, spanning human and animal microbiomes, oceans, lakes, soils, sediments, and buildings.
europmc-pmc7164821:
Hayward and co-authors compare the community burden of seasonal and pandemic flu using the Flu Watch cohort in England, in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine. Volunteers were followed over five winters, 2006 to 2011, with blood tests before and after each season, weekly illness reports, and nasal swabs. The study covered 5,448 person-seasons of follow-up.

Blood evidence showed flu infected on average 18% of unvaccinated people each winter. Most infections caused no illness: only about a quarter of confirmed infections produced swab-proven disease. Standard surveillance therefore misses most flu. Pandemic and seasonal strains are compared for severity, symptom patterns, and how often people consult a doctor, across age groups and study years.
europmc-pmc7223321:
Fan and co-authors review how mesenchymal stem cells protect tissue and calm the immune system. Their article appeared in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences. These stem cells are being tested against many diseases. They can mature into several cell types, from bone to fat. They also release signals that steer immune responses.

That immune steering can cut either way depending on the disease. In inflamed tissue, the cells may dampen harmful reactions. Elsewhere, they support repair and regrowth of damaged tissue. The review sums up recent progress on both fronts. It focuses on the mechanisms behind regeneration and immune control. Understanding those mechanisms decides where cell therapy can realistically help. The authors map the evidence for future regenerative medicine.
europmc-pmc7246821:
Blake and co-authors describe a digital learning package built to protect healthcare workers' mental health during COVID-19. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Frontline staff faced the greatest psychological risk. The team developed the package within the first three weeks of the UK outbreak. They used an agile, rapid three-step process with public involvement.

The package offers evidence-based guidance, support, and signposting to further help. It was made for all UK healthcare employees. A peer panel of 10 healthcare workers reviewed it for relevance and ease of use. Details such as captions on videos were added for inclusion. The authors report the build as a model for fast crisis resources. Protecting staff wellbeing, they argue, is part of the outbreak response itself.
europmc-pmc7273821:
Pierrakos and co-authors take stock of a decade of research on biomarkers for sepsis. Their review appeared in Critical Care. Biomarkers, measurable signs in the body, could help diagnose sepsis, guide treatment, and predict outcomes. An earlier review by the same group had already found 178 different markers, and the field kept growing.

Searching PubMed from 2009 to September 2019 produced 5367 new references and 258 biomarkers, 80 of them new. Most had been tested in fewer than 5 studies, and 81 in just a single study. Only C-reactive protein and procalcitonin had deep clinical testing. Nine markers beat one or both of those standards for diagnosis in head-to-head work. The authors urge better clinical evaluation before new markers are adopted.
europmc-pmc7333021:
West and co-authors report a cross-sectional survey study in JAMA Network Open. It compares resilience among US physicians with resilience in the general US working population. It also tests how resilience relates to burnout among physicians. The surveys were carried out in 2017.

The team invited physicians from a national physician file and surveyed employed adults through a probability-based panel. Both groups completed a short two-item resilience scale and items on burnout. The authors report that physicians scored slightly higher on resilience than other workers. Among physicians, each added point on the scale came with much lower odds of burnout. Even so, many doctors with top resilience scores still reported burnout. Readers get a large national comparison, plus a clear limit on what resilience alone can fix.
europmc-pmc7402621:
Thoms and co-authors solve the structure of a viral sabotage protein in Science. Once SARS-CoV-2 enters a cell, its protein Nsp1 shuts down production of the host's own proteins while viral proteins still get made. How it manages that trick was a key puzzle.

Using cryo-electron microscopy at 2.6 angstrom resolution, the team captured Nsp1 bound to the human 40S ribosomal subunit, the smaller half of the protein factory. Nsp1 plugs the tunnel where host messenger RNA must enter, physically blocking it. Cell studies showed this shutdown nearly abolishes the innate immune response. The binding pocket, they note, is a possible drug target: free the tunnel and the cell can defend itself again.
europmc-pmc7440121:
Czeisler and co-authors survey adult mental health in the United States late in June 2020. Panel surveys ran from June 24 to June 30, 2020, with 5,412 adults taking part. The team asked about anxiety, depression, substance use, and suicidal thoughts.

Overall, 40.9 percent of respondents reported at least one adverse mental or behavioral health condition tied to the pandemic and its stresses. Symptoms of anxiety or depressive disorder were common, and many adults had started or raised substance use to cope. About 10.7 percent had seriously thought about suicide in the 30 days before the survey, with far higher shares among young adults, unpaid caregivers, and essential workers. The authors urge community efforts built for these groups, with health messages that reach them first.
europmc-pmc7447521:
Harrison and co-authors study brain waste clearance in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The glymphatic system flushes waste, including tau protein, from the brain. Failed clearance may let tau build up and drive disease.

In the mouse model, glymphatic function varied by brain region. That pattern matched where tau gathered, region by region. The team then targeted aquaporin-4, a water channel key to glymphatic flow. Changing flow through this channel changed how fast tau cleared. Stronger clearance meant less tau buildup in the model. The results tie weak clearance to tau spread in this model. They also mark glymphatic flow, and aquaporin-4 in particular, as a possible treatment target for tau diseases.
europmc-pmc7551521:
Dong and co-authors systematically review SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidates. Many drug and vaccine efforts began soon after the virus emerged. Several vaccine types had already reached clinical trials.

The review covers inactivated, nucleic acid and vector vaccines. It sums up lab and clinical data for each type. Safety issues that need care are highlighted. Lessons come from vaccines for SARS and MERS viruses. Those lessons may aid design against the new virus. As of September 17, 2020, 36 candidates were in clinical tests. Another 146 were in preclinical work. Readers get a broad view of the vaccine race.
europmc-pmc7561721:
Vollset and co-authors forecast population trends for 195 countries and territories through the year 2100. Future population size shapes health care needs and resource plans for nations. How many children women have is a key input to any such forecast.

The team built new models for births, deaths and movement between countries. Birth rates were modeled from schooling levels and birth control need met. Death rates were modeled by age group through the end of the century. Movement between countries drew on growth and development measures over time. They compared a main forecast with other paths the future could take. They also weighed effects on economies and on power between nations. The ranges carry doubt from the data and the models used. Planners can use the work to prepare for older populations and new health needs.
europmc-pmc7573621:
Gong and co-authors meta-analyze brain activity patterns in major depression and bipolar disorder. The two disorders share many clinical features in practice. Brain markers that split or join them are still unsettled.

The team pooled resting-state MRI studies of brain activity. They included 50 studies with 1399 depression patients. Controls in those studies numbered 1332 people. Another 15 studies covered 494 bipolar patients and 593 controls. Both disorders showed higher activity in the insula. Medial prefrontal areas also showed shared change. Cerebellum activity was lower in both disorders. Other regions differed between the two conditions. The results may guide more targeted treatment for mood disorders.
europmc-pmc7766021:
Tiseo and co-authors project world antimicrobial use in farm animals to 2030. Demand for animal protein is rising, and intensive farms rely on routine antimicrobial use. That use fuels resistance in germs that can reach people. The team gathered sales data for chicken, cattle, and pig systems in 41 countries for 2017.

Global sales in 2017 came to an estimated 93,309 tonnes. Sales are projected to rise 11.5% by 2030, to 104,079 tonnes. All continents are set to increase use. The 2030 figure sits below older forecasts, thanks to falls in use in China, the largest consumer. Export-heavy nations report their data more often, a gap the authors note.
europmc-pmc7777221:
Guest and co-authors set out a sports nutrition society position stand on caffeine and exercise. It sums up a critical reading of the literature to date. Caffeine is among the most used aids in sport. The panel gives dose, timing, and caveats for its use.

Caffeine boosts many parts of performance, from muscle endurance to sprint and jump power. Gains are most steady for aerobic endurance work. Doses of 3 to 6 mg per kilogram of body mass work best. Most athletes take it 60 minutes before exercise. Response varies with genes and habit. Very high doses add side effects without extra gain.
europmc-pmc7779021:
Kalvari and co-authors present Rfam 14, an expanded archive of RNA families. Each family pairs a multiple sequence alignment with a covariance model. The model can search for more members of that family. Rfam now holds 3,444 families.

Work with experts improved microRNA, viral, and bacterial RNA coverage. Syncing with miRBase created 356 new microRNA families and updated 40. A set method now guides the naming of viral RNA families. It started with Flavivirus and Coronaviridae. Coverage of metagenome-based families also grew. In total, 759 new family groups joined Rfam 14. Expert users can now build and submit family groups through Rfam Cloud. New site tools include a sequence search and views of family groups with pseudoknots.
europmc-pmc7793621:
Kroll and co-authors present a fast CRISPR knockout method for larval zebrafish. Hundreds of human genes link to brain disease. The mechanisms behind those links lag behind. Zebrafish larvae are a handy model, but older CRISPR routes suit large screens poorly.

The team built a simple tool to check guide RNAs without sequencing. Their method turns over 90% of injected embryos into full knockouts in the first generation. These fish copied known mutant traits well. Examples include altered clock rhythms and escape responses to irritants. Day-night movement patterns also matched. Several genes could be knocked out in one fish. The route from gene to behavior now takes one week instead of months.
europmc-pmc7931121:
Friedenreich and co-authors present a review of movement, weight, and sitting time in the causes of cancer. An estimated 4 in 10 cancers can be prevented through changeable risk factors. The review gathers the population evidence on three linked habits: physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and obesity. It asks how strongly each one shifts cancer risk.

The authors summarise what large studies show across cancer types. They then explore the biology that may explain the links. Hormones made in the body are one route. Insulin sensitivity is another. Chronic inflammation forms a third path. Together these systems can raise or lower the chance that a tumour starts. The review gives public health planners a clear view of the stakes. It also shows where the proof is firm and where it is thin.
europmc-pmc7946321:
Li and co-authors report a systematic review and meta-analysis of mental illness in health care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Frontline staff worked under extreme strain. Earlier reviews found high rates of disorder but missed studies in Chinese. This review searched both English and Chinese sources to give updated figures for depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Data were pooled across 65 studies with 97,333 health care workers in 21 countries. Moderate depression affected 21.7% of workers across the pooled studies. Anxiety affected 22.1% of workers in the same pool. Post-traumatic stress disorder was also common. Rates of depression and anxiety ran highest in studies from the Middle East. The authors call the burden high and the need for support urgent. They also ask for research on which forms of help actually work.
europmc-pmc7963221:
Rappazzo and co-authors report a study of an engineered human antibody with broad power against SARS-like viruses. Future coronaviruses may spill over from animals again. A shield that works across the family would be valuable. The team started from antibodies taken from a survivor of the 2003 SARS outbreak. They then bred the antibodies for stronger binding in the lab.

One refined antibody stood out. It strongly neutralised SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, and two bat SARS-related viruses. It also bound the target region across a panel of related viruses, hinting at wider cover. In mice, it protected against both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2. The authors present it as a template for defences that outlast a single virus. The work looks ahead to outbreaks that have not yet happened.
europmc-pmc8006021:
Orsburn reviews the history of Proteome Discoverer, a software suite for proteomics data analysis. The program turns tandem mass spectrometry files into protein identifications. It is the vendor software for Orbitrap instruments, made by Thermo Fisher Scientific. The first version came out in 2007, as a replacement for the aging BioWorks framework.

The review traces the software across its 11 main versions. Early releases wrapped the Sequest and Mascot search engines. Later ones added tools for labeled and label-free quantification, crosslink analysis, and glycoproteomics. Orsburn stresses one lasting strength: users can view and check the spectra behind each identification. Free and commercial versions are both in wide use.
europmc-pmc8061021:
Tang and co-authors review IDO1 inhibitors now moving through clinical trials for cancer immunotherapy. IDO1 is a heme enzyme that burns tryptophan into kynurenine. Tumors exploit that pathway to escape immune attack. High IDO1 levels also track with poor prognosis across cancers. Blocking the enzyme could free T cells to work again.

The review starts with the enzyme's biology and structure. It then surveys the medicinal chemistry behind current candidates. Small molecules dominate the trial pipeline. Peptide vaccines take a different route to the same target. The authors give special attention to PROTAC degraders. Those molecules destroy IDO1 outright rather than merely blocking it. Trial results and setbacks both feature in the survey. The field's next design problems close the review.
europmc-pmc8108421:
Graham and co-authors study the first 100 patients at their Neuro-COVID clinic who were never hospitalized. Half had lab-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, half tested negative. All had neurologic symptoms lasting over six weeks. The group skewed young and female, with an average age in the early forties. Their complaints painted a consistent picture of stalled recovery.

Brain fog led the list at 81% of patients reporting the symptom. Headache followed at 68%, then numbness or tingling at 60% of the group. Loss of taste and smell each touched over half. Fatigue gripped 85% of the whole group as well. Loss of smell split the two halves sharply: 74% of confirmed cases versus 36% of the test-negative group. Lab-positive patients scored worse on attention and working memory tests. Quality of life sagged in both groups alike. Time since onset did not predict feeling better.
europmc-pmc8120021:
Zhang and co-authors review lysosomes as far more than the cell's stomach. These acid sacs digest worn parts and invaders alike. Newer work casts them as sensing and signaling hubs. They help run nutrient checks and immune defense too. When lysosomes fail, disease follows across the body. The review tours the damage organ by organ.

In clogged arteries and Gaucher disease, sick lysosomes skew macrophage signals. In brain diseases, failed cleanup lets toxic proteins pile up. Pancreatitis and autoimmune disorders carry their own lysosome faults. Tumors lean on lysosomes for growth, spread, and drug resistance. Immune cells inside tumors bend to them as well. Therapies aimed at lysosome proteins now move toward the clinic. Some target the acid pump, others the membrane gates. Restoring the cell's recycling plant is the shared aim.
europmc-pmc8498921:
Zhao and co-authors build the Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas, a data portal for brain tumor genomics. Gliomas are the most common and deadly brain tumors in adults. Rich genomic data aid study and care, but access is often limited. This atlas serves a large Chinese patient cohort.

The portal holds nearly 2000 primary and recurrent glioma samples. Data types span exome, RNA, and methylation measures. Clinical detail covers age, sex, treatment, tumor grade, and survival. Built-in tools let users probe mutations and gene activity. Survival and gene link analyses run inside the portal. The authors aim to drop barriers for glioma researchers worldwide.
europmc-pmc8763921:
Nearing and co-authors compare 14 methods that test which microbes differ between groups in microbiome studies. Labs use these tools as if they were interchangeable. Few large checks had tested that habit. The team ran all methods on 38 datasets of bacterial gene data, each with two sample groups.

The tools found wildly different counts and sets of significant microbes. Pre-processing choices changed the results as well. For many tools, hit counts tracked sample size and sequencing depth. Two methods, ALDEx2 and ANCOM-II, gave the most stable results. The authors urge a consensus approach that runs several methods before claims are made.
europmc-pmc8854421:
Ravi and co-authors ask why T cells fail inside glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor. Immunotherapy works poorly against this cancer. The tumor's surroundings seem to switch T cells off. The team built a computer model joining spatial and single-cell gene data. It covered 45,615 immune cells from 12 tumor samples. A suspect cell type emerged from the model.

The suspects were myeloid cells releasing interleukin-10. They sat in mesenchymal-like tumor regions. The authors link them to T-cell exhaustion. A lab model using human brain tissue confirmed the effect. Patient T cells placed in the model lost function. Blocking the JAK/STAT pathway restored them. The same rescue held in living animals. The work names a target for future immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc8858821:
Zhang and co-authors measure high uric acid levels across China's adult population. Hyperuricemia feeds gout and kidney disease. Two national surveys give the trend. The first covered 166,861 adults in 2015–16. The second covered 168,351 adults in 2018–19. All gave blood after an overnight fast. Sampling spanned 31 provinces.

Prevalence rose from 11.1% to 14.0% in three years. Men carried far higher rates than women. The male rate reached 24.4% in the second survey. The female rate reached 3.6%. Risk factors included city living and high red meat intake. Heavy beer drinking, inactivity, and high body mass also raised risk. Hypertension and poor kidney function appeared too. The authors call the rise alarming. They present it as a growing public health burden.
europmc-pmc9008121:
Chen and co-authors review how non-coding RNAs drive cancer drug resistance, and how to target them. Most RNA in cells never becomes protein. Three non-coding kinds run much of cancer's control wiring. Micro, long, and circular RNAs all feature. They steer growth, death, spread, and genome steadiness. They also rewire the paths that drugs attack. Resistance to all four therapy kinds traces back to them. Chemo, radiation, targeted drugs, and immune therapy all suffer.

The review maps resistance routes by RNA kind. It then treats the RNAs as warning markers. Some flag resistance before treatment starts. Others reveal it as it forms. Targeting the RNAs themselves is the hopeful turn. Delivery is the hard part of that plan. The authors weigh carrier options frankly. The field's promise and its bottlenecks share the page.
europmc-pmc9021021:
Bethlehem RAI and a large consortium built brain charts that track human brain structure across the whole lifespan. They pooled 123,984 MRI scans from 101,457 people, aged from before birth to 100 years. The charts plot centile scores for brain measures against age, much like height and weight charts for children. They revealed growth milestones that had not been reported before.

An individual's scores stayed stable over repeat scans, and the charts held up across study methods. Centile scores also flagged atypical brain structure in brain and mental disorders. The team released the charts as an open resource for research and care.
europmc-pmc9326521:
Diller and Tabor review the role of the extracellular matrix in wound healing. The matrix is a 3D scaffold of collagens, elastin, and other proteins in all tissues. It anchors cells, carries signals, and calls in repair cells. Injury breaks this scaffold, and healing must rebuild it.

The review walks through the four healing phases: clotting, inflammation, growth, and remodeling. In each phase the matrix is torn down and laid down anew. Second-intention wounds, like ulcers and burns, rebuild with stiff, weaker scar tissue. Products that borrow matrix proteins are listed. Synthetic scaffolds that mimic the matrix are also covered. The authors argue that restoring native structure is the route to stronger scars. The advanced wound care market keeps growing meanwhile.
europmc-pmc9636021:
Cutler and co-authors present Omnipose, a deep network tool for segmenting bacterial cells in images. Microscopy can now track form and molecules in single bacteria. Faithful cell outlines are the step that gates all such work. Odd cell shapes and optics break older outline tools.

Omnipose uses gradient outputs from a distance field to trace borders. That design fixes errors its forerunner Cellpose made on hard cells. Tests covered mixed bacterial cultures side by side. Antibiotic treated cells with warped shapes were segmented well. Long and branched cell forms also came through clean. Gains reached non-bacterial subjects and varied image types. Three-dimensional objects were handled by the same tool. A final test read shape changes in cells under attack by rival bacteria. The authors bill it as a shape proof route to cell outlines.
europmc-pmc9800921:
Huang, Lang, and Li review the IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway and its role across cancers. Interleukin-6 is a versatile immune signal in the body. It switches on the JAK2 and STAT3 relay inside cells. That relay guides cell growth and division choices.

When the pathway stays on too long, tumors benefit. It helps build the inflamed setting tumors thrive in. Spread and invasion programs also answer to its signals. The review first explains each of the three players. It then tours the pathway cancer by cancer. Liver, breast, and colorectal cancers open the tour. Gastric, lung, pancreatic, and ovarian cancers follow. In each, abnormal pathway activity tracks worse outlooks. The authors aim to guide drug work on key pathway points. Blocking the relay is the shared hope across cancers.
flammarion-death-and-its-mystery-before-:
Camille Flammarion was a French star man with a love of the strange. His Death and Its Mystery ran to three books from 1921. Book one, Before Death, came out in the dress of E. S. Brooks. It deals with signs of the soul at work while men still live.

Dreams that come true, views at a range, and deaths felt far off fill the text. Flammarion stacks tale on tale from his vast post bag of years. He holds the count too great to brush off as chance. The set is the great store of the field in its late prime.
fontenelle-histoire-des-oracles-french-1:
Bernard le Bovier de Fontenelle, the French man of letters, wrote his Histoire des oracles from the learning of the Dutch scholar Van Dale. This edition of 1721 kept the work before French readers. Fontenelle treats the pagan oracles of Greece and Rome, once thought to speak with the voices of gods or demons.

His verdict is elegant and deadly. The oracles were priestly frauds, kept up for profit and power, and they faded when politics changed. Wit does the work of demolition in graceful French prose. The book became the Enlightenment's classic doubting account of pagan divination. Oracles, one might say, were laughed out of court by the politest executioner in Paris.
frus-1861-d121:
Charles Faulkner wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 April 1861. The dispatch is document 121 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Faulkner stayed at the Paris post until Dayton could arrive. His April report came three days after Fort Sumter, from a capital full of war talk. It shows an outgoing envoy still serving the new chief through the handover. His service bridged two parties and two cabinets in the space of a few weeks. Bridging two cabinets in weeks was a strain few envoys of the age could match.
frus-1861-d21:
Henry Sanford, the American minister to Belgium, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 May 1861. The dispatch is document 21 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Brussels sat close to both Paris and London, and Sanford prized news from each. His reports mixed court talk with press and market word. For Washington, such letters were a cheap way to keep eyes on Europe's mood in the war's first spring. Belgium's king, Leopold, had wide family ties in Europe, which made Brussels talk worth hearing. Talk in Brussels often reached Seward before the same news came by formal note.
frus-1861-d221:
By the date of 22 November 1861, Seward had new word ready for Mr. Marsh. Congress received it as Document 221 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the autumn of the war's first year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d121:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, dated 7 August 1862. Congress received it as Document 121 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d21:
By the date of 11 February 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 21 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d221:
On 1 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart of the British legation, in a letter printed as Document 221 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter opened the month's run of Seward-Stuart exchanges.

July began with McClellan's army pulling back from Richmond, a retreat that looked like defeat abroad. Foreign governments read Union weakness as a reason to push for a truce. Against that mood, Seward kept his tone even and his letters frequent. This one belongs to the effort to steady nerves in the first days of a bad month. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d321:
Two Dayton reports are dated 3 September 1862, and the first stands as Document 321 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went from William L. Dayton in Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Dayton wrote three days after Bull Run, before the defeat's full weight had reached Paris. The French government was then drafting its proposal for a joint truce, the fall's central danger. Reports from these days show the envoy gathering the court's mood while the ground shifted under his information, a fair picture of his craft. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d421:
On 30 May 1862 Horace J. Perry reported from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward, five days after his last letter home. The report is Document 421 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Frequent short reports kept Washington current in an age when mail moved by steamer. Perry covered the Spanish court's view of the war, its Cuban concerns, and its part in the Mexican affair. In the last days of May 1862, French forces had just been checked at Puebla, news that changed the tone in Madrid. Perry's dispatches let a reader follow that shift as the legation saw it, week by week.
frus-1862-d521:
On 24 September 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. His report is Document 521 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Pike's letter was dated two days after Lincoln issued the preliminary emancipation order, but the news had not yet reached the Netherlands. He wrote instead of the Dutch scene as it stood: cautious, commercial, and waiting on American battle news. The gap between the date on the page and the facts on the ground is the story of all these letters. Seward, reading in October, could correct for it; the modern reader should too, and will find the Hague file a clear window on that lag.
frus-1862-d621:
On 10 January 1862 Jacob S. Haldeman reported from Stockholm to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 621 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Haldeman opened the year reporting Swedish goodwill and the north's reading of the war after the Trent settlement. Sweden and Norway sent the Union settlers and sailors rather than trouble, and their government's neutrality was never in question. Still, Seward wanted every post reporting, and Stockholm's letters fixed the friendly north in his survey of Europe. The report is part of the early-1862 round of the Department's work. In that round it confirmed, capital by capital, where it stood. The crisis with Britain had by then passed.
frus-1863p1-d121:
Third in its set comes this letter of 16 March 1863 from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 121 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

By the third sheet, a batch turns from the great heads to the finer ones. Seward's file for Britain held many small claims and talks, each worth its own page. This letter is the third of the 16 March set. It shows the depth of the brief that one envoy carried, and the care with which Washington stocked him for it.
frus-1863p1-d21:
For the last time in 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 29 December. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 21 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, Seward's last to London in the old year.

Seward wrote days before the freedom edict for the enslaved took force on New Year's Day. That act would change the war's face abroad, and his envoys had to be ready to speak for it. This letter belongs to that hinge in time. It shows Washington briefing its London man at the close of a year that had tested the Union and its foreign ties alike.
frus-1863p1-d221:
The mail from London dated 25 June 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 221 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d321:
A formal note dated 13 November 1862 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 321 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d421:
From the British legation in Washington on 23 March 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 421 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada bordered the Union along a long, thinly guarded line. British worries about that frontier, and American worries about plots hatched there, fed part of this mail. It dates from the spring when British debate over aiding the South was still live, and every note counted. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d521:
Under the date 21 May 1863, the record holds a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d621:
Secretary William H. Seward took up his pen on 22 September 1863 and wrote to William Stuart, Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863. With Lyons away from Washington, Stuart kept the British side of the correspondence going through the autumn of 1863.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d121: A second message from Stalin to Roosevelt dated November 12, 1943 stands as Document 121 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It pairs with the Stalin letter just before it, in the last exchange before the Tehran meeting sixteen days later. The catalog record gives the date and the two names and nothing narrower. The letter is kept in the Foreign Relations series, in the voyage run of papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d21: After a gap of more than three weeks, Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on August 8, 1943, and the message became Document 21 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The pause and the return both matter in this correspondence, which rose and fell with the war's turns. The record gives the date and the two leaders' names only. Printed in the Foreign Relations series, the letter resumes the thread that led to Tehran in November.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d221:
Minutes record President Roosevelt's meeting with the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 15 November 1943. It was held at two in the afternoon in his cabin aboard the battleship Iowa, as he sailed toward the Cairo conference. The printed excerpts cover French forces, Balkan strategy, and high command.

On rearming France, the chiefs note a plan to equip eleven or twelve French divisions. Admiral Leahy warns that de Gaulle would use such divisions as a lever for power in France itself. Roosevelt orders the present plan to proceed, with no new commitments. He also approves the chiefs' Balkan and eastern Mediterranean policy paper as it stands, and states his wish that General Marshall command the whole effort against Germany.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d321:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 407, in revised form, at Cairo on 26 November 1943, setting the broad lines to follow at the coming conference with the Soviets at Tehran. It is the Anglo-American playbook for their first staff talks with Stalin's officers.

The Western chiefs should first agree their own strategy in Europe. They should win their leaders' approval before facing the Soviets. They should consult each other before answering any Soviet proposal. And they should hold an agreed line on Balkan or Aegean operations. On Turkey they will back the Soviet wish to force her into the war, but refuse any diversion of forces that harms approved operations. The paper also reverses the Moscow pattern: this time the West should make specific requests of the Soviets, from bombing coordination to Siberian ports and air bases against Japan.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d421:
Louis Dreyfus, the American minister in Iran, telegraphed Secretary of State Hull from Tehran on 3 December 1943, number 1086, reporting the Declaration on Iran signed there on 1 December. The message gives the declaration's contents in four numbered points for Washington's record.

The three powers recognize Iran's contribution to the war against the common enemy. They see that the war has caused Iran special economic difficulties, and state their intent to go on providing such economic help as they can. Iran's postwar economic problems are to receive full consideration from the international conferences and agencies dealing with such matters. And the three powers reaffirm their desire for Iran's sovereign independence and territorial integrity, under the Atlantic Charter. Dreyfus notes the declaration was issued at the Iranian prime minister's request, and judges it has strengthened the American position in Iran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d521:
Marshal Stalin wrote to President Roosevelt on December 20, 1943, less than three weeks after the two men met for the first time at Tehran. The message passed between the Soviet leader and the President in their direct wartime correspondence. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Stalin's messages to Roosevelt were usually brief, formal, and carefully weighed, and each one mattered out of proportion to its length. A December letter belongs to the season when the alliance was converting Tehran's promises into the campaigns of 1944. For readers, it is the Soviet voice in a record often told from Washington and London, speaking for itself.
frus-1944-quebec-d121:
Roosevelt answered Churchill's Warsaw telegrams on September 5, 1944, in a personal and secret message sent from Hyde Park. It is short, and it closes the urgent exchange that had run through the previous day. The president relied on a report from his Office of Military Intelligence about the fighting in the Polish capital.

That report claimed the fighting Poles had left Warsaw and the Germans held full control. On that basis Roosevelt said the relief problem had been solved by delay and German action, and nothing more could be done. He added that he had long been distressed by the failure to help Warsaw's defenders. He hoped Poland would still end the war among the victors.
frus-1944-quebec-d21:
Prime Minister Churchill sent this message to President Roosevelt on August 8, 1944, one of two from him bearing that date in the volume. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume's pre-conference papers.

Churchill's August correspondence pressed British concerns as American power grew: the Mediterranean, the future of Italy and Greece, and Britain's shrinking share of the common effort. Two messages in a day show him working several fronts at once. For readers, the message captures a prime minister determined that victory should not leave his country a spectator at its own alliance's table.
frus-1944-quebec-d221:
Hull pressed the Argentine meat question again on September 12, 1944, in a memorandum for Roosevelt's talks with Churchill. Effective implementation of American Argentine policy, he wrote, depended on British economic cooperation, and London had so far given only tentative, highly qualified promises. Rumor held that Britain intended to sign a four-year meat contract.

Hull argued the food situation made a long contract unnecessary. Judge Byrnes had reported production in Allied areas a third above normal, with war reserves becoming surplus at peace. Beef could reach Britain from America, Canada, Australia, and other South American suppliers, including America's surplus utility beef. He proposed more lend-lease beef in exchange for reduced British purchases in Argentina, and spot buying instead of any long agreement.
frus-1945-50-intel-d121:
Hoover wrote to Attorney General Clark on 8 August 1946, the same day the National Intelligence Authority wrote to Clark. The FBI director's letter answers the board's move from inside the Justice Department. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Hoover rarely accepted a ruling against the bureau without putting his objection in writing to his own chief. His letter of 8 August belongs to the peak of the Latin American fight, when the board's decision on the field was being delivered. Readers can read the day whole: the authority's letter and Hoover's response, claim and counter-claim, preserved side by side. The volume's fairness in printing both is what makes it history rather than a victor's tale.
frus-1945-50-intel-d21:
General John Magruder, who now ran the Strategic Services Unit in the War Department, wrote to three intelligence chiefs at once on 1 October 1945. His unit was the surviving core of the dissolved OSS. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Magruder's letter went to the Army's intelligence chief, the Navy's, and the State Department's new research and intelligence head. That mailing list is the post-OSS world in miniature: three services and one department, each holding a piece. Readers meet here the man trying to keep the remnant alive while the pieces were argued over. His papers through the autumn form the volume's thread of survival, written from inside a unit that everyone expected to vanish.
frus-1945-50-intel-d221:
Dated 18 September 1947, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) to the Intelligence Advisory Board. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 221, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Congress was then debating the National Security Act, the law that would soon create the CIA and the National Security Council.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d321:
The General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Group (Houston) addressed a memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) on 29 July 1947. The State Department prints it as document 321 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d421:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote to the Army's assistant chief of staff for military intelligence, Bissell, on 8 May 1950. The memo is document 421 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Within weeks, war in Korea would test every part of the system these men ran. In May the work was still one of charts, duties, and shared reports. The memo shows the CIA chief dealing with Army intelligence at staff level, where the real links were made. Bissell's office linked the Army's field reports to the joint picture the CIA tried to build.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d121:
The Cabinet Committee could not agree on Germany, the Secretary of State told the President on 29 September 1944. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, sets the State Department's thinking against the Treasury's. It answers the Quebec paper of 15 September.

That Quebec paper, with its talk of the Ruhr, the Saar, and turning Germany into a farming and pastoral country, reflects mainly Secretary Morgenthau's views. The Treasury memorandum, Hull writes, is decidedly at odds with the line worked out in the State Department. He reports the practical ground already won: the surrender instrument has been approved in Washington, and the American and British zones were settled at Quebec.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d21: Roosevelt wrote to Stalin on 18 November 1944, raising the Soviet channel again after a run of Churchill letters. The message is document 21 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. Any summit needed Stalin's agreement on timing and place, so presidential letters to Moscow carried weight that staff messages to the Soviet government could not match.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d221:
Leo Crowley, head of the Foreign Economic Administration, wrote to Stettinius on 13 January 1945 about Moscow's credit request. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, suggests the two men take the matter to the President together. Harriman's cables of 4 and 6 January had raised questions fit for the coming conference.

Enclosed is a rough draft of the points Crowley wants in Washington's reply, both to Molotov's proposal and to Gromyko's note on the Fourth Protocol. The first point draws a bright line. Projects under the Lend-Lease Act belong to the war supply program. They must be kept wholly apart from any projects financed by long-term credits for postwar needs. The study of those credits, the draft says, is now under way.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d321:
A group photograph and a famous memoir help the editors pin down one Malta meeting in this short note. The session's substance survives only in Secretary Stettinius's book. A few words more appear in Churchill's history and Admiral Leahy's memoir. Times and names come from the official trip log.

The note even prints the caption of an Army photo of the Combined Chiefs at Montgomery House on January 31. Marshall, King, Brooke, and Portal are all named in the frame. Small notes like this one let readers check the main record against pictures and later books. They anchor names and faces to a single crowded week.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d421:
Antonov came back with answers, and Kuter's minutes of February 9, 1945, record them. The Soviet general opened by saying he had laid every point before Stalin. His first day's comments had been personal views only. Now he could give definite and official replies to each question.

On Far East operations, he reported no change of intent and only minor changes of plan since October. Units meant to move east early in 1945 were now fighting in the center of the Russian front. Their transfer would wait. The minutes catch the moment the Pacific bargain moved from asking to terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d121:
Churchill proposed announcing the press ban in advance in telegram number 103 to President Truman, sent July 4, 1945. The message is document 121 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The three leaders had already agreed that reporters would not be allowed at Terminal, while photographers would.

A public announcement now, Churchill argues, will avoid disappointment and stop newspapers from sending their best people to Berlin. Each government should let it be known that no press will be admitted and that only official communiqués, issued as agreed from time to time, will come out of the meeting. He says he is sending a similar telegram to Stalin, who, a note adds, accepted the idea on July 6.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d21: Stalin accepted at once in this reply to Truman, dated May 20, 1945, and given here in translation. He had received the President's message about the arrival of Hopkins and Harriman in Moscow by May 26. He readily accepted the proposal to meet them. The date — May 26 — was quite convenient for him. The short letter, transmitted through the Soviet Embassy in Washington, opened the door the Hopkins mission would walk through six days later.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d221:
Joseph Davies set out his creed on foreign policy in a memorandum dated July 3, 1945. The paper is document 221 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Davies, who chaired the President's War Relief Control Board and had been ambassador to Moscow, sent it to Truman along with his survey of the conference agenda.

Foreign policy, Davies writes, is nothing more than rules governing a country's relations with peoples outside its borders. Its first purpose is protection from invasion and attack, freedom from fear. Its next is to preserve the people's standard of living and way of life, freedom from want.
