He urges clear statements of American policy, defense of the western hemisphere as a neighborhood of friends, and grounding in justice, liberty, and the Four Freedoms.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d321:
Censorship is the point Melbourne adds in his Bucharest cable of July 15, 1945. He first notes General Schuyler's two messages of July 14, which set out the least changes needed in how the Rumanian armistice was run. Melbourne then turns to Article 16 of that armistice, which covered censorship.

Control of censorship, he wrote, was a great political and cultural weapon held by Soviet officials alone. With the war over, he argued, three-power control of censorship could no longer be put off on military grounds. While the armistice lasted, Washington should claim a right to help decide what Rumanians could print and read.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d421:
German coal is the subject of Murphy's despatch No. 539 from supreme headquarters, dated June 28, 1945. He transmits a staff memorandum on the present coal situation, written by his economic officer Rainey. With it goes the Potter-Hyndley report on coal in northwest Europe, dated June 1945.

Murphy points Washington above all to three paragraphs of that report's summary. The coal supply problem in western Europe, he stresses, is extremely critical. Everything touching the production and movement of German coal must take the highest priority. Shortages in France, Belgium, Holland, Denmark, and Norway demand export of all available western German coal if civil order is to survive the winter.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d521:
Reconstruction aid for Poland is urged in a briefing book extract dated June 29, 1945, from the paper on suggested American policy toward Poland. To carry out the policy of a truly independent, democratic Polish state, it argues, America should be ready to help. Subject to legislative authority, it would assist through credits or otherwise. The help would rebuild Polish agriculture and industry.

Immediate action to supply urgently needed equipment and relief materials, it says, will promote a healthy American influence in Poland in an enduring way. That influence bears especially on the holding of free elections, the final step in the Yalta program. The efforts, the extract adds, should be national rather than international in form.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d621:
Ambassador Harriman sent extracts of a study of Soviet oil output from Moscow on June 29, 1945. The secret report is document 621 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It was prepared for U.S. talks on oil and reparations that summer.

The study puts Soviet crude output at about 21.5 million tons in 1945. That is down from 31.1 million tons in 1940. Baku's fields faded for lack of new drilling during the war. German forces wrecked the Maikop field and much of Grozny, and the big Bashkiria field also fell off. The study concludes that the Soviet Union cannot export oil in the early postwar years, save in small amounts for set ends. It also expects Moscow to keep its grip on oil output in the parts of Eastern Europe it holds.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1021:
American staff drafted this undated working paper on separating the Ruhr and Rhineland from Germany. It argues that disarmament alone cannot guarantee Germany will never attack again. So long as the Ruhr and Rhineland stay under German rule, the paper says, Germany keeps the means to wage a major war.

The paper proposes five rulings. The two regions would be permanently detached from Germany. Before occupation ends, they would form an international protectorate under the United Nations Security Council. Belgium, France, and the Netherlands would run it for the council. Its output would serve all Europe without favor. Truman's own note on the copy reads: not presented, but discussed; decided they should remain in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1121:
London's team tabled this proposal on 19 July 1945, the third day of the Potsdam Conference. Like the Soviet paper of the day before, it set down an opening stand for the three-way talks. Each team wanted its terms on paper before the trading grew hard.

Britain had fought the war for six years and was worn down in men, money, and ships. Its team sought a peace that guarded British interests without taking on new burdens. A formal proposal from the first week fixes that starting offer in the team's own words. The final terms can be read against it to see what London held and what it gave up.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1221:
A second Hurley dispatch to the Secretary of State bears the same date, 29 July 1945. Two cables in a day from the China post signal a file moving too fast for one report. Hurley's embassy dealt with a government, an army, and a rival party all at once.

Back-to-back dispatches let an envoy split subjects: one for the urgent, one for the standing picture. Together they kept Washington's China brief full during the summit's close. This one is the day's companion piece. Read as a pair, the two cables show the tempo of a post where the next war was already taking shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1321:
Parten, chief of staff of the American reparations team, wrote to Pauley, its head, on 21 July 1945. The note ran inside the mission that judged Germany's capacity to pay. Parten ran its staff work; Pauley carried its findings to the summit.

Internal notes of a mission fix facts, assign tasks, and ready the chief's brief. This one dates from the heart of the reparations fight at Potsdam. It shows the mission's machine at work behind its famous head. The figures that leaders quoted in the great rooms began in staff traffic of exactly this kind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1421:
The Soviet delegation at Potsdam submitted a text on 14 July 1945, in the volume's closing run of conference papers. The date falls just before the conference formally opened, when delegations were tabling their opening positions.

Early texts at a summit stake out ground. A paper tabled before the leaders even sat down shows a delegation arriving with its asks already drafted. Readers can follow this Soviet text forward through the talks: which of its points the final protocol kept, and which the other powers bargained away. The closing run of the volume gathers many such texts, letting the drafting fight be read whole.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-121:
State Department minutes record a meeting held on July 27, 1945, late in the Potsdam Conference. By then Attlee had returned as Britain's new prime minister, and the talks pushed toward their close. Formal minutes like these anchor the second Potsdam volume. They state the business done in a sober, ordered form.

The worth of minutes grows with time. Memories fade and claims conflict, but the written record holds. Readers find who spoke, what was proposed, and what was left for the final text. Set beside the note-takers' rougher sets, these minutes give the day's work its official shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-21:
Thompson's minutes record the foreign ministers' meeting of July 19, 1945, with Eden in the chair. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The day's agenda held German political questions, Poland, and German economic problems.

Before the agenda, Byrnes asked to reopen one point in the Council of Foreign Ministers paper. Its third section limited council duties to governments that had signed surrender terms. Some governments, Byrnes noted, were at war but had not signed armistice terms. France, for example, was at war with Italy without being such a signatory. He asked that the drafting committee reconcile the rival views on the wording. Molotov said the question was not quite clear to him. The exchange shows the council's membership rules still unsettled three days into the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d721:
Hurley wrote once more to the Secretary of State on August 1, 1945, in document 721. It is the last of his letters in this run of the second Potsdam volume. The pair of August 1 letters bookend the conference's closing day. From Chungking, Hurley kept Washington's China policy tied to the talks in Germany.

A closing letter in a series has summary force. The ambassador states where his mission stands as the ground shifts. Readers gain a sense of China as the conference left it: ally, problem, and prize at once. The document ends the Byrnes-Hurley thread on the day Potsdam itself ended.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d821:
Schoenfeld reported from Hungary on July 26, 1945, in document 821. The representative in Budapest wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. His letters, with Barnes's and Melbourne's, build the volume's Balkan wall. This one entered the second Potsdam volume as the conference neared its end.

Three missions reporting in parallel give readers a regional picture. Hungary's path can be set beside Bulgaria's and Rumania's. Schoenfeld's part of the wall is steady and detailed. The document shows a professional doing his duty in a post the maps were leaving behind. His reports remain a prime source for Hungary's first postwar summer.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d921:
Soviet delegates proposed this plan for advance deliveries from Germany, circulated at Potsdam in late July 1945. Until a permanent agency for reparations exists, urgent removals would go to nations that suffered, to help them rebuild. Each delivery would later be booked as reparations, restitution, or a purchase.

A Berlin sub-commission of the Allied Commission on Reparations would run the system. It would list the industries open for removals and approve deliveries from them. Raw materials from current output or stocks would need its approval too. The plan also demands uniform records of account. Each occupying power must report all property removed from Germany within six months.
frus-1955-57v21:
East Asian security, Cambodia, and Laos share Volume XXI of the 1955–1957 set. SEATO's growth leads, with council meetings and ANZUS work. The Bandung meeting of Afro-Asian states also draws long study.

Cambodia follows, with aid and army training beside worry over the Prince's neutral course. Laos takes the largest block, on backing the Royal Government against a Pathet Lao coalition. The papers show small kingdoms treated as front lines. Each grant and training team was weighed for how it would read in Peiping and Hanoi. Aid ran second to politics in each file's math.
frus-1961-63v21:
Africa fills Volume XXI of the 1961–1963 set. North Africa leads, with Algeria's war and its end in the first blocks. Libya, Morocco, and Tunisia follow in country runs.

Ghana and Guinea take the next blocks, their leaders courted in the files. The Horn follows. Rhodesia, Portuguese Africa, and South Africa close the volume. The papers show a continent of new flags. Each recognition, aid grant, and base talk was weighed against Soviet moves, and the counting never paused for long. South Africa's files close on the South West Africa fight.
frus-1964-68v21:
Volume XXI of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964-1968, covers the Near East region and the Arabian Peninsula. Short opening chapters treat the region as a whole and the Indian Ocean. Country chapters then cover Iraq, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia. The longest chapter follows Yemen, where civil war drew in Egypt and Saudi Arabia from opposed sides.

The records are embassy cables, memos, and notes of talks with kings and ministers. They show U.S. concern with oil, bases, and Soviet inroads. In Yemen, the papers trace U.S. efforts to end foreign meddling and calm the war. The volume gives the Gulf and peninsula side of Johnson-era policy.
frus-1969-1976-chile-vol-21:
Volume twenty-one of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1969 to 1976 covers Chile from 1969 to 1973. The State Department's Office of the Historian compiled the volume from declassified records. It documents one of the darkest chapters of Cold War policy in Latin America.

The papers follow Washington's alarm at Salvador Allende's election in 1970. They record the order to make the economy scream, the Track I pressure to block Allende's confirmation, and the Track II covert action run beside it. Aid cuts, coup plotting, and contacts with Chilean officers fill the file. The record ends with the September 1973 coup that brought Pinochet to power.
frus-1977-80v21:
Cyprus, Turkey, and Greece fill Volume XXI of the 1977-1980 Foreign Relations series. A section on the Eastern Mediterranean region opens the volume. Cyprus follows, then Turkey, then Greece. The papers deal with the slow Cyprus talks after 1974 and the U.S. arms embargo on Turkey. One talk record has Ankara's foreign minister glad to delay steps until after a Greek election. U.S. arms sales would proceed in the meantime.

The Greece section covers ties under the Karamanlis government and the path back toward NATO's military arm. Base rights and air space disputes fill many pages. The volume shows a triangle of allies at odds.
galsworthy-to-let-1921:
John Galsworthy published To Let in 1921 as the closing novel of The Forsyte Saga proper. The title comes from the empty Forsyte houses standing to let after the First World War. Galsworthy set the story in 1920, with a new generation in charge.

Fleur Forsyte, Soames's daughter, falls in love with Jon, the son of Irene and Jolyon. Neither knows at first why their families hate the match. The old scandal of Soames and Irene rises again to crush the young lovers. Beneath the romance, Galsworthy records an age passing: the solid Forsyte world dissolving into a looser, sadder England.
gao-gaoreports-b-293105-21:
GAO's decision of April 4, 2007, filed as B-293105.21, B-293105.22, and B-293105.23, returns to Greenleaf Construction's fight over a housing contract in Ohio. The Department of Housing and Urban Development had again awarded the home management and marketing work to Chapman Law Firm Company. Greenleaf again claimed a conflict of interest. This time GAO denied the protest. The contracting officer had reasonably found that the winner's owner had sold his stake in the Ohio closing agent firm.

The digest adds a point on proof. The owner's early reluctance to give up more pay for his stake did not taint the notarized papers. Those papers showed a clean end to the money ties.
gao-gaoreports-b-295421:
Dated February 18, 2005, GAO file B-295421 records Gray Graphics Corporation as the protester. The Government Printing Office had awarded McDonald and Eudy Printers a printing services contract. Gray Graphics held the low bid but was found nonresponsible and so barred from award. It protested that finding. GAO denied the protest. The finding rested on records of late deliveries under the firm's recent contracts. On such proof, the judgment was a fair one.

The contract was a one-year requirements deal, with one option year. In bid law, a sound finding on a firm's fitness ends the matter, even for the low bidder.
gao-gaoreports-b-296221:
Linguistic Systems protested the rejection of its quote for translation work in GAO decision B-296221, dated June 1, 2005. The buyer was the General Services Administration. The firm read a closing time of 12 PM as midnight. It thus missed the close. The system shut before it could file.

GAO denied the protest. A posted set of answers named the close as 12 Noon. That post changed the call in plain terms. The firm should have seen noon was the true close. A vague time note does not beat a clear fix. The ruling warns bidders to read all posts, not just the first call.
gao-gaoreports-b-297121:
Cartographics protested a Forest Service task order for map work in GAO decision B-297121, dated November 15, 2005. The order went to Photo Science. The work was digital maps of the Targhee National Forest. The firm held its own map deal with the agency. It said the order should have come under its deal, at its lower price.

GAO dismissed the protest. GAO lacks power to hear fights over task orders under such open deals. That bar is set by law for this kind of order. The price claim thus could not be heard here. The order stood with no GAO review. Task order fights of this type go elsewhere, not to GAO.
gao-gaoreports-b-297321:
Laerdal Medical protested a Navy award for medical training gear in GAO decision B-297321, dated December 23, 2005. The winner was Medical Education Technologies. The gear was simulator tools for medical training. The firm hit the tech marks for the bids. It said the review was flawed in how it weighed the tools.

GAO denied the protest. The record showed the tech review was sound. Marks tracked what the tools could do. A protest on tech marks must show a flaw in method or facts. Mere dissent with the marks is not enough. No such flaw was shown here. The award thus stood on a sound tech review.
gao-gaoreports-b-297421:
STR protested a sub deal award for grants software in GAO decision B-297421, dated December 22, 2005. The prime holder was SRA International. The sub winner was Infoterra. The software would serve the Agency for International Development and the State Department. The prime had run the pick in large part.

GAO dismissed the protest. GAO hears sub fights just when the sub deal is in truth by the state. Here the prime drew the test terms, scored the replies in large part, picked the good, and would run the sub deal. That depth of prime control did not meet the by-the-state test as GAO read the facts. The fight thus fell outside GAO power.
gao-gaoreports-b-311321:
Guam Shipyard lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-311321, dated June 9, 2008. The Navy sought washroom work on Barge YRBM-25 in Guam. The job fits low-care, touch-free wash gear. The award went to Gulf Copper Ship Repair, Inc. That firm scored high on past work and bid a high price. Guam Shipyard bid low and scored low on past work.

GAO denied the protest. The scores and the pick were fair on the file. Each fit the call's terms and the rules of the buy. Past work can tip a race when the call weighs it. A low price does not beat a strong past on such terms.
gao-gaoreports-b-400321:
Delex Systems, Inc. wanted two Navy training orders set aside for small firms that held a shared contract. GAO took up the pair as B-400321 and B-400402 on August 5, 2008. One order would revise Naval Strike Air Warfare Center course work. The other covered Tidewater naval air training courses.

GAO dismissed both protests at the door. By law, it lacks power over protests of delivery orders under such shared contracts when the orders are worth less than $10 million. These orders fell below that line. The text lays out the rule and why the small firm set-aside claim could not be heard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-221:
Means-Tested Programs, GAO-05-221 of March 11, 2005, asks a plain count: of those who can claim aid, how many do? Aid plans for low earners must stay open to those in need and stay clean of abuse. Chiefs need facts on both sides. The share of those who qualify but stay out is the key fact on the access side.

GAO gives that share for 12 aid plans, from food aid to housing vouchers. It names what lifts or blocks take-up. It lists steps at each level of government to boost both access and clean claims. It checks if agencies track the share at all.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-421:
Gasoline Markets, GAO-05-421 of June 17, 2005, weighs a clean-air win with a price tag at the pump. The Clean Air Act makes the worst-air zones burn a set fuel blend. The blend cuts the fumes that foul air. It takes an added part such as ethanol. Mild zones may choose a blend of their own, with federal leave. Each zone's blend can be its own.

GAO asks how wide such blends run, and where they will spread. It asks how much they cut car fumes and lift air health. It asks how they strain the fuel flow, since one zone's fuel can not fill the next. It prices their mark.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-521:
Billions in defense payments parked in suspense accounts are examined in GAO report GAO-05-521, issued on June 2, 2005. For years the department could not match many payments to the right accounts. It could not settle gaps between its check records and the Treasury's. Congress let it write off old items whose papers were lost. GAO was told to review how that write-off power was used.

The records were too poor to show the true size of the write-offs. Department books list a total value of $35 billion written off, or a net value of $629 million. GAO said neither figure can be trusted. Many items had been netted at local offices before reaching the suspense accounts. That hid which accounts were over- or undercharged. It also hid whether any payment broke the Antideficiency Act. The write-off process worked fairly but took heavy effort. New rules were not being enforced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-621:
Industrial loan corporations, once tiny lenders for workers, are the subject of GAO-05-621 (September 15, 2005). Their assets grew over 3,500 percent from 1987 to 2004, from $3.8 billion to over $140 billion. Some are now among the largest finance firms. They lend like banks and follow the same safety rules, so their risk to the deposit fund looks much like a bank's.

Their parents face a weaker watchdog, though. The deposit insurer's power over holding companies and sister firms is narrower than a bank supervisor's. That gap is untested in hard times. GAO flags the issue for Congress, noting these charters also ease mixing shops with banking.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-721:
GAO issued GAO-05-721 on July 22, 2005. The report looks at how the Environmental Protection Agency plans staff and funds for Clean Water Act work. Tight budgets at federal and state levels put past gains at risk. GAO asked how far the agency's budget process weighs the size and spread of its workload. It also asked what the agency is doing to plan better.

GAO found that the agency bases budgets mostly on past practice. Year to year shifts are small, even as duties grow and some work moves to states. The agency does not run the deep, bottom-up checks of work and needs that GAO says are called for. New workforce planning steps show promise. But GAO said two agencywide efforts need better coordination. Skill surveys also need to spot gaps more clearly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-821:
Welfare work rates across states are compared in GAO-05-821, issued August 19, 2005. States must show that welfare clients take part in work. The rate decides if a state faces a penalty. State rates for 2003 ran from 9 to 88 percent. GAO asked how states define the work that counts. It checked state controls on the data. And it weighed federal guidance and oversight.

GAO found states define the 12 work classes in clashing ways. Five of 10 states studied count care for a disabled family member. Five do not. Some states changed their definitions, so their rates cannot be compared across years. Controls on reported hours vary just as widely. The federal health department gives limited guidance, GAO said. It urged the department to use its oversight role so the measure means the same thing in every state.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1021:
Alternative mortgage products and their risks fill GAO-06-1021, issued September 19, 2006. These loans let borrowers defer principal or part of interest for the first years. That can lower early payments. Growth in such lending has been rapid. GAO tracked market trends and the risks for borrowers and lenders. It read the disclosures borrowers get. And it covered the regulatory response.

Headings carry the findings. The products' share of new mortgages grew threefold from 2003. Borrowers could face payment shock when deferred sums come due. Most loans are too new to show default results, so the impact stays unclear. Disclosures often fail to state the risks clearly or place them where borrowers will see them, GAO found. Draft joint guidance would tighten lending practice. States in GAO's sample also moved on the risks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-21:
Small town air service and the grants meant to save it are judged in GAO-06-21, dated November 30, 2005. Big legacy airlines face hard times, and low-cost carriers pull riders from small airports. Many small towns struggle to keep decent flight service. Congress set up the Small Community Air Service Development Program in 2000 to help. GAO reviewed how the Transportation Department runs the program.

Early projects show mixed results, as the title says. The department weighed the legal eligibility tests when it picked grant towns. GAO urged it to grade the full program before Congress renews it in 2008. For special Air Service Development Zones, GAO urged a clearer pledge of what support the department will give. The department broadly agreed with the report. It said it would weigh the advice as the program moves forward.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-421:
Data brokers gather personal facts, and agencies buy access to them. In GAO-06-421 (April 4, 2006), GAO checks privacy practice at agencies and resellers. Breaches at resellers had raised concern. GAO studied the Departments of Justice, Homeland Security, and State, plus the Social Security Administration. It asked how each uses personal data from resellers.

GAO measured reseller policies against the Fair Information Practices. Those are widely accepted principles for protecting private data. It checked agency policies the same way. The aim was to see how closely both sides follow the principles. Readers learn where personal data flows. They also see how privacy rules are applied in practice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-521:
Soldiers and citizens abroad vote by mail, and the system to help them grew. In GAO-06-521 (April 7, 2006), GAO reviews absentee voting help for the 2004 general election. The close 2000 presidential race raised concern about such voters. The Defense Department's Federal Voting Assistance Program leads the help. The services and the State Department share the work. GAO had made recommendations in September 2001.

GAO compared help efforts in 2000 and 2004. It checked actions taken on its earlier advice. It also named challenges that remain. Assistance increased for 2004, GAO found. Both departments generally concurred with the report. Readers get a full election case study.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-821:
Safety oversight of rail transit is examined in GAO report GAO-06-821, released on July 26, 2006. Subways, light rail, and streetcars form a vital part of the nation's transport network. States must name oversight agencies to watch safety and security, under rules from the Federal Transit Administration. GAO described how the State Safety Oversight program is designed. GAO also asked what is known about its impact and what might strengthen it.

GAO found that the program was built as a shared effort. The transit agency sets rules and guidance, and state bodies carry out the oversight. Federal agencies and the rail systems themselves also play parts. In practice, the depth of oversight varied. GAO concluded that additional federal leadership would enhance the program. Clearer direction, GAO said, would help states guard riders better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-121:
Federal civilian law enforcement work sits in far more corners of government than most people expect. In report GAO-07-121, dated December 19, 2006, GAO surveyed that workforce. It counted officers in 104 federal civilian components as of June 30, 2006. An officer here could investigate crimes, serve search warrants, make arrests, or carry a firearm. The survey also recorded job series and legal authorities.

The 104 components reported 137,929 law enforcement officers in all. They sat inside 14 departments and 28 other federal entities. Just seven components held 93,263 of the officers, about 68 percent. The Justice Department reported 58,489 officers and Homeland Security reported 49,835. Together those two departments held about 79 percent of the total. The report gives Congress a single roster for a scattered workforce.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-21:
Small fees, taken over a working life, can shrink a 401(k) balance by a wide margin. GAO studied those fees in GAO-07-21, a report dated November 16, 2006. Workers now rely on 401(k) plans for much of their retirement income. GAO sorted the kinds of fees plans charge and who pays them. It reviewed what workers are told about fees. It also checked how the Labor Department watches plan fees.

Investment fees make up most of the total, GAO found. One survey put them at 80 to 99 percent of plan fees. Record-keeping fees come second. Workers pay most investment fees through lower returns. Fee facts reach workers in scattered documents, GAO said. No single statement lets them compare options side by side. The Labor Department lacks the data to police fees well. GAO urged a plain fee summary for every plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-221:
Low-level radioactive waste piles up at hospitals, labs, and power plants that use nuclear material. GAO looked abroad for better ways to manage it in GAO-07-221, issued March 21, 2007. GAO surveyed 18 countries that lead in producing such waste. It compared their methods with U.S. practice. Topics included waste inventories, removal of strong sources, disposal choices, and reserve funds. U.S. regulators and waste firms weighed in as well.

Most surveyed countries keep full national waste databases, GAO found. Fourteen of the 18 move high-activity waste off work sites promptly. Most require used sealed sources to go back to suppliers. Only 3 countries had disposal sites for the strongest waste class. The United States uses these tools less or not at all, GAO said. It asked the nuclear regulator and the Energy Department to judge the foreign methods within a year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-321:
The commission that tends U.S. war cemeteries abroad passed its financial audit with one technology caveat. GAO reported the results in GAO-07-321, dated March 1, 2007. The law charges GAO with auditing the American Battle Monuments Commission. The commission runs 24 military cemeteries and 25 memorials and markers. Most stand on foreign soil. GAO audited fiscal years 2006 and 2005. It checked fair reporting, internal controls, and legal compliance.

The statements were presented fairly, GAO concluded. Controls over financial reporting were effective as of September 30, 2006. Tests found no reportable breaches of the laws checked. One reportable condition remains, tied to computers. User guidance for the foreign staff payroll is lacking. Security and access controls were weak at some sites. A past flaw in property and payable records was fixed in fiscal year 2006. The commission is working on the technology gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-521:
Job help for people with disabilities works better in some states than others, and GAO-07-521, issued May 23, 2007, hunts for the reasons. State rehabilitation agencies coach clients toward work. Many clients draw Social Security disability benefits. A prior GAO report, GAO-05-865, found wide gaps in the job rates states reach for those clients. This study digs into the spread.

GAO merged Social Security and Education Department data and surveyed the state agencies. It asked how earnings results shifted over time. It tested whether state economies, client traits, or agency tactics explain the gaps. Raw league tables mislead, GAO warns, since a weak state economy drags results down. The Education Department's data also lack key facts, such as how severe a client's disability is. GAO renewed its 2005 advice: judge agencies with the economy in view.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-921:
Fuel economy rules for cars and light trucks fill GAO-07-921, dated August 2, 2007. Standards now require 27.5 miles per gallon for cars. Light trucks must reach 22.2 for model year 2007. The safety agency sets and enforces the rules. Makers that miss the mark pay penalties or use credits. A size-based system now governs light trucks. GAO reviewed studies and heard leading experts. It weighed the program's strengths and flaws.

The rules cut oil use but carry dated features, GAO found. Car standards lack the size-based design trucks now use. The agency needs fresher data on new fuel-saving technology. GAO suggested Congress grant matching reform power for cars. It also suggested funds for technology tracking. Flexibility to adjust the program over time matters too. The Transportation Department agreed to weigh the points. The environment agency agreed outright. Energy officials did not comment.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-21:
Efforts to choke off nuclear smuggling networks are reviewed in GAO report GAO-08-21 (October 31, 2007). For decades, the United States has fought networks that supply gear to weapons programs in states such as Pakistan and Iran. GAO focused on seven countries where such activity has been reported. It judged three lines of work.

The United States won a UN resolution and new watch lists for risky technology. Other proposals stalled, though. GAO found weak data on the risks and on what U.S. aid achieves abroad. It told the State Department to run and record regular risk reviews. Enforcement agencies drew parallel advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-221:
Head Start oversight is revisited in GAO report GAO-08-221 (February 12, 2008). About 1,600 local groups run the preschool program with nearly $7 billion in grants. GAO raised doubts about federal oversight in February 2005. The children and families agency promised a risk review of the program. That review still has not come in full.

Data from the yearly grantee survey also remain shaky, GAO found. Site monitoring has improved, with help aimed at struggling groups. Yet risk is not judged across the whole program. GAO made four recommendations. They press for a full risk strategy and better survey data to steer oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-321:
Port-related user fees are the subject of GAO report GAO-08-321, released February 22, 2008. GAO examined the Harbor Maintenance Fee, the Merchandise Processing Fee, and inspection fees charged on air and cruise passengers and commercial vessels. GAO judged the fees against tests of equity, efficiency, revenue adequacy, and administrative burden.

GAO found the fees vary in how rates are set, collected, and reviewed, and they often fail to match the cost of the services they fund. Harbor fee collections have exceeded harbor maintenance spending since 2003, building a large trust fund surplus. Collection delays and weak coordination also raised costs. GAO made eight recommendations to three departments and suggested Congress review the harbor fee link. The agencies generally agreed.
garland-daughter-middle-border-1921:
Garland's Daughter of the Middle Border won the 1922 Pulitzer Prize for biography, a note in this printing stresses. Pictures show his mother Isabel and his wife Zulime Taft, called the new daughter. Book one opens with his first winter in Chicago.

The sequel carries his life from the pioneer boy of the first volume into manhood. Marriage to Zulime Taft and years as a striving writer fill the middle chapters. A return East and a backward look at the frontier close the arc. Issued in 1921, the book crowned the career of the great chronicler of the Middle Border in fitting style.
geley-unconscious-conscious-1921:
Gustave Geley sought the root of strange feats in From the Unconscious to the Conscious, his book of 1921. Geley ran the chief lab for such study in Paris. He holds that man is not a fixed self, but a stream that flows from a deep hid source. That source, pressed, can push out the stuff that forms shapes in the dark room.

His scheme tries to join mind science to the seance. Death, to him, is a shift of the stream, not its end. The book is the creed back of his lab. Its bold reach still draws fans.
graves-truth-about-the-protocols-1921:
Philip Graves, a Times writer in Constantinople, blew the Protocols hoax wide open in three pieces in August 1921. The Times put them in book form in London the same year. The Protocols claimed to be a secret Jewish plan to rule the world, and had spread far.

Graves sets the Protocols side by side with Joly's talk in hell of 1864. Line by line, the fake is shown to be a copy, with names swapped and the rest near word for word. His proof is the key work that named the Protocols a fake for all to see.
hamsun-pan-worster-1921:
Knut Hamsun published Pan in Norway in 1894, and W. W. Worster Englished it for Knopf in 1921. Lieutenant Thomas Glahn spends a summer in a hut in Nordland, hunting and fishing with his dog Aesop. At the trading post he meets Edvarda, the merchant's daughter, and falls into a proud, halting love.

Glahn tells the tale himself, two years later, and his telling keeps slipping. Pride, jealousy, and wild joy in the northern summer drive him to strange acts. Hamsun builds the novel from Glahn's senses: light, scent, blood, and weather. Worster's translation became the classic English Pan. The book stands apart from Hunger and Growth of the Soil as his lyric peak.
hd-hymen-1921:
Hymen, published in 1921, is a collection of poems by H. D., the pen name of Hilda Doolittle, the imagist poet Ezra Pound had launched in London. The title poem is a ritual piece for voices, built like a Greek chorus.

The poems take up marriage, myth, and the gods of Greece, retelling old stories through women's eyes. H. D.'s early imagism, with its hard, clear images, here grows more ceremonial and strange. Sea, heat, and white light run through the verse. The book shows a poet moving from imagist precision toward the mythic scale of her later epics.
heike-monogatari-sadler-1921:
A. L. Sadler translated the whole Heike Monogatari into English in two parts, in 1918 and 1921. The Tale of the Heike is Japan's great medieval war epic, telling the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185. The Taira clan, called the Heike, rises to glittering power, then falls to the Minamoto in five years of civil war.

Blind lute priests first spread the tale, chanting its battles and deaths across Japan. Its opening lines on the bell of impermanence set the Buddhist tone of the whole. Sadler's version, from the Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan, first gave English the complete epic. Pride, loyalty, and the fall of the mighty fill its pages.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle closes his life of Frederick the Great with book twenty-one, Afternoon and Evening of Friedrich's Life, 1763 to 1786. The Seven Years War is won, Prussia stands as a nation, and twenty-three years of peace remain to the king. Carlyle warns that little of this quieter reign belongs to world history in his grand sense.

Rebuilding, law, farming, and the management of a tired kingdom fill these pages instead of battles. Carlyle keeps glancing past 1786 toward the French Revolution he sees ripening in Europe's decay. The volume, and the whole vast biography, ends with an old king's death and a younger historian's thunder about the age coming next.
hobhouse-rational-good-1921:
The Rational Good, published in 1921, is Hobhouse's study in the logic of practice, his fullest statement in ethics. The liberal philosopher asks what makes a good rational: not appetite, not command, but harmony realized through reason.

He defines the good as a harmony of feelings, purposes, and relations that can grow without internal war, and tests pleasure, duty, and perfection against it. Social ethics follows: a rational society is one whose order lets each part develop. The argument is systematic and humane. The book crowns the philosophical side of the New Liberalism Hobhouse had helped to build.
howard-bury-mount-everest-reconnaissance:
The first Everest reconnaissance of 1921 came home with more than maps in 1922. Mount Everest: The Reconnaissance, 1921, the official account led by Charles Howard-Bury, tells the march to the great peak. His party crossed Tibet and probed the routes to the top.

On the high snows they found tracks they could not name, and the report prints the find in plain words. Porters called the maker of the tracks a wild man of the snows. From that report grew the Abominable Snowman of world fame. The book is thus both climbing history and the start of a mystery.
husserl-logische-untersuchungen-1921:
Husserl issued a second edition of his Logical Investigations in the years around 1921, revising the work that had made him famous in 1900. By then he was the master of a movement, and his own thought had moved on through the Ideas of 1913. The new edition let him bring the young breakthrough closer to the mature system.

He rewrote passages, added clarifications, and rethought parts of the sixth investigation in light of his later work. Some sections he left standing, judging them still sound. The result is phenomenology's classic in its definitive form, with the founder's second thoughts visible on the page. Comparing the two editions shows a philosopher arguing with his younger self. The volume is thus a document in the history of his thought, as well as a work of philosophy.
hutton-the-angami-nagas-1921:
John Henry Hutton worked as a colonial administrator in the Naga Hills of Assam, and he wrote about the peoples he governed. His 1921 book studies the Angami Nagas, one of the major groups of those hills, drawing on years of direct contact and local testimony.

Hutton describes village government, kinship, farming, and the great feasts of merit by which men gained honor and standing. He also covers the ancestor cult, omens, and the customs that shaped birth, marriage, and death. The book became a standard source on the Angami and a model of the administrator-ethnography of its period.
hutton-the-sema-nagas-1921:
Hutton wrote this 1921 volume as a companion to his book on the Angami Nagas, turning here to their neighbors the Sema, now often called Sumi. Like its partner, the study grew out of his years as an administrator in the Assam hills.

The account centers on the morung, the bachelors' hall where young men lived and learned tribal custom. Hutton also describes headhunting, warfare, farming, and the feasts that marked rank and wealth. Sema religion, with its spirits, omens, and rites, fills much of the book. Together the two volumes preserve a detailed picture of Naga life in the early twentieth century.
iamblichus-on-the-mysteries-taylor-1821:
Iamblichus wrote On the Mysteries in reply to a sharp foe of rite. Thomas Taylor gave the work English dress in 1821. Iamblichus was a Greek sage of the late Roman age. The book defends theurgy, the work of rites that lift the soul to the gods.

Porphyry had asked how mere rites could move high gods. Iamblichus holds that the gods gave the rites and work through them by their own will. Signs, names, and gifts all take their place in his scheme. The book is the base text for all rite magic of the West since.
il-proteo-metallico-o-sia-delle-trasform:
Fulvio Gherli, a doctor of philosophy and medicine from Modena, published this Italian work in Venice in 1721. Its long title calls it a philosophical, medical, and chemical work. It deals with surface changes in metals and with metal based cures. Gherli also aimed to expose false chemists.

Pages test how acids act on silver and other metals. Vinegar and lemon juice are set against strong waters that dissolve metal. From such tests Gherli draws cures for grave ills of the body. The book shows early chemistry at work in the service of medicine.
j-p-jacobsen-mogens-and-other-stories-19:
Short tales by Jacobsen fill Mogens and Other Stories, given here in the 1921 English version. The title tale tells of young love, fresh and brief as spring. Other tales turn darker, with plague, fear, and death stalking their pages.

Jacobsen polished every sentence until it shone like a cut gem. Few writers in Danish have matched his care for sound, color, and mood. Love and plague sit side by side, beauty and dread in one hand. The book gathers the full range of his short fiction and shows why later writers held his craft in awe.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-21:
Isaac Jogues and his captivity dominate Volume 21, published in 1898. Thwaites covers Quebec and the Hurons in the years of Jogues's ordeal. Mohawk captors seized the priest, tortured him, and held him as a slave for months.

Jogues writes of his pain with a restraint that deepens its horror. Fingers crushed, body scarred, he still seeks chances to teach and baptize. Fellow priests report his calm faith under cruel, daily abuse. Many readers rank his letters the most famous captivity account in the set. A saint's suffering, told in his own quiet and steady words, fills this volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-the-books: Aaron the Bookseller was an Italian dealer in Hebrew and other ancient manuscripts. He flourished at the beginning of the fourteenth century. He spent seven years in Toledo, hunting Arabic and Hebrew books with success. From there he sent the young students of Perugia a catalogue of eighty Hebrew and Arabic manuscripts. Once, in his absence, Immanuel de Romi and friends broke open his book-cases and copied some works in haste. Immanuel then added a bitter satire on Aaron, written as a letter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-121:
Abba is the Aramaic word for father, or my father. With its Greek form it occurs three times in the New Testament. It is a call to God that shows a close, filial bond between the speaker and God. Mark, chapter 14, verse 36, uses it, and Paul uses it for new converts made children of God.

The entry stresses that this use was not new or only Christian. Jewish saints of the time used the same call in prayer. Children in a drought cried to Ḥanan, grandson of Onias, "Abba, give us rain." The old Ḥasidim, too, spent an hour in quiet thought before prayer, to set their hearts toward their Father in heaven.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abel-meholah-da: Abel-meholah is a name found three times in the Old Testament. In Judges, chapter 7, verse 22, Gideon chased the Midianites as far as its lip, near Tabbath. That lip may be the bank at the edge of the Jordan valley. In First Kings, chapter 19, it is the home of Elisha. In chapter 4 of the same book it marks a limit of the district of Baana, one of Solomon's officers. Eusebius and Jerome set it ten Roman miles south of Beth-shean.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abinadab-father: Abinadab is the name of three men in this entry. The first was a man of Kirjath-jearim who kept the Ark in his house for the twenty years after the Philistines gave it back, by First Samuel. The second was the second son of Jesse, one of three brothers who followed Saul to fight the Philistines in the valley of Elah. The third was a son of Saul, killed at Gilboa fighting the Philistines, as Samuel and Chronicles record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abrahamson-augu:
August Abrahamson was a Swedish giver and founder of the Sloid Seminary of Nääs, near Göteborg. He was born on Dec. 29, 1817 at Karlskrona, to parents from Germany, and died on May 6, 1898 at Nääs.

Apprenticed at fourteen to a hardware merchant, he built one of Sweden's largest businesses. He retired in 1868, bought the Nääs estate, and founded free schools there. In 1872 he opened a manual training school for boys, then one for girls in 1874. A teacher training branch followed, led by his nephew Otto Salomon. By his will the seminary gained his whole estate, and students worldwide still train there free in sloid work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-isaac-821: Isaac Adler was an American doctor and teacher of medicine. He was a son of Rabbi Samuel Adler. He was born at Alzey, Germany, in 1849. He came to America in 1857. He finished at Columbia College in 1868. He studied medicine at four German schools and took his degree at Heidelberg in 1871. From 1875 he served as a visiting doctor at the German Hospital in New York. In 1892 he took a chair at the New York Polyclinic school. His papers treat points of the doctor's craft.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-jannu:
Alexander Jannaeus, also called Jonathan, was king of Judea. He was born about 126 B.C. and died in 76 B.C. He was the third son of John Hyrcanus. He came to the throne in 102 B.C. His brother Aristobulus had kept him in prison. The widowed queen Salome freed him, and he married her, though she was thirteen years his elder. He took the high priest's office as well.

His whole aim was to make Judea great and strong. His first campaign struck at Ptolemais. Ptolemy Lathurus landed an army to save the town. Alexander dealt with him in bad faith, and paid for it. Ptolemy took Asochis on a Sabbath, with 10,000 prisoners. At Azophon on the Jordan he crushed Alexander's whole army. The dead were hacked apart and boiled in caldrons, so men thought the victors were cannibals. Only Egypt's own troubles saved Judea then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-algeria-1221:
Algeria sits on the coast of North Africa. The entry traces Jewish life there across many rulers. Carthage, Rome, and the Ottoman Turks all held the land in turn. Jews were present from the first centuries of the common era. Old grave stones with Latin names point that way.

Later waves came from Spain in the seventh century. Some Berber tribes took up the Jewish faith, the entry reports. Under Arab rule Jews paid set taxes and faced dress limits. The long entry runs into the French period. It closes with notes on the Jewish press and late strife.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-altar-jonas-jon: Jonas Altar, also called Jonathan ha-Levi, was a Bohemian rabbi. He was born in 1755. He died on March 25, 1855, in Goltsch-Jenikau. He stood for the strictest form of the old faith. A pamphlet of his shows that stance well. It came out in Prague in 1826. In it he fought Aaron Chorin on one point of rite. He held that the head must stay covered at prayer. He also wrote pieces for a weekly paper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amora-plural-am:
Amora is a word that means the speaker. It came from a verb that means to say or speak. In one sense it names a hall officer. That officer stood at the side of the teacher. He spoke out loud what the teacher said in a low voice. He gave the sense in Aramaic for the crowd.

In a wide sense it names a whole age of teachers. That age ran from the death of Judah I in 219. It ran to the close of the Babylonian Talmud about 500. Those teachers spent their work on the Mishnah. Schools in Pumbedita won fame for sharp debate. A jest says they could thread an elephant through a needle's eye.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-angelology-1521:
Angelology is the branch of theology that treats of angels. Angels, from a Greek word for messenger, are beings above humans who dwell in heaven. They reveal God's will to people and carry out his commands, the entry explains. Belief in them runs through Jewish history from its earliest stages.

To survey that long history, the entry uses three periods: biblical, Talmudic and Midrashic, and medieval. It notes that Jewish teaching on angels never became one fixed system, unlike Catholic doctrine. In the Bible the word for angel first means simply a messenger. It gains the fuller sense when joined with God's name, as in angel of the Lord.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antonio-hector-: Hector Antonio was the brother of Diogo Antonio and agent of the Portuguese Maranos in Rome about the middle of the sixteenth century. He was sent to settle his brother's accounts. He also carried a complaint to Pope Paul III against the chief inquisitor, Cardinal-Infante Don Henrique. The Portuguese ambassador at the Vatican pressed for the fugitive Marano's arrest at once. The pope's own intercession saved him. Even so, the entry says, his work for his suffering brethren brought no success.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arsaces-1821: Arsaces, a Parthian king, is held by some scholars to be the sixth king of that name. First Maccabees tells how he trapped Demetrius, who had rebelled against him. Demetrius married a daughter of Arsaces and, by Josephus's account, died in captivity. The same king appears in First Maccabees chapter 15 among the rulers to whom Rome sent its edict forbidding the persecution of the Jews. He is also known as Mithridates I.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-anshel-be: Asher Anshel ben Moses Baer was a Talmudist who lived in the second half of the eighteenth century. Two of his works are named, both printed at Furth in 1785. Ben Emunim, Son of Faith, is a homiletic commentary on the Bible, built of sermons and readings. Hiddat Shimshon, Samson's Riddle, is a work on ethics, divided into three parts. The entry gives no birthplace, no teacher, and no death date for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auerbach-leopol:
Leopold Auerbach was a German physician and biologist. He was born at Breslau on April 27, 1828, and died there on Sept. 30, 1897. He studied at Breslau, Leipsic, and Berlin, and took his doctorate in 1849. The next year he began medical practice in Breslau. At the same time he studied tissue and nerve disease under Purkinje.

Auerbach taught at Breslau University from 1863. For the last quarter century of his life he held the chair of general biology and histology there. His fame rests on his work on the cell. His "Organologische Studien" of 1874 treats the build and life of the cell nucleus and the first stages of the fertilized egg. The entry credits him with showing that the nucleus is not dissolved in cell division but reshaped. He also found that the nuclei of oval eggs rotate in joining, and he uncovered the cell structure of the capillaries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ayas-leon-1021: Leon Ayas served as an interpreter for the French army in Algeria. He worked in the campaign against Abd-el-Kader and died in 1846. He took several wounds in the expeditions around Oran. In one of them he captured a lieutenant of Abd-el-Kader. At the battle against the Bou-Maza he showed special bravery. At a sharp moment of the fight he killed five Arabs. He was wounded in that action, and he died of those wounds the following year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azov-turkish-az:
Azov is a town in the government of Ekaterinoslav, Russia. It stands on the left bank of the Don, about twenty-four miles from Rostov and five miles from the sea. In old times, as Tanais, it was a Greek trade center. Mithridates took it in 115 B.C. The Huns wrecked it in the fourth century, and the Chazars held it after its rebuilding in the eighth.

Jews have lived in Azov since early times, probably from the first century B.C. Under the Chazars they traded between Azov, Constantinople, and the Russian towns. The entry quotes a note in a Pentateuch written at Azov in the year 1274. A sick man named Shabbethai gave that Bible to the Karaite synagogue in the Crimea. Of 25,488 people in Azov in 1892, about 600 were Jews. They had a synagogue and a Talmud Torah school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-babylon-lxx-b-1:
Babylon was the chief city of Babylonia. For long ages it was the capital of the kingdom and empire that ruled the Tigris and Euphrates valley. Its native names include Babu-ili, gate of God, and Tintir, seat of life. Hebrew tradition groups it with Erech, Accad, and Calneh, and so gives it great age. No native record, the entry notes, tells how the city began.

The ruins lie about fifty miles south of Bagdad, on the east bank of the Euphrates. They stretch five miles from north to south. One great mound, called Babil, covers 120,000 square feet and rises 64 feet high. Water works found beneath it point to the famed hanging gardens. In Genesis the city appears twice: once among the cities of Shinar, and once in the tale of the confused tongues. After the fall of Samaria it fades from the Hebrew story for a time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-badis-muzaffar-:
Badis, oldest son of King Habus of Granada, took the throne in 1038. Berbers who wanted his younger brother Bologguin as king fought him. Arabs and his vizier Samuel ibn Nagdela backed Badis and won. Once secure, though, Badis feared an Arab plot and planned to have the Arabs of his capital slain at Friday prayer in the mosque.

His new vizier, Joseph ibn Nagdela, had to swear to keep the plan secret. He still warned several noble Arab families to stay away that Friday, and few Arabs came. Badis first blamed Joseph, then agreed the warning had been wise. The entry ends grimly: Joseph was later murdered, four thousand Jews died with him, and Badis himself was poisoned soon after.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bamah-2421: Bamah is a Hebrew word that ordinarily means a "high place." The entry is a single short note on one verse, Ezekiel xx. 29. There the word serves as a general name for a place of idol worship. Ezekiel plays on the word, the entry says, as if it were built from "ba" (come) and "mah" (whereunto). On that reading, a bamah is a place people come to for worship. Readers are sent to the article on high places for the larger subject.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barfat-2521: Barfat is a name used by Jews in Provence and northern Spain. A Barfat certifies as witness in an agreement between Pedro II of Aragon and the Knights of St. Jean. A Niçak Barfat appears in Spain in 1346. Isaac ben Sheshet and his brother Don Crescas also bore the surname. Of many etymologies, the entry favors Bloch's: it should read "Berfet," shortened from "Perfetto," the equivalent of "Shallum." In Hebrew it is sometimes written "Parfat." Gross connects it with "Profiat," though that name is nowhere a family name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bashuysen-heinr:
Heinrich Jacob Bashuysen was a Christian printer of Hebrew books and an Orientalist. He was born at Hanau, Prussia, on Oct. 26, 1679 and died about 1750. Between 1709 and 1712 he set up a printing house in Hanau that issued over 100 works.

Bashuysen printed Abravanel on the Pentateuch and turned parts of Maimonides and rabbinic comment on the Psalms into other tongues. He taught Oriental languages and theology at Hanau, then led the school at Zerbst from 1716. He belonged to academies in Berlin and London. He also planned a full rendering of Maimonides and a larger history of the teachers of the Mishnah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bedarrides-gust:
Gustave Emanuel Bédarrides was a French magistrate born at Aix-les-Bains on Feb. 20, 1817. He entered court service in 1840 at Aix and rose step by step through posts there. In 1862 he went to Bastia as chief prosecutor.

From 1864 Bédarrides served at the Court of Cassation in Paris, rising to head a chamber in 1877. Age barred him from the court's top post in 1890, but he retired with an honorary title. He also led the central consistory of French Jews as its vice-president from 1872 until his death in 1899. He held the rank of commander of the Legion of Honor, as the entry notes at its close.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belkovsky-grego:
Gregoire Belkovsky was a Russian writer on political economy, born at Odessa in 1865. As a student he joined the Jewish nationalists of that city and lectured at a free Sabbath school. A prize treatise won him a gold medal at the university.

Belkovsky finished his degree in 1889 but refused a professorship tied to baptism. From 1893 he lectured at Sofia, in Bulgaria, and published books there on Roman law and banking. He spread Zionist teaching in print and in person. By 1899 he sat on the movement's larger action committee for Russia. On the Jewish question he wrote in favor of farm colonies as schools of productive labor for his people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benedetti-salva:
Salvatore de Benedetti, an Italian scholar, was born on April 18, 1818, at Novara and died on Aug. 4, 1891, at Pisa. Since public schools in Italy were closed to Jews, he studied at a college in Vercelli meant mainly for future rabbis. He chose teaching and journalism instead of the ministry.

After bold work for the Mazzini faction in 1848, he turned to science and letters. From 1862 he taught Hebrew at the University of Pisa until his death. His books include a life of Moses drawn from legend and a translation of Judah ha-Levi's poems.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bequest-3021:
Bequest means a gift of personal property left in a last will. The entry sets Jewish law beside modern English and American law on that theme. Unlike modern law, Jewish law draws no firm line between gifts of land and gifts of goods. It also allows an oral bequest to stand as valid.

A key rule holds that the words of a sick man count as if written and handed over. The entry then defines degrees of sickness, and the split between a sick-bed gift and a death-bed gift. It works through what happens when a man gives all he owns or keeps a part back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-arbel-1721: Beth-Arbel appears only once in the Bible. Hosea names it as a city destroyed by Shalman. The entry weighs rival views of both names. Its favored site is modern Irbid. That lies east of the Jordan. Shalman has been read in several ways. Schrader made him a Moabite king. Conder favored Shalmaneser III. Others chose Shalmaneser IV. The Greek version suggests a different reading. It gives Beth-Jeroboam and Shallum instead. That would point to Shallum's fall of Jeroboam's house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bethany-b-3221: Bethany is a place named in the Gospels. It does not appear in the Old Testament. John puts it near Jerusalem. He says it was about fifteen furlongs away. Jerome set it at the second mile-post. The site is the village El-Azariyeh. It climbs the Mount of Olives' southeastern slopes. Its Arabic name preserves "Lazarium." Christians sometimes called Bethany by that name. The village is a small green oasis. Its figs may have given Bethany its name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-birth-new-3321:
New Birth means the renewal of a man's nature. Sin's impurity is cast aside. The man becomes a righteous child of God. Ezekiel first voiced the idea, the entry says. He promised a new heart and spirit. Washing rites suggested the image of change. Naaman emerged from the Jordan like a child.

The Rabbis called such a person a new creature. A proselyte counted as new-born in law. His old family ties no longer held. The entry argues Paul borrowed this doctrine. Jesus' words to Nicodemus rest on it too. Baptism gave the Jewish idea a new form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blum-julius-als: Julius Blum, called Blum Pasha, was a financier. He was born at Budapest in 1843. In 1869 he directed the Austro-Egyptian bank. Alexandria was its seat. In 1877 Egypt made him finance state secretary. The khedive appointed him that year. Two years later he became finance minister. He was also raised to pasha then. He held the ministry until 1890. Then Vienna's Credit-Anstalt took him as director. Many orders decorate his record. They include the K.C.B. and the Legion of Honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonafos-menahem: Menahem ben Abraham Bonafos, also called Bonafoux Abraham of Perpignan, was a French philosopher. He worked at the end of the fourteenth century and the start of the fifteenth. His book Sefer ha-Gedarim explains technical terms in Hebrew works on philosophy, ethics, and medicine. It draws at times on Arabic and Greek. Editions came out at Salonica in 1567 and at Berlin in 1798.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bone-bona-arabi:
Bône, called Beled el-Anab in Arabic, is a town in the province of Constantine, Algeria. The Romans knew it as Hippo Regius. Jews lived there in the first centuries of the common era, as tombstones nearby attest.

Under pagan Rome local Jews held full freedom. Persecution began in the fourth century, when the city became Augustine's see. Vandals destroyed Bône in 431, and Arabs rebuilt it in the seventh century. Almohade pressure later drove many Jews east or forced conversion. Exiles from Spain swelled the community in the fifteenth century. It held 1,000 souls when the entry was written.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bristol-3721:
Bristol is a commercial seaport city in Gloucester and Somerset, England. Jews settled there very early. The city was a center of the slave trade between England and Ireland till 1172.

Eighteen Bristol Jews of the twelfth century are known by name. Moses of Bristol, father of a noted author, leads that list here. In 1210 King John extorted 10,000 marks from a Bristol Jew, Abraham. The king's men pulled the victim's teeth one by one till he paid, the chronicle says. The Jewry stood on the quay, with its synagogue in Small street. From the mid-eighteenth century a congregation grew again and won able ministers in time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calendar-hebrew:
Calendar, in the Hebrew sense, is a system for arranging the days of the year. The Jewish day runs from evening to evening, after the order of the Creation account. The entry repeats that rule from Exodus and Leviticus. It also sorts the word day into two senses: a full span of twenty four hours, and the light part alone.

Long middle sections work through dawn and twilight terms, months, and festival dating. Rules for fixing new moons and leap months rest on both sighting and reckoning. At the end come dense tables. They match Hebrew months against common year dates, row by row, for many year types. The piece serves as a working table, not just a history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carcas-4021: Carcas was one of the seven chamberlains who served King Ahasuerus in the book of Esther. The king ordered them to bring Queen Vashti before him, as Esther tells it in its first chapter. The Septuagint gives a different name for him. The Targum explains five of the seven names as symbols but leaves Zethar and Carcas without a gloss. The entry is only a few lines long. Nothing else is told of Carcas, his office, or his fate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castel-sarassin: Castel-Sarassin is the chief town of the department of Tarn-et-Garonne, in France. A fairly important Jewish community lived there in the Middle Ages. When the Pastoureaux attacked in 1320, the Jews, rather than fall into enemy hands, killed one another. Only two survived the first slaughter, and they then threw themselves from the tower. One source puts the martyrs at 200. Grätz, following Latin works that place the scene at Verdun, held 500 to be nearer the truth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cattle-hebrew-p:
Cattle is a term for all domestic animals. Such animals were the chief wealth of nomadic and pastoral peoples. They mattered greatly in early Hebrew life. Abel kept sheep, and Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were shepherds in the full sense. Their herds gave them tents, clothing, and food, plus material for sacrifices.

After settlement in the promised land, Israelites kept herding beside farming. Some tribes, such as Reuben, Gad, and Simeon, stayed pastoral. The stock of Israel was chiefly sheep and goats, horned cattle, and asses. Camels and horses were not common in Bible times. Horned cattle thrived only in well-watered spots, like the Jordan valley and Bashan. Scripture also commands kindness to animals, the entry notes. God gave man rule over them, along with care for them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chicago-israeli: Chicago Israelite, The, was an American weekly newspaper devoted to Jewish interests. It was founded in January 1885. Leo Wise edited it first and for several years ran a personal department called Notes and Comments. Emil Hirsch, Levi Eliel, and Julius Wise at times did that work in his place. Julius Wise wrote under the pen name Nickerdown. The paper made a feature of local news. It covered the congregations, lodges, and aid and other societies of its city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-climation-or-ac:
Climation, or acclimatization, means how a person adapts to a new climate, and the entry treats it as a live question for statesmen. Moving to a strange land reshapes the whole body, Virchow showed, and the change reaches later generations too. Could Europeans settle the tropics, stay healthy, and keep their kind there? That was the puzzle.

Jews supply the best test case, the entry argues. They live and hold their identity in nearly every climate on earth. Writers quoted praise their ease in hot and cold lands alike, from Surinam to Malabar. Figures from Algiers back the claim. Sober and temperate living gets part of the credit, and a trace of Semitic blood is said to help other nations adapt as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-hermann-l-:
Hermann L. Cohn, a German ophthalmologist, was born at Breslau on June 4, 1838. He studied chemistry and physics at Heidelberg under Bunsen, Kirchhoff, and Helmholtz, taking a philosophy doctorate in 1860. Medicine followed at Breslau and Berlin, with a medical degree in 1863. He settled in Breslau as an eye doctor in 1866.

His life work grew from one finding: many German schoolchildren needed glasses early. He traced the harm to the schools themselves. His 1867 study examined the eyes of 10,060 schoolchildren and proposed fixes for lighting and desks. Books on school hygiene followed for decades, plus a study of 50,000 Breslau pupils in 1899. Nearly 250 essays came from his pen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-constantine-anc:
Constantine, the ancient Cirta, is a city in Algeria and capital of its department. It was once the capital of Numidia. Grave inscriptions show Jews living there in the first centuries of the common era. Rome held the city until the Arab conquest of 710, and many Jews likely left in the fifth century for freer towns under the Vandals.

Peace lasted from the Arab conquest to the mid-twelfth century, then Almohad persecution came. Spanish rule from 1509 to 1555 brought severe suffering. Under Turkish beys the community shared the common Algerian lot. A muqaddam and council governed it. Under France it became a consistory seat for eight towns. The district counts 6,800 Jews, with 3,321 in Constantine itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cowen-laurence-: Laurence Cowen, originally Cohen, was a journalist and politician born at Hull in 1865. He reached London in 1888 and joined the staff of Ariel, Israel Zangwill's paper. Later he founded the journals Commerce and Finance and edited both. His firm, the Columbus Company, owned those papers and The Topical Times. He founded the Article Club for leading makers. Servia gave him the Knight Commander's Cross of the Order of Takovo in 1899. In Oct., 1900, he lost a bid for Coventry as a Liberal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cymbals-4821:
Cymbals are musical instruments of percussion, known to most nations of antiquity. They marked time for dances, singers, and other players. In the Bible they sound at religious ceremonies above all. Levites were set apart as cymbalists. The metal was brass, or copper with a little silver, to judge from a pair found in an Egyptian tomb. Sizes varied widely. Psalm verses distinguish high-sounding cymbals from loud ones.

One pair served in the Temple, the article notes. A special officer, Ben Arza, had charge of them. His stroke gave the Levites their signal to chant the psalms. Repairs could spoil the tone, the Talmud warns. Yet the sound carried far, and the memory of it lasted. Arab practice, with large cymbals for worship and small ones for dance, is set beside the Bible picture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dessauer-leopol:
Leopold Dessauer, known on stage as Ludwig Dessoir, was a German actor born at Posen on December 15, 1810, the son of a Jewish merchant. He made his début in 1825 in his home town. After years of travel he reached the Leipsic Stadttheater in 1834, then Breslau, Prague, and Vienna. From 1847 he played in Berlin, with few breaks, until 1872.

Many ranked Dessoir above his great rival Dawison, despite a plain figure and a weak voice. His Othello, first played at Berlin on October 6, 1849, and his Lear, Shylock, and Hamlet were called classical creations. His private life was bitter: his second wife went mad after their child's death. He died in Berlin on December 30, 1874.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deuteronomy-502:
Deuteronomy is the fifth book of the Pentateuch, called Debarim, or Words, in Hebrew from its opening phrase. Its English name comes from the Septuagint and rests on a mistranslation, the entry explains. A phrase meaning a copy of this law was read as this second law. Yet the name fits, since the book repeats many earlier laws in new form beside much new matter.

The book consists mainly of speeches that Moses is shown giving just before his death, across the Jordan. The first speech reviews the travels in the wilderness and urges Israel not to forget God. The long second speech, running through chapter 26, sets out the laws Israel must keep in the Promised Land, and the spirit in which to keep them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dishon-5221: Dishon is a name borne by two men in the Genesis lists of Seir's line. The first Dishon was a son of Seir and a head of the aboriginal Idumean tribes. The second was a son of Anah and grandson of Seir. He was also a brother of Aholibamah, the second wife of Esau. The entry cites Genesis xxxvi and First Chronicles i for both men, and notes a list of the second Dishon's sons in Genesis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dreyfus-samuel-: Samuel Dreyfus was rabbi of Mülhausen, Alsace, who died in June 1870. He was among the first pupils, one of the first matriculates, of the rabbinical school of Metz. The entry calls him an excellent Hebraist and preacher. He hoped to rise to chief rabbi but never did, and felt the miss keenly. He published several works and wrote for L'Univers Israélite. He also founded a monthly, Le Lien, which failed and was soon given up.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ed-witness-5421: Ed, meaning witness, is a name the English versions give an altar east of the Jordan. The entry says the name is not in the Hebrew text or the Septuagint. Those texts say only that Reuben's and Gad's children called the altar a witness. The altar was to show that the Lord is God, binding both banks of the river. The entry thinks the altar's true name fell out by a copyist's slip. Dillmann proposed Gal-ed, the name found in Genesis, as the lost word.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-5521:
Eleazar is a name borne by many men in the Bible and later Jewish history. The entry treats them in turn, and the first is the weightiest. This Eleazar was the third son of Aaron and became high priest. His two elder brothers died after offering strange fire. Eleazar then took charge of the oil, the incense, and the inner sanctuary. Before Aaron died, Eleazar was clothed in his father's garments.

Later parts take up the other men of the name. One Eleazar ranks among the three chief captains of David's army. Another, a son of Mattathias, died at Bet-Zekaryah in 162 B.C. He crept under a war elephant and speared it, and the beast fell on him. The entry also names a priest who guarded the Temple treasure. In a famed tale he gave Crassus a gold beam to save the rest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-embden-emden-57: Embden is a family name drawn, most likely, from Emden. The entry traces the lines of that family across Europe. One Carl Adam Emden rose high in a prince's service. He was made a noble in the year 1791. Henry Heine wed a woman of the family in time. The poet's wife Henriette was an Embden by birth. Kin of the name held rich farms in Surinam as well. Students of the name show up at Leyden across the years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-evil-merodach-5:
Evil-merodach, son of Nebuchadnezzar, was the third ruler of the New Babylonian empire. He reigned from 561 to 560 B.C. His Babylonian name, Amil-Marduk, means man or servant of Marduk. No inscriptions of his reign have been found. Only the Hebrew Bible and Berosus speak of him, the entry says.

The Bible tells that in his first year he freed the captive King Jehoiachin. He seated him at his table, dressed him as a king, and raised him above other captive kings. Berosus, by contrast, says he ruled unjustly and lewdly. A party at court soon deposed him. He was killed on the order of Neriglissar, his brother-in-law, who took the throne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-execution-13021:
Execution here means carrying a court's judgment into effect in civil cases, and the entry follows the Shulhan Aruk's order of steps. After judgment for a debt, the debtor in town is told first and given time to seek a fresh trial. The court then waits through a set run of Mondays and Thursdays. A writ called petihah places him under the lesser ban for ninety days.

Those ninety days rest on a kind guess: thirty to seek a loan, thirty to sell property, thirty for the buyer to raise the price. On further default a second writ, adrakta, orders seizure of the debtor's land. His bond is then torn up. Judgments for goods or land skip the ninety-day delay. The entry closes with the forms the writs take.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-faria-juan-de-6: Juan de Faria was a Marrano poet, and the entry about him is only two sentences long. While living at Brussels in 1672, he wrote a poem honoring his friend Miguel de Barrios and his book Coro de las Musas. Barrios, in turn, called Faria and Aaron Dormido the nightingales of the Mosaic nest. That phrase is quoted from Barrios's Relacion de los Poetas, the entry's sole source. No birth, death, homeland, or other work is given for Faria in the text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-finder-of-prope:
Finder of property is a legal entry on lost and found goods in Jewish law. One who finds and picks up lost goods gains a special right in them. That right holds against all but the true owner. Scripture lays a duty on the finder. He must seek out the owner and give the goods back. The duty is stated first for lost cattle, then for all lost things.

Later parts set out how goods are taken up and held. They cover lost deeds, which in some cases must not be given back. They tell how a find must be announced and cared for. Rules follow for beasts, money, and books while they wait for an owner. The close deals with proof of ownership and with finds owned by non-Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-finland-6121:
Finland was a Russian grand duchy and had once been part of Sweden. Its Jewish population was small and stood in an odd legal place. Old Swedish rules let Jews hold synagogues in only a few large cities. Those rules gave Jews no right to live in Finland for good. Still, a census of 1885 counted 973 Jews there. Most lived in Helsingfors.

Laws on passports let Jews travel and trade but not settle in country districts. A decree of 1858 let retired Russian soldiers and sailors reside in Finland. Jews held that it covered them too. Rules of 1894 let domiciled Jews trade in three towns. In 1895 there were about 120 Jewish families, mostly artisans and small traders.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-folz-hans-6221:
Hans Folz was a German playwright and physician of the fifteenth century. He is said to have been born at Worms. Records name him as a barber-surgeon at Nuremberg. Folz wrote many farces and Shrove Tuesday plays. In them he brought in Jewish figures, mostly for comic effect. Their parts are usually made ridiculous and contemptible. One play contrasts the religion of Talmud and Midrash with Christianity, to the latter's gain.

That play holds a garbled form of the Adon 'Olam hymn, sung by its Jewish figures. The entry calls it the oldest German rendering of the prayer in rime. Another farce turns on a student who wins a Jewish maiden and then mocks her parents and faith. Folz also wrote on Adam and Eve in 1480 and a rimed dispute of 1479. He was a forerunner and master of Hans Sachs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankl-grun-ado:
Adolf Frankl-Grün was an Austrian rabbi born at Ungarisch-Brod, Moravia, on January 21, 1847. He was schooled in his home town, at Leipnik, and at Eisenstadt. At Eisenstadt he taught Hebrew at a rabbinical school. He then studied at Breslau and Jena and at the Breslau seminary. In 1877 he took a doctor's degree from Jena and his rabbinical degree from Breslau.
