McManus and co-authors published a study in 2023 on germ films that grow in the lungs. The germ in question lives in soil and water, often in slimy films of cells. It can infect people whose lungs or defenses are weak. Labs grow the films in distinct ways, and it was not known if the films match.

The team grew films by two methods and compared them side by side. One method took four weeks in a salt broth. The other took one day with a chemical trigger. The films differed in look and in the glue that holds them together. Both held a plant-like fiber and both resisted two strong drugs. Cells inside the films died at far lower rates than free cells. The authors say growth method shapes the film, but some traits are shared.
pmc-10748121:
Tahesin Samira Delwar and colleagues present a radar transmitter design in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Radar use is spreading in cars and sensors, raising demand for strong transmitter front-ends. Their design works at twenty-four gigahertz, a common radar band. It is built in a standard sixty-five nanometer chip process. The front-end joins an up-conversion mixer with a power amplifier.

The mixer lifts a low input signal to the radar band using a local oscillator tone. Its design adds a second signal path to improve linearity, so the output stays clean. The paper walks through the design choices and their trade-offs. Such front-ends sit at the heart of compact radar units. The work should interest radio engineers who build sensing and safety systems for vehicles.
pmc-10750421:
Fakher Rahim and colleagues review gut-targeted supplements for autism spectrum disorder. Their meta-analysis and umbrella review appeared in twenty twenty-three. Interest in the gut-brain link has grown quickly in autism care. Probiotics, prebiotics, and combined synbiotics are the interventions tested.

Thousands of records were screened for controlled trials. Trials covered young children through adults with autism diagnoses. Ten studies reported on autism-related behaviour symptoms. Results were pooled across supplement types and age groups. Safety data were reviewed alongside behaviour outcomes. Evidence remains mixed and based on small samples overall. The review gives families a cautious summary of current claims.
pmc-10753721:
Melek Ayadi and co-authors compare natural fibers for building insulation panels in this 2023 study. Green building goals push the search for plant-based insulation. The team characterized fibers from seagrass and alfa grass in depth. Hemp, the standard natural fiber, served as the benchmark. Anatomy, microstructure, and chemistry were all measured. Porosity and heat breakdown behavior were part of the panel.

Density measures rounded out the physical picture. Such traits decide how a fiber panel traps heat. Seagrass washes ashore in heaps, so use would valorize waste. Alfa grass is abundant around the Mediterranean. The study asks whether either can replace synthetic insulation. It is a materials characterization paper. Results feed panel makers' material choices.
pmc-10754021:
Shihui Hou, Jie Yang, Fei Xiao, and Huanzi Dai published a 2023 case report on a patient whose kidneys and heart were attacked at once after a streptococcal infection. Strep infections commonly trigger acute kidney inflammation. Heart damage after strep usually means rheumatic fever, a different disease. This patient developed both kidney inflammation and non-rheumatic heart muscle inflammation together, a combination rarely reported.

The authors argue the pair forms a cardiorenal syndrome driven by the immune response to the bacterium, one storm hitting two organs. Treatment combined antibiotics with immune-suppressing therapy, and the patient recovered well. Single cases cannot prove a mechanism, but they can name a pattern for others to recognize. The report urges doctors to check the heart when kidneys fail after strep, and the kidneys when the heart does. Understanding this post-streptococcal syndrome, they write, is the route to earlier diagnosis and treatment.
pmc-10755621:
Steven Kozlowski and co-authors compare uptake of biosimilar drugs between two forms of Medicare in this 2023 study. Biosimilars are near copies of costly biologic drugs and can widen access while cutting cost. Forty were approved in the United States by early 2023. Managed Medicare plans have tools, like prior approval, that may push use toward cheaper options.

Using claims and encounter data from 2015 to 2022, the team tracked twenty biosimilars across seven product types. Uptake ran higher in Medicare Advantage than in traditional Medicare for six of the seven types. The typical edge was about thirty percent higher share. One cancer drug went the other way, and its case is examined closely. The study maps how plan design shapes the spread of lower-cost drug copies.
pmc-10773921:
Huihui Li and co-authors read the gene activity of piglets struck by a deadly diarrhea virus to learn why some die and others resist. Their study appeared in 2023. Twelve Min piglets, taken before their first milk, were split into infected and control groups. Eight received the virus at three days old; four of them died within days, while four survived. The team measured virus levels across the gut and sequenced gene activity in the small intestine of each group.

Dying piglets carried far more virus and worse gut damage than the resistant ones. The gene profiles separated the groups sharply, pointing to immune and gut-barrier pathways that differ between death and survival. The authors say these response signatures could guide breeding or treatment against a disease that costs pig farms heavily.
pmc-10777221:
Mario Villasenor leads a team with a tracheostomy emergency case. Their case from twenty twenty-three deals with a cannot ventilate event. A set share of tracheostomy patients face major complications.

A young adult with brain injury came for a bladder scope. He had repeat urine infections as the reason. During anesthesia start, he desaturated and air stopped moving. Chest compressions ran while the tube was pulled. He was intubated by mouth with a video scope. The removed tube held a mucus plug turned crystal. A checklist and emergency pathway are urged.
pmc-10792721:
Raj Yadav and four colleagues measure how common hernia is among surgery patients at a large care center, in a twenty twenty-three study. Records covered two years of admissions, more than two thousand patients in all. Hernia is one of the most frequent reasons for surgical admission and lost function. The team counted cases and sorted them by type and urgency.

Hernia made up about twelve percent of admissions. Groin hernia was by far the most common type, at over two thirds. About one in eight hernias was stuck and could not be pushed back. High blood pressure was the most frequent extra illness. The authors urge early diagnosis and repair to cut harm.
pmc-10800921:
Cheng Liang and co-authors wrote a study, dated 2023 in its text, on the resistant starch in rice and the genes that set its level. Resistant starch escapes digestion, trims calorie uptake, and helps guard against diabetes. Rice feeds half the world, so raising its resistant share could matter widely. The team grew seventy-two rice lines with mid to high amylose and measured three forms of the trait: in raw milled rice, in hot cooked rice, and in cooled, set rice.

Each form varied widely and answered to a different mix of starch-making genes. One master gene, Waxy, mattered for all three and ruled the cooked and cooled forms. Gene activity peaked about seventeen days after flowering, a window flagged for breeding. Long starch chains and mid-size granules favored the cooled form. The map gives breeders targets for healthier rice.
pmc-10824321:
Katia Boniface, a solo author, reviews how vitiligo starts and grows. The review deals with a long term autoimmune skin disease. Skin loses its color cells, called melanocytes, in patches.

How the disease works is now a hot field of study. Cross talk among skin, fiber, and immune cells is mapped. Signs that lead to loss of color cells are set out. Resident memory T cells play a key part in return of patches. New cure paths grow from this clearer picture. The review is a story form sum of the field.
pmc-10840421:
Meiyu Zhang and co-authors published this study, whose text is dated 2023, on early puberty in girls. Some girls' puberty races fast and needs prompt care, but telling fast from slow forms takes months of watching. The team sought blood marks that split the kinds early. They followed 121 girls with early breast growth and sorted them after six months into fast, slow, and benign groups.

A base level of luteinizing hormone ran higher in the fast group, while a carrier protein for sex hormones ran lower. Set cut points on the two marks caught most fast cases with fair accuracy. The fast group also stood taller in bone age and body mass. The authors say the two cheap blood tests can flag girls who need swift care, sparing others long watch-and-wait.
pmc-10903321:
Myeong-Hun Bae studies how exercise lifts school life satisfaction in Korean children and teens, and what carries the effect, in work from 2023. Happy school life feeds learning and mental health. Exercise is a plausible lever, but the paths from sport to satisfaction differ by age.

A national survey from 2020 gave data on about twenty-nine hundred children and fifty-seven hundred teens. A path model tested three middle factors: body health awareness, self-esteem, and depression. All direct and indirect paths mattered in both groups. Children scored higher on every measure. Some paths ran stronger in teens, others in children. The author draws age-tuned advice for schools.
pmc-10976621:
Behavior analysis began with simple learning through direct consequences, but its reach now extends to language itself. Krystyna Pomorska and Paweł Ostaszewski trace that growth in a 2023 article, focusing on a framework that explains how words gain meaning through learned relations. Skinner laid groundwork for studying language, yet only this century could analysts explain how a stimulus can change function without any direct training.

Working with that generalized relational responding lets therapists analyze and shift behaviors once outside their scope. The authors describe newer tools built on these frames and expect the approach to keep opening new populations and problems to behavioral therapy.
pmc-10994621:
Ali Hadi Sabhan compared two ways to treat stones in the ureter, the tube that carries urine from the kidney, in a study published in 2023. One group had a stent placed first and the stone removed weeks later. The other group had the stone removed at once, with no stent placed first.

The study covered 126 patients, split between the two groups. Both groups had near the same surgery time, hospital stay, and rate of clear scans after care. Small problems were rare in both groups and were handled well. Sabhan concludes that removing the stone at once is safe and works as well as the delayed route. That can spare patients an extra step and its side effects.
pmc-11532321:
Alberto Vandenbulcke and co-authors discuss surgery for a rare benign tumor of the neck in a 2024 article. Chondromas are cartilage growths that can form in the channels where nerves leave the spine. When they press on a nerve or the spinal cord, removal becomes necessary, but the route in must protect both nerve function and spine stability.

The authors describe removing such a tumor at the lower neck through a side approach, without needing added spine hardware. They also review eleven reported patients who had surgery for the same condition. Most had nerve symptoms, and surgeons used front, side, or back routes depending on tumor position. The authors stress that matching the approach to each tumor's anatomy is the key to full removal with a stable spine.
pmc-11571321:
Yu Hao, Yuxin Tie, Lijun Zhang, Fan Zhang, and Chaolun Sun grade how well cities in Henan Province, China, manage public health emergencies, from a resilience angle. Fast growth raises the odds of sudden urban health crises. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Thirty one gauges span six stages, from readiness and early warning through recovery and learning. A paired weight method blends expert weights with data driven ones, and a ranking model scores each city. Four cities showed robust skill, while three lagged. The frame joins resilience theory with whole process balance theory, the authors note, giving cities a way to spot weak stages.
pmc-11572221:
Andrew Annalora, Jacki Coburn, Antony Jozic, Patrick Iversen, and Craig Marcus wrote a 2024 paper on how foreign chemicals reshape gene activity in liver cells. The body handles drugs and pollutants with a family of enzymes. Those chemicals also switch how genes are spliced, meaning how their messages are cut and rejoined, which can change the proteins made.

Working with rat liver cells kept in a layered culture, the team exposed them to three chemicals and read the full set of gene messages. They checked both which genes turned up or down and how splicing changed across the genome. Each chemical left a distinct splicing landscape. The work shows splicing is a broad, drug-sensitive layer of response, not a side note.
pmc-11573221:
Nan Xu and Yifeng Wang published a research paper in 2024 on a decision system that watches opinion risk in campus social networks without wasting computing resources. Monitoring everything is slow and costly. Their first stage sorts network text with a hybrid algorithm that prunes paths dynamically while finding the shortest route through the data.

On top sits a sentiment classifier blending convolutional and recurrent networks with an attention layer. The sorting stage beat the classic shortest-path method on precision and speed. The recurrent variant classified long texts accurately, and adding attention lifted sentiment accuracy by about four points. The authors offer the stack to campus managers who must spot risky opinion surges early.
pmc-11574321:
Xuanyu Zheng, Xueming Li, and Qihai Chang show that a single-site laser radar can estimate sideways features of gravity waves in the upper air, in a paper from 2024. Such lidars were thought to read only temperature and vertical wave motion. Sideways motion was beyond their reach, or so it was believed.

By integrating the wave signal over area as it varies in time and space, the authors derive that the echo carries the sideways wavenumber. That proves the horizontal activity can be estimated from one site. Data from an observatory near Beijing confirmed the method works. It suits short-scale horizontal waves. The authors note that beam spread, laser sharpness, and height resolution must be chosen well for reliable reads.
pmc-11575021:
Soheila Khojand and four co-authors sequenced sixty-two almond samples to chart the genetic diversity of Iran's almond stock, in this 2024 study. Iran grows many local types alongside breeding lines and imports, and breeders need a map of how they relate. Genotyping-by-sequencing found about sixty-three thousand reliable markers spread over the eight chromosomes.

Diversity ran high across the collection. Family ties faded fast with distance along the genome, a sign the varieties have crossed heavily. Neither geography nor clustering by origin separated the trees, and most variation sat inside groups rather than between them. The authors offer the survey as a base for breeding and conservation planning.
pmc-11582021:
Ducharme and co-authors re-examine a great fault zone on the Greek island of Evia, in a 2024 geology paper. The zone slices between two rock stacks that were squeezed under high pressure long ago. Soft rock layers thinned as the upper stack slid, flattening the whole package.

Field work shows the strain split unevenly by rock type. The soft, layered matrix took most of the flattening, while harder blocks of marble and other rocks kept older fabrics inside them. Quartz vein patterns record an earlier, warmer squeeze, and some soft layers show a later, colder one. New isotope dates help pin the timing. The study refines how geologists read ancient detachments that shape mountain belts today.
pmc-11585221:
Augustus Osborne and colleagues track newborn deaths in Sierra Leone across 2008 to 2019 in a 2024 study. The country cut its newborn death rate over that span, yet gaps between groups stayed wide. The team used three rounds of the national health survey to measure those gaps.

The newborn death rate fell from about forty-nine deaths per thousand live births in 2008 to about thirty in 2019. Gaps tied to a mother's wealth and schooling shrank over the period. The gap tied to a mother's age, though, grew wider. The team measured inequality by region, by where families live, and by the baby's sex as well. Their results show where health programs still need to reach, even as the national rate improves.
pmc-11585621:
Kang Zou and eleven co-authors present a 2024 study building a tool to predict death in intensive care patients with gastrointestinal bleeding. Such bleeding can turn fatal quickly, and doctors need early risk estimates. The team drew records from two large critical care databases. They built a nomogram, a scoring chart, from patient factors and made it available as a live web tool.

The study covered over thirty-six hundred patients in total. The tool sorted patients well in its home data and fairly in the outside database. Patients classed as high risk died at about one in four, versus under three in a hundred in the low-risk group. The authors report good accuracy and clinical usefulness across checks. They offer the tool to help intensive care teams spot high-risk bleeders early and plan care.
pmc-11586921:
Huifang Kang and five co-authors study how adding nitrogen changes a carbon material in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The material is graphdiyne, a flat carbon network with both single and triple bonds. The team asked how nitrogen doping alters its magnetoresistance. That is the change in electrical resistance when a magnetic field is applied. They made samples with several doping levels and checked them with imaging, spectroscopy, and transport tests.

Lightly doped samples showed negative magnetoresistance, tied to a quantum effect called weak localization. Heavier doping flipped the sign, giving strong positive magnetoresistance. The authors trace the switch to the rise in charge carriers that doping brings. The results suggest a way to tune carbon electronics by doping. Such control could serve sensors and spintronic devices.
pmc-11591621:
Anna Christakou and co-authors tested whether motor imagery, mentally rehearsing movement, improves balance and function in older people with early dementia, in a 2024 trial. Dementia erodes thinking and daily function, and imagery offers practice without physical strain. The trial ran at an Athens day care center of the Alzheimer Association.

A total of 160 participants were split three ways: exercise plus imagery, exercise alone, and neither. The exercise arm ran 24 physiotherapy sessions over twelve weeks, drawn from a standard home program. The imagery group added a half hour of guided mental rehearsal after each session. Balance and function tests came before, midway, and after the program.
pmc-11592521:
Paweł Topolewski and co-authors review whether a liver cancer patient's response to pre-transplant treatment predicts how they fare after a liver transplant, in a 2024 systematic review. Bridging therapy treats the tumor while the patient waits for a donor organ. Whether response to it forecasts recurrence and survival was unsettled.

Searching two databases under standard review rules, the team found five studies. Four carried a serious risk of bias and one a moderate risk, which tempers the findings. Patients whose scans showed a complete or partial response tended to do best after transplant. Poor response or growth during bridging went with worse survival. Data were too thin to judge tissue-based response. The authors urge future transplant scoring models to fold in scan, tissue, and molecular features of the tumor.
pmc-11594321:
The authors asked what sets diffuse exophytic nasal papillomas apart from focal ones, in an 18 patient cohort study from a single center, published in 2024. The team checked clinical records, tissue features, and human papillomavirus DNA, including viral load, for each case.

Twelve patients stayed in the final analysis. The seven with diffuse growth were younger and the growth sat on the nasal septum far more often. Virus DNA showed up in every diffuse case, mostly one strain, but in only two of five focal cases. The paper maps a distinct profile for the diffuse form.
pmc-11596521:
Prakash Ramachandran, Madara Brice, Elena Sutherland, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It shows how a bile acid drug calms the liver scarring of fatty liver disease, and pinpoints which liver cells it acts on.

The drug, INT-767, switches on a receptor that is a leading target for this disease. In mice fed a scarring diet, the drug slowed new scar buildup, though it did not undo scars once the diet stopped. Treated livers made less of the tough collagens that stiffen tissue. Blood markers of scar collagen tracked the benefit over time. In human liver samples, gene data at bulk and single-cell level blamed star-shaped storage cells for the abnormal basement membrane the drug restrained. Cell culture tests confirmed the targets.
pmc-11597721:
Maísa Miranda Araújo and co-authors present a 2024 study on diagnosing a triple condition in women after weight-loss surgery. Osteosarcopenic adiposity combines weak bones, low muscle, and excess fat. Women years past a gastric bypass can carry all three, but rival rule sets define the condition differently.

The study checked 178 women at least two years after surgery, with an average age near forty-five. Three diagnostic rule sets were applied and compared. The condition's rate came out at 2.2, 2.8, or 6.2 percent depending on the rules. Two rule sets agreed moderately with each other, while the third barely agreed at all. All were good at ruling the condition out but poor at catching true cases, with one set the most accurate overall.
pmc-11599421: Marah Mansour and co-authors report a rare abdominal wall hernia with an unexpectedly long sac in a 2024 case paper. A Spigelian hernia pushes through a weak seam at the belly's edge, and it is easy to miss on examination. The report centers on how imaging settled the diagnosis. Computed tomography proved decisive for spotting it, sizing the problem, and planning surgery early enough to protect the trapped contents. The operation corrected the hernia successfully. The authors stress quick, image-guided action in such cases.
pmc-11600921:
Wenjie Cheng, Wei Chen, and Ruipeng Jia review a fiery form of cell death and its role in urinary system cancers, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. These cancers are a growing global burden, with poor outlooks at late stages. The death form, called pyroptosis, drives inflammation and helps control tissue balance and stress responses.

The review lays out how the process works and how it is regulated inside cells. It then traces what is known about its links to cancers of the urinary tract. By sparking inflammation as cells die, the process can shape tumor growth in complex ways. The authors aim to point clinicians toward new treatment directions that target this pathway.
pmc-11603621:
Delirium after surgery is a common and serious confusion state, especially in older patients, and is linked to worse recovery. Wenhui Zhang and co-authors pooled randomized trials to ask whether esketamine, a drug used during anesthesia, lowers the risk. They searched four databases for trials in patients having planned surgery under general anesthesia. They found seventeen trials covering about thirteen hundred patients, and checked trial quality with a bias tool.

Across the trials, patients who received esketamine at the start of anesthesia developed delirium at well under half the rate of control patients. Rates of side effects such as nausea, dizziness, and slowed breathing did not differ clearly between groups. The esketamine group had less low blood pressure and reported slightly less pain a day after surgery. The authors conclude that esketamine during induction appears to cut delirium risk without adding side effects.
pmc-11607421:
Noriko Akutsu and Yoshihiro Kangawa simulate how a growing crystal surface roughens, and find two celebrated theories competing on the same face. Using a lattice model with Monte Carlo simulation, they study kinetic roughening of the singular (001) surface during steady growth. At low temperature, two roughening transitions are known as the driving force increases. The first is the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang transition, where steps around islands stay well defined on a thermodynamically rough surface. Its roughness exponent matches the theory's universal value.

Island-on-island structures prove crucial to forming that KPZ rough surface. At higher temperatures, an additional Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless rough region and a re-entrant KPZ region appear at large driving force, where the crystal grows adhesively. The authors assemble a temperature-versus-driving-force roughening diagram. Crystal growers choosing temperature and supersaturation are, knowingly or not, choosing which roughening regime their surface lives in.
pmc-11608121:
Ajith and thirteen colleagues watched brand-new particles form in the air over Rehovot, Israel, and tracked how they grew. Such particles, born from gas, can seed clouds and harm lungs. The team logged particle sizes, air chemistry, and gases in two spring campaigns, in twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-three. The second run fell during a bonfire festival, a natural test of smoke's effect. Airborne organic matter sorted into traffic-like, wood-smoke, and aged types.

New particles formed often by day in clean nucleation bursts, and at night in bursts that never grew. Day events lined up with higher sulfuric acid in the air. Wood smoke thickened the soup of gases that feed or block growth. The twenty twenty-four study helps modelers say when city air makes its own particles, a step in linking traffic, fires, and health.
pmc-11608221:
Xiaoting Hao and colleagues engineered enzyme shape inside microreactors in 2024. Enzymes work less well outside cells. Industry still wants their precise chemistry. Tiny hybrid reactors were built here. A tailored ionic liquid joined the design. Lipase enzymes were the test case.

Reactor conditions reshaped the active site. Enzyme behaviour changed alongside shape changes. Special liquid parts stabilised protein structure. Heat unfolded treated enzymes more slowly. Flow operation ran continuously in tests. Performance improved over standard setups. The authors expect wider biocatalysis use. Real-world production is the long-term aim. Stability under heat was a key gain.
pmc-11609121:
James Roberts, Caroline Wakefield, and Robin Owen asked whether imagining a movement captures its path through space, not just its timing. Imagined and real movements are known to take similar times, which hints at a shared brain representation. To test the spatial side, they used an obstacle task: a movement tends to bend away from an obstacle seen on the trial just before. Participants reached with and without a virtual obstacle, and the trial before each real reach was either imagined or really performed, in work published in twenty twenty-four.

Imagined trials took longer than real ones. A real reach did bend after a real obstacle trial, just as expected. But after an imagined obstacle trial, the next reach showed no such bend. The authors conclude that mental imagery holds only a limited version of a movement path, even though its timing matches real movement well.
pmc-11610121:
Gholamhossein Jowkar and co-authors published a study in 2024 on rebuilding ancient gene sequences. Insertions and deletions of letters shape how genomes evolve. Modeling long inserted blocks is costly, so most tools treat each letter on its own. The team tested whether that shortcut distorts rebuilt ancestors.

Their method infers single-letter inserts and deletes along a family tree in fast, linear time. They ran it on mammal proteins and on fake data with known answers. The rebuilt ancestors kept the same gap-length pattern seen in the input. Inserts in mammal proteins ran longer than deletes, matching a known bias toward deletion. The authors say their tool is the only one that tracks insert and delete events over time.
pmc-11611121:
Anicca Liu and colleagues gather Florida stakeholder lessons for the next pandemic. Their study from twenty twenty-four interviews leaders across sectors. Florida chose a low-restriction path through COVID-19. State-level preparedness advice informed by experience was lacking.

Twenty-five current and former leaders gave semi-structured interviews. Voices came from government, universities, and private business. Transcripts were coded into challenges, successes, and recommendations. Communication and coordination themes run through the findings. Successes and failures of the Florida response are both catalogued. Future planning can borrow the concrete fixes proposed. Preparedness is a system property, not a stockpile count.
pmc-11614021:
Al-Kindi and co-authors review what COVID-19 did to leukemia care at one academic center in a 2024 study. Acute leukemias, both the myeloid and lymphoblastic forms, are fast blood cancers that cannot wait for care. The pandemic strained hospitals and may have changed who arrived, how sick they were, and how they fared. The team studied their own center, Sultan Qaboos University Hospital in Muscat, Oman.

They pulled records for all patients treated there from 2017 to 2021, one hundred fifty-one in total. Patients found before the pandemic were compared with those found during it. The leukemia rate rose in the pandemic years in their data. The comparison spans frequency, clinical features, and outcomes. Such a ground record helps centers plan cancer care that holds up in the next crisis.
pmc-11615321:
Tatsuo Nozaki and three co-authors dated two seafloor ore deposits to pin down when an ocean ridge sank beneath Japan, in a study published in 2024. Ridge sinking triggers heat change and hot water flow, but its timing is hard to fix. The ores formed on a mud-covered mid-ocean ridge, so their ages mark the event. A rare metal dating method gave clean lines: about 89 million years for one site and 48 million for the other.

Five signs agreed that both ores grew on such a ridge in a shelf sea. Their ages match the rocks around them. The team reads the pair as formed just before the Izanagi-Pacific ridge sank under the ancient Japanese islands. The dates give the deep past of the islands a firmer frame.
pmc-11619521:
Timothy Griffin and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on why knee osteoarthritis hits women harder than men, using mice as a model. Obesity raises the risk, and the team asked whether a rich diet harms male and female joints through different routes. They fed mice a high-fat or normal diet for twenty weeks.

Both sexes gained much weight on the rich diet. The team then measured body metabolism, gut microbes, gene activity in joint tissues, and the cartilage damage itself. Splitting every result by sex and diet showed where the paths diverge. Such maps may explain the human gap and point to treatments tuned by sex, an angle joint research has often skipped.
pmc-11621321:
Shuyao Zhang and five co-authors emulate a trial of diabetes drugs in veterans with kidney disease. Their 2024 study compares GLP1 receptor agonists with DPP4 inhibitors. The newer drugs may slow kidney decline and heart events. Real-world effects on hospital use and death were unclear.

Records from 2006 to 2021 built the comparison. Over sixteen thousand matched pairs were followed for about two years. The agonist group used acute care less often each year. Deaths from all causes also ran lower. Acute heart events, though, did not differ clearly. Emulated trials can guide practice while true trials catch up.
pmc-11622121:
Takalani Mbedzi and co-authors describe daily life for families who care for mental health users in rural South Africa, in work from 2024. Sixteen family members from eight clinics in the Vhembe district shared their stories in open talks. Recovery-focused care casts families as part of the care team, yet rural families get scant support for that role.

Carers dwelt on duty without pause. Endless worry and strain brought forgetfulness, poor sleep, high blood pressure, and pain. No change in their loved one, and thin town support, left them feeling helpless. Fear of harm and shame drove lonely lives. The authors urge stronger town services.
pmc-11624121: Kushal Pradhan and co-authors present a 2024 case report on a failed attempt to place a breathing tube with a flexible scope, a method held as the standard for hard airways. Such failures can stem from the patient, the gear, or the operator. In this case, the scope failed because suction stayed on continuously, an equipment error. The report walks through the event so airway teams can spot and avoid the same trap.
pmc-11624721:
Siyuan Wang leads a team of ten authors pricing cleaner air in China in heart attacks avoided and money saved. China carries both heavy particle pollution and a rising cardiovascular burden. Their model projects ten-year disease costs and quality-adjusted life years under three air scenarios: twenty fifteen pollution levels, the national target, and the far stricter World Health Organization guideline.

Risks were drawn from a national survey of older adults, with pollution effects taken from WHO risk curves. At twenty fifteen pollution, the model foresaw about thirty-five million cardiovascular events and ninety-six billion dollars in costs over a decade. Meeting the national target cut events by several million. The exercise translates air policy into health-system arithmetic.
pmc-11626621:
Alia Zayed and four co-authors report the first finding of an invasive mosquito in Yemen in a paper from 2024. The species, Aedes albopictus, spreads dengue and chikungunya and adapts to many settings. Teams screened twenty-two sites in three districts with traps, sprays, and water checks during routine surveillance in September 2023.

Adults and young stages turned up in Hawf, a town near the Oman border, sharing containers with a kindred vector species. Trade and travel across the border may have brought it in. The authors urge close monitoring inside Yemen and joint border surveillance with Oman, plus disease watch where both vectors now live.
pmc-11627421:
Abutayeh and five co-authors tested pomegranate peel extracts against bacteria in twenty twenty-four. Drug resistance is rising worldwide, pushing the search for new germ fighters. Pomegranate peel, about half the fresh fruit's weight, is rich in plant compounds with germ-killing potential.

Using Jordanian fruit, the team made extracts with different solvents and methods, then tested them on four bacterial strains. Water-based extracts worked strongly against three strains, including a tough Pseudomonas type. An alcohol extract worked best against the fourth strain. Pairing a microwaved water extract with the antibiotic gentamicin restored effect against resistant Pseudomonas, even at low doses. The authors call the peel, a safe food by-product, a promising partner for conventional antibiotics.
pmc-11630821:
Ariel Zylberberg, Akram Bakkour, Daphna Shohamy, and Michael Shadlen argue that the value people place on things shifts as they decide, in this 2024 study. The classic view treats choice between familiar items as a comparison of fixed values, with noise causing slow or inconsistent picks. The authors suggest the values themselves move with changing inner states.

They reanalyzed data from a task where people chose between snack foods. Their algorithm, named Reval, uncovered clear swings in how much each item was valued within a single session. Those shifting values predicted choices and response times better than the values people stated outright. They also matched brain signals in a region tied to value more closely. A new model of evidence building, with linked samples over time, supports the idea that value is built during the act of deciding and then colors the next choice.
pmc-11631221:
Kirk Bansak and Elisabeth Paulson survey what the public wants from human and algorithmic choice-makers in high-stakes settings, in a two thousand twenty-four social science paper. Algorithms more and more share choices about bail and bank loans, and public acceptance matters.

About nine thousand respondents chose between paired choice-maker profiles in pretrial release and loan scenarios. Profiles varied in type and in performance metrics, including error rates for white and minority applicants. Efficiency led people's judgments; fairness ranked last, consistently across scenarios, subgroups, and choice-maker type. Even at equal performance, respondents preferred human choice-makers on average, though that preference varied widely between people.
pmc-11631721:
Joseph Kim, Yohan Kim, and Andres Saenz reported an unusual encephalitis case in 2024. Autoimmune encephalitis inflames the brain through antibodies. One rare type targets the LGI1 protein. It causes memory, mood, and sleep problems. Brief face and arm jerks are typical.

The patient developed sudden vocal cord paralysis. Both vocal cords failed at once. Larynx problems are not known in this disease. Other autoimmune diseases can affect the larynx. This case adds a new warning sign. Doctors should watch airway symptoms closely. The report stresses atypical presentations. Quick recognition can protect the airway.
pmc-11633021:
Ricarda Duerst and Jonas Schöley improve forecasts of weekly deaths in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. In the winter of two thousand twenty-two to twenty-three, German excess death estimates near ten percent raised questions about their reliability. Forecast errors set how much trust such numbers deserve.

Using weekly death data from twenty-three countries, they build prediction intervals from past forecast errors rather than from model assumptions. These empirical intervals proved better calibrated than standard parametric ones. They also show that a ten percent weekly excess is not very unusual in summer or winter under normal conditions. The authors stress that interval choice can change how severe an excess looks.
pmc-11637521:
Christoffer Dharma and co-authors work on better counts of mental health among gay, bisexual, and other sexual minority men, in a methods paper from 2024. Community surveys can skew who takes part. Broad population surveys can miss men who hide their identity. Both flaws bend the rates that planners rely on.

The team weights a Canadian community survey so it matches a national health survey. The method aims to fix both kinds of bias at once. Adjusted rates for low mood, service use, and anxiety fell between the two raw sources. The paper gives health agencies a way to plan with firmer numbers.
pmc-11639921:
Tao Wang and co-authors present a 2024 study on why a native Chinese pig breed resists viruses better than commercial pigs. The team reanalyzed public gene data from blood cells of Dapulian and Landrace pigs after a mock viral challenge, a standard stand-in for infection.

Comparing the breeds surfaced candidate resistance genes, including three named TIMD4, RNF128, and VCAM1. Deeper analysis built a control network for the Dapulian response: five small regulatory RNAs steering twelve genes, several central to immune signaling. The network shows how the local breed mounts its antiviral reply at the level of gene regulation. The authors offer the findings as leads for breeding hardier pigs and for understanding broad-spectrum resistance.
pmc-11640321:
Cédric Sueur and co-authors model the giant huddles formed by Japanese monkeys on one island, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. On Shodoshima, huddles can top fifty animals, far larger than in other groups. Huddling keeps animals warm and builds social bonds in cold places.

A computer model let each virtual monkey join or leave by simple chance rules. Heat, group size, and solo choices drove the pattern in the model. Cold did favor larger huddles, yet joining and leaving rates mattered just as much. The island group's size likely blends weather with high social tolerance, the authors say.
pmc-11640421:
Yasemin Ozgür-Gunes and co-authors argue for a neglected cell type in this 2024 review. Oligodendrocytes wrap nerve fibers in fatty insulation inside the brain and spinal cord. Gene therapy trials have mostly aimed at other brain cells instead. The authors ask why these cells keep being passed over.

One reason is doubt about how much the cells drive disease. Another is practical: common gene switches barely turn on inside these cells. So most past studies either saw no gene activity there or never checked. The review makes the case for testing these cells as targets in several brain diseases. It also urges researchers to report what happens in them.
pmc-11642521:
Johana Vásquez-Procopio and co-authors track six essential metal nutrients in the blood of pregnant women in Mexico City, and link them to birth outcomes, in a 2024 study. Pregnancy raises demand for iron, zinc, and their peers to build the baby. The team followed 206 women from a local cohort across all three trimesters, from 2017 to 2020.

Iron and magnesium fell as pregnancy advanced, while copper rose. Women with an underactive thyroid ran low on zinc and magnesium throughout. Statistical checks tied falling magnesium to higher odds of gestational diabetes. Other metal shifts also lined up with outcomes at birth. The authors conclude that a mother's metal balance, watched over time, is a real factor in how a pregnancy ends, and they argue it deserves a place in prenatal care.
pmc-11642721:
Filip Jurić and co-authors tracked skin temperature over healing collarbone fractures in children, testing whether heat imaging could follow the repair. Twenty-seven children aged four to eighteen, most of them boys, took part. Heat camera readings were taken above the break and on the healthy side on days one, four, eight, fifteen, and twenty-two, alongside ultrasound checks of the new bone.

The temperature gap peaked at about zero point seven degrees during the growth phase of the healing callus, around days four to eight, when the gap was statistically clear. Once the callus showed on ultrasound, the gap shrank steadily and vanished by day twenty-two. The authors say heat imaging might one day flag callus formation and cut the X-rays children now get at follow-up.
pmc-11642821:
Serxio Álvarez-Olcina and co-authors built 3D-printed bone scaffolds that can heat up inside a magnetic field, a treatment called magnetic hyperthermia. The scaffolds mix polylactic acid and hydroxyapatite, two materials suited to bone repair, with iron-oxide nanoparticles that turn a magnetic field into heat. Such heating could kill leftover cancer cells or resistant infections at an implant site while the scaffold supports new bone.

The team compared two ways of adding the particles: mixed through the printing material, or coated onto the printed surface. Both versions passed cell-safety checks and reached the heat levels needed for moderate or strong treatment. Detailed heating curves map how temperature depends on particle amount, field strength, and distance from the coil.
pmc-11643721:
Ceccherini and colleagues read spit prints that split two bile duct ills in this twenty twenty-four study. Both ills scar the bile ducts and end in liver scar and rot. No blood mark can yet tell the two ills apart in wards.

Inside, spit from sick folks of one ill met past files of the kin ill. Two score proteins swung hard tween the two ill bands. Most swung bits serve the cell's frame web and guard acts. Frame web shifts tie to liver scar and growth paths in the field. Spit thus bears a cheap print for duct ill sorts.
pmc-11644821:
Assel Jexembayeva, Marat Konkanov, Lyazat Aruova, Akpan Kirgizbayev, and Lailya Zhaksylykova wrote a 2024 paper on mixing recycled plastic into bitumen, the sticky binder in asphalt roads. Plastic from bottles, called PET, is a major waste stream. Adding it to bitumen might make roads stronger and more water resistant while using up waste.

The team made mixes with six doses of plastic, from one to twelve percent, and ran standard tests for softening, brittleness, stretch, and hardness. Mixes with five and eight percent plastic performed best overall. They also photographed the mix surfaces and checked their inner structure with X-rays. The results give road builders a recipe range to test in real pavements.
pmc-11644921:
Shaoxin Wang and ten co-authors survey the core sensor for a space observatory that will hunt gravitational waves from orbit. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Ground detectors are hampered by shakes and by short arms, so a space mission can hear lower tones. The signal is faint, so a test mass must float almost free of all stray forces.

The inertial sensor shields the mass and, with a drag-free control loop, keeps it on a near-perfect free path. That gives a steady frame for laser measures between craft. The paper walks through the sensor's parts and key tricks, and it looks at where the tech may go next.
pmc-11645021:
Juraj Machaj and co-authors published a 2024 study on catching fake Wi-Fi access points that sabotage indoor positioning. Phones locate themselves indoors by fingerprinting the Wi-Fi signals around them, a cheap and widespread method. But Wi-Fi is unlicensed: anyone can broadcast a spoofed access point with a copied identity. A spoofer can bend the fingerprint and drag position estimates astray.

Earlier work mostly measured how much damage spoofing does, or caught anomalies while maps were being built. Defenses that fit live positioning systems lagged. This study works on detection within the fingerprinting approach itself, watching for the fingerprints that do not belong. The stakes range from mall navigation to hospital asset tracking and emergency response, anywhere indoor position is trusted. The authors treat positioning as a security problem, not just an accuracy one: a location system that cannot tell friend from impostor will eventually be lied to.
pmc-11646421:
Sarah Hasnain and Shelley Arnott present a 2024 study on how prey behavior shapes the impact of an invasive predator in lakes. The invader is a small predatory water flea that eats other plankton. Its main prey, Daphnia, can sit at different depths in the water, and that choice varies between individuals.

The team ran tank experiments with plankton communities. Where Daphnia stayed apart from the predator in depth, predation on smaller species was heavier. Those tanks also grew more algae, since fewer grazers survived to eat it. Where the prey overlapped more with the predator, the effects were milder. The results show that small behavior differences in native prey can steer the whole impact of an invasion.
pmc-11648121:
Li and a large team of co-authors report a gene fault behind a rare growth and vessel disease in a paper from 2024. Nine patients from seven families shared small head size, short stature, facial differences, eye scarring, and moyamoya disease, where brain vessels narrow. All carried two copies of the same variant in TOMM7, a gene for a part that imports proteins into mitochondria.

Edited stem cells carrying the variant made swollen mitochondria, aged faster, and formed poor vessel tubes. Energy output shifted from respiration toward sugar burning. Zebrafish lacking the gene showed like skull and brain vessel defects, backing the causal claim.
pmc-11648321:
Jamy Ard and co-authors present an expert panel discussion from two thousand twenty-four on obesity medicines in the age of GLP-1 drugs. These long-acting drugs mimic a gut hormone and have shown strong effects on weight and metabolic health. With obesity affecting more than two in five adults in the United States, access and long-term care are pressing issues.

The panel, gathered by a medical journal, brings together specialists in obesity medicine. They discuss clinical use of the new drug class, now called third-generation anti-obesity medication. They also weigh effects on health systems and society, and the need for fair, lasting access. The discussion format lets each expert speak from practice, with Ard opening as moderator and society president.
pmc-11649521:
Tae Hee Han and co-authors measure how glutamate receptors at the fruit fly's neuromuscular junction open and close, and how their partner protein Neto shapes that behavior. This junction is a classic genetic model for synapse biology. Its receptors come in two types, A and B, and they need Neto to assemble and work. Until recently, rebuilding these receptors outside the fly had failed, so their gating was unknown.

Using patch clamp recordings with fast chemical application, the team studies native receptors and lab-built ones in human cells. The two receptor types gate in strikingly different ways, and the two Neto variants tune them further. Single-channel events expose more contrasts. Shut-off after activation is extremely fast: the decay of synaptic currents tracks the desensitization rate of this receptor family. The authors say the data will help interpret the effects of mutations seen in whole animals.
pmc-11651421:
Melina Klein, Alexa von Bosse, and Christophe Kunze studied people with early-stage dementia using a tablet app in Germany in two thousand twenty-four. The app aims to spur thinking and physical activity, supporting independence at home as care capacity shrinks. The team asked what users need and how they experience such tools.

They combined interviews with watching people test the app. Most users were hesitant at first but tried it after encouragement, and some needed much more help than others. Content that felt personally relevant mattered most, and users valued social contact with the researchers. The authors stress one-to-one support, while noting its time and cost in real care settings.
pmc-11653021:
Jorge Valencia-Ortega and colleagues track mother signalling proteins across pregnancy. Their longitudinal study from twenty twenty-four follows one hundred healthy women. Organ-derived signals may predict newborn size and body fat. The team measured four such proteins at several pregnancy stages.

Newborn weight and length were recorded at birth and one month. Body fat share at one month used a special infant device. Mother nutrition before pregnancy and weight gain were also tracked. Statistical models linked protein levels to newborn measures. Each protein was tested against size and fat outcomes separately. Early prediction of newborn growth patterns could guide feeding care. The study adds pregnancy timing detail that single measures miss.
pmc-11653821:
Camille Velarde Crézé and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on a fast-track method for building expert consensus when a health crisis will not wait. Classic Delphi surveys take rounds of questionnaires over months, too slow for emergencies. Their hybrid design squeezes the process into preset steps: one group session, then two rounds of online questionnaires.

A ready toolkit of survey templates, analysis code, and a user guide removes setup delays. The team piloted the method on a tobacco control question and finished in eighteen days. Experts found it workable and useful in real conditions. The authors offer the process to policymakers who need defensible consensus at crisis speed.
pmc-11655321:
Takato Mizuho and co-authors ran a field study in a grocery store on whether shoppers remember promotions delivered by robots or screen agents, in a 2024 paper. Agents stood at two store locations pitching products. The team guessed that hearing pitches from different agents would aid memory, and that physical robots, feeling more socially present, would beat virtual ones.

Neither guess held: recall did not differ across the conditions. One pattern did emerge. With the physical robot, shoppers who rated its social presence higher also remembered more; with the virtual agent that link vanished. The authors call the work a stepping stone for memory-focused promotion research.
pmc-11655521:
Kirsten Zantvoort and co-authors ask how much data a machine learning study in digital mental health really needs, in a 2024 paper. AI tools promise better care, but many studies train on small datasets, and their claims may not hold up. The team used records from 3,654 users of one digital therapy study to map how prediction quality grows with sample size.

They trained models to predict who would drop out of the program, varying the dataset from 100 users up to the full set, and trying many feature sets and model types. Small sets, at or below 300 users, made models look better than they were. Fancy models overfit small data but won on large data. Results settled only somewhere between 750 and 1,500 users. The authors propose a minimum of 500 to 1,000 users for such studies.
pmc-11655921:
Françoise Vendittelli and co-authors published this consensus study in 2024. Birth plans let pregnant women record their wishes for labor and delivery. In France few women write them, and their contents vary so much that studies of their effects are hard to compare. The team set out to win national agreement on what a birth plan should contain, using a modified Delphi process of repeated expert voting.

A steering committee drafted 103 candidate items arranged in eight sections. Panels of perinatal professionals and service-user representatives rated each item over three rounds, with participation in the high thirties and low forties. An external board then checked the final text for understandability. The agreed plan keeps eight sections and nineteen subsections. The authors say a shared structure should make birth plans more useful for women and easier to evaluate.
pmc-11656021:
Liu, Zhang, and Zuo review the many roles of macrophages in skin disease and skin tumors in this 2024 article. Macrophages are long-lived eating cells of the innate immune system, spread through every tissue. The skin, the body's largest immune organ, gives them a wide stage.

The review gathers current findings disease by disease. It covers eczema-like dermatitis, psoriasis, systemic sclerosis, lupus, rosacea, and blistering disease. It then turns to melanoma and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. In each setting macrophages can drive inflammation, calm it, or feed tumor growth. The authors aim to expose disease mechanisms and point to therapies that retrain these cells rather than just suppressing immunity.
pmc-11657121:
Qiao Feng and eight co-authors test if a sugar-fat index sharpens a plain age-kidney-heart score for folks past artery wire care. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Both marks had each been tied to bad ends past such care. Near one thousand two hundred fifty heart patients at a Chengdu ward were tracked for a mean of near thirty-one months.

Past set cut lines, high scores on each mark more than doubled the rate of grave heart and brain hits. Both held as fate marks past full checks. Put in the plain risk frame, the pair lifted guess force by clear steps on all counts. The team backs the joined score for risk sorts.
pmc-11660321:
Russell, Chan, Davies, Gibson, Harniess, Rendle, and Wray set out the SPIRITUS study protocol in twenty twenty-four. Non invasive ventilation helps children with sleep disordered breathing. Many children use it less than prescribed, risking undertreatment. Few interventions to improve adherence have been tested.

The study runs in three mixed methods phases. First it will identify toolkit components that tackle known barriers. Then those components are tested for feasibility and family acceptance. The team will also learn which health outcomes matter most to families. Interviews and surveys feed both qualitative and descriptive analysis. The study is registered and runs from twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-five. Results will be shared widely with stakeholders.
pmc-11662921:
Zhuoxin Zhang and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four study of gene and nutrition links to colorectal cancer in Hakka Chinese people. A folate-processing gene variant and a nutrition score had each been tied to some cancers. Their joint role in bowel cancer here was unknown.

Over six hundred patients and more controls were enrolled and genotyped. Nutrition score groups differed clearly between patients and controls. Smoking, blood pressure, diabetes, and family history also differed. Gene type distributions varied as well. The study helps local doctors weigh inherited and lifestyle risks together for bowel cancer screening.
pmc-11663721:
Jiwon Lyu and ten co-authors wrote this review, published in 2024. It explains how granulomas form in tuberculosis. A granuloma is a tight ball of immune cells that walls off the bacteria. These balls can protect the host, but they can also help the disease spread when they break down.

The authors sort the many cell signals that build a granuloma into those that help and those that harm. Too little or too much of a signal can both weaken the wall, they argue. What matters is a response that is strong, balanced, and timed well. The review also compares these balls across many animals, from zebrafish to cattle and primates. Knowing what makes a granuloma hold could point to new drugs and better vaccines.
pmc-11664321:
A conference collection gathers the abstracts of the Annual Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Conference held in October 2023, published in 2024. ASCAT is a major meeting for doctors and researchers who treat inherited blood disorders. The hosted text runs through dozens of short research summaries, each with its own author list and topic tag. One early entry reports transfusion independence after a gene therapy, exagamglogene autotemcel, in patients with beta-thalassemia who once needed regular transfusions.

Other abstracts span new therapies, gene therapy trials, and bone marrow transplant work. Together they snapshot a field in rapid motion, as one-time gene treatments move from trials toward routine care. Clinicians and patient groups use such collections to track which centers are testing what, and how fast results are arriving.
pmc-11669321:
Wen-Hsin Tseng and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on the obesity paradox in bladder cancer, using Taiwan's national health insurance database. Heavier patients often survive some diseases better than lean ones, against intuition. From over fifteen thousand bladder cancer patients, careful filtering left 10,352 for analysis by weight class.

Most patients were men over sixty. Despite carrying more other illnesses, obese patients died less: overall mortality was about three quarters that of normal-weight patients, and cancer-specific mortality was also lower. Underweight patients fared worst on both counts. The pattern held across clinical stages. The authors say weight should inform, not mislead, prognosis talks, while mechanisms remain to be explained.
pmc-11674321:
Jiaxin Cindy Tu and co-authors published this brain network study in 2024. It examines families carrying genes that guarantee Alzheimer's disease. Brain hub regions, the highly connected nodes that keep information flowing, seem especially fragile in such diseases. One theory blames their own heavy activity for wearing them down. The team refined a hub disruption index to test how connectivity breaks down in these mutation carriers.

The breakdown pattern matched a targeted attack on hubs rather than random damage. Strikingly, it was already visible about twelve years before expected symptoms. It grew steadily worse as dementia advanced. The disruption tracked regional connection strength and followed the spread of amyloid plaques seen on brain scans. That order fits the activity-wear theory. The authors say mapping hub damage could sharpen diagnosis. It might also guide treatments aimed at the most burdened brain regions.
pmc-11674921:
Reem AlWhaibi and co-authors survey video game habits and self-rated spatial skills in students in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Spatial reasoning matters for study and work in science fields, and games are suspected of training it. The team asked how play frequency, type, and length relate to perceived skill.

Over five hundred sixty Saudi university students filled an online survey. Frequent players, about two thirds of the group, rated their spatial skills higher than rare players, above all at adapting to spatial tasks. Action and open-world players reported the largest gains. Men and women benefited alike. The game camera's viewpoint also linked to skill gains. The authors see games as candidate training tools.
pmc-11675021:
Molaya Chaisen and colleagues published an imaging comparison study in 2024. They tested whether routine CT scans can screen bone health. Osteoporosis is usually measured with a DXA scan. Many patients already get abdominal CT scans anyway. Vertebra brightness on CT may reflect bone strength. The team studied just over one hundred patients. Each patient had both scan types within a year. Vertebra measurements were compared with DXA results. People with metal artifacts were excluded carefully.

CT values correlated moderately with DXA scores overall. Lower thresholds caught most osteoporosis cases sensitively. Higher sensitivity came with more false alarms though. The spine vertebra L1 performed as a useful site. Opportunistic screening needs no extra radiation or visits. Positive CT flags could prompt formal DXA testing. The trade-off between sensitivity and specificity needs care.
pmc-11675121:
Zhe Lin and co-authors craft a new yardstick for chaos synchronization. Coupled chaotic systems can lock steps despite their wild sensitivity. Old gauges lean on phase space paths and the governing equations themselves. Their DTSPC method reads only sampled time series from the pair.

It studies the gap series between the two systems and scores its peak patterns by entropy. Rich pattern mixes mark loose coupling; plain mixes mark tight lock. Tests on paired Lorenz systems, alike and unlike, span wide settings. The gauge caught non-monotone shifts and tangled borders between regimes. Transitional behavior, often missed, shows up sharply in the score.
pmc-11676321:
Eva Cutrim, Karla Penha, and Patrícia Silva lead a team lab test of charcoal toothpaste and powder, asking what the fashionable black cleaners do to tooth enamel. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Charcoal products promise whiter teeth, but their abrasiveness is debated. The team brushed stained enamel samples under controlled cycles.

Four products were compared: charcoal paste, charcoal powder, peroxide whitening paste, and a regular paste. Charcoal brushing did not change color more than the others. But it softened the enamel and roughened its surface. The powder carried no fluoride and leached the most calcium from the samples. Plain toothpaste left the enamel least disturbed. The authors conclude charcoal's whitening claim is unproven while its wear is real. Dentists get numbers for a common patient question.
pmc-11676721:
Selvam and co-authors build AISMPred, a learning tool to spot anti-inflammatory small molecules. Peptide drugs are specific but slow and costly to develop. Small molecules offer stability and oral use instead. Their data set held 1,750 molecules with activity values. Features came from PaDEL and Mordred descriptor tools.

A hybrid feature set joined both descriptor types. Fifteen models were built across three feature sets. Five classifier types were tested in the build. The extra trees model with hybrid features scored highest. The authors offer the tool for faster drug screening.
pmc-11676821:
Megan Wu, Chandan Sarkar, and Bin Guo published a review in 2024 on a protein called PAK2 in cancer spread. PAK2 is an enzyme that helps control cell shape and movement. Signals from small switch proteins turn it on. It then affects how cells stick, crawl, and survive.

Recent work ties PAK2 to growth and cell death in many cancers. Newer studies give it a direct role in metastasis, the spread of cancer. That makes the enzyme an appealing drug target. The review gathers what is known about its actions in different tumor types. Understanding those pathways may shape future therapies. Blocking spread would address the deadliest stage of cancer.
pmc-11677121:
Antonella Cotoia and co-authors published a review paper in 2024 on how food and gut microbes shape brain swelling after a traumatic brain injury. A blow to the head does direct harm at once, then a slower wave of swelling adds more. The gut and brain talk to each other, and that talk can stoke or calm the second wave.

The review pulls together animal and human studies on fats, proteins, and helpful live microbes. Certain diets shift the gut mix in ways that ease brain swelling. Tailored feeding plans may help the brain heal and guard it from further harm. The authors present diet and gut care as promising add-ons to standard treatment.
pmc-11677921:
Matthew Garnett and co-authors present a 2024 study on making cellulose gel beads with even inner structure. Such beads serve drug and cell work, but the drop method leaves them lumpy inside and uneven in strength. Salt in the mix was long treated as stray waste. The team instead added salt up front and tuned the mix thickness, then set the beads in an acid bath.

Three-dimensional views showed salt-first beads held the most even pore web through their depth. A probe test tied stray salt from the bath to strength swings. Pre-added salt screened that effect out, and strength steadied. Even beads matter where dose or cell load must match from bead to bead. The fix is cheap: control the salt, not just the gel.
pmc-11679121:
Seieun Kim and co-authors survey what makes people accept health devices, in a 2024 study. The devices split into wearables worn on the body and radar sensors that monitor without touch. Acceptance decides whether such tools ever help, so the authors modeled its drivers statistically.

Over eleven hundred valid responses fed the model. Beliefs that a device performs well and is easy to use shaped attitudes, which in turn drove the intention to use it. Trust carried weight of its own, and perceived risk cut against acceptance. Age group changed how strongly attitude and trust converted into intention. The kind of device changed the trust effect too: radar and wearables persuade differently. Designers get a map of which reassurances matter for which audience.
pmc-11683121:
Lauren DePoy and ten co-authors tested whether scrambling the body clock in young mice leaves lasting marks on reward-seeking and risk behavior, in this 2024 study. Broken sleep rhythms are tied to mental illness and drug use, and the teen years are a sensitive window for both. The team shifted the light cycle of young and adult mice by twelve hours.

Four weeks later, mice whose rhythms were scrambled as teens, but not as adults, explored more boldly and preferred cocaine more strongly. In self-dosing tests, females with a teen scramble history took more cocaine, while males showed weaker drive. Gene activity in the brain's clock center also changed, in sex-specific ways. The authors warn that teen rhythm disruption may prime later drug problems.
pmc-11688021:
Ya Gao, Yalin Wang, Wenbo Li, and Fenglian Wu compared stitching methods for facial wounds in 2024. Face injuries need care that heals well and leaves the smallest scar possible. Sixty patients treated over one year were split between standard care and a cosmetic suturing method paired with a device that reduces tension across the wound.

Follow-up at one, three, and six months used a standard scar rating scale. The combined-method group scored better on scars, had narrower scars, and reported much higher satisfaction than the control group. The authors recommend wider use of cosmetic sutures plus tension reduction for facial skin trauma, based on these results.
pmc-11688721:
Xuexin Yu and five co-authors study whether low mood links long-term loneliness to memory loss. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses a United States aging study with close to five thousand adults aged fifty and older. Loneliness was checked at up to three points over eight years. Low mood was then checked, and memory was tested two years later. Two groups with staggered dates were pooled.

More years of loneliness linked to worse memory, in a step-wise way. Low mood explained part of that link. The share it explained grew with more years of loneliness. The authors say treating low mood may soften, but not erase, the harm of lasting loneliness.
pmc-11689221:
Kathryn Nearing, Leslie Wright, Christin Williamson, and Cory Sedey-Seitz describe a training program for older adult research staff in a 2024 paper. Older adults are often left out of clinical trials, which limits how well results apply to them. Their university program trains community older adults, average age sixty eight, for roles on trial teams.

Graduates, called Older Adult Research Specialists, design outreach, recruit and consent participants, and help keep them in studies by solving practical barriers. They also teach research teams how to include older adults well. Training runs fourteen weeks and is competency based, built on health navigation skills. Four cohorts, forty three graduates, have completed it so far.
pmc-11689721:
Molly Ream and six co-authors survey VA clinicians who treat older veterans, in twenty twenty-four. They ask whether unmet social needs differ for rural and urban patients. They also ask what helps or blocks social life in the country. A third aim was to gauge interest in a group program for veterans with trauma stress.

Eighty-four clinicians took part, split by how much of their load was rural. Rural clinicians saw more lack of support, low contact, and loneliness. Yet they also saw close towns and strong will to help. Their blocks were few choices and long distances. Most rural clinicians wanted to run the group program.
pmc-11690221:
Zeyu Liu and three co-authors interview older climate activists about working across age groups. Their twenty twenty-four study spoke with forty-five activists aged sixty-five to eighty-nine. Each gave at least ten hours a week to climate work. The team sorted their views into themes about the young and the old in joint action.

Care for future kin drove much of their work, the team found. Activists praised joint work, but named blocks to it as well. They also saw chances for each age group to mentor the other. A strong shared thread was duty: a sense that they helped cause the problem and must help the young fix it.
pmc-11692021:
Neha Dewansingh and three co-authors study, in twenty twenty-four, links between thoughts about one's own aging, the move out of work, and sleep health. Good sleep matters at all ages, yet sleep often gets worse in later life. A keen sense of aging has been tied to good habits like exercise, but its tie to sleep was less known.

The team used a national midlife study with over six hundred adults. A higher sense of aging went with worse sleep health for both those still at work and those who had left work. The link was stronger for those who had left work. The authors say this was a surprise, given past work on gains. They call for study of why the end of work may turn such thoughts into a sleep risk.
pmc-11692121:
Eleanor Skemp, Tanish Sathish, Yichen Zhang, and Brian Carpenter published a study in 2024 on racial and ethnic differences in willingness to participate in Alzheimer's disease research. Minority populations are underrepresented in such research. That affects both the generalizability of findings and the equity of care.

The researchers used a 2022 national survey of 1,274 adults in the United States, with deliberate oversampling of Black respondents. Participants were asked whether they would join a research registry or a cohort study, and about their reasons. Black adults were more likely than white or Hispanic adults to say they were unwilling to do either. They were also less likely to see participation as a contribution to the wider community. Hispanic adults voiced more concern about time, unwelcome health news, and the use of their data against them. The differences were small, the team notes, but they can guide how studies conduct outreach.
pmc-11692221:
Alma Hernández de Jesús and co-authors present a 2024 study on how family doctors involve relatives in dementia care. Family members often spot the first signs of memory loss and carry much of the daily care. The authors interviewed eighteen family physicians across the United States about how they work with families.

Doctors said strong, open contact with family shaped care at every stage. Relatives helped reach an early diagnosis by reporting changes they had seen. They joined talks about goals, keeping the patient at home, and respecting the patient's wishes. Physicians also taught families about the disease and linked them to resources. Tricky family dynamics sometimes needed the doctor's help as a go-between.
pmc-11696621:
Joe Jabre shows how a chatbot-written script automates a trick for finding normal values in nerve test data, in a 2024 paper. The e-norms method extracts healthy reference ranges from mixed patient datasets, which contain both normal and abnormal studies. It matches traditional healthy-volunteer norms well, but one step, spotting the plateau where normal values lie, was done by eye through an old spreadsheet macro. Jabre had ChatGPT write a Python script to find the plateau automatically.

The script's normal values compared favorably with the visual method's. Automating a judgment call makes the method faster and more consistent across labs. The paper doubles as a case study in clinicians using AI to write working code for a niche, real task.
pmc-11698921:
New cell therapies that aim T cells at cancer can also strain the heart. Malak Munir, Ahmed Sayed, Daniel Addison, and Narendranath Epperla review the toll in 2024. Three cures fall in scope: lab-armed T cells, bridge drugs that link T cells to cancer, and T cells pulled from the tumor itself. Reports tie them to racing or wild heartbeats, weak pumping, heart swelling, and bleeds. Such events now cap how long folk live after the cures work.

The review sorts rates, risk traits, and care steps for each ill. A storm of immune signals explains part of the harm, but not all of it. Gaps the team flag include which hearts are at risk before treatment and how to guard them. They call for heart checks to be built into these cures from the start.
pmc-11700221:
More rehab after leaving hospital did not clearly lift quality of life for intensive care survivors, finds a 2024 review and meta-analysis by Motohiro Shimizu and co-authors. The team gathered randomized trials of stepped up rehabilitation started after discharge, searching six databases and two trial registries up to early 2024.

Nine trials fed the pooled estimates for the physical and mental halves of a standard quality of life scale, plus harms. Bias and certainty were graded with standard tools. The authors frame the work as the current state of the evidence: whether extra sessions, longer programs, or tighter protocols help survivors is still an open question.
pmc-11705621:
A team of doctors compares meditation with counselling for burned-out health workers in a paper from 2024. Burnout and mental strain are common among healthcare providers. One group of about one hundred workers practiced rajyoga meditation for three months. A similar group received stress management counselling and weekly positive messages. Both groups took mental health scales and heart tracings over twelve weeks.

The meditation group improved more on depression, anxiety, stress, and burnout scores. Burnout rates fell visit by visit in that group while satisfaction rose. A machine learning step could also spot burnout from raw heart tracing data. The authors suggest meditation as a practical support, with heart data aiding early detection.
pmc-11706721:
Zhibin Liu and Myoung Ok Kim published a review in twenty twenty-four on treatment strategies for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. The cancer is common worldwide and concentrated in Asia, with China carrying over half the global burden. Surgery remains the main treatment for locally advanced disease, often joined by chemotherapy and radiation.

The review tracks how precision medicine has added targeted drugs and immune therapies to that backbone. It also confronts the stubborn problems: treatments that work only modestly and tumors that learn resistance. Mapping the current landscape, the authors argue, is the first step to sequencing old and new tools better. Their perspective aims at raising outcomes in a cancer that still kills most patients.
pmc-11709621:
Timothy Ciesielski and co-authors hunted for signs of recent natural selection around APOE, the gene whose variants shape Alzheimer's risk. Risk and the strength of the famous APOE-4 variant differ by ancestry, hinting that evolution may have acted differently in different groups. The team scanned chromosome data from over two thousand five hundred people in twenty-six populations.

Neither of the two variant sites that define the APOE forms showed selection anywhere. But several regulatory sites that control APOE did: nine ranked in the top one percent on one selection score. Two sites stood out on both scores, one in Kinh Vietnamese and one in Han Chinese samples. The authors suggest selection at a control site may sharpen APOE-4's effect in the Vietnamese group.
pmc-11709721:
Andrew Ho and ten co-authors published a 2025 study of brain changes in 128 people who had mild cognitive impairment before death. Mild impairment can affect memory alone or several thinking skills at once. The team compared these patterns with the diseases found in the brain at autopsy.

Alzheimer’s pathology appeared at similar rates in memory-type and other-type cases. The memory-type group was older at death and showed more small strokes deep in the brain and more tangles in one region. Vessel damage, including worn white matter and protein buildup in vessel walls, was common in both groups. The findings show that similar symptoms can rest on quite different mixtures of brain disease.
pmc-11710121:
Morteza P Kouhsar and co-authors share a 2025 conference abstract on DNA methylation and psychosis in Alzheimer's disease. Delusions and hallucinations strike about forty percent of patients over the disease course, and this subgroup shows a distinct biology. The team built methylation networks from 153 post-mortem frontal cortex samples.

Five methylation modules tracked with psychosis in the first cohort, and one of them replicated in a second cohort. That module was rich in T cell receptor signaling genes. It also shared gene regions linked to schizophrenia and years of schooling. The authors argue that these molecular splits could guide tailored treatment for patients with psychosis.
pmc-11710221:
