Lei Chen and co-authors present a 2025 conference abstract on walking speed and executive function in people who feel their memory slipping. Slow gait and weak planning skills often travel together in early decline. The team recruited patients at a hospital in Chengdu, China, with either felt decline or mild impairment.

The sample held 63 people with felt decline and 23 with mild impairment. Each person took memory and thinking tests plus a ten-meter walk. Walking speed tracked with schooling, global scores, word fluency, and processing speed in the full group. Within the felt-decline group, speed tracked mainly with processing speed and age.
pmc-11710421:
Mahsa Shanaki Bavarsad and co-authors present a 2025 tissue study that maps a protein tied to cell contacts in the human brain. Loss of contacts is a strong sign of decline, and new scans aim to track it in life. The scan target is a protein on the small sacs that nerve cells use to send signals.

They stained and scanned slices from donor brains with distinct brain diseases and from healthy donors. They also ran protein tests on frozen tissue from the same cases. Levels of the target protein fell in all disease groups, with patterns by area and disease. A second contact protein did not track as closely as hoped. The authors back the target but urge more checks.
pmc-11710821:
Gleb Bezgin and co-authors present a new way to map tau tangles in a 2025 methods report. Tau tangles build up inside brain cells in Alzheimer's disease and spread in a set pattern over time. Their method, called Manifold Component Analysis, lays that spread out as a simple two-dimensional profile for each person.

The team applied the method to tau scans from 753 people in the TRIAD cohort. Profiles showed the biggest change, about a quarter, at the middle spread stages. Each thinking test matched a distinct spatial pattern in the profiles. Memory scores tied to early stages, while higher skills tied to later ones. The authors offer the method as a fast lookup tool for tracking disease stage.
pmc-11712521:
Allison Caban-Holt and co-authors report what Black Americans told focus groups about donating their brains to research after death, in this 2025 paper. Brain donation drives Alzheimer's research, yet Black donors make up only about two percent of donations to the national coordinating center. The team wanted the reasons from the community itself.

Eighty-three adults joined groups in Florida, New York, North Carolina, and Ohio in late 2023. Awareness of how brain donation works was low, and many did not know it is separate from the organ donor mark on a driver's license. Many assumed donation would disfigure the body and rule out an open-casket funeral. Few had ever been asked to donate. Most were open to learning more and welcomed research led by Black scientists. Religion was not a major factor, but family agreement mattered. The findings will shape a community education program.
pmc-11712621:
Seung-Eon Roh and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a protein that marks active links between brain cells and fades early in Alzheimer's disease. The protein is made by one class of nerve cells and strengthens the grip of calming cells that keep brain rhythms in tune. Some of it later sheds into spinal fluid, where low levels track with worse memory.

Using a glowing form of the protein in mouse cortex, the team watched it move as they turned partner circuits up or down. Quieting the calming cells sped the protein's shedding, while waking them made it build up at the links. Daily swings in this traffic may help refresh the cell groups that store memories.
pmc-11713421:
Hannah Baumeister and co-authors build a data-driven model of brain shrinkage patterns in memory clinic patients, in this 2025 paper. Clinic patients differ widely in the cause of their aging problems. The authors ask whether distinct patterns of tissue loss appear in this mixed group, as they do in Alzheimer's disease.

The team applied a method that sorts patients into subtypes and stages at the same time. Their data came from eight hundred thirteen people in a German cohort, some healthy and some with noted decline. Brain scans supplied the measures of tissue loss. The authors test whether the patterns found hold up in new patients and carry clinical meaning.
pmc-11713621:
Jenna Adams and co-authors present a shared protocol in 2025 for marking brain regions on scans. The medial temporal lobe holds small areas that fail at different rates in Alzheimer's disease. Research groups have drawn these areas in their own ways, so their results are hard to compare. A working group of many labs set out to build one common method grounded in real tissue.

Four experts marked stained tissue slices from three human specimens. They charted four areas, from the front to the back of the lobe, and checked where their marks agreed. Shared landmarks then set the range for each area on scans. A single shared method should make studies from different labs easier to compare.
pmc-11715421:
Paul F Hill and three co-authors split memory for place into two parts: whether a thing is recalled at all, and how crisp the recall is. Plain pass-fail tests merge the two, which can hide fine loss. Their task asked folk to place seen items back on a ring with a dial. A stats model then read both parts from the gap between the true and placed spots.

Thirty-five healthy older adults and nine with mild thought loss played five rounds. The mild group scored lower on both parts than the healthy group. Crispness also swung a lot from person to person, apart from plain recall scores. It did not track scores on the word and space tests in clinic use. In a scanned subset, work in the memory zone during learning foretold later crispness. The split may give trials a finer gauge of early loss.
pmc-11725321:
Vít Škrhák and four colleagues introduce CryptoBench, a dataset and benchmark for cryptic protein binding sites, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Structure-based site predictors are usually trained on ligand-bound protein shapes. That flatters their performance, especially for cryptic sites that appear only in free proteins. A fair test needs unbound structures as the starting point.

The dataset assembles over eleven hundred structures from bound-unbound protein pairs. Pairs were grouped, clustered by sequence, and filtered for real binding-site change. Predefined cross-validation splits make it the largest cryptic-site dataset to date. Baseline tests compared a top structure-based detector, a general site predictor, and a new sequence-based network. The sequence approach, using protein language model embeddings, outperformed expectations. The authors offer the benchmark to drive honest method development.
pmc-11726921:
David Fisman, Maarten Postma, Myron Levin, and Joaquin Mould-Quevedo review how flu and flu like illness drive missed work and lost output in adults across Europe and North America. Even healthy working age adults miss work when sick or when caring for others. The review came out in twenty twenty-four.

The authors drew on dozens of studies from Canada, Europe, and the United States. Lost time was worst for those with no flu shot, those under sixty-five, and those hit hard by illness. Care for sick kin added a large share of the loss. The review also weighs shots, age, and preventive drugs, and calls for more work on adults with other health issues.
pmc-11727421:
Aircraft telemetry links rely on error correcting codes set by the IRIG-106 standard, among them low-density parity-check codes tuned to the radio waveforms in use. Andrew Cummins, David Mitchell, and Erik Perrins ask whether randomly puncturing and shortening these codes can squeeze out more spectrum efficiency without losing reliability. Puncturing drops some coded bits and shortening fixes some data bits, and both reshape the code rate to fit the channel better. The authors focus on codes built for advanced range telemetry waveforms.

They analyze the code families mathematically to predict how the reshaped codes behave at large sizes, then run simulations to check real decoding. The simulations confirm the sturdy performance the design promises. pmc-11790221:

pmc-11793121:

pmc-11794221:

pmc-11806221:

pmc-11829121:
Amanda Ramdass and Sephra Rampersad read the full genome of a Serratia strain pulled from oil-soaked soil in work dated two thousand twenty-four. pmc-11936321:
Caryl Feldacker leads a team on hand data entry work in Malawi health care. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with a nurse led HIV care program. Mobile health apps and record systems often fail to link.

pmc-11975521:
Jingjing Wu and co-authors review a simple speed measure for judging how old a person's arteries are in a 2024 paper, published in Chinese with an English summary. pmc-11978421: Anna Annunziata and co-authors report a fifty-two-year-old man with the recessive form of Bethlem myopathy, a muscle disease marked by slow weakness and stiff, bent joints. pmc-12022621:
Malgorzata Pawlowska reviews hepatitis B in pregnancy and childhood as world elimination plans advance, in work from 2024. Stopping mother-to-child spread is a pillar of the global plan set in 2016. High virus loads in mothers call for drug cover late in pregnancy.

pmc-12078121:
Yuyan Fan, Ning Yang, Jialu Zhuo, and Ting Han test whether a blood inflammation score predicts how fast mild COVID-19 clears in this study published in 2024. pmc-12199921:

pmc-12506921:

pmc-12510721:

pmc-12722421:

pmc-12725621:

pmc-12728921:

pmc-12729221:

pmc-12732321:

pmc-12732821:
