pmc-12733021:
Roni Chaim Mukamal and co-authors published a qualitative study in twenty twenty-five on telemedicine for older adults with dementia, seen through their caregivers' eyes. Aging populations are swelling dementia numbers, and remote care promises better access and continuity. The study ran at a university hospital geriatrics service in Brazil.

Eleven caregivers of patients who had video consultations were interviewed and their answers analyzed thematically. Caregivers found telemedicine useful, reachable, and safe, and felt it strengthened their bond with the care team. Missing physical examination and occasional technical glitches were the main complaints. Most favored blending remote and in-person visits. The authors urge policies for digital inclusion and training on both sides of the screen.
pmc-12733321:
Mariana Carvalho de Menezes and colleagues reviewed food environment research in two thousand twenty-five. Their focus was low- and middle-income countries. Food systems shape population health through many pathways. They drive a linked syndemic of undernutrition, obesity, and climate change. Research in poorer countries lags behind richer ones.

 The review maps the state of the field there and aims to bridge that gap. Studying where people buy and eat food matters for policy. Such evidence can guide healthier food environments in places carrying a double burden of hunger and obesity.
pmc-12733721:
Sriharsha Talapaneni leads a team that reviews valve size mismatch. Their review from twenty twenty-five deals with aortic valve replacement. Mismatch means the new valve is too small for the body.

A small valve raises flow strain and harms heart reshaping. It can also cut how long a patient lives. The team searched two data sets for proof on this flaw. Both surgery and catheter valve paths are covered. Rates, flow effects, and fix plans are all summed up. Ways to dodge mismatch at implant time are stressed. Both open and catheter paths matter here.
pmc-12734521:
Avdeev leads a large team reporting light coupling work from twenty twenty-five. Photonic chips guide light on tiny paths and serve fields from telecoms to self driving cars. Getting light from a fiber into a chip path with low loss is a key hurdle.

The team reviews coupling methods and presents refined designs for silicon nitride chips. Their focus is inverse tapers built with a new fabrication method. The design works for both main light modes. Tests at a common infrared wavelength showed very low loss per chip edge for one fiber type. Low loss at this step helps the whole chip system waste less signal.
pmc-12735321:
Larissa de O Garcia and co-authors examine films of Prussian blue relatives grown by electric deposition, in a research paper from 2025. These open-framework materials suit batteries and other electrochemical uses because their chemistry can be tuned. The team grew films holding iron, cobalt, or nickel.

Electric tests showed each metal gave distinct charge behavior. Iron and cobalt films grew smooth and pyramid-shaped, while the nickel film cracked, with cube clusters on top. All shared the same cube crystal frame, shrinking steadily from iron to nickel. Inner chemistry shifted toward one iron state as the metal changed. The results show how metal choice sculpts these electrode films.
pmc-12735421: Tkaczyk opens a theme set on plant germ ills and their curbs in this twenty twenty-five note. Fungi, germs, cell bugs, and kin forms all strike crops and wild plants each year. Such ills rank high among threats to food stores, farm health, and green land balance. The set gathers work on how to spot these germs fast and how to hold their spread in check.
pmc-12738621:
Muhammed Aksu and co-authors study a cancer-linked protein in liver tumors in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The protein, YAP, helps control cell growth and is active in primary liver cancers. A chemical mark on one of its sites, set by a family of kinases, can switch it on.

Using mouse models, the team compared tumors carrying YAP forms with and without that mark. With the mark, bile duct type cancers were more common. Without it, tumors shifted toward the liver cell type. Gene tracing confirmed the different cells of origin. Two new transplantable cell lines with mixed features were also created. The authors point to a related signaling pathway as a possible treatment angle.
pmc-12739121:
Tang Li and Tao Shi present a 2025 study that turns old Chinese weather writings into fine climate data. Scribes logged frosts, snows, and cold snaps for centuries, but prose resists tidy coding. The team built a weather word lexicon by meaning clusters that grow as new terms appear. On that base they set a graded index that weighs storm force, farm harm, money harm, social harm, and deaths. Weights mix a math rule with expert calls.

Cold records from two far-apart provinces were then coded and charted. Their Qing-era trends match known climate work, with shared swings and clear local splits. A forest model checked the index and scored well. Archives of words can thus yield hard climate series.
pmc-12740421:
Haoran Deng, Xuchun Ding, Shiping Zhu, Xue Song, and Yufei Guo built a deep learning system to predict chronic lung disease early, in twenty twenty-five. The disease, COPD, is hard to catch soon enough, and past models used scattered data poorly. Their network fuses three streams: chest scans, lung function measures, and exposure data on the patient's surroundings.

A two-tower module lines up image and non-image features so they can be compared. A generative module fills gaps in exposure data, and a gating step reweights the streams by patient traits like smoking history and age. On a public COPD gene data set, the system scored an area under the curve of point nine two, with high catch and clearance rates. It beat single-stream models. The authors say the design can support precise early action.
pmc-12741121:
Letouzey and co-authors test, in a 2025 study, whether heat cameras can give an objective read on a newborn's condition in the first minutes of life. Doctors judge newborns with the Apgar score, which rests partly on the eye of the observer. Infrared thermography, which maps skin temperature without touch, might firm up that judgment. The team ran a feasibility study at a large maternity hospital.

They filmed 223 full-term babies born by cesarean across their first ten minutes, at four set times. Babies with low one-minute Apgar scores showed visibly different surface heat patterns at first, then warmed and converged with the stronger group over time. The authors stress that the study shows the method is workable as a side aid, not that it predicts outcomes. Larger, wider studies must come first.
pmc-12745321:
Diego García-Mata and co-authors study a hormone signal inside breast tumors in a 2025 paper. The hormone is adiponectin, made by fat tissue, and its receptor is a docking site on cells. The team asked whether levels of the hormone and its receptor differ between tumor tissue and the fat right beside it, in women past menopause with breast cancer.

Forty women took part, half with normal weight and half with obesity. Tumor tissue held more of the receptor than the nearby fat did, in both weight groups. The hormone itself showed no such gap. In women with obesity, fat near larger or more advanced tumors held more receptor than the same tissue in normal-weight women. The authors say the receptor, not the hormone, marks the tumor setting in this group.
pmc-12748121:
Annelaure Damont and co-authors tracked the full urine chemistry of mice fed a diet labeled with carbon-13, in a 2025 study. Tracing single pathways with labeled inputs is standard, but this team aimed at the whole metabolome at once. Three mice ate pellets made from labeled spirulina and wheat for six weeks, while three controls ate a normal diet.

All mice grew normally, and urine was collected daily. A high-grade instrument identified 238 metabolites without doubt by comparing labeled and plain samples. Whole-urine labeling passed 90 percent after 22 days, yet each single compound labeled at its own pace over the 39 days tracked. The work maps how fast body pools turn over.
pmc-12749321:
Irving Hernández-Prior and co-authors test diet change and nutrient supplements in people with Down syndrome, in work from 2025. People with the condition often face nutrient gaps, weak detox paths, and gut imbalance, yet these traits are poorly tracked. The team used records from an institute in Mexico City.

A panel of 121 blood and body markers was read before and after ten months of care. One group cut certain foods only, while the other also took supplements. Most marker shifts came with the combined plan. Signs of gut overgrowth by bacteria and fungi fell under that plan. The authors say diet plus supplements can shift the body profile in this group, and call for controlled trials.
pmc-12752221:
Fatokun and six co-authors reviewed heart risks of cancer care in Africa for this paper from twenty twenty-five. Cancer cases on the continent topped one million in twenty twenty-two and may double by twenty forty. Combination therapies save lives but can damage the heart. The review asks what that means for African patients and systems.

Several drug families are tied to weak heart muscle, inflammation, or artery spasm. African care faces late diagnosis, scarce screening, and thin trial representation. Poverty and other illnesses compound the strain. The authors call for cardio-oncology programs inside cancer centers. Earlier screening and better access to heart care top their list of fixes.
pmc-12752321:
Osama Alkhatib, a solo author, reports two cases of gum and mouth lining harm tied to nicotine pouches, in a 2025 paper. The pouches, sold as a tobacco-free swap for snuff, have spread fast since 2019, yet mouth effects are barely logged. Two healthy young men showed harm exactly where they parked their pouches. One, after eleven months of daily use, had gum recession and a white patch at a canine tooth. The other, after eighteen months, had gum recession near the back teeth.

Checks ruled out wide gum disease, bite strain, and hard brushing in both cases. The white patch raises concern, since like lesions in snuff users can turn precancerous, though no biopsy was taken. The author urges dentists to ask about pouch use and to biopsy odd patches. Users, he says, should be told to quit before harm deepens.
pmc-12752421:
Yijing Xin, Xifeng Qian, and Yanmin Yang studied muscle loss with obesity in two thousand twenty-five. The combined condition is called sarcopenic obesity. It may accelerate heart, kidney, and metabolic syndrome. A Chinese aging study supplied nine years of data. Muscle status followed Asian expert criteria. Heart events were tracked prospectively afterward.

Thousands of older participants entered the analysis. Sarcopenic obesity linked to far more advanced syndrome stages. Related body patterns showed similar strong links. The reference group had healthy muscle and weight. Event risk analysis used survival models over time. Preserving muscle in older adults looks vital. Weight alone misses this compounding danger.
pmc-12752821:
Oliveira and co-authors recheck colon growths under newer rules to see how many mild polyps were really serrated lesions, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Three hundred eight growths from the upper colon, cut between two thousand five and two thousand fifteen, were re-read. A repair gene's protein was stained in the kept lesions.

About thirteen percent of mild calls rose to serrated lesions on review. No missed cancer-like change turned up. Judge agreement swung from fair to none across pairs, a sobering spread. All checked lesions kept the repair protein switched on. Readers get a measure of how much names drift moves diagnoses.
pmc-12753621:
Akmal Zubair and Safa Wdidi review four new cancer strategies and weigh real promise against hype, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The four are personal vaccines, immune therapy, gene editing with CRISPR, and therapy with bacteria. Trials were gathered from four major databases.

Personal vaccines train the immune system on marks unique to one patient's tumor. Immune drugs help some patients a lot and others little, the review notes. Bacteria can shrink tumors and carry drugs to them, while gene editing can fix tumor mutations but is not yet ready for routine human use. Harm to healthy tissue and drug resistance still block all four. Readers get a balanced map.
pmc-12757121:
Quan Zou, Mengting Niu, and Xiaoqing Ru introduce a set of studies in a twenty twenty-five editorial. The topic is circular RNAs, short pieces of genetic material that form closed loops. These loops resist being broken down, so they last well in the body. Many of them show up in set patterns that differ by tissue and by disease.

Circular RNAs can be found in blood, urine, and other body fluids. That makes them strong candidates for tests that spot or track disease. The editorial sums up six studies in the set, both new work and reviews. Together, they use many data types and computer methods to place these molecules in a wider frame.
pmc-12764221:
Jonathan Philip Chung and Robert Andrew Paul published this study in 2025. It compares two Zeiss laser systems for fixing nearsightedness. The procedure carves a thin lens of tissue inside the cornea, which is then removed to reshape the eye. A private clinic in Western Australia reviewed fifty procedures done on each system, the older VisuMax 500 and the newer 800. Vision and refraction were checked before surgery and one month after.

Both systems gave similar vision gains and similar final prescriptions. Safety profiles showed no meaningful gap. The newer machine's real edge was speed: suction time fell from an average of thirty-four seconds to thirteen. One suction loss occurred, in the older group. The authors call for larger studies over longer follow-up before firm verdicts.
pmc-12765321:
Yaru Quan, Huijie Yang, Wei Li, and Linxian Li review immunogenicity and quality traits of messenger RNA vaccines. Their 2025 piece says that quality control must rest on traits that are key for quality, known as critical quality attributes.

The team works through key traits in a set way. They look at how each trait shapes how well a vaccine can bring on an immune response. They set out the tech rules at its base, where work on it stands now, and key items for quality control. They also set out what those items mean, and the signs used to gauge the immune response. A core theme is the need to study how the quality traits link to that response. That link, they say, is at the base of work to keep both efficacy and safety in place, as the platform grows fast.
pmc-12770321:
Yiqiu Han and colleagues challenge a basic rule of thumb in physics: that ordered states of matter melt away at high temperature. Ice, magnets, and superfluids all lose their order when heated enough. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team builds explicit local models in which ordered phases survive to any temperature, however high. The trick is a trade: order in one part of the system frees another part to fluctuate wildly, and that extra disorder pays the entropy cost of keeping order.

Their construction uses interacting bosons and sidesteps known theorems that ban long-range order or entanglement at high temperature. As a demonstration, they sketch a simple model of high-temperature superconductivity built on the same principle. The work reframes heat not as a universal enemy of order, but as a resource that the right coupling can spend.
pmc-12780721:
Dan Liu and co-authors ask whether more chemotherapy after surgery helps stomach cancer patients who already had it before surgery, in a 2025 study. The team reviewed records of patients who had drug treatment, then radical surgery. After matching like with like, 180 patients remained: 116 who got further chemotherapy and 64 who did not. Overall survival did not differ between the groups.

No subgroup by tumor depth, spread, or response gained from the extra drugs either. One tissue feature changed the story: mature tertiary lymphoid structures in the tumor bed. Patients lacking them lived longer with the extra chemotherapy, while patients who had them did better without it. Statistical tests confirmed the treatment effect hinged on that feature. The authors propose it as a guide for who should get more treatment.
pmc-12781721:
Lei Wang and co-authors reviewed ketogenic diets as an aid against cancer treatment resistance in two thousand twenty-five. Many cancers rely on fermenting glucose even when oxygen is present, a trait called the Warburg effect. A ketogenic diet is high in fat and low in carbohydrate, which shifts body metabolism.

That shift may starve malignant cells while sparing normal tissue, the review argues. Early animal and small human studies link the diet to weaker growth signaling and better response to chemotherapy and targeted drugs. It may also ease inflammation and alter gene marks. But large randomized trials are still sparse, adherence is hard, and standard protocols are not yet set.
pmc-12784521:
Xiang Li and eight co-authors build a prediction tool for a severe sepsis effect in a study from twenty twenty-five. Sepsis can weaken the heart muscle for a time, a state tied to high short term death risk. Standard scores miss much of its complex pattern.

The team studied more than a thousand adults with this condition from a large care database. About one in five died within twenty-eight days after intensive care. They screened risk traits with three methods, then built and compared eight machine learning models. Curves and decision tests judged how well each model sorted risk. The aim is a sharper tool for early care choices.
pmc-12785521:
Natalya Bondar and colleagues map epigenetic marks in mouse brains after social defeat stress of different lengths. Their study from twenty twenty-five compares ten and thirty days of stress. Stress disorders like depression resist simple molecular explanation. Duration may matter as much as stress itself.

Thirty days produced stronger depressive-like behaviour in the mice. A key activating histone mark was mapped across the prefrontal cortex. Changes were slight but spread over many sites. Earlier fifteen-day data and gene activity data were integrated. Promoter regions showed duration-dependent mark shifts. Longer stress rewires gene control more deeply, it seems. Timing could guide when interventions work best.
pmc-12800221:
Justin Slager and co-authors score cancer cell state changes from pictures of their organelles. The epithelial-mesenchymal shift helps tumors spread and resist drugs. No easy gauge existed for in-between states along that path. Cell Painting images plus fast microscopy fed a boosting classifier instead.

The model learned stage-by-stage organelle reshaping as breast cells shifted under a growth signal. It tracked the shift's timing, its halfway states, and its reversal. Human breast and lung cancer cells scored correctly under new triggers like low oxygen. The method thus travels across species, inducers, and cancer types. A screening platform for resistance-breaking drugs is the prize.
pmc-12812721:
Hou, Jiang, Wang, Yang, and Zhang packaged garlic oil into nanodisks for lung injury in this study from twenty twenty-five. Garlic oil fights inflammation and oxidation but dissolves poorly in water. The team loaded it into flat nanoparticles about one hundred fifty nanometers wide. Mice with chemically induced lung injury received the disks by vein.

Disk-treated mice showed cleaner lung tissue than untreated injured ones. Inflammatory factors dropped and oxidative stress markers improved. A protective pathway switched on while an inflammatory one switched off. The disks beat plain garlic oil at the same dose. About fifty-five percent of the oil was successfully encapsulated. The authors offer the design as a template for other oily drugs.
pmc-12812921:
Wan, Huang, Kong, Li, and Lu analyze gut microbes in children with global developmental delay, dated twenty twenty-five in the head. Global developmental delay means a young child falls behind in several skill areas at once. Causes are diverse and often unclear.

The gut microbiota composition and function of affected children were profiled and compared. The gut brain axis is a growing research theme in child development. Distinct microbial patterns, if confirmed, could suggest dietary or probiotic support routes. The study adds data from an area where microbiome research in developmental conditions is still thin.
pmc-12816021:
Akanksha Gajbhiye and ten co-authors traced how kidney damage from a chemotherapy drug leads to hearing loss in mice, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Hearing loss is far more common in people with chronic kidney disease, but the link's mechanism was murky. The drug model reliably injures kidneys in a pattern like human disease.

Treated mice developed severe kidney injury and, weeks later, clear hearing loss on two tests. Sound-sensing cells died and their connections withered. The ear's inner barrier grew leaky, its lining cells changed, and ion channels shifted. A kidney injury protein surged in the ear too, alongside an inflammation switch. The authors name barrier breakdown and that protein as key links between the two organs' failures.
pmc-12820321:
Kamyar Mazloum Jalali and Elahe Mosayebnejad Roudbaneh hunt new mutations in a hepatitis B virus gene in a 2025 study. The virus's HBx protein helps it persist and is tied to liver cancer, yet its variation in Middle Eastern patients is little mapped. The team screened the HBx region in fifty Iranian patients with chronic infection and sequenced four samples with distinct screening profiles.

Several changes appeared, including two glycine swaps and a proline swap never reported before; changes at one glycine position recurred across samples. Computer models of the protein hinted at small shape shifts near control regions. The authors stress the modeling is preliminary. Even so, a regional mutation map guides surveillance of a cancer-linked virus.
pmc-12820521:
Yinghui Wei and a large team of co-authors study who gets a formal long COVID code in health records in England in two thousand twenty-five. Long COVID is the lasting illness that can follow a COVID infection. Codes in records are known to miss many cases, so who gets coded shapes what the data seem to say.

The study used a secure platform that holds records for near eighteen million adults. Only a small share, about two in a thousand, had a long COVID code by March of two thousand twenty-two. Coded cases were more often women, adults under sixty, people with obesity, and people who saw doctors more often. The results warn that coded counts reflect care patterns as well as illness.
pmc-12822121:
Yueying Li reflects on her own decade with eating disorders to show how Chinese culture and state pressures shape the illness in women, in work from twenty twenty-five. Eating disorders are rising among Chinese women, yet most research frames them through Western psychiatry. Lived experience in a non Western setting is rarely centered.

Beauty pressure, fierce competition, and Confucian gender norms stood out as social drivers. Care itself is hampered by scarce psychiatric resources, trauma blind treatment, deep stigma, and a long moral framing of food and waste. Li argues the disorders mirror wider tensions of gender and governance, not just private psychology. Recovery, in her view, also means reclaiming selfhood beyond those constraints.
pmc-12829221:
Qian and co-authors map chemical changes in the blood of patients with NK/T-cell lymphoma. Shifts in cell metabolism are a known mark of this cancer, but the full blood picture was unclear. The team used a broad, untargeted scan of plasma from 92 patients and 28 healthy controls. The method paired liquid chromatography with high-resolution mass spectrometry.

Blood profiles differed clearly between patients and healthy people. The changed compounds clustered in purine, arginine, proline, and pyrimidine pathways. Three compounds were combined into a test model with good diagnostic performance. The authors suggest such a blood test could aid early, non-invasive screening for the disease. More work would be needed before clinic use.
pmc-12830521:
Jiawei Zhang and co-authors mine single cell data for natural killer cell marker genes and build a breast cancer outlook score from them, in work from twenty twenty-five. Killer cells patrol tumors and can speed or slow growth. Their exact weight in breast cancer was murky.

Twenty-nine marker genes emerged from single cell sequencing of breast tumors. Machine learning turned them into a risk model on a large cancer atlas set. The model predicted survival well there and on an outside gene data set. High and low risk groups differed sharply in immune cell makeup. Enrichment checks backed the split. The authors offer the signature as a guide for therapy planning and target hunting.
pmc-12830721:
Amani Arjan and four co-authors studied foot infections in people with diabetes at referral hospitals in the northern West Bank, Palestine, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. The team read the charts of patients treated in two thousand twenty-two at Rafidia Surgical Hospital in Nablus. They logged which germs grew from the wounds and which drugs still worked against them.

Gram-negative germs caused more cases than gram-positive ones. The top three were Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Many strains resisted key drugs, and some resisted several drug classes at once. Longer infections and longer hospital stays went with a higher risk of amputation. The team calls for early care, well-chosen drugs, and steady local checks on drug resistance.
pmc-12830821:
Tudor Selescu leads an eleven-author team showing that the wet dog shake depends on a cold-sensing molecule, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Shaking water from fur or feathers helps warm-blooded animals thermoregulate. The behavior is well described in mammals, less so in birds.

The molecule is TRPM8, the main cold transducer in mammals. A new TRPM8 activator triggered shaking in rodents and in birds, mimicking water spray. Sprayed mice lacking normal TRPM8 function shook later, proving dependence. Both lineages apparently converged on the same sensor for cold wetness. The authors argue evolution reused one molecular solution for a shared physical problem: getting dry before getting cold.
pmc-12830921:
Liča Lozica and co-authors report in two thousand twenty-five the first known circovirus infection in Croatia's Eurasian griffon vultures. Circoviruses infect many birds; the best known causes beak and feather disease in parrots and spreads through trade. Griffon vultures are endangered, and Croatia's population is the country's last vulture species.

Several young vultures at a rescue center on the island of Cres showed feather damage like the parrot disease: retained sheaths, discolored and pinched shafts, gnawed tips, and feather loss. Lab tests on feathers confirmed a circovirus, and blood work fit a viral infection. Two chewing louse species were also found on the birds, both known from this vulture before. The authors flag the finding for conservation monitoring.
pmc-12831521:
Bruna Rodrigues Barbosa and co-authors report a rare case of brain inflammation caused by human herpesvirus 6 in an elderly man with a healthy immune system. Their case report appeared in 2025. The virus infects nearly everyone in childhood and usually harms only people with weak immunity. The patient, aged 84, had well-controlled diabetes and past treated cancers but no immune suppression. He developed worsening unsteadiness and bouts of double vision, with signs of body-wide inflammation.

Spinal fluid testing found the virus's DNA. Antiviral treatment brought complete recovery of his nerve function. The authors warn that the test needs care: some people carry the virus woven into their chromosomes, which can mimic active infection. They urge doctors to consider this virus in older adults with unexplained decline.
pmc-12836821:
Yun Ren and co-authors expose mice to high heat and study what it does to male fertility in 2025. The work links hotter weather, as the climate warms, to damage in the testes and in sperm. It gives a lab model for a harm that is hard to study directly in people.

Heat-exposed mice ate and drank less and lost weight, and their testes and sperm stores shrank. Sperm counts, survival, and membrane health all fell, while misshapen sperm rose. Two genes that shape the sperm tail dropped, and more cells died by a self-destruct path. Chemical signs of cell stress also worsened. The authors say heat harms reproduction at many levels at once.
pmc-12837321:
Yanshuang Jiang and Yuxuan Liu built and checked a survey scale for student engagement in language classes where students learn with computers as partners, in a study published in 2025. Seven hundred ten junior high students in Mongolian-language schooling took part. Engagement in such mixed human and machine settings had no well-tested measure.

The authors drafted items from past research and interviews, then tested them in two waves. The final scale has five parts: deep thinking, talk with the teacher, work with the computer, active group learning, and enthusiasm for learning. Statistical checks confirmed the five-part shape and showed strong consistency across items. The scale gives teachers and researchers a trusted way to gauge how such classes are working.
pmc-12838421:
Shaowen Wang and six co-authors build a forecast model for glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumor, and land on two candidate marker genes. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. Survival stays poor, current markers are not exact, and tumors resist drug therapy.

The team mined gene data from tumors and healthy brain in public atlases. A fourteen-gene signature, built through layered statistical selection, split patients into high and low risk groups. An outside cohort confirmed the split. High and low groups also differed in mutation patterns and immune cell mix. Deeper checks flagged two genes tied to a form of cell death called ferroptosis. Tests in tumor cells and a mouse model probed their effect on sensitivity to that death path.
pmc-12839221:
Olesia Kalmukova and eleven colleagues tested whether melatonin protects kidneys in rats fed a fattening diet. Obesity injures kidneys partly by scrambling circadian rhythms and raising oxidative stress. Melatonin, the body's own clock regulator, might counter both. Male rats ate normal or high-calorie food for six weeks. They then received melatonin in drinking water or plain vehicle for seven more weeks.

Obese rats developed belly fat, kidney enlargement, scarring, and tubular damage, with raised injury markers. Melatonin softened the scarring and lowered several damage signals. It also improved tubule and glomerular injury and cut inflammatory signals in fat. In lean rats it shifted a clock protein in kidney cell nuclei. The twenty twenty-five study supports melatonin as a candidate shield against diet-driven kidney damage.
pmc-12849621:
Tsz Ho Kwan, Denise Pui Chung Chan, and Shui Shan Lee present a 2025 survey of HIV prevention pill use in Hong Kong. The pills, called PrEP, stop HIV infection when taken ahead of risk. Most users take daily pills, but long-acting shots are in growth. In Hong Kong the pills get no public subsidy. The team asked how many men who have sex with men use PrEP and what shot options they would pick.

An online survey drew 437 replies from adult men in the city without HIV. About 17 percent had ever used PrEP, and 16 percent used it now. Current users tended to earn more and to report higher-risk sex patterns. Past users who had stopped gave reasons the team also tracked. The results show cost and access gaps that local health planners can act on.
pmc-12852921:
Saubi, Jamisola, Suglo, and Matsebe built a joint learner in twenty twenty-five to guess and tune rock break and ground shake in open-pit blasts. Data came from one hundred twenty real blasts at a Botswana gem mine. Ten blast facts fed a set of model kinds tried side by side.

A paired net and forest blend won on both break and shake reads. Powder load and burden drove the break scores most in their checks. A slope walk on the learned face found settings with fine break and low shake. Engineers can slide the facts and read the trade at once.
pmc-12853821:
Adrien Borgel and colleagues show two breast cancer subtype labels describe largely the same tumours. Their study from twenty twenty-five covers estrogen receptor negative cancers. Both subtypes are defined by androgen signalling activity. Different classifier systems, though, drew the groups separately.

Public and hospital datasets were classified both ways for comparison. Overlap between the two groups proved substantial. Shared tumours switched on androgen and growth pathways together. Tumours matching only one label carried more immune signals. A four-gene signature captured the overlapping group well. The test worked on fresh and preserved samples alike. Clearer subtype borders should improve trial design and treatment choice.
pmc-12876221:
Psoriasis makes skin grow too fast and draws in immune cells, and a protein called S100A4 is abundant in the diseased skin. Huiqin Wang and co-authors probe its role with mice bred to lack the gene, using a cream that triggers psoriasis-like lesions. The study appeared in 2025, though the catalog lists it under 2026. Single-cell gene data showed how each skin cell type changed with and without the protein.

Mice without S100A4 fared better, with less swelling of the skin layer and fewer immune cells moving in. A skin cell group tied to the disease shrank, and two flare signals, TNF and IL-17, quieted down. The team traced skin thickening to a switch involving the Klf9 and Krt15 genes, which the missing protein helped set right. Their results point to S100A4 as a driver of psoriasis and as a possible target for treatments.
pmc-12882221:
Yalemtsehay Debebe and three colleagues published an environmental study in two thousand twenty-five on bacteria that eat a common weedkiller. The herbicide 2,4-D washes easily into surface and ground water, so microbe cleanup is attractive. Termite mound soil in Ethiopia was the hunting ground.

Five bacterial isolates grew using the herbicide as their only food and energy source. The best performer was identified as Enterobacter cloacae. It tolerated a wide acidity and temperature range, thriving best in mildly acidic, cool conditions. Added to farm runoff water, it broke down over ninety percent of the herbicide, against under ten percent without it. The authors propose it for cleaning contaminated water.
pmc-12884421:
Meng Gong, Xiangting Wang, and Xiaolin Liang review RNAs that act as building parts of cell structures, not just as messages, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Ribosomal RNAs have long been known as ribosome parts. New finds add RNAs that form speckles, paraspeckles, the nucleolus, and even parts of the cell skeleton frame.

The first skeleton-forming RNA, tied to tubulin, anchors the new class the authors name. Each member RNA holds its own web of partner contacts. Knowing these parts clarifies normal cell life and hints at disease targets. Methods and open questions close the review. Readers meet RNA in a fresh role: as brick, not just blueprint.
pmc-12912321:
Jiarong Chen, Wanqing Wu, Tong Liu, and Shenda Hong present a 2024 study on rebuilding a full heart tracing from just one lead. A standard heart test uses twelve leads, but that setup is bulky and can bother patients. Wearable devices use one lead, yet they capture far less detail.

The team built a model that learns by hiding parts of the signal and guessing them back. From any single lead, their model rebuilds the full twelve lead tracing. They also built a test suite that checks the output at three levels: the raw signal, key features such as heart rate, and final diagnosis. Their model reached the best scores they report on these tests.
pmc-12982921:
Zhou and co-authors show a poplar gene that boosts salt tolerance, working through a stress hormone path. The gene, PagHB7a, belongs to a plant-only family of switch proteins. It was among the genes most switched on by salt in earlier poplar work. New tests confirm salt and the hormone ABA both raise its activity. ABA-linked switch proteins bind its control region directly. Poplars with extra copies of the gene handled salt far better.

Trees with the gene knocked out fared worse under salt. Gene-wide reads showed shifts in salt, hormone, and oxidation pathways. The results cast PagHB7a as a positive lever in the salt response. It is a candidate for breeding tougher trees.
pmc-12993521:
Fatima Ezzahra Atmani and a large team of co-authors turn sardine fish scales into a dye-hungry sponge for wastewater, in a two thousand twenty-six environmental materials paper. Textile dyes are persistent pollutants, and cheap biosorbents are in demand.

The scale material proved porous and rich in surface groups. It grabbed methylene blue and Congo red fast, reaching equilibrium within thirty minutes through chemisorption. Capacity topped out near one hundred eighty-eight milligrams per gram for Congo red and one hundred thirty for methylene blue, ranking among the best bio-derived adsorbents reported. Adsorption was spontaneous and exothermic, and the material regenerated well across cycles. The authors pitch fishery waste as treatment infrastructure.
pmc-13037621:
Pratiwi and a large team test if a growth hormone gene shapes laying and meat traits in local Indonesian chickens, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The gene is a natural candidate since it steers growth in many species. Local Kampung hens and Sentul roosters are valued native breeds. Breeders want gene markers that predict better birds.

They typed two cut sites in the gene across fifty-four birds. One site varied between birds, while the other did not. Neither site linked to egg timing, egg counts, or carcass weights. Added and dominant effects were also absent. Deep sequencing found two new small deletions in both breeds. The team concludes these sites do not steer the traits studied here.
pmc-13064721:
Stephen Saklad reviews how to solve common snags with long acting shot forms of mind drugs, in a 2025 journal article. The shots treat grave mental illness well, yet their use is tangled by timing and drug clash traps. A missed date can let signs break through.

The guide starts with the clock: set call and text nags, and kin in the plan, keep shots on time. Each drug has its own grace span past the due date, from a week to two. Past the span, catch up may mean a shot at once, pills as a bridge, or a full restart. Clash rules cover drugs that drain or swell the shot's level in blood. For shakes and unrest, the guide backs a dose cut or a switch to a calmer drug.
pmc-13081421:
Fatemeh TajikRostami and co-authors present a 2025 study on why rectal cancer patients respond differently to pre-surgery treatment. Chemotherapy and radiation before surgery, called neoadjuvant therapy, fully clear the tumor in some patients and not in others. The team compared gene activity between the two response groups.

Public gene data yielded 606 genes that differed between complete and incomplete responders. Network analysis pointed to five key genes at the center of the response pattern. Groups of biological terms tied to growth control also stood out. The authors argue that genetic variation between patients helps explain the split outcomes. Treatment gains, they suggest, will need a precision medicine approach that reads each tumor's profile.
pmc-13128621:
Qi Zhang and co-authors present a study the catalog lists under 2026. The topic is unresectable liver cancer, meaning surgery cannot remove it. One arm pairs artery chemoembolization with donafenib, a targeted drug. The other adds camrelizumab, an immune therapy antibody. The single-center records cover 278 patients treated from 2021 to 2024. Propensity matching then balances the groups at fifty-eight patients each.

Tumor response, time without growth, survival, and side effects are compared after matching. Regression models hunt for factors that predict outcomes. Liver cancer teams get a head-to-head read on whether adding immune therapy earns its cost and risk. Matching strips out the bias of doctors steering sicker patients to one arm. The triple-versus-double question is live in clinics now, so matched real-world data carry weight beside trial results.
pmc-13133221:
Punga and a large team found in twenty twenty-six that a little-known protein is part of a gene-muting team in cells. The team, named MIER, uses a cut tool to loosen packed genes so they can be read or shut. The new part helps that cut tool meet its lead protein.

When the gene for this part was fully cut out, packed genes changed how open they were. Cells also moved less well from place to place. In zebra fish, loss of the part harmed growth of the young in the egg. The team plans a new name for it that states its job.
pmc-13135421:
Julie Kurek, Cheyenne Falat, Laura Bontempo, and David Gatz present an emergency case of a toddler with a seizure, in two thousand twenty-six. The girl was nineteen months old and was brought in after a witnessed seizure. Seizures in young children alarm families and can have many causes, from mild to life-threatening.

The case walks through the possible causes one by one. History, the physical exam, lab tests, and imaging narrow the list step by step in the emergency setting. The final diagnosis comes as a surprise, and the authors reveal it only after the work-up. They then discuss the outcome and what the case teaches about sorting urgent causes from benign ones.
pmc-13135521:
In twenty twenty-six Arshad and a large team studied how clinics care for women with polycystic ovary syndrome. Guides urge a full check and clear teaching at a first visit. How clinics do this was not well known. The team looked at eight expert clinics in five lands. Staff talks set out staffing, referrals, and note keeping. They checked notes of over thirteen hundred first visits for tests guides call for.

Care changed a lot from clinic to clinic and land to land. Checks on mood were noted for only a few women. Teaching on long-term heart and weight risks was noted even less. Cash, team mix, and clinic setup drove most of the change. Clinics with full mixed teams kept to the guides more. The team says system shape, not staff judgment, explains most gaps. They urge stronger teams and better joint work.
pmc-13138621:
Linda Visser, Jan-Henning Ehm, and Janin Brandenburg present a study dated two thousand twenty-six on how school results and mental health move together in teenagers. Grades, anxiety and depression symptoms, and ADHD symptoms all link to each other. How the three change together over time was much less studied.

The team used a large United States study that followed nearly twelve thousand children from age nine or ten across four time points. School records and inner distress were related, but neither predicted later change in the other. ADHD symptoms tied to both. Depression symptoms, in turn, pointed to later falls in ADHD symptoms, a result the authors discuss with care.
pmc-13144421:
Hannes Kramml and a large team sequence, in twenty twenty-six, the genomes of three Clusia tree species to explain their diverse ways of doing a drought-proof form of photosynthesis. That form, crassulacean acid metabolism, splits carbon dioxide uptake and fixation in time, so leaves can keep stomata shut by day. Clusia spans weak, inducible, and strong versions of it, a rare range. Humboldt first noted the trait in this genus over two hundred years ago. Genome mechanisms behind the diversity were unknown.

Comparing the three genomes, the team finds genome doubling followed by transposon-driven return to two copies likely shaped the gene families involved. Genes for recycling a key carbon compound via leaf starch stand out. The work frames how these physiotypes, distinct metabolic styles, evolved.
pmc-13144821:
Hrvoje Budincevic and nine colleagues report seven years of stroke care data from a national registry in Croatia. The registry, called RES-Q, tracks how well hospitals treat stroke. Croatia joined the registry in two thousand seventeen. The team compared care in the first quarters of recent years.

Stroke centers across the country entered over five thousand patients. Clot-busting drug use rose from ten percent to about twenty percent over the period. Mechanical clot removal also climbed, reaching near fourteen percent of patients. Times from arrival to treatment improved as well. The authors note gaps in prevention care, such as statin use and help to quit smoking. A registry covering every center, they add, would sharpen the picture.
pmc-13156121:
Ji-Su Shim and co-authors measure the burden of chronic cough in South Korea in this 2026 study. Refractory or unexplained chronic cough resists standard treatment and lacks options. Seven referral clinics enrolled 200 patients prospectively. Half had the refractory type, and half had cough under one year.

Structured interviews and records covered quality of life, mood, work loss, and care use. Refractory patients were older and had coughed far longer, a median of 80 against 4 months. They also paid more out of pocket and used more tests, visits, and medicines. Quality of life scores, though, did not separate the groups clearly. Long duration itself drives cost and frustration. The CHORUS data quantify an unmet need for cough clinics.
pmc-13158421:
Junying Song, Yifu Zhu, Yufei Zhang, Zhou Yu, and Baoqiang Song pack neural stem cells into a hydrogel to heal diabetic wounds, in a 2026 study. Diabetic ulcers stall because their local environment turns hostile. Stem cells are prized healers, but neural stem cells had barely been tried on skin. In dishes, the cells boosted vessel growth, antioxidant strength, and energy health in vessel-lining cells.

The gel carrier proved gentle on the cells it held. Dressed on diabetic mice, the loaded gel sped closure, calmed inflammation, grew vessels, and supported nerve-friendly repair. The authors present the platform as a clinically plausible dressing that fixes the wound's environment while delivering living help.
pmc-13163521:
Paola Lima and six co-authors report a study in 2026 of loss and grief among Brazilian frontline health workers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Hospitals stretched work hours to meet surging demand, while many deaths left staff little time to grieve. The team interviewed twenty four frontline workers by phone in late 2024 and early 2025.

Using grounded theory, the authors built their account around a core theme of strain and strength in a war like setting. Workers described harm to health services, sudden deaths, and the absence of families at the bedside. The study shows how grief built up under crisis work, and what helped staff keep providing care despite exhaustion.
pmc-13163821:
Kun Wu and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on a computer system that grades knee alignment for joint replacement surgery. Surgeons sort knees into types by the angles of the thigh and shin bones. The type guides how a new joint should be set. By hand, the grading is slow, and no one had tracked how types shift from before surgery to after.

Their system reads X-rays and spots the bone points on its own, then works out the angles and type. On a held-out test set, its points landed close to hand marks and its type calls were right four times in five. In a group of more than nine hundred patients, fewer than one in ten kept their type after surgery. Most shifted to three types. Once base gaps were weighted out, no type shift group fared better in the short term.
pmc-13164721:
Yuki Tanaka and a large team of co-authors hunt for the blood zinc level that separates better from worse survival in liver cirrhosis, in a two thousand twenty-six hepatology paper. Zinc deficiency is common in cirrhosis, but its prognostic cutoff was unknown.

Among seven hundred twenty-one zinc-naive patients, survival worsened dose-dependently as zinc fell, and seventy micrograms per deciliter emerged as the threshold. Below it, matched zinc-treated patients lived a median of about eighty-six months against forty-eight untreated, with an adjusted hazard ratio of zero point six four. The authors suggest monitoring and supplementing to stay above the line, while demanding prospective trials to confirm.
pmc-13179921:
Imran Qureshi and co-authors study bowel cancer patients who had an earlier cancer in a 2026 paper. Bowel cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide, and it shares risk factors with other cancers. Using a national cancer database from 2004 to 2022, the team matched patients with and without a prior cancer so the groups were alike. More than half a million patients were included in total.

Patients with a prior cancer were less likely to show several aggressive tumor traits and advanced stage disease. They were slightly more likely to get treatment, but also faced more delays and readmissions after surgery. Overall death risk was higher for them, except in the earliest stage. Readers see why a cancer history should shape bowel cancer care plans.
pmc-13180121:
Abbas, Samlowski, and Hedayat report a single cancer case in twenty twenty-six. The patient had a rare fat tissue cancer that had spread to other sites. Such spread cancers in soft tissue often respond poorly to standard drugs. Responses, when they occur, tend to be brief.

The team added a drug called pembrolizumab to a drug the patient already took, pazopanib. This was the fourth line of treatment tried. The tumors shrank a lot after just five doses, with little harm from side effects. After fifteen doses, scans showed the response held, and a biopsy found no live cancer in a sampled lesion. The patient then stopped all treatment and stayed in remission. The authors suggest the pair merits more study.
pmc-13181321:
Ermyas Brhane Reda and colleagues published a 2026 nutrition survey from the Tahtay Maichew district of northern Ethiopia. Their subject was what children between six and twenty-three months old eat during a critical window for growth and brain development. Little local information existed on how varied those young diets are.

Mothers of nearly a thousand children recalled everything each child ate and drank during the previous day. The team then looked for household, demographic, and health-service factors linked with more varied diets. Findings like these help local health workers see which families most need support in feeding their youngest children a wider range of foods.
pmc-13181821:
Hicks, Magalhaes, and Bernard study a brain link that joins two key parts. One part helps store facts and find the way in space. The other part sits at the back of the head. Work in mice and rats shows the two parts fire at the same time. Both parts also hold lots of sex hormone sensors. In women, those hormone levels fall a lot at midlife.

Past work used small groups of young adults, so age gaps stayed unclear. The team asks how this link shifts across adult life. They also ask if sex and hormone change help shape the shift. Their aim is a fuller map of the link in grown men and women.
pmc-13182921:
Bacteria carry stowaway viruses in their DNA, and Dominique Holtappels, George Rickus, Túlio Morgan, Rafael de Rezende, Britt Koskella, and Poliane Alfenas-Zerbini survey those stowaways in a plant-attacking species group. They compared five hundred and eighty-seven genomes of the Pseudomonas syringae complex, cataloging defense systems, attack proteins, and the embedded viruses, called prophages.

The group held a rich shared arsenal: one hundred and thirty-nine defense mechanisms in all. Different virus families carried very different gene sets, so the perks a host gains depend on which viruses it hosts. Genes for attack and defense also move sideways between bacteria, riding these elements. The team says the pattern helps predict how such bacteria adapt to their surroundings.
pmc-13188121:
George Wang and six co-authors published a 2026 case series on a rare pattern of brain tumor spread: high-grade glioma reaching the dura, the tough membrane around the brain. Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive adult brain tumor, yet spread to the dura is exceedingly rare, partly because patients survive only briefly. The team presents four cases from one center and reviews the published literature.

The report details how this spread looks on MRI scans, a key need since the pattern is underreported. It also weighs how the tumor might reach the dura, and how such cases should be diagnosed and managed. The authors aim to help clinicians recognize the pattern when it appears, rather than mistaking it for a new tumor of the membrane itself.
pmc-13191521:
Renan Falcioni and co-authors compare albino and red poinsettia leaves to learn how plant color trades against photosynthesis. Their study appeared in 2026. Four tissues, white and green from pale plants, red and green from red plants, formed four distinct pigment-structure syndromes. Imaging, chemistry, gas exchange, and microscopy showed the showy bracts keep a working photosystem but hold few, poorly stacked chloroplasts and barely take up carbon.

Instead the bracts act as protective antioxidant sinks, spending light energy safely. The plain green leaves, especially on red plants, do the real feeding. The authors say breeding for color silently rewires the leaf's whole economy, splitting the jobs of display and dinner between tissues.
pmc-13193921:
A disease driven by antibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, a protein on the brain's insulation, can present as brain inflammation, and a common virus may be tangled up in it. Runzhe Chen and co-authors describe five newly diagnosed patients whose illness looked like encephalitis and whose lab tests also showed Epstein-Barr virus findings. Every patient tested positive for the disease antibody on a live cell based assay.

Treatment told a suggestive story: three patients' spinal fluid measures briefly improved on antiviral therapy, yet real clinical recovery came only after corticosteroids, at high or low dose. Harder cases needed added intravenous immunoglobulin or the drug tocilizumab. The authors read the pattern as a hint that virus driven immune activation can coexist with this disease rather than explain it outright. They stress the idea needs testing in larger, prospective studies before it guides care.
pmc-13197221:
Victoria Niven, Immanuel Sakkilian, Paul Harper, and Jennifer Gallagher model how dental teams can prevent tooth decay in children, in a 2026 paper. Decay stays common in England and hits poorer children hardest. The dental workforce holds several grades of staff, not just dentists. The team asked which mix of staff delivers proven preventive care with least time and fewest workers.

Their model drew on child population data, health service figures, and decay surveys. Guidance on best preventive care set the care steps, and past research set the timings. Six staffing mixes were compared in the model. Mixing dentists, dental therapists, and dental nurses with extra duties proved most efficient. The authors say skill mix could stretch preventive care to more children.
pmc-13197621:
Lingling Song and colleagues report a 2026 study on how a parasite harms the eye. Toxoplasma gondii infects about a third of the world's people. In the eye it can threaten sight, yet how it drives damage was unclear.

Infection pushed eye surface cells toward a state change linked to scarring and invasion, in both lab cells and mouse eyes. A parasite protein called ROP16 drove that shift by switching on two host signal paths. Parasites lacking the protein caused less change, while extra protein caused more. Blocking either signal path eased the cell shift and eye damage in mice. The paths are promising drug targets for this infection.
pmc-13198021:
Keita Tashiro and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a routine blood marker can forecast survival for one of colorectal cancer's grimmest presentations. Cancer already spread across the peritoneum when found. No international guideline currently endorses the marker, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, in colorectal practice. Even though tumor cells that cling strongly to peritoneal surfaces are known to express it heavily. A living hint that blood levels might carry prognostic information.

The study used two large Japanese cohorts. The first gathered just under seven hundred patients treated across sixteen hospitals in the nineteen nineties and two thousands. It set marker cut-off values by an information rule. That rule best separated survival results. With a second tumor marker treated in parallel. A prospectively registered checking cohort of well over one hundred patients from twenty-eight institutions then tested whether those cut-offs held up.
pmc-13200421:
Hyunji Park, Huso Yi, and Minah Park published this vaccine study in 2026 from South Korea. RSV is a top cause of lung illness in small children, and child vaccines for it are nearing use. The team asked what shapes parents' plans to vaccinate. They surveyed 402 parents of children aged five and under, testing a classic health belief model, then an extended one that adds vaccine hesitancy as its own outcome.

Seventeen percent of parents had no plan to vaccinate. In the plain model, felt risk and prompts to act carried knowledge into plans. In the extended model, prompts to act drove plans most, while felt blocks drove hesitancy most of all. Adding hesitancy made the model steadier and richer. The authors urge training for providers to talk through parents' doubts.
pmc-13201721:
Changing a single building block in a huge protein machine is technically hard, and a 2026 methods article authored by Adel Beghiah offers a workaround. The research article presents plasmid sub-fragmentation, a way to perform site-directed mutagenesis on large multi-subunit protein complexes by splitting their genes into short, manageable pieces.

The authors demonstrated the method on the genes for the E coli Complex I, a large respiratory enzyme. They divided a 15.1 kilobase sequence into twenty fragments of about nine hundred bases, mutated them with ordinary polymerases, and reassembled the pieces accurately. The approach promises easier functional studies of other large protein complexes with repeated subunits.
pmc-13202421:
A wound dressing that fights germs and reports wound acidity by changing color is presented in a 2026 materials study authored by Miaoshen Kou. The research article builds a hydrogel from silk fibroin and hyaluronic acid, using one plant-derived molecule, rhein, to supply every active function.

Laboratory tests showed the gel killed more than ninety-four percent of three bacterial types, including drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, in the reported assays. It also scavenged free radicals strongly and kept cultured cells healthy under the tested conditions. Its color shifted distinctly across the acidity range typical of wounds, which would let clinicians read wound status visually without separate sensors or electronics.
pmc-13202821:
Danassis and seven co-authors test a shared care plan for brain drains in a study from twenty twenty-six. External ventricular drains relieve fluid pressure in the brain, but they can bring a severe infection of the brain spaces. Vague diagnosis and mixed prevention habits may raise infection rates and drug use.

The study in a Berlin intensive care unit compared care before and after a joint standard plan was put in place. Adult patients with drains were split into the two time groups. The team tracked infection rates and antibiotic use. The aim was to see if one clear, shared plan could cut harm and spare drugs.
pmc-13203321:
Shaodong Zhong, Heng Zhang, and Jin Huang present a study the catalog lists under 2026. Stomach cancer kills many patients around the world, largely when it spreads. Spread needs cancer cells that can invade and move well. The team searched a large public cancer data set for genes tied to spread. They trace a chain of four linked genes and one signal path.

Gene scans and survival models picked the key genes from the data set. Lab tests, including blots and wound-healing tests, checked the chain in cells. The chain controls how strongly stomach cancer cells invade and move. It also links to how long patients live. Drug researchers get a named target chain rather than a loose gene list. Blocking a link in the chain could slow spread, though that step needs its own trials. The study joins big data with bench tests in one arc.
pmc-13203721:
Barley hay could replace poor-quality roughage in sheep diets, and a 2026 feeding study headed by Xiaoyuan Wang measures the trade-offs. The research article feeds forty-five young sheep diets in which barley hay replaces a quarter, half, three quarters, or all of their usual roughage, then tracks rumen fermentation and blood markers.

Barley hay encouraged fiber-degrading microbes in the rumen, which improved feed digestion in the flock. Blood tests also showed higher concentrations of protective immune proteins in the hay-fed animals. Although switching feed caused minor short-term stress signals, the full replacement diet performed best overall, and the authors recommend barley hay as a practical primary roughage.
pmc-13206621:
Tatiana Dragan and a large team survey health staff on the use of patient-reported outcome measures in head and neck cancer care, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. These cancers and their care can harm speech, swallowing, looks, and mood. Patient questionnaires can track those harms, yet routine use stays patchy. The team sent a thirty-item survey to staff across centers and got 133 replies.

About a third never used the measures, a third used them at times, and a third used them often. Users mostly handed out paper forms during treatment and early follow-up. The survey also weighed what staff see as the value of the tools and what blocks their spread. The authors call for easier, digital paths into daily care.
pmc-13206921:
Alma Diaz-Herreros and co-authors present a 2026 mouse study of a protein that may help control blood sugar in diabetes. The protein, pVHL, supports the cells in the pancreas that make insulin. Its levels fall in mice fed a rich diet that brings on type 2 diabetes. The team injected a virus carrying the gene for the protein straight into the pancreas. They then tracked blood sugar after sugar loads over fifteen days in two mouse strains.

Treated mice showed smaller rises in blood sugar than untreated diabetic mice. By the last day, levels of a stress-linked protein and one sugar transporter had fallen. Levels of a second transporter and of insulin itself had risen. Both mouse strains showed the same pattern of change. The authors read this as proof of concept that restoring the protein helps. Much more work would be needed before any use in people.
pmc-13211521:
Haoqing Yang and co-authors survey blood parasites in domestic chickens in southern China in a 2026 study. Three bird malaria-like parasites threaten poultry health, but their spread in the region was poorly mapped. The team collected 941 blood samples in Hunan and Guangxi between mid-2024 and late 2025.

Gene tests found infection in about a quarter of the birds. One species, Plasmodium juxtanucleare, dominated at about twenty-four percent, while a second appeared in under two percent and a third was absent. Birds older than ninety days carried more infection. Black-bone and partridge breeds were hit harder than three-yellow chickens. The gene sequences matched known strains closely. The authors urge steady monitoring and targeted control.
pmc-13212421:
Jeremy Tze En Lim and colleagues compare, in 2026, recovery after neck spine surgery between older and younger patients with degenerative cervical myelopathy. The operation removes a damaged disc from the front of the neck and fuses the bones, aiming to relieve spinal cord pressure.

Registry records covered 219 patients treated between 2005 and 2014, with only 31 aged seventy or more. Both groups improved substantially, and satisfaction rates were similar at two years. Older patients, though, gained less in neurological symptoms, neck disability, and physical quality of life, and stayed longer in hospital. Age seems to shrink the size of recovery rather than block it.
pmc-13213121:
Nihat Yiğit and co-authors compare in 2026 two treatments for broken wrists in frail older patients for whom anaesthesia itself is risky. One option sets the bone and holds it in a cast; the other fixes it surgically with a plate on the palm side.

Sixty patients aged sixty-five or more, all with serious health risks, were split evenly between the two treatments at one hospital. At six and twelve months, pain, wrist function, grip strength, and daily independence matched closely between groups. X-ray measures of bone angle favoured the plate slightly on two measures. For high-risk patients, the results suggest a cast can serve about as well as surgery.
pmc-13213621:
Hyun Wook Choi and colleagues announce in 2026 a boron version of the famous buckyball, the sixty-carbon soccer-ball molecule that launched nanoscience. Similar cages made of other elements had resisted discovery, because carbon's bonding is unusually suited to closed shells.

Firing electrons off clusters of eighty boron atoms produced a strikingly simple spectrum, the fingerprint of a highly symmetric structure with a healthy energy gap. Among candidate shapes, only the simulated buckyball matched the measurement. Its electronic structure and bonding closely echo the carbon original. Bulk synthesis becomes the next goal, and the authors foresee a new boron-fullerene chemistry growing from this eighty-atom cage.
pmc-13214321:
Mengistu Tesfa Alula and co-authors rechecked malaria tests in a 2026 study in northwest Ethiopia. Right diagnosis drives right care, blocks drug resistance, and cuts spread of the disease. Yet lab errors that call sick people well, or well people sick, stay a hidden load in regions where malaria is common.

The team retested routine cases from health centers with a lamp-based gene test that is more exact than standard checks. They then set the fresh results against the first calls made at each center. The gap shows how much wrong diagnosis the routine system hides. Their findings push for stronger lab checks in daily care.
pmc-13214921:
Victoria C. Sanfrancesco, Daniella Della Mea, and David A. Hood review in 2026 how muscle mitochondria talk back to the cell when stressed. Two quality-control programmes, the integrated stress response and the mitochondrial unfolded protein response, switch on protective genes through three master transcription factors.

Healthy skeletal muscle depends on a flexible mitochondrial network, yet the signals that start these programmes in muscle remain poorly charted. The review gathers evidence across exercise, ageing, and disuse, three states that stress the system in different ways. Gaps in the initiation steps stand out clearly. Filling them could yield therapies that keep muscle resilient when metabolism is pushed by disease or inactivity.
pmc-13215421:
Jip Martijn van Oostrum and co-authors report a 2026 Dutch qualitative study on using deepfake technology in grief treatment. Deepfakes can make a realistic moving image of a deceased person appear to speak.

After watching a video of a deepfake grief session, 159 bereaved people and 126 mental health workers each listed reasons for and against the method. Bereaved respondents saw a chance to say goodbye and feel close again. Professionals saw promise as an add-on to existing therapy yet warned about consent, misrepresentation, and clients growing dependent. Both groups backed careful, therapist-guided use with safeguards.
pmc-13218221:
Yang Liu and the BE-China registry investigators report how airway clearance techniques are used by bronchiectasis patients across China, in a 2026 multicentre cross-sectional study. Bronchiectasis permanently widens the airways, trapping mucus, and guidelines recommend clearance techniques to help patients cough it out. How often Chinese patients use these techniques, and who uses them, was unknown.

The registry gathered data from 9,647 patients at ninety-two hospitals between January 2020 and March 2024. Only 12.2 percent used airway clearance regularly at baseline, and use varied by region. Users tended to have longer disease duration, more severe disease, heavier cough and sputum, and more intensive drug and ventilatory treatment. Modeling tied use to comorbidity burden, daily sputum production, expectorant and antibiotic use, and noninvasive ventilation. A European registry showed the same pattern of heavier medication burden among users. The authors suggest clinicians target clearance training to the patient groups most likely to benefit.
pmc-13219021:
Andrea Guzmán-de Antonio and ten co-authors built a model to predict how fast kidney transplant patients clear the drug tacrolimus, in this 2026 study. The drug guards against organ rejection, but the right dose varies widely between patients. A simple ratio of drug level to dose and weight serves as a stand-in for how the body handles it.

The single-center study covered seventy-seven stable adult recipients. One gene variant, in a drug-processing gene, flagged fast clearers with high accuracy when positive but missed many of them. Adding age and time since transplant sharpened the model, while extra gene variants added little. The authors back a combined gene-plus-clinic approach to dosing, with wider testing still to come.
pmc-13219321:
Luote Dai, Saizhi Wang, and Jiajia Chen surveyed 452 Chinese university faculty on why feeling ownership of research might spark teaching innovation, in this 2026 study. The direct link, it turned out, was not there. Ownership paid off only by a side road: it strengthened academic identity, and that identity carried the effect into the classroom.

Support from the institution made the first link stronger, while professional identity did not change the second link. Effects ran strongest at research-oriented universities, weaker at applied and vocational schools. The authors advise leaders who want fresher teaching to feed researchers' sense of belonging to their academic role, not merely demand new methods.
pmc-13220121:
Joe Bradley and co-authors report a 2026 physics study on how to measure the tiny particles in milk. Milk holds fat drops and much smaller protein clusters called casein micelles, and most sizing tools cannot tell the two apart.

The team combined two methods on homogenised milk, meaning milk treated so the fat stays evenly mixed. A microscopy method tracked particle motion in the liquid, while a frozen-sample imaging method cut and viewed thin layers directly. Together they showed two overlapping size groups without first separating the milk. The authors note that different tools rarely give the same answer, so using both gives a fuller picture.
pmc-13222921:
Samy Selim and eight co-authors published this study in 2026. It squeezes a desert plant, Heliotropium arbainense, with supercritical carbon dioxide, a high-pressure method that pulls out plant chemicals without harsh solvents. The question is whether extraction pressure changes what comes out and how well it works.

Extracts made at higher pressure carried more of the prized phenolic and flavonoid compounds, led by gallic acid, and simply yielded more material. Both extracts killed a broad range of bacteria and a yeast, but the high-pressure one worked at lower doses. Against ovarian cancer cells in dishes, the high-pressure extract also proved more potent overall, though the low-pressure one triggered slightly more cell death of certain kinds and calmed inflammation a touch better. The authors conclude that pressure is a dial worth tuning when mining plants for useful compounds.
pmc-13223521:
Luz Alejandra Lorca and co-authors evaluate a frailty scale built for stem cell transplant candidates, in a 2026 prospective observational study from Chile. One hundred two patients with blood cancers completed the scale before transplantation. Items fall into objective, subjective, and laboratory groups, and the team tested consistency, structure, and whether scores matched clinical expectations.

About fifteen percent of patients classified as frail, nearly half as pre-frail, and the rest as fit, with multiple myeloma the commonest diagnosis. The scale's three dimensions explained most score variance. Only one validity hypothesis held: patients with poorer performance status scored frailer. Other comparisons across risk and age groups did not confirm, tempering the authors' endorsement.
pmc-13224421:
For womb cancer that has spread or returned, adding immune checkpoint drugs to chemotherapy has become a leading first-line plan.
