They split results by repair status of the tumor's DNA-proofreading system and by levels of a surface marker the immune drugs target. Growth delay and survival were the measures.

The combination delayed growth in every subgroup, whatever the repair status or marker level. Survival, though, improved clearly only in patients whose tumors had broken proofreading, where the risk of death fell by more than half. Patients with working proofreading gained no measurable survival benefit. The marker's level did not change who benefited. The authors conclude that proofreading status, more than the surface marker, should guide expectations for this treatment pairing.
pmc-13226821:
Marie Biedermann and colleagues present a 2026 case of a food-poisoning bacterium causing a life-threatening heart emergency. Campylobacter jejuni is the leading cause of bacterial diarrhoea, yet heart complications are rare. A 47-year-old man arrived with sudden chest pain and breathlessness, and ultrasound showed fluid squeezing the heart, a tamponade, alongside fluid around the lungs.

Although he reported no gut symptoms, laboratory analysis grew the bacterium from both the heart fluid and his stool. Growing it from pericardial fluid has been reported only three times before. Bloodstream spread in an otherwise healthy man is the likely route, and the authors warn that resistant strains complicate antibiotic choice in such invasive infections.
pmc-13229321:
Jiangxue Tian, Handong Li, Shuran Lv, and Peng Wu build a 2026 fire-risk forecasting system for urban villages, the dense, informally built neighbourhoods where fire hazard runs high. Their model pairs a long short-term memory neural network, tuned by an improved grey-wolf optimisation algorithm, with incremental learning that refreshes predictions without retraining from scratch. Real incident records from fifty-five Beijing urban villages trained and tested the system.

Prediction error fell by more than ninety percent compared with a standard network baseline. The authors report high accuracy, stability, and adaptability across the villages studied. Because the model updates as new incidents arrive, they propose it as a practical monitoring tool for fire services watching fast-changing, high-density districts.
pmc-13229921:
Tushar Saini and colleagues present in 2026 a forty-seven-year-old man whose blocked stomach outlet looked like duodenal cancer but was groove pancreatitis instead. He drank heavily, and scans plus camera views first suggested a primary tumor of the duodenum. The rare condition sits in the groove between the pancreas head, duodenum, and bile duct.

Biopsies found no cancer, and a team review settled on segmental groove pancreatitis using the typical scan pattern. Treatment stayed conservative with stomach drainage, acid control, pancreatic enzymes, nutrition support, and stopping alcohol. Both the blockage and the lesion cleared within seven days. Careful checks before major pancreas surgery can spare patients a very large operation when this mimic is the cause.
pmc-13230321:
Ana Luiza Rocha Soares Menegat and colleagues pool in 2026 early evidence on a new keyhole operation for belly wall hernias. The PeTEP method repairs the hernia from outside the belly cavity and can also address separated stomach muscles. Four studies with ninety-nine patients formed the whole evidence base.

Average operating time was a little over two hours in the pooled results. Blood collections appeared in about one in ten patients, and about one in five had some complication, none needing another procedure. Slight bulging showed in a small share of cases, and no hernia returned during short follow-up of one to twelve months. Longer head-to-head studies are needed before the method can be judged against older repairs.
pmc-13230621:
Junhyeok Jeong and colleagues report in 2026 evidence that a copper oxide superconductor sits between two classic pairing regimes. Underdoped cuprates show only arcs of the electronic surface, leaving open whether electrons pair weakly or form tight pairs early. The team studied clean inner layers of a four-layer cuprate with light-based and magnetic methods.

Measurements revealed a small electron pocket coexisting with a surprisingly large superconducting gap. Ratios tying the gap and the transition temperature to the pocket energy reached near the top values expected for flat superconductors. Oddly, the crossover appeared as carrier numbers rose, within a very narrow doping window. The result gives a concrete footing for theories of pairing in these doped insulating materials.
pmc-13231721:
Xianzhong Zhu and colleagues test in 2026 a receptor-activating compound against skin scarring in a mouse model of systemic sclerosis. In that disease, helper T cells of the follicular type help drive the scarring process. Mice received a scarring drug under the skin for four weeks, with half also given the compound Ficz on a regular schedule.

Treated mice grew thinner skin with less collagen and lower levels of several scarring genes. Their blood held fewer follicular helper T cells, and skin levels of a helper signal from those cells also fell. Staining confirmed the helper cells sat inside the skin lesions of untreated mice. Turning on that receptor may calm both the cells and the scarring together.
pmc-13232621:
Xue-Ting Zhen and colleagues train in 2026 a deep learning tool that spots loose DNA circles in routine cancer slides. These circles, called ecDNA, carry extra cancer genes and help tumors resist drugs, yet finding them needs costly sequencing. Their platform, ecPICK, learned from thousands of stained slide images across twenty cancer types.

Predictions from ordinary slides matched lab-confirmed circle levels closely in validation checks. The tool also flagged patients with worse outlook beyond what standard factors explain. Circle-rich zones carried quiet immune activity, dense scar-like collagen, and altered cell energy patterns in spatial gene maps. Cheap slide-based mapping could sort patients faster and hint at how circles reshape their neighborhood.
pmc-13232721:
Regina Rab and eleven colleagues test whether tumor-destroying gene therapy can broaden the reach of immune checkpoint blockade, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Checkpoint inhibitors fail many cancers because the tumor microenvironment protects them. The team used a bacterial enzyme gene delivered into tumors. The enzyme converts a prodrug into a toxic purine base inside the tumor.

In mouse triple-negative breast cancer, the combination beat checkpoint therapy alone. Even distant tumors not expressing the enzyme were strongly repressed. Treated tumors showed fewer suppressive regulatory T cells and more activated killer cells. Rapid immune clearance followed the cytoreduction. Because the toxic base also destroys quiescent support cells, the microenvironment's shelter collapses. The authors argue this could sensitize stubborn cancers to immune attack across many subtypes.
pmc-13233621:
Nico Wunderling, Boris Sakschewski, Johan Rockström, Bernardo Flores, Marina Hirota, and Arie Staal modeled how close the Amazon rainforest is to a tipping point, in this 2026 study. Warming and tree clearing both dry the forest, and dryness can feed on itself as trees recycle the rain they need. The team coupled a tipping model with a tracker of how moisture rides the air across the basin.

With warming alone, the danger threshold sat near four degrees, with up to a third of the forest at risk. Adding deforestation dropped the threshold to roughly one and a half to two degrees. Under that pairing, most of the forest could flip to a degraded state, driven by drought spreading from place to place. The authors urge holding warming low and stopping clearing.
pmc-13233721:
Léa Ribet and co-authors review how fermentation can make bread easier to digest and more nourishing, in a review paper from 2026. Bread is a staple food, yet some people report gut trouble after eating it. Conditions like wheat sensitivity and irritable bowel syndrome are complex and poorly understood.

Yeasts and lactic acid bacteria used in baking can free minerals and cut trigger parts like gluten and certain sugars. Picking microbes with the right traits strengthens these gains. Fermentation can also yield helpful compounds during baking. The authors caution that microbe choice still lacks standard rules, and clinical proof stays thin. More trials are needed before health claims can stand firm.
pmc-13234021:
Anna G. Willocks, Ksenia M. Bykova, and Elena Moltchanova published a 2026 study building childhood reference values for a test of chewing and swallowing solids. The test counts bites, chewing cycles, swallows, and time while a child eats a cracker, and a phone-style application now administers it. The team tested 114 healthy children between four and nineteen years old, evenly split between boys and girls.

Age significantly shaped every efficiency measure, and the team converted the results into normative tables for clinical use. Scores from the app did not match the older hand-recorded norms, with the widest gaps in the youngest children, so the methods cannot be swapped casually. The authors offer the app-based norms as a first reference for spotting swallowing problems and oral motor delays.
pmc-13234121:
Seyed Reza Miri Shaktai and colleagues published a 2026 aquaculture study on feeding silymarin, a milk thistle extract, to Caspian trout larvae. Silymarin protects the liver and fights oxidation, but its free form absorbs poorly. The team compared plain silymarin against a nanomicelle version, tiny carrier droplets meant to deliver more of it. Each was mixed into feed at the same dose for sixty days. A third group got no supplement at all.

The nano form clearly outperformed. Larvae on the nano form ended heavier, gained more, and grew faster than both other groups. Plain silymarin did nothing that could be measured for growth. The nano group also showed stronger activity of one antioxidant enzyme and richer stores of valuable long-chain omega-3 fats in their bodies. Other measures did not differ. The authors back nano delivery for young farmed fish.
pmc-13235221:
Makoto Tsujita and colleagues followed in 2026 kidney transplant recipients in Japan to test whether lasting anaemia tracks declining graft function. Anaemia after transplantation is common and has been linked to worse graft outcomes. Records covered more than three hundred recipients at one hospital over two years. Kidney function was averaged repeatedly, while blood haemoglobin entered the models as it changed over time.

Kidney function declined steadily across the follow-up period in the main model. Higher haemoglobin at any point went together with better kidney function over time. Use of anaemia-stimulating drugs by itself showed no independent link to the function trend. Recipients receiving those drugs nevertheless lost function faster in supporting comparisons, including a matched analysis. The authors read persistent anaemia as a sign of underlying graft problems rather than a direct cause.
pmc-13235921:
Cheng and colleagues study how business analytics students engage with AI-supported learning. AI tools are now woven into coursework, yet little work has asked what keeps students using them over a whole course. The team treats AI use as part of the course itself, not a one-off choice to try a new gadget.

They ask how students' views of AI-supported learning shape their wish to keep using it. They then link that wish to interest in the subject and to plans for a career using analytics. The chain matters for teachers: a tool students abandon early cannot deepen interest, while one they value may steer both grades and ambitions.
pmc-13236721:
Damian M. Bailey and co-authors exposed in 2026 twelve healthy men to six hours of low-oxygen air and normal air on separate occasions. The study asked how organ systems coordinate to defend the brain's energy supply when oxygen falls. Blood markers of stress and vessel injury were measured alongside ultrasound estimates of brain oxygen and glucose delivery. Five participants developed acute mountain sickness symptoms during the low-oxygen session.

Brain fuel delivery stayed well maintained under low oxygen, including in those who felt sick. Slow rhythmic oscillations across body systems grew stronger and more synchronized during oxygen shortage. Those oscillations were even more pronounced and connected in the men with mountain sickness symptoms. Blood markers showed no extra oxidative damage or vessel unit injury in the sick group. The authors suggest mountain sickness may reflect a protective adaptation rather than simple failure.
pmc-13239121:
M. M. Guerisoli and colleagues ran the first multi-year survey in 2026 of the guigna, the Americas' smallest cat, in Argentine Patagonia. Thirty-five camera traps in a protected area logged over eight thousand trap nights and 176 independent guigna events, one of the highest detection rates recorded anywhere for the species. Models weighed landscape features against species-interaction factors, and activity patterns were compared across years, seasons, and coat types.

Guignas favored thick forest with plentiful prey and avoided open vegetation and places with rival predators. They were mainly nocturnal despite little human disturbance, and black-coated and spotted individuals kept the same schedule. The authors credit rich resources and low human impact inside the reserve. The study fills a near-total knowledge gap for Argentina and names what to explore next.
pmc-13239221:
Abebaw Hailu Fikire, Elena Viktorovna Korchagina, and Nidhi Chaudhary systematically reviewed forty-four studies from 2020 to 2024 in 2026. They defined what efficiency and sustainability mean inside food supply chains and built a framework that links their drivers. Inefficient food chains undermine food security and poverty reduction worldwide. The review followed PRISMA guidelines across two major indexing databases.

Publication in the area grew over the period, with one open-access publisher leading output and first authors from the United Kingdom and Italy most active. Efficiency, in their framing, means trimming cost and time, while sustainability adds environmental and social responsibility across the chain. The authors aim the framework at scholars choosing new questions, at policymakers, and at practitioners. Their closing claim is that the field now has clearer signposts for where the unsolved problems sit.
pmc-13239621:
Owais Dar and a large audit team summarise the first United Kingdom and Ireland audit of advanced heart failure referrals, published in 2026. Around a million Britons live with heart failure, and transplants or implanted pumps can save advanced cases, yet only a few hundred procedures happen each year.

Seven transplant centres reported roughly one hundred referrals a month for assessment. Referral rates differed sharply by region even after age was considered, and many referred patients turned out to have conditions ruling the therapies out. Distance and local deprivation did not explain the gaps, while women made up only a third of those assessed. The authors see unequal access needing national attention.
pmc-13239921:
Ali Moradi and colleagues report an unusual cause of episodic paralysis in a 2026 case paper. A 31-year-old woman with mast cell activation syndrome suffered repeated bouts of weakness, cramps, and near-fainting, often after carbohydrate-heavy meals or exercise, and one attack came with severely low blood potassium.

Her pattern fitted hypokalemic periodic paralysis, a muscle channel disorder usually seen in teenage boys with affected relatives. She had no family history and lacked the flushing that her other syndrome would predict during attacks. pmc-13240121:
Anwu Huang and colleagues connect diet quality for gut microbes with survival in a combined heart, kidney, and metabolic syndrome in a 2026 study. The dietary index for gut microbiota scores eating patterns by how well they feed helpful gut bacteria, and its link with death risk in this high-risk group was unknown.

National survey data covered 13,562 American adults with the syndrome between 2007 and 2018, followed for about eighty-two months on average. The lowest scoring group died at the highest rate. Each extra point on the index came with roughly a tenth lower risk of death overall and a slightly larger drop in cardiovascular death. The pattern held across patient subgroups.
pmc-13240921:
Ratsavong's team in Vientiane asked why toddlers stay underfed where food is at hand in Laos's capital. 333 mother-child pairs filled out a structured survey. 47 caregivers also gave in-depth interviews. Two districts, one urban and one peri-urban, were covered.

About 27 percent of children under two were stunted, with low weight near fourteen percent. What set thriving children apart was not food access alone. Parents who gathered feeding advice from varied sources, and turned knowledge into daily practice, had better-fed children. The team advises hands-on, show-how feeding outreach for urban and peri-urban families in Laos.
pmc-13241521:
Pasvolsky and colleagues at MD Anderson report outcomes for older myeloma patients treated with a four-drug induction and stem cell transplant. Twenty-seven were aged seventy or older, with a median age of seventy-four.

Older patients often received gentler conditioning and lower lenalidomide doses than younger ones. Even so, response depth matched: nearly every older patient reached a very good partial response or better after transplant. No transplant-related deaths occurred in either group. pmc-13242121:

pmc-13242221:
Jyoti Prakash Panda and Mala Kaneria report a rare infection next to a transplanted kidney, in work from 2026. The germ belongs to a group that often strikes people with weak immune systems, most often on skin, in lungs, or across the body. A lone pocket of pus beside the kidney, with no spread, is very rare.

Their patient was a man aged thirty-four, eight months past his transplant, with pain and fever after a minor knock. Scans showed a fluid pocket first taken for a blood clot. Normal germ tests found nothing, but a special stain flagged the germ group, and culture named the species. Drainage plus a tailored drug mix cured him, though side effects and drug clashes made care hard.
pmc-13243321:
Mitsuaki Hirai and colleagues asked health workers how a water and sanitation improvement program actually landed in Zimbabwean facilities. Their qualitative study appeared in Discover Public Health in 2026. pmc-13243621:
Xinxing Liu, Fuwu Yan, Xiaorong Li, Pinbin Zhao, and Yuhu Cheng published a 2026 engineering study on a curious problem: car throttle pedals that vibrate when the horn sounds. pmc-13245821:
Raja presents five clinical cases in this 2026 Cureus case series, all married women with years of bodily complaints such as pain, stomach trouble, dizziness, fatigue, panic, and broken sleep. pmc-13246421:
Zhiqi Yu and colleagues build a learning model to predict poor recovery after nerve fiber decay in a 2026 study. Wallerian degeneration follows nerve injury in the brain and often leaves lasting disability. No tool existed to flag which patients will fare badly.

Just over half the patients had a poor outcome at three months or later. The best model is explained with charts that show how each factor pushes the risk. Such a tool could guide early rehab choices.
pmc-13246921:

They also warn that antibody tools for measuring the code need rigorous validation first.
pmc-13248421:

Across six teams, the researchers logged two hundred three hours of observation plus interviews and group talks. Managers, the authors argue, must match support to each pattern instead of using one fix for all.
pmc-13248521:

The model projects illness counts and costs through 2040 under lower and higher emissions paths. Results diverged by region, shaped by changing heat patterns and by where vulnerable groups live. The authors argue the approach lets officials test interventions at specific points in the chain, and time regional responses before heat waves arrive.
pmc-13249921:
Girasol and a Brazilian team simulated therapy lasers traveling through human skin, in a 2026 Lasers in Medical Science study. pmc-13250221:

pmc-13250321:

The team repaired it with a three-layer flap of nearby skin while also straightening the curve, and recovery went smoothly with good function and appearance. Old records suggested a childhood repair as the likely cause. The authors urge careful checks during surgery itself.
pmc-13251221:
E Moens and co-authors published this expert consensus study in 2026 on community first responder systems. When a heart stops outside hospital, fast CPR and a quick shock decide survival. Registries of defibrillators and backing from national health plans helped systems last.
pmc-13251521:
Kadyan and co-authors show that a mother's fat choices during pregnancy and nursing shape her pups' guts and brains into adulthood. Their brains showed stronger synaptic plasticity signals, quieter inflammation, and lipid profiles tied to membrane health. Omega-6 also left lasting microbiome marks, distinct from saturated fat. The authors frame maternal omega-3 as long-term neuroprotection delivered through the gut-brain-immune axis.
pmc-13251821:

An approved drug given during sleep loss protected it, and given just before testing it briefly restored access. Shining light on the tagged memory cells in the brain also brought the memory back, pointing to a recall failure rather than a lost trace.
pmc-13252821:
Shiqiong Yan and colleagues review machine learning for predicting bleeding during surgery in this 2026 paper. Bleeding mid-operation threatens patient safety, and prediction models are multiplying, but their quality and readiness for wards were unclear.

Searching seven databases to April 2025, the team kept 23 studies with sample sizes from 48 to over 48,000. Tree-based models were the most common, and accuracy varied widely. Feeding models both records and images helped. Only six studies tested their model on outside patients, and accuracy often fell sharply there. Every study carried a high risk of bias by a standard tool, so the authors urge stricter building and reporting.
pmc-13253221:
Hongfang Liu and colleagues hunt for predictors of new chromosome errors in embryos across three kinds of fertility testing in a 2026 retrospective study. pmc-13253921:
Aiman Waheed and colleagues sequence a drug-resistant bacterium in a 2026 study from Peshawar, Pakistan. Genes for attachment and iron uptake were also present, matching a classic, not hyper-virulent, type. The authors stress better species naming and wider genome checks, while noting one isolate cannot show regional patterns.
pmc-13254021:
Xintao Zeng and a large team review how alterations in the gene KMT2C reshape gastrointestinal cancers in a 2026 article. Because the impact depends on mutation type, partner mutations, and tissue context, the authors map the resulting therapeutic weak points carefully.
pmc-13254321:
Mohamed Ismail, Assem Hassan, and Osama Shehata test concrete wear in cold weather in a 2026 study. Abrasion, surface wearing away, matters for bridge decks, highways, and runways in cold regions. Colder temperatures raised both strength and wear resistance across mixes, and cutting binder content caused the largest losses.
pmc-13254721:
Shaozi Zhong and colleagues test a compound from the herb danshen on aging bone stem cells in a 2026 laboratory study. pmc-13255221:
Pfisterer-Heise and colleagues built a core outcome set for research on centralizing hospital services into fewer, higher-volume units. Because studies measure different outcomes, their results resist comparison. The team combined a systematic review, focus groups with patient representatives, interviews with medical societies and insurers, and a survey of researchers, all based in Germany.

A longlist of outcomes went through two Delphi rounds judged against a strict agreement threshold. The final set contains twenty-seven outcomes spanning every domain of an established taxonomy, with nine addressing quality of care. The authors say future centralization studies should report across these domains, though agreed measurement instruments still need work.
pmc-13255421:
Jinghang Yu and colleagues ask whether an extra thigh-bone cut is needed in hip surgery for young children in a 2026 study. Walking-age children with developmental hip dysplasia often get open reduction plus socket reshaping, sometimes with a femoral osteotomy added. The team compared 52 children, 59 hips in total, treated with or without the extra cut.

After roughly three and a half years, socket angle gains and hip growth measures were statistically the same in both groups. The authors conclude the femoral cut is unnecessary for children with dislocation grades up to the third level when the other two steps are done.
pmc-13255521:
Merve Koseoglu and co-authors use machine learning to predict dental student grades in a 2026 study. Schools hold rich pre-university data on students, from exam scores to family background, but rarely use it to forecast success. The team gathered 96 records on dentistry graduates, including high school grades, entrance exam scores, and parent education and income.

Entrance exam scores and rankings predicted later grades better than traits like hometown, gender, or school type. The best models explained at least 74 percent of grade variation and sorted course grades with over 70 percent accuracy. The authors say such models can flag students who may need support early.
pmc-13255721:
Duncan Jaroslow and co-authors report a 2026 glasshouse study of an Australian spittlebug, Bathyllus albicinctus, and the plants it can live on. Spittlebugs worldwide spread Xylella fastidiosa, a plant bacterium that has devastated olives, grapes, and citrus overseas. The pathogen has not reached Australia, yet knowing which local insects could carry it guides preparation.

In no-choice tests, where each insect got a single plant species, survival and growth varied with the host plant offered. The insect's sex and the season also shifted the results. Some plants supported the bug well and others poorly. The authors say mapping these preferences now, before any incursion, helps risk assessors predict which crops and native plants a local vector could threaten if the bacterium ever arrives.
pmc-13255921:
Pingbo Yin and colleagues study how the frontal cortex handles opposite tasks in a 2026 neuroscience paper. Two groups of female ferrets learned sound tasks with reversed rules, so the same sound meant opposite actions and rewards. The team recorded single brain cells and field signals in the frontal cortex during the tasks.

Surprisingly, cell responses looked similar across the opposite tasks. Responses were stronger and longer for target sounds, which signal a change of action, than for reference sounds. Activity fell into three dynamic profiles from separate cell clusters. The authors propose the frontal cortex holds an abstract code of task structure, sent onward to deeper brain areas.
pmc-13256121:
Barbara Toffoli and colleagues present a 2026 real-world comparison of oral versus injected semaglutide in type 2 diabetes care. Semaglutide is unique among its drug class for offering both forms. Records covered 434 patients at an Italian diabetes center, with a median age of seventy and thirteen years of diabetes.

More patients stopped the oral form than the injection. Among those followed eighteen months, both forms lowered blood sugar and body weight comparably, with starting values best predicting response. In fifty-five matched patient pairs, the pattern held, while the oral form reduced diastolic blood pressure more. Adding SGLT2 inhibitor drugs strengthened cholesterol improvements in both groups. The authors conclude the two forms are broadly interchangeable in everyday practice, with adherence the practical difference.
pmc-13257121:
Tomohiko Aoe presents a 2026 overview and hypothesis article on fibromyalgia, a chronic widespread pain disorder. Diagnosis still rests on symptoms alone, with no objective test. Pain arrives with fatigue, poor sleep, thinking problems, anxiety, and low mood for many patients.

Fibromyalgia is now classed as nociplastic pain, where the central nervous system processes signals abnormally. Brain imaging work from the author group split patients by pain threshold into low and normal groups. Those groups may reflect different underlying mechanisms rather than one uniform disease. Sorting patients by mechanism could guide more fitting treatment choices. Clinicians get a concise map of causes spanning brain, psychological, environmental, and genetic factors. The subgroup idea is offered as a testable proposal, not settled fact.
pmc-13258121:
Emad Hafaf and colleagues present a 2026 study of stockout risk in supply chains, meaning the risk that needed stock runs out. Their framework tests whether longer lead time, the wait between ordering and delivery, causes stockouts. It mixes causal inference methods, which aim to isolate cause and effect, with machine learning prediction and time series forecasting. The data covered 20,000 supply chain incidents.

Propensity score matching gave the most credible causal estimate, an average treatment effect of 0.882, confirming a strong link between lead time and stockout risk. An instrumental variable test gave a weaker, non-significant result, which the authors blame on a weak instrument. Random Forest and LightGBM models predicted best among the machine learning methods. A moving average forecast tracked stockout patterns over time with a score of 0.883.
pmc-13259421:
Fangmin Liang and coauthors join hot water and screw push prep steps to lift lignin yield in a 2026 study. Most plant lignin burns for heat since plain pulls leave it weak in use. The two step prep comes first, then an alcohol wash pulls the lignin out.

Yield rose by about a fifth next to raw stock runs. Key bond breaks freed far more active hydroxyl groups on the lignin. Weight spread shrank, which marks a more even good. Most plant fiber stayed whole for split use, and sugar goods came out too. Plants gain a route to sell lignin as a chem good, not burn it.
pmc-13259621:
Yan Shen and co-authors review bacteria reprogrammed as living medical devices. Synthetic biology hands engineers gene editing, DNA assembly, and directed evolution to rebuild microbes for set tasks. Their 2026 review surveys what designer bacteria already do in diagnosis and therapy.

As sensors, tuned strains sniff out disease markers and flash readable signals for early detection. As treatments, they ferry drugs to targets, coach immune responses, or rebalance gut communities. Precision improves over conventional therapy in these designs. Stable colonization, immune reactions, factory-scale production, and missing rules still stand between prototypes and patients, the authors caution.
pmc-13259821:
Fabian Tollens and colleagues reported in 2026 on a cloud platform that links imaging and clinical data for prostate cancer surgery planning. Their single-center study drew on 249 men who had radical prostatectomy, with 176 cases reviewed from past records and 73 enrolled going forward. The team fed MRI scans, lab values, and pathology data into the International Radiomics Platform.

Models built on the platform predicted spread beyond the prostate capsule far better once imaging measures joined standard clinical factors. The same imaging features added little for forecasting positive surgical margins or nerve-sparing choices. Quantitative radiomics features gave no extra gain beyond routine imaging. The authors conclude that platform-based analysis is workable in daily care, while its limits for some surgical choices remain clear.
pmc-13260021:
Karina Zierden and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective cohort study of removable dental prostheses held by double crowns with spark-eroded friction pins. The devices were fitted in one general dental practice and followed for up to thirty years. In total, 196 prostheses and 563 abutment teeth, the natural teeth that anchor them, were observed. Mean follow-up was 14.07 years, with a maximum of 31.66 years, and survival was analyzed by standard time-to-event methods.

About 30.61 percent of prostheses and 39.43 percent of abutment teeth failed during follow-up. Mean survival was 22.66 years for prostheses and 20.29 years for abutment teeth. Survival differed by jaw classification, number of replaced teeth, opposing teeth, number of abutments, crown-to-root ratio, pocket depth, location, and tooth vitality. Devices replacing eleven or more teeth performed worst, while one classification group performed best.
pmc-13260921:
Guankun Wang, Long Bai, and Hongliang Ren wrote a 2026 viewpoint article on giving AI copilot robots thinking ability in endoscopic surgery. Endoscopic surgery works through small holes or natural passages, guided by camera views. Vision-language-action models, which turn camera input and text orders into robot actions, could serve as copilots. The authors argue that thinking would let such robots combine multiple cues, read the surgeon's intent, and infer how hidden tissue behaves, reducing doubt and mental burden.

The article sets the copilot at watched autonomy levels, proposing and watching options and carrying out bounded moves under the surgeon's watch, not acting alone. Key challenges include soft tissues that change shape without warning, how patients differ, and sudden events such as bleeding. Done well, the authors argue, such thinking could turn copilot robots from reactive actors into thinking partners, improving precision and safety in clinical practice.
pmc-13262421:
Benito Baldauf and co-authors track infections from implanted heart devices in Germany in a 2026 journal article. These devices treat faulty heart rhythms but can become infected at the device pocket or along their wires, causing a serious heart infection. The team used insurance claims to get a national picture for 2015 to 2019.

Among 282,205 patients who had device work, 6,577 people, or 2.33 percent, had major infections within three months. Pocket infections occurred in 1.91 percent, and wire-linked heart infection in 0.82 percent. Death in hospital reached 8.36 percent for pocket infections and 15.0 percent for the heart infection type. Infected patients also needed many more procedures than others.
pmc-13263021:
Sookyung Kim and colleagues survey motorcycle food delivery workers in South Korea about fatigue and crash risk in a 2026 journal article. Earlier work focused on actual accidents, but this study also covers near misses and anxiety about accidents. An online survey of 336 workers fed statistical models linking job fatigue and health habits to a combined traffic risk index.

Work fatigue was tied to higher overall risk and to every subscale, including near misses and anxiety rated by self and others. Inconsistent helmet use and low physical activity also tracked with higher risk scores. Current smoking tracked with more near misses. Shorter reported breaks oddly tracked with lower risk, which the authors say needs better measurement in future work.
pmc-13263121:
Chang Gyo Jung and colleagues map soil genes that drive nutrient breakdown across the continental United States in a 2026 journal article. Soil microbes release enzymes that free carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus from organic matter. Using DNA data from soils plus climate, landform, and plant data, the team trained a machine learning model to predict where the genes for these enzymes are most common.

The model explained well over half of the variation seen today. Rainfall was the strongest influence for carbon and nitrogen genes, while slope length mattered most for phosphorus genes. Under future climate paths to 2100, carbon and nitrogen gene shares fell in wetter regions and rose in drier ones. Phosphorus gene shares fell markedly in semiarid and Mediterranean-type regions.
pmc-13263221:
A retraction notice published in 2026 withdraws a 2019 paper on stem cell derived neurospheres from the journal Stem Cells International. The original paper claimed a one-step method turned human umbilical cord stem cells into ball-shaped nerve cell clusters with unique gene activity and helpful secretions. The publisher investigated after concerns arose about an image in the paper.

One panel, labeled as one treatment condition, overlapped with an image in another paper by the same group showing a different cell type. The authors supplied raw data, but review raised further concerns. As a result, the journal and publisher judged the article's results no longer reliable and retracted it. The notice records that the authors disagree with the retraction.
pmc-13263921:
Linnéa Good and colleagues report a 2026 crossover study on how one night without sleep changes blood metabolites in young adults. Forty-two adults took part, including eighteen with obesity and twenty-four with normal weight. Each person completed a night of total sleep deprivation and a night of normal sleep, with morning blood samples tested by targeted metabolomics.

Tryptophan rose after sleep loss only in participants with obesity. Histidine, kynurenine and creatinine fell only in the normal-weight group. Both groups shared some changes, including a lower kynurenine to tryptophan ratio and higher medium-chain acylcarnitines. Readers gain a clear picture of shared and weight-specific responses that may help explain metabolic risk after poor sleep.
pmc-13264021:
Kanoko Yoshida and colleagues connect a mitochondrial enzyme's failure to how the placenta is built in pregnancies with high blood pressure. These troubles strike up to a tenth of all pregnancies and lack proven cures. Fusion of placental cells into a shared layer is vital, and their 2026 study finds it blocked when membranes stiffen.

Blocking the enzyme DHODH switched on interferon-induced membrane proteins through a gene-switch factor. Those proteins loaded the membrane with stiff fats, draining its flow and halting cell fusion. One of them also worsened a blood ratio used to grade how bad the disease is. The chain offers fresh targets for a condition managed today mostly by early delivery.
pmc-13264121:
Henrik Normannseth, Stein Andersson and Christoffer Hatlestad-Hall describe a 2026 brainwave dataset from healthy women, organized for open reuse. Sixty-nine women aged nineteen to forty recorded resting brain activity with eyes closed and open using a sixty-four channel system. A second task played tones at five loudness levels to measure how brain responses grow with volume, a marker studied in mood research.

Files follow the Brain Imaging Data Structure standard and sit on an open repository. Tables add age, contraceptive use, menstrual cycle notes, depression scores and impulsivity measures. Researchers can probe resting rhythms, loudness responses and hormone-related variation without collecting new recordings, and machine learning teams gain a clean, well-documented example set.
pmc-13264221:
Ryoki Semba, Tetsuya Katsumori and Hiroshi Miura report two trauma cases highlighting a spinal cord risk during artery blocking treatment in a 2026 paper. Bleeding between the ribs from injury can be stopped by embolization, where material blocks the damaged vessel through a catheter. A nearby artery that feeds the spinal cord sometimes branches from the same vessel, and blocking it by mistake can cause paralysis.

In the first case doctors spotted that critical artery during imaging and avoided it. In the second it sat at the image edge and went unrecognized, yet treatment still avoided it and bleeding stopped without nerve harm. Both patients recovered without neurological complications. Careful mapping of that artery before embolization is the central lesson.
pmc-13264921:
Laura E Pernoud and a large team present a 2026 protocol for the LIFE study, on lifestyle risks for long-term disease across the stages of reproductive ageing in women. The menopause shift raises the risk of heart disease, metabolic disease, depression, and dementia. Inflammation and lifestyle changes are thought to play a part, but the links are unclear.

The study enrolls women aged 40 to 65 and sorts them as before, during, or after menopause. Body measures and blood samples are taken, and activity and sleep are tracked for seven days with wearable devices plus a sleep diary. Thinking skills are tested with two standard tools, and surveys cover mood, sleep, balance confidence, and diet. Data gathering was due to finish in April 2026. The team hopes to show how lifestyle shifts across menopause shape inflammation, belly fat, and brain health.
pmc-13266021:
Iman Wehbe and Abdelaziz Tlili review messenger RNA therapies for lung cancer (2026). Lung cancer causes vast global death tolls, with late finding and resistance limiting care. Success of mRNA vaccines against infection showed the platform's speed. Adapting it to cancer is the review's focus.

Uses covered include cancer shots, targeted protein therapy, and immune-tuning therapy. Gene editing and cell resetting methods also feature. Delivery hurdles and tumour resistance receive detailed attention. Fat-based tiny carriers are central to current designs. The authors expect mRNA methods to reshape precise lung cancer treatment with further work.
pmc-13266221:
Christophe De Block and the team analyse meal-time glucose control for a weekly combination diabetes treatment (2026). IcoSema combines weekly insulin with semaglutide in one product. Two completed phase three trials supplied continuous glucose monitoring data. A modified algorithm detected meals from sensor traces.

Data from 1,650 people were analysed, with about two meals detected daily per person. The combination clearly improved post-meal glucose measures. Comparators were weekly insulin alone in one trial and daily multi-injection therapy in the other. Final treatment weeks provided the sensor data. Full effect details follow in the complete report.
pmc-13266721:
Zhengqiang Tang and co-authors pool in 2026 evidence on whether a blood inflammation score predicts trouble after surgery for aortic dissection. The score, called SIRI, combines counts of neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes taken before the operation. Their review searched three databases and combined eight studies covering 2,404 patients.

Higher scores linked clearly to aorta-related adverse events after surgery, in both major dissection types. Kidney injury, renal failure, infection, and several other complications also occurred more often when scores were high. No clear link appeared for major adverse events overall or for death in hospital. Clinicians may find the simple score useful when judging risk before surgery.
pmc-13266821:
Liting Cai and colleagues report in 2026 on two RNA-reading proteins in lung squamous cell carcinoma and their link to an immune checkpoint protein. Both proteins, YTHDF1 and YTHDF2, help cells interpret chemical marks on RNA messages. The team combined public cancer data, tissue staining from 60 tumors, and lab experiments in cancer cells.

Both proteins were higher in tumor tissue than in nearby normal tissue, and higher levels tied to more advanced stage. Raising YTHDF1 in cells increased PD-L1, the protein tumors use to blunt immune attack, and reduced killing by T cells. The effect depended on the RNA mark the protein reads. Findings suggest a new path by which this cancer may evade immunity.
pmc-13267821:
Ao Men and colleagues report a 2026 study building a chart to predict heavy fluid build-up after liver cancer surgery. Removing part of the liver can leave fluid collecting in the belly, called ascites, which complicates recovery. The team studied 232 patients operated on at one center between 2021 and 2025. Of them, 66 developed massive ascites and 166 did not.

Four factors independently predicted the problem: platelet count, a liver enzyme level, portal vein hypertension, and how long the operation lasted. The team built a nomogram, a scoring chart, from these four. It sorted patients with strong accuracy and stayed well calibrated under repeat testing. Benefit checks suggested the chart helps real decisions across a wide risk range. The authors offer it for tailoring care after surgery.
pmc-13267921:
Xiaoyu Feng, Jianmei Gong, and Shuangying Ma wrote a 2026 review drawing together interview studies on living with lymphedema after gynecological cancer. Lymphedema is lasting swelling, often in the legs, after lymph nodes are removed or damaged. The team searched ten databases up to February 2026 for studies reporting patients' own experiences.

Twelve studies with 141 patients qualified. The combined findings fell into three themes. First, the swelling's impact reaches body, daily life, and feelings. Second, patients understand and adapt to the condition in widely different ways. Third, support needs span medical care, information, and emotional help. The reviewers rated confidence in the combined findings as moderate. They urge fuller support and wider research coverage.
pmc-13268921:
Difei Yu and co-authors review in 2026 how liquid biopsy tests might guide kidney-sparing care for cancer of the upper urinary tract. Removing the whole kidney and ureter is the standard for high-risk disease, but it sacrifices kidney function. Choosing patients safely for lesser surgery is hard because scans and scope biopsies describe shape better than tumor biology.

Urine-based tests, covering gene methylation, mutations, RNA panels, and proteins, look most ready for detecting cancer and sorting patients before surgery. Tumor DNA in blood, by contrast, tracked hidden aggressive disease and leftover cancer after operations. The authors stress that these tests should add a decision layer on top of imaging and pathology, not replace them, and that outcome trials are the next step.
pmc-13269121:
Marcel Krumrein and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on tiny light guides built into silicon carbide, a hard crystal used in electronics. Inside the crystal sit color centers, flaws that can hold and read out quantum information, meaning data stored in single particles. The team added a mirror to boost the light signal.

Their mirror reflected over 80 percent of light at its peak, across a wide range of colors. At very cold temperatures, the centers gave about 104,000 light counts per second in standard tests. A second checking method raised that to about 125,000 counts. The authors calculate that such rates could allow a correct single reading more than 98 percent of the time.
pmc-13269321:
Danwei Yang and David D Kim published a journal article in 2026 on heart and metabolic diseases and quality of life in the United States. They tracked how much each condition lowered self-rated health from 2001 to 2022. Six conditions were compared, including stroke, diabetes, and obesity.

National survey data on adults showed overall quality of life rising after a low in 2012. Stroke lowered it most, followed by heart disease and then diabetes. The losses tied to diabetes and heart disease shrank steadily over the two decades. The loss tied to obesity, by contrast, grew after 2012. The authors argue that health values used in policy studies need updating over time, not one fixed figure.
pmc-13269521:
Jay J W Han and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 following up patients after belly hernia repair with a muscle-release technique. Surgeons measured the force needed to pull the wall tissues together before and during repair. The question was whether leftover tension predicted later problems.

Of 100 patients in the first study, 77 had follow-up beyond one year. Their hernias were wide, with a median width of 13 centimeters. Median closing force was 4 pounds, down from 11 pounds at the start. Only one hernia returned, a rate of 1.4 percent among those checked in person. No tension measure was linked to hernia return, wound problems, or patient-reported pain and quality of life.
pmc-13269921:
Sofya Tishina and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a weakness in pancreatic cancer, one of the deadliest cancers. Its main driver gene, KRAS, switches on an interferon program, a cell alarm system, that loads cancer cells with proteins for a form of cell death called necroptosis. Removing one guard protein then triggers that death.

In mouse models, deleting the guard protein wiped out most early pancreatic lesions. Drug blockade of the same guard cut tumor burden in aggressive mouse models and in mini-tumors grown from patient tissue. A cross-cancer analysis linked the death program to Ras pathway activity and interferon signatures. The authors present the alarm program as a treatment opening in this cancer.
pmc-13270021:
Robert S Dean and co-authors published a review and combined analysis in 2026 on surgery for tears of the inner knee meniscus root, comparing repair with partial removal of the meniscus. Twelve studies with over five years of follow-up were pooled. Outcomes included patient scores, arthritis grades, and failure needing further surgery.

The studies covered 797 patients, 83.7 percent of them women, followed for an average of 84.1 months. Both operations improved patient scores clearly. Repair, though, gave better function scores and lower arthritis grades, 1.8 against 2.4 on the scale used. One patient score averaged 72.8 after repair against 46.5 after removal in the comparison reported. The authors title repair as the superior option at five years and beyond.
pmc-13270121:
Hanna Koch and a long list of co-authors propose in 2026 dropping the word synthetic from the name of researcher-built microbial communities. Groups of cultured microbes are now widely used to study how microbes interact with each other and with hosts, from plant roots to the human gut. The authors argue that synthetic carries needless negative baggage for a tool with growing practical uses.

They suggest Defined Microbial Community as the standard term for applications. The shift in practice is real: single strains proved unstable and weak, while defined multi-species mixtures better capture natural diversity and have improved plant resilience and growth in trials. A neutral, descriptive name, the group argues, will help the field communicate with regulators, industry, and the public.
pmc-13270221:
Biazin Yenealem Mekuriaw and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on what pregnant women in a resource-limited setting know about neurodevelopmental disorders, conditions affecting child brain development. A hospital-based survey of 404 pregnant women used standard questionnaires for knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions. Factors linked to each score were tested.

Average scores converted to 43.6 percent for knowledge, 38.5 percent for attitudes, and 72.8 percent for perception, rated inadequate, poor, and good in turn. Lower schooling and past substance use went with lower knowledge, while strong social support raised it. A diploma or higher and strong support also favored better attitudes and perceptions. A family history of mental illness went with less favorable views, the analysis found.
pmc-13270521:
Nicole Hanania and co-authors report in 2026 a two-step recipe for building unsymmetrical diarylethylenes, including versions carrying heavy hydrogen for drug studies. These molecules, with two different aromatic rings on one carbon of a double bond, appear in polymers and drug candidates, yet the deuterium-labeled forms were hard to make. Their route starts from cheap, off-the-shelf aromatic compounds and aldehydes.

First the partners join into a phosphorus salt with reliable positioning. Then a Wittig-style step with ordinary or deuterated formaldehyde finishes the double bond. Yields were good, and the heavy hydrogen landed with high isotopic purity. The authors pitch the sequence as simple access to versatile building blocks for synthesis and medicinal chemistry, where deuterium can slow a drug's breakdown.
pmc-13271021:
Gavin Feinberg and co-authors described a 61-year-old man whose Tourette syndrome tics improved markedly on a drug called cariprazine. Tourette syndrome causes repeated motor and vocal tics, and his case was complicated by bipolar disorder and years of treatments that failed to control functionally disabling tics. Cariprazine, an antipsychotic that acts on dopamine receptors, was started and its dose adjusted gradually.

Over roughly two years his tic severity fell substantially and stayed down, with the drug well tolerated and his mood stable. Single cases cannot prove a treatment works, but the authors argue the result is worth attention. Cariprazine may deserve formal study for tic disorders in patients whose other conditions limit the usual drug choices.
pmc-13271621:
Ruimin Hu and six colleagues review why the lipid bubbles delivering genetic medicines also provoke inflammation, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-six. Lipid nanoparticles carried the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines to success. Their immune stimulation helps vaccination but harms gene editing and anti-inflammatory therapy.

The review dissects mechanisms: specific lipid components, the cell entry pathways activated, and innate sensors that detect the nucleic acid cargo. Particle structure, injection route, and where particles accumulate all modulate the response. Engineering countermeasures are surveyed, from structure-guided lipid design onward. The double-edged nature is the theme: the same property is feature or bug depending on the therapy. Taming it widens nanoparticle medicine's map considerably.
pmc-13271921:
Yanwei Li is lead author of a 2026 retrospective real-world study of anlotinib as third-line or later therapy for recurrent or spread head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Anlotinib is a multi-target drug that blocks blood vessel growth signals. Patients had already failed at least two prior drug regimens, leaving few options.

Among 68 patients treated at one centre between January 2021 and October 2023, fourteen had partial tumour shrinkage and 39 had stable disease, giving a response rate of 22.1 percent and disease control of 74.6 percent. Median time without progression was 6.3 months and median survival 8.4 months. Tumours with an inflamed immune profile, marked by a PD-L1 score and more killer T cells, responded better.
pmc-13272621:
Enrique Gracia wrote a 2026 perspective asking whether ending violence against women by 2030 is a realistic goal. That aim is target 5.2 of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. He uses the European Union as his case, where wealth and gender equality are high by world standards.

Gracia argues that rates stay high, progress has stalled, and some advanced, gender-equal countries show oddly high levels. Prevention work also seems not to reach younger people well, he says. In his view, past efforts have not cut rates across whole populations, and real declines will need scaled, proven prevention, lasting political will, and stronger accountability.
pmc-13272921:
Amira Moustafa leads a 2026 study of new liquid salts made from the drug isoniazid, for polishing carbon steel. Polishing helps steel resist rust and wear, but older methods can eat away metal. The team tested these salts as greener guards during polishing in strong acid.

At a low dose, the guard effect reached mostly 80 percent. More of the salt worked better, while more heat worked against it. Surface tests showed a guard layer on the steel, and computer work supported a mixed binding mode. Tests also probed harm to a germ that attacks steel, suggesting a dual-purpose guard for harsh settings.
pmc-13273221:
Cynthia Rodríguez-Nava and co-authors set out a practical method in 2026 for labeling antibody fragments used in tissue staining. Immunohistochemistry reveals proteins in tissue slices, but full antibodies are costly, vary between batches, and enter tissue poorly. Small engineered fragments called scFvs offer a cleaner option.

Their method attaches biotin, a tiny tag, directly to these fragments by chemistry. Tagged fragments then plug into standard streptavidin detection systems, so no second antibody step is needed. The fragments also slip into tissue more easily than full antibodies. The authors report that the protocol sharpened antigen viewing while saving time and cost. They present it as a robust and scalable route for steadier staining in research and diagnostic labs.
pmc-13273421:
Lidia Gazzola leads a 2026 multicentre survey of how acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections are managed in Italy. These common infections range from cellulitis to major abscesses and carry clinical and organizational burden. A 107-item questionnaire went to nine expert Italian centers, with one senior specialist replying for each.

Practice varied widely in organization and care pathways, the survey found. Infectious disease specialists were central, but round-the-clock availability was limited, and access to microbiology and wound care varied. No center had a fully structured care pathway, dedicated teams were in a minority, and links with general practitioners and community care were generally lacking. Monitoring and cost evaluation were inconsistent.
pmc-13273521:
Yu-Sun Guo leads a 2026 case report of a sacral nerve implant that pushed out through the skin twice in a patient doing heavy labor. Sacral neuromodulation treats overactive bladder, urine retention, and fecal incontinence with an implanted pulse generator. Extrusion is uncommon but can cause severe complications and loss of benefit.

Salvage treatment included urgent cleaning with 2 liters of antibiotic solution, moving the device to a deeper pocket about 2 centimeters down, and seven days of antibiotics after surgery. At seven months there was no recurrence. The authors also reviewed nine related cases, summarizing triggers and best treatment, and stress strict limits on activity after surgery.
pmc-13273721:
Chew and colleagues report a 2026 systematic review done for a Lancet Commission on heart and blood vessel care in the Asia-Pacific region. The review compares how health systems deliver this care. It also looks ahead to needs in 2050.

The authors gathered evidence across many countries in the region. Wealthier systems offered broad access to tests and treatment. Lower-income systems faced gaps in access and broken care pathways. Patients often paid high costs or reached care too late. The review projects rising demand as populations age. It urges stronger primary care and fairer funding. Coordinated regional action is presented as the path to better heart health.
pmc-13274921:
Sankhadip Bhadra and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a yeast mutation that disables just one member of a vital enzyme family. Six related kinases, called PIKKs, run DNA-damage alarms, growth, and nutrient sensing, and a three-part helper complex called TTT matures all of them. The team found seven mutations in one helper gene, tti1, that made fission yeast sensitive to DNA-damaging chemicals.

One mutant, tti1-N18, selectively wiped out the function of the checkpoint kinase Rad3, the yeast version of human ATR. The other five kinases, including the ATM counterpart, worked largely normally. That surgical specificity suggests the helper grips each client differently. The authors note the human version of the complex is a known drug target, hinting at therapeutic openings.
pmc-13275721:
Junqi Ma and colleagues review COVID-19 mRNA vaccines and their future direction in a 2026 article. The pandemic turned mRNA from an experimental idea into a proven vaccine platform. First products in fatty nanoparticle carriers protected strongly against severe disease.

Protection against infection faded over time, and new variants partly escaped vaccine defences. Mucosal immunity in the nose and throat stayed limited, and responses differed in groups such as older adults. The review covers immune markers, repeated dosing questions, and new RNA formats such as self-amplifying RNA. It closes with uses beyond COVID-19, from other respiratory viruses to cancer therapy.
pmc-13276321:
Salahshour, Safaei, Rahimian, and Hazratgholi reported this diagnostic pitfall in twenty twenty-six. A sixty-two-year-old woman had severe anemia, very low platelets, and many liver lesions. Biopsies kept reading the lesions as hemangiomas, harmless knots of blood vessels. She even received a session of therapy meant to shrink such growths.

The lesions kept growing fast, and new scans looked atypical. A fresh biopsy finally showed the truth: a rare cancer of vessel-lining cells in the liver. Her course worsened with kidney failure that needed dialysis. She died after two cardiac arrests a day apart. The authors warn that a supposed hemangioma that grows or acts oddly demands a second look.
pmc-13276821:
Jens Verlinden and colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study that makes Sudan virus safer to study. Sudan virus is a deadly relative of Ebola, and work on it normally needs the highest level lab safety. The team removed a gene the virus needs, called VP30, so it can grow only in specially made cells.

The contained virus grew much like the wild type in those helper cells and stayed contained in other cells. VP30 proteins from related viruses worked in the system, while one from Marburg virus did not. The setup also allowed quick drug screening and confirmed strong action by remdesivir. Mutations tied to drug resistance were pinpointed along the way.
pmc-13278021:
Natalia Buenache leads a 2026 study of a blood test for leftover cancer cells in multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow. Checking bone marrow for residual disease predicts outcomes but is invasive and can miss patchy disease. The team tested a sensitive DNA sequencing method on cell-free DNA in blood from 84 trial patients, using 292 samples over time.

Detectable tumor DNA in blood predicted relapse more accurately than the standard bone marrow flow test, with far fewer false alarms. Patients with detectable DNA faced a much higher risk of progression or death. Automated sample preparation matched manual methods. A blood-based check could make repeated monitoring easier, the authors propose.
pmc-13278721:
Ibrahim Alharbi and colleagues report a new kidney finding in a child with a GLIS3 gene disorder, in a 2026 case. The ten-year-old Saudi girl carried the classic trio of newborn diabetes, underactive thyroid from birth, and congenital glaucoma. The gene shapes development of the pancreas, thyroid, kidneys, liver, and eyes.

Routine monitoring uncovered a complex mass in her left kidney that she had not felt. Biopsy after detailed imaging showed a benign multicystic nephroma with mixed tissue features. Such a tumour had not been reported in this disorder before, widening its known effects beyond simple kidney cysts. Doctors chose active surveillance over surgery, given the harmless nature of the lesion.
pmc-13278921:
Aidana Rakhmankulova and colleagues chart cervical cancer across Kazakhstan over a decade, in a 2026 nationwide study. HPV shots for girls began in 2024 in the country, so a pre-vaccine baseline matters. Registry data covered cases from 2014 to 2023.

Recorded cases climbed while incidence and death rates peaked around 2022. Five-year survival sat near sixty-five percent overall, with advanced-stage disease driving most lost years. Treatment with chemotherapy or radiation marked higher risk in adjusted models, reflecting more severe cases. Burden measures such as disability-adjusted life years also peaked in 2022. The authors offer the analysis as the benchmark for judging the years ahead.
pmc-13279321:
Hong Yang and colleagues published a 2026 analysis of how bacteria in the upper and lower airways change as ventilator-associated pneumonia develops. It strikes patients ventilated over 48 hours and carries high mortality. Reanalyzing gene sequencing data from 123 samples in public databases, the team compared intubated patients without pneumonia, a phase just before pneumonia appeared, and confirmed cases. They tracked diversity and makeup in both airway regions.

Bacterial diversity in the upper airway rose sharply in pneumonia groups, while lower airway diversity barely moved, yet their makeup differed across all three stages in both regions. Genera including Prevotella, Leptotrichia, and Peptostreptococcus emerged as candidate early warning markers with strong accuracy in their tests. Bacteria moving from upper to lower airway grew more in step by day seven, hinting at a window for action. The authors call for testing in fresh patient groups before any marker guides care.
pmc-13279421:
Mengying Mao and colleagues published a 2026 multi-site study building a prediction model for postherpetic neuralgia, the persistent nerve pain that follows shingles. The team followed 1,361 patients from two hospitals in Hangzhou and Zhejiang, of whom 511, about 37.6 percent, developed the outcome. They screened 36 candidate factors and focused on SIRI, a blood index combining several immune cell counts that reflects body-wide inflammation.

Inflammation measured by SIRI predicted who developed lasting pain on its own. Selection narrowed the model to six factors: age, SIRI, initial pain strength, delay before treatment, rash location, and a neutrophil-to-albumin ratio. Among eight machine learning methods, the XGBoost model performed best, with accuracy scores between about 0.86 and 0.90 across training, internal test, and external patient groups. The authors also converted the model into a simple paper risk score, aiming at a first-visit tool to flag patients for early, aggressive pain prevention.
pmc-13279921:
Yuqin Ye and colleagues give a 2026 review of a mixed cell death mode in brain and spinal cord trauma. Traumatic brain and spinal cord injury cause high death and disability rates in the world. The death mode, PANoptosis, blends three death types in one: pyroptosis, apoptosis and necroptosis. A hub complex starts all three at once. It links to rust stress, nerve swelling and second wave harm after trauma.

Mitochondria, the cell power cores, sit at the centre of the story. Their balance loss can start and run PANoptosis in many cell types. The review lists imbalance signs: poor new core growth, odd split and fuse acts, faulty clean up and shed vesicles. It then maps how each sign feeds the death hub. Drug ideas that guard power cores to block the death blend close the review.
pmc-13280221:
Mathieu Tiret and colleagues report a 2026 study of flea beetle resistance in cabbage kin. The cabbage stem flea beetle grows as a threat to winter Brassica crops in Europe, oil and vegetable plants of the cabbage family. Genetic basis of resistance was poorly understood. The team ran a genome wide association study, which scans the full genome for trait links. They joined pooled gene reads with a large feeding test on one hundred thirteen Brassica oleracea types.

Resistance showed moderate heritability with a mostly polygenic base, meaning many small gene effects. Types split sharply: cabbage head types were mostly susceptible, while cauliflower types and wild groups resisted far more. One major effect zone on chromosome C01 stood out despite the small effect back cloth. Resistance alleles piled up in wild groups, while susceptible alleles ruled in head cabbage. Wild kin hold the resistance stock for breeding.
pmc-13280721:
Diyana Muhammed and colleagues published a 2026 study of SelfCheck-Eval, a framework for catching made-up answers from large language models without needing reference data or model internals. Hallucination is an obstacle to using these systems in medicine, finance, or education. Existing detectors lean on general questions, so the team built a test set from an American mathematics examination, where wrong reasoning can sound convincing. Their framework combines three checks covering meaning, specialized checks, and consistency with context.

Evaluation exposed a sharp split. Detectors handled life stories well but stumbled on math reasoning errors. The weakness persisted across three improvement strategies: fine-tuning on inference data, preference learning, and guided reasoning steps. The authors conclude the failure is structural rather than a matter of more tuning. They argue for specialized black-box detectors for any model, open or closed, before such systems can be trusted in high-stakes work.
pmc-13281321:
Camille Wirth and colleagues shared a 2026 case report on a heart fix that backfired in a very sick patient. The patient was on a heart and lung support machine for severe lung artery pressure. The heart then weakened under stress, and fluid backed up into the lungs. Doctors made a small hole between the heart's upper chambers to drain the pressure. The step is used to ease lung pressure in some patients and to unload the heart in others.

Here it did the reverse. Blood slipped the wrong way through the hole, starving the body of oxygen. Pressure also loaded the weak heart further, and the patient got worse. The authors say the balance of pressures on each side of the heart decides whether the hole helps or harms. They urge great care before using it in like cases.
pmc-13281421:
Temesgen Gebeyehu Wondmeneh measured anemia in toddlers across nine African countries for a 2026 study. Anemia in this age group can slow growth and brain gains. The study used fresh health survey data from 2021 to 2024. It counted more than fourteen thousand children aged six to twenty-three months. Rates were judged by new 2024 global cutoffs, which are stricter than the old ones. The author weighed severity, from mild to severe, against family and health factors.

Even with the new cutoffs, about six in ten toddlers had anemia. Most cases were mild or moderate, and severe cases were few. Girls tended toward milder anemia than boys. Schooling of the mother, health cover, worm care, and varied food all guarded against severe anemia. Fever, low weight, and being a twin or triplet made anemia worse. The author urges action on food, care access, and mother schooling.
pmc-13281821:
Killian Sheriff and colleagues taught software to model metal mixes at any recipe in a 2026 study. A metal's traits swing with its recipe, from neat ordered mixes to jumbled ones. Simulating each recipe from scratch is slow and costly. Learning models can help, but they often fail outside the recipes they trained on. The team used information theory to pick the most telling atom patterns to teach. The model then learned the full landscape of each mix.

They tested it on four mixes, from two-metal pairs to a four-metal blend. It foretold fault energies, local atom order, heat storage, and phase maps across recipes. Its calls matched lab data closely throughout. The authors say smart sampling, not brute data, is the key step. The method could speed the hunt for alloys built for heat, strength, or wear.
pmc-13282321:
Sedra T Alabed and Diana Finkel wrote a 2026 narrative review on tuberculosis that shows only as eye inflammation. Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection best known in the lungs, but it can inflame the uvea, the eye's middle layer. Diagnosis is uncertain because no test directly proves the eye disease. The authors set out how doctors weigh eye patterns, exposure risk, blood immune tests, and the exclusion of look-alike diseases.

Certain eye patterns raise suspicion more, including a snake-like retina pattern, blocked retinal veins, and lumpy iris or choroid lesions. A positive immune blood test shows past exposure, not that tuberculosis caused the eye problem. A negative test does not fully rule it out either. Guidance supports tuberculosis antibiotics in selected patients. The review urges lower treatment thresholds for high-risk eye patterns, and caution when findings are vague and only the blood test is positive.
pmc-13283121:
Fluid racing over a sensor skin, spiked with nanoparticles and swimming cells, is modeled in 2026 by Muhammad Azhar Iqbal's group. The flow mixes tiny metal grains, heat, magnetism, and living cells that swim. Good models can aid drug delivery tools, chip labs, and plant sensors.

A trained neural network learned to predict flow traits with high accuracy. Inputs covered squeeze flow, heat source effects, and chemical change in the fluid. The model also fits ore slurry lines, mine water units, and coating tasks. Magnetic control and grain mix can tune heat flow and sensor response. The authors offer the model as a design aid for engineers who build smart sensor systems for harsh settings.
pmc-13283421:
Calcified shells around old brain bleeds form an armoured-brain picture in Aasim Ali's 2026 shunt case from Pakistan's literature. The shunt was placed in childhood for high brain pressure. New headache after 20 days prompted brain imaging for shunt problems.

The patient was a 35-year-old man with a mild, diffuse headache at arrival. Brain checks showed no clear nerve deficits or eye signs of pressure. CT scans showed crescent collections with thick calcified shells on both sides. That shell pattern is called armoured brain in the report text. MRI confirmed the collections and showed a mild shift of the brain midline. A small fresh bleed may have triggered symptoms.
pmc-13283621:
Stephanie Tow, David Bell, and Shana Harrington surveyed young para sport athletes in 2026 about early specialisation and injuries. Little is known about specialisation in this group, whose medical and body factors may reshape what counts as early or risky. The web survey, tested first by five young para athletes, went out through national para sport bodies to athletes aged eight to eighteen.

Twenty-five athletes replied, average age thirteen and a half. Most played several sports all year, averaging more than eight months in a main sport. Among the youngest group, all played multiple sports year-round. About four in ten of all respondents reported a sport injury in the past year. Injury shares looked much alike whether the main sport ran past eight months or not.
pmc-13283921:
Blood cell shredding after a pit viper bite was diagnosed without key lab tests in a 2026 Nepal case from Prabhat Kaphle and colleagues. The complication, called MAHA, is extremely rare with green pit vipers. Rural clinics often lack the blood smear tools that confirm it.

The 47-year-old woman developed swelling, bruising, blood in urine, and clotting failure. Low red cells and low platelets tracked over time fit the MAHA pattern. No species-matched antivenom was available at her treating facility. Supportive care plus blood product transfusions carried her to full recovery. Kidney harm never developed, and syndromic vigilance got the credit.
pmc-13284421:
Noam Shalem and colleagues report a 2026 imaging study on personal targeting for focused ultrasound treatment of tremor. Standard care aims at a thalamic site using fixed landmarks, yet up to one fifth of patients get poor tremor control. The team tested whether maps of brain tracts could guide a better target for each patient.

Scans from 81 patients treated between 2014 and 2021 were reviewed, with outcomes tracked for up to two years. Good lesions sat in one front-side zone of the dentatorubrothalamic tract, while poor lesions ringed that zone. A model using tract features predicted the best target well. The authors propose a shared sweet-spot map, while noting more testing is still needed.
pmc-13284521:
Won Ro Park, Yong Jae Kwon, and Dong Ha Lee compared in 2026 two ways of gauging bone strength: the standard DXA scan and density readings taken from ordinary CT scans. CT values, called Hounsfield units, had matched DXA fairly in the spine, but other bones were barely studied. The team reviewed 214 patients who had both scans, measuring CT values at five spots in four limb bones.

Inner bone readings in the upper and lower shin bones correlated moderately with the lowest DXA scores. One outer region of the upper arm bone also tracked the scores. Average CT values at several spots differed clearly between osteoporotic and normal groups. The authors suggest routine CT scans can supplement bone checks when DXA is unavailable.
pmc-13284721:
Yuna Miyachi and Kenta Nakai built a deep learning model in 2026 that predicts where RNA gets spliced, reading DNA stretches up to one hundred thousand letters long. Splicing trims non-coding segments from gene messages, and errors cause disease. Older tools miss far-away control signals because long sequences cost too much to process, and many models cannot explain their calls.

Their model, SpliceSelectNet, stacks transformer layers in a hierarchy, mixing local and global attention to catch near and distant signals at single-letter precision. It topped benchmark tests for splice site prediction and for spotting harmful splicing changes. Systematic fake mutations showed the model's attention scores track real functional importance, and long-range perturbation tests confirmed it senses distant regulators. The authors present it as both accurate and biologically readable.
pmc-13285221:
Mario Gilberto Siqueira and co-authors report long-term results, published in 2026, for a nerve transfer that restores shoulder outward rotation after upper arm nerve injury. Turning the shoulder outward is vital for daily tasks, yet repair efforts often focus on lifting the arm and bending the elbow. Seven patients had a radial nerve branch rerouted to power the infraspinatus muscle.

All seven regained some outward rotation after follow-up with a median near five years in this small series. Five reached the level the authors count as a good result. The team argues the transfer works and should join the set of options nerve surgeons consider for upper plexus injury, where each added motion widens what patients can do.
pmc-13285421:
Jia Zeng and five co-authors review trials of short exercise breaks, called exercise snacks, for aches from long sitting. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Long sitting is a world health risk and is tied to neck and back pain. Brief bouts of movement through the day are a fair way to break up desk work.

They gather the blind trials in desk-bound adults. Breaks span stretching, walking, stair climbs, and quick muscle work, each for a few minutes. Most trials find snacks cut aches next to plain sitting or rest. Stretch, strength, and mid-paced work beat slow walking. But most trials carry a high risk of bias, so the claim stays soft.
pmc-13285621:
Why does Bundibugyo ebolavirus still lack a licensed vaccine? Aniso Mohamed Abdi and co-authors press the question in a 2026 letter after fresh outbreaks in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Licensed Ebola shots guard only the Zaire species, leaving Bundibugyo and Sudan species bare despite repeat deadly outbreaks.

Animal proof for Bundibugyo and mixed-species shots exists, so the block is not science, the writers argue. Weak profit pull stalls late trials for germs that strike rarely in poor lands. Even Zaire shot access lags where risk runs high. The letter calls the gap a structural failure of preparedness and urges funding paths that do not wait for rich markets.
pmc-13285921:
Yuki Suzuki reviews DNA origami for drug delivery and cell control in a 2026 survey of intelligent nanomedicine. Folding a long DNA strand with short staples builds tiny shapes with exact size and spots for cargo.
