Engineered cancer cells expressing HLA-G proliferated, migrated, and formed colonies faster, progressed through the cell cycle readily, and resisted apoptosis. In mice their tumors grew faster, with stemness and metabolic programs on and mitochondrial activity up. HLA-G raised VEGF-C and its receptor signaling.
pmc-13475521:
Julia Hawthorne and co-authors review calcium use in 2026 during resuscitation for heart arrest inside hospitals. Calcium was long given for its hoped heart-boosting effect, despite thin proof. Records covered 599 arrest events at one academic center from 2011 to 2024, all lasting at least five minutes. About thirty-nine percent received calcium during the event.

Calcium use tracked with far lower rates of restored pulse, survival to discharge, and good brain outcome. Adjusted math kept the link strong on all three outcomes. Longer resuscitation time did not explain the pattern. The authors urge restraint and fresh trials before routine in-hospital use.
pmc-13476321:
Lorenzo Onorato and four colleagues pooled in 2026 studies on preventive antibiotics of the fluoroquinolone class for high-risk patients with low white-cell counts and blood cancers. They combined 18 trials and observational studies covering 12,586 patients, comparing preventive treatment with ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin against no preventive treatment.

Death rates did not differ between groups, even after excluding low-resistance settings. Preventive treatment did cut fever episodes and bloodstream infections, with a strong effect on the latter. Resistant strain counts did not differ. The authors conclude that preventive treatment reduces fever and bloodstream infection but offers no survival benefit.
pmc-13476621:
Yi Chen and co-authors show in 2026 that a tag system for proteins is required to build kidneys before birth. The system, UFMylation, had been tied to kidney shrinkage in adult mice when its ligase failed. Pups lacking that ligase in the kidney grew malformed kidneys that mimicked loss of a growth switch called YAP. Lab work found YAP itself receives the tag at one key site.

Tagging shields YAP from the cell shredder, letting it enter the nucleus and switch genes on. One of two tag-removing enzymes proved to be the main brake on YAP. Removing that brake steadied YAP and lifted its activity. A fresh cause for birth kidney faults is named.
pmc-13478021:
Elisabetta Cerchiara and co-authors describe a blood cancer case that breaks the usual genetic rules, in a 2026 report. These cancers are normally driven by one of three gene faults. The faults were thought to exclude each other. Their patient was a seventy-one-year-old man with polycythemia vera. His blood values stayed poorly controlled on standard treatment. Worry about progression led to broad gene sequencing.

The scan found a dominant second driver mutation. The first driver's clone had shrunk below the scan's detection limit. Older samples confirmed the two clones had traded places over time. Tissue findings still fit the original disease picture. The team settled on a broader diagnosis category. The case shows extra clones can reshape a disease's course. Step-by-step gene testing can miss that story. The authors argue full profiling should guide diagnosis and outlook in the sequencing era.
pmc-13478521:
Alwabli presents a task offloading strategy in 2026 for the Internet of Vehicles, where connected cars generate computing jobs too heavy to run on board. The four-tier design spreads work among the vehicles themselves, roadside units, edge servers, and the cloud, weighing delay against energy use for every assignment. Learning agents, trained centrally but acting independently in each vehicle, decide where each task goes as traffic and channels shift.

Against nine rival methods, from simple rules to rival learning systems, the strategy posted low average delay and low energy use in the simulations run. It also achieved a high task success rate and settled into stable behavior faster than the competing approaches tested alongside it. Tuning the balance between delay and energy shifted the system between safety-style services, which prize speed, and tolerant services that prize saving power, which the author frames as sustainability.
pmc-13479221:
Jeremy Howick and colleagues present a 2026 proposal for a model of empathic leadership aimed at crises in modern management. Business writing celebrates empathic leadership, yet two gaps persist. The proposed model imports what healthcare research shows about empathy: understanding another's perspective, communicating that understanding, and acting on it. The authors argue this sequence can guide leaders facing staff burnout, conflict, and rapid change. A defined model also lets organizations train the skill deliberately instead of treating it as a personality trait. The paper offers the model as both an explanation of good crisis leadership and a teaching foundation.
pmc-13479621:
Tina Nanyangwe-Moyo, Laura J. Rosa Pereira, and Mathieu Jean-Patrick Poirier published a 2025 evaluation of how well tobacco control research handles gender. Each study was scored on whether it named its gendered target group and assessed how policies land differently by gender. Forty of the forty-three studies did identify specific target groups and their challenges, a stronger showing than the authors' framing might suggest. pmc-13480221:
Reid Whitlock and co-authors report how common blocked-artery heart disease is in Manitoba, and what care people with the disease receive. Their study, published in 2026, linked health records for adults across the province. They counted cases from 2006 to 2019 and tracked blood fat levels, drug use, heart events, and hospital costs.

About one in ten adults had the disease, and the mean age was near 69 years. Just over half were taking drugs to lower blood fats, which means many were not. Among those with a blood test, fewer than half met the target level. Heart events were common and hospital care cost tens of millions of dollars. The authors stress a clear gap in care.
pmc-13480521:
Daniel C Cano-Blanco and co-authors present a 2026 catalyst study on breaking down nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas. Live X-ray probing during reaction showed the gases cycling through a shared pathway where the cobalt-cerium base stores and releases oxygen while rhodium sites turn over. The three-way border between the oxides flexes oxidation states with ease and frees lattice oxygen for the work. Rate studies matched that shared cycle picture. Designing oxide borders on purpose, guided by live spectroscopy, may yield cheaper gas clean-up catalysts that use less precious metal.
pmc-13480921:
Ren and colleagues set side by side in 2026 three decades of ischemic stroke data for China and the United States. Trends were split by age and birth group, and the team cast counts ahead to the year 2035.

Rates of living with past stroke rose in both. Raw case loads will still swell by 2035 in both lands, as crowds age. The authors urge more stroke proofing and care funds.
pmc-13482621:
Barre and Mohamud survey Mogadishu households in 2026 on what would make them pay for renewable energy, modeling the decision with the theory of planned behavior. The model explained 42.8 percent of the spread in readiness to pay, a moderate showing its adjusted figure of 40.2 percent roughly confirms for this sample. pmc-13483521:
Yingxuan Rong and co-authors compare three keyhole surgery routes for pinched neck nerves in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Neck pain, arm pain, daily function scores, and complication rates stayed statistically even across all three. Rankings crowned the wide channel only on speed. pmc-13483621:
Hajjam, Al Amad, and Nasher measure silent malaria in one district of Yemen, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. People with no symptoms can still carry the parasite and pass it on. The district lies in Al-Hodeidah, the main zone for malaria in Yemen. The team sampled homes in stages and tested blood with a rapid test.

About one in twenty of those tested carried malaria with no signs, and most cases were the falciparum kind. Schooling was linked with lower risk. Lack of window screens and homes near still water were linked with much higher risk. The authors call for screen use, care of still water sites, and more word spread in the area.
pmc-13486721:
Bozorgzad Fahadan and colleagues pitted two exercise therapies against each other for women with chronic low back pain that has no specific structural cause. Their 2026 trial randomly assigned 51 middle-aged women equally among the two programs and a control group, scoring pain, disability, balance, and position sense before and after.

Both programs cut pain by roughly two and a half to three points on the scales used in this trial. Disability scores fell by about fourteen points under both programs, far beyond the control group's change. Postural training pulled ahead specifically on lumbo-pelvic position sense, the ability to feel where the lower back sits. Bozorgzad Fahadan recommends blending both approaches, matched to each patient's particular deficits.
pmc-13486821:
Hosseinnezhad and Sabri designed a portable radon sensor around a cadmium telluride crystal, simulating the whole tool before building it. It distinguished decay energies sharply, with resolution better than two percent at the main alpha energy tested. pmc-13487821:
Makoto Nojo and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 35-year-old woman with repeated night-time anaphylaxis that was first blamed on Anisakis, a fish parasite. In vitro fertilization avoided exposure to seminal plasma and led to a healthy birth, which the authors present as a practical route to pregnancy for similar patients.
pmc-13487921:
Cheng and Li fuse sensor data with teacher scores to grade sports skills in twenty twenty-six. School sports marks often rest on one teacher's eye, which can be biased and slow. They tested it on close to four thousand skill samples from two hundred forty-five students. The fused model scored above ninety percent, well past either stream alone. It stayed steady when data went missing or a sensor failed. It also graded each sample in a flash. The authors call it a help for teachers, not a swap.
pmc-13488021:
Ahmet Yuce and colleagues study a blood ratio as a marker of erectile dysfunction in a 2026 retrospective analysis. The ratio divides fibrinogen, a clotting protein tied to inflammation, by albumin, a common blood protein. The ratio averaged clearly higher in patients than in controls, and higher values tracked with worse scores on a standard five-question erection scale in the reported analysis. A high cutoff was very specific but missed many cases, so the authors frame the ratio as support for diagnosis rather than a stand-alone test. They argue the link fits vessel and inflammation theories of the condition.
pmc-13488221:
Chun-Yan Sun and colleagues build a scale that gauges how well caregivers can support teenagers who self-injure without suicidal intent in a 2026 scale development study. The final scale holds thirty-two items across five dimensions, after weak items were cut by factor analysis. Scores hung together well, the five parts split cleanly, and a second model backed the structure in the reported checks. The authors offer the tool for assessing families and targeting support programs.
pmc-13490021:
Zengpeng Sun and others describe an exceptionally rare liver tumour containing two distinct cancers side by side. In 2026, the case report concerns a fifty-four-year-old man with hepatitis B-related liver scarring and three liver lesions, two cancers and one benign growth. Imaging suggested different findings for each lesion, and biopsy showed one as hepatocellular cancer and another as cholangiocarcinoma.

Surgery was not feasible, so the patient received interventional therapy, immune care, and chemo. By nine months, both cancers had shrunk a lot, by roughly sixty percent and seventy-two percent, with good general condition and normal routine blood tests. The authors review only two earlier definitive cases and offer this outcome as a reference for treating unresectable collision tumours.
pmc-13491821:
Yunanji Zhou and four colleagues quantify in 2026 the hidden cost of delivering liquid traditional Chinese medicine to older rural patients with chronic lung disease. Modeled distance to care averaged roughly ten kilometers for rural residents against under three for urban ones, and one in nine rural patients sat beyond fifteen kilometers. Delivery costs for rural areas beat urban benchmarks under every assumption tested, with the most expensive rural deliveries reaching several times city prices. No subsidy level in the scanned range produced stable cooperation among all parties, so the authors demand local pilot data before any national scheme.
pmc-13492321:
Yunjuan Sun and others describe implanting a leadless pacemaker in a pregnant woman without iodinated contrast and with minimal X-ray contact. In 2026, the case concerns a woman thirteen weeks pregnant with intermittent complete heart block, pauses up to 5.2 seconds, and repeated fainting. As a dancer, she declined a standard transvenous pacemaker.

Guided mainly by transthoracic echocardiography, the team tracked the guidewire, sheath, giving catheter, and device in real time, using belly shielding and only a low dose of fluoroscopy in the end. The approach shows that sound scans can largely replace contrast and X-rays for leadless pacing when fetal safety demands it.
pmc-13492421:
Lee, Cho, and Park wrote in 2026 a commentary on a fresh study of blood thinners and hidden cancer. These drugs cut stroke risk but can unmask slow bleeds. The study team tracked shifts in hemoglobin, the red blood protein, in the year after the drugs began.

About one in thirteen patients lost a large chunk of hemoglobin with no clear bleed to blame. Those patients went on to get a cancer diagnosis at a higher rate than peers whose levels held steady. The link ran strongest for gut cancers, and the same group also faced higher death and major bleed risks. Lee and co-authors frame the drop as an early alarm bell that should spark a search for hidden tumors.
pmc-13492521:
Sonja Hoover and four colleagues price out in 2026 what a community cancer support center actually spends guiding patients through their illness. Michelle's Place, a California nonprofit, offers navigation plus education and support groups to patients and families. The team collected salaries, staff time diaries, and non-labor costs, then split spending between core navigation work and extras aimed at relatives.

Core activities such as intake assessments and hunting down financial assistance consumed roughly four hundred sixty-four dollars of that figure. Family-oriented extras added about one hundred seventy-five dollars per client. Published cost figures for nonprofit navigation programs are rare, and the authors offer theirs as a budgeting anchor for funders and planners.
pmc-13493821:
Diella and co-authors tested intensive robot-assisted walking training for people with hereditary spastic paraplegia, an inherited condition that stiffens the legs and weakens walking. The team measured walking, balance, motor skills, and quality of life before and after, plus three months later.

Timed walking, balance scores, and a broad motor function scale also improved, and a severity rating suggested symptoms eased. Detailed gait analysis, however, showed no significant change in how the walking pattern itself looked. Patients reported better perceived physical health. The authors call for studies in more uniform patient groups.
pmc-13494221:
Scull and Benitez review bovine leukemia virus, a widespread cattle infection, through a One Health lens that links animal, human, and environmental wellbeing. Their 2026 review gathers evidence on milk output and composition, udder health, farm economics, and the unresolved question of whether the virus reaches people.
