Immune weakening from the virus also invites mastitis, compounding losses. Reports of viral traces in human tissue recur but fall short of proving transmission, the authors stress. They call the virus a silent drag on food security deserving coordinated control.
pmc-13495321:
Pengchao Zhang and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, two platelet-rich plasma protocols for mild meniscal tears in the knee. The meniscus is a cartilage pad that cushions the joint, and low-grade tears often ache without needing full repair. One protocol gave a series of ultrasound-guided shots around the meniscus over six weeks. The other paired scope surgery with a single shot inside the joint.

The review covered forty patients, twenty per protocol, followed for six months. No serious problems occurred. Both groups improved strongly: pain scores fell by about five points, and knee function scores climbed steeply. Pain paths matched between groups. Function scores leaned higher at six months for the surgery-plus-shot group. The authors stress the gap is descriptive only, a hint for a proper trial rather than a verdict, since patients were not assigned by lot.
pmc-13495521:
Dene Betz leads a large team comparing, in a 2026 mouse study, gene activity in the brain cortex beside a stroke and on the opposite side. Recovery peaks in a brief window after stroke, and repair was thought to center on tissue near the injury. The team sequenced RNA from both regions seven days after a clot-based stroke in male and female mice.

Both sides, injured and untouched, switched on the same inflammation program, rich in signals tied to reactive microglia, the brain's immune cells. The far side showed no distinct profile of its own; it echoed its injured partner. The shared response held in both sexes, and six weeks later both sexes grew comparable new wiring from the far side toward the injury. The authors argue that stroke recovery is a whole-cortex affair, not a local one, which widens where therapies might aim.
pmc-13495921:
Deng and co-authors use Denmark's national registries to ask whether a mother's thyroid disease, or the medicines used for it, raises her child's risk of cancer. Thyroid problems are common in women of childbearing age, but earlier evidence was patchy. Their 2026 case-control study matched 2,521 children diagnosed with cancer between 1973 and 2016 against 63,014 children without cancer. It then pulled mothers' diagnoses and prescriptions from national registers.

One condition stood out: children of mothers with goiter, an enlarged thyroid, had roughly double the odds of any childhood cancer in the adjusted analysis. Higher odds again appeared for leukaemia and lymphoma in particular. Neither underactive nor overactive thyroid showed a clear link, though the authors caution those analyses had limited statistical power. Reassuringly, mothers' thyroid medication itself carried no increased risk. The team stresses the small numbers behind the goiter finding and calls for replication first.
pmc-13499521:
Amna Nazir, Sadaf Ambreen, and Yasir Nawaz trace the family trees of genes that drive or suppress breast cancer. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Cancer grows when growth genes switch on wrongly and guard genes fail, and those genes have deep evolutionary histories.

The team pulled protein sequences from major databases for humans and other vertebrates. They aligned the sequences and built branching trees for eleven growth genes and ten guard genes. Counts of sister copies varied widely by gene. The growth genes cluster around jobs like gene switching, signaling, and RNA handling. The guard genes cluster around keeping cells stable. The trees show all studied genes descend from shared vertebrate ancestors, with later copying shaping each family.
pmc-13499921:
Cierra M Keith leads a 2026 study asking whether memory failure works the same way in Alzheimer's disease that begins early in life as in the usual late-onset form. Holding onto new memories, called episodic memory, is the hallmark problem in both, yet onset groups might lean on different brain regions. Using memory clinic data for 180 people with the amnestic, memory-led form of the disease, the team compared several memory measures and their ties to volume and thickness in signature brain areas.

No difference appeared in memory performance between early-onset and late-onset groups on any examined measure. Links between memory processes and brain structure were likewise mostly similar across groups. One exception stood out, since memory consolidation tied more strongly to thinning in a left parietal region in the early-onset group. That region helps integrate senses and language, hinting it carries extra weight there.
pmc-13500721:
Rahul Biswas, Rakesh Salunke, and Sadik Khan present a 2026 remote-sensing study of ground movement across the Mississippi River Delta. The team processed 461 pairs of Sentinel-1 radar images from 2020 to 2024, covering about 22,043 square kilometres of southeastern Louisiana and coastal Mississippi. They used a small-baseline interferometric method that tracks slow surface change over time. A key step filtered the radar signal using different quality thresholds for each land cover class, such as developed land, farmland, forest, and marsh.

Measured line-of-sight speeds ranged widely, from sinking near 43.71 millimetres per year to rising near 30.23 millimetres per year. Marsh and wetland ground sank fastest, especially organic-rich, low-lying areas, while parts of the southwestern coast rose where sediment accumulates. Readings at two NOAA stations were checked against satellite navigation measurements for validation.
pmc-13501721:
Razan Ahmed Alawaz leads a three-author team reporting a 2026 case of chronic oculomotor nerve palsy in a teenager, traced to an old sphenoid sinus lesion. A 16-year-old boy had a long outward drift of the right eye and growing limits on eye movement from early childhood. Examination showed restriction of inward, upward, and downward gaze, a wide outward squint, and a fixed dilated pupil, matching third cranial nerve palsy. The right eyelid did not droop despite the motor deficit.

His history included a sphenoid sinus lesion treated years earlier with endoscopic surgery and partial removal. Tissue study had shown a histiocyte-rich lesion wrapped in fibrosis. MRI showed surgical changes and arrested development of that sinus, with no returning mass. It also showed fatty wasting of two eye muscles from denervation. The authors stress that sinus disease near the cavernous sinus can damage eye nerves in children.
pmc-13503021:
Jason Liew reports a 2026 lung case in which a year's worth of tuberculosis investigation ended with a steroid prescription instead. A 65-year-old non-smoker with diabetes and hypertension carried a waxing and waning cough for twelve months, with chest infiltrates that migrated between scans and a stubborn right upper lobe opacity. At a specialist centre, sputum smears, gene assays, and cultures all came back negative, ruling the infection out rigorously.

Attention then shifted to the blood and the pattern: a peak eosinophil count of 3.8 billion per litre on the reported scale, IgE of 729 international units per millilitre, and edge-heavy consolidations on high-resolution imaging. Vasculitis, fungi, and parasites were excluded. The patient declined the airway scope that would have sampled his airways, so chronic eosinophilic pneumonia was diagnosed clinically. Prednisolone at 30 milligrams daily produced dramatic relief within 48 hours and complete clearing of the shadows in four weeks.
pmc-13503721:
Siva Venkadesh and ten colleagues present a shared brain atlas that lines up regions across five species, in a 2026 paper. The set spans mouse, rat, marmoset, macaque, and human brains. Past atlases were built one species at a time, which blocked fair comparison across them.

The team built the atlas from averaged brain forms with matched tissue maps, then checked it four ways. Checks covered match with known human maps, fit inside species maps, steady placement across species, and dye-tracer links in mouse and marmoset. Each region got a score for how sure its match across species is. Sense and movement links held up well across species, while links for higher thought drifted more. The atlas is free for others to use.
pmc-13503921:
Caio Márcio Vasconcellos Cordeiro de Almeida leads a team selecting cacao clones for farms in Rondônia, Brazil, in a 2026 study. Brazil could grow its share of world cacao as output slips in the top producer states. Local clones must yield well and hold steady across years under tree shade.

The team tracked 30 clones in shaded plots over seven harvests. Yields ranged widely, nearly sevenfold from worst to best, with a mean near 476 kilos of dry beans per hectare. Genetic spread and heritability were high, which favors selection gains. A factor model best captured how rankings shifted across years. Two years of harvests sufficed to pick clones in late breeding rounds. Five clones combined top yield with the steadiest record.
pmc-13504821:
Marco Carfagno leads a team exploring how people with eating disorders rethink illness and recovery during group therapy, in a 2026 interview study. Recovery is often counted as symptom loss alone, which can miss what change means to the patient. Group settings may reshape those meanings.

Ten adult outpatients spoke at the end of a group program set within broader care. Early on, most framed their illness through food, weight, and control. Over time they spoke more of feelings, relationships, and self-worth. Recovery became a winding path of awareness, acceptance, and connection rather than a finish line. The group gave belonging and a mirror for reflection, though it also stirred shame and fear of judgment. The authors name feeling skills and identity work as recovery targets.
pmc-13505021:
Saime Esin Güney leads a team comparing mouth health in child leukemia survivors at early and late stages after treatment, in a 2026 study. Cancer drugs given in childhood can scar growing teeth and dry the mouth. Whether those harms fade with time was the open question.

The study covered 38 survivors aged five to eighteen and 20 healthy siblings. Tooth decay scores ran higher and saliva flow lower in survivors seen within about three years of treatment than in those seen later. Tooth shape faults, like small teeth and odd roots, appeared in most survivors but few siblings, and they did not fade with time. Age and time since treatment each predicted decay scores. The authors urge close dental watch in the first years after treatment.
pmc-13505121:
Aykut Can Balkanlıoğlu and Izzet Acikan test cold plasma surface treatment for early dental implant hold. In 2026, the forward-looking single-center randomized within-patient trial compares untreated implants with cold atmospheric plasma, vacuum plasma, and argon jet plasma, each applied sixty seconds before placement. The trial analyzed forty implants in ten patients. Implant hold dips transiently before biological secondary hold takes over.

All implants remained in place with no adverse events, and baseline stability quotients were comparable. Controls dipped at day twenty-eight while plasma-treated implants rose steadily, with a clear group-by-time interaction. At day fifty-six, plasma groups exceeded controls by 10.0, 8.9, and 8.3 stability units respectively. The authors call for larger forward-looking, site-standardized trials.
pmc-13506121:
Justin Hyde and colleagues review how aneurysmal bone cysts behave when they grow in the spine or sacrum rather than long bones. These blood-filled cysts are benign yet locally aggressive, and in the spine they often start in the rear elements and push toward the canal. The review, built mainly on the last ten years of literature, covers diagnosis, biopsy, surgery, and add-on treatments.

Imaging can hint at the diagnosis through fluid levels inside an expanding lesion, but scans cannot rule out cancer look-alikes, so biopsy stays essential. Treatment is tailored to nerve pressure, stability, deformity, and lesion size. Options run from scraping the cyst out to wider removal with stabilisation, sometimes helped by blocking its blood supply, injecting doxycycline, or giving denosumab. Cyst return links most strongly with incomplete removal and younger age, and the authors ask for prospective spine-specific comparisons.
pmc-13507021:
Bing Sun, Jieyang Zhu, Yi Jiang, Sihui Chen, and Tao Zhang build, in 2026 work, a survival forecast for osteosarcoma based on genes tied to cell organelles. Osteosarcoma is the most common malignant bone tumor, often seen in teens. The team screened gene data from patient cohorts and kept three genes linked to outlook: ACSS2, CLTCL1, and PLD3.

Their three-gene score divided the cohort into high-risk and low-risk groups whose survival differed clearly, and it held up in a second cohort. Risk groups also differed in response to four drugs in lab data. Cell tests supported a real role for ACSS2 in tumor behavior. The score could help sort patients and point to new treatment targets.
pmc-13507221:
Junkyu Park and colleagues explore, in 2026 work, side-effect patterns of GLP-1 obesity drugs in real-world reports and search computationally for herbs linked to those patterns. Reports came from the United States adverse event system for 2015 to 2025, totaling 142705 reports, with 4090 tied to obesity use. Stomach and gut events dominated, and most reports involved female patients.

Onset clustered in the first month, while one drug showed more late cases after a year. Strong signals appeared for gallbladder, pancreas, kidney, and clotting events for some drug pairs. Network models ranked familiar medicinal herbs as top candidates for study. The authors stress that all herb links are hypotheses needing lab and clinical proof.
pmc-13507821:
Ayushi Saxena and six co-authors review whether a fast form of brain stimulation works as well as the standard daily form for hard-to-treat depression, in 2026 work. Standard treatment uses magnetic pulses over several weeks of daily visits. The faster option, called accelerated iTBS, compresses sessions into a much shorter span. The review gathered 25 studies that compared the two approaches in adults whose depression had not eased with usual care.

Across those studies, the fast approach matched the standard one on easing depression symptoms. Effects on thinking skills looked just as safe in both groups. Shorter schedules also lowered the travel and time burden that can block access to care. The authors present the fast option as a practical choice for clinics and for patients who cannot manage weeks of daily visits.
pmc-13508221:
Meng Zhou, Liru Zhao, Dongbo Li, and Zhongle Cheng combine a rapid lab fingerprint method with machine learning to spot drug-resistant bacteria, in 2026 work. The target germ, Acinetobacter baumannii, causes hospital infections, and its carbapenem-resistant form limits treatment choices. Standard resistance testing is slow. The team collected 301 bacterial samples, over half of them resistant, and took two spectra from each. Five learning models were trained on part of the data and judged on a held-out set, split by sample to avoid leakage.

A flexible way of slicing the spectra into bins beat fixed slicing for every model. The best model reached near-perfect sorting scores on the test set, with accuracy above nine in ten. An explanation method highlighted which parts of the fingerprint drove the calls. The authors argue this pairing could flag resistant infections sooner, guiding drug choice and infection control while tests still run.
pmc-13508321:
Xuan-Geng Deng and five co-authors compare two ways to stop spinal fluid leaks during neck disc surgery, in work published in 2026. The surgery, called ACDF, treats worn or injured neck discs. A tear in the membrane around the spinal cord is a rare but serious slip during the operation. Standard care patches the tear and seals it with glue. The newer method plugs the space around the implant with bone wax, walling the leak off. Records covered patients with such tears from 2020 to 2025.

Among 1,311 operations, twenty-three patients had a leak, and all tears were small. Twelve were patched and eleven were sealed with wax. The patch route failed twice, needing extra drainage for lasting leaks. The wax route had no failures and no other complications after surgery. The authors suggest wax sealing is a dependable backup when patching proves awkward.
pmc-13508621:
Furkan Bahar and five co-authors compare clotting and bleeding risks between the two first-line drug routes for advanced melanoma, in 2026 work. Vein clots are a leading cause of illness in cancer patients, and both immune therapy pairs and targeted tablet pairs are standard openers. Adults starting either the immune pair or the targeted pair were matched one to one on background traits, giving 1,043 patients per group. Clots, bleeding, and death were tracked for six months.

The immune pair carried clearly higher clot risk: seven percent against about four percent in six months. Lung clots and leg vein clots each ran higher too. Bleeding, including brain and gut bleeding, did not differ between the groups. Deaths ran slightly higher with the immune pair, though that gap missed statistical firmness. They suggest clot prevention planning should weigh which melanoma opener a patient receives.
pmc-13510221:
Pengcheng Xu and co-authors report a 2026 gene study of a Chinese Han family with hearing loss passed down through the family. More than one hundred twenty genes are known to cause forms of hearing loss that come with no other symptoms. The team set out to find the cause in this family and to test what the fault does.

They checked the family in the clinic and sequenced over four hundred deafness-linked genes in the child at the center of the case. Two faults in one gene, CDH23, were found in her, one from each parent. Both faults were new, and checks in the rest of the family matched a recessive pattern. Lab tools predicted how the faults would disrupt the gene's message. The case widens the known range of faults in this gene.
pmc-13510721:
Kotova and colleagues tested in 2026 whether two anti-inflammatory drugs ease the effects of long stress in zebrafish, small fish widely used to study mood disorders. Stress that lasts for weeks can inflame the brain, and that swelling is tied to anxiety and depression. The team wanted to know if calming the swelling also calms behavior.

Fish went through two weeks of unpredictable stress, with or without drug treatment. Minocycline, given for the full two weeks, cut depression-like freezing in a tail test and lowered both pro- and anti-inflammatory gene signals in the brain. Nimesulide, given for one week, had a narrower effect: it eased anxiety-like behavior and brought two stress-raised inflammatory genes back to normal levels. The contrast shows the two drugs act on stress in distinct ways.
pmc-13511721:
Sab Siddiq, Shabnam Cheetham, Clare E. Pain, Eve M. D. Smith, Sizheng Steven Zhao, Liza J. McCann, and David M. Hughes gather evidence on extra health conditions that travel with rheumatic diseases starting in childhood, in a 2026 systematic review. The three diseases covered are juvenile idiopathic arthritis, childhood-onset lupus, and juvenile dermatomyositis, a muscle and skin condition. Three major databases were searched without limits, following standard review guidance.

Patients faced a higher risk of a wide range of added conditions in both childhood and adult life. That extra burden reaches beyond the primary disease and weighs on quality of life across the whole life course. The authors urge proactive, multi-specialty watch and care for these added conditions. Current studies show weak spots, above all thin long-term follow-up, so firmer risk figures for childhood-onset disease still need building.
pmc-13514021:
Andrew Rogers and colleagues lay out a review protocol on substance use disorders among adults with chronic pain. Their protocol from twenty twenty-six targets nicotine, alcohol, and cannabis specifically. Opioids dominate the pain-and-addiction literature by far. The other substances are common yet poorly quantified in pain populations.

The planned review will pool prevalence across existing studies. Pain and substance use influence each other in both directions. Clinicians need real rates to plan screening and care. Standard review methods will structure the search and synthesis. The protocol fixes those methods before results are known. Documented prevalence can reshape pain clinic routines. Undercounted problems stay undertreated problems, the authors imply.
pmc-13515021:
Yang Wu and a team of co-authors report virus work from twenty twenty-six on Getah virus in pigs. The virus has spread again in recent years and caused gut illness outbreaks on pig farms. It belongs to a virus group that also holds major human and animal threats.

The team isolated a strong strain from the gut contents of sick piglets. In mice, the strain proved lethal. They then traced how a viral protein breaks down a host defense protein, using the cell waste system to remove it. That trick weakens the host response to the virus. The work warns of outbreak risk and shows one way the virus evades defense.
pmc-13515321:
Li and colleagues published a 2026 study on a bird flu virus taken from chickens in Jiangsu, China. H9N2 flu circulates widely in poultry and can infect people occasionally. The isolate, gathered in March 2025, came from a chicken flock. The team read its genes and tested it in mice, chickens, and ducks.

Gene trees placed the virus in a fast-spreading Chinese lineage mix. Key changes hinted at stronger copying power inside mammal cells after infection. In mice, the virus grew in lungs and noses with no prior training rounds. Chickens caught and passed it more readily than ducks did. Chicken-to-duck spread worked better than duck-to-duck in their pens. Stronger farm surveillance is the team's closing plea to authorities.
pmc-13517021:
Gabriela Christina Kuhl and four colleagues engineer a safer therapeutic bacterium in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. Live bacterial medicines need two things regulators demand: they must not escape control, and their added genes must stay put. The team used CRISPR-based editing to swap one gene in a standard E coli strain. The swap removed the bacterium's ability to make certain amino acids, so it starves without supplements, and inserted a therapeutic gene in the same step.

The built-in starvation worked and lifted when the missing nutrients were fed. The chromosome-based strain kept its therapeutic activity, the red-cell-bursting effect of its cargo protein, and grew as well as the plasmid version. Both versions delivered DNA into those cells. Kuhl's team presents the single-step design as a cleaner chassis for future live medicines.
pmc-13517121:
Guillermo Eduardo Cuéllar-Nevárez and five colleagues review how to diagnose tuberculosis in people living with HIV in a 2026 article. The pairing is deadly because weakened immunity makes TB hide: fewer bacilli, odd symptoms, disease outside the lungs. Standard tools, sputum smears, cultures, and chest X-rays, miss many such cases. The authors walk through each option's accuracy, practicality, and barriers to real-world use.

Rapid molecular tests now catch the germ and drug resistance early, though sputum-free and body-wide disease still slip through. A urine test helps the severely ill, and a newer version promises more. Blood signatures and computer-read chest images may sharpen screening and triage. Cuéllar-Nevárez's team argues no single test suffices. They propose combined algorithms matched to local resources, stitching microbe tests, urine tests, imaging, and host-response tools into one pathway.
pmc-13519021:
Sejoong Ahn and a large team mine a Korean emergency department registry in 2026 for clues on steroids in septic shock, a debate usually argued from intensive care data. Records covered 5,127 adults treated between 2015 and 2023 across many centers. Timing and dose were examined among patients given hydrocortisone after blood-pressure drugs began.

After adjustment, steroid use linked to lower 28-day mortality, with odds reduced by about a quarter. The benefit concentrated in patients also receiving vasopressin. Among 1,529 hydrocortisone patients, waiting longer to start, starting at higher pressor doses, and exceeding 300 milligrams per day each linked to higher mortality. Ahn and colleagues stress the findings are observational and hypothesis-generating, not proof.
pmc-13520121:
Siddiq and colleagues trace how a yeast gene's control region evolved in this 2026 study. The gene, TDH3, helps yeast process sugars. Its promoter became more active in the baker's yeast lineage. A promoter is the DNA stretch that sets how strongly a gene runs. The team compared promoters across Saccharomyces species to find which DNA changes caused the rise and how they acted.

Much of the increase came from changes sitting between the well-known binding sites of two regulator proteins, not at the sites themselves. Those changes raised expression levels while leaving the timing pattern of the response untouched. Their effect appeared only when a third regulator, TYE7p, was present, suggesting the changes work by shaping how the whole regulator complex assembles on the DNA.
pmc-13520321:
Chenjiao Hou and colleagues describe in 2026 miniature heart tissues grown from reprogrammed human stem cells, used to test drug harm and benefit without animal hearts. The tissues beat on their own and copy key features of real heart muscle.

Known heart-damaging and heart-protecting drugs were applied to the tissues, including a cancer drug noted for heart injury and a birth-defect drug used as a harm check. Beating, survival signals and injury models for heart attack and thickened heart muscle were tracked. Responses matched expected drug effects, supporting the tissues as a screening platform. Further validation would be needed before routine drug decisions rely on them.
pmc-13520521:
Kai Zhao and Xiangcai Meng test in 2026 whether a brief hydrogen peroxide soak can raise medicinal compound levels in peony roots used for two traditional remedies. Farmed roots have lost quality as demand grew, while mild stress is known to switch on protective chemistry in plants.

Fresh roots from two peony lines were soaked at several peroxide strengths. At the middle strength on day two, eight measured compounds rose markedly in one line, with gains ranging from roughly one fifth to over three quarters. Six compounds rose in the other line as well. Follow-up tests with blockers probe whether reactive oxygen signalling drives the gains.
pmc-13521021:
Chen and colleagues studied in 2026 the blood ratio of heterophils to lymphocytes, a simple immune marker in poultry, in Yellow-legged Ma chickens. The basis of this ratio inside tissues was unclear. The team picked birds with very high or very low ratios from 113 chickens and split them by sex. They combined liver and spleen tissue checks with blood chemistry and gene and metabolite profiling.

Chen found no clear differences between high- and low-ratio birds in tissue structure, liver enzyme levels, or oxidative stress markers. The molecular picture split sharply by sex, though. Hens with low ratios showed stronger immune gene activity across T cell and cytokine pathways. Roosters differed instead in chemokine, Toll-like receptor, and related signalling. One gene, CCR2, stood out as a shared node. The authors frame the ratio as a sex-dependent window on liver immune state, useful for breeding.
pmc-13521821:
Xin Lin and Baoai Wang review three blood index values and their links to outcomes after a sudden stroke, in a paper from 2026. The stroke type studied is caused by a blocked brain artery. Harm after such a stroke comes from inflammation, stress-driven high blood sugar, and long-term metabolic problems acting together.

Each index reflects one of those strands. One combines immune cell counts, one compares blood sugar with a long-term average, and one joins fats and sugar in a single score. Raised values of the first index link to worse severity, worse function, and higher death rates. The review gathers what is known about all three and argues they complement each other. Used together, they may help grade risk early.
pmc-13522421:
Firew Tekle Bobo and co-authors examine, in a 2026 Australian study, how national data sources define and count psychosocial disability, meaning disability linked to mental health conditions. Five sources were compared, including disability and health surveys, a mental health survey, the Census, and records from the National Disability Insurance Scheme. Definitions were reviewed first, followed by a comparison of prevalence figures.

The sources proved inconsistent, because each was built for a different purpose and covered different conditions. Broad surveys included developmental and degenerative conditions, while the insurance scheme covered only severe illness with major limits on daily function. Reported rates ranged widely, so the authors warn researchers and policymakers to account for these differences before using the figures for planning or funding choices.
pmc-13522521:
Ibrahim Aldawood, Ahmad Althumali, Syed Mansoor Ali, and Saad Aldawood grow nickel oxide films of different thicknesses on flexible plastic in a 2026 materials study. Nickel oxide conducts positive charges and is transparent, making it useful as a charge-transport layer in solar cells. Films from ten to forty nanometers thick were deposited on plastic coated with a clear conductor and then examined by several methods.

Thin films formed scattered islands, while thicker films became compact and much smoother, with roughness falling sharply. Light emission peaked at thirty nanometers, and electrical resistance fell as thickness grew, reflecting more charge carriers. The authors identify films in the thirty to forty nanometer range as the most promising for flexible solar and light-based devices.
pmc-13523121:
Mehul Desai and six co-authors published a 2026 systematic review of how needle and device choices affect injections under the skin. Such injections deliver many modern drugs, and small design details can change pain, anxiety, and safety. The team searched four databases and kept 62 studies that tied needle traits, such as thickness, length, and tip shape, or device traits to patient outcomes.

Thinner and shorter needles consistently cut reported pain and side effects like bruising and bleeding. Tapered, lubricated, and hidden needle designs lowered anxiety and raised satisfaction. Autoinjectors and prefilled syringes also helped. Results varied across studies, and many were too small or changed several traits at once. The authors call for cleaner studies that vary one trait at a time.
pmc-13523221:
Ella Petter and colleagues use tumor size dynamics to find mutations that shape treatment response in lung cancer in a 2026 study. Standard genetic studies rely on survival outcomes, while clinicians in practice follow how tumors shrink and grow on scans. A new framework was built to model repeated tumor readings from roughly seventeen thousand radiology reports at a major cancer center.

The method found twenty-seven mutations linked to uneven response to common treatments, with both protective and harmful effects. Two findings were validated in an external drug sensitivity screen. Thirteen further mutations tracked rates of growth and response across the whole treatment course, nine of them invisible to conventional survival models. Results held in an advanced-stage subgroup, supporting tumor dynamics as a complement to survival analysis.
pmc-13523321:
Ngwa Niba Rawlings, Mark Stephen Bailey, and Orin Courtenay pool evidence on volatile pyrethroid spatial repellents in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. These devices release insecticide vapor to protect a surrounding space from mosquitoes and sand flies. Forty-nine studies with more than one hundred fifty datasets were included, covering human infection trials and trap-based insect studies, mostly testing one active ingredient.

Trial data suggested protection of about half against malaria parasites and about one third against dengue and Zika viruses, with a single trial giving similar protection against leishmania. Trap studies showed substantial falls in captured insects, with estimates varying by trap type. Outdoor use looked no worse than indoor use. The authors present spatial repellents as a promising complement to existing vector control tools.
pmc-13523521:
Shuai Yang and others test, in a 2026 imaging study, whether pairing two magnetic resonance mapping methods can grade knee cartilage wear and meniscus injury in knee osteoarthritis. Standard scans show structure late, while mapping reads tissue chemistry earlier. One method, sped up by AI compressed sensing, was paired with conventional mapping.

The study took in 56 patients with knee osteoarthritis and 30 healthy volunteers between August 2025 and February 2026, all scanned at 3 tesla. Both measures were higher in patients than controls across regions, and values separated mild from severe subgroups. Joint mapping reached the strongest accuracy for cartilage wear and slightly better accuracy for meniscal injury than either method alone. The authors propose the pairing for earlier, stage based management decisions.
pmc-13524921:
Victor Miguel Sierra Marquina, Maria del Carmen Pardo, and Alba Maria Franco-Pereira develop an overlap measure for judging biomarkers. Their 2026 statistical methods paper targets markers that must separate three stages of Alzheimer's disease. Tests sort people into probable Alzheimer's, mild cognitive impairment, or normal aging, and the usual scoring tools were built for two groups.

Their overlap measure extends a known index to three groups, with both parametric and nonparametric forms plus bootstrap confidence intervals. Practice runs checked how well the estimators behaved. They set it against the volume under the ROC surface, the standard three-way accuracy measure. A longitudinal neuropsychological data set on biomarker tracking of disease stages shows the method. The authors aim to speed drug work by finding markers that track progression earlier.
pmc-13525421:
Jinhu Wu and co-authors took apart the roles of each metal in a catalyst in a 2026 study. The catalyst blends iron, cobalt, nickel, and molybdenum in a glassy, unordered mix shaped into tiny rings. It drives the oxygen-making half of water splitting well and lasts long, but which metal does what was hard to see in such a mixed frame.

The team watched the catalyst at work with live light probes. Cobalt stood out as the main active site, turning into a high-charge form as it works. Iron and molybdenum back it up in ways the probes could split apart. Knowing each role helps chemists tune mixed catalysts by design rather than by trial.
pmc-13526721:
Xiaoli Chen, Zhuo An, Changhong Li, and Jinxia Zhao test, in a 2026 lab study, whether pooled antibodies from rheumatoid arthritis patients can drive the bone eating cells behind joint erosion. These anti-citrullinated protein antibodies mark the disease, yet their direct effect on osteoclast growth was debated. Antibodies were purified from pooled blood of 37 positive patients.

Purified antibodies kept an intact structure and bound citrullinated vimentin. Monocytes from healthy donors and patients were then grown into osteoclasts with standard growth factors, with or without the antibodies. Antibody treatment did not clearly raise osteoclast numbers, marker gene expression, or bone resorption pit area against controls. The authors conclude any bone effect likely needs a richer tissue setting or special antibody properties their setup missed.
pmc-13527121:
Christopher F. Sharpley, G. Lorenzo Odierna, Vicki Bitsika, and Christopher B. Watson review, in a 2026 systematic narrative review, sensory hyposensitivity in major depression, meaning dulled responsiveness across the five senses. Individual studies had reported blunting in single senses, yet no review had covered vision, hearing, taste, touch, and smell together.

The search gathered fifty-one individual studies and five reviews focused on smell. Findings were organized by the form the blunting takes, the brain processes proposed to underlie it, and its possible function. Explanations split between peripheral sensory dulling and central cognitive dysfunction. The authors propose hyposensitivity may serve as an escape from an aversive environment, giving the depressed person a form of relief. Clinical translation ideas and future research directions close the review.
pmc-13527921:
Esa Ala-Ruona and eight colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for a randomized trial of integrative music therapy for adults with depression-related problems, including anxiety, work stress, and exhaustion. Participants aged 18 to 65 will receive improvisational music therapy twice a week for six weeks, starting each session with slow paced breathing.

Four groups will compare the core therapy with versions adding music listening, vibroacoustic treatment, or both; one group waits as a control. The main outcome is psychological distress, with depression, anxiety, burnout, quality of life, and difficulty naming emotions also measured. Registered in advance, the trial aims to show which combination of elements helps and who responds best.
pmc-13528021:
Ning Yao and seven colleagues chart chickenpox in Chongqing, China, in a 2026 study of disease patterns, immunity, and costs. Routine records from 2011 to 2024 held 301,714 cases. Over half were in children under fifteen. A 2024 blood survey of 960 people measured protection levels. Cost data came from thousands of clinic and hospital cases.

Overall, about seventy-eight percent of people carried antibodies. Children showed a clear gap, at about seventy-one percent protected. Two vaccine doses protected far better than one dose. Adults over fifty had the highest levels and the lowest recent case rates. Hospital care for children cost more than for older patients. The authors recommend wider two-dose coverage to cut both illness and costs.
pmc-13530021:
Xiao-Wei Jia and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six mouse study of a fat-derived factor that browns white fat through nerves. The factor FSTL1 is released by fat cells. Browning burns energy, but how the factor drives it was incomplete.

Extra FSTL1 browned white fat, raised energy use, and improved sugar uptake in male mice. Fat-specific extra amounts protected mice on a rich diet. Without the factor, mice chilled easily and gained weight. The factor worked by growing sympathetic nerves into fat, not directly on fat cells. Cutting those nerves erased the benefit.
pmc-13531621:
Jakub Chmiel and co-authors link in 2026 the tally of cardiovascular risk factors to dangerous plaque features across all heart arteries. Light-based imaging inside the vessels of 131 patients catalogued 534 plaques and their traits. Risk factors split into changeable habits and conditions versus fixed traits such as age and family history.

More risk factors meant more plaques, more thin-capped fatty plaques, and more fragile features such as cholesterol crystals and tiny vessels. After adjustment, only the changeable burden predicted higher vulnerability. The message supports aggressive control of pressure, lipids, diabetes, weight, and smoking.
pmc-13532221:
Anastasia Lambropoulou and colleagues find in 2026 two soil-bacterium peptides that restore frontline antibiotic power against enzyme-armed resistant gut bacteria. Screening natural products surfaced pinensin A and B from a soil species. These bacteria-killing enzymes, metallo-beta-lactamases, shrug off nearly every beta-lactam drug and have no approved blocker.

Both peptides returned the drug meropenem to full effect in 30 resistant clinical strains, dropping needed levels below the treatment threshold. The secret is tight zinc grabbing: the enzymes need zinc, and the peptides bind it at extremely low amounts. Further work as drug boosters is warranted.
pmc-13534421:
Ritu Gauraha, Ayush Kumar Agrawal, and Parul Dubey present in 2026 a hybrid framework that classifies sentiment in deepfake social media posts while showing its reasoning. Fake text is hard to judge, and most accurate models act as black boxes. Their dataset held 25,572 tweets split evenly between human and machine writing.

The method pairs transformer text embeddings with fuzzy rules that people can read. Across ten-fold checks it reached high accuracy and F1 scores, beating a strong baseline by a clear margin. Readers gain both performance and explanations that help analysts trust each call.
pmc-13534521:
Ozge Gundogdu, Erol Egrioglu, and Eren Bas propose in 2026 a forecasting method for nonlinear time series that blends Pythagorean fuzzy sets with a hybrid neural network. Fuzzy methods capture uncertainty well, yet their inputs grow large and lag choice is often unsystematic. Dimension reduction first compresses membership data into cleaner inputs.

A modified network paired with simple smoothing then models both linear and nonlinear patterns, with swarm optimisation setting all parameters. Tests on rolling windows of two major stock indices beat existing approaches. Readers in finance and engineering gain a systematic, ready-to-build forecasting framework.
pmc-13534821:
Natalia Castoldi and a team of co-authors probe spine bone quality in teens with scoliosis, in a case study dated twenty twenty-six. Eight patients gave small bone samples from the curve's apex during corrective surgery. Three tools checked the samples: fine CT scans, electron imaging, and nano-scale hardness tests.

Bone volume share matched healthy values, and the struts ran a bit thicker than usual. Mineral spread was wider than in reference data. One mineral peak fell as the wedge angle of the curve grew. The study gives a rare direct look at bone inside the bent spine.
pmc-13535121:
Nicholas McClellan, Li Chen, Sophia Matossian, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It photographs the tiny blood vessels at children's fingernail edges to tell apart subtypes of juvenile muscle inflammation and to gauge how active the disease is.

Capillaroscopy is painless and shows microcirculation directly. Seventy-six young people took part: healthy controls, juvenile dermatomyositis, childhood lupus, and overlap myositis. Software measured the vessel patterns; unsupervised clustering sorted patients into three camps, dominated by branched vessels, by enlarged vessels, or by neither. The branched camp tracked with a distinct clinical picture. Feature comparisons separated the diseases, and in muscle disease the vessel measures moved with clinical activity scores. Ten newly diagnosed patients were rechecked at three months. The authors pitch nailfold imaging as a cheap bedside biomarker for a rare disease family.
pmc-13536021:
About a quarter of people who survive acute pancreatitis develop diabetes within three years. Djibril Ba and co-authors ask whether machine learning can spot them early. They used a large federated health records network covering 2017 to 2024. The cohort held 58,746 pancreatitis patients with no prior diabetes. Five model types were trained across four prediction windows. Simple logistic regression won.

Its accuracy averaged 0.72, with a discrimination score of 0.79. Top predictors included age, pancreatic necrosis, body weight, and blood pressure. Visit counts and past lab values also mattered. The authors say routine records already carry much of the signal needed for early warning.
pmc-13536121:
Jai Das and a large team of co-authors set out a trial protocol in two thousand twenty-six for heat adaptation in rural Pakistan. Parts of the country often pass forty degrees Celsius, and most heat research targets cities or rich settings. Rural, low-income communities have little evidence to guide them.

The cluster-randomized trial covers twenty-two clusters, split evenly between intervention and control. The bundle pairs community education with structural fixes: roof and wall treatments, shading, ventilation, clean energy, and shared outdoor shelters. Surveys will track health and behavior, while wearables and sensors record heat exposure and indoor conditions. Approvals and consent plans are in place, and results will be shared with communities and policymakers.
pmc-13536621:
Shuang Zhang and colleagues compare in 2026 ultrasound cycloplasty with Ahmed valve implants for neovascular glaucoma, a severe eye pressure disease driven by abnormal new vessels. Eighty patients, one eye each, were split evenly between the two treatments and followed for six months. Pressure, drug counts, pain, vision, and complications were tracked over time.

Both methods lowered eye pressure well, and success rates were similar across the groups. By six months the ultrasound group showed steadier pressure and lower pain scores. The valve group had more complications, mainly tube blockage and plate exposure, favouring ultrasound on safety and comfort.
pmc-13536721:
Haoyu Wei and Xinhong Yang describe an inherited low fibrinogen case in a 2026 family report from China. Fibrinogen is a blood protein needed for clotting, and low levels can cause bleeding. A 28-year-old pregnant woman and her mother both showed low fibrinogen levels on lab tests. Gene sequencing searched for the cause, and delivery care was planned around the clotting weakness.

Testing found a new single-letter deletion in the FGA gene carried by both women, matching their low activity and low protein levels. Before a planned cesarean birth with spinal anesthesia, the patient received extra fibrinogen by vein. The baby girl was delivered safely without heavy bleeding. The authors stress combined lab and gene testing for diagnosis, counseling, and safe birth planning.
pmc-13536821:
Wei-Zhi Huang and co-authors probe how lidocaine, a common numbing drug, affects human mouth cells in a 2026 laboratory study. Beyond pain control, the drug may influence cancer growth and healing after surgery. Two cell lines were tested, one mouth cancer line and one normal gum line, using growth, flow, gene, protein, and electrical measures. Combinations with two standard cancer drugs were also checked.

Cancer cells grew less under lidocaine, with shifts in cell cycle, cell death, energy membranes, low-oxygen signals, and self-cleaning activity. Gum cells responded differently, with distinct cycle, death, and stress patterns. Lidocaine strengthened both cancer drugs in both cell lines. Electrical patterns for the drug alone resembled those for a drug pairing. The authors suggest wider roles for numbing drugs in oral cancer care.
pmc-13538221:
Franck Zekre and co-authors test blood antibodies to two gum bacteria in early spine arthritis in a 2026 cohort analysis. Both bacteria drive gum disease and have been linked to joint arthritis, raising questions about spine disease. Serum from 554 people in a French early back pain cohort was tested and sorted into spine arthritis types, with or without skin or bowel features, plus chronic back pain controls. Smoking was also considered.

Antibody levels overlapped strongly across all groups, with no clear gap between any arthritis type and controls for either bacterium. Adjusting for age, sex, weight, and smoking changed nothing, and smoking itself showed no sway on patterns. The authors conclude that blood responses to these two bacteria show no major link to early spine arthritis, while wider mouth imbalance remains possible.
pmc-13538521:
Esperança João Rafael and colleagues survey self-medication for COVID-19 among health students in Maputo, Mozambique, in a 2026 online study from November 2022. Students from three health training institutions answered questions on herbal and standard medicine use during the pandemic. Among 390 eligible respondents, most reported treating themselves, raising concern about habits that future clinicians may carry into practice and patient advice.

Herbal use dominated, led by eucalyptus steam inhalation, lemon, ginger, garlic, and onion across twenty-three plant types. Standard medicines reached about one third of students, led by an antibiotic also used without prescription. Three in ten students mixed both approaches. The authors call for curriculum teaching that confronts false beliefs, flags resistance risks from stray antibiotic use, and promotes evidence-based care.
pmc-13538821:
Jonas R Schaarup and colleagues test whether nerve damage to heart control tracks early heart failure in type 2 diabetes in a 2026 Danish clinic study. Two hundred patients from two outpatient clinics underwent reflex tests for the nerve condition, blood tests for a heart strain marker, and risk scoring, with symptom grading by a standard scale. Adjusted models probed the link overall and in symptom-free patients.

Forty percent of tested patients had the nerve condition, and over half of them showed raised heart strain marker levels versus under a quarter without it. Full adjustment tied the nerve condition to about sixfold higher odds of raised marker levels. The link held in patients without symptoms and at low-to-moderate risk scores. The authors suggest nerve testing could flag earlier heart failure stages.
pmc-13540321:
Elisa Buzzatti and a large Italian team report a 2026 letter. The subject is infection during treatment with gilteritinib. That oral drug treats a form of acute myeloid leukaemia. The cancer has returned or stopped responding in these patients. Trial reports lump infections into broad labels, leaving clinicians short on detail.

Eighteen centres tracked 123 adults from April 2020 to January 2025. Sixty percent had at least one documented infection. Lung infections came first, then bloodstream sepsis. Most episodes arrived within ninety days of starting treatment. Fungal disease clustered in patients with a stem cell transplant. Death from infection reached eighteen percent, far lower among responders.
pmc-13540721:
Rebecca McKee and co-authors present a 2026 field study of how predator hunting styles shape prey traits. Steady trait gaps between animals, often called personalities, can aid or harm survival. The team asked whether ambush hunters and active hunters push prey traits in unlike directions. They worked with hispid cotton rats in the Florida Everglades.

The team scored three traits in caught rats: boldness, activity, and docility. Released rats were then tracked in the wild, where snakes hunt by ambush and mammals and birds hunt on the move. Against the standard guess, bold and active rats were not simply at more risk. Shy but active rats died more often to active hunters. The pattern for ambush hunters ran the other way. Mixed predators may keep trait variety alive in prey.
pmc-13540821:
Baraah Abu Alsel and six co-authors pooled the evidence on a blood pressure drug in a 2026 review. Telmisartan is widely used for hypertension, alone and in combination pills. The team gathered trials comparing telmisartan-based plans with placebo, usual care, or other drugs.

Twenty-four trials with 6,521 patients met their rules. Telmisartan-based therapy lowered office systolic pressure by about six points and diastolic by about five against the mixed comparators. The size of the benefit depended on what it was compared with, and the certainty of evidence was rated low. Side effects and safety were weighed alongside. The authors present the pooled numbers as a guide, not a verdict, for prescribers.
pmc-13540921:
Leilei Zhang and six colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a deep learning model that predicts how candidate drugs will be absorbed, distributed, broken down, excreted, and whether they will prove toxic. Such ADMET traits decide clinical success, yet traditional models generalise poorly when data are thin.

Their model fuses a language-style network reading molecular sequences, a second network digesting global property descriptors, and fingerprint encodings of local substructures. It outperformed traditional methods and most rival pre-trained models on standard benchmarks. Fine-tuning on a self-built database of nearly half a million entries produced ninety-seven property predictors. A free online tool now offers 133 prediction endpoints.
pmc-13542121:
Xiong Li and colleagues simulate a drug carrier question in 2026. The compound is wogonin, from a traditional Chinese medicine herb. The carrier candidate is graphene, a flat carbon sheet. How the compound grips the sheet guides carrier design. The study works at atomic level throughout.

Quantum calculations ran alongside molecular dynamics runs. The dynamics lasted twenty nanoseconds of simulated time. Both agreed the molecule lies flatter on graphene. Its electron cloud spreads wider across the surface. Charge transfer was negligible between the pair. Gentle stacking forces dominate the grip. Binding energies were strongly favourable at two levels of theory. In simulated water, the pair stayed together throughout.
pmc-13542421:
Pound, Ainslie, and Wolf price out two technical rule changes in America's federal milk marketing orders, the Depression-era system that sets minimum dairy prices by end use. In 2025 the agriculture department dropped 500-pound barrels of cheddar from the cheese price survey and restored an older formula, the higher-of rule, for pricing fluid milk's skim component. Their 2026 analysis estimates what each change does to the prices farmers and processors actually face.

Removing barrels nudges the cheese survey price, and with it protein values, modestly upward, with the effect strongest when margins are thin. Restoring the higher-of rule lifts average class I skim prices by roughly a quarter of a dollar per hundredweight compared with the averaging rule it replaced. It hands the asymmetric risk of price spikes back from processors to producers.
pmc-13542521:
Seyed Hossein Mousavi and five co-authors pool Iranian studies on how often hospital patients survive resuscitation after their heart stops. Their systematic review and meta-analysis came out in 2026. Restarting the heart is only the first step; leaving the hospital alive is the outcome that matters most.

Forty-seven studies met their rules. Pooled across them, about three in ten resuscitation attempts succeeded at first. Of those successes, about a third of patients survived to discharge. Across all attempts, fewer than one in ten patients left the hospital alive. Trends over time showed resuscitation success improving, while survival after success slipped. The authors blame weak post-resuscitation care and urge investment in intensive care capacity and team coordination.
pmc-13543521:
Zilin Wang's team published a 2026 study building a prognostic score for kidney cancer from genes tied to mitotic catastrophe, the cell-death route triggered when division goes badly wrong. Using cancer atlas data and outside cohorts, the team distilled a nine-gene signature and scored patients with two survival-learning methods. Scores were checked against stage, scan features, immune makeup, and mutations, and one standout gene, CCNF, was tested in cells and mouse tumours.

The signature separated high- and low-risk patients, with accuracy above 0.9 for one-, three-, and five-year survival in the main cohort. High scores tracked with advanced stage, blood-vessel growth, suppressive immune cells, and higher levels of the checkpoint proteins LAG3 and TIGIT. CCNF contributed most to the score; boosting it made cancer cells grow, move, and invade faster, through the mTOR pathway. It is offered as both marker and possible target.
pmc-13543621:
Li Xiao and colleagues published a 2026 survey of whether China's tuition-waived medical students, trained free in exchange for contracted rural service, actually intend to honour their contracts. The programme exists to staff underserved countryside clinics. Questionnaires based on the theory of planned behaviour reached 1,130 students in Hubei Province in 2023, and 1,114 valid replies were analysed for attitudes, social norms, and perceived control.

About seventy-five percent intended to comply. All three theory components mattered significantly. Several things nudged intention upward: voluntarily choosing the programme, believing rural work has value, family support, and a mother with more education. Peer compliance and familiarity with rural practice helped too, as did feeling that rural systems need highly trained doctors. Winning hearts before graduation, the authors argue, matters as much as the contract's legal weight for keeping doctors in the countryside.
pmc-13544321:
Qing Sun and co-authors share a dataset on how Chinese university students plan their careers, in a 2026 data paper. The survey was built on the theory of planned behavior, which links goals to attitudes, social norms, and a sense of control. Students answered questions on each of these themes.

The dataset covers 1,400 students across 28 provinces and 12 fields of study. It records their career goals, their views on planning, the pressure they feel from others, and basic background details. The authors give summary statistics and simple links between goals and the survey themes. They offer the data as a base for career teaching in universities and for studies that compare students across fields or regions.
pmc-13544621:
Amanda Lopes-Araujo and co-authors test whether gene variants change how much mercury Amazon river dwellers accumulate from eating fish, in work from twenty twenty-six. Mercury rides fish into riverside communities and ranks among the worst pollutants. Bodies differ in how they clear it.

The team picked people at both extremes of exposure and read four detox related genes. Two variants stood out: one form of a glutathione gene and one genotype of a fat handling gene clustered in the highly exposed. Both hint at weaker detox. Two other genes leaned the same way without firm proof. The authors urge screening that flags high risk residents early and prevention tuned to local genetics.
pmc-13544721:
Ngokwe and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a lipoma, a benign fat tumor, inside the mouth of a 52-year-old woman. Oral lipomas are rare compared with lipomas elsewhere, and this one grew slowly without pain, pushing her face out of symmetry. The team removed it through the mouth under local anesthesia.

Tissue study after removal confirmed the diagnosis of a simple lipoma. At follow-up the facial asymmetry had faded and the wound healed well. Working through the mouth leaves no visible scar, which matters on the face. The report walks the full path from first exam to final check. It reminds clinicians that a soft, painless, slow mouth swelling in a middle-aged adult is often this harmless tumor, best confirmed by removing and testing it.
pmc-13545721:
Daniela Denier led a 2026 study of children with primary sclerosing cholangitis, a liver disease whose course varies widely from child to child. Instead of judging risk from a single blood test, the team modeled how one enzyme, GGT, moved over three years in 782 children from an international consortium. Statistical grouping sorted the children into four patterns of change.

The four groups fared very differently, with five-year survival without a transplant ranging from 74 percent to 98 percent. Children whose high GGT fell back to normal within a year did nearly as well as those who stayed low throughout. Baseline and six-month readings predicted group membership well, which could help doctors judge early whether treatment is working.
pmc-13546521:
Beibei Hua and colleagues examined in 2026 the role of FANCI, a protein from the Fanconi anemia DNA repair pathway, in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Using several public cancer datasets plus single-cell data, they found FANCI switched on at high levels in tumors, where it separated cancer tissue from normal tissue with high accuracy. High levels also tracked with shorter survival.

In cell experiments, raising FANCI pushed cancer cells to grow, spread, and resist death, while silencing it slowed tumors in mice and stalled the cell cycle. The protein was found physically bound to its pathway partner FANCD2 inside the nucleus. The authors propose FANCI as a possible marker for diagnosis and prognosis, and as a candidate drug target.
pmc-13546721:
Seikh Masudur Rahman and colleagues surveyed in 2026 what Bangladeshi consumers believe about broiler chicken meat and what shapes how much of it they buy. Interviews with 369 consumers in rural, semi-urban, and urban areas measured common fears on a five-point scale and linked purchases to income, schooling, job, and place of residence.

Concerns about hygiene at processing points scored highest. Next came beliefs that broiler meat carries unsafe chemicals, growth hormones, heavy metals, and even cancer risk. Many also saw it as less nutritious than local Deshi chicken. City living and more schooling raised consumption, while higher income and professional jobs lowered it. The authors urge better food safety communication to correct misconceptions.
pmc-13547221:
Junchen Liu and colleagues asked in 2026 how deep a residual neural network should be when forecasting electricity demand a short time ahead, a task grid operators depend on for scheduling. They tested two versions of the architecture across many depth settings on two real datasets, one from New England with strong seasonal swings and one Malaysian dataset rich in weather variables.

Depth helped in a bent, dataset-dependent way rather than a straight line. Medium-depth networks suited the seasonal New England data best, while shallower networks did better on the Malaysian data, where extra layers added complexity without gains. Squeezing the weather inputs through principal component analysis made the Malaysian models steadier across depths. The authors advise choosing depth together with the data's character.
pmc-13547321:
Hamza Tahiri and co-authors built in 2026 an automatic tuning method for a sliding mode controller, a robust but fiddly controller for robot arms, applied to a three-joint manipulator. Their optimizer adds three tricks to an existing stochastic algorithm. A chaotic shuffle spreads starting guesses, a learning step flips candidates to speed convergence, and periodic long jumps near the best solution escape traps.

On a standard benchmark suite the tuner ranked first among twelve algorithms. In the robot test, tracking a looping figure-eight-style path, it produced the smallest tracking error of all rivals, settled fastest, and repeated its performance almost identically across runs. The authors present it as reliable automatic tuning for nonlinear robots facing disturbances.
pmc-13547421:
Yuanyuan Wang and colleagues fed mice a combined supplement of Rosa roxburghii fruit and kiwifruit for 28 days in 2026 to test claims of better stamina and faster recovery from fatigue. Fifty mice were split among resting controls, exercised controls, and three dose levels, then put through a swimming endurance test. Blood and tissue chemistry captured the usual fatigue markers and the body's fuel stores.

Supplemented mice swam longer, stored more glycogen in liver and muscle, and cleared exercise waste products faster, with lower urea nitrogen, lactic acid, and muscle damage enzymes. Oxidative stress markers fell while protective enzymes rose. No organ damage appeared. The authors credit fuel storage and oxidative balance for the effect, at least in mice.
pmc-13547621:
Do Thi Cat Tuong and colleagues reviewed in 2026 plant bioactive compounds as feed additives that might replace antibiotic growth promoters in livestock and poultry. These plant chemicals span phenolics, terpenoids, polysaccharides, and sulfur compounds, and studies link them to better growth, improved nutrient use, calmer gut communities, and antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial effects in farm animals.

The appeal is doing all of that without feeding drug resistance or endangering food safety. Practical hurdles remain: the right dose varies, absorption is inconsistent, compounds can break down during feed processing, and ingredients are hard to standardize from batch to batch. The review maps what is known, names the gaps, and sketches what must be solved before plant additives take a routine place in sustainable production.
pmc-13548521:
Rong Lei and eight colleagues wrote to add a missing piece to a new sepsis measure. The measure, called the blood pressure response index, ties blood pressure to the dose of drugs used to hold it up. Low values have been linked to higher death rates. The letter asks whether blood flow, not just pressure, changes that link.

The team used records from a large intensive care database and its heart scan companion set. They studied adults with sepsis who got pressure-raising drugs and had a heart scan within a day. Cardiac index, a measure of how much blood the heart pumps, was worked out from the scans. Patients with the same pressure response could have quite different flow. The authors argue that flow should be read beside pressure when judging risk in sepsis.
pmc-13548621:
Mustafa Güneşdoğdu and Samet Hasan Abacı test a bay leaf oil preparation against the Varroa mite, the honeybee parasite behind many colony losses, in a 2026 field and modeling study. Beekeepers need alternatives to synthetic mite killers. The team turned laurel essential oil into a nanoemulsion, a fine droplet mix that stays stable and spreads well, then measured its chemistry and performance in real colonies.

The oil was dominated by 1,8-cineole at about forty percent. Droplets averaged roughly seventy nanometers and held together well. Mite numbers fell with dose, reaching about seventy percent control at the highest strength, clearly beating the standard drug used for comparison. Computer docking suggested the oil's parts grip a mite nerve enzyme tightly, supporting a poisoning mechanism. The authors present the preparation as a greener candidate for mite control.
pmc-13548721:
Seung-yoon Han and colleagues test whether the angle of the head relative to the neck can flag nonspecific neck pain in women factory workers, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Forward head posture is measured by this cervicovertebral angle from a side photograph. Among 135 workers, sixty-four had neck pain and seventy-one did not, and the team ran both logistic regression and decision tree models to find useful cutoffs.

Workers with pain held their heads about two degrees further forward on average. Each added degree of angle lowered the odds of pain slightly, even after adjusting for body size and age. Both models settled on a cutoff near fifty-one and a half degrees, with a second, lower tree threshold. Accuracy was modest, however. The authors advise treating the angle as a supplementary screening hint, never a diagnosis on its own.
pmc-13549521:
Ahmet Polat and Emin Can Balci raise a sunk knee joint face in a young man with no bone fill. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Such lone mid knee sinks are rare, and lifts are most oft propped with bone graft or swap fill. The man, aged eighteen, came past a fast bike crash with knee pain and swell. Scans showed a lone sink with small shift.

The face was raised true and held with a lock plate, no fill at all. Bone knit by three months. At one year the face held with a hair of sink, no harms, and his knee score leapt. Picked cases may not need fill.
pmc-13549621:
Zhi Yang and co-authors linked a heat sensor to sex change in ricefield eels in a 2026 study. The eel starts life female and turns male later, a rare sex flip among farmed fish. Warm water was known to push the flip, but the sensor that reads the heat was unknown.

The team show that a channel called Trpv4, open to calcium and keenly heat-sensitive, sits in the gonad's support cells. Warmth raises its signal and wakes male-making genes in the ovary. That chain ties the weather outside to the gonad switch inside. Eel farmers may one day steer sex ratios with water heat.
pmc-13551721:
Wei Zhao, Rongjie Tang, Jing Tian, and Dengfeng Gao published a 2026 prospective cohort study of insulin resistance markers and heart disease risk in Chinese adults with early metabolic problems. Direct insulin resistance measurement is impractical in large groups, so eleven substitute scores built from glucose, lipids, and body measures were tested. Data came from a national aging study spanning 2011 to 2020, with marker levels in 2012 and 2015.

The authors compared single measurements, cumulative exposure across both time points, and trajectory patterns grouped by clustering. Survival models estimated risk of newly diagnosed cardiovascular disease, and curve analyses checked for nonlinear links. Their aim was to show whether long-term exposure and changing patterns predict risk better than one baseline reading in people with prediabetes, prehypertension, or early lipid problems.
pmc-13551821:
Xinchang Lun and ten colleagues tracked a fungal infection in mainland China in a 2026 study. The fungus, Talaromyces marneffei, was tracked in hospital patients from 2022 to 2024. Past work focused on HIV patients in narrow regions. Here the data came from sequencing tests on patients with acute lung infections. The team mapped where and when detection rose and what germs appeared with it.

The study covered 2,316 reported cases. Detection clustered in space and peaked twice a year. Men and people aged 41 to 50 were hit most. A yeast-like fungus was the top co-detected germ. Dew point, a humidity measure, explained nearly half the spatial pattern. Paired factors explained more than single ones. The team aims the results at surveillance in humid areas.
pmc-13551921:
Markus Harboe Olsen, with a large trial team, published a 2026 report on data checks in a trial of preterm infants. The SafeBoosC-III trial enrolled 1,601 infants at 70 sites. Site visits for data checks are costly and were strained by the pandemic. The trial used central checks instead. Staff ran monthly data reviews and completeness checks. Most errors were spotted by eye.

Central checks kept missing data near one percent of all data. Reviewers looked at close to 44,000 data points. They flagged a few hundred points for review. About a fifth of the flagged points were fixed after checks. The team argues that human review plus statistics guards trial truth. They call for standard rules for central checks in future trials.
pmc-13554021:
Yang Yang and Leilei Fan scan a fat-carrying protein, APOC1, across thirty-three cancers in a 2026 study. The protein had been tied to several cancers, yet its wider role stayed unclear. The team combined gene, protein, and drug data from large public banks. They also used tissue maps and single-cell data to find which cells make the protein.

High levels appeared in most cancers and meant worse outcomes in kidney, brain, and stomach tumours even after other factors were weighed. The source proved to be macrophages, immune cells that settle inside tumours. High levels came with both immune attack signals and immune brakes, plus more cells that suppress attack. Tumours rich in the protein answered some drugs poorly yet may suit others, a lead for paired immune therapy.
pmc-13554121:
Routhu Srinivasa Rao and three colleagues build a two-part learning model to find gut diseases in scope images in a 2026 report. Gut diseases carry a heavy global burden, and early spotting improves outcomes. Their design pairs a small image network, good at fine detail, with a larger one that reads the whole scene. An attention block then stresses the regions that matter most while muting background noise.

Tricks such as mixed training images and averaged weights steadied the learning. The finished model sorted images with accuracy above eighty-four percent overall. It beat single-network versions and other standard models on the same tests. Scores for rare classes also rose, which matters when some diseases appear far less often than others in clinic sets.
pmc-13554221:
Aflah Hanafiah leads a ten-author team uncovering a surprise role for a silencing protein group in waking genes up in a 2026 study. The group, a Polycomb complex, usually keeps genes quiet by folding DNA into loops. At genes marked as ready-but-waiting, those loops held the genes poised for action. Removing a key part of the complex broke the loops and stalled nerve cell growth.
