Trained as an exercise scientist, he built his career on the idea that spinal networks below an injury can process sensation and relearn movement, much like a small brain.

The tribute traces his locomotor training work, from manually moving the limbs of spinal-injured rats toward the robotic rat stepper of the late nineteen-nineties. Later came human gait-training robots and an exoskeleton case that restored some voluntary control in chronic paralysis. It also covers his push into neuromodulation, pairing electrical stimulation with training as a therapy. The authors credit his persistence with opening a new era of rehabilitation engineering that still shapes devices in clinics and labs today.
pmc-13621621:
Xiaoyan Huang and Qian Zhu report, in 2026, the first documented case of internal abdominal bleeding caused by tissue left behind after a medical abortion. A thirty-three-year-old woman arrived with sudden heavy vaginal bleeding and mild abdominal pain thirty-three days after ending a first-trimester pregnancy with the standard two-drug regimen. Ultrasound showed a mass inside her uterus plus a significant pool of blood in her abdomen.

Surgeons performed emergency scraping of the uterus, and tissue examination confirmed retained products of conception with degenerated pregnancy villi. The authors propose that blood escaped backward through a fallopian tube from the retained tissue, a route clinicians rarely consider. Blood in the abdomen in women of childbearing age usually points to a burst cyst or a tubal pregnancy. Their message: after abortion care, retained tissue belongs on that differential list, since the disguise invites dangerous misdiagnosis.
pmc-13622921:
Eun-Ha Jung, Hyun-Kyung Yim, and Ji-Hyun Min present a 2026 lab study on whether sugar-free fizzy drinks spare the teeth. Zero-calorie sodas are booming as health awareness grows, but fizzy drinks erode enamel through acid, not just sugar. The team bought 135 drinks sold in South Korea and split them into zero and regular groups by calorie rules. Each drink's acidity was measured fresh with a pH meter.

Both groups averaged a pH near three, well into the range that dissolves enamel, and the difference between them was not significant. Nearly all drinks sat below pH four. The authors warn that zero drinks carry about the same erosion risk as regular sodas despite their lack of sugar. Consumers, they say, should not treat the zero label as tooth-safe. Dentists may use the finding when counseling soda drinkers.
pmc-13623521:
Zhu and colleagues launch in 2026 AIDrugDesigner, a free web server that puts deep learning molecule design within reach of researchers who cannot code or maintain model software. Designing molecules with preset properties is central to drug discovery and notoriously slow by hand.

The server has two modules. The generation module creates candidate molecules four ways: aimed at a chosen target, guided by a pharmacophore pattern, conditioned on desired properties, or by designing the linker between two fragments. The optimization module then polishes molecules a user supplies, improving drug-likeness, the fat-water balance measure called LogP, and ease of synthesis. Tests across several design tasks showed the platform's versatility. By wrapping many generative strategies in one interface, the authors aim to lower the technical barrier to AI-assisted drug design.
pmc-13623621:
Xialing Zhu and six co-authors built an ultrasound model to tell benign from malignant gallbladder lumps before surgery in a 2026 paper. The study covered 166 patients with confirmed diagnoses, only 36 of them malignant, split into training and test sets. From standard and contrast ultrasound images they extracted hundreds of texture features each.

A few clinical signs separated the groups, including lump size and blood lipid levels. Models trained on standard images, contrast images, and both reached good discrimination, with the contrast model ahead in training. A final chart combining the image score with clinical indicators was built for bedside use. The authors argue such radiomics can sharpen preoperative decisions for a cancer that is often found late.
pmc-13623721:
Qiaoyin Tan and co-authors pilot a tech-aided summer program to curb teen weight gain, in a trial from two thousand twenty-six. Twenty-five teens aged eleven to fourteen split into camp and control groups. The camp mixed gym lessons, food talks, walks, an app, and two trackers.

Campers liked the app a bit more by week two. App use slid once the in-person camp ended, though. Camp days logged over two hours of brisk motion on the gauges. Trackers showed weekday motion above weekend motion. Weight trends leaned kind for campers but stayed murky in stats. Readers get a workable camp with a home-tail problem.
pmc-13624021:
Ratchada Kitsommart and colleagues run a randomised trial in Bangkok, Thailand, testing whether a glucose solution given by mouth can treat low blood sugar in newborns who show no symptoms. At-risk babies born late-preterm or at term often dip in blood sugar after birth; the standard fix, intravenous glucose, separates mother and baby and needs a drip line.

Four hundred babies whose blood sugar stayed low after a first feed received either the glucose solution on the cheek lining or a placebo, followed by feeding, in a double-blind design. Fewer babies in the glucose group needed intravenous treatment, but the gap was small enough to be chance. Blood sugar climbed higher after treatment in the glucose group, no baby overshot into high sugar. Older newborns and those born small or large responded less. The authors say the solution's clinical role needs more study.
pmc-13624121:
Zhang and co-authors test how the Gata4 gene steers fibroblast movement by tissue source. Fibroblasts help repair tissue and lay down matrix. Heart, lung, and tail fibroblasts came from young mice. Cells grew on soft 8 kPa pads that mimic body stiffness. Gata4 was cut with a virus-borne Cre tool.

Heart cells moved faster and straighter on soft pads than on hard plastic. Base Gata4 was highest in heart cells and lowest in tail cells. Cre cut Gata4 by over 90 percent in all three types. Loss of Gata4 shifted movement in split ways by source. The authors say repair programs must weigh cell origin.
pmc-13624321:
Xianfeng Ye and colleagues describe a three-bacterium team from cucumber root soil that protects the plant against Fusarium wilt, a fungal disease. The partners, strains of Achromobacter, Bacillus, and Flavobacterium, feed each other: the Flavobacterium member cannot make one amino acid it needs and depends on the others, a dependency organising the alliance.

Inside the partnership, the other two strains handle most carbon and nitrogen processing while the dependent partner quiets those same functions. Together they build layered biofilms, structured films on the root surface, far better than any strain alone, and that architecture lets two of the partners slip inside the root and live there. Once resident, the Flavobacterium switches on the plant's system-wide defences, priming it against fungal attack. The authors present cross-feeding dependency, usually seen as a weakness, as an engineering principle for building protective microbe teams for farming.
pmc-13624421:
Lirong Liang and co-authors trace how a common anesthesia drug can leave lasting marks on the young brain. Baby mice breathed sevoflurane for two hours a day over three days early in life. As adults, those mice showed damage in the hippocampus, a brain area tied to memory and social recognition, and they performed worse on memory tests.

The damage centered on perineuronal nets, mesh-like coatings that wrap certain nerve cells and limit their change. Sevoflurane lifted a chemical brake on a gene that makes MMP9, an enzyme that chewed up those nets. Restoring a net-building protein or blocking MMP9 protected the nets, steadied cell connections, and reversed the memory problems, pointing to a way to guard infants under anesthesia.
pmc-13624821:
Da-In Eun, Hyeonhoon Lee, and Hyung-Chul Lee, publishing in 2026, propose a bedside score for how well the blood delivers oxygen. The true delivery index needs invasive lines and heavy equipment, so they built the Easy DAO2 index from pulse pressure, heart rate, hemoglobin, and fingertip oxygen, scaled to body size. Records covered about 95,000 operations at an Asian hospital and about 90,000 intensive care stays in the United States.

The team tracked how long each patient spent below a very low cutoff of the new index. In both surgical and intensive care groups, longer time spent that low went with a higher risk of death within seven days in hospital. A score from routine monitors could thus warn teams earlier, without extra invasive steps.
pmc-13626221:
Dalai Xu and colleagues report a rare hernia that struck ten months after stomach cancer surgery. A 71-year-old man had his whole stomach removed by keyhole surgery, with the food pipe joined to the small bowel in a Roux-en-Y rebuild. A scan on day seventeen already showed the join riding up into the chest, though nothing was blocked, and the clue passed quietly.

Later he developed position-linked upper belly pain, and a fresh scan showed the join and a swollen bowel loop pushed through the diaphragm's opening into the right chest. Emergency keyhole surgery pulled the bowel back, found it alive, and stitched the gaps shut, and he recovered smoothly. The authors, reviewing past cases, warn that early upward drift of the join is a red flag worth acting on.
pmc-13627021:
Daiping Hua and co-authors present a case report the catalog lists under 2026. A hormone disorder makes the body resist parathyroid hormone. The classic type often shows a set body pattern and starts young. A 59-year-old woman came in with fading memory, odd behavior, unsteady walking, and seizure-like spells. Her case starts late and does not fit the classic mold.

Blood tests showed low calcium, high phosphate, and high parathyroid hormone. Brain scans showed matched calcium deposits deep in the brain. A brain-wave test showed seizure-type discharges. Gene tests found a new variant in a known gene, never reported before. Doctors get a reminder that this disorder can appear late and mostly in the brain. Gene testing can settle odd cases where blood and scan signs point one way but age and shape do not. The report adds one new variant to the shared record.
pmc-13627221:
Elisabet Stener-Victorin and colleagues review how fatty liver disease, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovary syndrome intertwine in women. Fatty liver affects about 38 percent of adults and diabetes about 11 percent, while polycystic ovary syndrome, here called PMOS, affects 10 to 13 percent of reproductive-age women. Their 2026 narrative review links the three through hormones, insulin resistance, and inflammation.

Excess androgens drive liver fat genes, switch on scarring cells, and suppress a binding protein, building a scar-prone, fat-toxic liver. Shared pathways span fat-tissue failure, faulty fat signals, and weak mitochondria, with adolescence, pregnancy, and menopause as vulnerable windows. Stener-Victorin and colleagues urge life-stage screening and early action.
pmc-13628121:
Daeseok Oh and three co-authors study brain white matter in lasting shingles pain in a 2026 paper. This chronic nerve pain lowers quality of life long after the rash heals. A brain scan measure based on water movement along white matter tracts has proven sturdy in other brain disorders. They tested whether it sets these patients apart from healthy peers.

The patient group showed clearly higher values on the new measure and on two standard ones. The new measure separated patients from controls better than the standard ones. In a combined model it was the only independent predictor of patient status. The authors propose it as a marker of widespread white matter disruption in this pain condition.
pmc-13628521:
A meadow stays productive through drought or heavy grazing partly because its species react differently to the same stress. Manuel Pitzer and co-authors test that insurance idea in this 2026 study, measuring how 96 grassland species respond to land-use pressure in the field and in a shared garden.

Heavier land use shrank the variety of responses in both settings. Communities rich in varied responses held their function steadier over time, yet lost species with fewer replacements, so their makeup grew less stable. The trade-off, the authors argue, means response diversity guards what a grassland does, not who lives there.
pmc-13629821:
Karina Pereira-Lima and six colleagues studied first-year resident doctors who screened positive for depression. They asked whether residents with disabilities spot their symptoms and seek help in unlike ways. The data came from a long study of interns from 2020 to 2022. It held 940 residents who reported their disability status. About one in eight had disabilities.

Residents with disabilities were far more likely to spot their own symptoms. They were also much more likely to seek treatment than peers without disabilities. The pattern held when mental disabilities were left out of the checks. The authors suggest that living with disability may counter a training culture habit. That habit treats distress as normal. The finding offers a route to cut stigma. It could lower barriers to care for all trainees.
pmc-13630821:
Mehmet Emin Gönüllü and three co-authors propose a blood-based index for wound risk after surgery in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Wound problems after an operation are a common cause of illness. Routine lab markers of inflammation and nutrition might flag risk early. The team built a combined index from two ratios. One ratio pairs C-reactive protein with albumin; the other pairs two white cell types. They also tracked how the index changed over the first days.

The study looked back at eighty-six general surgery patients. The authors tested how well the index and its change predicted wound problems. They used standard statistical checks and internal validation. A simple score from routine labs could help staff spot high-risk wounds sooner. The authors present the index as exploratory, so more testing is needed.
pmc-13631321:
Cezary Cybulski and twelve colleagues tested a reported genetic warning sign in breast cancer. They found it did not hold up. Their study appeared in 2026. An earlier study had linked a common variant in the PCSK9 gene to more spread and worse survival. A claim like that has real weight if true. So the team checked it in two groups. One held 1,052 women carrying BRCA1 mutations. One held 467 with familial breast cancer of unknown cause. A control group of 1,404 joined them.

Neither patient group showed any link between the variant and breast cancer death. Time to death after the cancer spread showed no link either. The authors conclude the variant carries no prognostic weight in these groups. Other genetic or environmental factors could still modify any effect elsewhere.
pmc-13631821:
Patrick O'Donoghue and co-authors report a shin wound case where two blood flow imaging tools guided surgery in one stage, in work from twenty twenty-six. Shin wounds in older adults are hard to judge and can rot if dead tissue is missed. Standard checks of color and bleeding are rough guesses.

The patient was a ninety-one year old man hurt in a road crash, on blood thinning drugs. A handheld heat camera first flagged a cold zone over the worst bruised skin. After a first cut back, a dye based glow scan found more low flow tissue to remove. A skin graft and vacuum dressing followed at once. The graft took fully at first review. The tools play complementary roles, the authors say.
pmc-13632121:
Qi Zhang and fourteen colleagues published this 2026 study linking steady access to food with healthy aging in the United States. Food insecurity means having limited or uncertain access to enough food. The team used two large national surveys of adults aged sixty and older. One survey held more than forty-two thousand such participants, and the other held about three thousand. Healthy aging was judged across illness, thinking, physical limits, mood, and self-rated health.

People with secure food access scored better on every part of healthy aging in both surveys. They were more than twice as likely to count as aging healthily in the larger survey, even after accounting for income, habits, and other illnesses. The pattern held across sex, race, lifestyle, and body weight groups. The authors argue that food security deserves a central place in plans for aging well, especially where resources are thin.
pmc-13632921:
Amin Danial Asham, writing alone, presents a new control method that lets a two-wheel robot follow any set of waypoints, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Most past work assumes the path is a smooth curve, not a loose set of points. Asham built a fresh error model for a differential drive robot, which steers by changing the speed of each wheel. A sliding mode controller then pushes the tracking error toward zero.

The design keeps working even when the robot's exact dynamics are unknown, and its stability is proven. Tests in simulation beat a widely used rival method at sharp turns and sudden direction changes. Live trials on a real robot confirmed the gains. The method suits robots that must thread tight point-to-point routes.
pmc-13634121:
Ya-ting Zheng and six co-authors test a new pig vaccine in a 2026 paper. The target virus causes heavy losses in piglets and breeding failures in China, and newer strains have spread for over a decade. Standard oil-based vaccines work but often cause local reactions. A water-based additive offers a safer option with strong immune effects.

Their killed-virus vaccine paired that additive with a booster ingredient chosen from several candidates. In mice it gave strong protection after two doses. In piglets, shots into muscle produced higher antibody levels than the control vaccines and full survival after challenge, with less virus shedding. Shots into skin worked less well.
pmc-13634621:
Ferdaous Kasmi and Karima Marc report milky chest fluid caused by Behçet's disease in a case report from two thousand twenty-six. The fluid, called chylothorax, usually follows trauma or cancer. In Behçet's disease, a body-wide vessel inflammation, it is very rare.

A woman aged thirty-five with five years of the disease arrived short of breath with a dry cough. Scans showed big vein clots above the heart and fluid on both sides of the chest. A tap drew milky fluid rich in fats, confirming the diagnosis. Other causes were ruled out. Blood thinners, steroids, an immune drug, repeated taps, and a low-fat diet cleared her breathing and shrank the fluid.
pmc-13634921:
Claire Hughes and a large international team published this 2026 study of what shields young children when their parents feel distressed. Parental distress tends to travel with children's anxiety, withdrawal, and low mood. The team studied eight hundred forty-nine parent-child pairs in England, Hong Kong, and mainland China, children about five. Parents rated their distress and their child's struggles. Observers scored warm guidance during joint tasks; speech samples measured how much parents treated the child as a mind of its own.

Parental distress linked to more child problems and less warm guidance everywhere. The shielding effects differed by place. Warm guidance softened the link in mainland China; treating the child as an independent mind did so in England. The second pattern proved site-specific under closer modeling. The authors argue protective parenting travels across cultures unevenly, widening the field beyond its usual Western samples.
pmc-13635721:
Shujie Xu and seven co-authors show how gut viruses steer nitrogen between host and microbes. Their 2026 mouse study follows a low-protein diet's effect on the gut virome. Dietary protein shapes growth and nitrogen balance. How gut phages translate diet into body outcomes was poorly known.

Low protein remodeled phage-bacteria dynamics in the gut. Stressed bacteria released fewer free phages, weakening bacterial lysis. Some phages carry genes that grow their hosts while blocking nitrogen recycling. The result is a nitrogen trap: plenty of bacteria, little return to the host. Adding back normal-diet phages partly restored nitrogen flow. The team names this a viral shunt inside the gut.
pmc-13640221:
Tianyu Tan and ten colleagues report a 2026 cohort study of HIV incidence among men who have sex with men in the Chinese city of Chongqing. The analysis covers a decade of data from the city's disease control center, from 2013 to 2022.

The cohort included 2,134 men who began HIV-negative. Overall incidence ran at about five infections per hundred person-years, and the rate declined across the decade. Lower education, finding partners offline, unprotected anal sex, and recent popper use each raised risk. The authors credit broad prevention programs for the decline while urging continued condom promotion and outreach.
pmc-13642421:
Niklaus Schaefer led a 2026 analysis testing whether a simple liver blood index, APRI, predicts survival after yttrium-90 radioembolization for primary liver cancer. Patient selection for this arterial radiation treatment remains hard, since standard liver function scores do not fully capture hepatic reserve. The team drew on the prospective European CIRT study, analyzing 103 patients with bile duct cancer inside the liver and 377 with hepatocellular carcinoma, with cutoffs chosen from the data.

Higher APRI tracked with clearly shorter survival in both cancers, above 0.4 for cholangiocarcinoma and above 0.7 for hepatocellular carcinoma, and the links held after matching and other checks. The cutoffs separated survival under body-surface-area dosing but not under partition-model dosing. Doctors get a cheap, easy-to-use marker for outlook, with the caveat that tumor type and dosing method shape its value and further study is needed.
pmc-13648821:
Ann Huang and five colleagues explore the hidden variety inside trained neural networks, showing that many different internal mechanisms can sit within one connected region of equally good solutions. They introduce a method that walks through weight space along directions that leave network behaviour unchanged, using local curvature to guide the path.

Applied to recurrent networks, image-recognition transformers, and game-playing agents, the method found representations more different from the original than separately trained models, and it exposed a reward-hacking strategy in one agent. It also measured how model size and task complexity shape the solution region. The authors argue this diversity matters for understanding, merging, and editing models.
pmc-13649321:
Kgosi Tavares and three colleagues pull back the curtain on a drug firm's front group in the opioid trade. The firm, Mallinckrodt, set up the Alliance for Balanced Pain Management in the mid-2010s. The team read 132 files from a public trove of court-freed opioid papers.

The files show the firm chose the group's name, drew outside groups in, and staged a 2014 summit to court press. Its sites, ads, opinion pieces, and posts all pushed one line: misuse was the fault of doctors and patients, not makers. The group also served to sign up fresh allies. The authors say such fronts must be unmasked so health groups are not co-opted.
pmc-13649421:
Jing Liu and five colleagues pooled trials that compared two sleep drugs, ciprofol and propofol, for painless gut scope exams. They searched two databases for adult trials through May 2026 and split results by drug dose.

Eleven trials with 2,084 people met their rules. Wake-up time ran a bit longer with ciprofol, by under a minute, at mid-range doses. Start time and patient and doctor ratings did not differ much. Ciprofol, though, came with fewer drops in blood pressure, less pain at injection, and fewer breathing problems. All trials ran in China, and methods varied a lot between them. The authors call their dose findings early leads that need larger world trials.
pmc-13649721:
Jianbin Liu and two colleagues report a newborn death in China tied to two new faulty copies of a gene that moves glycine, a brain chemical, into cells. Faults in this gene cause a form of glycine brain disease, and most affected babies die in their first months. Fewer than ten gene variants had been reported before this case.

Gene reads from amniotic fluid and both parents found the pair of changes, one from each parent. In lab cells, both changes left the gene's message intact yet cut its protein output hard. A review of past cases found shared signs: clubfoot, excess fluid in the womb, and slow growth. The case is China's first documented newborn death from this gene pair.
pmc-13650621:
Graycen Horne and one colleague map where a lipid-transfer protein is switched on inside the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, a standard laboratory animal. The protein, PPIT-2, ferries a key membrane fat between compartments, and its human relatives matter for insulin release, yet its expression pattern in the worm was largely unknown.

The team inserted a glowing tag into the worm's own gene, so the protein lit up wherever the animal naturally makes it. The signal shone strongest in the excretory system and its canals, with additional glow in the skin-like hypodermis, sperm, the developing vulva, and fluid spaces near the germline. The pattern overlapped notably with a fat-building enzyme, marking candidate tissues for studying how this carrier supports membrane traffic and fat balance. The report establishes the map as a starting point for functional experiments.
pmc-13651521:
Ruizhi Li and four co-authors overturn a textbook belief about oxidizing formaldehyde on palladium. At high voltages the reaction was thought to hand its electrons straight over, making formate with no hydrogen intermediates, since any surface hydrogen should be burned away at once.

Their instrument is a two-faced palladium membrane: one side runs the formaldehyde reaction while the other side reports hydrogen that has soaked through the metal. Hydrogen kept arriving across a broad voltage range, up to strongly positive potentials, showing the high-voltage path still makes hydrogen atoms. Charge counting showed the palladium lattice filling heavily with hydrogen. Spectra and models support a sequence where carbon-hydrogen bonds break, leaving hydrogen atoms to choose between soaking in, pairing into gas, or oxidizing. The team even used the made hydrogen to hydrogenate styrene in a second liquid, and they propose anodic hydrogenation as a synthetic plan.
pmc-13651621:
Lewis Hamilton and nine co-authors break a classic thermoelectric trade-off using molecules with two loosely paired electrons. Turning heat into power needs materials that conduct well and generate high voltage from a temperature gap at once, and those two virtues usually fight each other.

Theory said that stretching these diradicaloid molecules would narrow their energy gap and drag their conduction resonances toward the electrode's Fermi level, lifting conductance and voltage together. Measurements on molecular layers confirmed the unusual pattern: longer molecules conducted better. The voltage per degree climbed past values prized in the field, so the power factor grew with length instead of sagging as in plain conjugated molecules. The authors argue that exotic quantum transport seen in single molecules survives into hands-on self-assembled films, a step toward wearable and waste-heat thermoelectric devices.
pmc-13659521:
Shengwei Mo and Boju Pan present a pancreatic tumor so rare that it imitates far more common growths. Their patient, a woman in her late fifties, came to a surgical clinic after a scan found a lobulated mass in the tail of her pancreas. Imaging showed mixed signal patterns and strong enhancement, and routine tumor markers in her blood gave no clear answer, leaving the growth's identity open.

Tissue examination after removal identified a sclerosing epithelioid mesenchymal neoplasm, an entity most pathologists will never see. Publishing the imaging features alongside the final diagnosis builds the small shared record that future cases will be judged against. For radiologists and surgeons, the lesson is practical. An unusual enhancement pattern in a pancreatic tail mass may deserve a wider differential than the common cancers and cysts that dominate the list.
pmc-13661221:
Xinjie Shi and seven co-authors study how lake microbes changed over centuries in Lake Daihai in northern China. Their twenty twenty-six paper uses ancient DNA preserved in a sediment core, combined with stable isotope measurements. The question is how climate shifts and human pressure each shaped the tiny life of the lake.

The team reports that microbes were long assembled by steady, predictable processes. After the Little Ice Age ended, random chance played a larger role as human impacts grew. Community structure changed about ten times faster than community function, because key bacteria provided backup roles. Readers gain a long view of how lake ecosystems absorb disturbance.
pmc-13664621:
Raghavendra Patwardhan, Shruti Morjaria, Gargi Nandi, Syed Hasan, and Santosh Sandur review how oxygen-linked chemistry is timed across the cell cycle, in work from 2026. Cells make reactive oxygen forms as part of energy work, and long held views cast defense systems as mere cleaners of those forms. The authors argue the picture is richer.

Defense proteins shift in amount, activity, and place as the cell moves through its growth and division stages. The review walks through the main defense systems one by one, from enzymes that clear peroxide to the glutathione and thioredoxin sets. Their roles overlap and change stage by stage. The authors propose the cycle itself be seen as a redox-run process, with timed oxygen signals as an extra layer of control.
pmc-13677621:
Rodrigo Oliveira and six co-authors published an animal science study in twenty twenty-six on a Bacillus-based probiotic fed to grazing Nellore bulls. Probiotics are being tried as an alternative to ionophores in pasture systems. The question was whether they improve intake, growth, and digestion in cattle finished on tropical pasture.

Twenty-eight bulls grazed Marandu grass paddocks and got a corn-based supplement daily for one hundred twelve days. Half received the probiotic; half did not. The supplemented bulls ate less pasture and gained less weight each day, with no gain in digestibility. The study is a useful caution that a probiotic helping in one system may not help on pasture.
pmc-13678221:
Marble Nasasira and co-authors published this tuberculosis study in 2026 from Uganda. Bedaquiline is a key drug against drug-resistant TB, but it can stretch the heart's QTc interval, a rhythm risk. The team read records from fourteen treatment sites, spanning 2017 to 2022, for 532 patients. They counted new cases of the stretch and hunted its predictors.

The rate came to twelve new cases per thousand person-months. Low body mass raised the risk, so thin patients need the closest heart tracing watch. Cure rates matched between those with and without the stretch, near seventy percent in both. Most patients were men, and a third also had HIV. The authors urge monthly heart tracings as the drug's use grows, with extra care for the underweight.
pmc-13678721:
Grandjean and coauthors update a tool that maps atoms in chemical reactions. Atom maps show which reactant atom ends where in products. Those maps guide reaction sorting and synthesis plans. The tool learns maps from a large language-style model.

Past checks used a flawed test set with wrong maps. The team built a clean set of more than 4,500 reactions. They retrained the tool on two large reaction banks. A new scoring method checks maps by graph match, not text match. That switch cuts false fails from text quirks. The update gives a firmer base to judge map tools.
pmc-13679821:
Makenna Marty, Jonathan Zuo, Linan Wang, and Marc Attiyeh report a rare 2026 surgical case that held two surprises. An eighty-three-year-old woman came in with belly pain, a high white cell count, and raised bile levels. Scans showed a swollen gallbladder with stones, a picture that looked like a common gallbladder attack.

Because her pain grew worse, surgeons removed the gallbladder at once. They found it hanging free and twisted, a rare state that mimics the common one. Lab tests on the tissue then found a small, aggressive cancer that had spread to one nearby node. Later scans showed no leftover disease. Since the organ had hung free of the liver, no further liver surgery was done, and drug treatment was advised instead.
pmc-13682021:
Heerva and co-authors study smoking and survival across cancers in Finland in a 2026 paper. Smoking after a cancer diagnosis is known to harm survival, but large real world proof across many cancers was scarce. The team found patients with solid cancers treated at two university hospitals from 2009 to 2019. Smoking status was pulled from medical notes by a checked computer method and linked to death records.

Among nearly sixty three thousand patients, status was known for about forty five thousand. Five year survival was highest in never smokers, lower in former smokers, and lowest in current smokers. The gap held across most cancer types and even in patients treated with curative intent. Readers see strong grounds for making quit support a standard part of cancer care.
pmc-13683421:
Xinyi Fang and co-authors review how three parts of the cell trade fats and signals in type 2 diabetes, in a paper from 2026. The three parts are mitochondria, the cell's power centers; the endoplasmic reticulum, which builds proteins and fats; and lipid droplets, which store fat. Each is well studied alone, but their joint work is less clear.

The review gathers evidence from gene studies, imaging, and lab tests. The three parts meet at contact sites that pass fats and calcium between them. They shape fat storage, fat burning, cell cleaning, and stress signals. When the network breaks down, fat handling goes wrong in the liver, fat tissue, muscle, and the pancreas. That damage feeds insulin resistance and tissue harm. Drug ideas that target the network are also covered.
pmc-2375021:
Huang, Sherman, Tan, and co-authors present the DAVID gene functional classification tool. Modern experiments often yield lists of hundreds of genes with no clear story. DAVID uses a fuzzy grouping method to condense such lists into organised classes of related genes, which the authors call biological modules.

Grouping by shared function helps researchers see themes instead of noise: cell growth, immunity, or other joint roles. The module-centred approach differs from tools that rank genes one by one. For labs facing a long gene list, a clear grouping is often the first real clue about what an experiment changed.
pmc-2746121:
Terwilliger and Berendzen present a fully automated procedure for solving crystal structures by MAD and MIR methods. Those methods use special X-ray signals to find atomic positions in a crystal. Hand solving was slow and depended heavily on expert judgement at each step.

Their scheme turns structure solution into an optimisation problem, scored step by step by computer. Automation let more structures be solved, faster, by less specialised users. The work helped shift crystallography from a craft bottleneck toward a routine pipeline, feeding the rapid growth of known protein shapes.
pmc-3618321:
Hänzelmann, Castelo, and Guinney present GSVA, a method for gene set variation analysis of microarray and RNA-Seq data. Gene set analysis condenses expression profiles into summaries of pathways or signatures. Compared with single-gene analysis, it reduces noise and the sheer number of results, and adds biological interpretability.

GSVA estimates how much each pathway varies in each individual sample, rather than only comparing groups. Sample-level scores let researchers tie pathway activity to clinical traits directly. The method is widely used in cancer studies to characterise tumours one patient at a time.
pmc-4015721:
IntHout, Ioannidis, and Borm compared two methods for meta-analysis in 2014. Meta-analysis pools results from many trials of the same question to get a clearer answer. The standard DerSimonian-Laird method is used almost everywhere for random effects models.

The authors show that the standard method often gives error rates that are too high. A less used method, named for Hartung, Knapp, Sidik, and Jonkman, performs far better in their tests. It is also simple to apply in practice. Their work gives trial reviewers a strong reason to switch methods, so pooled results are less likely to claim effects that are not real.
pmc-4053721:
Law, Chen, Shi, and their co-authors presented the voom method in 2014 for RNA sequencing data. RNA-seq counts how many times each gene's message is read in a sample. Those counts need care before standard linear models, built for other data types, can be used on them.

Voom charts how the spread of the log counts changes with their size, then gives each data point a weight based on its precision. Those weights enter the limma framework, a trusted set of tools for gene studies. The method lets labs use mature linear model tools on RNA-seq counts, with results that respect how noisy each count is.
pmc-4284921:
Collins, Reitsma, Altman, and their colleagues issued the TRIPOD Statement in 2015. Prediction models help health providers estimate the risk that a disease is present or that an event will occur later. Such models guide real decisions, so their reports must be clear and complete.

TRIPOD lists what a report of a prediction model should include, for both diagnosis and prognosis models. Poor reporting had made many models hard to judge or reuse. A shared standard lets readers check how a model was built and tested. That improves trust in risk tools used at the bedside and in clinics.
pmc-7619421:
Bhagyashree Dasari Rao and Snezhana Oliferenko compare the cell membranes of two related fission yeast species whose membrane fats differ sharply. Their study came out in 2026. Membrane electrical properties shape how the proteins embedded in them behave.

One species builds membranes from mostly unsaturated fats plus the standard fungal sterol. The other uses many saturated fats with an unusual short chain, plus a bacterial-style sterol mimic gained by gene transfer. Using fluorescent dyes that report on the membrane environment, the pair found similar overall polarity in both species. Yet the second species showed a higher dipole potential, an internal voltage of the membrane. Mutant and model membrane tests pointed to its sterol and its saturated fats as the support. Membrane character emerges from the whole lipid mix, not single ingredients.
prierias-de-strigimagarum-latin-1521:
Silvestro Mazzolini, called Prierias, was the papal theologian who first answered Luther in print. His three Latin books on the marvels of witches and demons appeared in 1521. The work is the first Dominican demonology after the Malleus Maleficarum, and it carried huge influence at the papal court.

Prierias defends the reality of witches' deeds against the old skeptical canon. His learning marshals Scripture, law, and reported cases in scholastic ranks. Rome's theologian here lends the hammer his weight. The book shows the Vatican's own scholar building doctrine for the hunts. Students of the Malleus tradition read Prierias as its first great reinforcement from the top of the church.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
Short news jokes fill the front of Punch for January 21, 1920, under the standing head of Charivaria. The weekly, then in volume 158, made its humour from small items in the daily papers and turned each into a dry one-paragraph jest.

One item suspends, in fancy, a French duellist who lost his temper and threatened to shoot his rival. Another sends a man to an asylum with coal-shock after half a ton of coal arrived without warning. Wrexham's plan to drop Welsh lessons, a Dublin arrest with gelignite, and demobilised men at shooting galleries all draw the column's raised eyebrow.

Punch for April 21, 1920, in volume 158, leads with Charivaria and its string of short jokes taken from the week's papers. Crime in Ireland and dry America supply the first laughs this week.

Irish criminals are sorted into three classes: those who cannot be caught, those who cannot be convicted, and those who cannot be kept in prison. Dry America is so dry, the column says, that Scotsmen there pin stamps to their letters. A Deptford man offers to walk to Brighton with a jar on his head, a boy is knocked down by a funeral car, and an American lady gains her thirteenth divorce.
quimby-manuscripts-1921:
Phineas Parkhurst Quimby healed by the mind decades before his papers saw print in The Quimby Manuscripts of 1921. Horatio W. Dresser edited the writings of the Maine clockmaker turned mental healer. Quimby held that disease begins in mistaken belief, and that truth, rightly grasped, sets the body free.

His ideas seeded two movements: New Thought took them up gladly, and Christian Science grew from soil he tilled. Dresser published the manuscripts to fix Quimby's place as the source. Readers meet here the rough, earnest notes of a pioneer whose influence ran far beyond his lifetime.
russell-analysis-mind-1921:
Bertrand Russell published The Analysis of Mind in 1921, a set of lectures on psychology and philosophy. Russell defends neutral monism, the view that mind and matter share one basic stuff. Sensations and images, arranged in different ways, make both minds and physical things. He draws on the behaviorism of Watson and the work of William James.

Chapters treat desire, memory, belief, and consciousness itself. Russell doubts that consciousness is a special inner light. The book became a landmark of early philosophy of mind. Its plain style suits general readers. Later philosophy of psychology still starts debates from its positions.
rutherford-harp-of-god-1921:
Joseph Franklin Rutherford, the Judge who led the Bible Students after Russell's death, published The Harp of God in 1921. The book offers proof of a Creator and of his plan for mankind in catechism form. It became the Jehovah's Witnesses' first great textbook.

Questions and answers walk the student through creation, the fall, the ransom, and the coming kingdom on earth. Rutherford plays the Bible as a harp of ten strings, each string a doctrine sounding in harmony with the rest. Millions of copies went out as the movement's chief tool for teaching new believers.
sapir-language-1921:
Edward Sapir was a scholar of speech who studied the Native languages of North America and taught at Ottawa and Chicago. His 1921 book Language is a plain introduction to how speech works and changes. Sapir had already spent years writing down grammars of tongues few outsiders had studied. It remains one of the most loved books in its field.

Sapir covers sound patterns, grammar, word building, and the slow drift of languages over time. He shows how speech shapes thought without trapping it, an idea later linked to his name and Benjamin Whorf's. Students still read him for his clear style and his feel for language as art.
sawyer-wonderfull-discoverie-edmonton-16:
Elizabeth Sawyer kept a poor home at Edmonton, north of London. The Wonderfull Discoverie of Elizabeth Sawyer, printed in 1621, tells how she came to be hanged as a witch. Her case grew out of quarrels, a curse, and a neighbor's death.

The pamphlet mixes her confession with stern moral warnings, as Stuart crime print often did. It asks readers to see God's hand and the Devil's snares in a poor woman's fall. Within the year, her story reached the stage as The Witch of Edmonton. That play kept her name alive long after the gallows.
say-letters-to-malthus-1821:
Jean-Baptiste Say wrote his Letters to Malthus on the great question of gluts, and John Richter's English translation appeared in 1821. The two economists were friends who disagreed in public. Malthus feared that a whole economy could produce more than it could sell, leaving workers idle; Say denied the possibility.

Say argues that production itself creates the income with which goods are bought, so a general glut cannot last. Particular goods can overflow a market, he grants, but the cure is more production of what is wanted, not less of everything. Malthus answered in kind, and the friendly fight shaped the classical creed for decades. The letters are courteous, clear, and sharp at once. Economists still argue the ground these two friends staked out in 1821.
say-treatise-prinsep-1821:
Jean-Baptiste Say was a French writer on trade whose Treatise on Political Economy first appeared in 1803. This English version, translated by Prinsep, was published in 1821 and carried his ideas across the Atlantic. Say wrote in the line of Adam Smith but with his own sharp twists.

The book is famous for Say's Law, the claim that making goods itself creates the means to buy them, so supply creates its own demand. Say also gives the entrepreneur, the risk-taking organizer of production, a central place in economic life. For decades his treatise served as the continent's leading guide to the subject.
shahnama-warner-vol-8-1921:
Volume 8 of the Warner Shahnama appeared in 1921, the eighth of nine volumes. Arthur and Edmond Warner had begun their English Book of Kings in 1905. Firdausi's Persian epic, which they translated, ends with the fall of the Sasanian Empire to Arab armies.

This volume brings the story near that end, through the last shahs and the invasions that broke their power. Persian tradition tells these events with grief and pride, honoring rulers who lost an empire. The translation keeps the poem's couplets in English verse where it can. Readers approaching the final volume can feel the weight of a thousand years of kings passing into memory.
shankara-vivekachudamani-madhavananda-19:
Shankara, the eighth-century teacher of Advaita Vedanta, wrote the Vivekachudamani, the Crest-Jewel of Discrimination, as a manual for seekers. Swami Madhavananda's 1921 translation comes from the Advaita Ashrama, the order's publishing house. The poem is the beloved handbook of its school.

In verse dialogue, Shankara teaches the student to split the real from the unreal until the self stands clear as pure awareness. Body, mind, and world are coverings; Brahman alone, he argues, is finally true. Generations of Hindu students have learned their first Vedanta from these verses, often by heart. The translation keeps the verses' direct, questioning music as far as English allows.
shelley-adonais-1821:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote Adonais in 1821 after learning that John Keats had died in Rome at twenty-five. Shelley blamed harsh reviewers for hastening Keats's death, fairly or not. The poem appeared in Pisa that same year, in the form of a classical pastoral elegy.

Shelley mourns Adonais, his name for Keats, through shepherds, dreams, and the figures of other poets. Grief slowly turns to triumph as he argues that the dead poet's spirit joins nature and outlives his enemies. The famous lines call life a dome of many-colored glass that stains eternity. Adonais is often ranked as Shelley's greatest short poem and one of the finest elegies in English.
spr-proceedings-vol31-1921:
Parts seventy nine through eighty one and an appendix make volume thirty one, dated 1921. The SPR is now a veteran body, near forty years from its founding. Its journal keeps the founding mix of experiment, case, and criticism. Trance mediumship still supplies the longest reports.

New sittings test fresh mediums under the old safeguards. Telepathy work continues, scored with the care of long practice. Spontaneous cases arrive from a public schooled by war to ask such questions. Volume thirty one sustains the primary archive into the 1920s. Its pages show a field both older and no nearer settlement. The open file remains the society's gift.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5021:
Millard Fillmore gives three yearly addresses in one set. Their dates run from December 2, 1850, to December 6, 1852. Three stars part each address from the next. The first looks back on a sudden call. A painful turn of heaven raised Fillmore mid-session. The country then lay in mourning for its lost chief. His first word to Congress met the need of that moment.

Grief filled all hearts in that season. No broad statement of views fit the time. Now Congress meets again in calmer days. Fillmore takes the chance to set out his course. He states it in a general way for both fields. Dealings abroad form one field of that course. Work at home forms the other field. Nations, like men in a state of nature, are equal. They hold set rights and owe set duties to each other.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Volume 21 of The Tales and Novels of J. de La Fontaine contains The Spectacles, The Bucking Tub, and The Impossible Thing. Convent tricks lead the volume, as the poet admits at the start of the first tale.

He had lately vowed to leave the nuns alone, their freaks having filled his page so often, and fears the subject may fatigue the mind. Yet his muse still inclines to hold the veil up to public view. She pursues scene after scene among the sisters. Their artful straying runs through soft loves. The fastest clerk alive could not record it in full. The Spectacles turns on a pair of glasses that show more than they should; the tub and the impossible task close the set in broader farce.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Number 21 of volume 1 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated April 1, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a long notice for one set of books: John Jackson's History and Manuals of Vertical Writing. The Theory and Practice of Vertical Writing costs one dollar and a quarter. The Teaching of Vertical Writing costs fifty cents. Jackson is named as the system's originator.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
Part 21 of Don Quixote, Miguel de Cervantes' novel, appears in John Ormsby's translation. Chapter eleven tells of the strange adventure the valiant Don Quixote had with the car or cart of The Cortes of Death. The knight rides on in deep dejection.

He turns over in his mind the cruel trick he believes enchanters played on him, changing his lady Dulcinea in his sight. Grief over that imagined change hangs on him as the road brings a fresh, deathly encounter. Cervantes mixes mourning with stage-like spectacle, as a cart tied to death itself crosses the knight's path.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, August 25, 1827 leads with Liverpool's town hall and a history of the port's rise. Within a century and a half, the article says, Liverpool advanced from a small, inconsiderable hamlet to national importance. In Leland's time it had only a chapel, its parish church standing four miles off at Walton. In 1571 its inhabitants begged Queen Elizabeth for relief, styling themselves her poor decayed town of Liverpool.

Prince Rupert besieged the town in 1644, and traces of his trenches surfaced when the infirmary's foundation was dug. An act of 1698, allowing a new church, begins the rapid progress the article celebrates. Population figures chart the climb: 25,787 inhabitants in 1760, then 94,376 in 1811, then 118,972 in 1821. Verse about the Mersey's inglorious stream turning to opulence closes the extract. Readers watched a magazine measure civic pride in census numbers and old sieges alike.

No. 583 of The Mirror, dated December 29, 1832, presents a natural tunnel in Virginia. Rock bridges, the writers argue, rank among nature's sublimities as artificial bridges rank among human works. Virginia held several, including the Rockbridge that named its county, yet the specimen pictured here was little known beyond its neighbourhood.

Lieutenant-Colonel Long of the United States Army described the tunnel for an American journal of geology and natural science. He named it himself for its likeness to built tunnels. It pierces rock above Stock Creek in Scott County, a stream rising in Powell's Mountain and joining the Clinch River two or three miles below. His summer excursion narrative follows in his own words.
the-return-of-sherlock-holmes-pg221:
Arthur Conan Doyle's thirteen adventures are listed here. A Strand Magazine heading for October 1903 tops the list. The empty house case opens the collection for readers. Watson dates that case to spring of 1894. London was fascinated by Ronald Adair's murder then. Fashionable society felt dismay at the inexplicable crime.

Watson notes that investigation details were withheld at first. The prosecution case seemed overwhelming without them all. He can complete the chain only after nearly ten years. A companion record carries the same opening text. That record lacks the magazine heading found here. Readers should expect the same thirteen stories in both.
tischner-telepathie-hellsehen-1921:
Rudolf Tischner gave his land its first full study in Ueber Telepathie und Hellsehen, out in German in 1921. The name means on thought leaps and far sight. Tischner was a healer in Munich. He ran his own tests with cards, draws, and hid marks, then weighed the hits gainst the odds that mere chance could give the same sums.

His prose is strict, calm, and free of cult zeal. The book founds the field's line in the German tongue. Fans there cite it as their charter. Its care set a bar for all who came next.
tob-0021:
Thecla, a young woman of Iconium, hears Paul preach and leaves her fiance and family to follow the apostle. The Acts of Paul and Thecla tells her story, and early Christians cherished it for centuries. This entry draws on a verified pre-1930 public-domain edition.

Condemned to beasts and fire, Thecla escapes again and again, and in the arena she baptizes herself in a tank of water. Some church fathers condemned the tale; many believers read it as a call to courage. Thecla became a famous saint, with shrines across the Christian East. Her story remains early Christianity's boldest tale of a woman apostle.
tob-0121:
Ignatius Donnelly was a lawmaker and writer from Minnesota. His 1882 bestseller Atlantis: The Antediluvian World said the lost isle was real. It sank in one great flood, he held, and its heirs seeded all the peoples of the earth. Each flood tale in the world, for him, told of that one drowning.

He piles up rocks, myths, like words, and old authors in a bold, sure case. Scholars scoffed, but the crowds bought the book. It built the whole modern craze for Atlantis on its own. As false history it is a wild, fun read, and its mark lies on a century of lost land tales.
tob-10221:
William James delivered the lectures that became The Varieties of Religious Experience in 1902. A psychologist and philosopher, James studied religion as lived experience rather than doctrine. He drew on hundreds of firsthand accounts, letters, diaries, and autobiographies from people of many backgrounds.

Chapters sort conversion, mysticism, saintliness, and prayer, asking what these states do for the people who have them. James takes extreme cases seriously without mocking or simply believing them. The result helped found the psychology of religion. Readers still use his test: judge religious experience by its fruits in a life, not only by its claims.
tob-10521:
Three Initiates, a pen name most now link to the New Thought writer William Walker Atkinson, put out The Kybalion in 1908. The short book claims to teach the old Hermetic lore of Egypt and Greece. It sums that lore up in seven rules said to govern all things.

The rules are mind, matching, shaking, the pull of opposites, rhythm, cause and effect, and gender. As above, so below is the key line. Was the lore truly old, or new work in old dress? That fight still goes on. True or not, the book has shaped a whole age of occult thought.
tob-4021:
Books Three and Four of Locke's Essay, gathered in volume two, turn from the origin of ideas to language and to knowledge itself. Book Three asks how words hook onto ideas, and how badly they can mislead when they do not. Book Four asks what we can truly claim to know, and with what certainty.

Locke's famous distinction between primary qualities, like solidity, and secondary qualities, like color, stands here, along with his degrees of knowledge and his defense of probability where proof runs out. The volume completes empiricism's founding document. Paired with volume one, it shows a philosophy trying to be honest about the limits of the human mind.
un-ga-res-21: Judges of the International Court of Justice had been picked, and Resolution 21 of the General Assembly, passed on 10 February 1946, hurries the court into life. The Secretary-General must call its first meeting at The Hague as soon as it can be arranged. The Carnegie Foundation, which owns the Peace Palace there, had agreed to talks on the terms for the court's use of the building. A secretary and stopgap staff would help the court until it named its own registrar.
un-ga-res-a-69-21:
Staff work for the Palestinian cause is renewed in Resolution A/69/21, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Assembly had read the yearly report of its Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People. That committee has tracked the question since 1977, with the help of a small UN unit, the Division for Palestinian Rights.

The text notes with thanks the work of the Secretary-General under the last vote on the point. It holds that the division's staff support lets the committee carry out its task in full. That support, it says, keeps world eyes on the question of Palestine and on the urgent need for a just peace.
un-ga-res-es-10-21:
The General Assembly, not the Security Council, adopted Resolution ES-10/21 in October 2023. It came at the Assembly's tenth emergency special session. The war in Gaza had begun after the attack of 7 October 2023. The Assembly voiced grave concern at the worsening situation in the occupied Palestinian territory.

The resolution condemned all violence against Palestinian and Israeli civilians. It called for an immediate, durable, and sustained humanitarian truce, leading to a halt to the fighting. All parties were told to obey international humanitarian and human rights law. Civilians and civilian objects had to be protected. Aid, supplies, and basic services had to reach everyone in need in the Gaza Strip. The text also restated the duty to respect the Geneva Conventions in all circumstances. Because it is an Assembly text, its call carried political weight rather than binding orders.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: The General Assembly adopted Resolution 21 on 10 February 1946, at the twenty-eighth plenary meeting. It arranged the first meeting of the International Court of Justice. The Assembly told the Secretary-General to call the Court together at The Hague as soon as its judges were elected. He was to name a temporary secretary and staff. He was to open talks with the Carnegie Foundation on the terms for the Court's use of rooms in the Peace Palace.

General Assembly resolution 69/21 (2014) concerns the Division for Palestinian Rights of the Secretariat, the office that supports the Assembly's Palestinian rights committee. The Assembly judges the Division's work useful and helpful and asks the Secretary-General to keep funding it. Its tasks include watching developments and holding international meetings. They include running the 'Question of Palestine' website and its information system, and publishing materials. They include training Palestinian government staff. They include holding the annual exhibit for the International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People on 29 November.

Resolution ES-10/21 was adopted by the General Assembly at its tenth emergency special session in October 2023. Its title is Protection of civilians and upholding legal and humanitarian obligations. It answered the sharp rise in violence from 7 October 2023 and the fast worsening crisis in the Gaza Strip and the rest of the occupied Palestinian territory.

The Assembly called for an immediate, durable, and lasting humanitarian truce leading to an end to the fighting. It demanded full respect for the laws of war. It demanded steady delivery of water, food, medicine, fuel, and power to civilians in Gaza. It also demanded access for aid agencies and the release of civilians held captive. It demanded no forced transfer of the Palestinian population.
un-sc-res-121: Japan applied to join the United Nations. Resolution 121 records the Council's answer. The Council adopted it on 12 December 1956. No member dissented. The meeting was the Council's 756th. The text is a single formal step. The Council states that it examined Japan's application. It recommends that the General Assembly admit Japan to membership.
un-sc-res-1321:
Sierra Leone's peace remained fragile in the autumn of 2000. On 20 September 2000 the Security Council extended its mission there, UNAMSIL. The new term ran until 31 December 2000. The Council also set a deadline for itself. It would review the situation again no later than 31 October. Earlier resolutions had built the mission up after rebels seized peacekeepers that spring.

The short extension kept United Nations troops in place through the year-end. It bought time to judge whether the ceasefire could hold. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter. Sierra Leone's war, fought over government control and diamonds, still had more than a year to run.
un-sc-res-1421: Dated 2002 in the catalog, Resolution 1421 records formal action by the United Nations Security Council. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1521:
Liberia's civil war drives Resolution 1521, the Council's sanctions text for that country. Guns from the war had spread across West Africa, and thousands of people had died. Even with fighting over, the Council kept strict limits in place.

The measures target the trade that fed the war, above all Liberian timber and rough diamonds, along with arms sales and travel by listed figures. Panels of experts were to watch for cheating and report back. For readers, the text shows how the Council uses trade bans to keep a fragile peace from collapsing.
un-sc-res-1621:
MONUC gained election reinforcements on 6 September 2005. Congo's transition rested on the Global and All Inclusive Agreement signed at Pretoria in 2002. Elections were the base for lasting peace and the rule of law, the Council stressed. Transitional bodies had to hold free, fair, and peaceful polls and keep the electoral commission's timetable. Armed groups in the east still threatened the vote.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council approved the Secretary-General's recommendations and concept of operations for the elections. It authorized a temporary rise in MONUC's strength of 841 personnel, soldiers and police, to help secure the polls. The extra deployment would end by 1 July 2006 at the latest, and its short-term character was underlined. MONUC was encouraged, within its means, to give the electoral process its full support. The Council stayed actively seized. The boost covered the run-up to polling day.
un-sc-res-1721:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1721, adopted on 1 November 2006. Elections could not be held on time, and the transition period had expired the day before. The African Union had ruled on how the country should be run until a vote was possible. The crisis kept causing large-scale suffering and displacement.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council backs the African Union plan in full. The president stays as head of state for one final transition of at most twelve months. The prime minister also stays, barred from running in the coming election. He gains full powers to deliver the road map, including command over the security forces. Elections must happen by 31 October 2007.
un-sc-res-1821:
The Golan Heights force closed out 2008 with a routine renewal. On 27 June 2008 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 31 December 2008. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission that month. The Council welcomed the force's work on staff conduct rules. UNDOF enforced the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse. Its members had to meet the United Nations code of conduct in full.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 without delay. A closing report was due at the term's end. It would cover events and steps taken toward 338. UNDOF's patrols kept the separation zone quiet. That calm had held, with rare breaks, since the force arrived in 1974.
un-sc-res-1921:
Nepal is the subject of Resolution 1921 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 12 May 2010. A ten-year civil war had ended there in 2006. The United Nations Mission in Nepal, called UNMIN, watched over arms and fighters after the war.

The text renews the mission's mandate until 15 September 2010, at the Nepali government's request. It notes worry that parties had not yet agreed on a new constitution. It calls on the government and the Maoists to set a clear plan for former fighters. The mission was told to prepare its withdrawal by the same date.
un-sc-res-21:
Trust rule over the Pacific islands once held by Japan was set in Security Council Resolution 21, passed on 2 April 1947. The Charter's trusteeship system could take in lands held under old League mandates. The islands north of the equator had been given to Japan by the League in 1920. Japan, beaten in the war, no longer held any sway in them.

The Council approves the terms of trust for the islands as a strategic area, a class of trust land watched by the Council itself, not by the Assembly. The United States would run the islands under those terms. The trust lasted till the islands chose their own paths, most as free states in the 1980s and 1990s. The catalog year of 1921 is wrong.
un-sc-res-221:
Oil tankers bound for Beira, with fuel for Rhodesia's illegal regime, drew a rare call to action at sea on 9 April 1966. One tanker had already arrived at Beira, in Portuguese Mozambique. Another was on its way. A pipeline ran from Beira to Southern Rhodesia. The Council had already ordered states to cut the regime off from oil. Resolution 221 answers those reports.

The Council decided that the situation was a threat to the peace. Portugal was told not to let oil be pumped through the pipeline to Rhodesia, nor to accept oil at Beira meant for Rhodesia. All states had to divert any of their own ships believed to be carrying such oil. Britain was called on to stop suspect tankers from reaching Beira, by force if needed. It could arrest and hold the tanker named in the text after unloading.
un-sc-res-321:
Portugal's attack on a Senegalese border post was condemned on 23 October 1972. Senegal's complaint told of regular Portuguese troops striking the post at Nianao on 12 October 1972. Earlier Council texts, from 178 (1963) to 302 (1971), had condemned Portuguese violence in Senegal again and again. Lisbon refused to comply with any of them. Incidents along the borders of Guinea-Bissau, Angola, and Mozambique kept growing.

The Council condemned the frontier violation and the attack on Nianao. It recalled resolution 294 (1971) on Portuguese acts of violence and destruction. Portugal was told to stop at once, and for good, every act of violence and destruction against Senegal. Lisbon also had to respect self-determination and independence for the peoples of its territories, as the 1960 declaration set out. The Council declared that if Portugal failed to comply, it would meet to weigh other steps.
un-sc-res-421:
South Africa's mandatory arms embargo gained its watchdog on 9 December 1977. Resolution 418 (1977), passed that November, had judged South Africa's arms build-up a threat to the peace. It banned arms sales to Pretoria under Chapter VII. The Council now judged that the ban needed machinery to check its progress. The Secretary-General already owed a report on the embargo's working.

The Council set up a committee of all its members under rule 28 of its rules. The committee would examine the Secretary-General's report on the embargo. It would study ways to make the mandatory ban bite harder and advise the Council. It would seek from every state fresh word on the steps taken to apply resolution 418. All states were called to cooperate with the committee in full and supply the facts it sought. The Secretary-General had to give the committee every help it needed.
un-sc-res-721:
Fighting in Yugoslavia deepened in the autumn of 1991. The parties had signed a ceasefire deal in Geneva on 23 November. The Secretary-General's personal envoy had carried that agreement to the Council. On 27 November 1991 the Council backed his warning to the parties. A peacekeeping operation, he had said, could not be deployed without full respect for the Geneva deal.

The Council also restated its arms embargo from resolution 713. It deplored the heavy loss of life and wide damage in the fighting. Neighboring states felt the effects as well. The Council stayed seized of the matter until a peaceful solution came. The envoy's warning framed the mission that followed months later.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 121 was adopted unanimously on 12 December 1956. It recommends to the General Assembly that Japan be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The Council had examined Japan's application. Its file before the Council included documents from 1952 and from the autumn of 1956. Acting on a membership application is one of the few steps the Charter reserves to the Council and the Assembly together. No state can join the United Nations without a Council recommendation first.

Sierra Leone's battered UN mission gained a short lifeline in 2000. On 20 September, the Council adopted Resolution 1321. The force, UNAMSIL, had been built in 1999 to back a peace deal. That spring, rebels had seized hundreds of its peacekeepers as hostages. Fresh troops and reviews had followed in August and early September.

Three short lines do the work here. The mandate runs to 31 December 2000. The Council will review the state of play by the end of October. It stays seized of the matter in the meantime. The bridge carried the mission toward its stronger form of 2001. That form finally broke the rebels' grip on the country.

Two lines are all this bridge measure needs. On 3 July 2002, acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that the provisions of its resolution 1357 of 2001, on the former Yugoslavia, would stay in force until 15 July 2002. The matter stayed under review while the follow-on arrangements covered by that earlier text were settled.

Liberia's sanctions regime is rebuilt from the ground up on 22 December 2003, after its civil war. Expert panels had found the old measures still being breached, mainly through arms buying. A peace agreement had been signed in Accra in August, and a transitional government had taken office in October.

The old prohibitions are ended and the old sanctions committee dissolved, then a fresh set of measures is imposed under a new committee. These cover arms, rough diamonds from Liberia, and timber, matched to the new situation on the ground. West African states are told to stop armed groups from using their territory to attack neighbours, and reviews are set to test whether the transitional government meets the Council's conditions.

Resolution 1621, adopted on 6 September 2005, reinforces the UN mission in Congo ahead of historic elections. The Pretoria transition agreement of 2002 was moving the country toward its first free national polls in four decades. The Council called on the transitional institutions and all Congolese parties to keep the elections free, fair, and peaceful, and to respect the electoral commission's timetable exactly.

To guard the process, the Council authorized a temporary increase in the strength of MONUC, the UN mission, which already operated under Chapter VII. Donors funding the election effort were thanked and pressed to keep giving. The text also records continuing alarm at hostilities in the east and at attacks on civilians by armed groups.

Côte d'Ivoire's transition is extended one final year under African Union terms in Resolution 1721, adopted on 1 November 2006. Elections had proved impossible on schedule. The transition and the mandates of the president and prime minister expired on 31 October 2006. The AU Peace and Security Council had set new terms on 17 October 2006.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council endorses the AU decision. The president remains head of state for a final transition of no more than twelve months. The prime minister's mandate is renewed on the same terms, barred from standing in the coming election. The prime minister receives powers including rule by ordinance and authority over the defence and security forces, to deliver disarmament, voter identification, and elections by 31 October 2007. The High Representative for the Elections is renewed for twelve months as arbitrator of electoral disputes and certifier of all stages.

Summer 2008 brought the Golan force to the table once more. The chief's report of 16 June 2008 told of a calm line. UNDOF's term was set to lapse at the month's end. The force had stood on the heights since 1974. Resolution 1821 passed on 27 June 2008.

Six more months were set, to 31 December 2008. Both sides heard the old call to act on the 1973 text. The staff code clause runs long in this text. Zero tolerance for sexual abuse is the theme. Troop states must drill their men, probe claims, and punish guilt. A report was due when the term closed. The twin frame of these late texts is plain: still guns on the line, strict rules for the watch.

Resolution 1921, adopted on 12 May 2010, extends the UN Mission in Nepal, UNMIN, one more time while setting its exit. The deadline for Nepal's new constitution was 28 May 2010, yet the parties had reached no agreement on the text or on extending the Constituent Assembly. Discharge of disqualified Maoist army personnel, including minors, had been completed under a December 2009 action plan. Nepal asked for UNMIN to stay until 15 September 2010.

The Council renews UNMIN until 15 September 2010. It decides that UNMIN should start arranging its withdrawal at once, handing over leftover monitoring duties by that date. It calls on the government and the Maoist party to agree on a timed plan, with clear targets, for integrating and settling Maoist army personnel. A report on carrying out the resolution is due by 1 September 2010.

Pacific islands once held by Japan came before the Council on 2 April 1947. The islands had been German colonies before the First World War. The League of Nations then gave them to Japan as a mandate. Japan lost them in the Second World War. Resolution 21, adopted unanimously, set up a trusteeship for the islands.

The Council approved the terms of the trusteeship and made the United States the administering authority. The islands were classed as a strategic area. Because of that, the United States could build bases and station forces there. In return, it had to move the islanders toward self-government. It had to protect their lands and rights. It also had to build up education, health services, and the local economy.

Resolution 221 is a UN Security Council enforcement step against Rhodesia's oil lifeline, adopted on 9 April 1966 by ten votes to none with five abstentions. After the white minority regime's unilateral independence declaration, oil tankers were heading for Beira in Portuguese Mozambique, from where a pipeline could pump fuel to landlocked Southern Rhodesia.

The Council declares the situation a threat to the peace, calls on Portugal not to allow pumping or accept Rhodesian oil at Beira, and asks all states to divert their suspect vessels. Most strikingly, it authorizes Britain to use force if necessary to stop such ships, and specifically to arrest the tanker Joanna V if her cargo were discharged. The episode became known as the Beira Patrol.

Senegal's charge against Portugal wins backing in Resolution 321. It passed on 23 October 1972, with twelve votes in favor and three members not voting either way. Senegal's foreign chief laid out the case in the hall. Portugal replied by letter. Past texts since 1963 had dealt with Portuguese strikes on Senegalese soil. The strikes came from the colony of Guinea-Bissau, next door. A UN rights team's report of 1971 set out the facts in depth.

The Council voiced deep dismay at Portugal's flat refusal to obey those texts. It condemned the strikes and told Lisbon to respect Senegal's soil and borders. Calm would come, it argued, when all African lands near Portugal's colonies were left in peace, and their peoples freed to rule their own fate.

South Africa's arms buildup is the subject of Resolution 421, adopted on 9 December 1977. A month earlier, in Resolution 418, the Council had ruled that South Africa getting arms threatened world peace and had placed a required arms embargo on the country. Members now wanted a way to watch how well that ban was working.

The resolution creates a Security Council committee made up of all Council members. The committee must study the Secretary-General's report on the embargo, look for ways to make the ban work better, and ask states what they have done to enforce it. All states are called on to cooperate and share information, and the Secretary-General must give the committee the staff and help it needs.

Yugoslavia was tearing itself apart in late November 1991. A ceasefire signed in Geneva on 23 November offered brief hope. The Secretary-General's envoy, Cyrus Vance, had brokered it. Yugoslav leaders told him they wanted UN peacekeepers deployed quickly. Resolution 721 gave the Council's answer that month.

Members approved the envoy's peace efforts warmly. They endorsed his warning to the parties. No peacekeeping force could deploy without full respect for the Geneva deal. The Yugoslav sides were urged to honor it completely. The Council promised to act fast on any peacekeeping proposal. That promise led, within months, to the huge UNPROFOR mission in Croatia and Bosnia.
unamuno-tragic-sense-of-life-flitch-1921:
Miguel de Unamuno published Del sentimiento trágico de la vida in Spain in 1913, and J. E. Crawford Flitch Englished it in 1921 as Tragic Sense of Life. Unamuno argues that man thinks with his whole being, not with reason alone. Reason says we die for good; the heart refuses to accept that verdict.

From that clash Unamuno builds his philosophy of faith, doubt, and hunger for eternal life. He writes as a wrestler, not a professor, and names his own unbelief honestly. The book influenced thinkers far beyond Spain in the century after. Flitch's Macmillan translation was a landmark for Unamuno in English. It remains the fullest statement of his thought.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s21-21:
